title: Color Vision — Then and Now
affiliations: Justus Liebig University of Giessen
abstract:
Many of the central questions in color vision have been with us for more than a century: How precisely can we discriminate colors? How stable are surface colors under changing illumination? And how should brightness and luminance be related to perception? This long tradition has produced a remarkably solid framework of theories, measurements, and standards. Yet its very success can also create the impression that the central questions have largely been settled.
In this lecture I will argue that several classical problems in color vision remain surprisingly open. My current work revisits these questions using a new generation of experimental tools. Virtual reality allows color constancy to be studied in photorealistic scenes under nearly natural viewing conditions while maintaining full experimental control. Deep neural networks provide end-to-end models of vision that link color processing directly to tasks such as object recognition. Robust ranking paradigms enable large-scale online experiments to evaluate photometric standards and heterochromatic brightness. Finally, gamified tasks make it possible to measure color discrimination at unprecedented scale, helping to overcome the curse of dimensionality in color space.
It is an exciting time in vision research, when new techniques allow us to find new answers to very old questions.

title: Distinguishing imagination from reality in a generative brain
affiliations: University College London
abstract: Our perception of reality is generative: to resolve ambiguous sensory input, our brain predicts the most likely interpretation using an internal model built on past experiences. This same mechanism allows us to generate sensory signals in the absence of input, giving rise to mental imagery. Since perception and imagery rely on the same generative mechanism, how do we know at any given moment that what we are experiencing is real and not just imagined? I will present studies that aim to answer this question using psychophysics, neuroimaging and computational modelling. The results suggest that higher-order brain regions monitor the precision of sensory signals to infer whether they reflect reality or imagination. I end by discussing a novel research direction in which we will explore the interaction between reality inferences and our internal model of the world.

title: The Early Role of Vision in Multisensory Development
affiliations: Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia
abstract: Developmental processing relies heavily on vision, which serves as a key organizer for integrating information from other senses. Vision indeed helps to shape how auditory and tactile signals are interpreted, supporting the development of coherent spatial and body representations. When visual input is missing early in life, as in blind infants and children, these representations are often altered, leading to difficulties in multisensory integration. Understanding how vision guides early sensory interaction reveals its foundational role in building a unified perception of the world and informs the design of accessible technologies that translate visual information into sound, vibration, or movement.

Real-time neurofeedback training to modulate glutamate concentration using functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy
affiliations: 1. University of Regensburg (DE)
abstract: Real-time neurofeedback training enables participants to learn to modulate their brain activity in a desired direction. However, existing neurofeedback trainings either rely on indirect measures of brain activity or lack spatial specificity, which limits the effectiveness of the technique. Here, we introduce a real-time neurofeedback training using functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS) to directly modulate excitatory activity within a volume-of-interest (VOI) located in the occipital lobes (mainly consisting of early visual areas V1 and V2). fMRS is an MRI-based technique that allows non-invasive, near real-time measurement of the concentration of glutamate, a major excitatory neurotransmitter, in a predefined VOI. College-age participants (fifteen per condition) either trained to increase or decrease glutamate concentration using veridical feedback about their performance, or trained with random feedback as a control condition. Participants were unaware of their group assignment and of the purpose of the neurofeedback training. The following procedure was used. First, pretraining glutamate concentration was measured, followed by thirty neurofeedback training trials. Each trial included a sixteen-second induction phase during which participants applied self-selected mental strategies to modulate glutamate levels relative to the pretraining concentration. Performance was subsequently provided as veridical or random visual feedback. Glutamate concentration in the VOI was measured using consecutive two-second PRESS scans in a 3T MRI scanner. The results showed that within a thirty-minute training period, participants successfully learned to increase or decrease glutamate concentration relative to the pretraining concentration, whereas no significant concentration changes occurred in the control group. This indicates that real-time neurofeedback training using fMRS enables participants to rapidly learn to modulate excitatory activity in a predefined brain region. The developed procedure overcomes limitations set by previous neurofeedback training techniques and could support treatment procedures in patients with maladaptive excitatory processing.

title: Perceptual learning of a Form-from-Velocity task in eccentric visual locations with varying levels of sustained attention performance
affiliations: 1. University of Regensburg (DE)
abstract: Individuals with central vision loss rely on peripheral vision, leading to the development of a ‘preferred retinal locus’ (PRL) through oculomotor and perceptual learning. The mechanisms guiding PRL location selection are still under investigation. One proposed factor influencing PRL location selection is the individual ability to sustain attention at that location. To investigate the link between sustained attention and perceptual learning, we assessed sustained attention in eight peripheral locations (8° eccentricity) in 19 normally sighted participants (18-30 years). Participants fixated centrally and directed their attention for 2.5–4 seconds to a cued eccentric location before identifying the orientation of a Landolt-C gap (up, down, left, right) at that location, amidst full-ring distractors in the other seven locations, followed by 100 ms masks across all locations. Participants then underwent perceptual learning of a speed discrimination task at their highest (HPL) and lowest (LPL) sustained attention performance locations. We used a form-from-velocity (FFV) task where different orientations of a virtual, motion-defined, triangle should be detected among moving dots. The target figure was distinguishable by a difference in speed of the target moving dots compared to the background moving dots. White coherently moving dots on a black background were used with randomly alternating overall motion direction (upwards, downwards, left, right). The target form was triangularly shaped and presented in two directions (apex pointing up/down; 2AFC). Participants had to indicate on each trial the orientation of the triangle, while fixating a central fixation cross. Results indicate a significant learning effect, demonstrated by significantly increased hit rates in the FFV task after training (p=.01) at both locations. Additionally, there were lower speed difference thresholds at the HPL in comparison to the LPL (p=.002). The results show that speed discrimination performance in the peripheral visual field may be modulated by differences in sustained attention abilities.

title: Excessive exposure to a task-irrelevant feature jeopardizes the long-term retention of perceptual learning
affiliations: 1. Institute for Psychology, University of Regensburg (DE)
abstract: Repeated exposure to a visual feature (e.g., a coherent motion direction) enhances discrimination sensitivity for that feature, reflecting visual perceptual learning (VPL). Previous studies showed that, once acquired, VPL can persist for months after the exposure period. Here we made a surprising observation, namely that excessive exposure to a task-irrelevant feature jeopardizes the long-term retention of VPL for that feature. In a first behavioral experiment, thirty college-age participants performed a rapid-serial-visual-presentation-task at screen center while being exposed to a near-threshold task-irrelevant coherent motion direction in the visual surroundings. Participants were randomly assigned to short-exposure (six sessions) and long-exposure (twelve sessions) groups. Discrimination sensitivity for the direction was assessed before the beginning, immediately after, and again three months after the exposure period. Both groups enhanced discrimination sensitivity for the exposed direction, reflecting VPL. During the retest three months later, discrimination sensitivity remained enhanced in the short-exposure group but returned to preexposure levels in the long-exposure group, indicating that the long-term consolidation of VPL had failed. To understand the neural mechanisms underlying the consolidation failure, a follow-up imaging experiment was conducted. Fifteen new participants completed the long-exposure behavioral protocol and underwent additional exposure sessions in the scanner before the beginning, midway through, immediately after, and at retest. Again, we found that VPL for the exposed direction was not retained at retest. Functional magnetic resonance imaging showed that activity in area MT+, crucial for coherent motion perception, remained high in the preexposure and midway scans but declined sharply in the posttraining and retest scans. This indicates that attenuated neural processing of the task-irrelevant feature after the first exposure period impairs the long-term consolidation of VPL. Our results suggest that a moderate amount of exposure is optimal for inducing and retaining VPL.

title: Representing the Future Objects in Working Memory
affiliations: 1. Zhejiang University (CN)
abstract: It is widely acknowledged that we can recall the past state of an object, but can we also 'remember'”' the state of an object that has not yet formed but holds the possibility to form in the future? This study explores how these possibility for a unified future object shapes visual working memory. Participants viewed puzzle-like stimulus pairs. Crucially, some pairs have possibility to be combined into a single, completed object (possible condition), while others remained separate pieces (impossible condition). Participants were asked to memorize the spatial gap between the pieces and, after a brief delay, move one of the piece to reproduce that distance. We found that the remembered distances were significantly shorter for possible pairs than impossible pairs. This finding persisted across varied orientations and shapes in follow-up tests, suggesting the representation of possible pairs was different from impossible pairs in working memory. To probe the neural signature of representing a possible future, we employed EEG during a change-detection task. During encoding  (0–500 ms), possible pairs captured attention similarly to a single piece but significantly different from impossible pairs, indicating they were rapidly integrated into a unified object representation. Critically, during maintenance (500–2000 ms), the match condition demanded the most attentional resources. This might reflects holding a ‘future object’ in mind for change detection task is a double duty: one must preserve both the holistic, integrated form and the specific shape details of the pieces. Mismatched pieces, lacking this integrated future, required only simple shape memory. Our findings suggest a fascinating expansion of memory's reach. Working memory does not merely record the past; it actively sketches the shape of objects to come, holding space for objects that exist only in potential.

title: Two routes to scene memory: attention and image-intrinsic memorability
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
2. Department of Computer Science, Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
3. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior Universities of Marburg, Giessen, and Darmstadt (DE)
4. Center for Applied Computer Science and Data Science, Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
abstract: What we remember depends not only on image properties but also on how we sample visual information. While models such as ResMem predict memorability from visual features, gaze reinstatement during recognition has also been linked to memory. Here, we ask whether these mechanisms depend on image content and how they interact to support memory. Participants (N = 40) viewed 144 natural indoor scenes containing faces, text, both, or neither (36 each matched for predicted memorability using ResMem) during incidental encoding, followed by an old/new recognition test with eye tracking at both phases. For each image, we quantified human memorability (hit rate) and encoding–recognition gaze similarity (gaze reinstatement). Behaviorally, scenes containing faces were most memorable, text-only and both-content scenes showed intermediate memorability, and scenes containing neither were least memorable. Gaze reinstatement was highest for faces, intermediate for both-contents and text-only scenes, and lowest for scenes without faces or text. Critically, the relationship between gaze reinstatement, model predictions, and memorability dissociated across content. For face scenes, memorability was high and well predicted by ResMem, but independent of gaze reinstatement. In contrast, for text-only scenes, memorability was strongly predicted by gaze reinstatement but not by ResMem. These findings suggest two routes to scene memory: an image-intrinsic route captured by current models, and an attention-dependent route not reflected in model predictions.

title: Temporal components of correct and incorrect item retrieval from visual working memory
affiliations: 1. University of Cambridge (UK)
abstract: Accessing information held in working memory is among the most fundamental operations in visual cognition, but the time course of this retrieval process is poorly understood. In cued recall tasks, microsaccades (fixational eye movements) following cue onset are preferentially directed towards the location of the target item. In this study, we conducted a series of experiments in which participants were shown an array of visual items, each with a unique orientation and colour. After a brief delay, one target item was indicated by a cue of the same colour and participants were instructed to reproduce its orientation from memory. This task requires at least two processes: matching the colour cue to one of the items in memory, and retrieving the orientation of the matched item. The onset of the microsaccade bias is a physiological marker providing an upper-bound on the duration of the cue-to-item matching process. We developed a formal model that distinguishes baseline and item-directed microsaccade rates, estimating the transition point between these rates while accounting for stable directional bias. We compared the estimated transition points across experimental manipulations designed to influence the retrieval dynamics, systematically varying the number of memory items and the signal strength of colour and orientation features. The results argue against a strictly sequential retrieval process across non-spatial feature dimensions and items. Swap errors, defined as reports matching the orientation of a non-target item, were observed at sufficient rates to characterise microsaccades in this subset of trials. These microsaccades were preferentially directed toward the reported rather than the cued item, while showing qualitatively similar temporal dynamics to target-oriented trials. This demonstrates that swap errors originate from failures of the cue-to-item matching process. Taken together, these findings offer new insights into the temporal architecture of working memory retrieval and the mechanisms of access to stored representations.

title: The Beep-Speed Illusion: Perception rather than bias
affiliations:
1. University of Erfurt (DE)
2. University of Trier (DE)
abstract: When two objects move randomly across a screen and occasionally change direction, brief beeps synchronized with the direction changes of one object lead participants to indicate the synchronized disk as moving faster than the other in a forced-choice paradigm. This effect is observed both with and without eye movements, and across different object speeds and motion trajectories. We refer to this phenomenon as the Beep-Speed Illusion. We propose two potential explanations for the Beep-Speed Illusion. First, attentional mechanisms may enhance the processing of the beep-synchronized disk, leading to an increase in its perceived speed. Alternatively, decisional biases in response behavior may underlie the effects observed in our experiments.  With regard to attentional explanations, our results show that guiding visual attention toward one of the visual objects, rather than presenting beep sounds, elicits a similar illusion. This finding suggests an attentional origin of the Beep-Speed Illusion. With regard to decisional biases, our results indicate that simple response biases (i.e., selecting the synchronized object) cannot account for the illusion, as the same pattern of results emerges when observers are instructed to select either the faster or the slower object. Furthermore, the Beep-Speed Illusion is also observed in an equality judgment paradigm, in which participants indicate whether the two objects move at the same or at different speeds. This rules out more complex decisional biases arising from forced-choice tasks. In sum, our findings provide little evidence for decisional biases as an explanation for the Beep-Speed Illusion and instead point to differences in attentional processing between the synchronized and unsynchronized objects.

title: Exploring pivotal moments in visual potential: Gaze behavior during visual and tactile exploration of sculptures
affiliations: 1. Laboratory of Experimental Psychology, Department of Brain and Cognition, University of Leuven (BE)
abstract: As observers move around a sculpture, shifts in viewpoint generate a sequence of geometric events in openings, ridges, cusps, occlusions, and T‑junctions. From the set of all visual experiences obtainable when traversing any orbit through space, these critical events in visual potential might attract attention and guide perceptual processing. In contrast, tactile exploration affords full access to the 3D form from a fixed visual position, enabling interaction with shape without the accompanying visual transformations produced by moving around the sculptures. To investigate how these two modes of exploration affect perceptual processing, we conducted an exhibition‑based study using eight sculptures by Joos Vandewalle, selected to vary in color, geometry, and structural complexity. In a within‑participants design, observers either freely moved around each sculpture to interact with its visual potential or explored it by touch from a fixed viewpoint using both hands. Participants wore mobile eye‑tracking glasses and a fiducial marker on top of the head, tracked by a ceiling camera. Fixations were coded into eight areas of interest, including outer edges, inner edges, surface regions, and pedestal in either a visual exploration trial or a tactile exploration trial. During visual trials, our data revealed a significantly lower proportion of fixations on surface regions compared to tactile trials. Heat maps showed a high density of fixations at emerging or disappearing openings, ridges, cusps, and contour junctions, precisely those locations where changes in visual potential occur. During tactile trials, although those salient aspects also attracted attention, the gaze also seemed to linger more on the surface of the sculptures, converging with our quantitative analysis of the areas of interest.

title: When Sound Leads Vision: Temporal Dynamics of Cross-Modal Prediction
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior, Universities of Marburg, Giessen, and Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: In everyday life, the brain continuously integrates information across sensory modalities, forming expectations about what is likely to occur next. These cross-modal predictions allow input from one modality (e.g., audition) to anticipate and modulate processing in another (e.g., vision). Here, we manipulated the temporal synchrony between auditory and visual streams and used time-resolved fMRI multivariate pattern analysis to test whether leading auditory input can predictively shape representations in visual cortex. Participants (N = 30) viewed sixteen 10-second naturalistic videos depicting everyday cooking actions (e.g., chopping, peeling, blending, pouring, frying, grating). Audio tracks were shifted by 3 seconds to precede the visual input (“leading” condition), follow it (“lagging” condition), or remain synchronized (“synchronous” condition). Participants monitored audiovisual congruency by detecting occasional mismatches between sound and video. We performed pairwise decoding of the sixteen stimuli within each ROI to assess the discriminability of stimulus-specific activity patterns across conditions. Leading sounds yielded higher decoding accuracy than lagging sounds in scene-selective PPA and object-selective LO, indicating that predictive auditory cues enhance visual representations of upcoming events across visual regions. In contrast, decoding accuracy in multisensory regions IPS and IFG tended to be higher in the lagging than in the leading and synchronous conditions, consistent with increased demands for temporal conflict monitoring. Time-resolved decoding further revealed that decoding in PPA exhibited a steeper rise when sounds led the visual input, whereas in IFG the rise was steeper when sounds lagged. Together, these findings demonstrate that anticipatory signals from one sensory modality can predictively shape representations in another, highlighting the temporal dynamics of cross-modal predictive processing.

title: Where does the multisensory orienting advantage arise? ERP evidence at 50 ms cue-target onset asynchrony
affiliations: 1. The University of Queensland (AU)
abstract: Research using response times demonstrate a multisensory (audiovisual bimodal) orienting advantage at short cue–target onset asynchronies (CTOAs 50 ms), suggesting that multisensory integration (MSI) facilitates exogenous attentional orienting. Drift diffusion modelling indicates that this advantage is primarily expressed as a reduction in non-decision time, implicating faster sensory encoding and/or response-related processes rather than enhanced evidence accumulation. To localise this effect, the present study uses EEG to dissociate early sensory processing (N1) from later attentional selection (N2pc, P3a) and motor execution (RP), testing whether multisensory facilitation reflects early sensory gain, downstream attentional prioritisation, or speeded motor execution.  Participants performed a speeded visual orientation discrimination task following spatially non-predictive unimodal (visual), crossmodal (auditory), or bimodal (audiovisual) cues presented at a 50 ms CTOA. Analyses focused on target-locked P1 and N1 as indices of early visual processing, N2pc and P3a as markers of attentional allocation, and response-locked motor potentials to assess motor execution.  We replicated previously published response time findings. EEG measures indicated a modality × validity interaction in target-locked N1 amplitude, such that validity effects were larger for targets following bimodal cues than following unimodal or crossmodal cues. This effect was driven by greater negativity on invalid trials, which may reflect increased processing demands associated with attentional reorienting to targets appearing at invalid locations. Given the short cue–target interval, early target-locked components likely reflect a combination of cue-related and target-evoked activity. However, the observed validity-dependent modulation suggests that these effects are not solely driven by cue-evoked activity. Importantly, no corresponding modulation was observed in response-locked motor potentials, indicating that the multisensory advantage is unlikely to reflect changes in motor execution and instead arises at earlier perceptual or attentional stages.

title: Perceptual cues underlying surface softness of touched textiles
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University (DE)
2. Unversity of Tokyo (JP)
3. Leibniz Institute for New Materials (DE)
abstract: Softness is a core dimension in human haptic material perception. Previous research has predominantly focused on compliance as a physical correlate of softness and on normal deformation (“pressure”) as the primary exploratory procedure. However, softness is also reliably perceived during lateral stroking, indicating that surface softness constitutes a distinct and relevant aspect of haptic experience—for instance when interacting with textiles, biological tissues, or human skin. Despite its importance, the perceptual mechanisms underlying surface softness judgments are poorly understood. While earlier industry-oriented studies have reported correlations between perceived surface softness and various physical parameters (e.g., acoustic emissions), the perceptual cues driving these judgments are still unclear. In the present study, we systematically investigated candidate cues including friction, roughness, and deformability during active touch. Thirty-eight participants explored 38 textile samples spanning fibrillary (e.g., velvet, fur) and non-fibrillary (e.g., silk, denim) materials using controlled lateral stroking movements. Visual and auditory information was minimized via an opaque curtain and headphones. Exploration force was monitored using motion tracking and regulated through real-time auditory feedback. Each stimulus was explored for 4 seconds. Participants provided magnitude estimates of perceived surface softness and rated surface descriptors on Likert scales. Kinematic and force parameters were recorded continuously. A principal component analysis of the descriptor ratings revealed four dimensions: smoothness/hairiness, roughness/friction, deformability, and velvetiness. Linear mixed-effects modelling showed that perceived surface softness increased with hairiness, velvetiness, deformability, and applied force, but decreased with perceived roughness/friction. Notably, the physical coefficient of friction and movement speed did not significantly predict surface softness judgments. These findings demonstrate that surface softness is a multidimensional percept arising from multiple interacting perceptual cues. Future work will further disentangle the relative contributions and underlying mechanisms of these cues.

title: Efference Copy Signals Improve Haptic Precision During Active Information Acquisition
affiliations:
1. HapLab, Experimental Psychology Department, Justus Liebig University (DE)
2. INM Leibniz-Institute for New Materials (DE)
3. Physics Department, Saarland University (DE)
abstract: Haptic perception can integrate cutaneous input from the fingerpad, proprioceptive signals about body position, and efference copy signals that can be used by sensory processing to predict the consequences of movement. Although all contribute to perception, the specific role of efference copy signals remains to be fully understood. To date, such signals are known to suppress task-irrelevant sensory input during self-generated movement (Juravle et al., 2010 Voudouris & Fiehler, 2017). However, their role when movements are aimed at acquiring information remains controverse. To investigate this, we conducted a spatial frequency discrimination experiment on grating stimuli using the method of constant stimuli (reference: 15.3 mm or 16.3 mm interelement distance comparison stimuli spanning 11.3–19.3 mm or 12.3–20.3 mm, respectively), across three conditions: (1) In the active condition, participants explored the stimulus with the index finger by freely moving their arm back and forth kinematic parameters were recorded for each trial. (2) In the passive-arm condition, these recorded trajectories were replayed using a motor-controlled armrest. (3) In the passive-stimulus condition, participants’ arms remained stationary while the stimulus probe moved according to the same recorded trajectories. The order of the latter two conditions was counterbalanced across participants. We hypothesized that perceptual precision would be highest with full sensorimotor signals (active), intermediate with cutaneous and proprioceptive input (passive-arm), and lowest with cutaneous input alone (passive-stimulus). Results showed that just noticeable differences for spatial frequency were lower in the active condition than in both the passive-arm and passive-stimulus conditions, with no significant difference between the two passive conditions. These findings indicate that when movements are aimed at information acquisition, efference copy signals enhance haptic perceptual precision.

title: Foraging tempo revisited: How does time pressure contribute to individual differences in target selection behaviour?
affiliations:
1. Department of Cognitive Science, University of Malta (MT)
2. Faculty of Psychology, University of Iceland (IS)
abstract: An unexpected finding in the human foraging study by Kristjánsson, Jóhannesson & Thornton (2014) was that a minority of individuals (25%) showed little if any difference in run patterns under feature versus conjunction conditions. We termed these individuals “super-foragers”. Since that time, similar cohorts have been reported in many other studies, and attempts have been made to understand the characteristics of such individuals. In the current presentation, we will briefly review what we know to-date about individual differences in the context of foraging, and will then focus on new studies from our group linking run-pattern preferences to more general cognitive mechanism, in particular “processing speed”. Thornton, Nguyen & Kristjánsson (2021) demonstrated experimentally that manipulating the “foraging tempo” with which participants were allowed to select consecutive targets strongly influenced patterns of runs. Building on this finding, we will present new data exploring whether independently measured individual differences in the ability to make decisions under time pressure can be related to observed patterns of runs during human foraging tasks.
session_title: Symposium: Strategies for searching: better understanding visual foraging through the study of individual differences

title: How working memory shapes visual foraging behaviour: insights from individual differences
affiliations:
1. Université Paris-Cité (FR)
2. Université de Bordeaux (FR)
abstract: Previous research has shown that visual foraging strategies vary with task difficulty. In easy tasks, where targets and distractors differ by a single feature, participants typically adopt a proximity-based strategy, selecting the nearest target and frequently switching between target types. In difficult tasks, involving conjunctions of features, most participants adopt a category-based strategy, focusing on one target type at a time. However, individual differences are observed, with individuals showing category-based and proximity-based strategies in the same foraging task. The present study aimed to examine whether increasing working memory load – by increasing perceptual and motor load – would favour category-based strategies in all observers. We also investigated the relationship between individual differences in foraging strategy and individual differences in executive functioning. Each participant completed eight exhaustive visual foraging tasks (four feature-based and four conjunction-based), in which the number of target types (two vs. three) and response modality (mouse clicks vs. gaze fixation) were manipulated. Participants then performed three cognitive tasks assessing executive functions (inhibition, attentional flexibility, and visual working memory). Preliminary analyses indicate that increasing the number of target types favours a category-based strategy, and lengthens inter-target times. Participants with higher working memory spans were also more likely to change strategies with task difficulty, showing higher adaptability in foraging tasks. Overall, these findings highlight the role of executive functioning in foraging behaviour, with visual working memory playing a central role in both foraging behaviour and selection strategy.

title: Immersive virtual reality for probing visual foraging across the lifespan.
affiliations:
1. University of Bristol (UK)
2. University of Plymouth (UK)
abstract: Psychological assays of human search behaviour have traditionally relied on the visual search paradigm, often treated as a simplified proxy for naturalistic visual foraging. However, relatively little is known about how visual foraging operates across the lifespan, particularly in large-scale environments where age-related changes in cognition may interact with strategy use and exploration. Such changes may be exacerbated in neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, contributing to a growing interest in visual foraging as a potential early behavioural marker of atypical cognitive decline. To address this, we developed an immersive virtual reality paradigm to examine visual foraging. Across a series of task manipulations, search behaviour was systematically influenced by target features and spatial distribution, revealing trade-offs between patch exploitation and exploration. These effects emerged largely independent of explicit instruction, suggesting that visual attention drives foraging strategy even when behaviour requires complex, large-scale movement. A follow-up study combining the paradigm with cognitive assessment and neuroimaging in younger and older adults revealed that group-level age differences in visual foraging performance were relatively modest, consistent with accounts of adaptive compensation in ageing. However, cognitive profiles, rather than age per se, differentiated more and less efficient foragers. These findings position immersive visual foraging as a tool for studying cognitive ageing. Rather than reflecting uniform decline, age-related differences in behaviour appear to be shaped by variability in underlying cognitive function, pointing to visual foraging as a sensitive behavioural lens on the earliest shifts in cognitive ageing, and highlighting the importance of understanding search behaviour through the lens of individual variability.

title: Visual foraging patterns as distinguishing features: A predictive model for PSP vs. Parkinson's Disease
affiliations:
1. University of Essex (UK)
2. Durham University (UK)
abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a rare neurodegenerative condition associated with disturbances in motor movement, including deficits in eye movement control. Its rarity means diagnosis is typically delayed by around 3.5 years compared to more prevalent movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we examined whether foraging behaviour could distinguish between PSP and PD patients, using the Bells Test as a clinical screening tool. Three patient groups: PD (N = 29), PSP (N = 28), and age-matched controls (AMC, N = 27), each completed one trial, searching for 30 bells embedded among distractor items on an A4 sheet. We applied a generative model to characterise search strategy, which predicts the sequence of item selections using latent parameters: proximity (bias toward nearer bells), momentum (bias toward continued forward motion or reversals), and absolute direction (bias toward a consistent search direction). PD patients and controls exhibited similar behaviour, both showing strong directional biases consistent with 'reading-like' search patterns, and both achieving comparable item-by-item prediction accuracy (~40%). PSP patients, by contrast, showed markedly disorganised search with no consistent directional or distance-based strategy, reflected in substantially lower prediction accuracy (~15%). Importantly, the model only requires the order of target selections from a single trial, suggesting that it could potentially be implemented as a practical tool in clinical settings. These findings suggest that foraging strategy captures meaningful differences between the two patient groups, and we discuss additional analyses aimed at evaluating the model's capacity to discriminate between PSP and PD at the individual level.
