title: Cooking in a kitchen with a toilet? Understanding Functions Based on Scene Context and Phrases
affiliations: 1. LMU (DE)
abstract: Constantly, we interact with objects to complete goal-directed actions. Single objects are directly manipulated, and scenes provide the contextual information needed to understand them. While scenes appear to carry action information, context has seldomly been manipulated systematically. The scene grammar framework suggests that scenes can be decomposed into “phrases” – subclusters of objects including an anchor object, which predicts the location and identity of other objects in the phrase. While these conceptual units are thought to reflect functional organization, whether action-possibilities are assessed based on these phrases remains largely unexplored. Across four Experiments, we assess if action understanding is based on phrases alone, or if it relies on context. To test this, we use so-called chimera scenes which gradually change from one category (e.g., from a bathroom) to another (e.g. a kitchen) by switching out phrases one-by-one (e.g. swapping the toilet in a bathroom with a stove, the shower with a fridge etc.).   When categorizing scenes in Experiment 1, participants showed faster RTs for intact versus chimera scenes. Matching actions and scenes in Experiment 2, a new group of participants demonstrated higher accuracy and faster responses for intact scenes, and a gradual impairment correlated with the number of inconsistent phrases in the scenes. In Experiment 3, scenes served as primes in a lexical decision task, and the amount of (in)consistent scene information affected RTs. In Experiment 4, using eye-tracking, participants showed increased attention to action-related objects and to consistent scene context when assessing scene-action fit.  In sum, we demonstrate that inconsistent scene context disrupts action understanding, introducing uncertainty even when only a small subset of objects is incongruent. We suggest that contextual information contributes to efficient action understanding, rather than action-related objects alone, and that actions are thereby understood by integrating phrase- and scene-level information.
session_title: Scene and Object Perception and Recognition

title: How Viewpoint Angle and Scene Congruency Shape Object Recognition
affiliations:
1. School of Informtion Science, Yunnan University (CN)
2. School of Psychology, University of Southampton (UK)
3. Institute of Brain and Psychological Sciences, Sichuan Normal University (CN)
abstract: In natural scenes, objects are rarely viewed from a single fixed angle. Although previous research has separately examined viewpoint effects in object recognition and the influence of scene congruency, much less is known about how these two factors jointly shape object processing under naturalistic viewing conditions. To address this gap, we used stimuli generated from three-dimensional modeling to approximate natural viewpoint variation and examined the interaction between viewpoint and scene congruency across two experiments.   In Experiment 1, participants performed a behavioral object-classification task in which target objects were presented from different viewpoints in semantically congruent or incongruent scenes. The results showed that scene congruency facilitated object recognition and reduced the cost of viewpoint variation. In particular, back views, which provided less diagnostic visual information, produced greater recognition difficulty, whereas congruent scene context attenuated this disadvantage.   In Experiment 2, we used a repeated detection task (RDT) combined with EEG to investigate the neural dynamics underlying this interaction. ERP analyses revealed enhanced N300/N400 responses for incongruent scenes, indicating increased demands on semantic integration. In addition, viewpoint manipulation modulated both earlier and later processing stages: back views elicited larger N200 and N400 components than more canonical views, suggesting greater perceptual conflict and semantic processing cost.   Together, these findings show that scene congruency can compensate for viewpoint-related recognition difficulty, with viewpoint effects emerging at earlier stages of processing and the influence of scene congruency becoming more evident during later semantic integration.
session_title: Scene and Object Perception and Recognition

title: New scene representations are learned more effectively during active than passive tasks
affiliations:
1. LMU (DE)
2. ENIB (FR)
3. TU Le Mans (FR)
abstract: When we search for objects in a room, we use our previous knowledge of scenes to direct our attention to locations where the object could be. This scene knowledge, a.k.a. scene grammar, follows a hierarchical structure (Võ, 2021). Currently, it is not clear how we learn scene grammar. For instance, do we simply learn through repeated exposure to objects being in the same location or is a more active task, such as search, required to successfully learn object identities and locations? In this study, we aimed to determine how adults learn a new, artificial scene grammar. Participants encoded objects through either a passive viewing or an active search task. The passive viewing task highlighted objects in the scene which participants gazed at one after another. In the active search task, participants were given a target object which they searched for. To ensure that participants had no previous scene grammar for the objects or the scenes we presented them with artificial objects in artificial virtual reality scenes.  Participants then performed two recall tasks. First, an odd-one-out task where participants were presented with three objects and asked to choose which one was the odd one out. Secondly, participants were given a scene reconstruction task where participants had to place the artificial objects in the correct locations within the scenes. Eye tracking and behavioural responses indicated that participants learned the object locations faster and, in more detail, when they encoded objects via the active search task compared to the passive viewing task. However, participants only showed superior memory regarding which objects were grouped together in the rebuild task and not the odd-one-out task. These results suggest that participants learn new scene grammar more effectively through an active search task and only recall the new scene grammar representations when required for the task.
session_title: Scene and Object Perception and Recognition

title: Stage-wise Correspondence is Insufficient: DNNs and the Brain Differ in Representational Transformations
affiliations:
1. MARCS Institute for Brain, Behaviour, and Development, Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia (AU)
2. School of Psychology, Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia (AU)
3. School of Computer, Data and Mathematical Sciences, Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia (AU)
abstract: Object recognition unfolds in the brain along a spatiotemporal hierarchy, with representations transforming from being predominantly visual at early stages of processing to increasingly abstract at later ones. Deep neural networks (DNNs) parallel this progression: Activations in lower layers align with early neural processing higher layers correspond to later neural processing stages. While this stage-wise correspondence is well established, it remains unclear whether the representational transformations across stages are the same in these two systems. Investigating this possibility requires stimuli that evoke distinct activation patterns at different stages of processing. To probe how representations evolve across DNN layers, we extracted activation patterns from a pretrained DNN for 26,107 images and computed representational dissimilarity matrix (RDMs) at each layer. We then applied a ‘greedy’ procedure with optimal-stopping to assemble a subset of 200 images that minimised correlation between layer-wise representations. Using this optimised image subset, we recorded electroencephalography (EEG) from 20 participants, and examined the correspondence between the resulting human RDMs and the DNN layer RDMs, replicating previous findings of early-to-early and late-to-late correspondence. Finally, we quantified representational transformation as changes in pairwise RDM values from early to late stages in DNNs and in the EEG over time. We found that while the direction of representational changes was preserved across DNNs and the brain, the relative magnitude of these changes did not match. These results reveal a critical gap in DNN-brain comparisons: while DNNs capture the stage at which representations emerge, DNNs and the human brain diverge in how representations are reorganised, underscoring that stage-level correspondence alone is insufficient for validating DNNs as models of human vision. Biological and artificial vision may solve object recognition through meaningfully different representational transformations, highlighting the need for future work to investigate how these changes unfold in each system.
session_title: Scene and Object Perception and Recognition

title: Computational mechanisms for flexible intuitive physics in humans
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior (DE)
abstract: Objects with different physical characteristics behave in entirely distinct ways: rigid bodies, such as boxes, and deformable objects, like ropes, respond very differently to manipulation. How do our internal models of the world support the ability to predict and interact with such diverse object classes? In video game physics engines, domain-specific models (such as rigid-body, soft-body and particle-based simulations), tailored to simulate specific object classes, are commonly used. Do we similarly possess distinct internal models for different physical objects? Do we use a single, versatile internal model across all objects? Or do we use a mixture of shared and object-specific mechanisms? To investigate these questions, we designed a game-like task to probe, in a controlled yet ecological way, how human participants interact with objects with diverse physical characteristics. Participants are shown, on a computer screen, an ‘arena’ including an object, a simple manipulator (a rectangular pusher) and a goal indicated by a shape and location within the arena. Using the keyboard, they can rotate and translate the pusher, and their task is to use it to push the object into the goal. On each trial, the object belongs to one of three categories: box, rope, and granular (e.g. a pile of pebbles). We compare the behavior of human participants on this task with graph neural network (GNN)-based models trained to predict the physical dynamics with varying degrees of flexibility. We present initial results assessing the degree to which these different models approximate human behavior, shedding light on the computational mechanisms of flexible intuitive physics in the human mind.
session_title: Scene and Object Perception and Recognition

title: Object category information is dynamically shifted by scene context
affiliations:
1. University of Warwick (UK)
2. University of Cambridge (UK)
abstract: Our knowledge about how the world is structured has a powerful influence on our perceptions. Being in a kitchen, there are certain items we’re more likely to see than others, and a large body of EEG/MEG research shows that the congruency between scenes and objects modulates neural activity, particularly at semantic stages. However, it remains unclear whether contextual information changes the temporal emergence of behaviourally relevant object representations, rather than simply modulating response amplitude. This study aimed to test whether a prior visual scene shifts the timing of object category representations in the brain, and whether such temporal shifts relate to facilitated recognition behaviour. MEG data were collected while participants viewed objects preceded by congruent scenes, incongruent scenes, or scrambled images (no‑context condition). Object category classifiers were trained on activity to no‑context objects and tested on congruent and incongruent trials. Cross‑condition decoding and temporal generalisation analyses were used to determine whether object category information occurred earlier or later in time when preceded by different scenes. Our results showed that behaviourally, object recognition was faster following congruent scenes compared to incongruent and no‑context conditions. Neural decoding showed that object category information could be decoded for both congruent and incongruent trials between ~100–500 ms. Crucially, temporal generalisation revealed that category information present in no‑context trials emerged earlier in time if objects followed congruent scenes. This temporal shift was not observed for incongruent trials, which showed temporally-aligned category representations. Further, the temporally shifted and enhanced decoding for congruent trials was correlated with faster behavioural recognition speeds. These findings demonstrate that scene context accelerates the emergence of categorical object representations when they are congruent. Our results support predictive processing accounts in which contextual expectations dynamically reshape the timing of semantic representations, facilitating object recognition in natural scenes.
session_title: Scene and Object Perception and Recognition

title: A polygon illusion
affiliations:
1. University of California (US)
2. Glendon College (CA)
3. Hokkaido University (JP)
abstract: If a spot moves around inside an outline square that is also moving, the motion of the spot is judged relative to the square, not to the earth. Thus if a spot moves vertically up and down inside a surrounding square that moves horizontally left and right, the spot’s motion will look oblique, not vertical. We have developed this theme into what we call a ‘Polygon illusion’ that describes the polygonal motion path of a moving spot. It requires two polygons: Polygon 1 is the actual motion path followed by the moving spot, say a triangle. Observers do not perceive or notice this triangular path. The spot moves around the perimeter of Polygon 2, say a circle, which is made to move along some appropriate path.  Observers falsely perceive the spot as moving around a circular path (following Polygon 2) and completely ignore Polygon 2’s motion path.  So the spot’s motion is judged relative to the local polygon, not relative to the earth. Note that any two polygons can be chosen without restriction to produce this illusion

title: Visual Perception of Longitudinal Waves: Theory and Observations
affiliations:
1. City-St Georges, University of London (UK)
2. UC San Diego (US)
abstract: Longitudinal travelling wave motion is a physical phenomenon that forms the basis of acoustics and seismic transmission. Our theoretical analysis of physical longitudinal wave motion reveals that it exhibits profound nonlinearities neglected by the physics community. We then simulated longitudinal motion in visual form with a random-dot field in which each dot particle oscillates sinusoidally about a fixed position at the same frequency but with a phase advance proportional to its distance from the origin. The resultant longitudinal density wave is essentially sinusoidal at very low oscillation amplitudes, becoming progressively distorted as oscillation amplitude increases. When the maximum velocity of each dot particle reaches that of the propagation, the density function approximates a series of narrow travelling spikes, splitting into double spikes at even greater amplitudes.   To study such phenomena, we generated wave motion of 6 cycles around 2:1 random-dot annuli, to preclude eye movements by central fixation. Perceptually, the motion splits into a transparent combination of forward motion of the crests and backward for the troughs, rather than a uniform travelling wave, revealing the emergent, or higher-order, tendency to integrate like motions across cycles separately for the two opposing directions. This split motion percept persists for drift-balanced contrast versions, but is eliminated when the dot density increase is compensated by reducing contrast, at high amplitudes. Remarkably, the speed for perceptual cancellation of either forward crest or backward trough motion percepts by adding a (‘rigid’) velocity component scales with oscillation amplitude, but with a nonlinear decrease for the forward crest motion.   Uncompensated longitudinal waves evoke no motion aftereffect (MAE) at any amplitude, except when the contrast of the forward crest motion is selectively reduced, revealing an MAE from the now-dominant retrograde trough motion. This result implies that the opposing transparent motions generate opposing MAEs that cancel when balanced.

title: A rotating wheel illusion reveals distinct stimulus and contextual contributions to perception
affiliations: 1. King's College London (UK)
abstract: It is established that dynamic changes in contrast near luminance edges can drive vivid motion illusions. Such illusions can provide insights into the hierarchical neural architecture serving perception. We empirically study a rotating wheel illusion recently introduced in various forms by a Japanese artist online on X (@jagarikin). The illusion occurs when a wheel (doughnut-like) typically configured with four equal radial sectors of alternate lower/black and higher/white luminance is spun around and appears to either expand or contract despite having no veridical radial motion. The inner and outer circumference of the wheel has narrow strips with luminance edges at the boundaries which contribute to the illusion. We carry out an experiment to measure factors that modulate illusion strength by manipulating four properties: rotation speed, edge size, edge contrast and wheel contrast. In a psychophysical forced choice task, we compare the strength of test stimuli to a simultaneously presented reference stimulus of fixed parameters in blocks of multiple trials. We show that these four characteristics drive the illusory strength. By percentage, participants are most sensitive to speed changes as a driver of the illusion. To study context, we carry out a similar task in which arrows of varying sizes are introduced at the centre of the test stimulus in directions congruent or incongruent with the radial illusory motion. The effect of the arrows shows substantial individual differences, generally either increasing illusion strength regardless of arrow congruence or decreasing the illusion and showing distinct effects for the arrow directions. Few participants are agnostic to the contextual arrows. We test correlations between sensitivity to the lower-level parameters and context measures and unveil a complex set of idiosyncratic interactions. Findings suggest a hierarchical system with contrast, spatial and motion processes contributing to the illusion, all potentially subject to individual top-down modulation.

title: Measuring the Mainz-Linez Illusion using orbital displays.
affiliations:
1. Department of Cognitive Science, University of Malta (MT)
2. Department of Psychology, Faculty of Philosophy, University of Novi Sad (RS)
3. Laboratory of Experimental Psychology, University of Belgrade (RS)
abstract: The Mainz-Linez Illusion (MLI) – introduced at ECVP 2025 – is a powerful example of how static background elements can alter the perceived behaviour of moving targets. Specifically, rectilinearly moving targets are seen to deviate from their physical paths and follow the curves traced by static background elements. In the current presentation, we use an “orbital” variant of the display to quantify several aspects of the illusion. The orbital Mainz-Linez illusion (OMLI) uses a single static inducing circle whose contour is sinusoidally modulated. Targets physically orbit with a fixed radius, but as per the original MLI, appear to follow the curves of the modulated inducing circle. First, we demonstrate that the illusion requires targets to be close to equiluminance with respect to the wider background. This allows us to create a display in which a low-contrast target object – with illusory deviation – is paired with a high-contrast control object – perceived veridically – that is placed 180° away. Measurements are obtained by physically modulating the amplitude of the control object trajectory to systematically match the curves of the inducing circle. We use the method of constant stimuli to obtain the physical amplitude that matches the illusory deviation under various display conditions. On average, estimates of illusory deviation appear to vary between 30-40% of the physical curves. However, this magnitude is also subject to modulation by a number of factors, including eccentricity, configuration – in terms of the number and placement of target/control objects – and the parameters of the inducing circle.

title: Judging a Row by Its Endpoints: Measuring the Bookend Effect
affiliations:
1. Department of Cognitive Science, University of Malta (MT)
2. Department of Psychology, University of California San Diego (US)
3. Department of Psychology, Glendon College (CA)
4. CVR, York University (CA)
5. Psychological and Brain Sciences, Dartmouth College (US)
abstract: Last year at ECVP, we introduced a new example of perceptual grouping called the bookend effect. When several targets undergoing illusory motion are placed in a row on top of an oriented black and white zig-zag background, the whole group appears to move in the direction set by the two outermost elements (the ‘bookends’). Surprisingly, this happens even when the inner elements (the ‘books’) create strong illusory motion signals in the opposite direction. We hypothesized that spatial proximity and shared physical motion lead the visual system to construct a single, unified object representation for the entire group of targets. Within this group, the outer bookend elements have a strong influence on the perceived motion direction of the whole. Importantly, this isn't due to crowding, since the static and dynamic features of the inner elements can easily be reported. However, these inner features appear to contribute little, if at all, to determining the perceived direction of the group's motion. Here, in a series of experiments and stimulus variants, we investigate the conditions under which the bookend effect emerges and whether the inner books can ever modulate the overall motion percept. We quantify this by measuring perceived group direction using a standard adjustment probe. Initial findings reveal a consistent pattern of motion capture across variants, confirming almost no influence of the inner books until bookend motion/form is severely degraded.

title: Reconstructing motion direction from temporally disordered position sequences
affiliations: 1. Department of Psychology, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (DE)
abstract: The idea that visual perception operates in discrete temporal windows rather than continuously has gained increasing support. However, how motion is perceived based on a sequence of discrete snapshots remains unclear. One possibility is that motion direction is not derived from chronological order but reconstructed from priors for coherent spatial changes among elements presented within a temporal interval.  We tested this hypothesis using an adaptation of Rolfs et al.’s (2025) high-speed motion paradigm. Participants viewed an object moving along a curved trajectory over or under a central fixation point, with its successive positions presented in a randomized order rather than in the order in which the object would physically move. Trajectory amplitudes were 4, 8, and 12 dva, with each position shown for one frame (0.7 ms). Across conditions, we manipulated the proportion of rightward and leftward positional shifts (0%, 30-33%, 50%, 68-72%, 100%).   Participants were asked to identify both the curvature and direction of motion. Participants showed 100% correct curvature identification, confirming stimulus visibility and task compliance. Crucially, the perceived direction of motion was systematically biased toward the direction defined by fewer, and therefore on average larger and faster, positional shifts. This result was consistent across all participants tested (N = 5), with little interindividual variability.  We propose that within a temporal integration window, positions are treated as a set rather than as an ordered sequence, and that large jumps introduce new windows of integration. Direction is then resolved at a higher processing level as an ordered sequence of average spatial positions (centers of mass) of successive temporal windows.  These findings are consistent with the idea that motion perception reflects postdictive reconstruction over temporally extended, discrete events rather than direct tracking of sequential change.

title: The cellular basis of the human face inversion effect
affiliations:
1. CNRS-Universite de Lorraine (FR)
2. Université de Lorraine-CHRU-Nancy (FR)
3. KU Leuven (BE)
4. Fudan University (CN)
abstract: Human face identity recognition (FIR) is severely disrupted by picture-plane inversion, yet the cellular mechanisms of this robust face inversion effect (FIE) remain unknown due to behavioral and neuroanatomical limitations of non-human primate models of face recognition. Here we recorded extracellular spiking activity in the human Fusiform Gyrus (FG), a hominoid-specific structure that is key for face recognition. Nine epileptic patients implanted with a hybrid macro/microelectrode in the middle portion of the FG performed an automatic unfamiliar face individuation task associated with large inversion effects at the neural population level (EEG, iEEG). Within a rapid 6 Hz stream of the same repeated face identity across size changes, images of different face identities appeared every fifth image (1.2 Hz) during 70-seconds stimulation sequences. Across participants and sessions, this frequency-tagging stimulation identified 193 single- (122) and multi- (71) units responsive to face identity change at 1.2 Hz and harmonics. 166 units showed a significant identity discrimination response for upright faces (UP+ units, 86.0%) and only 58 for inverted faces (INV+ units, 30.0%), including 31 units responding to both conditions. This neuronal face inversion effect was more prominent in the right than the left hemisphere. Despite these differences, the firing rate for upright vs. inverted faces measured in their respective pool of significant units did not differ, and the time-course of the face identity discrimination response was similar for upright and inverted faces (~130-450 ms). In summary, most neurons are tuned to changes of face identity either at upright or inverted face orientation, with no difference in spike rate modulations across orientation. Instead, supporting a long-standing evidence accumulation hypothesis, the human FIE appears to be accounted for by a much larger proportion of midfusiform neurons tuned to changes of face identity for upright as compared to inverted faces.
session_title: Symposium: Recent Advances in Face Perception and Identification: From Cells to Cognitive Mechanisms and Applied Identification

title: A cross syndrome investigation of face selective processing abilities in Williams Syndrome and Down syndrome
affiliations:
1. School of Psychology, University of East Anglia (UK)
2. William James Center for Research, Ispa – Instituto Universitário (PT)
3. Department of Psychological Sciences, Birkbeck College, University of London (UK)
4. College of Health, Medicine and Life Sciences, Brunel University (UK)
5. Department of Psychology, Bournemouth University (UK)
6. Centre for Genomics and Child Health, Blizard Institute, Queen Mary, University of London (UK)
7. School of Psychology, University of Surrey (UK)
abstract: Individuals with Williams syndrome (WS) and Down syndrome (DS) are reported to show differences in their face processing relative to neurotypical comparison groups, i.e., strengths and weaknesses, respectively. Yet the evidence base for these claims remains limited, particularly with respect to their face-selectivity. Our cross-syndrome investigation assessed recognition memory and perceptual discrimination ability in adults with WS and DS alongside large neurotypical comparison samples, for upright faces and a comparably complex comparison category: bicycles. In line with neurotypical individual differences research, there was notable variability in face abilities within syndrome groups, as well as between them. Overall, the first two stages of the Cambridge Face Memory Test for Children proved particularly sensitive to group differences: individuals with DS performed more poorly than those with WS and NT children over 5 years of age, whereas individuals with WS showed difficulties only relative to NT children over 10 years. When modelling the developmental trajectories of face abilities relative to general object abilities, we found that the relationship between skills across categories did not differ across groups (NT, WS, DS). These latter findings critically challenge notions of the exceptionality of face processing differences in these syndrome groups, and prompt reconsideration of the theoretical accounts that highlight social differences.
session_title: Symposium: Recent Advances in Face Perception and Identification: From Cells to Cognitive Mechanisms and Applied Identification

title: Predictors of lineup accuracy in 2D and 3D displays: An individual differences approach
affiliations: 1. University of Stirling, Stirling (UK)
abstract: Face processing ability varies widely amongst people and has clear consequences for eyewitness accuracy. Indeed, eyewitness identification is error prone and has led to wrongful convictions in approximately 70% of the cases re-examined by the Innocence Project. Applied work typically concentrates on improving the lineup presentation procedures or estimating the impact of individual differences in face processing ability but seldom looks at both. While there is some evidence suggesting that so-called super-recognisers are consistently proficient across most face processing tasks, including lineup identification, this is not true for ‘typical’ perceivers whose ability can vary widely depending on the test used. For the first time, this research examines whether, and how, eyewitness accuracy interacts with individuals' face processing ability in different 2D and 3D Virtual Reality (VR) line ups. The aim of this project was to establish the best predictors of lineup identification, and to examine the extent to which they predict identity recognition in 2D and 3D lineups displayed in VR. Eight hundred and forty participants completed a battery of online face processing tests, followed by laboratory (in-person) basic vision assessment, and eight non-violent mock crimes and lineup tasks in VR. The results and implications for practice will be discussed as a part of this talk.
session_title: Symposium: Recent Advances in Face Perception and Identification: From Cells to Cognitive Mechanisms and Applied Identification

title: Context-induced distinctiveness in face learning: Evidence across multiple facial appearance cues
affiliations:
1. University of Liège (BE)
2. Simon Fraser University (CA)
abstract: Traditionally, the impact of distinctiveness on face learning has been studied for faces deviating from a population norm, showing recognition advantages compared to typical faces. However, distinctiveness may depend on the observer’s face diet or on the immediate learning context. Namely, faces typical at the population level may become distinctive relative to others learned concurrently, thereby shaping their representation. To test this idea, we developed an odd-one-out learning paradigm grounded in a cost-efficient encoding hypothesis. Specifically, facial information that renders a face distinctive in a given context would be disproportionately weighted during learning, reducing the encoding of finer-grained information relative to faces learned concurrently. Participants learned four FaceGen‑generated faces. Before learning each one individually, they viewed a group image in which one face was made distinctive by a single salient feature (counterbalanced), while the remaining three shared that feature. In Experiment 1, distinctiveness was induced via skin tone (Caucasian, non‑Caucasian N=96) to examine whether it could reverse the other‑race effect. In Experiments 2 and 3, distinctiveness was induced through hair (blond, black N=80) or eye colour (blue, brown N=80), to examine the impact of peripheral and central salient features on learning. Recognition was tested with the salient feature preserved (superficial test) or removed (e.g., skin tone or hair removed eyes closed fine test). Overall, context‑based distinctiveness seems to promote superficial encoding of faces. Although the other‑race effect appeared reversible at a superficial level, memory representations for distinctive same‑race faces were more robust, consistent with experience‑based tuning. Therefore, face representations are shaped by contextual distinctiveness during learning, favouring efficient encoding strategies that depend on both feature diagnosticity and prior visual experience.
session_title: Symposium: Recent Advances in Face Perception and Identification: From Cells to Cognitive Mechanisms and Applied Identification

title: Navigating toward domain-specific accounts of face identification: evidence from individuals with developmental prosopagnosia and super-recognizers
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: One of the classic debates in visual cognition concerns whether face recognition relies on general visual mechanisms (i.e., a domain-general view) or face-specific mechanisms (i.e., a domain-specific view). One line of support for the domain-general view comes from neuropsychological patients who, after brain injury, show concurrent deficits in face recognition and navigational skills. However, it is currently unknown whether this link is merely coincidental (i.e., observable only in prosopagnosia) or genuinely interdependent (i.e., such that variation in one ability predicts variation in the other across the full spectrum of face-recognition abilities). We tested these two accounts in participants with developmental prosopagnosia, super-recognizers, and control participants. In Study 1, participants completed a recently validated ecological route-learning task. In Study 2, participants completed a battery of laboratory tasks associated with navigational skills. Results showed no group differences in either study, suggesting that face recognition and spatial navigation are not directly associated, providing support for domain-specific accounts of face recognition.
session_title: Symposium: Recent Advances in Face Perception and Identification: From Cells to Cognitive Mechanisms and Applied Identification

title: How the Brain Builds Confidence: The Neurobiological Basis of Decision Evaluation
affiliations: 1. Laboratoire des Systèmes Perceptifs, Ecole Normale Supérieure, PSL (FR)
abstract: Feelings of confidence in our decisions arise from an evaluation of the evidence supporting those decisions. For perceptual decisions, sensory evidence can be maintained in visual working memory well beyond stimulus offset. This persistence provides a basis for computational accounts in which confidence depends on evidence that continues to evolve following the decision. Under such a framework, the strength of the maintained sensory evidence should directly constrain the quality of confidence evaluations. However, the neural mechanisms governing the maintenance and transformation of this evidence remain poorly understood.   Here, we investigate how sensory evidence is maintained and transformed across the entire decision window using a perceptual discrimination task with orthogonal stimulus features (colour and orientation). On each trial, participants provided a perceptual response according to the task-relevant feature and subsequently rated their confidence on a 4-point scale. Critically, the task design allows us to dissociate stimulus-specific representations from decision-related processes in the post-stimulus interval.   Twenty participants completed the task while EEG was recorded. Analyses focused on post-stimulus dynamics of both sensory representations and decision-related signals. This approach enabled us to track the temporal evolution of stimulus evidence and decision after stimulus presentation.   We find that stimulus-specific information persists after stimulus offset, remaining significantly above baseline for ~800ms. Moreover, this maintenance signal exhibits a gradual decline over time, consistent with accounts of evidence degradation. Finally, results suggest that greater accuracy of post-stimulus sensory maintenance, quantified as lower decoding error, contributes to the efficiency of confidence judgements.   Together, these findings suggest that confidence is supported by dynamically evolving post-decision representations. This work provides new insight into the neural mechanisms linking evidence accumulation, sensory maintenance, and confidence evaluation.

title: Neural adaptation of the sense of confidence
affiliations:
1. LSP, DEC, ENS-PSL University (FR)
2. CNRS (FR)
3. Paris Brain Institute (FR)
4. INSERM (FR)
5. Paris School of Economics (FR)
abstract: When we make a decision, we can feel more or less confident in our choice. It has been proposed that a general metacognitive mechanism serves to evaluate confidence across all forms of decision-making. Here, we aimed to provide causal evidence of this general metacognitive mechanism, and examine its neural basis. We developed a confidence adaptation technique where prolonged exposure to high (or low) confidence decisions altered how humans evaluate their confidence in a different decision-making task. We found the evaluation of visual confidence was adapted in line with the predictions of a dual-channel model: there was a pattern of increased confidence sensitivity following adaptation. We could then examine neural activity that predicts this change in confidence. We found such activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, and the insula (commonly correlated with confidence in previous studies), changed according to the alteration in confidence evaluation. The change in the insula strongly predicted the change in behaviour, suggesting this region is critically engaged in evaluating confidence.

title: Confidence Sharing Improves Children's Collaborative Decisions
affiliations:
1. Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (ES)
2. Ecole Normale Supérieure (FR)
abstract: Confidence, our subjective sense of decision accuracy, represents a key marker of metacognitive experience. While research in adults demonstrates that confidence coordinates collaborative decisions, whether children can access and utilize these metacognitive signals for social coordination remains unknown and yet is critically important for education.We studied 38 dyads of children (8–11 years) completing a visual perception task.Children judged grating orientations and rated their confidence on a 6-point scale on each trial, first individually then collaboratively. An individual staircase maintained accuracy around 70%. We quantified metacognitive sensitivity and efficiency using Signal Detection Theory, analyzed Confidence Matching Scores during disagreement trials, examined confidence dynamics when participants changed their mind, and employed mixed-effects inference respecting the dyadic nesting of observations.Joint decisions demonstrated significantly higher type-1 perceptual sensitivity than individual decisions. Metacognitive sensitivity improved for joint decisions, however no effects were observed in M-ratio. During disagreement trials, dyads followed the more confident partner 92% of the time, with no age bias. The remaining 8% of non-following trials were characterised by significantly smaller confidence gaps, with the majority involving a difference of 1 point. Collective benefit (d′joint/d′max) was positively associated with relative sensitivity (d′min/d′max), indicating that more evenly matched dyads gained greater collective benefit. When participants changed their mind to align with the collaborative decision, they did so from a position of low confidence and confidence recovered to baseline levels on the subsequent trial without lasting disruption.Children effectively use subjective confidence as a social signal to coordinate perceptual decisions appropriately, abandoning strict confidence weighting when signals are nearly equivalent. Collaborative gain is greatest in evenly matched dyads. These findings demonstrate that collective functional metacognitive awareness does not require extended development and that collaborative learning can leverage confidence to enhance outcomes, directly informing educational interventions and metacognitive training programs.

title: The neural basis of stimulus-driven overconfidence
affiliations:
1. Hertie-Institute for Clinical Brain Research (DE)
2. Centre for Integrative Neuroscience (DE)
3. MEG Center, University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: An essential part of decision-making is confidence - the ability to judge how likely our choices are to be correct or incorrect. Despite its fundamental role, the neural computations underlying confidence judgements are still poorly understood. While confidence and accuracy are inherently correlated, confidence judgments can be biased and thus dissociated from accuracy. Such dissociations provide a window into the underlying computational mechanisms. One such case is the positive evidence manipulation, where subjects are overconfident for strong evidence that supports their choice. Here, we employed this manipulation in a magnetoencephalography (MEG) study, in which participants performed an orientation discrimination task with simultaneous choice and confidence reports. We found that neural choice and confidence representations were similar with and without stimulus-driven overconfidence. However, in the overconfident high-evidence condition, both the mean and variance of neural choice signals were increased. Furthermore, a simple computational model of choice confidence predicted both the increase of the neural choice signals and of subjective confidence across individual subjects. Our results suggest that overconfidence is not due to a cognitive bias, but reflects a stimulus-driven change of the distribution of neural choice signals.

title: Evidence against domain-general metacognition: Distinct confidence rating strategies in visual perception and recognition memory tasks
affiliations: 1. Department of Experimental Psychology, University of Oxford (UK)
abstract: Metacognition is often described as the monitoring and control of one’s own cognitive and behavioral processes. People use their confidence in a judgment to adjust their subsequent actions for example, they may slow down when the road is unclear to gather more information, allowing for more accurate decisions. Given the ubiquity of metacognitive processes in mental operations (e.g., visual perception or recognition memory), researchers are curious about whether there is a single, unified system that can read out various forms of information from different domains (the domain-generality hypothesis). While previous research has conventionally addressed this question by correlating measures of metacognitive accuracy across tasks, we critique this approach, arguing that such correlations may be spurious, arising from shared third variables or inherent properties of modeling metacognitive efficiency using the signal detection theory (SDT) model. Consequently, whereas previous research has focused on performance correlations, our approach focuses on assessing domain-generality via more robust, quantifiable characteristics of confidence rating strategies. We reasoned that if metacognition is domain-general, individuals should maintain the same confidence rating strategies across different types of tasks. In the initial study, we manipulated difficulty in both visual perception and recognition memory tasks to test whether participants maintained the same computational strategies (e.g., being Bayesian or heuristic in confidence ratings) across tasks by examining the property of criteria setting under the unequal variance SDT model. The results indicate that participants’ computations of confidence were similar within tasks but not across tasks, providing evidence against the domain-generality of metacognition. At least, the metacognitive system for visual perception may differ from that for memory.

title: Size discrimination versus stimulus detection across levels of visual awareness.
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology and Cognitive Science, University of Trento (IT)
2. Centre de Recherche Cerveau et Cognition, CNRS, Université de Toulouse (FR)
3. Department of Neuroscience, Biomedicine and Movement Sciences, University of Verona (IT)
abstract: An accurate representation of object size is a fundamental visual process supporting effective interaction with the environment. Size computation relies on early mechanisms that encode stimulus properties according to the retinotopic organization of the visual system. Under normal viewing conditions, physically larger stimuli typically elicit stronger and earlier neural responses than smaller ones. While behavioural evidence suggests that size discrimination depends on conscious awareness, it remains unclear whether this is reflected at the neural level and whether size information can be processed without awareness. To address this question, we recorded EEG activity while participants performed a size discrimination task under Continuous Flash Suppression (CFS), which allows manipulation of visual awareness. On each trial, a small or large ring was presented to one eye while a dynamic high-contrast flickering mask was shown to the other. A staircase procedure was used to estimate individual perceptual thresholds, ensuring a balanced proportion of conscious and unconscious trials. Participants performed a forced-choice size judgment and rated perceptual clarity using the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS). Catch trials were included to assess performance in the absence of the stimulus. Behavioural results showed that size discrimination critically depended on awareness: accuracy was above chance only in conscious trials, whereas performance in unconscious trials did not differ from chance and was comparable to catch trials. Consistently, ERP analyses revealed size-related neural differences only under conscious perception, with no differences between unseen stimuli and catch trials. However, time–frequency analyses revealed residual unconscious processing. Although no power differences emerged, unseen stimuli elicited increased low-frequency (delta-band) phase synchronization compared to catch trials, suggesting that stimulus presence is registered without awareness. Overall, these findings indicate that while unconscious processing does not support size discrimination, it may encode basic stimulus presence, highlighting a dissociation between feature processing and detection across levels of awareness.

title: Tiny convolutional neural networks reveal computations underlying human gloss perception
affiliations:
1. University of Oxford (UK)
2. Justus-Liebig-Universität Gießen (DE)
3. University of Auckland (NZ)
abstract: A central goal of visual neuroscience is to explain how the brain infers object properties such as texture, curvature, and gloss from images. Here, we used machine learning not as a direct model of the brain, but as a tool to identify the computations underlying human gloss perception, a visual task long regarded as a challenging inference. We rendered thousands of object images with varying shapes, viewpoints, and illumination, and collected gloss judgments through crowdsourcing. Human judgments were highly consistent across observers, yet systematically deviated from physical ground truth. We compared these responses with convolutional neural networks trained either to estimate physical specular reflectance or to reproduce human judgments. By progressively reducing network size, we identified the minimum computations required for each objective. Estimating physical reflectance required deep networks, whereas human judgments were captured by remarkably shallow networks with as few as three convolutional layers. Strikingly, a tiny model containing only a single filter predicted human judgments better than the best-performing ground-truth network. Generalization tests on independent external image sets showed that human-like networks also reproduced known gloss illusions, generalized to computer-generated object images with a broader range of optical properties, and extended to photographs of real objects. However, for objects with high-contrast textures, the model overestimated gloss by responding to texture. When the model was retrained on both textured and non-textured objects after adding a second filter, the original gloss-sensitive filter was retained, while the added filter acquired selective sensitivity to texture and suppressed texture-driven errors. These findings suggest that human gloss judgments rely on simpler, more general-purpose computations than previously thought, and highlight the value of tiny, interpretable neural networks for uncovering biologically plausible computations underlying material perception.
session_title: Symposium: Artificial Intelligence as a Window into Material Perception: From Minimal Models to Active and Individualized Representations

title: Spatiochromatic Representation in Discrete Autoencoders
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
2. Lancaster University Leipzig (DE)
3. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Understanding how the human visual system efficiently encodes both colour and spatial structure remains a central challenge in vision science. Here, we investigate this question using artificial neural networks trained for colour conversion on natural images with discrete representational constraints. Specifically, we trained vector-quantised variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs), characterised by a latent code constrained to discrete representations. We systematically varied the number of discrete embedding vectors (K), input–output colour spaces (e.g., RGB to CIELAB), and random initialisations. To characterise the learned representations, we generated images by sampling from individual embedding vectors, as well as their combinations. Across different random initialisations, embedding vectors converged to highly consistent and interpretable outputs, revealing a stable organisation of colour representations. With a small codebook (K=6), networks reliably produced three chromatic categories (red, yellow, blue) alongside three achromatic values (black, grey, white). Increasing the codebook size to K=8 introduced an additional chromatic category (green) and a finer subdivision of achromatic values. Further increases in K (11, 16, 32) primarily refined chromatic space, yielding intermediate hues (e.g., brown, beige), while the number of achromatic representations remained relatively stable. For larger codebooks (K≥32), a qualitative shift emerged: some embedding vectors encoded both chromatic and spatial information. Sampling from these vectors produced oriented patterns such as horizontal or vertical colour stripes, indicating the emergence of spatiochromatic units. Importantly, similar spatial and chromatic effects could also be achieved in smaller codebooks through combinations of vectors. These combinations resulted either in spatial mixtures (e.g., striped colours) or perceptual colour blending (e.g., red and blue yielding purple, or red and grey producing pink), resembling mechanisms of spatial integration and neural colour opponency. These findings suggest that key aspects of human spatiochromatic encoding can emerge from efficient representation learning under capacity constraints.

title: Unravelling constancy mechanisms in haptic perception of materials using DNN modelling
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Haptic perception of the materials an object is made of is crucial for interacting with it. The sense of touch often extends our visual perception of materials, as we can sense differences (e.g. fake vs. real wood or satin vs. silk) which might be very difficult to see. The underlying signals in the perception of such fine textures are high-frequency vibrations elicited on the skin by manual exploration of the material surface (sliding across the surface). Naturally, these signals depend not only on the spatial structure of materials’ surfaces but also on exploration speed, however our haptic perception of materials is speed constant. We used an unsupervised learning model to show that processing of sensory input relies on efficient encoding of these vibratory signals. The resulting low dimensional perceptual space resembles the tuning of the two main tactile afferents (RA and PC) involved in material texture perception, suggesting that both artificial and natural system evolve similar representations. Moreover, such representation reflects a simple characteristic of the relative frequency composition of vibratory signals – the slope in the frequency domain. The slope is sufficient for material category classification and can explain human correct and mistaken material classifications. We systematically varied exploration speed and showed that, while signal properties change with speed, the slope in the frequency domain is relatively invariant. Furthermore, we trained a supervised neural network to classify material categories based on vibratory signals, independent of exploration speed. We show that its deepest units express a similar level of speed constancy as the slope, while its shallower units likely only extract the Fourier spectrum. Overall, we showed that deep learning trained to perform ecologically relevant tasks is a powerful framework for explaining how sensory input is acquired and transformed from simple, input-like features, into more complex perceptually-relevant features.

title: Active Perception of Real-World Materials Using 3D Gaussian Splatting
affiliations: 1. American University (US)
abstract: In everyday life, we visually judge materials to make decisions. Previous research on material perception mostly uses static images with passive viewing, even though the appearance of real-world materials often changes across viewpoints due to complex interactions among lighting, materials, and shape. We developed an AI-based pipeline based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to build photorealistic, yet controllable, scenes from real-world captures. We use fake fruit detection as a benchmark for our method. Unlike mesh-based rendering, 3DGS captures digital twins of real-world scenes while preserving their natural appearance. Unlike photographs or videos, 3DGS provides intuitive viewpoint controls, making it a useful tool for investigating the role of active vision in material perception. To automate scene construction, we built a programmable spherical camera rig that captures many views of the scene using a mirrorless camera. We combine neural scene reconstruction with geometric constraints from our spherical setup. This allows us to refine object masks by using a ground-plane constraint and 3D-to-2D projection, including hole-filling based on surface curvature. We also assembled randomized yet physically plausible fruit arrangements using an optimization algorithm. Interactive viewing was supported by developing a real-time GPU viewer that renders 4K resolution at 120 Hz. We investigate whether material judgments elicit task-driven active viewpoint-control strategies in reconstructed scenes. Participants inspect 50 fruit arrangements and indicate which objects are plastic fruits, while they explore the scene using a mouse that controls an orbiting camera. In a control, they identify which fruits have stickers placed on them. We record the viewpoint and mouse behavior during the exploration task. We predict that the material-judgment condition will induce greater individual differences in viewing trajectories, longer dwelling time, and more repeated visits to ambiguous stimuli than the sticker-identification condition, as material discrimination depends on viewpoint-dependent cues such as gloss, texture, and translucency.

title: Personalized Modeling of Material Perception in Autism Spectrum Disorder
affiliations:
1. Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, Hokkaido University (JP)
2. Prometech CG Research (JP)
abstract: Real-world objects exhibit a wide range of material properties, and understanding how these are perceived requires considering not only group-level trends but also individual differences. This is particularly important for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), where individuals often exhibit sensory hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity, with substantial variability across individuals. Characterizing such diversity requires approaches that move beyond group averages and instead model perception at the individual level. In this study, we measured visual discrimination sensitivity across multiple material dimensions and developed personalized computational models of material perception using deep neural networks. Thirty individuals with ASD, recruited from clinical settings, and a group of age- and gender-matched typically developing (TD) participants took part in the experiment. Participants performed an odd-one-out task using a material perception dataset (Sawayama et al., 2022, Journal of Vision), in which stimuli were generated via physically based rendering and systematically varied along six material dimensions. At the group level, no significant differences were observed between ASD and TD participants in discrimination accuracy. However, substantial individual variability emerged in the computational modeling results. We evaluated multiple deep neural network models with different pretraining paradigms and found that self-supervised models (e.g., DINO) provided the best predictions of individual behavioral performance across both groups. Further analysis revealed distinct patterns in the levels of representation that best explained individual performance. For many TD participants, deeper-layer features yielded better predictions, suggesting reliance on higher-level representations. In contrast, ASD participants exhibited more heterogeneous patterns: while some individuals were best explained by deeper features, a substantial number were better captured by shallow-layer features, indicating a broader diversity in representational reliance. These findings suggest that personalized modeling can uncover individual differences in the perceptual features underlying material discrimination, providing insights into the heterogeneity of perceptual processing in ASD.

title: Developmental changes in exogenous visual spatial attention: faster facilitation effects improve position accuracy with age.
affiliations:
1. Indian Institute of Technology (IN)
2. Barnard College, Columbia University (US)
3. Stanford University (US)
abstract: Exogenous visual spatial attention — the automatic orienting to peripheral cues — is widely considered developmentally stable. However, this conclusion overlooks critical temporal dynamics: prior developmental studies have focused on cue-to-target intervals (CTIs) of 100 ms or longer, inadvertently obscuring developmental processes unfolding at shorter timescales. Here, we examined how exogenous cue facilitation and suppression change across development at a shorter, previously unexplored CTI.  We tested 184 participants (ages 6–40 years, cross-sectional) in a letter identification task with peripheral cues appearing 50 ms or 100 ms before the target. All error trials were classified as transposition errors (reporting a nearby non-target) or misidentification errors (reporting a stimulus not present in the display) to understand how spatial cues changed task performance.  Developmental changes emerged selectively at the 50 ms CTI, with valid cue benefits increasing with age and driven specifically by a reduction in transposition errors. No developmental modulation was found at 100 ms, indicating that developmental differences in exogenous attention are interval-sensitive and emerge only at shorter CTIs.   Our findings challenge the developmental stability of exogenous attention, revealing that facilitatory effects of valid cues become faster with age and qualitatively more refined: adults use the valid cue benefits specifically to reduce transposition errors — the error type that directly reflects spatial position encoding — rather than producing broad accuracy gains. This suggests that with development, exogenous attention is not developmentally stable — it gets faster, more precise, and more functionally selective with age.

title: The neural basis of categorical visual attention in humans: evidence from intracerebral EEG recordings
affiliations:
1. Université de Lorraine, CNRS, IMoPA (FR)
2. Service de Neurologie, Université de Lorraine, CHRU-Nancy (FR)
abstract: A major challenge in studying the neural substrates of visual attention in the human brain is attention’s fast and dynamic nature across large-scale networks. To address this, we used intracerebral electroencephalographic recordings (stereo-EEG) in drug-resistant epileptic patients implanted with multi-contact depth electrodes, enabling direct access to attention-related neural activity with high spatiotemporal resolution.   We employed a frequency-tagging paradigm with three image categories (faces, houses, cars) to reliably capture high-level visual representations. Participants (N=14, 7 women) viewed continuous sequences of natural images in which category-specific stimuli were presented as periodic oddballs at 1 Hz within a mixed-category stream presented at 4 Hz. This approach elicited category-selective neural responses at the tagging frequency, indexing populations tuned to each category. Attention was manipulated by instructing participants to selectively attend to one category while ignoring another, with both categories sequentially frequency-tagged at 1 Hz. Crucially, visual input was held constant across attention conditions, allowing isolation of attentional modulation. Neural responses were analyzed in the frequency domain by comparing normalized amplitudes between attended and ignored conditions.   Across 1882 cortical and hippocampal contacts, 739 showed significant oddball responses (z>3) to at least one image category. A significant main effect of attention, pooling categories together, was observed in 285 contacts across 12 participants, predominantly in bilateral ventral occipito-temporal cortex. This effect was supported by a linear mixed-effects model (β=1.02, p<.001). Category-specific attentional modulation was most often restricted to one (278 contacts, 14 participants) or two categories (56 contacts, 10 participants), mainly within ventral occipito-temporal cortex. In contrast, multi-category attentional effects were observed in a smaller subset of contacts (10 contacts, 4 participants), primarily in frontal, temporal, insular, and hippocampal regions. These findings reveal robust category-specific attentional modulation along the ventral visual stream, alongside more integrative, multi-category effects distributed in fronto-temporal networks, potentially reflecting higher-order attentional control mechanisms.

title: Revealing the hidden spatial distribution of visual attention through pupillometry
affiliations: 1. Utrecht University (NL)
abstract: Visual attention selects which visual information is processed at a given moment. Its spatial distribution, i.e. its size and shape, constitutes the attentional field. This field is central to our everyday behaviour, but how it is adjusted and changes over time is challenging to measure. Here, we introduce a pupillometry approach that uses luminance tagging to track changes in the attentional field continuously. Our method is based on previous work, which has shown that attending to a brighter location causes the pupil to constrict, whereas attending to a dark location causes it to dilate. Here, we use these properties to demonstrate changes in the attentional field. In two experiments, we demonstrated that both the size of the attentional field (Experiment 1) and the shape (Experiment 2) can be tracked using a luminance-tagged background. Crucially, the approach is bidirectional: a large attentional field can be tagged with a dark luminance on one trial and a bright luminance on the next. This bidirectionality ensures that the measure is not confounded by other factors known to influence pupil size, thereby making it suitable to use across a range of contexts. We further discuss implications for studying the temporal dynamics of attentional field adjustments and present possible directions for applying this method to understand attentional field differences across different states and traits of individuals.

title: Shifting of visual attention in time based on cue-interval regularities can operate in the absence of awareness
affiliations:
1. Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics (DE)
2. International Max Planck Research School for the Mechanisms of Mental Function and Dysfunction, Graduate Training Centre of Neuroscience, University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: In dynamic environments, adaptive behaviour crucially depends on anticipating the timing of upcoming events based on various temporal regularities and proactively increasing attention to peak at the expected time. Previous studies have shown that cue-interval associations make the interval predictable and lead to improved perception of and reaction time to visual stimuli. However, while it is established that some regularities, e.g. isochronous streams, can drive temporal attention automatically and involuntarily, it is not clear whether this applies to cue-interval associations. Understanding this is essential to models of visual attention, as in our natural environment, these regularities are often implicitly learned, and the prediction process is applied unconsciously. Here, we tested in two experiments the ability of interval-based temporal attention to operate in the absence of awareness or volitional use of temporal regularity. In the first experiment, participants provided speeded responses to a visual target embedded in a stream of visual stimuli. Unbeknownst to them, the interval between the target and the penultimate stimulus was consistently repeated in the stream. Subjective awareness of this regularity was reduced by using variable stream length and multiple target times, and was probed at the end of the experiment using a questionnaire about the task structure. We found that 81% of participants were classified as naïve based on their questionnaire responses, and within this group, responses were faster to temporally valid compared to invalid targets. The second experiment repeated this design with a challenging perceptual discrimination task, leading to 90% naive participants, and revealed higher temporal sensitivity (d′) for valid compared to invalid targets. Together, these results provide evidence that interval-based temporal attention can operate involuntarily without conscious awareness, and impact not only motor preparation but also directly visual processing.

title: When Covert Exogenous Spatial Attention Isn’t Purely Bottom-Up: Reward learning modulates an abrupt onset’s impact on asymptotic discriminability
affiliations:
1. Trinity College (US)
2. New York University (US)
abstract: The sudden appearance of a peripheral stimulus elicits a reflexive shift of covert spatial attention, yielding rapid and transient improvements in perception at attended locations. Classic accounts emphasize the largely bottom-up nature of this effect, yet recent work shows that “reflexive” attention is sensitive to learned regularities. Here we extend this work by asking whether learned reward associations modulate the allocation of covert exogenous spatial attention.     Twenty-two observers completed four sessions each of a speed-accuracy trade-off (SAT) procedure. Each trial contained two peripheral Gabor patches presented left and right of fixation. Observers indicated the orientation (clockwise/counterclockwise from vertical) of the post-cued Gabor after delays of 33–2133 ms. A spatially uninformative, abrupt-onset disk preceded the Gabors and was equally likely to be valid (near the subsequent target) or invalid (near the distractor). The disk’s luminance was deterministically paired with one of two outcomes: for one luminance-defined disk, correct responses earned $0.03 for the other, correct responses earned $0.00. Data were fit with a standard SAT model to estimate asymptotic discriminability and the rate of information accrual. Both reward-predictive and non-reward-predictive disks produced robust cueing effects. Critically, reward history modulated the magnitude of the attentional effect at asymptote: we observed a reward × cue validity interaction for the SAT asymptotic parameter, with larger cueing effects for reward-predictive onsets. In contrast, reward did not interact with cue validity for processing-time. Nonetheless, we observed a main effect of cue validity, consistent with prior SAT findings that exogenous cueing speeds the rate of information accrual.These results indicate that reward learning selectively amplifies the ultimate perceptual advantage conferred by covert spatial attention, without altering attention’s effect on the temporal dynamics of information accumulation. More broadly, findings underscore that exogenous attention is not purely stimulus-driven: its consequences are shaped by learned regularities.

title: The Trajectory of Visual Attention Teleport or Drift?
affiliations: 1. Helmholtz Institute, Utrecht University (NL)
abstract: Covert attention is a fundamental component of visual processing, but its ‘covert’ nature makes it challenging to measure directly. Thus, although signatures of covert attention are frequently used in all sorts of domains of visual cognition (visual search, visual working memory, attentional capture, reading, attentional spotlight tasks, object-based attention, etc.), relatively little is known about what a shift of covert attention actually looks like. Here, we address the following question: when covert attention shifts, and boosts sensory processing at some target location, is sensory processing along the path of this shift boosted as well? Or, does it ‘teleport’ without altering sensory processing along the way?  We conduct an EEG-eyetracking experiment (n = 24) paired with a cueing task and Rapid Inivisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT), using which we track attentional allocation to the start and end points of a covert attentional shift. We show successful markers of attentional shifts (RIFT responses at the endpoints, alpha lateralization, gaze position). Crucially, we also tag locations between these start and end points and observe no attentional modulations to the RIFT response at these locations. Thus, our results suggest that covert attention is directly shifted from start to endpoint without boosting the encoding of stimuli along the way. As tools that track attention are developed in order to better study the various domains of visual cognition, this outcome places important constraints on what can be tracked.

title: Tonic Arousal Modulates Response Speed but Not Attentional Orienting
affiliations: 1. University of Amsterdam (NL)
abstract: Human performance fluctuates over time even under constant task demands, potentially reflecting variations in internal states, such as arousal. While prior work has linked arousal to perceptual and decision-making performance, its influence on selective attention remains unclear. Here, we investigated how moment-to-moment fluctuations in tonic arousal modulate visuospatial attention, using pupillometry in combination with variants of the Posner cueing paradigm. Across five experiments (N = 377), we measured pre-stimulus pupil size as a trial-by-trial index of tonic arousal while participants performed exogenous and endogenous spatial cueing tasks. Task variants systematically manipulated cue predictiveness, inclusion of neutral trials, inhibition of return, and cue type (peripheral vs. central). Behavioural performance was assessed via response times (RTs) and cueing effects (invalid–valid RT differences), allowing testing for dissociations between global processing efficiency and attentional orienting. Consistent with the Yerkes–Dodson framework, we observed a robust quadratic (U-shaped) relationship between tonic arousal and RTs in four of five experiments: responses were fastest at intermediate arousal levels and slower at both low and high arousal. Mixed-effects model comparisons confirmed that quadratic models provided a significantly better fit than linear models. In contrast, cueing effects showed little evidence of modulation by arousal, suggesting that attentional orienting is largely unaffected by fluctuations in tonic arousal. These findings demonstrate that spontaneous fluctuations in tonic arousal strongly influence overall processing speed but do not consistently modulate the efficiency of spatial orienting. This dissociation suggests that arousal primarily affects global processing efficiency rather than the specific mechanisms underlying attentional reorienting. Together, our results refine current accounts of arousal–performance relationships by showing that the canonical inverted-U robustly characterizes response speed, but does not uniformly extend to selective attention.

title: Temporal expectations drive early visual processing
affiliations: 1. Utrecht University (NL)
abstract: Expecting a red light right after a yellow light is possible because stoplights follow predictable timing. Temporal expectations about relevant sensory events reliably improve response time and response accuracy. Improved accuracy is in part attributed to preparatory changes in visual areas. However, physiological evidence for this preparation relies primarily on endogenous neural markers (e.g., alpha oscillations), whose precise relationship to visual processing is debated. Here, we employed Rapid-Invisible-Frequency Tagging (RIFT), an invisible experimenter-induced neural marker of early visual processing intensity, while participants completed a temporal orienting task (manipulation of expected target timing). In line with previous research, behavioral performance (precision) improved when targets were presented at the expected time. Crucially, the RIFT response revealed that anticipating relevant events increased visual processing shortly before their onset. Using induced (rather than endogenous) neural oscillations, these results show that temporal expectations facilitate perceptual performance by driving the earliest stages of visual processing when anticipating relevant sensory events.

title: Tracing Pupils and Performance: Task Difficulty and Timescales of Arousal
affiliations:
1. University of Amsterdam (NL)
2. University of Basel (CH)
3. Vrije Universiteit van Amsterdam (NL)
abstract: A century after Yerkes and Dodson proposed that performance peaks at intermediate arousal, the neurobiological conditions under which this relationship emerges in humans remain debated. Arousal is increasingly understood as a multiscale process, expressed in fluctuations unfolding over different timescales, from fast, transient responses to slower changes in global state. These are reflected in pupil dynamics and relate to neuromodulatory influences, including but not limited to locus coeruleus-noradrenergic activity. Inverted-U arousal-performance relationships have been reported in both the auditory and visual domain, raising the question of what mechanisms underlie this relationship. We investigated how task difficulty and the timescale of pupil-linked arousal fluctuations shape the arousal-performance relationship in an auditory discrimination task. Sixty participants performed easy and difficult task variants (~90% and 70% accuracy, respectively) while pupil size was measured. Using a hierarchical Bayesian modeling, we estimated how task difficulty and pre-stimulus pupil-linked arousal predicted perceptual sensitivity. Overall, we found evidence for an inverted-U shaped arousal-performance relationship, but no evidence for modulation by task difficulty. Crucially, the strength and form of this relationship depended on the investigated arousal timescale. When infra-slow arousal fluctuations (<0.01 Hz) were removed, the inverted-U relationship became stronger, whereas isolating these infra-slow components abolished the inverted-U. Sliding-window analyses further showed a temporal dissociation across trials, with the inverted-U relationship emerging later within blocks, coinciding with attenuation of pupil decay. This suggests that early performance might be dominated by slower neuromodulatory fluctuations rather than intermediate-timescale fluctuations, influencing performance later in the block. Together, these findings demonstrate that arousal-performance relationships is not fixed, but depends on the temporal scale of arousal fluctuations being examined, providing a mechanistic refinement of the Yerkes-Dodson law that is likely generalisable across modalities.

title: Distinct effects of feature-based attention on serial dependence and central tendency bias in hue judgements
affiliations: 1. University of Helsinki (FI)
abstract: Serial dependence and central tendency bias (CTB) are similar, attractive biases toward recent stimulus history but operating on different timescales. Serial dependence is modulated by feature-based attention: when a different feature of the stimulus was attended in the previous trial, serial dependence diminishes compared to when the same feature was attended. We tested whether feature-based attention similarly affects CTB in hue judgments. If it does, the two effects could be caused by a shared mechanism, but if not, it suggests that they are at least partially separate. Sixteen participants estimated the hue or horizontal width of colored ellipses in two separate sessions. In each trial, an ellipse was presented for 500 ms after a pre-cue, and after a 1250 ms interval, participants adjusted a response probe to match the cued feature. The feature to be reproduced alternated between trials in a fixed pattern. To test the effect of attention on CTB, we manipulated the distributions of hue between the sessions. Stimulus hues in Hue trials were sampled from 160°–200° or 180°–220° in CIELAB space (L* = 55, C = 45) in both sessions, counterbalanced between participants. In Width trials, the distribution of hues was different between the two sessions: either 20° greener or bluer. Using a linear mixed-effects model for analysis, we did not replicate the role of feature-based attention on serial dependence in hue judgments.
