Instead, previous stimuli one and two trials back attracted current hue judgments regardless of whether hue was attended in the previous trials or not. We also found an attractive CTB independently of serial dependence. The center of CTB shifted away from the unattended stimulus distributions, demonstrating a repulsive attentional effect. In conclusion, feature-based attention differently affects serial dependence and CTB, suggesting that they may rely on at least partially distinct mechanisms.

title: Temporal evolution of idiosyncratic visual biases: heating up the visual system?
affiliations:
1. CNRS (FR)
2. Université Paris Cité (FR)
abstract: The perception of different families of visual stimuli has been shown to be governed by idiosyncratic biases. These biases are reliably different from one observer to the next, are generally conserved within each individual over time, but do undergo changes over time that are usually small and cumulative, demonstrating that the biases are measures of internal states of the visual system (Wexler, Duyck & Mamassian, 2015). But what causes the biases to change over time when they do so? Their temporal evolution could be driven by either external stimulation, or internal dynamics of the visual system. In order to distinguish between these two causes of temporal evolution, we performed an experiment in which we measured biases repeatedly, but varied the temporal intervals between the measurements, from 1 minute to 12 hours. We reasoned that, on one hand, if evolution of biases is driven by the perception of the underlying stimuli, the degree of change should be independent of the temporal interval between measurements if, on the other hand, temporal evolution is driven by internal dynamics of the visual system, changes in biases should be larger for longer temporal intervals between measurements. Interestingly, we found a result that contradicts both of these predictions: paradoxically, biases change more from one measurement to the next when measurements are performed at briefer intervals. This unexpected observation argues for a thermodynamic model in which repeated exposure to visual stimuli causes the visual system to go into a noisy or 'hot' state far from equilibrium, driving larger changes in biases. With longer intervals, the visual system cools down, returning to a more stable state.

title: A model of rhythmic attentional sampling of visual processing
affiliations:
1. Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Integrative Neuroscience and Cognition Center (FR)
2. Department of Psychology, New York University (US)
3. Center for Neural Science, New York University (US)
4. Institut Universitaire de France (FR)
abstract: Attention rhythmically samples visual information at low frequencies (<20 Hz), giving rise to periodic fluctuations in behavioral performance (VanRullen, 2016 Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2019 Kienitz, Schmid and Dugué, 2022). Despite accumulating empirical evidence, the circuit-level computations underlying these behavioral rhythms remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a computational model of rhythmic attentional sampling to explain and predict rhythmic perceptual outcomes. The model is grounded in the ORGaNICs framework –a class of biophysically-plausible recurrent neural circuits in which divisive normalization, a canonical computation describing how attentional allocation modulates visual cortex responses, emerges endogenously from the interplay between recurrent amplification and modulatory control (Heeger and Mackey, 2019). Crucially, the framework includes an input gain parameter that scales feedforward sensory drive, providing a candidate mechanism for attentional modulation. We exploit this by driving input gain rhythmically, instantiating periodic fluctuations in feedforward sensitivity. Applied to a population of spatially and orientation-tuned units, the model yielded phase-dependent fluctuations in detection sensitivity and closely fitted previous empirical evidence of rhythms in behavioral performance (Galas, Donovan and Dugué, 2025). Specifically, we captured two distinct modes of attentional sampling: sustained attention operating at the alpha frequency (~12 Hz) and exploratory attention rhythmically shifting between stimuli at the theta frequency (~6 Hz). Together, our work goes beyond previous empirical observations and provides a principled, circuit-level account of how rhythmic attentional modulation of recurrent sensory dynamics gives rise to structured fluctuations in perceptual sensitivity.

title: Atypical Development Disrupts the Perception-Action Dissociation: Evidence from Visual Illusions
affiliations: 1. York University (CA)
abstract: Visual illusions provide a powerful tool for probing the fundamental architecture of the visual system, particularly the well-established dissociation between vision-for-perception and vision-for-action. While adults typically show that actions like grasping are resistant to illusions that deceive perception, the developmental trajectory of this dissociation offers critical insights into how this functional specialization emerges. Our research demonstrates that this dissociation is evident in typically developing school-aged children, whose perceptual judgments are susceptible to the Ponzo illusion while their grasping movements remain accurately scaled to real-world object size. However, this foundational dissociation appears sensitive to developmental conditions, suggesting its emergence is not guaranteed. We explored this by testing two distinct pediatric populations. First, in children with amblyopia, a condition of atypical visual experience, we found a profoundly different pattern. Unlike their typically developing peers, these children were susceptible to the illusion in both their perceptual estimations and their grasping actions, suggesting that typical visual input is crucial for cementing the functional divide between the perception and action streams. Second, in autistic adults, we observed a convergent but distinct reduction in the perception-action dissociation. Autistic individuals showed susceptibility to both the Ponzo illusion and to the height-width illusion during grasping - contextual information that typically influences only perceptual judgments leaked into visuomotor computations. This pattern suggests that typical neurodevelopmental maturation, independent of visual experience per se, is equally critical for establishing functional specialization. Together, these findings illustrate that while the division of labor between perception and action pathways emerges early in typical development, it represents a fragile developmental outcome, contingent upon both the quality of visual experience and the integrity of neurodevelopmental maturation.
session_title: Symposium: Probing the Visual System: Illusions as Windows into Typical and Atypical Cognition

title: Altered Magnitude Matching Between Sensory modalities in Autism
affiliations: 1. University of Haifa (IL)
abstract: In a series of experiments, we examined whether sensory processing in autism reflects differences in both contextual calibration and experience-driven (statistical) sensory learning, and whether these processes operate in a modality-specific or amodal manner. Using a magnitude perception paradigm, autistic and non-autistic adults judged auditory and visual durations relative to the distribution of recently experienced stimuli, allowing us to assess how sensory evidence is calibrated by context across modalities. Across experiments, a consistent pattern emerged. Non-autistic participants showed modality-specific calibration, with stronger context effects within than between modalities, reflecting differentiated sensory coding. In contrast, autistic adults exhibited comparable context effects across modalities, alongside reduced sensory specialization, indicating a broader, more amodal integration of contextual information. To test whether this pattern reflected synesthetic cross-modal tendencies, we included a comparison group of adults with synesthesia. Synesthetes showed modality-specific calibration similar to non-autistic controls, ruling out synesthetic mechanisms as an explanation. Together, these findings demonstrate a converging pattern across calibration and sensory learning paradigms: sensory processing in autism is characterized by less differentiated, more amodal integration of contextual information, suggesting broader, less specialized sensory representations.
session_title: Symposium: Probing the Visual System: Illusions as Windows into Typical and Atypical Cognition

title: Ambiguous apparent motion perception in 5–7-year-old neurotypical children
affiliations: 1. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: In order to interact appropriately with our environment, we need to correctly interpret the motion of the objects within this environment. To do so, we need to connect the correct instances of these objects at different moments in time. This is not always an easy task, as the visual input can be highly ambiguous, for example when objects are occluded by other objects. To study how the visual system is able to solve this task, ambiguous apparent motion displays have been used in adults. In these displays participants can perceive different types of motion despite the visual input being identical. What motion is perceived depends on which objects have been connected across space and time, i.e., how object correspondence is solved. Research has shown that in adult vision the spatio-temporal relationship between objects as well as their features, e.g., their colour or shape, can influence the ambiguous apparent motion percept. Based on these findings different theories have been developed that suggest that object correspondence can happen at different levels of processing, at a lower-level spatio-temporal information has a large impact and at higher levels the influence of feature information is more important. The aim of the work presented here was to examine how children perceive ambiguous apparent motion and whether they use the same type of information to connect objects across space and time as adults do. We manipulated the ISI, colour and shape of the objects as well as the duration the display was presented and asked children between the age of 5 and 7 to report their motion percept. Our results showed that all factors influenced ambiguous apparent motion perception in children, but not in the same way as they do for adults, suggesting that correspondence might be solved predominantly at a lower-level in children.
session_title: Symposium: Probing the Visual System: Illusions as Windows into Typical and Atypical Cognition

title: Stress and visual illusions: Is there a relationship?
affiliations: 1. University of Trento (IT)
abstract: Stress is a pervasive condition in modern society, affecting individuals across both professional and personal contexts. Defined as the body’s response to perceived threats or challenges, it can be acute or chronic and has significant implications for mental and physical health. While extensive research has documented its adverse effects on cognitive functions such as memory, attention, and decision-making, far less is known about its influence on sensory processing—particularly visual perception. In this talk, I will present recent work examining how stress levels may modulate susceptibility to visual illusions. Using a computerized battery of 13 geometrical illusions in which participants performed an adjustment task, we quantified the degree to which each individual was deceived by the illusions. Negative emotional states were assessed using the self-report Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (DASS-21). In a subset of conditions, we attempted to manipulate stress level by presenting relaxing or unpleasant music during the task. Overall, our results revealed a positive relationship between stress and illusion susceptibility: individuals with higher stress levels showed greater vulnerability to visual illusions than those with lower stress levels. Additionally, some—but not all—illusions exhibited stronger effects under the unpleasant music condition. Taken together, these findings suggest that stress can shape visual perception, potentially biasing perceptual processing toward greater reliance on top-down expectations over bottom-up sensory input. They further indicate that stress may selectively modulate specific perceptual mechanisms rather than exerting a uniform influence across all illusions.
session_title: Symposium: Probing the Visual System: Illusions as Windows into Typical and Atypical Cognition

title: Learning Fast and Slow: towards a theory of perception
affiliations: 1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
abstract: How come, perceptual learning sometimes requires tens of thousands of trials to elicit tiny changes in sensitivity that barely generalise, while other times we can learn entirely new concepts from a single example? Why do some researchers in our field think perception is all about inferring parameters of physical reality, like distance, size or colour, while others focus on attention or eye movements as the central processes of making sense of sensory signals?  While these two questions might seem not to have very much in common, here, I will present the outline of a two-stage theory of perception (‘learning fast and slow’) that seeks to provide a unifying explanation of a wide range of phenomena.  The basic concept is that perception is structured around two core computations—disentanglement and selection—that have complementary computational demands and benefits. Disentanglement proceeds by slowly acquiring nonlinear transformations of raw sensory signals through massive quantities of passive observation (structured by unsupervised learning objectives), which discover latent causal structures “out there” that are responsible for sensory signals. Once acquired, such general-purpose representations enable perceptual constancy of world properties like shape, material or object identity, by rapid, largely feedforward discriminative inference. Selection, in contrast, operates “in context” with a particular behavioural goal in mind, to suppress task-irrelevant features, allowing zero-shot learning and heuristic deployment of resources in a largely top-down way. This involves computationally costly generative inference and is impacted more directly by action outcome (e.g., reward).  I will present some concrete examples of this framing of perception, and argue that it may also help us to understand how both heuristics and statistically optimal strategies make sense in perception and action.

title: Dissociable Visual and Non-Visual Semantic Coding in the Place Network Revealed by Language and Vision Models
affiliations: 1. University of Trento (IT)
abstract: Cognitive neuroscience has identified cortical regions that respond selectively to a broad range of object categories such as faces, places, body parts, tools, and animals. These regions respond strongly to visual images, but some also respond to words, and the perceptual/semantic nature of these representations is unclear. Here, we used fMRI-based Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) alongside computational models of vision (VGG-19) and language (OpenAI Large-3) to dissociate visuo-semantic and non-visual semantic contributions to word-driven responses across the place-selective network.   Participants (N=24) were presented with the names of 48 famous monuments. Representational spaces were derived from the pattern of activation produced by these monuments in the place-selective network: the parahippocampal place area (PPA), transverse occipital sulcus (TOS) and retrosplenial complex (RSC). These representational spaces were compared to computational representational spaces derived from a) a language model based on non-visual descriptions and b) a visual-feature based model constructed by averaging activations from the penultimate layer of VGG-19 across ten typical images per monument. Key analyses focussing on the independent contribution of visual and non-visual semantic models revealed different patterns across regions (region x model interaction: p=.007). Non-visual semantic information was represented strongly in RSC (p<.001) and TOS (p=.003), but not in PPA (p=.58). Conversely, for the visual model, visuo-semantic representations were present in PPA (p=.005) but not in RSC (p=.067) or TOS (p=.162).  This pattern of results indicates that, even in the absence of visual images, information about the visual properties of specific monuments is preferentially represented in ventral PPA, whereas non-visual semantic information is represented in RSC and TOS.  This functional dissociation within the place-selective network provides insights into the nature of visual and semantic representations within category selective regions, as well as functional specialisation across elements of category selective networks.

title: Deep Neural Networks Initially Align with Biological Vision but Quickly Part Ways
affiliations:
1. Universiteit van Amsterdam (NL)
2. Radboud University (NL)
abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) have become the dominant computational model of biological vision, yet it is well known that they classify objects primarily by texture while humans rely on shape. This fundamental divergence in strategy coexists with strong brain-network correspondence — a paradox that raises questions about what such correspondence actually reflects. Here we compare developing networks with developed human vision: we track DCNNs across training, sampling checkpoints densely during early epochs and more sparsely thereafter, evaluating alignment with adult human fMRI, adult human EEG, and adult macaque electrophysiology at each developmental snapshot. Brain alignment is largely established within the first four epochs, when classification accuracy remains below 15%. During this brief window, networks acquire sensitivity to low-frequency, shape-based structure: the coarse visual statistics that any system processing natural images must encode, regardless of task. These findings suggest that the correspondence between artificial and biological vision reflects their shared visual environment (the universal structure of natural images that both systems must represent) but not the convergence on how they recognise objects. The rapid divergence after early training, as networks develop texture-based classification strategies that humans do not employ, demonstrates that DCNNs ultimately solve object recognition in a fundamentally different way than human vision, despite their early alignment with biological representations.

title: Steerable autoencoders underlying remapping, spatiotopy, and visual stability
affiliations:
1. Glendon College (CA)
2. Dartmouth College (US)
3. NYU Abu Dhabi (AE)
4. Western University (CA)
5. Vector Institute for Artificial Intelligence (CA)
abstract: Whenever the eyes move, the locations of attended targets must be updated to keep track of them despite their shift on the retina, a process called remapping. Here we show that each attended target’s identity can be connected to the locations of its features in early visual cortex through a steerable autoencoder network. The network is trained to appropriately shift the feature activity to the target’s new location with each saccade. The model is a type of autoencoder architecture that takes an input pattern, here from early retinotopic cortex, passes it through several layers of encoding to generate a high-level, low-dimensional representation that corresponds to the object areas of visual cortex. The model receives and integrates the upcoming saccadic movement information in this layer. This then returns through decoding layers to produce an updated output pattern, again in early visual cortex. Autoencoders have been used to model object-based attention, to predict the subsequent images when targets are moving, and here to predict upcoming target locations when the eyes move – based on distributed information about eye position (gain fields). This autoencoder process is part of the overall architecture of the visual system, acting to link target properties together, even as the target or the eyes move.

title: A Neural Model of Lightness and Color Assimilation
affiliations: 1. University of Nevada (US)
abstract: In the phenomena of lightness and color assimilation, the appearance of one region of a visual image undergoes a shift in value or hue in the direction of that of a surrounding or neighboring region. Well known examples are the Bezold-Brucke effect and Helson assimilation. Here, I show that these effects depend on edge integration—a process by which the appearance of a region is computed from a sum of color induction effects from edges—and I propose a neural model of assimilation based on edge encoding by On-center/Off-surround, Off-center/On-surround, and four types of double-opponent color neurons, followed by filling-in of surface color from edges. In support of this model, I describe a psychophysical experiment in which a visual stimulus comprising an achromatic disk surrounded by an achromatic annulus is presented against a background field whose color is varied from cyan to magenta along the LM axis of a physiological MB/DKL color space. This background variation changes the color contrast at the outer annulus border, and this contrast change, in turn, induces a change in the hue of the disk. Importantly, when the direction of the color contrast of the outer annulus border reverses as the background chromaticity passes through the achromatic point, the magnitude of the hue induction in the disk also changes. This result mirrors a previous finding that the strength of lightness induction from a remote border depends on the luminance polarity of that border (Rudd, J. Vision, 2010). The polarity-dependence of the strengths of lightness and color induction are difficult to explain with low-level filtering models, but are consistent with the hypothesis that surface appearance is computed from edges encoded by half-wave rectified neurons such as the ones proposed in the model, followed by a neural color filling-in mechanism that performs edge integration.

title: Inferring Visual Properties by Predicting Future Video Frames
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior (DE)
3. Excellence Cluster “The Adaptive Mind”, Universities of Marburg, Giessen and TU Darmstadt (DE)
4. University of Auckland (NZ)
abstract: We investigated whether training a neural network to predict the future states of visual input could cause it to learn to infer world properties. We created 20,000 videos of objects rotating or translating under various lighting conditions. Each object had either a mirror-like reflective surface or was matte with one of 10 different surface patterns. We then trained an unsupervised recurrent neural network (PredRNN-v2) to predict the future frames of each video. After training, we analyzed the model’s latent representations for multiple factors (material, motion, illumination, and surface pattern) across three network layers and memory states (C, H, and M) by using linear decoding, feature-level selectivity metrics, and lesioning analyses. We found that the scene properties could be robustly decoded from the latent space representations across layers and memory states, indicating that the model developed a rich representation of environmental structure without supervision. The representations were generally distributed across many feature maps however, there were subsets of feature maps that showed selectivity for specific visual properties. Importantly, lesioning those units led to a significant drop in property decoding compared to lesioning randomly-selected feature maps, indicating the functional relevance of those features. Taken together, the results suggest that artificial networks that learn to predict the next visual input implicitly learn representations that partially tease apart object and scene properties. These representations also capture properties that are relevant for material perception in dynamic environments. This computational framework can shed light on how the brain learns underlying world properties from complex visual environments.

title: Oculomotor contribution to synchronization of cortical activity
affiliations:
1. Department of Neurosciences, Psychology, Drug Research and Child Health, University of Florence (IT)
2. Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, University of Rochester (US)
3. Center for Visual Science, University of Rochester (US)
4. Feil Family Brain and Mind Research Institute, Weill Cornell Medical College (US)
abstract: Humans actively shape their visual input through incessant eye movements. While rapid (micro-)saccades redirect the fovea toward objects of interest, slower fixational drifts continuously displace the retinal image even during attempted fixation. Traditionally considered disruptive, these oculomotor-induced luminance modulations are increasingly recognized as functional, contributing to the spatiotemporal reformatting of visual input and potentially enhancing visual encoding by helping form spatial representations.  Recent work has shown that saccades redistribute the spectral content of natural scenes, “whitening” spatial frequencies below a velocity-dependent cutoff and reducing input redundancy. Notably, the bandwidth of this whitening effect decreases with increasing saccade amplitude. To investigate the cortical correlates of this reformatting, we combined EEG and eye tracking while participants executed saccades of varying amplitudes across narrow-band noise fields at different spatial frequencies. The EEG fixation-related potential (lambda-wave) over occipital sites followed the predictions of the whitening hypothesis: its amplitude varied with stimulus spatial frequency for small saccades, but became invariant for larger ones, consistent with amplitude-dependent spectral equalization. Beyond this retinal effect, we observed that the lambda-wave amplitude was modulated by a signal proportional to saccade size, indicating an interaction between sensory reformatting and a motor-related component. In a second experiment, we further examined the role of fixational drifts by combining EEG, eye tracking, and gaze-contingent retinal stabilization. Participants fixated a grating flickering over time, either under natural viewing or retinal stabilization that eliminated drift-induced retinal motion. Although stabilization concentrated stimulus temporal power at the modulation frequency, it reduced the amplitude of the evoked steady-state visual potential, compared to natural viewing. Together, these findings show that self-generated retinal transients are a fundamental feature of vision, shaping early visual processing and likely serving as signals that the visual system actively exploits to optimize visual encoding.
session_title: Symposium: Vision on the Move: From Eye Movements to Visual Encoding (and back)

title: From monocular input to binocular action: How pre-saccadic motion shapes post-saccadic following
affiliations: 1. Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (DE)
abstract: The active visual system integrates pre-saccadic visual information to guide post-saccadic action. A key marker of this is the post-saccadic following response (PFR) – a short-latency drift of gaze in the direction of perceived motion immediately after saccade landing. Here, we tested whether PFR strength depends on monocular versus binocular motion input, using the physiological blind spot as a manipulation of monocular visibility. We first localized each participant’s blind spot in both eyes. Participants then made centrally cued saccades to peripheral apertures containing random dot motion tangential to the saccade direction. Stimuli were presented either binocularly or such that motion was visible to only one eye (falling within the blind spot of the other). Motion either remained visible after saccade landing or was removed during the saccade, isolating the contribution of pre-saccadic information. We observed a robust PFR that persisted when motion was removed mid-saccade, confirming its reliance on pre-saccadic information. Critically, PFR gain was reduced under monocular viewing. Moreover, we observed a brief interocular asymmetry in the early post-saccadic interval: the eye that received pre-saccadic motion input showed a stronger initial drift than the other eye – indicating that, at least briefly, post-saccadic motor output may not be fully yoked across the eyes. These findings point to eye-specific contributions to post-saccadic motor output and indicate that early post-saccadic drift can be modulated independently in each eye. This challenges the assumption that smooth drift responses (like the PFR) are strictly binocular at the motor level and suggests that pre-saccadic motion exerts eye-specific influence on motor output weighted by binocular reliability. This raises the possibility that early post-saccadic drift provides a valuable window into how the brain transitions from monocular input to binocular action – and that this transition may not be instantaneous.
session_title: Symposium: Vision on the Move: From Eye Movements to Visual Encoding (and back)

title: Feedback and feedforward contributions to perceptual stability during self-motion
affiliations: 1. Heinrich Heine Univeristy (DE)
abstract: Active vision requires the brain to maintain coherent perceptual estimates despite continual self-induced changes in retinal input. This implies that visual encoding is not purely feedforward, but is shaped by the integration of sensory evidence with efference-copy–based predictions generated by internal forward models. A key contribution will examine how these predictions support perceptual continuity and produce history-dependent biases, and how their impact depends on the degree of voluntary control over visual sampling. By manipulating prediction precision and sensory uncertainty across complementary paradigms, the work will quantify effects on perceptual stability and serial dependencies. Extending these measurements to atypical visual behavior will test whether observed differences arise from altered predictive signals, altered sensory encoding, or differences in how prediction and evidence are combined.
session_title: Symposium: Vision on the Move: From Eye Movements to Visual Encoding (and back)

title: Temporal dynamics of visual processing during the course of fixation
affiliations:
1. Vision and Control of Action Group, Department of Cognition, Development and Psychology of Education, Institute of Neurosciences, Universitat de Barcelona (ES)
2. Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, University of Rochester (US)
3. Department of Neuroscience, University of Rochester (US)
4. Center for Visual Science, University of Rochester (US)
abstract: During natural scene inspection, vision unfolds through sequences of saccades and brief fixation periods. Although information is processed across the visual field during fixation, the temporal evolution of this processing and the interplay between foveal and extrafoveal processing remain incompletely characterized. We first investigated whether the time course of change localization during fixation differs across regions of the visual field. Participants made a saccade toward a fixation point surrounded by four bars that could be located either all in the fovea (0.3º of eccentricity), all in the periphery (9º of eccentricity), or two in the fovea and two in the periphery. Upon saccade landing, one of the stimuli briefly changed its orientation, and at the end of the trial participants reported the location of the moving stimulus. While foveal change localization remained relatively stable throughout fixation, at 9º performance markedly improved over time. When foveal and peripheral stimuli were monitored simultaneously, a similar pattern emerged: peripheral performance showed a pronounced recovery during fixation, whereas foveal performance remained stable. To determine if this temporal modulation follows a graded, eccentricity-dependent profile, in a second study stimuli were presented at different eccentricities (0.3º, 2º, 6º, 15º), either in isolation or split across two eccentricities. Performance improved over time during the course of fixation, with larger improvements at greater eccentricities. When two eccentricities were monitored simultaneously, early fixation performance favored stimuli closer to the center of gaze, but peripheral performance rapidly recovered, following a time course comparable to when tested alone. Together, these findings reveal that fixation is not a static processing window but a dynamic period in which visual processing recovers following saccades in a graded, eccentricity-dependent manner. Peripheral processing appears to incur an early post-saccadic cost that is progressively compensated during fixation, highlighting fundamental spatiotemporal constraints in active vision.
session_title: Symposium: Vision on the Move: From Eye Movements to Visual Encoding (and back)

title: Heterochromatic brightness adapts to display channel balance
affiliations:
1. Shanghai University of Sport (CN)
2. Giessen University (DE)
abstract: Electronic displays are ubiquitous, yet consumer monitors differ substantially in the relative gains of their red, green, and blue primaries. It remains unclear whether heterochromatic brightness simply reflects these device differences, or whether the visual system adapts to the prevailing channel balance. We tested this question in three experiments using a brightness-ranking task. In Experiment 1 (N=12), observers viewed stimuli on a calibrated monitor while the green channel was scaled relative to red and blue at three levels. In Experiment 2 (N=122), we repeated the same manipulation online across observers’ own displays. In both experiments, brightness judgments shifted systematically with the imposed imbalance. As green gain increased, observers behaved as if green contributed less to brightness, in the direction opposing the physical manipulation, consistent with compensatory adjustment. Time-course analysis showed that this effect was absent initially but built up over the course of a block, suggesting adaptation over several minutes. To test whether this display-dependent effect extends across contexts, Experiment 3 measured observers’ brightness judgments in the laboratory on a common monitor and independently characterized their own displays. Observers using displays with relatively stronger red primaries later assigned lower relative brightness to red on the common monitor, whereas no corresponding effect was observed for green or blue. Together, these findings show that heterochromatic brightness is not a fixed readout of stimulus specification, but adjusts to display channel balance.

title: Timing is key: N1 latency variation as a neural marker of chromatic sensitivity
affiliations:
1. Newcastle University (UK)
2. University of Edinburgh (UK)
abstract: While individual differences in chromatic sensitivity are robustly captured by psychophysical measures, their relationship to individual differences in neural measures is less well understood. Such relationships are important for investigating possible compensatory mechanisms in colour vision deficiency (CVD). The N1 is a well-established VEP component associated with chromatic processing, but it remains unclear whether its shape and temporal characteristics reflect interindividual variability in chromatic sensitivity. Here we examine the relationship between psychophysical chromatic sensitivity thresholds and N1 amplitude and latency in a large sample of normal trichromats (NT) and individuals with CVD. 39 participants (20 NT, 19 CVD) completed various colour vision assessments, including the Colour Assessment and Diagnosis (CAD), to measure sensitivity thresholds for L-M and S-(L+M) axes. In a separate electroencephalography (EEG) task, participants viewed Gabor patches at four contrast levels in each direction of these chromatic axes. Each condition comprised 65 stimulus presentations (300 ms stimulus duration, 1000–1200 ms interstimulus interval), during which participants responded to rare vertical Gabors as an attentional control. VEPs were derived by averaging EEG responses to horizontal Gabors at occipital electrodes (Oz, O1, O2). Linear regression functions were fitted to the four amplitude and latency values for each chromatic direction for each participant. The slope of N1 latency, but not amplitude, as a function of contrast differed significantly between NT and CVD. Furthermore, latency slopes, but not amplitude slopes were positively correlated with CAD thresholds along the L–M axis across all participants. Individual N1 amplitude slopes exhibited correlations between chromatic directions, suggesting that interindividual variability in amplitude is probably driven by individual EEG acquisition factors, e.g. scalp impedance. These findings highlight the need for caution when interpreting interindividual variability in N1 amplitude, while supporting the use of N1 latency as a neural marker of chromatic sensitivity.

title: Journey into colour naming space: From 2D cone contrasts to 3D categories
affiliations: 1. Newcastle University (UK)
abstract: One person’s blue might be another’s green, or even white. Individual variation in colour naming occurs within all colour vision types, masking differences between individuals with colour vision deficiency (CVD) and normal trichromats (NT). Indeed, dichromats may deploy a similar range of colour terms to normal trichromats (Broackes 2010 Moreira et al. 2013), beyond the predicted hues “blue” and “yellow” of their cone-contrast spaces. Here we construct individual colour naming spaces that capture and quantify variations within and between colour vision (CV) types. As previously described (Hurlbert et al., ECVP 2025), colour naming was assessed with a forced-choice task. Participants (83 NT 18 anomalous trichromats 14 dichromats) selected the single best name of 11 basic colour terms (black, white, red, green, yellow, blue, brown, orange, pink, purple, gray) for each of 371 distinct colour samples successively presented against a large neutral background on a calibrated LCD monitor. Stimulus colours spanned 40 Munsell hues, 8 Chroma levels and 9 Values. For each participant, for each basic colour term, the convex hull enclosing all coordinates (in CIELAB or colour vision type-tailored cone-contrast space) named with that term was computed. The set of 11 convex hulls formed the individual participant’s colour naming space. For a given CV group, the average colour naming space was computed by averaging the individual convex hulls per category over the group.  An individual’s naming concordance with a given group was calculated from the intersection between the individual’s and the group average’s category convex hulls.  Colour category concordances with the NT group, computed in the 3D normal trichromat space (CIELAB), varied across basic colour terms for both normal trichromats and CVD individuals, and were significantly correlated between all CV groups. In particular, the colour naming space for dichromats exhibited 3D structure that was not explained by 2D cone-contrast coordinates.

title: Colour representations in the ventral visual pathway
affiliations: 1. Univeristy of Sussex (UK)
abstract: Colour information in natural scenes is highly correlated with other low and high level visual attributes such as entropy, fractal dimension, the presence of particular spatial features, and object and scene categories. If the visual system is sensitive to these reliable contingencies in inputs, intermediate and high-level colour representations in the brain may be in conjunction with spatial image attributes. We present recent work from our lab that has used neuroimaging to investigate joint colour-spatial representations in anterior visual areas. Using the Natural Scenes fMRI dataset we have used correlations between colour and other image properties to reveal functional distinctions in stimulus-provoked brain responses. We found that colour-biased regions in the ventral visual pathway are food-selective – now termed the ‘ventral food streams’. Since colour is a particularly reliable attribute of food (e.g., foodstuffs are often canonically coloured), we conducted several experiments using EEG and fMRI to attempt to isolate the colour tuning of joint colour-spatial representations in anterior visual areas. We describe the results of these studies, which have so far produced tuning functions which are quite noisy and variable. We discuss possible next steps in research to better isolate jointly tuned colour-spatial visual mechanisms.

title: Decoding Illusory Colour from Training on Colorimetric Colour: Evidence for Shared Neural Signals Around 300 ms
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: A central unresolved question is whether the brain represents illusory colour using the same neural code as physical colour, and at what time any such shared representation emerges. The present study addressed this question using EEG and MVPA. Participants viewed a modified Lotto and Purves cube illusion in which a central grey patch appeared yellow under a blue illuminant and blue under a yellow illuminant, embedded in a larger contextual cube. We successfully decoded illusory colour from occipital activity, with reliable evidence emerging around ~300ms after stimulus onset (BF >10). Importantly, decoding peaks aligned in time with those obtained for colourimetric colour stimuli. To test whether this effect depends on luminance information, we also included an isoluminant condition in which only chromatic information was available. In this case, decoding of illusory colour was weaker, with only modest Bayesian evidence (BF>3), suggesting that colour-only signals are sufficient to carry some but not strong information about the illusion, and that luminance contributes substantially to the full effect. In a grayscale condition, where only lightness variation was present, decoding was still possible (BF>10) but emerged much earlier, around ~100ms, consistent with previous research suggesting early processing of lightness constancy (MacEvoy, & Paradiso, 2001). Finally, a simultaneous contrast condition, in which the patch was presented on a uniform background defined by the mean scene chromaticity, produced a temporal profile closely resembling the full Purves condition, again with decoding emerging around ~300ms (BF>10). Together, our results suggest that colour constancy mechanisms can give rise to neural representations that closely resemble those evoked by physically defined colour, emerging relatively late. However, the comparable profile with simultaneous contrast suggests that decoding may not capture scene interpretation-related colour constancy mechanisms. The results argue that cross-decoding between physical and illusory conditions can be supported by non-chromatic scene features.

title: A Behavioural Task to Measure Cone-Opponent Mechanisms
affiliations: 1. University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: Colour opponency is a fundamental property of the human and many animal visual systems. Textbooks have long assumed that afterimages are colour-opponent and can be used to demonstrate this function. However, this idea has recently been refuted (Witzel, Communications Psychology, 2025), raising the question of how colour opponency can be demonstrated and investigated in a straightforward behavioural task. We introduce opponent flicker fusion to directly probe cone-opponency. This new technique leverages the perceptual mixture of alternating colours at high temporal frequencies (heterochromatic flicker fusion). Opponent colours produce an achromatic percept when mixed therefore, when such colours are alternated at high temporal frequency, they yield neutral grey. Opponent flicker fusion measures opponent colour pairs that produce grey by allowing observers to adjust the hue and saturation of one of two flickering colours until the flicker disappears against the isoluminant grey background. In one experiment, we sampled the fixed reference colour along an isoluminant hue circle in cone-opponent DKL space. As predicted, colours adjusted by observers to neutralise the referents corresponded to the cone-opponent colours along the hue circle. In a second experiment, adjusted colours were also cone-opponent when referent colours were sampled non-uniformly in cone-opponent space, thus excluding potential artifacts of the sampling method. A third experiment showed that opponent flicker fusion also worked with a temporal frequency below luminance flicker fusion (15Hz) after luminance flicker is neutralised through additional luminance adjustments. These results show that opponent flicker fusion allows probing the postreceptoral, second stage of colour processing because the separation between luminance and chromatic channels does not exist in the photoreceptors.   Opponent flicker fusion contrasts with the triangular distribution of afterimage colours that reflect cone adaptation at the first stage of colour processing. Together, afterimages and opponent flicker fusion provide behavioural tools to probe the physiological stages of colour processing.

title: Super-recognisers spontaneously and preferentially process face identity: Evidence from implicit experimental paradigms
affiliations:
1. The MARCS Institute for Brain, Behaviour, and Development, Western Sydney University (AU)
2. School of Psychology, University of New South Wales (AU)
3. School of Computer, Data and Mathematical Sciences, Western Sydney University (AU)
4. School of Psychology, Western Sydney University (AU)
abstract: Exceptional face recognition abilities are typically identified and studied via behavioural tasks that explicitly instruct observers to attend to face identity. Consequently, relatively little is known about how individual differences in face identity processing manifest under implicit task conditions (i.e., in the absence of explicit instructions to monitor identity). We address this outstanding question by exploring how super-recognisers—individuals with exceptional face identity processing abilities—differed from control participants on two implicit paradigms. In Experiment 1, 36 super-recognisers and 92 controls completed an “odd-one-out” task in which they selected which of three faces they found most visually distinct on each trial. Within each triplet, each face was a unique outlier in either valence, viewpoint, or identity, enabling participant’s selection to reveal which dimension they perceived as most salient. Although both participant groups tended to endorse identity as more salient than either valence or viewpoint, super-recognisers endorsed identity more than controls. In Experiment 2, 31 super-recognisers and 66 control participants completed a same/different expression matching task based upon a Garner Interference paradigm, where two sequentially presented faces could be either the same or different identities. We found that task-irrelevant identity changes detrimentally impacted expression-matching in both groups, but had a greater impact on Super-Recognisers’ performance. Additionally, across both experiments, our implicit indices of identity processing correlated with established face recognition test scores (e.g., CFMT+). Taken together, these results suggest that exceptional face recognition abilities are characterised not only by superior face memory or matching under explicit task conditions, but also by a tendency to spontaneously prioritise identity over other face dimensions. This prioritisation of identity occurs even when identity is task-irrelevant.

title: Human face categorization: Neural evidence for meridian asymmetries.
affiliations:
1. UCLouvain (BE)
2. Université de Lorraine (FR)
abstract: At the fovea, face identity recognition preferentially relies on horizontally-oriented face information. Since radially oriented input is privileged in the periphery, along the horizontal meridian (HM) the engagement of face-selective mechanisms is enhanced. We previously showed that subject-level radial bias predicts the speed of saccadic eye movements toward faces. Here, we investigated whether this functional link is due to basic-level face categorization in the periphery being shaped by the radial bias.  Thirty-two participants were tested using Fast Periodic Visual Stimulation (FPVS) combined with EEG. Face images were periodically embedded at 1.2 Hz within rapid streams of non-face objects presented at 6 Hz. This frequency-tagging approach allows face categorization responses to be objectively isolated at predefined frequencies with high signal-to-noise ratio. It enables dissociating high-level categorization responses to faces (1.2 Hz, i.e. face oddball frequency) from general visual responses to stimulus sequences (6 Hz, i.e. base frequency). Stimuli were presented at four peripheral locations (left, right, up, down). Neural response to face oddball frequency  was localized on occipitotemporal electrodes with a significant right lateralization. This neural marker of face categorization was strongest along the horizontal meridian. It was also stronger in the upper than in the lower visual field in line with past evidence. In contrast, the general visual response at 6 Hz was maximal in the lower visual field, consistent with known low-level visual anisotropies. Together, these results indicate a clear distinction in visual field anisotropy between high-level face categorization responses and low-level visual reponses. Basic-level face categorization in the periphery is most robust along the horizontal meridian, likely reflecting enhanced access to diagnostic horizontal information. These findings indicate that radial bias selectively modulates horizontal–vertical meridian anisotropies at high-level, category-selective stages of visual processing, following a pattern that is qualitatively distinct from low-level visual responses.

title: Impaired face identity recognition in horizontally compressed identities
affiliations: 1. Universite de Lorraine (FR)
abstract: Human face identity recognition (FIR) is a fundamental social ability driven by specialized neural pathways. While earlier behavioral studies suggested that FIR is surprisingly resistant to horizontal image compression—implying that spatial configurations may be secondary to recognition—those conclusions were largely based on accuracy rates for familiar faces during long response intervals. To provide a more objective assessment, we utilized electroencephalography (EEG) to track implicit neural markers in twenty-one participants as they viewed unfamiliar faces at five varying compression levels (0% to 90%). Although robust recognition signals were recorded over the occipito-temporal cortex at low levels of distortion (0–22%), these responses progressively diminished as compression increased, reaching near-total suppression at 90%. These results indicate that, unlike artificial intelligence models that adapt efficiently to linear transformations, the human visual system is significantly hindered by geometric distortion, providing evidence that spatial cues are indeed vital for identity recognition.

title: Fine-grained face race categorization shifts after virtual race embodiment
affiliations:
1. University of Fribourg (CH)
2. University of Nairobi (KE)
3. Waseda University (JP)
abstract: Social identity fundamentally shapes human interactions. Yet, its specific impact on visual processes remains poorly understood. A well-documented phenomenon is the Other-Race Categorization Advantage (ORCA), whereby individuals categorize other-race faces more efficiently than same-race faces. However, whether this effect is driven by perceptual expertise, social group affiliation, or an interaction between the two remains unclear. To address this question, we used a novel and promising methodological tool: Virtual Reality (VR). A large cross-cultural sample (N > 250) from Kenya, Japan, and Switzerland was embodied in avatars that either matched or differed from the participants’ natural race group. To enhance the illusion of virtual body ownership, participants completed three interactive tasks with visuotactile and visuomotor feedback. Race categorization performance was assessed pre- and post-embodiment using both race-prototypical and a continuum of race-morphed stimuli. The results revealed that embodiment did not modulate the ORCA, suggesting that rapid categorical processing of prototypical face race is robust to short-term changes in social identity. Conversely, embodiment reliably impacted the categorization of ambiguous race-morphed faces. Participants embodied in an other-race avatar were more likely to categorize ambiguous faces as belonging to their natural race group. These findings suggest that transient shifts in social identity selectively recalibrate fine-grained visual race boundaries without affecting robust categorization by race of prototypical faces. This study also highlights the value of VR embodiment as a tool for manipulating social identity and opens new avenues for investigating the interplay between group membership and visual processing, with potential implications for interventions targeting biases in face processing.

title: What makes a face difficult to remember?
affiliations:
1. University of Copenhagen (DK)
2. Aalborg University (DK)
abstract: Individuals vary in their ability to learn, recollect and recognize facial identity. However, face memory variability related to difficulty of the stimuli themselves is rarely considered. The aim of this study was twofold: (1) to investigate whether a gradient of trial difficulty exists on one of the most commonly used tests of unfamiliar face memory and (2) to relate this potential difficulty gradient to the performance of a deep learning model in order to identify a structuring principle for face stimuli difficulty. We tested 599 adult UK participants online with the Cambridge Face Memory Test (CFMT Duchaine & Nakayama (2006)), in which participants must learn the identity of six novel identities (Phase 1), recognize them among distractors (Phase 2) and finally recognize them under degraded conditions (Phase 3). In order to determine if a difficulty gradient for the 54 recognition trials (Phase 2 and 3) exists, we fit trial-level responses to a two-parameter Item Response Model (Lord, 1980). Then, we investigated whether this difficulty gradient corresponded with trial-by-trial performance in a deep learning model for face recognition (FaceNet, Schroff et al. (2015)), by correlating the IRT-derived trial difficulty parameters with the mean Euclidean distance between 128-dimensional vector embeddings of the target and distractor faces on each trial. We found substantial variability in difficulty across the 54 CFMT recognition trials (difficulty parameters ranging from -2.31 to 0.91), indicating that the CFMT trials form a graded continuum of recognizability. Further, this difficulty gradient correlated significantly (r = -.37, p = .006) with the mean Euclidean target-distractor embedding distance. These results suggest that the established gradient of face stimuli difficulty is statistically related to recognition based on deep learning. On that basis, deep learning models may inform the calibration of difficulty of new experimental paradigms and clinical assessments of face recognition ability.

title: Generalisation of Familiarity‑Related Neural Patterns to Emotional Facial Expressions
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: While emotional expressions are theorised to modulate face familiarity, their shared neural dynamics remain unclear. In this secondary analysis of openly available EEG data, we used cross-dataset multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to test whether neural representations of familiarity generalise across emotional expressions. Data was drawn from two previously published experiments: an emotion categorisation task, in which 24 participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice task on facial expressions (happy, angry, sad, neutral 384 trials), and a familiarity task, in which 22 participants viewed personally familiar and unfamiliar faces (100 trial-unique images) alongside an orthogonal attention task. Classifiers trained to distinguish familiar versus unfamiliar faces were cross-applied to emotional expression data, and vice versa, using re-labelling strategies (e.g., angry = familiar, neutral = unfamiliar). This approach enabled assessment of shared representational structure independent of task demands. Results showed that angry expressions aligned most strongly with familiarity-related neural patterns, with sustained cross-classification accuracy emerging from approximately 200 ms post-stimulus and peaking over posterior electrodes (Cohen’s d = 1.35). Happy and sad expressions exhibited weaker and more transient associations within the 200-400 ms window, while neutral expressions consistently aligned with neural signatures of unfamiliarity. These findings support behavioural accounts of threat prioritisation, suggesting that threat-related facial expressions recruit neural representations that overlap with familiarity processing. Overall, the results provide evidence for partially overlapping neural mechanisms underlying affective evaluation and identity processing in face perception.

title: Seeing without saying: ERP signatures of visual awareness beyond report
affiliations:
1. University of Verona (IT)
2. Istituto per le Applicazioni del Calcolo "M. Picone" Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche (IT)
abstract: A major challenge in the search for the neural correlates of consciousness is distinguishing electrophysiological signatures of perceptual awareness from activity related to report, decision-making, and other post-perceptual processes. No-report paradigms provide a critical tool for minimizing these confounds and identifying neural signals that more directly track conscious visual experience. In Experiment 1, we recorded EEG while participants viewed Mooney images, taking advantage of their disambiguation effect: initially ambiguous two-tone stimuli become readily recognizable after presentation of the corresponding original image. This design allowed us to compare unaware and aware perceptual phases under both report and no-report conditions. Behavioral results confirmed a reliable perceptual transition, with recognition and naming accuracy increasing from the unaware to the aware phase. ERP analyses focused on the Visual Awareness Negativity (VAN) and the Late Positivity (LP). A robust VAN emerged in the contrast between aware and unaware trials, regardless of report demands. By contrast, the LP was strongly attenuated in the no-report condition, suggesting that this later effect is shaped largely by post-perceptual demands rather than by awareness itself. Building on Experiment 1, which dissociated awareness-related activity from report demands, Experiment 2 tested whether this activity also tracks the psychometric dynamics of perceptual emergence. To do so, we parametrically manipulated stimulus recognizability by gradually increasing the grayscale contribution to Mooney images across alpha levels. Preliminary results indicate that awareness-related ERP activity scales as a logistic function of alpha level, mirroring the psychometric profile of perceptual recognition rather than reflecting simple linear changes in physical input. Together, these findings support the VAN as a strong candidate neural marker of visual awareness and show that combining no-report paradigms with parametric manipulations of recognizability provides a powerful approach for isolating neural activity genuinely linked to conscious perception.
session_title: Visual Illusions, Hallucinations, and Visual Awareness

title: People with more vivid visual imaginations are more likely to perceive illusory faces in objects
affiliations: 1. The University of Queensland (AU)
abstract: Differences in the vividness of visual imagery provide a window into how internally generated signals shape conscious perception. One unanswered question is the degree to which the vividness of visual imaginations can alter our perceptual experiences of the world. Here, we tested whether individual variation in imagery vividness predicts susceptibility to face pareidolia, an illusion in which faces are falsely perceived in inanimate objects.  Participants rated how face-like images of objects appeared and completed a standard measure of imagery vividness. Imagery vividness did not predict face-likeness ratings for canonical pareidolia images that strongly signal the presence of a face. However, imagery vividness positively predicted the tendency to report faces in non-face objects. These findings indicate that more vivid visualisers are more likely to impose face structure on ambiguous sensory input, consistent with stronger top-down influences on perception. Together, the results suggest that individual differences in imagination shape how strongly prior expectations bias perceptual decisions under uncertainty.
session_title: Visual Illusions, Hallucinations, and Visual Awareness

title: Remapping of metric spatial vision by orientation-specific adaptation
affiliations:
1. University of Nottingham (UK)
2. City St Georges, University of London (UK)
3. Cardiff University (UK)
abstract: Visual adaptation provides a powerful tool for probing the mechanisms underlying metric spatial perception.  Following adaptation to dynamic spatial patterns, pairs of dots placed in adapted visual field locations appear closer together than identical pairs presented in unadapted locations, indicating a compression of perceived space. Here we examine how adaptation to oriented patterns modulates this effect to investigate the involvement of cortical mechanisms. We report that spatial compression is anisotropic and, surprisingly, greater for dot dipoles aligned with a sine grating spatial frequency sweep adaptor than for dipoles aligned with the luminance gradient. For contrast reversing grating adaptors, compression asymmetry was greatest for low spatial frequency gratings (at 6 Hz) and decreased with spatial frequency up to 8 c/deg, at which point compression was isotropic. For a 3 c/deg grating, compression asymmetry was largely invariant as a function of temporal frequency, whereas compression magnitude decreased with temporal frequency. Compression asymmetry was still present for 60Hz (imperceptible) grating adaptors. The orientation dependence of the effect implicates cortical processing, while its persistence at high temporal frequences suggests adaptation within early visual cortex, likely involving magnocellular inputs to layer 4Cb of V1. We account for these findings using a gain field framework. Specifically, we propose that a global, extrastriate gain field is constructed by spatial aggregation of local V1 responses. The gain field transforms location by means of a ramp weighting function which scales the physical separations and implements a spatial metric mapping physical space onto perceptual space. Adaptation-induced changes in gain produce directional distortions of this metric, leading to corresponding changes in perceived separation and size.
session_title: Visual Illusions, Hallucinations, and Visual Awareness

title: Pupillary Signatures of Lightness After Scene Decomposition
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Visual illusions are widely used to investigate perceptual mechanisms. A prominent example is the lightness display introduced by Anderson and Winawer (2005): central disks are embedded in cloud-like regions that can be interpreted as occluding layers, producing systematic differences in lightness matches. This has been taken as evidence that the visual system infers reflectance through scene decomposition, effectively separating it from illumination and atmospheric conditions. However, such effects may reflect cognitive interpretation and response biases rather than perceptual inference. Observers may recognise the clouds as a separate surface and ignore them for their lightness matches, rather than experiencing different perceived lightness. We used pupillary responses to test whether the effect reflects perception or cognitive interpretation. Twenty participants viewed two versions of the display: one inducing a lighter and the other a darker central disk percept. The physical stimulus was identical across conditions only contextual interpretation varied. In a control condition, the entire background was rotated, disrupting the border relationships consistent with occlusion and transparency cues and presumably the illusion as well. If pupil responses track luminance only, dilation should depend solely on background intensity. Instead, modulation by background luminance was reduced in the illusion relative to the rotated control (F(31,589)=3.598,p<.001), indicating that perceived lightness influences physiological responses. In fact, the image with the dark background is overall less dark when the disk is perceived as light, and the one with the light background is less light with the disk perceived as darker. A cluster-based permutation analysis showed that this modulation emerged in a sustained window starting at~1.8s. Behavioural lightness matches replicated the illusion (F(1,19)=41.14,p<.001). These results show that the Anderson and Winawer effect reflects genuine perceptual processing. More broadly, this approach provides an objective (response bias-free) way to validate findings in perception.
session_title: Visual Illusions, Hallucinations, and Visual Awareness

title: Controlling the content of visual hallucinations through seeded flicker
affiliations: 1. University College London (UK)
abstract: Visual hallucinations induced pharmacologically, clinically, or experimentally often resemble specific geometric forms, including radial spokes/fans, concentric rings, and spirals. These ‘Klüver forms’ have been attributed to intrinsic properties of visual cortex, whereby wave-like activity patterns propagate through retinotopically-arranged lateral connections. Empirical evidence for this link derives from ‘seeded’ hallucinations, where flickering patterns in one visual-field location have been argued to elicit opponent forms in adjacent locations (e.g. spokes induce illusory rings, and vice versa). However, these reports rely on purely qualitative responses, taken in uncontrolled conditions. Here, we used quantitative psychophysical measurements to test whether flickering geometric stimuli can selectively induce spatially-opponent hallucinations in adjacent visual-field locations.   Participants (n=20 typical adults) viewed 15Hz flickering stimuli (either radial spokes/fans or concentric rings) for 2 minutes. Stimuli were either full field (as in the MacKay effect), foveal patterns with a blank surround, or peripheral patterns with a blank centre. Fixation was monitored. Hallucinatory percepts were reported using button presses, allowing classification as spokes, rings, or mixed forms. Across all conditions, opponent forms were significantly more frequent than congruent forms (e.g. central spoke stimuli induced more illusory peripheral rings than spokes), as predicted. However, this opponency was not exclusive: individual variability and the presence of mixed/irregular percepts demonstrate greater heterogeneity than previously reported. Opponent forms emerged rapidly after stimulus onset, with a slower rise in the frequency of congruent percepts, suggesting an additional role for processes like adaptation. Participant drawings corroborated these findings, revealing both a predominant opponent bias and more complex patterns (e.g. fractal structures) like those induced by unstructured flicker.   Our results provide quantitative support for models in which hallucination content reflects the interaction of stimulus-driven input and intrinsic cortical dynamics, but also highlight the need to incorporate the variability and phenomenological richness of the resulting perceptual states.
session_title: Visual Illusions, Hallucinations, and Visual Awareness

title: Hybrid images reveal time-dependent neural encoding of competing visual content
affiliations:
1. The MARCS Institute for Brain, Behaviour and Development, Western Sydney University (AU)
2. Department of Basic Neurosciences, University of Geneva (CH)
3. School of Psychology, Western Sydney University (AU)
4. School of Computer, Data and Mathematical Sciences, Western Sydney University (AU)
abstract: Ambiguous object recognition is usually studied using images that have a single ground truth, for example, by reducing the available information (e.g., deleting or occluding parts of an object) or by adding noise to the image.  Another form of ambiguity consists of encoding the information from multiple object identities in the same visual input, which constitutes a great tool to study the brain’s mechanisms to disambiguate each individual identity. However, less is known about how the visual system resolves objects in images with multiple competing ground truths, as in the case of hybrid images. Using a pre-trained diffusion model that creates visual illusions through noise decomposition, we created hybrid images in which information about two distinct object identities was embedded in the low and high spatial frequency bands (e.g., low spatial frequencies ‘fruits’ and high spatial frequencies ‘parrots’). Alongside control images, we presented these hybrids to 30 observers while we recorded 64 channel EEG and used multivariate decoding to examine which object identity was dominant in the brain as a function of time. The decoding prediction favoured the low spatial frequency object in the early stages of the neural response, but flipped to favour the high spatial frequency object at a later processing stage. These predictions suggest a different prioritisation for the low spatial frequency information compared to the high spatial frequency information. Additionally, we conducted a behavioural categorisation experiment where participants chose whether the image was animate or inanimate. The correlation between the behavioural and the classifier’s categorisation of the images was positive when there was information of the high spatial frequency in the brain. Our work with hybrid images provides new insights into how the object information is carried through the visual system and how the high spatial frequency information drives the final categorisation decision in this case.
session_title: Visual Illusions, Hallucinations, and Visual Awareness

title: Seeing the trees through the forest: Spatiotemporal routines in visual cognition
affiliations:
1. Lausanne University Hospital (CH)
2. University of Lausanne (CH)
3. The Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
4. Icelandic Vision Laboratory (IS)
abstract: Perception and cognition unfold within richly structured spatiotemporal environments. Despite this, research in these domains often relies on paradigms that isolate stimuli from their natural context. In this talk, I argue that even the most fundamental perceptual functions are inherently shaped by spatial and temporal structure. Drawing on examples from vision, attention, memory, and decision-making, I outline shared computational principles through which spatiotemporal context shapes perception and cognition. I further show how classic phenomena can be revisited when contextual factors, such as visual statistics, are taken into account. Finally, I introduce the concept of spatiotemporal routines: canonical mechanisms that integrate spatial and temporal structure to guide perception and behavior.
session_title: Symposium: Beyond local features: Spatiotemporal structure in perception and neural processing

title: Binding for whom? From features and observers to action in a structured world
affiliations: 1. Universiteit van Amsterdam (NL)
abstract:
The symposium challenges ‘brick-by-brick’ views of visual processing by emphasizing spatiotemporal context. I argue this critique doesn't go far enough. The problem isn't that features need context - it's that ‘features’ and ‘binding’ are artifacts of a paradigm we should leave behind.

The binding problem asks how separately processed features are combined into coherent percepts. But this question presupposes that features exist as separable primitives and that perception culminates in a representation for an observer. Both assumptions are unnecessary. Visual systems are tuned not to local features but to the statistical structure of the natural world, shaped by evolutionary and developmental history. In this framework, there are no segregated features requiring recombination—binding is a solution to a problem the brain only has for a small part of its processing.

More fundamentally: binding for whom? The question presupposes a Cartesian observer for whom features must be assembled. Yet the brain contains no such privileged viewpoint—let alone the proliferation of observers that binding theories quietly require, one for each operation that must be 'read' by something further downstream. The neuroconnectionist framework—using deep neural networks to express and test hypotheses about brain computation—replaces ‘are features bound?’ with ‘can downstream circuits drive appropriate action?’, dissolving binding into questions about information accessibility for behavior.

I discuss findings—from lesion studies, neural networks, and classic binding errors—that remain puzzling within the classical framework but become coherent and actionable once we abandon it.
session_title: Symposium: Beyond local features: Spatiotemporal structure in perception and neural processing

title: A half second of spatiotemporal, contextual processing precedes conscious perception
affiliations: 1. EPFL (CH)
abstract: Classical models of vision assume a largely feedforward process in which a stimulus is presented, propagated along the visual hierarchy, and ultimately gives rise to a conscious percept. Within this framework, consciousness appears as a continuous stream of percepts that closely follows incoming sensory input. Here, we present converging evidence suggesting a different picture: before a stimulus is consciously perceived, the visual system engages in a period of spatiotemporal and contextual integration that can last up to half a second. In addition, behavioral experiments, combined with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and electroencephalography (EEG), indicate that the conscious perception of a single element is not determined solely by its immediate sensory representation. Instead, perception depends on interactions among elements distributed across the visual field and unfolding over time. Information presented before and after a target stimulus can strongly influence how that stimulus is ultimately perceived. Hence, perception is constructed through extended contextual processing rather than instantaneously read out from the retinal input. We argue that such long unconscious processing periods are necessary to resolve the inherently ill-posed problems of vision, such as luminance, color, and, in particularly motion processing. In addition, segmentation and grouping are time consuming processes that depend on a large number of elements in the visual scene. Only after all these processes are accomplished, a coherent percept is rendered conscious. Conscious perception, therefore, may not reflect the immediate present but rather the outcome of a short period of postdictive processing that integrates events across time and space.
session_title: Symposium: Beyond local features: Spatiotemporal structure in perception and neural processing

title: Traveling Waves as spatiotemporal neural mechanism for perception and attention
affiliations:
1. Université Paris Cité and CNRS (FR)
2. Institut Universitaire de France (FR)
abstract: Neural processing unfolds through distributed spatiotemporal dynamics, and can manifest as traveling-wave-like patterns –smooth phase shift across the cortical space. Traveling waves have been observed across species, scales and recording types. Yet, their functional relevance in human is challenged by the methodological constraints inherent to noninvasive recordings. Our work focuses on developing theoretical models and analysis tools to reach a mechanistic understanding of traveling waves for human cognition, and in particular for visual perception and attention. The talk will present our recent research on both meso-scale (within a single visual region) and macro-scale (across the entire cortex) traveling waves. I will show that waves can travel across the primary visual area (V1) and organize perceptual processing over space and time. Additionally, waves can propagate between frontal and visual regions and support inter-areal communication during attentional exploration of visual scenes. Together, I will argue that traveling waves constitute a possible canonical brain computation underlying diverse brain functions.
session_title: Symposium: Beyond local features: Spatiotemporal structure in perception and neural processing

title: Overcoming the Reliability Paradox: A Psychometric Evaluation of an Object Foraging Task
affiliations:
1. University of Iceland (IS)
2. Reykjavik University (IS)
abstract: Cognitive tasks that effectively detect group differences often perform poorly at detecting individual differences: the reliability paradox. This happens because tasks designed to maximize group or condition differences actively suppress the between-person variance that individual-differences research depends on. Visual object discrimination varies across individuals and develops throughout childhood, yet the tasks used to measure it have rarely been evaluated for psychometric adequacy. Сhildren (N = 310, ages 4 - 8) completed a visual object foraging task. On each trial, children foraged through a display of 9 targets among 9 distractors. Item pairs were either from different object categories (basic-level) or the same category (subordinate-level) a control condition used black and white circles. Performance was measured as correctly selected targets per second. The visual similarity between items was quantified using activation patterns from the CORnet-S neural network, as well as human ratings for shapes and features. The object discrimination task overcomes the reliability paradox, as it produces both large developmental effects and reliable individual differences. The task demonstrated excellent internal consistency and high alternate forms reliability across sessions with different stimulus sets. Stable between-person differences accounted for a substantially larger proportion of trial-level variance than is typically observed in classic cognitive paradigms. Explanatory IRT models revealed that item difficulty was driven by shape dissimilarity for basic-level trials and by feature dissimilarity for subordinate-level trials. The difficulty rankings were highly stable across age groups.
