Interestingly, native and non-native speakers had differential item functioning for basic but not for subordinate discrimination, and girls and boys showed differential item functioning for both types of object discrimination. A short form of 18-item pairs retained excellent reliability (< 5 minutes of testing).  These findings provide a psychometric foundation for prior and future research using this paradigm. The language-independence at the subordinate level makes it well-suited for cross-linguistic applications.

title: Individual Priors Shape Real-World Object Search
affiliations: 1. Justus-Liebig-Universität Gießen (DE)
abstract: Real-world objects vary widely in appearance. With each person experiencing a different visual diet, the variability represented for a given object differs between individuals. For example, when thinking about clocks, some people might picture an analogue template (e.g., a round clock face), whereas others might think of a digital one (e.g., a rectangular display). This raises the question: how do people use their own prior knowledge while searching for an object whose exact appearance is unknown? Here, we used human drawings to investigate how object templates vary across people. Across two experiments, we demonstrate that idiosyncrasies in object templates predict individual differences in visual search performance. In Experiment 1, participants drew four exemplars from each of 12 real-world object categories before performing a cued search task in which they indicated whether the target category was present or absent. Using a deep neural network (DNN), we computed similarity between each drawing and target stimulus per trial and correlated it with the reaction time for each participant. Our results showed that higher similarity between a participant's own template and the target predicted faster search performance. Critically, templates were prioritised based on drawing order, with participants' first drawing serving as the strongest predictor of their search performance. Furthermore, individuals' own drawings predicted their search better than other participants' drawings, revealing that idiosyncratic object templates shape search behaviour. In Experiment 2, we replicate this effect in a foraging task. Here, participants drew exemplars of 5 object categories followed by a visual foraging task with large object arrays containing multiple targets from the same category. We show that participants systematically utilize their own most prioritized templates as they forage. Together, our findings indicate that search differs across people as a function of their prior experience with objects and their variability in the world.

title: Proactive deployment of attention in ageing: fixation-related neural dynamics during enhancement and inhibition of spatial priority
affiliations:
1. Leicester University (UK)
2. Chongqing Medical University (CN)
3. Nottingham University (UK)
abstract: Visual attention is shaped not only by stimulus salience and current attentional goals, but also by statistical regularities in the environment. Repeated experience with target and distractor locations induces lasting plasticity in spatial priority maps, facilitating target selection at high-probability locations (proactive enhancement) and suppressing likely distractor locations (proactive inhibition). While enhancement-based learning appears largely preserved in healthy ageing, evidence suggests that older adults may show reduced capacity to deploy inhibitory attentional templates stemming from a strategic shift toward enhancement-based control. Preliminary data from our laboratory suggests age-related decreases in saccadic selectivity and processing speed are accompanied by differences in quasi-stable EEG topographies and their transition probabilities during search. These data are consistent with neural alterations in proactive attentional control. To investigate this further, the current study compared younger and older adults on a visual search task combining eye-tracking and EEG. Displays contained 8 binary square wave gratings on a grey background with targets differentiated from distractors by orientation. Gratings were masked by multi-grey mosaics using alpha values designed to introduce a fixed level of ambiguity during orientation discrimination. Prior to search, a spatial cue varying in predictability (75% vs. 25% valid) indicated whether a subset of four objects was likely (positive) or unlikely (negative) to contain the target. We examine oculometric indices of search efficiency and fixation-related potentials (FRPs) at high and low probability target locations. We predict that proactive enhancement for positive cues will be preserved across age groups, whereas older adults will show attenuated FRP modulation and reduced search efficiency for negative cues, consistent with diminished flexibility in deploying suppression-based templates. These contrasts seek to uncover how ageing affects neural signatures of target selection, evidence accumulation, and evaluation in response to spatial statistical regularities during visual search.

title: All target-matching features of multi-dimensional search targets are prioritised independent of target-relevance: Electrophysiological evidence
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: When searching for an object, we mentally represent its features as a search template. However, real-world objects often contain multiple identifying features across dimensions, varying in probability and task-relevance. This study investigated whether participants represent multifaceted objects using only their most probable and relevant features. Participants searched for target categories defined by multiple shapes (dresses, shirts) and colours (purple, green), where one feature per dimension appeared on two-thirds of trials (high probability) and the other on one-third (low probability). It was hypothesised that participants would adopt a 'good enough' template, prioritising only the most probable and task-relevant features. To probe which features were represented, isolated features were extracted from the targets and presented as task-irrelevant visual probes acting as either spatially valid or invalid cues to target location. Task-relevance was manipulated across three experiments (all Ns = 20): Experiment 1 made shape relevant (identifying an embedded line's orientation), while Experiments 2 and 3 made colour increasingly relevant (requiring colour congruence judgments, or requiring direct identification of target's colour). Contrary to predictions, behavioural results showed that all partially matching probes influenced spatial attention regardless of feature probability or dimension relevance, producing faster target detection when spatially congruent. ERP data revealed that all probes elicited a late lateralised positive component consistent with the Late Directing Attention Positivity (LDAP), reflecting strategic attentional deployment toward the probe location. Early attentional capture/selection was less consistent: shape probes elicited a large, reliable N2pc across experiments, whereas colour probes produced a weaker and more variable N2pc. These findings suggest that during unpredictable visual search, individuals strategically tune attention toward all potentially relevant features of a multifaceted object, rather than narrowing attention to specific high-probability or task-relevant features alone and that the depth of processing to utilise these cues may vary across dimensions.

title: Mapping foraging strategy: How information availability shapes spatial exploration in a virtual environment
affiliations:
1. University of Essex (UK)
2. DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory (US)
abstract: Spatial exploration reflects how organisms gather, interpret, and respond to information about their environment. Foraging tasks, in which participants search for multiple targets across a space, provide a useful framework for studying exploration strategies. Here, participants navigated a virtual environment as first-person avatars, searching for items across a series of trials. We examined how movement ability and information availability shape foraging behaviour and developed a generative model to capture these strategies. The model predicts the order in which items are selected using three latent parameters: proximity (bias toward items near the previous selection), momentum (bias toward continued forward movement or reversals), and turning (tendency to turn left or right). We show that proximity and momentum are the strongest predictors of foraging behaviour in this task. We further demonstrate that information availability influences strategy: participants given access to a map were more inclined to reverse direction during search. We also evaluated different target selection rules, finding that a “winner-takes-all” rule outperformed both a stochastic alternative and a simple baseline. Taken together, these results show that our model captures foraging behaviour at the level of individual item selections, and we propose that this framework offers a useful approach for examining the cognitive processes underlying human visual exploration.

title: A neural model of top-down feature guidance of spatial attention
affiliations:
1. Laboratory for Experimental Psychology, Department of Psychology, Faculty of Philosophy, University of Novi Sad (RS)
2. Department of Psychology, Faculty of Media and Communications, Singidunum University (RS)
3. Department of Psychology, Faculty of Philosophy, University of Rijeka (HR)
abstract: In a singleton search paradigm, a salient distractor can capture attention, even if it is irrelevant. Such a bottom-up strategy can be prevented in a feature search paradigm when the target has a consistent value, allowing for the top-down control to be applied. However, when the task allows for both strategies, bottom-up seems to be preferred, and the participants would use the top-down strategy only to avoid switching between the two. Furthermore, whether a singleton distractor captures attention in a bottom-up manner or salience helps suppress irrelevant stimuli in a top-down manner can be influenced by the independently manipulated salience of the target and of the distractor.  This particular pattern of data was obtained from our 8 experiments and used to develop a neural model comprising 3 processing stages that emulate interactions among area V4, the inferotemporal (IT) cortex, and the posterior parietal (PP) cortex. Stage 1 is top-down attentional modulation from IT to feature maps in V4. Top-down attention interacts multiplicatively with feature maps, facilitating a relevant feature when a target template is present or suppressing an irrelevant feature when a salient distractor is present. This feedback provides re-entry signals to V4 that bias processing in the feedforward pathway from V4 to PP cortex, guiding spatial attention. Stage 2 is divisive normalization, which computes the contrast or saliency of locations within each feature map in V4. Stage 3 is a decision-making circuit in the PP cortex that selects a location based on the summed output from all feature maps computed in the second stage. Decision-making is modelled as a leaky competitive accumulator.  Using a single set of parameters, the model correctly predicted the pattern of response times from all our experiments. We propose a comprehensive, yet parsimonious model of attentional deployment under both top-down and bottom-up influences.

title: Applications of Physically Based Differentiable Rendering in Vision Science
affiliations: 1. Technical University of Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: Physically Based Rendering (PBR) is the physical simulation of light transport within a scene, i.e., how light participates in events such as reflections, refractions and scattering when interacting with objects. Recent advances have made the diffentiation of PBR possible and computationally tractable, allowing the reconstruction of physical scene properties (such as lighting, materials, shapes, etc.) from two-dimensional images using gradient-based optimisation. This enables us to optimise physically-interpretable parameters instead of reasoning about pixel-based images. Here we demonstrate the potential of differentiable PBR in two settings: (a) to find physically based model metamers to explain model sensitivities and invariances to physical object properties and (b) to create controversial scenes where two models disagree on the interpretation of a physical scene, using gloss appearance as an example. These examples display the promise of differentiable PBR for understanding perceptual inferences in humans and machines.

title: Humans perceive invisible materials and their properties by observing others’ actions
affiliations:
1. INM - Leibniz Institute for New Materials (DE)
2. Centre for Tactile Internet with Human-in-the-Loop (CeTI), Dresden University of Technology (DE)
3. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
abstract: Imagine watching someone gently squeeze a ripe peach at a market. Even without touching the fruit yourself, you can infer its softness, juiciness, and fragility from the subtle deformation of its surface and the careful modulation of the person’s grip. But how much information is conveyed purely by the movements of the hand? Here, we isolated action information by removing the material from view and presenting observers with hand movements alone. Using motion-capture gloves, we recorded typical exploratory actions performed by two individuals interacting with five materials (e.g., a sponge). From the recorded explorations, we rendered realistic hand interactions. Across three experiments, we asked observers to identify these invisible materials and their properties from hand interactions seen from different viewpoints (first-person, second-person, and side). In Experiments 1 and 2, observers identified and categorized the invisible materials from hand interactions, using forced-choice tasks. In Experiment 3, observers rated 14 sensory adjectives (e.g., softness) to assess the material qualities. Observers were able to infer both material properties and material identity from hand movements alone. Performance differed significantly across material categories, with the highest accuracy for granular (71%), viscous (58%), and deformable materials (56%), indicating differences in diagnosticity of the characteristic exploratory movements. PCA analysis revealed 4 material dimensions closely matching the categories in Experiment 2 and tactile and visual material dimensions found in previous studies. Viewpoint did not significantly affect performance, suggesting that hand movements convey robust material information across different perspectives. Together, we found that exploratory hand movements can provide visual cues that allow an observer of these movements to readily identify the explored materials and their qualities, even in absence of direct visual information about the material itself. Hence, this work provides insights for robot learning, where artificial agents must extract information about object properties from observed human manipulation.

title: Perception of material properties: Roles of 2D, 3D and cognitive cues
affiliations: 1. State University of New York (US)
abstract: Anticipating properties of a material such as slipperiness, ripeness, hardness or warmth from just its visual appearance is necessary for successful functioning. Most studies of material perception have concentrated on 2D perceptual cues while a few have used image statistics such as Fourier spectra or the responses of oriented linear filters.  The neural processing underlying material perception and the roles of 3D cues and semantic memory mostly remain to be understood. Towards these aims, we comprehensively investigated visual perception of fabrics varying widely in appearance and affordance. We took high resolution photographs from a fixed distance of 135 different fabrics that included most types of woven, knit, braided, bonded and felted materials.  Observers were shown grey-level images of the fabrics at high resolution without stereo, and asked to place materials along five-point rating scales ranging over ten opposing properties: soft/rough, warm/cool, stiff/flexible, sturdy/delicate, water-absorbent/repellent, shiny/matte, see-through/opaque, smooth/coarse, elastic/rigid, thin/thick. We conjectured that repeated 3D texture features are major cues, as are semantic memories associated with different types of fabric. A few fabric qualities can be distinguished using spatial-frequency bands (Giesel & Zaidi, 2013) but higher-order statistics are required to extract feature shapes, and 3D textures are perceived through shape-from-shading. The combined 10-dimensional ratings were subjected to dimensional reduction with a canonical-correlation analysis and the major axes correlated with image statistics estimated using gliders representing second, third and fourth order correlations, before and after whitening. The effect of shape from shading was estimated by redoing the ratings for high-resolution photos taken under diffuse light, and the effect of semantic memory by comparing fabric recognition performance under an auditory n-back memory suppression task. Together these manipulations reveal the range of cues used for material property perception and the differences from 2D texture discrimination.

title: Material perception in context
affiliations: 1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
abstract: Material recognition—distinguishing between substances like metal, fabric, wood, or glass—is essential for predicting object behavior and guiding interactions. Prior studies have shown that people can rapidly and effortlessly recognize materials and infer their properties, despite substantial variability in appearances. However, most previous work used isolated texture patches, ignoring potential effects of visual context. Unlike objects, materials are usually not defined by a diagnostic global shape, rendering them more ambiguous and potentially more prone to contextual influences. Here, we used AI-based image synthesis with careful, iterative prompting to seamlessly embed identical image patches—depicting materials such as eggshell, metal, or water—into eight different surrounding contexts. One context was congruent with the original material (e.g. eggshell patch embedded in the image of an egg), seven were incongruent (e.g. eggshell patch embedded in the image of a human arm). For each stimulus, 10 participants identified the material of the central patch and rated 17 properties (e.g., realism, softness, glossiness, temperature). Importantly, we tested different groups of participants so that no single person saw the same patch twice (irrespective of context). Our findings revealed a strong impact of the context on the interpretation of the central patch. For example, participants identified eggshell as human skin when embedded in the context of a human arm. Property ratings shifted systematically to reflect the categorization—e.g., the patch appeared “softer” and “warmer” in the arm context than in the egg context. A control experiment, in which material patches were paired with mismatched contexts, confirmed that these effects were not due to inattentiveness but genuine perceptual integration of the patch and the surroundings. Overall, the findings demonstrate that material recognition is highly context-sensitive, potentially more so than object perception, highlighting context as a key factor in material perception.

title: Probing Novel, Hybrid Material Representations via Natural Language and Semantic Embeddings
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior, University of Marburg, Justus Liebig University Giessen and the Technical University of Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: How do we perceive materials that are entirely novel or nonexistent in the real world?  Here we address this fundamental question by investigating how observers infer information about material properties from unfamiliar, hybrid combinations of different material categories. Building on our previous work (Schmidt et al., 2025), we utilized CNN-based interpolation (Vacher et al., 2020) to generate 12 cross-category morph sequences (e.g., sand–grass, moss–fur). We previously showed that perceptual scaling aligns with physical morph levels, driven by low-level features like RMS contrast and color saturation. Here, we investigated the semantic interpretation of these hybrid textures. Participants (N=100) provided free-text descriptions—including material labels, visual properties, and haptic attributes—across five interpolation steps (0%, 24%, 50%, 76%, and 100%). To quantify the responses, we used sentence-transformer embeddings to calculate mean cosine similarity between participants’ descriptions. Our results show that inter-observer consistency declines significantly as morphs approach the midpoint, indicating increased ambiguity and diverse recognition of novel material combinations. Furthermore, semantic similarity decreased as a function of distance along the morph continuum for example, the 0%-24% pair was semantically closer than the 100%-24% pair. This suggests that the semantic space of visual materials closely maps onto the image-based morph space. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) further revealed a path-to-distance ratio of 0.24–0.33, demonstrating that morphed material representations do not follow a linear trajectory between parent categories in semantic space. Interestingly, descriptions of haptic properties did not follow these systematic trends as closely as material labels or visual attributes, likely due to a lack of lexical diversity. Participants used similar terms regardless of the material in general, suggesting that crossmodal tactile inferences from visual material cues are less sensitive. Overall, this study provides insights into how visual, haptic, and semantic material feature spaces are represented and integrated in the brain.

title: Distangling the role of local motion and global shape information in material perception
affiliations: 1. Department of Psychology, Justus Liebig University (DE)
abstract: Recent studies using dynamic dot materials (DDMs) show that motion alone provides information about material properties of non-rigid deforming objects (Schmid & Doerschner, 2018 Bi et al., 2018). DDMs depict materials as moving dots attached to or embedded within objects. Without surface information, they convey material through local and global features of motion and shape. Recent work using point-light cloths (PLCs) suggests percepts remain robust to disruptions in local dot motion and rely on holistic processing, discounting local motion features (Erdogan et al., 2025). However, these displays are confounded by shape information conveyed by the spatial configuration of dots, a strong cue for material/object recognition. The visual system may extract global shape at each timepoint, with temporal integration allowing identification of e.g. cloth from moving dots. Hence, the critical question is whether local motion cues, in the absence of global shape cues, provide diagnostic information about materials? To answer this, we restricted access to global shape information with an aperture. Using dynamic dot stimuli from five material categories (liquid, smoke, rigid-breakable, jelly, fabric) we presented stimuli with intact or disrupted local motion (limited lifetime dots). Observers (N=40) viewed animations in three sequential blocks: a fixed aperture, an interactive aperture allowing shape exploration, and no aperture (https://next.hessenbox.de/index.php/s/X42ejA9pacnsadA). They completed free description, material categorization, and attribute rating task for each block. We found restricting global shape information and disrupting local motion both impaired performance. Critically, without global shape information, disrupting local motion reduced categorization to chance, whereas performance remained well above chance when local motion was intact. Descriptive and rating tasks showed similar patterns. Findings indicate contributions of both local motion and global shape in material perception from DDMs. Contrary to previous findings, we conclude that local motion cues are required for inferring material from motion when strong shape cues are absent.

title: Dynamic modulation of endogenous attentional sampling under cue uncertainty
affiliations:
1. Princeton University (US)
2. University of Pennsylvania (US)
abstract: Theories of rhythmic attention propose that attention samples from the environment in rhythmic cycles, with alternating states of enhanced or diminished perceptual sensitivity at an attended location. While previous studies have revealed robust theta-band rhythmic sampling when attention is drawn to an exogenous event, the cues that drive attention are often internally driven and ambiguous in real world. To investigate how perceptual uncertainty of visual cues affects the temporal dynamics of attention deployment, we designed a task that combined elements of perceptual decision making and spatial attention. A central cloud of red and blue dots was used as an endogenous cue, with the dominant color indicating the likely location of a target, which appeared at a varied delay following the cue offset. Cue uncertainty was introduced by varying the red-blue ratio. Participants reported the target location, then rated their confidence in the attended location on a five-point scale. When cue uncertainty was low or subjective confidence was high, detection performance fluctuated at a theta frequency (∼6–7 Hz), replicating previous findings using exogenous attention cues. Increased cue ambiguity disrupted this rhythmic coordination. Remarkably, in the absence of directional cue information, we observed slow, coherent behavioral fluctuations (~3 Hz) selectively in the left visual field. These results suggest that attention dynamics flexibly adapt to internal states of certainty, with subjective confidence modulating both the frequency and coordination of spatial attentional sampling.
session_title: Symposium: The rhythmic nature of perception and attention: Evidence, challenges, and open questions

title: Testing oscillatory modulations in temporal summary statistics across visual features
affiliations:
1. Psychophysics and Neural Dynamics Lab, Department of Radiology, Lausanne University Hospital and University of Lausanne (CH)
2. The Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
abstract: Several theories propose that perception and cognition operate through rhythmic sampling, with theta (4–7 Hz) and alpha (8–13 Hz) oscillations shaping attention and perception. Yet, evidence for such “behavioral rhythms” remains inconsistent and largely confined to simplified paradigms with brief stimuli, leaving open whether these dynamics generalize to more continuous and naturalistic settings. Here, we introduce a paradigm in which observers estimate the average of rapidly unfolding visual features across eccentricities, allowing us to probe the temporal structure of perceptual integration. Using a temporally weighted averaging model across orientation, size, and color tasks, we tested for periodic modulations, or “waving averages”, in how individual stimuli contribute to perception. Our results reveal a heterogeneous pattern: robust low-frequency waving averages (<2.5 Hz) for orientation and size, weaker effects for color, and higher-frequency components (~4–8 Hz) emerging only in a subset of participants and primarily in the parafovea. These results challenge the notion of universal behavioral rhythms, instead pointing to task-dependent and individual-specific temporal dynamics, while highlighting slower oscillatory processes as a more consistent feature of perceptual integration.
session_title: Symposium: The rhythmic nature of perception and attention: Evidence, challenges, and open questions

title: Oscillatory dynamics of attention in sensory tuning and perceptual processing
affiliations:
1. Department of Cognitive Neuroscience, Faculty of Psychology and Neuroscience, Maastricht University (NL)
2. Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Integrative Neuroscience and Cognition Center (FR)
3. CLLE, Université Toulouse Jean Jaurès, CNRS (FR)
4. Department of Experimental Psychology, Ghent University (BE)
5. Institute of Psychology, University of Muenster (DE)
6. Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science, New York University (US)
7. Institut Universitaire de France (FR)
abstract: Growing evidence suggests that attention samples sensory information rhythmically, leading to periodic fluctuations in perceptual performance. Fundamental questions remain about the mechanisms, neural basis, and functional role of these behavioral rhythms. I will present a series of experiments combining psychophysics and electroencephalography to explore these limitations. Using an exhaustive psychophysical protocol with attentional manipulation and reverse correlation analyses, we showed that sustained and exploratory attention differentially shaped sensory representations over time. Sustained attention elicited oscillations in perceptual performance at alpha frequencies (9-12Hz) and rhythmically suppressed irrelevant information, whereas exploratory attention elicited oscillations at theta frequencies (4-7Hz) and rhythmically enhanced task-relevant features. In a follow-up study, we demonstrated that these behavioral rhythms corresponded to neural oscillatory dynamics at matching frequencies. Time-generalized EEG classification accuracies showed alpha oscillations during sustained (spatial and feature-based) attention and theta oscillations during spatial exploration. Faster reaction times correlated with stronger theta power, supporting the functional role of theta oscillations in attentional processing. Finally, we investigated whether oscillatory phase determined not only when perception was optimal, but also what was perceived. Previous studies, in the auditory domain, suggested that perceptual content could depend on the timing (i.e., the phase of brain oscillations) of stimulus presentation. We tested whether a similar relationship existed in vision by inducing an association between visual stimuli (faces) and the phase of visually tagged brain oscillations. We assessed this phase-face association by presenting ambiguous stimuli at multiple phases and found that face-discrimination performance was biased over time, with early versus late delays favoring different faces. These biases were not reliably modulated by the phase of ongoing oscillations. Overall, these findings support a role for oscillatory dynamics in structuring the timing of perception, while suggesting that further investigations are needed to clarify the link between oscillatory phase and perceptual content.
session_title: Symposium: The rhythmic nature of perception and attention: Evidence, challenges, and open questions

title: Effects of neural oscillations on visual performance during attentional deployment
affiliations:
1. University of Nottingham (UK)
2. University of Leeds (UK)
3. CNRS (FR)
abstract: Oscillatory accounts of attention have predominantly emphasised the role of alpha-band activity in gating sensory processing and shaping attentional selection. Within this framework, alpha oscillations are thought to regulate the excitability of the visual cortex, by modulating perceptual performance in a rhythmic manner. However, accumulating evidence suggests that other frequency bands may play a more central role in attentional control than previously assumed. In particular, beta-band activity (∼15–30 Hz) has been implicated in top-down processes that support the enhancement of task-relevant information. In this talk, I will present causal evidence on the role of neural oscillations in attentional deployment using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and EEG. By probing the attentional network at specific temporal intervals, we assessed both electrophysiological and behavioural consequences of rhythmic brain activity. Across a series of experiments, we consistently observed that beta-band dynamics, rather than alpha-band oscillations, are critically linked to changes in visual performance. This pattern was evident across both covert and overt attentional shifts and was robust across different behavioural measures, including detection accuracy and decision bias. These findings challenge dominant alpha-centric models of attentional selection and suggest a need to revise current frameworks of rhythmic attention. More broadly, they contribute to the ongoing debate on whether perceptual and attentional processes are fundamentally rhythmic by highlighting the importance of identifying the specific frequency bands that causally shape behaviour.
session_title: Symposium: The rhythmic nature of perception and attention: Evidence, challenges, and open questions

title: Integrating fixed and flexible rhythms
affiliations:
1. University College London (UK)
2. University of Cambridge (UK)
abstract: Our sensory inputs contain temporal structure often paralleled by neural dynamics, notably, in the form of oscillations. How do we align neural processing with the input to optimize perception of sensory streams? Flexible rhythm, or entrainment, accounts propose that neural oscillations align flexibly with sensory rhythmic information. Fixed accounts instead suggest more rigid neural dynamics determined by different intrinsic processes. I first highlight this apparent incompatibility between existing accounts. Sensory rhythms in our environment will usually not coincide specifically with the rate of any fixed rhythm. To resolve these and other issues, I then propose that sampling rhythms reflect statistical (Bayesian) learning of the temporal properties of inputs, determined by several sources. We process the sensory world according to the probability with which the combination of sources has predicted information at that time. This mechanism can integrate constraints to determine optimal sampling. I present some recent MEG work where we test components of this account, along with considerations about the role of the motor system in supporting such temporally-specific perceptual processes.
session_title: Symposium: The rhythmic nature of perception and attention: Evidence, challenges, and open questions

title: Causal inference across features during transsaccadic integration in humans and RNNs
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, University of Cambridge (UK)
2. Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge (UK)
3. Department of Cognitive Science, Central European University (HU)
abstract: Transsaccadic integration supports uninterrupted processing of the visual environment by combining presaccadic memory with postsaccadic sensory input. This can be framed as a causal inference problem: integration should depend on the probability of stimulus stability (i.e., that pre- and postsaccadic signals share a common cause). An ideal Bayesian observer solves this by weighing the perceived discrepancy between observations against prior knowledge of sensory uncertainty and environmental volatility. Previous work shows that human observers approximate this process: when viewing stimuli that change during a saccade and reporting the postsaccadic feature value (color or orientation), the presaccadic feature biases perception only when the discrepancy is not too large.  In natural vision, features are often linked through shared object causes. An ideal observer should therefore use changes in one feature to infer changes in another, depending on their covariance structure. However, humans did not display such cross-feature integration in previous work, possibly because color and orientation covary weakly in natural scenes. Using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained on an analogous task, we show that networks approximate ideal observers, exploiting feature covariance when informative. Moreover, the degree of cross-feature integration closely tracks the statistics of the training environment.  We then extended our behavioral paradigm in a new experiment (n=14) using color and shape, which may share richer covariance. Replicating prior findings, participants showed causal inference behavior (reduced presaccadic biases for large discrepancies), but changes in the uncued feature did not modulate integration in the reported feature. These findings suggest that limited use of cross-feature statistical structure generalizes across feature dimensions. We propose that this reflects the covariance structure of the natural visual environment, contrasting with the training statistics required to elicit cross-feature integration in RNNs.

title: Mislocalization in saccades to tactile targets
affiliations: 1. Heinrich-Heine University Düsseldorf (DE)
abstract: Stimuli briefly presented around the time of a saccade are systematically mislocalized. This mislocalization is typically bi-directional, with probes presented both before and beyond the saccade target appearing compressed toward the target. Existing computational models attribute this effect to sensorimotor mechanisms that support visual stability across saccades. Alternatively, mislocalization might also be driven by purely sensory mechanisms. Here, I varied the sensory features of the saccade target by asking participants to execute saccades in complete darkness toward either tactile or visual signals. At the start of each trial in the tactile condition, participants fixated a tactile stimulus delivered to the left index finger. After 1 s, this stimulus was extinguished and simultaneously replaced by a tactile stimulus on the right index finger, which served as the saccade target. At varying times relative to saccade onset, a probe LED was briefly flashed (8 ms). After a 500 ms delay, a comparison LED appeared, and participants judged whether the probe had been located to the left or right of the comparison. Psychometric functions were used to estimate perceived probe location across multiple time bins around saccade execution. The visual condition was identical, except that LEDs defined both fixation and saccade targets. In this condition, I replicated the classic perisaccadic compression effect. In contrast, the tactile condition yielded an asymmetric pattern: probes presented before the saccade target were localized relatively accurately, whereas probes presented beyond the target were still perceived as compressed toward it. These findings demonstrate that saccade target features selectively influence perisaccadic mislocalization. Crucially, saccade dynamics were indistinguishable between the visual and the tactile conditions. Sensorimotor processes thus seem unlikely to explain these differences. Instead, the data show that perisaccadic mislocalization arises from uni- or multisensory spatial integration between transient visual probes and the saccade target signal.

title: Asymmetric detection of feature onsets and offsets across saccades
affiliations: 1. Marburg University (DE)
abstract: The window of visibility differs between foveal and peripheral vision. While foveal vision achieves high contrast sensitivity even for fine spatial information, contrast sensitivity is overall lower and shifted to coarser information in peripheral vision. Consequently, the available information about object features changes with every saccade, when they move from peripheral to foveal vision and vice versa. Nevertheless, humans typically do not register any changes during saccades. Here, I tested which changes in feature visibility are detected across saccades. Participants had to execute saccades to a black ring that could contain a Gabor stimulus. In the first task, contrast sensitivity for the Gabor was measured separately before and after the saccade. As expected, contrast thresholds were higher presaccadically in the periphery than postsaccadically in the fovea. In the second task, the Gabor either disappeared (offset) or appeared (onset) during the saccade (change), or it was either continuously present or absent (no change). Participants had to report if they noticed a change during the saccade. Three Gabor contrasts were tested: average of pre- and postsaccadic thresholds, twice the pre- and twice the postsaccadic threshold.  For perisaccadic Gabor offsets, change reports increased with increasing contrast. When the Gabor was continuously present, change reports were infrequent and decreased with increasing contrast. Strikingly, for perisaccadic Gabor onsets, change reports were indistinguishable from the continuous condition, indicating that participants could not register that the Gabor appeared during the saccade. In a second experiment, the Gabor was placed at the presaccadic fixation location and then onsets were more often detected than offsets. These results indicate that the visibility of changes is related to the typical experience during saccades: At the postsaccadic fixation location, information is typically gained, and onsets are hardly noticed. At the presaccadic fixation location, information is typically lost, and offsets are hardly noticed.

title: The Remote Distractor Effect and the Size-Latency Effect are caused by lateral inhibition in the Superior Colliculus
affiliations:
1. Marburg University (DE)
2. SUNY College of Optometry (US)
3. University of East London (UK)
abstract: The Remote Distractor Effect (RDE) and the Size-Latency Effect (SLE) are two phenomena that influence the timing of saccadic eye-movements. In the SLE, larger targets delay saccades systematically according to their eccentricity/diameter ratio. In the RDE, the ratio of distractor and target eccentricities also predict saccade latencies. Do these effects share a common neural mechanism of lateral inhibition in the Superior Colliculus (SC)? If so, one would expect that: (1) both effects should exhibit identical spatial and temporal profiles, (2) increasing inhibition should systematically enhance effect magnitude, and (3) both effects should be attenuated when using equiluminant stimuli, which produce weaker SC responses. Through a series of human psychophysical experiments, we found that the ring stimuli used in past SLE experiments evoke RDE-like effects with identical spatial and temporal profiles, once taking into account the smaller magnitude of the RDE. Saccadic latency cost increases monotonically with the number of distractors, consistent with an increasing degree of inhibition. Finally, neither effect was observed with equiluminant stimuli that produce weaker responses in the SC. These findings are consistent with the RDE and SLE being caused by the same underlying neural mechanism, most likely of lateral inhibition within the SC.

title: Saccadic omission of predictable chromatic information
affiliations: 1. Heinrich-Heine Universität Düsseldorf (DE)
abstract: When we move our eyes, we do not perceive the motion that is produced on the retina, a phenomenon known as saccadic omission. We have recently shown that intra-saccadic motion becomes habituated when certain speeds are repeatedly coupled to certain saccade amplitudes. Previous studies have shown conflicting findings regarding chromatic omission. Here, we asked if color might be omitted when presented contingently on a given saccade vector. Seventeen participants performed a color detection task for stimuli presented during saccade execution. In habituation trials, participants executed 100 saccades during which a full-screen color was presented for ~42 milliseconds. In these trials, participants had no other task than performing a saccade. We measured detection thresholds before and after saccade execution for the same colors shown in habituation trials. Participants were asked to locate the position of a colored stimulus flashed for ~42 ms that appeared randomly either in the upper or the lower half of the screen. Color contrast was varied across trials, and the median of the psychometric function was chosen as the detection threshold. We found raised detection thresholds after habituation, indicating that the sensorimotor system habituates to saccade-contingent color stimulation. Furthermore, intra-saccadic habituation was selective for the color presented during habituation trials. If participants were exposed to a red stimulus in habituation trials and tested with a yellow color afterwards, no habituation was found. Our data show that color, like motion, can become omitted during saccade execution, depending on the saccade-contingent stimulation history. We conclude that saccadic omission results from intra-saccadic habituation, flexibly silencing sensations that have been repeatedly experienced to co-occur with saccades.

title: Suppression of optokinesis during smooth pursuit eye movements: testing the stationarity tagging hypothesis
affiliations:
1. University of Leicester (UK)
2. Complutense University of Madrid (ES)
abstract: Performing smooth pursuit eye movements over a structured background requires suppression of optokinetic responses towards the reafferent retinal signal. This suppression is reflected in reflexive ocular tracking responses to brief background motion opposite to the direction of pursuit. When a patterned background is static and then moves, motion opposite to the direction of pursuit elicits a very small response. Motion in the direction of pursuit elicits a much larger response. The suppression of optokinesis is not simply motor: if the background moves with the pursuit target, a motion perturbation in the background elicits nearly symmetric responses. Another option is that responses to surfaces “tagged” as stationary are suppressed. In the absence of body motion, the retinal motion of stationary surfaces is anticorrelated to the eye movement—they produce purely reafferent signals. If these cues were used, we should see smaller suppression of optokinesis when background motion is presented without a static background. The ground surface, projecting to the lower visual field, provides another cue for stationarity, based on prior knowledge. Our preliminary data (n = 11) shows that the absence of a static background increases responses in the direction of pursuit but not those in the opposite direction. The effect of visual field was largest, again only for reflexive response in the direction of pursuit, with static backgrounds in the lower visual field having a suppressive effect on responses in the direction of pursuit. The processing of background motion signals in the re-afferent direction is qualitatively different from those in the pursuit direction only the latter is consistent with stationarity tagging. The suppression of optokinesis may only differentiate between target and background. Supported by grant PID2024-155243NB-I00 from Ministerio de Ciencia, Innovación y Universidades (Spain).

title: Anticipatory gaze strategies as a principle of active information sampling
affiliations: 1. Technische Universität Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: Vision does not only depend on the retinal input, but also on how it is actively sampled over time. While eye movements are known to reflect both stimulus properties and task demands, it remains unclear whether their consequences on visual sensitivity are strategically exploited or merely incidental. Here, we investigate whether humans proactively adjust gaze behavior to optimize perceptual encoding, by disentangling task-driven (anticipatory) from stimulus-driven (reactive) influences on eye movement control. Across two sessions, observers (N=15) detected either low (0.1 cpd) or high (10 cpd) spatial frequency gratings at varying contrasts. Stimuli spanned a wide visual angle, so eye movements were not necessary to perform the task. Crucially, low and high spatial frequency gratings were presented in both sessions. This allowed us to isolate the task-driven (session-dependent) and stimulus-driven (trial-dependent) effects on gaze patterns. Saccade amplitudes and velocities were strongly shaped by task demands, in line with predictions from optimal coding accounts: saccades were larger when participants looked for low spatial frequencies and smaller for high spatial frequency targets. Adoption of these strategies was related to performance, although effects varied across individuals. In contrast, stimulus-driven influences were comparatively weak, though reduced visibility increased the task-dependent effect. This suggests a trade-off between encoding benefits and movement costs. Together, these findings support anticipatory gaze strategies as a principle of active information sampling, and highlight the role of self-generated motion for visual perception.

title: Exploring eye-movement mechanisms of colour discrimination: An eye-tracking study.
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: The human visual system samples the world through eye movements due to limited processing capacity. When participants match the colour of real objects, their fixations tend to land on the brightest regions, as these areas provide more information about a surface’s reflectance. However, because the brightest regions are typically most saturated, it is unclear whether fixations are driven by luminance or chromatic contrast (chroma). Our study explores fixation patterns of participants engaged in a colour discrimination task using physically-based rendered objects with dissociated luminance and chroma. The hue for the two reference stimuli was set along the bisector of the purple and orange colour quadrants, with chroma set to the maximum radius in the DKL iso-luminant plane. Comparison stimuli were generated by rotating the hue in six steps of 5° clockwise and counterclockwise. Crucially, the stimuli were illuminated from above, so that surfaces exhibited a top-to-bottom luminance gradient.  To dissociate luminance from chroma, we held the lightness distribution constant and inverted the chroma distribution, such that the brightest pixels had the lowest chroma. Participants (N=25) were presented with the reference stimulus, followed by the comparison and the reference again, in a random order. Their task was to indicate whether the second or the third stimulus matched the colour of the reference. We analysed colour discrimination performance (JND) and vertical fixation position as a function of condition (natural or inverted lightness–chroma relationship) and quadrant. Consistent with previous research, JNDs were lower for the orange quadrant (F(1,24)=64.347, p<.001), but did not differ between conditions. Crucially, when chroma was highest in the darkest regions, fixations tended to land on lower positions on the objects (F(1,24)=15.538, p<.001). Together, the results suggest that participants adapt their fixation strategy to sample the most colour-informative regions, thereby maintaining consistent performance.

title: Objective and explorative comparison of gaze allocation across conditions – an alternative to ROI analysis based on a combination of DDN classification and reverse correlation
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Gaze analysis typically depends on hypothesised, subjectively defined regions of interest (ROIs) or on heatmaps. ROIs facilitate comparisons between conditions but limit objectivity and exploratory analysis, whereas heatmaps avoid predefined assumptions yet involve numerous pixel-wise comparisons that make meaningful differences difficult to detect. Here, we introduce an advanced approach for analysing gaze allocation which combines the advantages and overcomes the limitations of these traditional approaches. We employ deep neural networks (DNNs), using adapted versions of AlexNet, to classify experimental conditions based on gaze patterns. This is combined with reverse correlation techniques to reveal where and how gaze differs across conditions. We test this approach on data from an experiment examining how object-specific sounds (e.g., a church bell ringing) influence gaze allocation (N=7). ROI-based analyses indicate significant differences between conditions (congruent sound vs no sound), with greater attention directed toward sound-associated objects in the congruent condition. However, definition of ROIs implies a certain degree of subjectivity. In fact, our data show that small variations of ROIs change the statistical significance of the results. In contrast, our DNN-based approach successfully classifies task conditions from individual fixations. Crucially, classification accuracy could be used to test for significant differences between conditions. The results demonstrate that sound can systematically alter gaze allocation for some but not all images. Furthermore, averaging random fixation patterns classified as each condition by the trained DNN revealed task-specific, image-specific, and non-trivial viewing strategies - fixations were not always drawn directly to the sound source instead, they may shift away from salient features and be directed all over the image, or fall between salient regions and the sound source. Such patterns would likely remain undetected using traditional hypothesis-driven methods. Overall, this approach offers an objective, data-driven framework that enables comparisons between experimental conditions while also allowing explorative approaches.

title: Seeing Tools Together: Preliminary Eye-Tracking Evidence for Perceptual Shared Experience in Tool Observation
affiliations:
1. Suor Orsola Benincasa University (IT)
2. University of Parma (IT)
abstract: From the earliest forms of collective life, human technology thrived within social contexts where knowledge was developed, used, and shared collectively. Perceptual Shared Experience (PSE), the phenomenon where the presence of another person influences perception, exemplifies this social basis. Tools are particularly useful for studying PSE: as objects designed for action, they are embedded in cooperative practices and cultural transmission, fostering a form of perception inherently oriented toward shared use. To examine how social presence reorganizes attentional priorities during tool observation, we recorded participants’ eye movements as they viewed various tools, either alone or with another person. In this eye-tracking study, twenty-three participants (F = 10 meanage = 21.6 SDage = 4.4) looked at images of everyday tools (e.g., a hammer, a knife) either solo (solo condition) or with someone else (shared condition). Each tool was divided into two predefined Areas of Interest (AOIs): a functional part (e.g., the hammer’s head) and a manipulation part (e.g., the hammer’s handle). After a fixation cross was shown for 500 ms, stimuli were displayed for 2000 ms, followed by a 3500 ms blank screen. Gaze distribution over time was analysed using growth curve analysis (GCA). Results showed a main effect of AOIs and an interaction with social presence. In both conditions, functional parts initially attracted more gaze. However, in the shared condition, manipulation parts attracted gaze more quickly and surpassed functional parts at the end of the window exploration, a shift not seen in the solo condition. These findings suggest that social co-presence may accelerate attentional shifts from semantic to action-oriented features. Thus, these results highlight, for the first time, that PSE not only increases attention but also appears to redirect it toward action-relevant features, suggesting it may serve as an organizing principle of cooperative action.

title: Visual salience during a head movement
affiliations:
1. Royal Holloway, University of London (UK)
2. University of Munster (DE)
3. Western Sydney University (AU)
abstract: This experiment investigates teh effect of visual salience during a head movement. We compare the effect of salience of a visual target on detection reaction times and eye movements, varying when the target appears relative to head movement. 36 participants performed 11 (repetitions) * 6 (conditions) * 2 (directions) target detection task presented in a HTC Vive Pro Eye virtual reality headset with eye tracking. The task was to find a (salient) red O or a (less salient) black T as quickly as possible on each trial and press a button according to its position. In the stimulus area, there was one distractor (a black letter L) and one target, positioned 5º above and below a central cross. For condition 1 participants fixated the cross and the letters appeared. For condition 2 participants were instructed that the stimuli could be found by moving their heads to the left (or right -  blocked), and the stimuli (a second fixation cross and the letters) were presented 60º horizontally from initial fixation, outside the initial field of view. Conditions 3-6 were the same as condition 2, but the letters only appeared (3) during the head movement (after 40º) (4) after the second cross was fixated for 10ms (5) 50ms and (6) 100ms. In all conditions the more salient target was detected faster. The largest effect of salience was in condition 2 - information was being processed during the head-eye movement. Reaction times relative to stimulus onset in the visual field suggested that in all other conditions the abrupt onset of stimuli reduced the differential effect of salience.   The gaze trajectory was not altered by peripheral stimuli during the head movement.  In conclusion, we find that stimuli which appear due to head movement are processed differently from sudden onset stimuli.

title: Knowing the world and understanding the words: Scene expectations and language comprehension as sources of guidance for visual attention and long-term memory
affiliations:
1. Durham (UK)
2. University of Aberdeen (UK)
abstract: Prior knowledge about the visual world and linguistic input are two sources of cognitive guidance that often co-occur in everyday life. However, it is unclear whether and how they jointly influence attentional allocation and long-term memory for information in real-word scenes. In this eye-tracking experiment, participants memorised a series of indoor scene images, each presented for 15 s, while listening to sentences describing them. Scenes contained eight objects, five of which mentioned in the sentence and three non-mentioned. In half of the images, all objects were semantically consistent, i.e., expected in the scene, while in the other half, one mentioned object and one non-mentioned object were semantically inconsistent (i.e., unexpected). In a two-alternative forced-choice recognition test, participants were asked to discriminate between a studied scene and a foil scene that differed in one object, which was either a mentioned or non-mentioned at encoding, and either consistent or inconsistent. The results showed longer fixation durations on mentioned than non-mentioned objects during memorisation, regardless of semantic consistency, and on inconsistent objects but only when these were non-mentioned. Object mention improved memory accuracy and confidence, while semantic consistency did not influence memory. In addition, memory did not depend on total fixation duration on the tested object during encoding. These findings suggest not only that representing information both visually and verbally enhances memory, in line with a dual-coding account, but also that language may be a stronger source of attentional and memory guidance than prior knowledge about objects within scenes. Violations of semantic expectations within a scene lead to greater attentional allocation, but only when object identification is not supported by a label. However, this study also suggests that, in contexts allowing ample viewing and memorisation time, greater attentional allocation at encoding need not directly result in a more robust memory representation.

title: Tracking the Continuous Resolution of Visual Ambiguity Through Movement Trajectories
affiliations:
1. Western Sydney University (AU)
2. University of Geneva (CH)
abstract: Resolving visual ambiguity is a continuous process critical to adaptive human behaviour in complex environments. While traditional discrete-choice tasks have established a strong foundation for understanding final decision outcomes, we can now build upon this work to capture the complex, ongoing processes of evidence accumulation. This talk will demonstrate how continuous measures like computer mouse-tracking can be leveraged to provide a high-resolution window into the competitional dynamics of ambiguous perceptual decisions. We recorded computer mouse trajectories while online participants made high-level categorisation judgements about ambiguous images with competing conceptual interpretations (e.g., 'go right for animal' 'go left for object'). By parametrically manipulating visual ambiguity, we could index how evidence for these competing alternatives is dynamically weighted over the course of the reaching response. The spatial and temporal characteristics of the movement trajectories, such as the physical pull towards the unchosen alternative, capture continuously updating cognitive conflict. These trajectories reveal how ambiguity is resolved in a continuous fashion, providing a time-resolved readout of updating decisional processes. Ultimately, this work highlights the richness of movement trajectories as an accessible, powerful, and sensitive window into the unfolding dynamics of human perception, underscoring their utility in advancing our understanding of choice behaviour.
session_title: Symposium: What vision scientists can learn from continuous movement tracking during decision making

title: Linking categorisation behaviour and category-selective cortex through motor tracking
affiliations:
1. KU Leuven (BE)
2. Georgia Tech (US)
abstract: An important feature of the functional organisation of visual cortex is the presence in occipito-temporal cortex (OTC) of regions that preferentially respond to given categories of visual objects, such as faces, bodies, and scenes. To relate this functional selectivity to human behaviour, previous research has employed a distance-to-bound (DTB) approach, where multivariate brain activity is used to estimate a decision boundary that can then be linked to perceptual decisions. Using this approach, correlations have been found between activity in OTC, and reaction time (RT) when carrying out certain categorisation tasks. However, it remains unclear what determines (a) where in OTC these correlations can be found, (b) with which behavioural categorisation tasks they can be found, and (c) whether they would also be found for other behavioural markers. In the current work, we explored these issues by asking (a) wether category-selective functional regions of OTC would relate to behavioural performance (b) while participants categorised images as belonging or not to their preferred categories. Crucially, (c) we replicated the RT correlations, and asked whether we could extend them to more complex, time-resolved motor movements. We adopted a more basic DTB approach and considered simple, univariate activity, rather than relying on decoding to build our DTB. Our results show that activation in regions selective to faces, bodies, and scenes, is sufficient to relate to behavioural performance while categorising images as being faces, bodies, or scenes, respectively, but also while categorising images as being animate or inanimate. We found brain-behaviour correlations for RT, but also for motor movements, which extends the validity of the DTB approach to time-resolved behavioural performance. Overall, our data adds to evidence that OTC serves to guide categorisation behaviour, and expands this relationship to motor movements.
session_title: Symposium: What vision scientists can learn from continuous movement tracking during decision making

title: Continuous movement tracking during decision making regarding visual social scenes reveals the temporal dynamics of the competition between scene and people valence
affiliations:
1. KU Leuven (BE)
2. Vrije Universiteit Brussel (BE)
abstract: To infer the emotional meaning of complex social interactions, we combine cues from scene context and depicted people. In a recent study (https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.05.08.651182), we used images of social interactions in emotionally loaded contexts, e.g. funerals. Across the full set the valence of the people in the scene was partially dissociated from the valence of the scene context, e.g. people laughing at a funeral. For these incongruent images, behavioral annotations revealed greater reliance on people valence and not the scene valence and fMRI showed stronger contribution of high-level processing. However, these measures did not reveal how valence judgments unfold over time. To investigate these temporal dynamics, we employed continuous mouse-tracking in an online experiment while participants rated image valence during short trials (1200ms). We quantified response dynamics as the deviation or ‘divergence’ of mouse trajectories from the screen’s vertical midline as a function of time and compared the deviation with behavioral annotations and fMRI data. For some incongruent stimuli, trajectories initially deviate toward the wrong response that are later corrected. For congruent images, trajectory divergence correlates with scene/people/image valence (450-1200ms). For incongruent images, divergence first correlates with scene valence (450–850ms) and later with people/image valence (625–1200ms). Comparisons with neurally (fMRI) predicted valence reveals that several regions predict divergence with similar temporal properties. Specifically, for congruent stimuli, predictions from many ROIs predict behavioral divergence at most time points, with the best predictions from mid- and high-level regions. For incongruent stimuli, predictions of scene valence from low-level visual ROIs peak at early time points, while correlations with predictions for people and image valence peak later and are related to mid- and high-level ROIs respectively.  Our findings show the efficiency of continuous movement tracking in studying and understanding complex cognitive processes.
session_title: Symposium: What vision scientists can learn from continuous movement tracking during decision making

title: Introduction to Spatiotemporal Survival Analysis: New insights from distribution analyses of movement trajectories
affiliations: 1. RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau (DE)
abstract: While, to this day, mean reaction time and accuracy analyses dominate the research of the temporal dynamics of human behavior, more recent approaches have been proposed to better capture true human performance. For instance, continuous movement-tracking (CMT) allows to dynamically track responses from initiation to completion, revealing the accumulation of information, emerging response conflicts, self-corrections, and more before the response is completed. Similarly, event history analysis (EHA) has emerged as a powerful tool to analyze the entire distribution of time-to-event data. By looking at both hazard and conditional accuracy functions, the application of EHA has given new insights into response activation, time-locking of effects, changes of effects over time, etc. Here, we introduce a recently developed method that combines the advantages of both of these approaches, namely Spatiotemporal Survival Analysis (StSA). StSA combines the rich data of CMT with the distributional approach of EHA. This is achieved by extracting the spatial information as well as the temporal information of movement along the entire trajectory. Here, the hazard function H(t, space) gives the conditional probability of movement in a spatial bin, given the movement hasn’t occurred within it earlier. Likewise, the conditional accuracy function CA(t, space) gives the probability that, if a movement occurs within a certain spatial bin within time bin t, it was toward the correct target. Key advantages of such an approach are that (1) all available data is used, (2) the dynamics of continuous movement and processing are captured, (3) it offers a model-free and versatile use for any type of CMT data. Thus, StSA offers a powerful and intuitive way to investigate decision-making along the entire time-course of overt response behavior.
session_title: Symposium: What vision scientists can learn from continuous movement tracking during decision making

title: Modelling Hand Movement Trajectories in Rapid Chase
affiliations:
1. RPTU University Kaiserslautern Landau (DE)
2. KU Leuven (BE)
abstract: Many visual perception processes have been argued to be feedforward processes. In response priming, the Rapid Chase Theory postulates that primes initiate motor responses that are later taken over by targets depending on stimulus onset asynchrony (Schmidt et al., 2006). Continuous movement-tracking (CMT) is an efficient method for examining the dynamics of such a perceptual process. This method also enables modelling cognitive processes from the “outside in,” i.e., inferring latent activation processes from observable motor behaviour. If response priming is a feedforward process, then the motor response to primes and targets should closely reflect the underlying activation dynamics. To capture this, hand trajectories from 4 experimental conditions from Schmidt et al. (2006) are first analysed and then used to simulate hand movements. Each movement is characterized by a decision time (initiation latency) and an acceleration parameter (response force). Parameter distributions were estimated using Bayesian inference from a single experimental condition (strong target, high contrast). The remaining three conditions are then simulated by systematically adjusting these parameters according to differences in stimulus properties (target strength and contrast), rather than refitting the model. This approach tests whether a single set of inferred parameters can generalize across conditions when modulated by stimulus properties. Both empirical and simulated data are analysed using Spatiotemporal Survival Analysis (StSA). This distributional approach captures the time course of response activation without data trimming or averaging, instead leveraging the full dataset. Results show that early responses are driven by prime information and later overtaken by target-driven activation across all conditions. Target takeover times remain stable, while acceleration varies with stimulus properties. The simulations successfully reproduce this pattern, supporting feedforward accounts of visuomotor processing.
session_title: Symposium: What vision scientists can learn from continuous movement tracking during decision making

title: Dissociating feedforward encoding from recurrent integration: Evidence from EEG decoding, masking, attention, expectation, and NMDA blockade
affiliations:
1. University of Amsterdam (NL)
2. Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (NL)
abstract: A central question in visual neuroscience is what distinct functional roles are carried by feedforward and recurrent processes, and how these processes are selectively modulated by sensory input, top-down factors, and neurochemical mechanisms. Here, we report a set of three EEG decoding studies to dissociate feedforward encoding from recurrent processing across multiple manipulations targeting perceptual input strength, attention, expectation, and NMDA receptor function. Using visual stimuli that vary in feature complexity, we distinguish early feedforward encoding of local contrast, intermediate processing of collinearity associated with lateral interactions, and later processing of illusory surfaces associated with feedback-dependent integration. Time-resolved decoding revealed a consistent dissociation across studies: early feedforward signals (~80 ms) were largely preserved across manipulations, whereas later stages (~200–300 ms), reflecting recurrent processing, were selectively modulated. First, we directly compared perceptual impairments (masking) and attentional limitations (attentional blink) under matched behavioral performance. Masking strongly reduced later-stage decoding, consistent with disrupted recurrent processing, whereas attentional limitations preserved local recurrent processing while preventing global recurrent processing associated with conscious access. Second, manipulating expectation and attention showed that top-down influences selectively affected later processing stages, with expectation effects emerging only when stimuli were task-relevant and attended, and no modulation of early feedforward encoding. Third, pharmacological manipulation using the NMDA receptor antagonist memantine provided causal evidence for the role of recurrent processing, selectively altering decoding of illusory surfaces, a marker of feedback-dependent integration, while leaving earlier stages largely unaffected. Together, these findings demonstrate that feedforward and recurrent processes make distinct contributions to visual processing, with feedforward activity supporting robust early feature encoding and recurrent processing—spanning lateral and feedback interactions—supporting feature integration and conscious access. Across perceptual, attentional, and pharmacological manipulations, effects consistently target recurrent stages while leaving initial sensory encoding largely intact.

title: Computational role of ventral bank STS neurons in the hierarchical visual processing of socially interacting bodies
affiliations:
1. CIN / HIH, Univ Clinic Tuebingen (DE)
2. KU Leuven (BE)
abstract: Social interactions can be recognized from the dynamic relationships between moving bodies, even from highly impoverished stimuli as the ones by Heider and Simmel. The superior temporal sulcus (STS) has been proposed as possible neural substrate for this processing. Simple neural theories can account for this function by hierarchical processing, where at a first level individual agents are recognized, and then their spatio-temporal relationship during interaction is processed at a higher level. How the STS contributes to these computations at the single-cell level is completely unknown. METHODS:  We present a hierarchical neural recognition model that implements the proposed computational principles. In addition, we tested how neurons in the ventral bank of the superior temporal sulcus (STS) of macaques might contribute to this processing. For this purpose, we presented individual and pairs of monkey avatars whose spatial relationship was modified to make them consistent or inconsistent with social interactions. RESULTS:  Our model successfully recognizes social interactions from abstract stimuli as well as during third-party observation of interacting full bodies. The recorded ventral bank STS units showed robust tuning to individual agents and their spatial parameters. Beyond a normalizing effect induced by the presence of a second agent, we failed to find a consistent influence of social interaction. CONCLUSIONS: While two level models account successfully for social interaction recognition from different stimulus classes, our experiment suggest that single units in the ventral bank of the STS are not performing the critical computations for the analysis of social interaction in third-party social interaction perception. Within a potential hierarchical processing stream their role thus likely is the processing of individual agents and their spatio-temporal parameters.

title: Emergence and dynamics of visual content in high-level visual cortex
affiliations:
1. Psychophysics and Neural Dynamics Lab, Department of Radiology, Lausanne University Hospital and University of Lausanne (CH)
2. The Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
3. EEG and Epilepsy Unit, Geneva University Hospitals and University of Geneva (CH)
4. Human Neuron Lab, Fundamental and Clinical Neuroscience Departments, University of Geneva (CH)
5. Neurology division, Clinical Neuroscience Department, Geneva University Hospitals (CH)
6. Laboratory of Psychophysics, Brain Mind Institute, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (CH)
abstract: Recognition of meaningful visual scenes is thought to progress from low-level feature processing in early visual cortex to high-level representations in ventral temporal areas, via a rapid increase in evoked neural activity along the ventral stream. However, theories differ on how accessible visual content emerges. Some propose distributed broadcasting across large-scale networks, while others emphasize more locally sustained dynamics within ventral regions that maintain content-related information beyond the evoked response. Using decoding and representational generalization analyses on intracranial stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recordings from seven patients with epilepsy, we tracked the emergence and temporal dynamics of visual content across electrodes sampling multiple brain regions and cortical depths. Participants either passively viewed or actively discriminated the category (animals vs. food) of 2-second images that were intact, phase-scrambled, or progressively descrambled, matched for low-level features. Although evoked responses in the broadband signal were weak and evident only in a small subset of electrodes in visual temporal cortex, we observed sustained and stable representations of real images throughout the presentation, relative to scrambled images. These representations emerged following the actual revealing of image content (intact or progressively descrambled) and were amplified during the active compared to the passive task, primarily involving temporal electrodes.  These initial results suggest that visual content is maintained beyond the initial feedforward sweep and may involve recurrent, temporally extended representations in ventral regions during image perception. Future analyses will investigate the specific contributions of other areas, such as frontal cortex, and their potential interactions with ventral stream processing of visual content across different frequency bands.

title: The visual front-end as a theorem: deriving early vision rather than measuring it.
affiliations: 1. Eindhoven University of Technology (NL)
abstract: Early vision is usually characterized by measurement and then modeled to fit the recordings. Here the opposite program is persued: ask what an optimal observer is obliged to do and derive the front-end before recording it. The chain is short and forced. A sample of light is a finite aperture demanding only linearity, a location, a free width and maximal non-commitment (maximum entropy) yield a unique shape — the Gaussian. To read context, the observer must reach a neighboring point composing infinitesimal steps shows the translation operator to be the exponential of the derivative, whose expansion is the Taylor series. Local structure is therefore the local jet of derivatives. Because differentiating noisy data is ill-posed, a theorem of Schwartz lets us differentiate the smooth operator instead of the image: the derivative-of-Gaussian kernels are the front-end receptive fields. The same axiomatic temper governs intensity. The stimulus axis is a half-line whose only invariant metric is the ratio, forcing a logarithmic code — Weber–Fechner. A cone, confined to a decade-and-a-half of useful range, holds its operating point by subtractive-in-log feedback from horizontal cells, whose synaptic triad is, almost literally, a field-effect transistor regulating the gate.
