And the very Gaussian-derivative filters predicted above are those that emerge unsupervised from principal- and independent-component analysis of natural-image patches they are optimal regularizers, and steerable. Opponent color channels arise in the same way, as the decorrelating principal components of the cone signals. At every stage — sampling, differentiation, intensity coding, gain control, feature learning, and color — the optimal mathematical solution and the measured biology coincide. The visual system does not merely approximate good design it appears to instantiate the design that first principles make inevitable.

title: Simulation-informed estimation of minimally required fMRI runs for population receptive field (pRF) mapping
affiliations: 1. High Field MR Center, Center for Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering, Medical University of Vienna (AT)
abstract: Population receptive field (pRF) modelling characterises how visual information is represented in the human visual cortex. These models are estimated using retinotopy experiments with multiple runs of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Yet no principled guidelines exist for selecting the number of runs required for reliable parameter estimation. Too few runs risk unreliable estimates too many waste acquisition time and resources. We propose a simulation-informed framework that links contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) to pRF estimation accuracy and translates this relationship into a practical recommendation for the number of runs. We simulated pRF responses for the NYU retinotopy dataset’s bar stimulus with known ground truth and additive white Gaussian noise, establishing stimulus-specific relationships between CNR and pRF estimation error, quantified by median root-mean-square error (RMS) across simulations. RMS for pRF position (x, y) and polar angle follows power-law scaling with CNR, with exponents −0.81, −0.86, and −1.16, while eccentricity errors follow an exponential decay (rate ≈0.50). These relationships define the CNR required to achieve any desired pRF parameter accuracy. To translate these findings to empirical data, we analysed the NYU retinotopy dataset (n = 44, up to 12 runs/subject). Across subjects, the median voxel-wise CNR computed from pRF time series scales with the number of averaged runs following a power-law (exponent ≈0.41). This is lower than the ideal √N scaling (exponent 0.5), reflecting structured noise in fMRI data.  By connecting the empirical CNR-versus-runs relationship with the simulation-derived CNR-versus-error relationship, the framework yields a direct mapping from the number of runs to expected accuracy. Researchers can specify a target accuracy for any pRF parameter and solve for the required number of runs. This provides a principled tool for planning pRF experiments and comparing efficiency across stimuli. Ultimately, this reduces acquisition time while ensuring reliable pRF estimates and enabling clinically feasible retinotopy experiments.

title: Transformation from visual cues to perceived realism revealed by fMRI and MEG
affiliations:
1. National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (JP)
2. Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JP)
3. Justus-Liebig University Giessen (DE)
4. The University of Osaka (JP)
abstract: Although the human visual system easily perceives the realism of the visual world, the neural basis of realism perception remains unclear. Because any physical differences between real and unreal images can be reduced to differences in image features, prevailing neurocomputational models predict that realism should be encoded within ventral visual areas that hierarchically process visual features. Contrary to this prediction, our results demonstrate a spatiotemporal transformation from feature-based to percept-based representations of realism. Using fMRI recordings obtained while observers viewed a series of content-matched images with different levels of realism (100 %, 90 %, ……, 0 %) generated by neural style transfer, we found that activity patterns in early visual areas (V1-V3) aligned with subband image statistics, and ventral (VTC) and early dorsal (V3A/B) visual areas aligned with style features. In contrast, higher dorsal visual areas (IPS1-IPS5) exhibited a feature-independent representation that predicted perceived realism: even after removing the variance explained by image features, perceived realism remained predictable only in higher dorsal visual areas, but not in the other visual areas. Furthermore, source-localized MEG signals in early, ventral, and early dorsal visual areas successfully predicted perceived realism at early latencies (peaking at 110-130 ms), whereas those in higher dorsal visual areas did so at later latencies (peaking at 350-370 ms). Our findings indicate that perceived realism is not merely derived from combinations of image features, but is reformatted into an abstract perceptual representation in higher dorsal visual areas.

title: SYNS: A Decade of Natural Scenes for Perception Science
affiliations:
1. School of Psychology, University of Southampton (UK)
2. Centre for AI & Society, York University (CA)
abstract: This year marks the 10th anniversary of the Southampton–York Natural Scenes (SYNS) dataset, a multimodal resource developed to characterise the statistical structure of natural environments and to support normative and computational accounts of visual perception. SYNS provides densely sampled, spatially co-registered measurements of indoor and outdoor scenes, combining LiDAR-derived range data, calibrated stereo image pairs, and high dynamic range (HDR) images. This integration of geometric and photometric information enables direct quantification of the relationship between image structure and 3D scene layout under ecologically valid conditions. Over the past decade, SYNS has supported a programme of work examining how natural scene statistics constrain perceptual encoding and inference. This work has revealed regularities in depth distributions, surface orientation, and luminance and colour statistics that are consistent with efficient coding principles and Bayesian models of perception. The availability of ground-truth geometry alongside rich image measurements has enabled systematic evaluation of the cues supporting depth perception and figure–ground organisation and has provided a common benchmark for comparing human and computational models of vision.  We will review these contributions and highlight recent unpublished work that builds on this foundation. This includes analyses of how local image structure relates to scene geometry at object boundaries, and psychophysical investigations of how observers integrate multiple cues (e.g. contrast, orientation, disparity, and colour) when making depth judgements in natural scenes. Across these lines of work, a consistent theme is that relatively simple image statistics carry substantial information about 3D structure, and that human observers are sensitive to and exploit these regularities in a manner shaped by spatial scale and perceptual priors. Together, these findings place further constraints on models of depth estimation and contour processing and demonstrate how multimodal natural scene statistics can inform theories of visual inference.
session_title: Symposium: CPC @ ECVP: Perception as Inference Across Scales — from natural scene statistics to neural computation and clinical translation

title: Previews induce long lasting (~1s) visual processing
affiliations:
1. EPFL (CH)
2. CHUV (CH)
abstract: In classical models of vision, a stimulus is processed along the visual hierarchy, ultimately giving rise to its percept. Here, we demonstrate that the processing of even simple, briefly presented stimuli can extend over approximately one second and exhibits complex temporal dynamics. We presented a vernier stimulus flanked by one cube on each side for 20 ms in the visual periphery. Performance was markedly impaired compared to when the vernier was presented alone (a classic crowding effect), or when the vernier and cubes were presented for 160 ms (an uncrowding effect). Strikingly, a 20 ms preview of the cubes alone, presented prior to the 20 ms vernier–cube stimulus, resulted in performance comparable to that observed with the 160 ms presentation. This facilitative effect persisted for interstimulus intervals (ISIs) of up to 1 second, suggesting that the preview initiates or primes the processing of the cubes.Critically, inserting distractor stimuli (e.g., scrambled lines) during the ISI abolished the preview effect. To investigate the neural mechanisms underlying this phenomenon, we recorded EEG in the cubes preview, as well as in a control condition in which the scrambled lines served as the preview. Owing to the long ISI (600 ms), the EEG signals revealed two temporally distinct components: one associated with the preview and another with the subsequent vernier–cube stimulus. Notably, left versus right vernier offsets could already be decoded from neural activity following the preview—that is, several hundred milliseconds before the onset of the vernier–cube stimulus. We propose that the presentation of a stimulus, such as a preview, elicits neural activity that persists for at least one second and can strongly influence the processing of subsequent stimuli.

title: Combining previews and backward masking reveals long lasting temporal dynamics of crowding
affiliations:
1. Laboratory of Psychophysics, Brain Mind Institute, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (CH)
2. Laboratoire des Systèmes Perceptifs, École Normale Supérieure (FR)
abstract: Crowding, the deterioration of the perception of a peripheral target when surrounded by flankers, is commonly explained by feedforward-only models. They predict: the more flankers there are, the worse the performance. On the contrary, empirical evidence has shown the opposite can be true, i.e., performance can improve with an increase in flankers, a phenomenon known as uncrowding. Uncrowding emerges when flankers form coherent structures and are presented for at least ~160 ms, suggesting the involvement of feedback processes.   We investigated whether uncrowding can be disrupted by using backward masking in a vernier offset discrimination task with three conditions: a vernier presented alone, flanked by lines (crowded), or by cubes (uncrowded), presented for 120 ms. A subsequently presented line-mask reduces performance in all conditions. Performance was particularly impaired in the cubes condition, indicating that uncrowding is comparatively more vulnerable. Presenting a flanker-only preview (e.g., only cubes for 20 ms before the target) restored performance.   These results indicate that the cube-percept can be modified by temporally surrounding stimuli even after 120 ms presentation time. In several parametric studies we quantified how these modifications are time-sensitive. While the duration of the mask does not impact its disruptive effect, an 8ms ISI between target and mask improves performance. Likewise, the duration of the preview does not have a large effect but presenting the target 60-120 ms after the preview’s offset resulted in optimal performance similar to the no-mask condition.   These results suggest that perceptual grouping unfolds over time, extending beyond stimulus presentation. With a 120 ms presentation of the cubes, the cubes-percept remains fragile as processing can be manipulated by time-sensitive tools: disrupted by a subsequent mask or kickstarted by a preview.

title: Distinct system-level computations underlie perceptual variation across the visual field
affiliations:
1. New York University (US)
2. University of Texas at Austin (US)
abstract: GOAL: Human visual performance varies across eccentricity (distance from gaze) and around polar angle (circular dimension). Perception typically decreases with eccentricity. At isoeccentric locations, performance is superior along the horizontal than the vertical meridian—horizontal-vertical anisotropy—and along the lower than the upper vertical meridian—vertical meridian asymmetry. Whereas retinal factors and cortical surface area account for eccentricity effects, they only partially explain polar angle variations. Here, we investigated whether and how system-level computations transforming visual input into perception underlie these heterogeneities. METHODS: Twelve participants performed an orientation discrimination task with Gabors embedded in dynamic white noise. Using the equivalent noise method and perceptual template model, we estimated three computations limiting visual performance in noise: gain—the system’s ability to linearly amplify the signal nonlinearity—how inputs are nonlinearly transformed and internal noise— intrinsic variability within the visual system, independent of external stimulation. These parameters were evaluated across eccentricity (fovea, parafovea, and perifovea) and around polar angle. RESULTS: We observed the expected performance variations across eccentricity and around polar angle. Performance declined with eccentricity, driven by decreased gain and nonlinearity alongside increased internal noise. Observers with stronger eccentricity effects showed greater gain decreases. Crucially, only gain varied with polar angle—it was higher along the horizontal than the vertical meridian, and along the lower than the upper vertical meridian. These gain asymmetries became more pronounced at further eccentricity and higher spatial frequency, directly paralleling performance asymmetries. CONCLUSION: This dissociation aligns with known variations in neuronal count and tuning. By revealing distinct system-level computations underlying performance differences along eccentricity and around polar angle, our findings link perceptual phenomena to neural architecture. This link provides insights into how the human brain encodes information under neural constraints and refines models of human perception.

title: Testing models of peripheral vision
affiliations:
1. Laboratory of Psychophysics, Brain Mind Institute, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (CH)
2. Department of General Psychology, University of Padova (IT)
abstract: Peripheral vision is worse than foveal vision in terms of spatial resolution, which is often modelled by blur. If blur were the main determinant, then all tasks should be affected in the same way. We examined this hypothesis with two tasks: the Honeycomb illusion (Bertamini et al., 2016), in which fine barbs disappear in peripheral vision while global structure remains visible, and a visual pop-out task, which requires the preservation of the odd-one-out target. The same observers (N = 20) completed both tasks. We first fitted the parameters of an eccentricity-dependent blur model to performance in the Honeycomb task and then tested whether these parameters generalised to the pop-out task. The model captured key aspects of barb disappearance but failed to account for search performance. We then trained autoencoders with latent bottlenecks as models of compression. Two of the four models reproduced barb disappearance in the Honeycomb illusion, but none preserved the pop-out target. Hence, models that explained one task failed on the other. These findings show that candidate models of peripheral representation do not generalise across tasks and thus argue against a single representational constraint, such as blur or compression, as a sufficient account of peripheral perception.

title: Anisotropy of small-number enumeration in peripheral vision
affiliations:
1. Ecole Normale Supérieure (FR)
2. CNRS (FR)
3. KU Leuven (BE)
abstract: Humans can rapidly and accurately enumerate small numbers of items (typically up to four) without counting, a phenomenon known as subitizing. Small-number enumeration has been studied extensively, with most studies using centrally presented displays and/or free viewing. How small numerosities are enumerated in peripheral vision has rarely been systematically examined. However, peripheral vision is characterized by specific contextual interactions among neighboring items, which may modulate enumeration performance. A prominent property of peripheral processing is its radial-tangential anisotropy: interference among items is stronger along the radial than the tangential direction. This anisotropy has been shown for large-number numerosity perception however, whether it also modulates small-number enumeration, which depends on distinct processes, remains unclear. We presented displays of 3 to 6 discs. On each trial, all discs were presented within a single peripheral sector. Discs were arranged either radially or tangentially. Enumeration performance was measured using bias, defined as the signed deviation between reported and presented numerosity, and precision, indexed by the coefficient of variation (CV). Radial arrangements were reported as less numerous than tangential arrangements across all numerosities however, they were also less precise, yielding higher CVs than tangential arrangements. A Bayesian observer model reproduced the dissociation between bias and precision, suggesting that radial arrangements were associated with greater internal noise than tangential arrangements, with noise increasing further with both numerosity and eccentricity. These findings indicate that small-number enumeration in peripheral vision is strongly shaped by radial-tangential anisotropy and highlight the importance of spatial interactions in determining enumeration performance.

title: Temporal dynamics of feedforward and feedback processes in visual perception: data and model using the flip tilt illusion
affiliations: 1. Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics (DE)
abstract: Visual perception relies on both fast feedforward sensory signals and slower feedback processes involved in perceptual hypothesis testing. This study investigates their temporal dynamics through visual psychophysical experiments and computational modeling. Feedback processes are stronger in the central visual field, according to the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy theory (Zhaoping, 2019) and recent anatomical evidence (Majka et al., 2026). Accordingly, we examine perception in the central visual field using stimuli that normally evoke the flip tilt illusion only in the peripheral visual field. This illusion concerns the perceived orientation (tilt) of a pair of dots, defined by the alignment between the two dots. When the pair is heterogenous (i.e., one black dot and one white dot on a gray background) rather than homogeneous (two black or two white dots), the perceived tilt is orthogonal to the actual tilt, this is the flip-tilt illusion, which is typically absent in the central visual field because feedback processes veto misleading feedforward signals arising from V1 responses to the dot pairs (Zhaoping, 2020). We used four types of stimuli: uniformly oriented hetero-pairs (uniform-hetero), uniformly oriented homo-pairs (uniform-homo), and equal mixtures of the uniform-hetero and uniform-homo stimuli whose orientations were either parallel (parallel-mixed) or orthogonal (orthogonal-mixed) to each other. Each stimulus was presented in the central visual field for a brief duration t before being masked, the feedback process should be interrupted when t was sufficiently short.  Observers reported whether the perceived orientation was tilted clockwise or counterclockwise relative to vertical.  For uniform-homo stimuli, performance was worse at shorter t, but perception remained veridical. In contrast, uniform-hetero stimuli yielded veridical perception at long t but induced the flip tilt illusion at short t. Performance for parallel-mixed and orthogonal-mixed stimuli across t reflects interactions between feedforward and feedback processes. A model of the two processes accounts for the data.

title: Humans aim for the center when crossing a moving gap
affiliations:
1. Univ Gustave Eiffel, COSYS-PICS-L (FR)
2. Univ Gustave Eiffel, Université Paris Cité, LaPEA (FR)
abstract: Visual control of locomotion is essential for catching preys, reaching goals or avoiding threats. Some studies have shown that locomotor interception relies on nulling changes in target bearing angle. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that humans tend to cross a moving gap close to its centre, suggesting that they rely on an interception strategy directed towards the gap centre instead of avoiding obstacles. In the present study, we tested this hypothesis by asking participants (N=21), immersed in a minimalist virtual environment, to walk towards a target located 15-m ahead while two moving obstacles crossed their path orthogonally. Spatiotemporal dynamics of the gap formed by these obstacles were manipulated across four conditions: (i) a control condition in which the gap size and the gap-centre velocity were maintained constant (ii) a size-only condition in which the gap size increased while the velocity of its centre remained constant and two conditions in which the gap-centre velocity was either (iii) accelerated by expanding the gap from the front or (iv) decelerated by expanding it from the rear. Initial lateral distance of the gap from the participants was also manipulated according to 5 offset conditions, resulting for participants to arrive at different positions in the gap if they did not regulate their behaviour. Results show that in all our conditions participants dynamically regulated their locomotion by adjusting both their speed and direction in order to cross the gap closer to its centre, even when such regulations were not required to safely pass between obstacles. These findings confirm that participants cross gaps in their centre and suggest that they mainly use an interception strategy rather than avoiding obstacles. These results will be discussed in light of constant bearing angle strategy

title: Do we anticipate the position of an object differently when we cause its motion?
affiliations: 1. Laboratoire interdisciplinaire des sciences du numérique (FR)
abstract: How our ability to act on the environment shapes visual processing remains an underexplored research field with some studies suggesting that the experience of controlling one’s actions and their consequences may influence how we predict the future position of a moving object. This study sought to deepen our understanding of the relationship between self-agency and visual anticipation across three experiments using the representational momentum (RM) paradigm. Experiment 1 (N=32) showed that a key press triggering a dot's movement reduced motion anticipation compared to a computer-initiated movement. Experiments 2 and 3 added the notion of freedom of choice by presenting two dots to the participant and letting them choose which one to set in motion (free choice), instructing them which dot to set in motion (constrained choice), or letting them observe the dot’s motion without any involvement on their part (passive observation). Our results showed again that anticipation is reduced when we initiate the movement of the dot (free and constrained choice) compared to the computer initiating the movement. However, freedom of choice did not modulate this effect. Experiment 3 was the same as experiment 2 but with additional affordant contextual cues (tunnels along the dots’ trajectories) that could bias visual anticipation. The comparison between experiments 2 and 3 showed that the addition of affordances increased anticipation without interfering with the effect of self-agency. This study suggests that being the author of an object’s motion influences its visual anticipation independently of one’s freedom of action and contextual cues.

title: Catch Me If You Can: Combining a Tactile Bracelet and Belt to Enhance Grasping Range
affiliations:
1. Institute of Cognitive Science, University of Osnabrück (DE)
2. feelSpace GmbH (DE)
3. Department of Neurophysiology, University Medical Centre Hamburg-Eppendorf (DE)
abstract: To enable visually impaired people to grasp distant objects placed outside their reach, we have developed GRETA, the assistive system that integrates the tactile bracelet with the feelSpace naviBelt for spatial navigation. We built the system based on our previous work on the automated hand navigation system (HANS) that can guide the hand of the bracelet user to the target object without the assistance of an external operator. The new integrated assistive system is controlled via auditory commands processed by the Android app, enabling autonomous exploration of the surrounding space. The system processes depth information (obtained from the smartphone via ARCore Depth API) and matches it with the objects detected in the scene by HANS. Upon finding the specified target object, based on its distance from the user, the system decides whether to send vibrations to the bracelet (fine-grained movements of the hand) or to the belt (coarse-grained movements of the whole body). The system automatically switches between the currently active device in real-time based on the user's position change, taking into account the speed of movement. We are testing the system in several scenarios, differing in the distance and number of obstacles the user has to pass to reach the target object, for the initial validation of the system with a group of blindfolded, normally-sighted participants. Afterwards, we plan to prepare a detailed training protocol for blind users. The protocol will enable to learn how to use the system in real-life contexts without any assistance from another person. Overall, the integration of the bracelet and the belt within a single assistive system vastly enhances utility, enabling users to grasp target objects not only in scenarios when they are immediately within reach. It is a crucial step in the project life cycle, moving it much closer to real-world applications.

title: High lights and low lights: A dissociation between illumination and contrast in obstacle avoidance
affiliations: 1. University of Aberdeen (UK)
abstract: Previously, we showed that safety margins during manual obstacle avoidance increase under mesopic lighting. In many XR applications, users interact with the environment without seeing their real hands, instead relying on virtual representations. We investigated in two experiments how illumination and obstacle contrast affect safety margins when avoiding virtual obstacles with virtual hand representations. Participants performed an obstacle avoidance task in a mirror setup. A virtual cuboid appeared as a mirror reflection in the workspace. Motion tracking markers on the index finger and the ulnar side of the hand were visualised as two rectangles moving in the x-y plane. In Experiment 1 (N=25), workspace and obstacle illumination was either high or low. In Experiment 2 (N=24), overall illumination was low, but the area beneath the obstacle had either high or low contrast relative to the background. In both experiments, collision feedback was manipulated: the area beneath the obstacle turned red upon contact. Safety margins were affected by illumination and contrast in opposite ways. Replicating our previous findings, safety margins were larger under low illumination even with virtual hands. In contrast, safety margins were larger for high-contrast obstacles. Collision feedback also increased safety margins. Our findings indicate that only illumination levels in the mesopic range increase sensory uncertainty. The increased safety margins for lower light levels might therefore be an automatic response to increased noise in the perceptual system. Manipulating contrast levels changes the saliency of the obstacle. Increased saliency of the obstacle might be seen as a warning signal which overshadows the light level effect. Overall, these findings show that safety margins are not determined by uncertainty alone, but by context-dependent interpretations of risk. (Supported by ESRC grant ES/V005170/1 to CH)

title: Pushing the envelope: Active viewing drives boundary extension
affiliations: 1. The New School (US)
abstract: When we actively move to view a scene, planning those movements requires predicting what we will see next.  Sensorimotor predictions lie at the core of the “active learning” advantage, wherein observers better remember information if they can control what they see, and when they see it.  Compared to passive viewing, active viewing may increase memory precision because it better aligns incoming visual input with the observer’s current preparatory and attentional state.  Here, we asked whether visual predictions generated during active viewing not only enhance memory for what was seen, but also bias memory toward details which were never visible.  In Experiment 1, observers viewed scene images by either using their mouse to actively move a small viewing aperture, or passively watching a replay of another participant’s viewing trajectory.  After a 3-s exploration period, they completed a recognition memory test in which they discriminated the final view visible through the aperture from a decoy view which was slightly zoomed-in or zoomed-out.  Active viewers showed robust boundary extension, more frequently selecting zoomed-out decoys than zoomed-in decoys passive viewers showed the opposite pattern, consistent with boundary contraction.  If active viewing drives greater boundary extension due to motor predictions, active viewers should specifically misremember having seen information in the direction their viewing trajectory was headed.  In Experiment 2, we displaced the decoy view forward or backward relative to the participant’s last heading direction.  Active viewers’ memory was biased toward unseen information in front of their viewing trajectory, and this bias was stronger than for passive viewers.  Thus active exploration drives memory toward predicted future views — not just any unseen content.  Together, these experiments demonstrate that sensorimotor predictions cause us to actively fill in what lies beyond a visible boundary.  We conclude that active viewing constructs richer, yet more inferential, memory representations than passive viewing.

title: Pantomimed action detection reflects intuitive knowledge about visuomotor feedback
affiliations: 1. Johns Hopkins University (US)
abstract: Visually guided action arises from a complex synergy between perceptual and motor systems when someone grabs a cup to take a drink, for example, the mechanics of their reach are updated online in response to evolving perceptual input. To what extent are ordinary observers aware of this component of others’ goal-directed behavior? Here, we explored this question through “pantomimed actions” — actions directed towards imaginary objects. We created a stimulus set of videos where agents performed both genuine object-directed actions (e.g., stepping over a box), and pantomimes of those actions (e.g., stepping over an imagined box of similar dimensions). We asked both (a) whether naive observers who watch these videos can distinguish real actions from pantomimed actions, and also (b) which kinds of information underwrite this performance. In Experiment 1, subjects watched videos of real and pantomimed actions side-by-side, with a black ‘censor bar’ covering the real (or imagined) object’s location. Under these conditions, subjects were able to distinguish the two action types at rates above chance for example, they could tell whether someone was stepping over a real (vs merely imagined) box, and also whether someone was shuffling between two real (vs merely imagined) poles. Moreover, subjects' text descriptions of their pantomime detection strategy reflected rich inferences about which features of the movement should be diagnostic. However, in Experiment 2, subjects viewed the same actions but with body movements instead depicted by simple ‘pose skeletons’ (dots connected by lines on a black background) generated from the original videos. Under these conditions, observer performance dropped to chance, despite the kinematic information being preserved across experiments. Together, these results suggest that ordinary people can relate differences in action kinematics to differences in sensory conditions, but that this capacity must be grounded in contextual information about the actor’s relation to their environment.

title: The Integration of Shape Information Across Spatial Scales during the Visual Perception of 3D Object Geometry: Evidence from Deep Neural Networks, ERPs and Eye Tracking
affiliations:
1. University of Southampton (UK)
2. Nottingham Trent University (UK)
3. University of Birmingham (UK)
abstract: The visual perception of 3D object geometry requires the computation of image shape features across different spatial scales from local edges to complex parts, the derivation of 3D spatial configuration, and the integration of these features into structured representations of 3D object geometry. In this talk we outline a series of studies that aim to elucidate the underlying computational processes that support 3D object recognitiion. Using converging evidence from behavioural studies, event-related potentials (ERPs), eye tracking and computational modelling, we show that 3D object recognition occurs in parallel across multiple spatial scales of image features and configural properties. Some limitations of deep convolutional neural networks as models of 3D object recognition are also discussed. We outline a novel multi-pathway parallel architecture for 3D object recognition that combines both compositional (parts-based) and image-based computational pathways.

title: Reward Learning Reshapes Neural Representations of Visual Perception and Imagery
affiliations:
1. School of Psychology, University of Southampton (UK)
2. Department of Psychiatry, University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: To interact effectively with our environment, we must distinguish objects not only based on their perceptual features (e.g., whether a stimulus is a face) but also on their learned significance (e.g., whether a face is familiar or important). These functions are supported by regions along the ventral stream of visual processing. In particular, visual categorisation is supported by category-selective regions along the occipitotemporal ventral stream, such as the fusiform face area (FFA) and parahippocampal place area (PPA), during both perception and imagery. More anterior regions of the temporal cortex support the representation of higher-level information such as familiarity, meaning, and behavioural relevance. However, it remains unclear how learning, particularly reward and punishment, shapes these category representations over time and across tasks. To address this, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure brain activity across two sessions in which participants viewed or imagined faces and houses. Between sessions, they learned that one category was associated with reward and the other with punishment. As expected, occipitotemporal category-selective regions showed reliable responses to faces and houses in both tasks. After learning, brain responses increasingly reflected the motivational value of the categories: multivariate activity patterns across a distributed network more strongly distinguished rewarded from punished stimuli. Crucially, the strongest effects emerged in anterior temporal regions, which are downstream of occipitotemporal category-selective regions. Importantly, these value-related effects did not differ significantly between perception and imagery. These findings show that learning about reward and punishment systematically alters how visual categories are represented at higher levels of the ventral stream. In particular, the anterior temporal cortex appears to integrate learned value into category representations, linking perceptual inputs to their acquired meaning and behavioural relevance. The generalization of these effects across perception and imagery suggests that learned value is embedded in abstract, task-independent representations.

title: Colour Inference in the Wild: #theDress Ten Years On
affiliations: 1. School of Psychology, University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: #TheDress was born in the world-wide web more than 10 years ago, when the ambiguous photo of a dress revealed striking individual differences in colour perception – many see it white and gold, many others blue and black. Subsequently, research has established that these are not merely differences in colour naming, but a continuous variation of perception. This variation is related to unconscious inferences about the lighting conditions in the photo and to a person’s sleep-wake cycle assumed to mediate inferred lighting conditions. Many candidate optical and physiological causes of the individual differences have been excluded. The perception of #TheDress can be primed by visual stimuli that manipulate the surround of the dress. New images that cause similar individual differences as #TheDress have been found and may be generated through a simple algorithm. However, the known determinants of #TheDress explain only a small amount of individual variation, implying that they only predict individual differences statistically across a large sample of participants. New results show that neither visual nor verbal primes of lighting assumptions affect #TheDress when they do not contain the dress itself. The original assumption that daylight variation is essential to the individual differences has been moderated. Rotating the hue of #TheDress gradually decreases the magnitude of individual variation, implying that individual differences might be stronger along the daylight locus, but not exclusive to it. The colours of #TheShoe, a picture of a shoe that many see turquoise and grey and others pink and white, vary in a direction almost perpendicular to the daylight locus. #TheShoe works by a similar principle as #TheDress: The perception of #TheShoe is correlated with #TheDress, and we can create new images with #TheShoe properties using the #TheDress algorithm. A more detailed understanding is necessary to provide reliable predictions of the striking individual differences.

title: Continuous Psychophysics in the Clinic
affiliations:
1. University of Southampton (UK)
2. University Hospital Southampton (UK)
3. Salisbury District Hospital (UK)
abstract: Standard clinical vision tests (e.g., acuity charts, perimetry) involve a trade‑off between ease of administration and informativeness: some are quick but narrowly focused, whereas others provide richer information at the cost of time and effort. This trade‑off limits the assessment of functional vision relevant to everyday visual performance in routine clinical practice. Continuous psychophysics offers a promising alternative, using an intuitive target‑tracking task to obtain reliable estimates of visual and motor function (Bonnen et al., 2015; Straub & Rothkopf, 2022). In a pilot study, we evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and reliability of continuous psychophysics in clinical settings and explored the association of tracking performance with visual acuity. Twelve adults with retinal disease (54–86 years) attending an intravitreal injection clinic completed two same‑day target‑tracking sessions and rated the task using the System Usability Scale (SUS). Participants used a mouse to track a randomly moving concentric Gabor target (10 trials per session); testing was binocular and unaided. The task was successfully integrated into clinical routine, with short session durations (≈ 4 minutes including self-paced breaks) and high completion rates (11 participants completed both sessions), supporting feasibility. Notably, participants rated the task as highly acceptable (mean SUS > 85; 0–100 scale, higher = better). Tracking performance indices showed excellent test–retest reliability (rs ≥ .84, ps < .05, N = 6) and a clear improvement between sessions in post‑injection assessments (N = 5), consistent with short‑term functional recovery and changes in optical correction (N = 1). Surprisingly, tracking performance was not significantly associated with visual acuity, suggesting that the task captures functional aspects not indexed by acuity alone. These findings support the translational potential of continuous psychophysics, and motivate larger studies and the development of methods to disentangle visual and motor contributions to target-tracking performance.
