title: Eye movements whilst watching TV could diagnose dementia
affiliations: 1. Loughborough University (UK)
abstract:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterised by progressive cognitive decline that impacts ocular motor control. Our previous research has shown that eye movement tasks can be used to predict AD in preclinical dementia (Wilcockson, et al., 2019) even as early as 12-years in advance (Begde, et al., 2024), or whilst in the prodromal subjective cognitive decline stage (Wilcockson, et al., 2025). However, the traditional ‘gold standard’ antisaccade task is susceptible to confounding individual differences, including working memory capacity, inhibitory control, and visual imagery (e.g., aphantasia; Wilcockson et al., in prep). These variables may compromise the reliability of the antisaccade task as a pure measure of neurodegeneration.

To address these limitations, we developed an ecologically valid, naturalistic task that measures the dissociation between top-down and bottom-up inhibitory control. Rather than viewing abstract stimuli, participants viewed video sequences while their eye movements were recorded. Participants were tasked with answering specific questions that required them to fixate on task-relevant stimuli rather than the most visually salient features of the scene. This design mirrors the inhibitory demands of an antisaccade task but within a familiar context. Four groups were recruited: AD, Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), older controls, and young controls.

Analysis revealed significant differences in gaze patterns between clinical groups and healthy controls. Both AD and MCI patients exhibited impaired top-down executive control, frequently failing to inhibit gaze toward salient but task-irrelevant stimuli. Furthermore, performance on this video task was significantly correlated with standardised memory scores, suggesting a robust link between ocular motor behaviour and general cognitive function.

These results indicate that eye movement measurement during naturalistic video viewing could serve as a non-invasive, accessible screening tool for cognitive decline. This approach may offer a more reliable and patient-friendly alternative to traditional diagnostic assessments, potentially facilitating earlier intervention and more accurate monitoring of disease progression.

title: Apraxia Disrupts the Spatiotemporal Structure of Grasping, Despite Preserved Aperture Scaling
affiliations:
1. York University (CA)
2. Imperial College London (UK)
3. University of Cambridge (UK)
4. Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust (UK)
abstract: Limb apraxia is a neurobehavioural consequence of stroke, characterized by impaired skilled action that cannot be attributed to basic motor impairments. It has traditionally been thought to selectively disrupt higher-level action representations while preserving basic visuomotor control. However, this view is supported largely by peak-derived metrics, such as maximum grip aperture (MGA), which may overlook potential deficits in the fine-grained spatiotemporal structure of movements. To address this gap, we assessed 25 patients with clinically-confirmed apraxia and 25 age-matched controls on an Efron-block width-scaling task (four objects, 5mm increments) involving reach-to-grasp movements (Experiment 1). We also examined 25 younger and 25 older healthy adults to determine whether any observed deficits were stroke-specific rather than age-related (Experiment 2). Consistent with previous findings, apraxic patients successfully scaled their MGA with object size, similar to controls. However, patients exhibited significantly slower movements and prolonged time to MGA. To assess the spatiotemporal structure of the movements, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) was used to measure the similarity between trajectory pairs across object sizes. The observed similarity matrix was then correlated with an ideal object size–based model. Although both patients and controls exhibited strong correspondence with the size model, apraxic patients showed significantly weaker correspondence compared to controls, even when using their ipsilesional hands. Bayesian analysis of Experiment 2 supported the null hypothesis, revealing that young and older adults showed equivalent object size–based trajectory organization patterns. Furthermore, both healthy age groups demonstrated stronger correspondence with the size model than apraxic patients’ ipsilesional hands. These findings uncover novel deficits in apraxic reach-to-grasp behaviour. While object-related aperture scaling remains intact, the spatiotemporal organization of trajectories is disrupted: a deficit that is distinct from healthy aging, and an impairment previously under-characterized in apraxia.

title: Bistable Perception as a Window into Non-Spatial Deficits in Spatial Neglect
affiliations: 1. Clinical Neuropsychology, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (DE)
abstract: Patients with spatial neglect show not only spatial deficits but also non-spatial impairments in visual perception and attention. One prominent non-spatial feature is a marked slowing of perceptual alternations during binocular rivalry (BR), which has been hypothesized to result from reduced habituation to the currently dominant stimulus – analogous to difficulties disengaging from attended spatial locations. In this study, we specifically tested this hypothesis in a group of patients with right-hemisphere lesions (N=31), spanning a range of neglect severity from none to severe, and an age-matched healthy control group. After viewing an unambiguous stimulus, participants were presented with an ambiguous BR display, composed of the previously seen stimulus (e.g., a house) and a new, previously unseen stimulus (e.g., a face). Compared to patients without neglect and healthy controls, neglect patients showed reduced switching to the previously unseen stimulus, consistent with diminished habituation. As a consequence of reduced habituation, neglect patients should show an increased sensitivity to saliency differences in the BR stimuli. We examined this in further experiments, replicating the result with contrast-modulated stimuli (high- and low-contrast gratings) and partially extending it to emotion-modulated stimuli (fearful, happy, and neutral faces vs. houses). We also tested whether the BR alternation rate findings generalized to another form of bistability, namely a structure-from-motion (SfM) sphere with an ambiguous rotation direction. The alternation rate of the SfM sphere also correlated with neglect severity, ruling out purely eye-based explanations that would account for only the BR results. Overall, our results are in line with the “reduced-habituation” hypothesis that might link spatial and non-spatial deficits in spatial neglect.

title: Connective Field Modeling Reveals Experience-Dependent Eccentricity Biases in Category-Selective Visual Cortex
affiliations:
1. University of Hamburg (DE)
2. Lucid Medical Diagnostics (IN)
3. LV Prasad Eye Institute (IN)
abstract: Category-selective regions in the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC) have been shown to exhibit systematic eccentricity biases: Face-selective areas seem to be preferentially linked to fovea, while place-selective areas have been found to feature a peripheral visual field preference. The present study tested whether these eccentricity biases emerge through early visual experience. We applied Connective-field (CF) modeling to resting-state fMRI data of normally sighted controls (n = 25), permanently congenitally blind individuals (n = 9), and individuals with reversed dense bilateral congenital cataracts (n = 20). CF-modeling allows us to estimate how downstream visual areas sample from retinotopically organized V1.  In normally sighted individuals, CF-modeling demonstrated eccentricity biases previously shown with task-based fMRI: We found more peripheral CF eccentricities for the place-selective collateral sulcus (CoS) than for the face-selective median fusiform-gyrus (mFus). Thus, we were able to extend CF-modeling to visual areas beyond early visual cortex and provided evidence that CF-modeling can quantify eccentricity-biased connectivity in higher-order visual cortex.  Compared to normally sighted controls, permanently congenitally blind humans’ CoS and mFus showed significantly higher eccentricities.  Congenital cataract-reversal individuals exhibited CF eccentricities that were significantly less peripheral than in permanently congenitally blind individuals in the mFus.  Together, these findings demonstrate that eccentricity-biased V1-to-VOTC connectivity can be recovered from resting-state data using CF-modeling and thus represents an appropriate approach to study experience-dependent development of retinotopic biases in the visual processing hierarchy. The altered sampling of higher order visual areas from V1 in individuals with congenital blindness provides evidence for an experience-dependent development of foveal and parafoveal representations in VOTC. The partial but not full recovery of typical eccentricity biases in VOTC in individuals who have suffered from a transient phase of congenital blindness suggests a sensitive (rather than a critical) period for the experience-dependent shaping of retinotopic representations in higher order visual cortex.

title: The role of elevated crowding and impaired integration in the visual deficits of Alzheimer’s Disease
affiliations: 1. University College London (UK)
abstract: Visual deficits are common in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), particularly in the ‘visual-variant AD’ subtype Posterior Cortical Atrophy (PCA). These cortical impairments can be detected using the Graded Incomplete Letters Test (GILT), which measures thresholds for recognising letters degraded by removing pixellated sections. Although GILT thresholds are strongly elevated in PCA relative to typical AD (tAD) and healthy ageing, it is unclear whether these impairments derive from higher-level deficits in processes such as global integration (difficulty combining fragmented elements into recognisable objects) or lower-level limitations such as elevated crowding (disruptions from clutter). To test whether these deficits drive impairments in incomplete letter recognition, participants with PCA (n=20), tAD (n=20), and controls (n=20) completed modified GILT variants designed to systematically probe these mechanisms, alongside independent measures of acuity and crowding. Relative to controls, PCA participants showed substantially decreased performance across conditions, with small, non-statistically-significant decreases in tAD. To probe global integration, pixel size was varied: larger pixels that concentrate information loss and increase the need to integrate fragmented features led to the poorest performance, with the best performance for smaller pixels that distribute degradation more evenly. Critically, these effects were not driven by absolute feature size: performance did not differ when whole letter sizes were varied. Adding background noise, which increases visual clutter and challenges global integration, led to additional performance decreases in PCA relative to controls. However, although independent measurements confirmed elevated crowding in PCA, these elevations were insufficient to account for the magnitude of GILT deficits. Reducing crowding (e.g. increasing letter size) also failed to improve GILT performance. Together, these findings indicate that impaired global integration is the primary driver of incomplete letter recognition deficits in PCA, with crowding contributing to a lesser extent. Test variants that more directly target these mechanisms could improve the detection of cortical visual loss.

title: Effects of lithium treatment on threshold and suprathreshold vision in individuals with bipolar disorder: interim findings from the Helios-BD study
affiliations: 1. University of Edinburgh (UK)
abstract: The HELIOS-BD study is a large-scale investigation of the hypothesis that lithium treatment in bipolar disorder acts at the level of the retina to quell hypersensitivity to light. The project integrates multimodal data from individuals with bipolar disorder, euthymic at time of testing, who are treated with lithium (current n = 31) or receiving alternative pharmacotherapy (current n = 43), as well as healthy controls (current n = 49 target n = 60 per group). Here we report findings from the psychophysics arm. To assess vision at threshold, we measured chromatic thresholds and colour and luminance contrast sensitivity functions. To assess processing away from threshold, we evaluated points of subjective equality for desaturated hues (orange and turquoise) and light grey. We also evaluated perceived contrast matching, with chromatic blue-yellow Gabors and luminance contrast-defined Gabors matched to red-green Gabors at four suprathreshold contrast levels. We find differences in contrast processing in the lithium-treated group for threshold tasks, which mainly rely on output from those units most sensitive to the signal, as well as for suprathreshold tasks, which rely on output of much larger and more inter-dependent neuronal populations. At threshold, the lithium-treated group exhibits elevated chromatic thresholds and decreased contrast sensitivity at 2-6 cpd for luminance and 6 cpd (the highest spatial frequency tested) for colour mechanisms. At suprathreshold, points of subjective equality and perceived contrast averages are similar to those of controls, but we observe somewhat broader just noticeable differences for desaturated hues and somewhat noisier perceived contrast matches (i.e., elevated standard errors across trials). These changes point towards increased noise in the visual system, with multiple retinal candidate sites. Noisiness persists at suprathreshold contrast levels, but does not lead to altered appearance in our euthymic observers.

title: Grasping with altered hands: (why) are some sensorimotor transformations more intuitive than others?
affiliations: 1. Bangor University (UK)
abstract: Hand- and arm-operated devices transform or remap the relationship between body movements and end-effector movements. This includes not only complex devices (body-powered prostheses, remote manipulators etc.) but also simple handheld tools. Controlling such devices with fluidity approaching that of natural limb movements requires construction of internal models equivalent to those of biological hands/arms—and is seldom achieved. Across several studies, we show that our ability to internalise tool properties in this way depends strongly on the nature of the induced transformation, suggesting some sensorimotor remappings are easier to internalise, or more intuitive(?) than others. We used motion capture to examine grasping movements made with handheld tools that induce different mappings between hand/arm and end-effector, including varying the gain and direction of grasp opening, and grasp-axis orientation. We also compared different mappings between arm-and-shoulder movement and opening/closing of a body-powered simulated prosthetic hand. Using (relatively) straightforward mechanical devices allows us to isolate specific aspects or sensorimotor remappings, holding other factors constant, while avoiding confounds such as temporal delays. With this approach, we aim to better understand fundamental aspects of human tool use, and to draw generalisable (as opposed to implementation- or device-specific) conclusions. As might be expected, we find that some ‘classes’ of transformation are more difficult to internalise than others. Perhaps more surprisingly, qualitatively similar transformations (e.g. gain of grasp opening) can be substantially harder/easier to internalise depending on quantitative aspects of the remapping. Our data also suggest that visual control strategies for tool use precede development of internal models truly equivalent to those of the hand/arm. We hope that a better understanding of the principles governing how readily different sensorimotor transformations are internalised can inform the design of devices that are fundamentally better suited to human sensorimotor control, and therefore more intuitive to use.
session_title: Symposium: Visuomotor transforms in prostheses, virtual reality, and teleoperation

title: Adapting to sensorimotor delays in continuous motor control tasks
affiliations: 1. Technical University of Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: With the increased use of human-machine technologies, we are also increasingly more exposed to sensorimotor delays. For instance, when initiating an action using a prosthetic or teleoperation tool or even our own hand in Virtual Reality (VR), the visual feedback of that action generally occurs at a delay as the system needs time to process the user input into an output. Such delays can vary from a few to several hundreds of milliseconds depending on the complexities involved, and the sensorimotor system somehow must deal with these delays for movement planning. In some cases, slowing down movements to let the feedback catch up can help in performing a visuomotor task, in other cases exposure to delay will lead to a shift in perceived timing through delay adaptation. Here we will particularly focus on delay adaptation in continuous movement tasks such as target tracking and interception. We show that delay adaptation occurs only in particular conditions that limit the solution space to requiring a temporal shift to increase performance and where the environment provides information that allows prediction of the target movement ahead of time. Furthermore, transfer of delay adaptation is limited to conditions that use the same control input even if the visual display for the task and feedback remains the same, but can survive spatial offsets between hand and controlled object locations in VR. Moreover, repeated exposure to the delay can lead to behavioural and/or perceived time-shift savings depending on the task. In short, delay adaptation for continuous movements strongly depends on the interplay of the control device, visuomotor task and the environment in which the task is to be performed. These findings are of particular importance for the further development of prosthetic, teleoperation and virtual reality tools and the environments in which they are to be used.
session_title: Symposium: Visuomotor transforms in prostheses, virtual reality, and teleoperation

title: Exploring the effects of spatial mismatches in teleoperation
affiliations:
1. University of Nottingham (UK)
2. UK Atomic Energy Authority, Remote Applications in Challenging Environments (UK)
abstract: Teleoperation has been, and is likely to remain, a widely used approach for remote control across many sectors (e.g., nuclear energy) despite increasing interest in AI/ML-based automation. During teleoperation, humans are faced with a fundamentally different visuomotor control loop whereby the human and robot are operating in completely different workspaces. A consequence of this is that visual information about the remote workspace (e.g., robot arms, target objects) must be relayed back to the operator via multiple camera feeds. In a qualitative project, we investigated the difficulties experienced by teleoperators in the nuclear energy industry when having to rely on such camera feeds to guide their movements. Think-aloud procedures, cognitive work analyses, and critical decision method interviews highlighted that spatial mismatches (e.g., direction, dimensions, orientation) between the operator’s movements and the visual feedback of the robot’s movements contributed to difficulties in teleoperation. For example, the operator might move leftward, but the visual feedback shows the robot arm moving rightward and movement dimensions can be mismatched across the different screens due to the different viewpoints of the camera feeds being relayed. In quantitative work, we subsequently investigated whether certain dimensionality mismatches were easier to deal with than others in a lab-based task. Participants used a stylus to control a cursor to collect targets in six different visuomotor mappings, each introducing a different dimensionality mismatch. Participants were significantly worse at controlling the cursor when there was a mismatch between the active dimensions in the stylus’ workspace and the remote workspace (e.g., when movements in the z-dimension in the stylus’ workspace controlled movements in the y-dimension on the screen). Collectively, this work has implications for optimising visualisation of the remote workspace to support teleoperation performance.
session_title: Symposium: Visuomotor transforms in prostheses, virtual reality, and teleoperation

title: Sensorimotor transforms and teleoperation in the nuclear industry
affiliations:
1. University of Reading (UK)
2. TOIA Tech (UK)
abstract: There are numerous instances where humans need to work in remote, inaccessible and/or hazardous locations. Examples include robot assisted surgery, space exploration, and nuclear maintenance and decommissioning. To work in these locations “human in the loop” remote telerobotic systems are used. The ideal telerobotic system should be “transparent” to the user, the system should be as effortless to use as real-world actions, however, these systems remain difficult, time consuming and costly to use. In this talk I will identify the fundamental role that perceptual psychophysics can play in addressing the optimisation of such systems. I will first identify the core issues to be solved, then draw links to how perceptual psychophysics is relevant. I will end by giving some examples my lab has been working on in collaboration with the nuclear industry. First, on the impact of (and adaptation to) sensorimotor transforms between vision and proprioception, and second, our work in building a bimanual visual-haptic virtual reality system. I will reflect upon my journey of getting into perceptual psychophysics specifically because it had no real-world application, to running a lab where virtually all of our work is applied.
session_title: Symposium: Visuomotor transforms in prostheses, virtual reality, and teleoperation

title: Revisiting Attneave’s Cat once more: An early recognition advantage for surprisal points over convexities and concavities.
affiliations:
1. University of Plymouth (UK)
2. Loyola University Chicago (US)
3. York University (CA)
4. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
abstract: An object’s shape is a critical cue to its identity and function. How does the visual system encode shape? A long history of theoretical and experimental research suggests that at early stages, shape is encoded in terms of curvature. Psychophysical studies suggest the importance of local curvature maxima (convexities) or minima (concavities), and physiological studies have found V4 neurons tuned to such features. Information-theoretic analyses show that high-curvature regions are informative and that, for closed contours, concave regions carry more information than convex regions with equal curvature. Nevertheless, informativeness (surprisal) is only approximately correlated with degree of curvature. Here, we explored whether the visual system prioritizes curvature extrema per se, or whether it instead prioritizes the most informative contour locations. In a match-to-sample experiment, five observers matched a smooth reference animal contour to one of two subsequently presented rescaled shapes (target and distractor), where (1) the points of maximum and minimum curvature, or (2) maximum information (surprisal) were extracted and connected with straight lines. We restricted the number of sampled points in the target and distractor, ranging from 4 to 32 points (ranked by magnitude). Performance increased with increasing number of points in both conditions, approaching ~90%. However, under very strong simplification (4 and 6 points), performance was significantly better for points sampled at locations of maximal surprisal (62%, 71%) compared to points sampled at locations of maximum curvature (51%, 62%), indicating an advantage for shapes based on highly informative points. Performance for the maximal surprisal condition was already above chance at the lowest level, contrary to the maximum curvature condition. These results suggest that shape representation might rely on features with high informational content rather than curvature extrema per se.

title: Arousal Modulates Performance but Not Decodable Visual Representations
affiliations:
1. University of Amsterdam (NL)
2. CNRS & Université de Paris (FR)
3. Vrije Universiteit (NL)
abstract: Arousal modulates behavioral performance, often following an inverted U-shaped pattern in which performance is best at intermediate arousal levels. It remains unclear whether such effects reflect changes in sensory and perceptual representations, or later decision-related stages. Here, we tested whether arousal influences early visual encoding or later perceptual integration.  Participants performed a perceptual task in which they detected Kanizsa illusory figures and discriminated local contrast in masked stimuli while EEG and pupillometry were recorded. We used multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode stimulus contrast as an index of early visual encoding and illusory shape perception as an index of perceptual integration, and related decoding performance to trial-by-trial fluctuations in pupil-linked arousal. To assess more sustained arousal changes, we additionally analyzed an independent dataset using sleep deprivation. Behaviorally, performance was optimal at intermediate arousal levels for both accuracy and reaction time. In contrast, EEG decoding of stimulus contrast and illusory percepts remained stable across trial-by-trial fluctuations in pupil-linked arousal, indicating that neither early sensory encoding nor later perceptual integration was systematically affected. Likewise, reduced arousal following sleep deprivation did not reliably alter perceptual representations. Together, these findings suggest that arousal-related changes in performance are unlikely to reflect modulation of visual representations. Instead, arousal may primarily influence post-perceptual processes, such as the transformation of perceptual evidence into decisions or responses. Ongoing analyses are testing this decision-stage account directly.

title: Color assimilation from objects moving behind an occluder occurs even without attention
affiliations:
1. University of Florence (IT)
2. CNR Institute of Neuroscience (IT)
3. University of Sydney (AU)
abstract: Visual input that reaches our retina is often interrupted by occlusions, yet perception remains stable and continuous. Previous research showed that object persistence and motion extrapolation contribute to perceptual stability, however, whether feature information is preserved during occlusion and at what level of processing remains unclear. We investigated this using a dynamic color assimilation paradigm, in which a target's perceived color shifts toward nearby inducing stimuli. In our experiments, two colored disks moved along trajectories passing behind occluders for approximately two seconds. One second into occlusion, a brief color probe appeared between the occluders, and participants judged its hue relative to a remembered standard. The perceived color of the probe was systematically biased toward the colors of the hidden inducers, demonstrating color assimilation from occluded objects (Sertakan et al., Current Biology, 2026). Critically, the bias was strongest when the probe appeared along the predicted trajectories of the moving objects, and disappeared when inducers halted before the occluders or when the probe appeared off-trajectory. This rules out generalized contextual spreading or response bias, implicating an active spatio-temporal representation of occluded motion. To examine whether this representation requires top-down attentional resources, in a second experiment we introduced a demanding task at fixation while the color judgment remained secondary. Strikingly, the magnitude of color assimilation was fully preserved under attentional load. This dissociation between dual-task performance and assimilation strength provides strong evidence that the spatio-temporal representation of occluded objects operates automatically, without top-down attentional allocation. The effect therefore cannot be attributed to focused attention on the moving objects, but reflects a genuinely automatic mechanism. Together, these results suggest that the visual system maintains precise, feature-rich representations of occluded moving objects through low-level, automatic processes — extrapolating motion and preserving feature content to support stable, coherent perception even when objects are temporarily hidden from view.

title: Differential depth and motion compression along the line of sight
affiliations:
1. York University (CA)
2. Glendon College (CA)
3. Dartmouth College (US)
abstract: Lengths seen along the line of sight at a distance appear compressed compared to widths and heights which are judged fairly accurately. How does this vary with eye height, and can we predict motion perception from length compression? We projected a display onto the floor at the end of a corridor and participants viewed it from 6, 12 or 18 meters while sitting on the floor, on a chair, or standing. For length judgments, three dots were projected that made an L shape with the two further away base dots at the same distance from the observer. The third dot was aligned with the rightmost of the first two and was closer to the observer. Observers adjusted the left-right separation of the two base dots to match the front-back separation of the right-hand pair of dots. The results showed a compression of perceived length of up to 400%. For motion judgments, the display was divided into two with a random dot pattern drifting left and right in the near half but toward and away from the observer in the farther half (and vice versa on half the trials). Observers adjusted the relative speeds of the two dot fields until they appeared to match. Motion toward and away from the observer was significantly slowed, by as much as 600% relative to left-right motion. For both length and motion settings, the effects of distance and eye height combined into one function governed by the viewing angle between the observer’s eye and the motion patterns but showing a larger effect for the motion judgements. The different perceptual outcomes for motion and distance judgements may arise from the local nature of the motion responses compared to the more global analysis needed for distance perception.

title: Cue-specialization in 3D cue integration
affiliations:
1. Justus-Liebig University (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior, Universities of Marburg, Giessen & TU Darmstadt (DE)
3. Excellence Cluster “The Adaptive Mind”, Universities of Marburg, Giessen & TU Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: While image patterns that elicit 3D percepts (e.g., shading, texture) are typically described as “depth cues”, they often do not actually specify depths. Instead, different cues are systematically related to specific 3D properties. For example, shading is related primarily to an object’s second-order curvatures, but does not capture how stretched or sheared it is (first-order). Instead, texture varies directly with first-order structure, but is broadly unaffected by subtle surface curvatures. This means that under typical conditions, when both cues are present, they actually provide complementary information about different shape properties. Is each cue’s “specialization” leveraged when these signals are integrated? Put another way, are they each treated as redundant depth cues or instead as complementary signals? To investigate this, we developed a class of 3D surfaces that maximized perceptual differences between shading and texture. Smooth, thin blobs were first strongly sheared in depth, and then perturbed with random patterns of shallow curvature. The resulting shapes look quite different depending on whether they are shaded or textured: shaded versions appeared fronto-parallel and bumpy, while textured versions appeared slanted and smooth. Participants adjusted a 3D probe to report their perceived shape for different surfaces in shading-only, texture-only, and combined-cue conditions. Interestingly, when both cues were available, observers’ perceived shapes were not a compromise between the two single-cue estimates, but rather retained the more informative aspects of both cues. Predictions from depth-based cue-integration models were both quantitatively and qualitatively off. Instead, participants’ perceived shapes were closer to predictions made by separately estimating curvature and shear from their respective “best” cues. This has important implications for cue-combination models, because it suggests that cues do not necessarily supply redundant estimates, but instead may be assigned specialized roles in estimating particular aspects of shape.

title: Investigating the Role of Local and Global Dynamics in Cascading Percepts
affiliations: 1. University of Amsterdam (NL)
abstract: Perceptually ambiguous stimuli displayed simultaneously tend to align in their perceived state. As an extension of previous research on multistable perception, this phenomenon could reveal substantial insights about the mechanism of our visual system as well as conscious perception. However, whether this so-called perceptual coupling arises from local, stimulus-driven interactions or global, top-down dynamics remains unresolved. We investigated this question using displays of multiple bistable motion quartets. In a first experiment, we applied exogenous manipulations to induce perceptual reversals in peripherally displayed motion quartets and measured their effect on a central ambiguous probe. We found that exogenous drivers of reversal in the periphery had only a small effect on the probe, corroborating previous indications that coupling is weaker between ambiguous and disambiguated stimuli. Effects relied on the visual distance and number of disambiguated stimuli to the probe. In a second experiment, we compared dominance durations for single versus multiple motion quartet displays, while constraining eye-movement in half of the trials. Contrary to some previous reports, we did not find shorter dominance durations for multi-stimulus displays in general. Preliminary results indicate however that the fixation cross acts as a moderator with shorter dominance durations occurring in multifigure setups only when no fixation cross is present. We integrate these findings in a cusp catastrophe network model incorporating local attention, inter-stimulus connectivity, and top-down influences. From this model, we derive new experimental predictions focusing on the role of eye-movements and visual attention.

title: Remapping peripersonal space through tool-based and movement training in virtual reality
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, University of Cyprus (CY)
2. Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento (IT)
3. CYENS Centre of Excellence (CY)
abstract: Background: Peripersonal space (PPS) refers to the multisensory representation of the space immediately surrounding the body and is critical for rapid defensive and goal-directed actions. PPS is a plastic that can expand after tool use. This study examined whether PPS remapping depends specifically on goal-directed tool-based pulling actions, defined as pulling objects toward the body using a tool, or whether it can also be induced by general motor activity in virtual reality (VR). Methods: Thirty-four healthy adults (17 women) completed a fully within-subjects 3 × 2 design with Training Condition (Tool-Based Pulling Training, Torso Movement, Whole-Body Movement) and Time (Pre, Post). PPS was assessed using a visuo-tactile detection task in immersive VR. Reaction times to tactile stimuli at five distances were fitted with sigmoidal functions, and the inflection point (x₀) indexed the PPS boundary. Bootstrap resampling (12,000 iterations) was used to estimate boundary distributions and to assess nonparametric significance. Findings: Tool-based pulling training significantly expanded PPS (Pre: 1.01 m Post: 1.45 m p = .021). Torso movement (1.28 m p = .180) and whole-body movement (1.31 m p = .160) showed non-significant increases. Model fits were strong across conditions (R² = .96–.99), indicating robust boundary estimation. Discussion: Goal-directed tool-based pulling actions selectively expanded PPS, whereas movement alone was insufficient. These findings suggest that functional actions bringing objects toward the body drive spatial remapping. VR-based tool-based pulling training may offer novel applications for enhancing near-body awareness and rapid responses in health, rehabilitation, and sport performance contexts.
session_title: Poster Session 1 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Relationship between Floriography and Flower’s Name, Image and Aroma
affiliations: 1. Kansai University (JP)
abstract: Recently, with the spread of flower aroma-based branding in companies, hotels, and stores, there is increasing potential for integrating floriography (the language of flowers) alongside visual and olfactory decorations. Therefore a sensory evaluation experiment was conducted to clarify the relationship between the impression received from the name, image, and aroma of a flower and its symbolism. Sixteen students (fourteen males, two females mean age 21.8 years) were presented with the names, images, and aromas of twenty selected flowers. They answered free-response first impression, twenty five impression items related to floriography and questions regarding flower recognition. The percentages of persons who had seen the flower before and knew its name were significantly different among flowers in their name and image, but almost zero for all flowers in their aroma. The impression tended to be strongly influenced by this recognition rate. For example, for rose, which had high recognition rates for both name and image, the impressions for the name and image were similar, but the impression for aroma differed significantly from the other two, possibly due to the low recognition rate for aroma. Three impression items highly related to the flower symbolism were extracted for each flower, and their mean evaluation was compared to the average evaluation for all flowers. The origins of floriography generally fall into two categories: those based on the flower's appearance or aroma, and those based on myths or anecdotes. In the former case, the mean evaluation was often closer to the flower symbolism. This suggests that when using flowers in architectural spaces, it’s necessary to pay attention to the origins of floriography. Moreover, it’s necessary to account for the generally low recognition of flower symbolism among the public.
session_title: Poster Session 1 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Shaping Tastes: Categorical and Graded Crossmodal Correspondences between Visual Geometry and Basic Tastes
affiliations:
1. National Cheng Kung University (TW)
2. MacKay Medical University (TW)
abstract: Crossmodal correspondences between visual features and gustatory sensations often follow systematic mapping rules. This study investigated the representational structure, bidirectionality, and robustness of associations between three basic tastes (sweetness, sourness, and bitterness) and two fundamental visual dimensions: angularity (round vs. angular) and symmetry (symmetric vs. asymmetric). Across three experiments, we employed a combination of explicit taste-matching and shape-matching tasks and Implicit Association Tests (IAT) to examine sweet–sour, sweet–bitter, and sour–bitter contrasts. Our results reveal a significant dissociation in how these visual dimensions encode taste information. Specifically, taste–angularity correspondences exhibited a categorical structure, where sweetness was consistently mapped to roundness, while both sourness and bitterness were grouped with angularity. In contrast, taste–symmetry correspondences followed a graded continuum, with sweetness, bitterness, and sourness ordered progressively along the symmetry-asymmetry axis. Furthermore, while bidirectional mappings were observed across most contrasts in explicit tasks, only the sweet–sour correspondence remained robust in the implicit measure, suggesting a stronger association that operates at an earlier processing stage. These findings indicate that visual geometry maps non-visual sensory attributes through distinct mechanisms—categorical for curvature and graded for symmetry—which are modulated by task demands and specific taste contrasts. Our results provide new insights into the hierarchical nature of how the visual system extracts and organizes crossmodal information.
session_title: Poster Session 1 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Presentation duration and feature information influence tactile correspondence mechanism in ambiguous apparent motion
affiliations: 1. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: It is difficult to keep track of a moving object, because objects are not continuously visible and their trajectories often intersect. Despite this incomplete and ambiguous information, we must establish correspondence between the correct object instances to perceive an object as moving from one position to another. In everyday life, we mostly rely on visual information. Nevertheless, we perceive objects also with our other senses, such as audition and touch and we can establish correspondence based on tactile and auditory information. Harrar and Harris (2007) showed that tactile correspondence depends on spatiotemporal factors, in particular the time between stimulus presentations. They used the Ternus display, an ambiguous apparent motion display, in which a tactile stimulation can be perceived as either moving by one step to the position of a neighbouring stimulus or as moving across that stimulus to the position of a third stimulus. Which motion is perceived depends on how correspondence is established between the tactile stimuli. In vision and audition, correspondence is also influenced by other factors, e.g., the stimulus duration and the feature information, such as the object’s colour or the sound’s frequency. The aim of this study was to investigate whether these factors are also important for tactile correspondence. We used a tactile Ternus display and manipulated the duration of the Ternus elements and the tactile appearance of the stimulus. Our results showed that both stimulus duration as well as feature information influence the tactile apparent-motion percept. Thus, correspondence in all three modalities is influenced by the same factors. This suggests that they may all rely on a similar mechanism to connect objects across space and time. Harrar, V., & Harris, L. R. (2007). Multimodal Ternus: Visual, Tactile, and Visuo - Tactile Grouping in Apparent Motion. Perception, 36(10), 1455–1464. https://doi.org/10.1068/p5844

title: An Ecological Model of Crossmodal Correspondences between Colour and Pitch
affiliations:
1. School of Psychology, University of Southampton (UK)
2. Department of Psychology, Justus-Liebig-Universität (DE)
3. Leibniz Institute for New Materials (DE)
4. Department of Psychology, Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz (DE)
abstract: Human senses provide fundamentally different types of information yet they are seamlessly integrated in a coherent multisensory experience that constitutes our perceived reality and helps us make sense of our environment. Crossmodal correspondences – perceived matches between signals from two different senses – allow access to multisensory experience by revealing how perceptual features are organised in the perceiver’s mind. In this study, we investigated the ecological origin of crossmodal correspondences, according to which such correspondences result from cumulative multisensory experience with the objects and materials in our perceptual environment. To test this account, we developed a quantitative ecological model that predicts colour-pitch correspondences by integrating ecological associations (objects and other phenomena) with each modality. For example, the model predicts the correspondence between blue and low pitch because both are associated with the sea and the sky. We tested the model in two experiments with different colour sets (24 colours varying in lightness, saturation and hue 30 colours varying only in hue). Pitch was controlled by using 20 loudness-matched pure tones with Mel-scaled frequencies. Ecological associations were elicited from participants in response to the colours, and their associations with colour and pitch were measured. The model combined these measures to computationally predict independently measured colour-pitch associations. The ecological model successfully predicted colour–pitch correspondences in both experiments, explaining 70–80% of the variance, and approaching the estimated noise ceiling. Results were robust across different measures of ecological associations and alternative mathematical formulations of the model. The success of the ecological model shows that perceivers combine sensory features across modalities, such as colour and sound, in ways that match their concepts of environmental phenomena, such as sea, sky, blood, and plants. More generally, these findings clarify how our multisensory experience is shaped by the interpretation of meaningful, functionally relevant phenomena in our environment.

title: Beyond Audiovisual Integration: Phonemic Features and Visual Articulatory Information Shape the McGurk Effect
affiliations: 1. MacKay Medical University (TW)
abstract: The McGurk effect is a speech illusion in which incongruent visual oral movements (e.g., /ga/) and auditory input (e.g., /ba/) are integrated to form a new percept (e.g., /da/). We examined whether two phonemic features that are prominent in Mandarin Chinese but not in English—aspiration and lexical tone—modulate the McGurk effect. Aspirated (/ph/) and unaspirated (/p/) consonants are both voiceless, with longer voice onset time for the former. Mandarin lexical tones are defined by fundamental frequency (F0) contours—Tone 1 (flat), Tone 2 (rising), Tone 3 (falling-rising), and Tone 4 (falling)—and are produced through laryngeal activity accompanied by subtle yet observable neck movements. In Experiment 1, aspirated (/pha/) and unaspirated (/pa/) syllables were paired with congruent (/pha/ or /pa/) or incongruent (/kha/ or /ka/) visual articulations, or else with a static face as an auditory-only control. In Experiment 2, the syllable /pa/ produced with four lexical tones was tested under the same three conditions. Participants judged whether the perceived speech matched a predesignated target syllable (i.e., /pha/ or /pa/ with a given tone). The McGurk effect was quantified by reduced accuracy in the incongruent relative to the congruent condition. Results showed that the McGurk effect was larger for the aspirated than the unaspirated consonant, and larger for Tone 1 than Tone 2. These differences could not be merely explained by performance in the auditory-only control. Our results demonstrate that the McGurk effect was susceptible to auditory phonemic features and visual movement beyond the oral area, including laryngeal-related movements in the neck. These findings suggest that the McGurk effect reflects the integration of phonetic gestures across articulatory domains, rather than a simple combination of auditory and visual signals, consistent with the view that speech perception is grounded in phonetic–gestural representations.

title: Development of haptic cross-section recognition in school-aged children
affiliations:
1. Italian Institute of Technology (IT)
2. University of Genoa (IT)
3. IHMC (US)
abstract: Cross-sectioning requires inferring the two-dimensional shape produced by slicing a three-dimensional solid. This ability relies on spatial representation, manipulation of 3D and 2D forms, and extraction of geometric structure. Developmental evidence suggests these skills mature during childhood. We investigated whether haptic recognition of solids’ cross-sections, assessed with a haptic version of the Santa Barbara Solids Test, improves across development and whether shape complexity and cut type affect performance. Because this task is typically studied visually, we considered whether children’s haptic performance might depend on haptic cues or abstract mental representations. We tested 37 typically developing children aged 6–11 years (M = 8.22, SD = 1.29). Children haptically explored 3D-printed solids and selected a cross-section among four 3D-printed options. Children in first and second grade completed 12 trials, whereas those in third and fourth grade completed 14 trials. Accuracy (correct/incorrect) was analysed with a binomial generalized linear mixed-effects model including age, shape, and cut as predictors, and subject as random intercept. Age, χ²(1) = 7.55, p = .006, and cut, χ²(1) = 16.68, p < .001, significantly predicted performance. Accuracy increased with age and was lower for diagonal than orthogonal cuts. The significant Age × Cut interaction, χ²(1) = 7.97, p = .005, indicates that age-related improvement was more pronounced for orthogonal than diagonal cuts. Shape was not significant, χ²(2) = 3.84, p = .147. Results suggest that haptic cross-section recognition improves with age, and diagonal cuts impose a greater processing cost than orthogonal cuts. Younger children showed a more diffuse error pattern, whereas older children’s errors appeared more concentrated in shape-cut configurations. This may reflect developmental differences in abstraction and spatial transformation. Future work will examine systematic error patterns and extend the paradigm to children with severe visual impairment feasibility testing has begun in one participant.

title: Conceptual colour understanding in the blind
affiliations:
1. University of Amsterdam (NL)
2. Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour (NL)
3. Oxford University (UK)
4. University of Nottingham (UK)
5. University of California San Diego (US)
6. University of Rochester (US)
abstract: Crossmodal correspondences (CMCs) are associations between different sensory modalities. Although CMCs have been studied extensively, research has predominantly focused on the audiovisual domain, for example, the Bouba-Kiki effect, in which a round shape is associated with Bouba and a spiky shape with Kiki. CMCs are well-studied in the visual modality, but CMCs involving tactile surface properties (e.g.roughness, softness) have received relatively little attention. Here, we study tactile-to-colour crossmodal correspondences.  Improved understanding of tactile-to-colour correspondences is not only of interest for a fundamentally improved understanding of CMCs, across diverse modalities. It may also provide insight into how colour is represented in the absence of vision, and thus offer a pathway for translating colour to blind individuals, who already rely heavily on touch.  In this study, we conducted several experiments to explore the underlying mechanisms of touch-colour associations and to provide a foundation for translating colour to blind participants.   First, a questionnaire on colour experience and CMCs was completed by 45 visually impaired participants (18 totally blind, 13 with very low vision <5%, 14 partially sighted). Totally blind participants still reported CMC colour associations, suggesting they maintain colour representations, whether acquired through prior visual experience or through language and learned representations.   Second, we compare visually impaired and sighted participants on behavioural measures of touch-colour association tasks and haptic sensitivity tasks, to assess how visual experience affects touch-colour correspondences.   Finally, we will present preliminary fMRI findings on haptic processing in blind individuals, providing insight into potential functional reorganization of neural representations underlying haptic perception in the absence of visual experience.   Together, these studies examine the theoretical framework of touch-to-vision associations and explore a practical application of translating colour for blind individuals. Moreover, the results provide further insights into how visual experience influences haptic processing.

title: The effect of auditory cue on visual search processing: the relation between the pip-and-pop effect and audiovisual integration capacity
affiliations: 1. Liaoning Normal University (CN)
abstract: The pip-and-pop effect describes the phenomenon wherein a nonspatial auditory signal significantly enhances visual search efficiency for a single target in a dynamic array, which may depend on audiovisual integration. However, how individual differences in audiovisual integration capacity modulate this effect remains unclear. The present study provides the first systematic examination of the relation between audiovisual integration capacity and the pip-and-pop effect across two experiments. In Experiment 1, we replicated the classic pip-and-pop effect using a dynamic single-target visual search task and found that individual audiovisual integration capacity significantly and positively predicted search performance specifically when auditory cues were present, but not in the no-sound condition. This dissociation suggests that audiovisual integration capacity selectively facilitates behavioral performance when auditory information is available to guide search. In Experiment 2, we extended this investigation to a dynamic dual-target visual search task. Although auditory cues enhanced dual-target identification accuracy overall, audiovisual integration capacity predicted behavioral performance in both the with-sound and no-sound conditions under high task load, reflecting shared demands on multiple-object tracking and attentional resources. Across both experiments, audiovisual integration capacity was not significantly correlated with the difference-based pip-and-pop benefit score, highlighting the multifaceted nature of the pip-and-pop effect, which likely involves additional mechanisms beyond audiovisual integration alone. These findings demonstrate that individual differences in audiovisual integration capacity may serve as an important modulating factor in the pip-and-pop effect, with its expression critically dependent on task load and the specific cognitive demands of the search context.

title: Intercepting accelerating targets with the help of sound
affiliations: 1. Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (NL)
abstract: We know that people are very poor at visually judging acceleration, and consequently do not consider visual estimates of acceleration when intercepting moving targets. As a result, their interceptive movements end up slightly behind accelerating targets and ahead of decelerating ones. If the target repeatedly accelerates in the same manner, people quickly learn to compensate for such errors. But if the acceleration varies from trial to trial, they keep making systematic errors. We have previously shown that providing information about the acceleration in the form of different background images (ice for a constant velocity sand for strong deceleration) does not help cope with acceleration. Here we examined whether an accompanying sound rather than a background image does help. We interleaved accelerating targets that were accompanied by a sound that increased in both volume and frequency with decelerating targets that were accompanied by a sound that decreased in volume and frequency. Adding such sounds reduced the systematic errors associated with ignoring acceleration considerably. The sounds did not provide actual information about the acceleration. Neither did the sounds influence the time taken to perform the interceptive movements. Presumably participants learnt to aim further ahead of the moving target when they heard the sound with increasing volume and frequency than when they heard the other sound.

title: From Eye Movements to Auditory Pitch Perception: Saccades Exert a Weaker Influence than Keypresses on Perceived Self-generated Tones
affiliations: 1. Vision Action Cognition (FR)
abstract: Sensory attenuation refers to reduced neural and perceptual responses to self-generated tones compared to tones triggered externally, due to predictive mechanisms.   Our previous study showed that the strength of action-outcome coupling (SAOC) influences the perception of sound loudness. Indeed, we observed that the perceived intensity of tones triggered by keypresses (strong coupling) was attenuated, in contrast to tones triggered by ocular saccades (weak coupling). Building on this earlier study, we investigated the influence of SAOC on perceptual attenuation for pitch. To date, no behavioral study has demonstrated any sensory attenuation effect regarding pitch perception, although it has been suggested that attenuation may manifest in this case as a change in the ability to perceive pitch differences.  A total of 140 participants were divided into three groups. They performed a pitch discrimination task in which test tones of varying frequency were triggered either by a saccade, a keypress, or played after a cue (no action required, or “passive” group). Test tones were presented 150 ms or 1500 ms after the action (or cue).   Results revealed lower discrimination sensitivity in the keypress group compared to the passive group (Cohen's d = 0.66). In contrast, no significant difference was found between the saccade and passive groups. Also, in the keypress group only, we observed a small effect of delay (Cohen's d = 0.14), with reduced sensitivity at the shorter interval.  This reduced perceptual sensitivity for keypress-triggered tones may reflect sensory attenuation. Importantly, the absence of a significant difference between the saccade and passive groups, together with the small size of the delay effect, suggests that this reduction in sensitivity cannot be explained by dual-task interference alone.  These results are consistent with the hybrid model of Dogge et al. (2019), which posits that different predictive mechanisms underlie sensory attenuation depending on the SAOC.

title: Hardware and software for a binocular multifocal display system
affiliations: 1. TU Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: Our Python software package multifocal offers a user-friendly API to interface the system with popular stimulus presentation libraries such as PsychoPy. Basic drawing is handled in a 3D coordinate system, allowing the user to specify where in the virtual volume a stimulus should be drawn multifocal then internally determines what should be drawn where on the physical monitor. We additionally implement depth-filtering techniques to blend light between two physical planes, which previous work has shown drives accommodation to intermediate depths. In addition, multifocal offers routines for photometric and geometric calibration. The photometric calibration allows color and luminance matching across the system's different planes using lookup tables and color correction models. The geometric calibration allows precise alignment of the drawing volume. For the binocular setup, it allows correct interpupillary and vergence calibration to enable correct image fusion.The system's luminance range depends strongly on the selection of the optical elements, the deployed display, and the calibration state. For the current hardware, calibrating the display itself to approx. 250 cd/m2 will result in a usable luminance range of approx. [0.0 - 12.0] cd/m2 at the eye. These hardware and software designs enable researchers to study human depth perception and address vergence and accommodation under laboratory conditions in ways impossible to do using conventional 2D displays.

title: An examination of behavioral characteristics during the execution of a button pressing task under observing 360-degree images
affiliations: 1. Tokyo Polytechnic University (JP)
abstract: I investigated the characteristics of depth perception during the observation of 360-degree video displayed on VR goggles (Meta Quest 3) and the motor models represented during reaching toward a target. In the experiment, participants observed 360-degree images through VR goggles. The subjects’ task was to press virtual buttons located 400 mm, 750 mm, and 1,200 mm away from the subjects’ initial position using a virtual hammer linked to a controller. In the 1,200 mm condition, the subjects had to walk to reach the button. The hammer’s trajectory was recorded. The results showed that while some participants were able to press the buttons, others experienced such a discrepancy between their perceived depth and the button’s actual position that they were unable to press the button on the first attempt. the time required to press the button increased exponentially as the distance to the button increased. One possible cause for this was that the error in subjective depth increased with distance, resulting in a suboptimal hammer trajectory. Other possibility was that the hammer’s travel time increased due to the greater distance. The results for the hammer trajectory length and tortuosity also increased exponentially with increasing the distance between the button and subjects. And the fractal dimension increased linearly. These results indicated that the increase was not due to the greater the distance, but rather that the hammer’s trajectory became more complex, thereby rejecting the hypothesis that the effect was caused by increased the distance. And these results suggested that when observing 360-degree images through VR goggles, the subject’s subjective depth error increases as the button moves further away from them. The error in perceived depth is thought to be caused by the fact that 360-degree video provides fewer depth cues than the real world.

title: Transitions in binocular rivalry qualitatively change with age
affiliations:
1. University of Graz (AT)
2. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: Our rich and complex subjective experience of sensory information is reduced by typical cognitive psychology paradigms to a few pre-defined discrete categories. In our previous study, we demonstrated the complexity of subjective visual experience during binocular rivalry. Rivalry occurs when dissimilar images are presented to each eye, resulting in conscious perception alternating between images separated by brief transition phases. We demonstrated that these transition phases occur in different yet categorizable perceptual forms, that they are affected by the type of stimuli, by contrast, and by attention. nPrior studies established that dominance durations in binocular rivalry increase with age while transition durations remain unchanged. However, there may be qualitative changes in transition appearance, which are not captured by quantitative measures. We, therefore, tested eighty-nine healthy adults (ages 18-64) with binocular rivalry induced by three stimulus types (gratings, images, moving dots) as well as their combinations (e.g., image and moving dots). Following each stimulus block, participants provided verbal descriptions and sketches of their transition experiences that were further categorized using qualitative content analysis. Our results confirmed that while dominance durations increased with age, transition durations showed no measurable change. Crucially, we observed significant age-related changes in the appearance of transitions that depended on stimulus content. First, the overall variety of transitions and the frequency of immediate transitions decreased with age for moving dot stimuli, which are associated with dorsal stream processing. Second, piecemeal transitions, which are thought to reflect interocular grouping failure, become more frequent with age for gratings but less frequent for moving dot stimuli. Finally, the increased frequency of halves during rivalry between images and moving dots implies an age-related decline in global competitive interactions between ventral and dorsal streams.These findings demonstrate that the aging visual system undergoes selective qualitative shifts in perceptual dynamics invisible to conventional quantitative measures.

title: Theta-burst stimulation of hMT+ modulates sensory eye dominance
affiliations: 1. The University of Hong Kong (HK)
abstract: Sensory eye dominance (SED) reflects an imbalanced weighting of the two eyes' inputs and is linked to visuomotor deficits, at least in clinical extremes (e.g., amblyopia). While traditionally attributed to the gain control mechanisms in primary visual cortex, SED has been more recently shown to implicate higher cortical regions, most notably, the human middle temporal complex (hMT+).  Whether hMT+ plays a principal role in governing SED, or whether its engagement reflects mere stimulus properties (SED is often indexed using motion stimuli) remains to be teased apart.  Here, we tested whether theta-burst stimulation (TBS) of the right hMT+ modulates SED. We tested 60 adults with normal vision. In Experiment 1, 40 participants received either intermittent (iTBS) or continuous TBS (cTBS) over the right hMT+, completing dichoptic motion and orientation tasks before and after stimulation. Both of these tasks can be used to quantify SED by capturing interocular threshold differences but crucially differ in terms of stimulus features. We found that iTBS, but not cTBS, significantly reduced SED magnitude in both tasks and reduced motion discrimination reaction times (RTs). In Experiment 2, we investigated the temporal characteristics of TBS-induced changes in SED. 20 new participants received iTBS or cTBS, and their SED was indexed using the dichoptic motion task at baseline and at multiple time points extending over 60 minutes post-stimulation. iTBS reduced SED from 30 to 60 minutes post-stimulation relative to baseline. Again, cTBS produced no reliable effects on SED. Motion RTs improved immediately following iTBS, though this benefit was not sustained across repeated post-tests. Our data suggests that hMT+ contributes to binocular balance beyond its established role in motion processing, pointing to a more complex network that governs eye balance than is conventionally considered.

title: BOOK OF THE DARK: IMPORTANCE OF ENVIRONMENTAL CUES FOR PERCEIVED DISTANCE ANISOTROPY
affiliations: 1. Laboratory for Experimental Psychology, Faculty of Philosophy, University of Belgrade (RS)
abstract: The anisotropy of perceived distance refers to upward distances being perceived as larger than physically equal downward distances or distances in front of us. This effect is mainly shown in situations with a reduced number of depth cues (dark room). Does perceived distance anisotropy depend on the number of depth cues present? Three experiments were performed, in which participants matched distances of stimuli in two directions, toward the horizon and zenith, but in situations with different amounts of depth cues present. In the first experiment, 29 participants matched distances of two dim light stimuli in a large dark room, monocularly and binocularly. In the second experiment, 17 participants matched distances of two red spheres in virtual reality, in two situations: empty dark space or with a brick wall surface on both directions. In the third experiment, 30 participants matched the distances of two white circles in an outdoor condition in the forest. Results of the first experiment showed a significant effect of direction on distance estimates, and no interaction with the viewing condition (monocular or binocular). In the second experiment, a difference in perceived distance in two directions is detected, with no interaction with the situation (empty space or brick wall). In the third experiment, the effect of direction on distance estimates is observed. In all experiments, the effect of perceived distance anisotropy is observed in the same direction distances toward zenith were perceived as larger than physically equal distances toward the horizon. We can conclude that perceived distance anisotropy is invariant to the amount of environmental information, which may have implications for health-related behaviors involving spatial judgment and navigation in low-visibility conditions requiring interaction with the environment. This research was supported by the Science Fund of the Republic of Serbia, #2424, Environmental Monitoring of Food and Waterborne Parasites – PARASITE_HUNTER.

title: Temporally demanding stereoscopic training drives effective binocular rebalancing
affiliations: 1. The University of Hong Kong (HK)
abstract: Optimal binocular vision requires balanced integration of inputs from the two eyes, yet most observers exhibit some degree of sensory eye dominance (SED), an asymmetry in how the two eyes’ inputs are weighted.  While dichoptic perceptual training can reduce SED by enforcing binocular cooperation, it remains unclear as to whether stereoscopic training is able to promote binocular balance, despite the obvious reliance of stereopsis on balanced binocular input.  Here, we asked whether training on a random-dot stereogram (RDS) depth-discrimination task reduces SED in visually normal adults and whether manipulating difficulty through changes in disparity differences versus stimulus duration differentially affects the extent of rebalancing.  Fifty observers were randomly assigned to one of two RDS training tasks completed over three consecutive days (3,600 trials total). In the disparity-manipulation task variant, stimulus presentation duration was fixed, while task difficulty was adjusted by varying the disparity difference between target and reference planes.  In the duration-manipulation task variant, the disparity difference was held constant, and difficulty was modulated by varying presentation duration.  On each trial, participants judged whether the target plane appeared nearer or farther than the reference.  Participants’ performance on both depth task variants, along with their SED (dichoptic signal-noise task) were indexed before and after training.  Results revealed that training improved depth-discrimination performance not only on the trained task, but also on the untrained depth task.  Critically, both groups showed significant reductions in SED after training (i.e., more balanced interocular weighting), with a reliably larger reduction following duration-manipulation than disparity-manipulation training. These findings demonstrate that stereoscopic training drives measurable SED plasticity in visually normal adults and suggest that heightened temporal demands may be particularly effective at promoting binocular rebalancing, perhaps by limiting the temporal window within which interocular suppressive mechanisms can engage.

title: Combined Monocular Deprivation and Perceptual Learning Promotes Long-term Binocular Balance
affiliations: 1. The University of Hong Kong (HK)
abstract: Both short-term monocular deprivation (MD) and visual perceptual learning (VPL) have been shown to alter sensory eye dominance (SED) in adults, yielding a more balanced binocular percept. However, each approach has limitations: MD effects are transient, whereas VPL is time-consuming to conduct. Here, we combined these two approaches to examine whether this produces a more robust and long-lasting shift in SED while remaining efficient to implement. Participants were assigned to one of the four groups, each undergoing a 3-day modulation period: MD only, VPL only, MD followed by VPL, and VPL followed by MD. During MD, observers viewed a movie for 1 hour during which the non-dominant eye viewed low-passed images, and the dominant eye viewed intact images. During VPL, participants trained on a dichoptic motion discrimination task. SED was assessed using the dichoptic motion task before and after modulation, with post-modulation measurements conducted immediately after, at 30 minutes, 24 hours, 1 week, and 1 month after the final day. All groups that received VPL (either in isolation or in combination) showed a reduced SED (i.e., a more balanced percept) that persisted for at least 1 week after modulation. These improvements in SED were accompanied by learning-related improvements on the task (i.e., reduced motion discrimination thresholds). The MD-only group showed a reduced SED immediately after modulation, but returned to baseline within 30 minutes, with no concurrent improvement in task performance. These results suggest that a 3-day VPL protocol is sufficient to induce binocular plasticity that consolidates over time, whereas MD alone, even across repeated sessions, does not produce long-term benefits. We speculate that when MD is delivered in combination with VPL, the MD-induced homeostatic shift towards the deprived eye may render respective neurons more susceptible to subsequent VPL-driven consolidation, potentially leading to longer-lasting changes in binocular balance.

title: Measuring suppression-related attenuation of stimulus information in binocular rivalry
affiliations: 1. University of New South Wales (AU)
abstract: Binocular rivalry (BR) is a perceptual phenomenon in which conflicting images presented to each eye cannot be fused into a stable percept, and perception spontaneously oscillates between the two images. While BR has been studied extensively, the role of attention in the neural dynamics of BR remains unclear. We used magnetoencephalography (MEG) to compare the neural information about a dominant BR percept and the associated suppressed stimulus, and how attention modulates this relationship. Participants (N = 16) viewed a stimulus with a rivalrous and non-rivalrous component, alternating whether their attention was directed to the rivalrous or non-rivalrous component. We used classification analyses to quantify the amount of information about each stimulus component contained in the MEG signal over time. As expected, classifier accuracy is greater for the attended than the unattended non-rivalrous stimulus, from ~200ms post stimulus presentation. For the BR stimulus, we decoded the image content of both dominant and suppressed stimuli, finding that information about the suppressed stimulus was surprisingly robust. Information about the suppressed stimulus was lower than the dominant stimulus, but was less attenuated than the unattended non-rivalrous stimulus. Overall, the decoding dynamics are consistent with the onset of BR involving similar processes to engaging covert spatial attention.

title: No empirical evidence for input-dependent noise in purely relative models of perceptual decision-making
affiliations: 1. University of Liverpool (UK)
abstract: In perceptual binary decision-making tasks, higher overall stimulus intensity often leads to faster and less accurate responses. This effect has been explained with models where difference in evidence is accumulated to a decision threshold while processing noise increases with overall stimulus intensity. Here we present empirical evidence from brightness discrimination tasks inconsistent with the proposal that processing noise scales with stimulus intensity. First, in tasks where participants make a decision when prompted by the experimenter (interrogation protocol), data show that accuracy does not decrease with increasing stimulus intensity, contrary to what input-dependent noise would predict. Second, in a task where participants can respond in their own time (free-response protocol), we observe that confidence increases with stimulus intensity even for equal-alternative conditions. Depending on how confidence is defined, input-dependent noise predicts that confidence should either remain stable or decrease or vary systematically with reaction time. We show that all these predictions are not supported by data. Finally, although data consistent with input-dependent noise have been observed in two-stimuli tasks, input-dependent noise predictions should also hold for single-stimulus tasks. Analyses of single-stimulus tasks show no systematic relationship between stimulus intensity and either reaction time or accuracy. Taken together, these results cannot be explained by the input-dependent noise hypothesis. We show how these results can instead be explained by response competition models.

title: Predicting Human Viewpoint Preference with Deep Neural Network Embeddings
affiliations: 1. University of Toronto (CA)
abstract: Humans prefer some object views over others, but the representational basis of these judgments remains unclear. Rather than treating canonicity as a discrete category, we approach it as a continuous perceptual variable around three-dimensional objects. We collected human ratings of viewpoint canonicity across multiple perspectives of the same objects to obtain average canonicity measurements. Using these ratings, we estimate the canonical fields (the maps of perceptual privilege) for this object set. Using these human behavioral ratings as ground truth, we show that deep image models accurately predict human canonicity judgments when anchored to the most canonical perspective (the view with the highest average canonicity rating). Specifically, distances in high-dimensional feature spaces (latent spaces) between the preferred view and other views closely track human ratings. These results suggest that the statistical distributions of object views in large image datasets may reflect human canonicity bias, because we often photograph objects from canonical perspectives.

title: Integrating the Simon Effect into Task-Switching: A Study on Cognitive Stability and Flexibility
affiliations: 1. University of Copenhagen (DK)
abstract: Task-switching experiments have been used to study cognitive stability (maintaining focus on the current task goal) and flexibility (efficient shift between tasks). These constructs are typically benchmarked by the task-rule congruency effect and the switch cost. However, the task-rule congruency effect is largely shaped by learned, instructed category–response associations, theoretically distinguishing it from the congruency effects observed in standard conflict tasks (e.g., Stroop, Simon, and flanker tasks). Comparing with the former, congruency effects more directly capture the degree of perceptual conflict between target and distractor stimuli in the standard conflict tasks. To better examine the relationship between perceptual conflict control and task switching, we introduce a novel paradigm that integrates Simon stimuli within a task-switching design. This allows us to measure the Simon effect (conflict control) and switch cost (flexibility) simultaneously. Results showed significant effects for both the Simon effect and switch cost, confirming that the paradigm successfully captures both conflict control (stability) and cognitive flexibility. A mixed-effects model of the delta plots further suggests that the Simon effect is significantly higher for the switch condition than for the repeat condition. However, no relationship between Simon effect and switch cost was observed, indicating no trade-off between stability and flexibility.
