title: Mind the snake in the shadows: Preattentive processing and autonomic responses to subliminal evolutionary threats
affiliations:
1. University of Trento (IT)
2. Paris Nanterre University - UFR STAPS (FR)
3. La Trobe University (AU)
abstract: In the course of evolution, human survival has largely depended on the ability to rapidly detect and respond to potential threats. Accordingly, the human visual system has evolved mechanisms that enable us to detect danger before conscious awareness. Previous studies have reported enhanced detection abilities and increased electrodermal activity in response to subliminal presentations of snake and spider images, with stronger effects in individuals with specific phobias. However, this advantage in the unconscious processing of evolutionarily threatening animals has not been consistently supported in the literature. Across two experiments, we subliminally presented spider and snake images, in both intact and scrambled versions, using the breaking Continuous Flash Suppression (bCFS) technique. In both experiments, we recorded the time required for the stimuli to break through suppression, as well as several physiological indices, including skin conductance, pupil dilation, and facial EMG. We also assessed participants’ levels of specific phobias using the Spider Fear Questionnaire (SPQ-12) and the Snake Anxiety Questionnaire (SNAQ-12) to investigate potential interindividual differences in physiological and behavioural responses. Additionally, in the second experiment, participants were asked to report how clearly they saw the stimulus and to categorize it. In both experiments, we observed shorter breakthrough times for snakes than for spiders, and faster responses to intact images than to their scrambled counterparts. Moreover, both animals were associated with higher electrodermal responses even before reaching visual awareness. In the first experiment, pupillometry analyses further revealed a clear preconscious advantage of threatening animals. When taking inter-individual differences in phobia level into account, the results suggest an avoidant response in arachnophobics compared to non-phobic participants. Together, our findings support the existence of a subcortical pathway that is preattentively activated to prepare the organism to react to potential threats. Moreover, this network appears to respond differently depending on individuals’ levels of phobia.

title: Reaction Times Reflect Distances in a Perceptual Similarity Space
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, Faculty of Arts, Charles University (CZ)
2. Institute of Psychology, Czech Academy of Sciences (CZ)
abstract: People frequently diverge in their similarity judgments, reflecting underlying differences in the cognitive processes and object features they prioritize. This study examines how choice behavior and response speed are shaped by the similarity-based embedding of object representations. We build on the previous work by Hebart et al. (2020) using the THINGS database. This embedding captures perceived similarity as distances in a high-dimensional psychological space.  Fifty participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice similarity judgment task. On each trial, a target image was presented above two candidate images, and participants selected the object that was more similar to the target. Task difficulty was operationalized in two alternative ways: either as the difference or as the ratio of each candidate object’s similarity to the target. Log-transformed reaction times were predicted from trial difficulty and mean pairwise similarity using Bayesian multilevel models with by-participant random intercepts and slopes. Reaction times varied systematically with representational distance, with easier trials yielding faster responses. Model comparison indicated that the difference metric provided a slightly better fit than the ratio metric. Slower participants showed stronger sensitivity to difficulty. The fixed effect of difficulty explained approximately 20% of the variance, whereas the full hierarchical model accounted for 42%, highlighting a substantial contribution of inter-individual variability. Our findings confirm that decision difficulty based on psychological distance predicts response speed, yet the substantial inter-individual variability uncovered by our hierarchical models suggests that people navigate these high-dimensional spaces using unique cognitive weights and feature priorities.

title: Opposing psychophysical laws in perceptual decision-making revealed by single-trial EEG modelling
affiliations:
1. University of Lausanne (CH)
2. University of Goningen (NL)
3. Utrecht University (NL)
abstract: Judging Gabor patches by their contrast can reveal properties of vision and decision-making processes hidden within the chain of processing that composes the reaction time (RT). In the case of visual contrast, Piéron's law states that increasing contrast results in a shorter reaction time following a negative power law. Fechner's law predicts that the time required to judge the difference in contrast between two patches is proportional to the logarithm of their physical intensity ratio. In this study, we demonstrate how these laws manifest in the RTs of participants performing a contrast discrimination task between two Gabor patches using electroencephalography (EEG). We manipulated the contrast of the Gabor patches so that the contrast difference remained constant while the pedestal contrast varied from trial to trial. We expected this manipulation to produce opposing effects on RT according to both laws: 1) increasing the pedestal contrast should decrease RT according to Piéron's law, and 2) should increase RT due to a more difficult decision according to Fechner's law. At the behavioral level, the manipulation revealed that participants' accuracy followed Fechner's law while their RT exhibited a combination of both laws. We analyzed the EEG using the hidden multivariate pattern method that models the single-trial signal as a sequence of an unknown number of trial-recurrent, sequential and time-varying EEG topographies. In this task, five of these brain events summarized the EEG signal occurring within participants' RTs. The single-trial estimate of the timing of events associated with visual processing followed Piéron's law. The timing of the decision and motor-related event followed Fechner's law and their buildup predicted correct response proportions with a very high accuracy. Overall, this shows that using this EEG-RT modelling approach we can decipher between visual, decisional and motor processes happening during the RT.

title: Adding ambiguity into already ambiguous spatial models
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Ambiguity detection, understanding if a text describing the arrangement of objects/subjects that has more than one valid interpretation, in mental models, is not well understood. I explored the differences in people’s ability to detect ambiguity depending on the point at which ambiguity is introduced i.e., Second Premise vs, Third Premise. I found that people are significantly better at detecting ambiguity when underspecificity is introduced by the third premise i.e., causing a model with only one viable solution to have more than one, compared to when the third premise simply adds underspecificity to the first two premises that already have more than one viable solution. Indicating that adding ambiguity to unambiguous situations is easier to process/detect than adding additional ambiguity to ambiguity. I suggest that this may be due to the third premise, which introduces ambiguity, encouraging re-evaluation of the model as whole which does not occur when the third premise adds more ambiguity to an already ambiguous situation. However, additional research is required in order to ascertain whether this is the case

title: The Efficacy-Proximity Paradox: Visual Framing, Affective Persistence, and the Behavioral Breadth of Climate Action
affiliations:
1. Nanyang Technological University (SG)
2. University of Warwick (UK)
abstract: Climate communication often heightens concern without translating it into action. This study examined how visual framing reorganizes cognitive, emotional, and behavioral pathways through which climate messages endure. These analyses are based on an interim subset of a preregistered study. Sixty-two participants (M_age = 26.68, SD = 8.39 53.2% male) viewed 2025 climate images drawn from CNN, Herald Sun, and The Straits Times. Stimuli were coded for equivalence and assigned to hazard, solution, or mixed frames. Participants completed Q-sorts of 40 images on efficacy, importance, and proximity, reported affect during viewing, sorting, and 24 hours later, described content, and listed green actions. Framing altered the cognitive structure of the image sets. In the hazard condition, efficacy was unrelated to importance (r = .04, p = .815) and modestly associated with proximity (r = .31, p = .048). In the solution condition, efficacy was more strongly associated with importance (r = .51, p = .001) and proximity (r = .75, p < .001), exceeding hazard and mixed conditions. Within the mixed set, solution images were judged more efficacious than hazard images (r = .55, p < .001), whereas hazard images were judged more proximal (r_pb = -.36, p = .022). Thus, what felt psychologically close did not necessarily feel actionable. Linear mixed-effects models showed that most affective responses declined by 24 hours, including positive affect (B = -3.99, p = .001), negative affect (B = -5.62, p < .001), anxiety (B = -0.50, p = .013), awe (B = -0.46, p = .036), and disgust (B = -0.83, p < .001). Hope was the most durable emotion: it showed no reliable overall decline, and solution framing sustained higher hope than hazard framing (B = 0.77, p = .039). Greater 24-hour hope predicted broader action breadth, whereas greater 24-hour anxiety predicted narrower breadth.

title: Confirmation Bias Under Social Influence: Gaze and Pupillary Signatures of Attentional Amplification and Effortful Belief Updating
affiliations:
1. Institute of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Liaoning Normal University (CN)
2. State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Science and Mental Health, Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CN)
3. Department of Psychology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CN)
abstract: Confirmation bias can preserve stable beliefs but also impair adaptive belief updating during social disagreement. Here, we tested whether this bias is implemented through dissociable attentional and arousal-linked mechanisms during social change of mind. Participants completed a two-stage social perceptual decision task: they first judged ambiguous visual images and rated confidence, then saw a dissenting advisor’s choice and confidence before deciding whether to stay or switch. Eye movements and pupil diameter were recorded during this revision phase. Participants showed a strong confirmation bias, staying with their initial choice more often than expected by indifference, despite initial accuracy on disagreement trials being near chance, and requiring the advisor to be much more confident before switching. Drift-diffusion modeling showed that evidence accumulation weighted self-confidence more strongly than advisor confidence, whereas a starting-point account was not supported. Participants also looked longer at their own confidence, and greater self-gaze predicted a higher probability of staying. An attentional drift-diffusion model favored a multiplicative mechanism in which gaze increased the impact of the attended confidence signal. In contrast, pupil dilation was larger on switch than stay trials. Together, these findings dissociate two components of confirmation bias: attentional sampling biases evidence in favor of the self, whereas pupil-linked arousal indexes the effort required to revise one’s mind.

title: Explicit expectations influence the content of false percepts
affiliations:
1. University College London (UK)
2. Maastricht University (NL)
abstract: False percepts are proposed to arise from overly strong top-down expectations (Corlett et al., 2019). However, a recent study (Haarsma et al., 2023) found that implicit expectations did not influence the contents of false percepts, and that expectations and false percepts activated different layers of early visual cortex, casting doubt on the hypothesis that expectations can lead to false percepts (Schmack et al., 2021). A potential reconciliation is that the implicit expectations in Haarsma et al. may not have been strong enough to cause false percepts, but stronger expectations can. The current study used explicit expectation cues to strengthen top-down expectations. Following a behavioural training session to explicitly learn the association between two cues and orthogonal gratings, participants (N=32) were scanned using 7T fMRI and presented with a cue (tone) followed by either a low contrast (predicted) grating embedded in visual noise (50% of trials), or with noise only (50% of trials). The task involved reporting the grating orientation and confidence in having seen a grating. Performance on grating present trials was significantly above chance and higher when confidence was high (M=83%) compared to low (M=60%). When no grating was presented, participants reported confidently seeing a grating on 56% of trials, suggesting false percepts did occur. Participants reported the expected (cue predicted) orientation in 55% of grating absent trials. This cue-driven effect was strongest when confidence was high (M=58%) compared to low (M= 49%). These results suggest that explicit expectations, unlike implicit expectations, can influence the contents of false percepts. Future investigations will focus on the neural correlates of this phenomenon.

title: Coarse (but Not Fine) Top-Down Control Over Consciousness: Evidence From VWM-Driven Conscious Access
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences, Zhejiang University (CN)
2. Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Neurocognitive Development and Mental Health, Zhejiang University (CN)
3. The State Key Lab of Brain-Machine Intelligence, Zhejiang University (CN)
abstract: Human visual consciousness is inherently limited, such that only a fraction of incoming information reaches awareness at any given moment. Visual working memory (VWM), the core system responsible for maintaining goal-relevant information, has been identified as a key driver of this prioritization. Specifically, stimuli that match the contents of VWM gain access to awareness more rapidly when initially suppressed from consciousness. However, it remains unclear at which representational level—coarse or fine—this top-down modulation operates. The present study addresses this question through a series of experiments that combine a VWM task with the breaking Continuous Flash Suppression (b-CFS) paradigm, in which high-contrast dynamic masks suppress target stimuli from awareness. Experiments 1a and 1b compared coarse (color) and fine (gap orientation) features within the same Landolt ring stimuli, revealing that only color matching in VWM facilitated conscious access. Experiments 2a and 2b extended this dissociation to the shape dimension, demonstrating facilitation for simple shapes (coarse) but not for complex polygons (fine). Experiments 3a and 3b further showed that VWM-driven conscious access operates at a categorical level of color representation and is neither enhanced by nor sensitive to precise color information. Finally, Experiments 4 and 5 employed global–local stimuli to identify the locus of this constraint. Experiment 4 showed that fine-level information under CFS suppression is resistant to top-down modulation, whereas Experiments 5a and 5b revealed that fine-level representations maintained in VWM are also ineffective as top-down signals. Taken together, these findings suggest that VWM facilitates conscious access in a coarse, but not fine-grained, manner. This constraint appears to arise from limitations in both unconscious visual processing and the representation of fine-grained information in VWM.

title: Development of visual expertise in medical education
affiliations:
1. University of Helsinki (FI)
2. Helsinki University Hospital (FI)
abstract: Visual reasoning skills are critical across medical specialties. Prior work shows experts achieve higher diagnostic accuracy with fewer saccades and longer fixations than novices. We examined how medical students learn to identify skin conditions during a dermatology course and compared their performance with experts, with a focus on diagnosis-specific differences. Fifth-year medical students (N=394) completed an online image-identification task in three sessions: before, during, and after the course. In a laboratory study, experts (N=7) performed the same task once with eye-tracking, and students (N=13) completed it twice (pre/post-course). On each trial, participants saw a written diagnosis and eight images and selected the matching image, then rated confidence. Each session included 47 diagnoses (most common in Finland) presented twice. The target image was randomly chosen from 15–30 exemplars.  Across sessions, students’ accuracy rose from 68% to 86%, decision times fell from 9.7 to 8.7 s, and confidence (5-point Likert) increased from 2.9 to 3.8. Substantial differences emerged across diagnoses: for the 12 easiest conditions, accuracy exceeded 90% pre-course for the 10 most difficult, accuracy remained below 75% post-course. Based on item characteristic curves, diagnoses were clustered into eight categories, revealing category-specific learning patterns. The lab study replicated the main behavioural findings. Despite improvements, students (62% to 82% 9.7 to 8.1 s) did not reach expert performance (97% correct, 6.4 s). Students’ average number of fixations decreased from 34 to 21, matching experts. Experts’ mean fixation duration was 217 ms contrary to expectations, students’ fixation duration were longer and increased from 220 to 249 ms. Eye-tracking metrics varied less across diagnoses than did behavioural performance. These results indicate that in dermatology, visual expertise development is strongly diagnosis-dependent and likely reflects both perceptual and rule-based learning. Results suggest teaching resources should be concentrated on diagnoses that remain difficult to learn.

title: Visuomotor learning enhances visual acuity and contrast sensitivity
affiliations:
1. University of Hamburg (DE)
2. LV Prasad Eye Institute (IN)
abstract: Visual perceptual learning (VPL) has been shown to improve contrast perception. Neural responses in rodents’ primary visual cortex (V1) have been shown to exhibit greater enhancement when animals perform VPL while running than in a stationary state, while results in primates are less clear. The present study examined which visual functions benefit from adding locomotion to a VPL task. Participants were assigned to one of three groups (control [n = 23], visual-manual training group [n = 20], and visuomotor training group [n = 22]). Participants in the two training groups completed assessment sessions before, immediately after, and one month after five sessions of VPL. The visuomotor group performed the training by using a Wobble board to select the relevant visual stimulus the visual-manual group responded with a mouse while sitting at a table. Participants of the control group did not participate in any training sessions and completed only three assessment sessions. During assessment sessions, Landolt-C visual acuity, Vernier acuity, contrast sensitivity function (CSF), and surround modulation were measured. In the VPL task, the visual target was defined as a uniquely oriented Gabor stimulus among other Gabor stimulus distractors. All stimuli were presented at the individual cut-off spatial frequency, with their contrast adjusted based on participants’ performance. The individual cut-off spatial frequency was defined as the spatial frequency corresponding to 50% contrast, extracted from the CSF curve. The visuomotor group showed larger improvements in Landolt-C visual acuity, Vernier acuity, and surround suppression compared to the other groups. Notably, these group differences increased after one month. Additionally, contrast sensitivity significantly improved immediately after visuomotor training. The present findings suggest that adding locomotion to a VPL task may enhance visual learning. As has been demonstrated for motor learning, visuomotor training seems to involve longer consolidation.

title: Facilitated but less selective visual cortical plasticity in children than in adults revealed by task-irrelevant perceptual learning
affiliations: 1. Universität Regensburg (DE)
abstract: Task-irrelevant visual perceptual learning (TIVPL) is a form of visual cortical plasticity characterized by enhanced detection sensitivity for features repeatedly exposed during the performance of another task. Theories of TIVPL suggest that it is tightly constrained by the contingency of internal reinforcement signals elicited by important events in the performed task, such as detecting a target among distractors. However, compared with adults, previous studies found evidence that TIVPL is less selective in children, suggesting that visual cortical plasticity may be subject to weaker constraints during childhood. Here, we investigated this hypothesis in children (7-12 years old) and college-age adults using psychophysics and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Over the course of three sessions on separate days, participants (fifteen per age group) practiced a rapid-serial-visual-presentation (RSVP) task at central fixation in which they detected the presence or absence of target images within a stream of distractor images. Together with the RSVP, task-irrelevant coherent motion directions were exposed in the visual surroundings. One direction was predominantly (66% probability) exposed in target-present RSVP-trials (paired direction). Another direction was predominantly (66% probability) exposed in target-absent RSVP-trials (unpaired direction). While performing the task, fNIRS (NIRx Medical Technologies) was recorded over occipital areas. Prior to and following the exposure period, detection performance for each motion direction was assessed. Children enhanced detection performance for paired and unpaired directions to a similar extent, whereas the enhancement was greater for the paired than the unpaired direction in adults. fNIRS recordings showed that activity (corresponding to oxygenated hemoglobin) in occipital areas was comparable between paired and unpaired directions in children but greater for paired than unpaired directions in adults. This suggests that TIVPL is less tightly constrained by the contingency of internal reinforcement signals in children than in adults, consistent with facilitated, yet less selective, visual cortical plasticity during childhood.

title: Not How Much You Remember, but How You Use It: Visual Working Memory Capacity as Strategic Stabilization
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences, Zhejiang University (CN)
2. Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Neurocognitive Development and Mental Health, Zhejiang University (CN)
abstract: Visual working memory (VWM) capacity is traditionally conceptualized as a limit on how much information can be maintained. However, increasing evidence links VWM capacity to attentional control and the regulation of cognitive resources. In natural tasks, memory use is not fixed but voluntarily determined, raising a critical question: how are individual differences in VWM capacity expressed when memory use is flexible? We addressed this question using a copying task that allows participants to trade off internal memory and external sampling. Across two experiments (N = 120), participants freely decided how many items to encode during each sampling episode. VWM capacity was measured independently using a visual change detection task. We manipulated task structure in two ways: sampling cost, which alters the incentive to rely on memory, and time pressure, which constrains the opportunity to adjust strategies. Increasing sampling cost reliably led participants to encode more items per sampling episode, replicating adaptive trade-offs between memory and resampling. However, this manipulation did not reveal any reliable relationship between VWM capacity and memory usage. In contrast, imposing time pressure produced robust capacity-related effects. Higher-capacity individuals showed more concentrated and less variable memory deployment across sampling episodes, accompanied by a reduction in mean usage. These findings suggest that VWM capacity in natural tasks is not primarily expressed as greater memory quantity. Instead, under constraint, capacity differences emerge in the stability of resource allocation. This dissociation highlights the importance of task structure in revealing individual differences and supports the view that VWM capacity reflects strategic control over memory use rather than storage limits alone.

title: The electrophysiology of iconic memory: Evidence from a partial report task
affiliations: 1. University of Verona (IT)
abstract: Despite extensive research, a thorough characterisation of the electrophysiological mechanisms underlying iconic memory is still missing. The aim of this study, therefore, was to exploit a partial report paradigm to disentangle neural activity associated with stimulus perception and icon formation and maintenance from that associated with post-perceptual processes. A total of 26 participants took part in the study. We recorded EEG while they performed a partial report task. They were shown circular arrays composed of six letters and lasting 100 ms. Afterward, an acoustic cue informed the participant on which side of the stimulus to report. The majority of the electrophysiological differences occurred in the time window between 850 and 1100 ms and consisted of a positive deflection over parieto-occipital electrodes ipsilateral to the side to report. We also performed a linear regression between participants’ accuracy and components’ amplitude, finding a positive relationship between accuracy and P1, and negative relationships between accuracy and P3, a component peaking at ~730 ms that we termed Visual Code Reactivation (VCR), and another component peaking at ~1060 ms that we termed Task-dependent Information Filtering (TIF). We also detected a negative correlation between the number of intrusions and TIF amplitude. Our results shed light on the distinct processes involved in iconic memory, suggesting the distinction between processes responsible for encoding and maintaining the neural trace of the visual stimulus and higher-order, task-related functions devoted to selecting an information subset for conscious report. In this regard, the TIF component could represent a filtering mechanism, preventing irrelevant information from being further processed. In conclusion, our results are the first detailed description of the electrophysiological processes sustaining iconic memory. They also have potential implications for the consciousness debate, particularly regarding the overflow argument, of which they could constitute an electrophysiological confirmation.

title: Outcome history shapes implicit perceptual learning without awareness of the eye of origin
affiliations: 1. Department of Experimental Psychology, University College London (UK)
abstract: Positive outcomes can shape visual processing for behaviourally relevant features such as locations, objects, or stimulus attributes. It remains unclear, however, whether such modulation can also arise when the source of those outcomes is not consciously accessible. To address this question, we employed a dichoptic visual detection task in which ongoing stimulation to both eyes was perceptually fused into a single centrally presented grating. Detection targets consisted of a brief Gaussian contrast decrement that appeared in one eye only, while target intensity was manipulated to estimate detection threshold. Crucially, although the target appeared in one eye, its eye of origin was not consciously accessible to participants. We first established baseline detection performance for each eye without eye-specific outcome differences. In a subsequent phase, we introduced a hidden eye-specific outcome structure: successful detections from one eye were followed by positive outcomes with high probability (100%), whereas successful detections from the other eye were followed by positive outcomes with low probability (20%). Because perceptual learning is strongly confounded by generic practice and baseline visual asymmetries, we analysed trial-by-trial responses using a continuous Generalised Linear Mixed Model to isolate outcome-related changes in performance. The model indicated greater learning-related improvement for the eye associated with the higher probability of a positive outcome, after controlling for baseline-dependent constraints, despite participants having no conscious awareness of the eye-specific contingency. These findings suggest that asymmetric feedback can modulate eye-specific perceptual learning. They are consistent with an implicit ocular prioritisation account, in which differential outcome history biases processing in eye-specific channels without requiring conscious or top-down attention. More broadly, the findings suggest that outcome-dependent learning may extend to early sensory stages where eye-specific information remains partially segregated.

title: Multidimensional Statistical Learning of Spatiotemporal Regularities
affiliations:
1. State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Science and Mental Health, Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CN)
2. Department of Psychology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China (CN)
abstract: To navigate the visual environment, the human brain must extract regularities that span across space and time. While temporal and spatial regularities can be acquired in isolation via statistical learning (SL), the joint acquisition of multidimensional regularities remains poorly understood. Here, we present a novel and robust form of visual SL for spatiotemporal regularities. Across four experiments, participants spontaneously learned regularities defined by coincident binding of temporal order and spatial configuration in visual chunks, even when regularities were task-irrelevant and remained unnoticed. This learning effect demonstrated remarkable generalization across (i) distinct spatial structures, (ii) varied temporal parameters, (iii) different combinatorial units (pairs vs. triplets), and (iv) multiple behavioral measures, including explicit familiarity judgments and implicit change-detection tasks. We further examined the relationship between this multidimensional SL and unidimensional SL using correlation and principal component analyses. Converging evidence revealed both domain-general and domain-specific components, moderated by observers’ awareness levels as identified by assessment types and confidence ratings. Relatively implicit measures yielded dissociable or even antagonistic patterns between temporal and spatial learning, whereas relatively explicit measures captured a positive coupling among all unidimensional and multidimensional effects. Together, these findings demonstrate reliable acquisition of spatiotemporal regularities, which engages an awareness-dependent hierarchical mechanism for integrating visual information over the spatial and temporal domains.

title: Bias in plain sight: Eye markers of contextual effects in visual working memory
affiliations:
1. Emotion Cognition Lab, Faculty of Psychology, SWPS University in Katowice (PL)
2. University of Bergen, Faculty of Psychology, Department of Psychosocial Science (NO)
abstract: Visual working memory (VWM)—the ability to maintain and use visual information—is crucial for many daily tasks, from navigation to grocery shopping. However, context can significantly affect our memories: the presence of similar items during memorization can not only reduce the memory accuracy but also bias the recall. Here, we investigate the information-processing dynamics underlying these biases by examining eye movements and pupillary responses during the encoding and reporting of colors. Participants memorized the colors of two squares, with similarity between their mean colors and color heterogeneity within each item manipulated across trials. They later reported the average color of each square using a color wheel. We first replicated the findings of Chetverikov and Hansmann-Roth (2016), demonstrating that the relative noise distribution between the memorized items influences the strength and direction of biases in line with the recently proposed Demixing Model. Preliminary results further suggest that eye movements and pupil size during encoding predict memory accuracy and biases. Finally, analysis of the response phase indicated that participants' gaze is often drawn to non-targets near the end of the response, even when the behavioral responses are biased away from those non- targets. This suggests that gaze position and pupil size provide a valuable source of information about internal dynamics of visual-information encoding and decision-making during the response, potentially clarifying how observers differentiate signals corresponding to different stimuli.

title: Visualizing Memory with AI: Generative Text-to-Image Models in Free Recall Tasks
affiliations:
1. Institute of Psychology, Czech Academy of Sciences (CZ)
2. Department of Psychology, Faculty of Arts, Charles University (CZ)
3. Department of Psychology, University of Chicago (US)
abstract: Research on long-term visual memory has traditionally investigated the free recall of visual scenes through verbal descriptions. Bainbridge and colleagues (2019) later introduced drawing as a method of free recall however, the level of detail captured in such drawings remains uncertain due to differences in drawing ability. Building on this approach, the present study examined whether generative multimodal models (GMMs) could serve as an alternative tool for assessing scene memory. We employed a design similar to drawing-based recall research while possibly overcoming limitations in participants’ drawing skills. Participants (N=52) first memorized 20 images from one of two scene categories (streets or rooms). The images were AI-generated, allowing us to create highly similar pairs depicting very similar scenes participants studied only one image from each pair. Then they completed a digit span task, followed by the free recall phase, consisting of recreating the previously viewed images using a text-to-image model (ChatGPT-4o). Afterwards, they completed a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task with foils that were highly similar to the memorized images. To evaluate the generated outputs, independent raters (N=80) attempted to match each generated image to its original source image in an 8-alternative matching task, providing a measure of recognizability. We then analyzed the effects of textual properties of the conversation transcripts, such as frustration levels and the number of objects or words, on recognizability of the final generated image. The raters selected the correct image significantly more often than expected by chance (probability correct=53%, effect size h=0.91). In addition, respondents selected the target pair (target image or very close distractor) in 94% of cases. Textual properties were not significantly related to image recognizability. Overall, the findings suggest that GMMs may offer a high-fidelity alternative to traditional hand-drawn recall methods for studying long-term visual memory for scenes.

title: Differential Network Metrics as Predictors of Specificity and Transfer in Perceptual Learning
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences, Zhejiang University (CN)
2. Department of Psychology, School of Education, Soochow University (CN)
abstract: Visual perceptual learning is characterized by specificity to trained conditions. Understanding the mechanisms behind this specificity remains a fundamental topic in perceptual learning research. In a previous ERP study (Zhang-et-al., 2013), half the participants (n=14) in Vernier learning exhibited location specificity (TI<0.5), while the other half demonstrated learning transfer (TI>0.5) across the visual hemifield. Here, we examined small-world network metrics to compare the changes in the topological properties of the whole-brain network between the specificity and transfer groups. We established functional connectivity between each pair of EEG channels by calculating the phase-locking value using a wavelet transform in the beta band. We then applied a threshold to obtain undirected binary small-world networks for each participant at trained and transfer locations before and after training. From these networks, we calculated the clustering coefficient, indicating local interconnectedness, and the shortest path length, reflecting global information integration. Before training, both groups exhibited similar small-world properties, characterized by high clustering coefficients and short path lengths. After training, while both groups displayed similar threshold reductions, the specificity group showed higher clustering coefficient (p=.003) and longer path length (p<.001), whereas the network metrics of the transfer group remained unchanged (ps>.111). Additionally, when the transfer effects were tested at the untrained location, the specificity group demonstrated trends (ps<.007) in network metrics similar to those at the trained location, while the transfer group displayed higher clustering coefficient (p=.035) with unchanged path length. We conclude that whether learning is location-specific is pre-determined by training-induced changes in network properties. While the transfer group maintained both local and global efficiencies, the specificity group exhibited over-optimized local efficiency at the expense of global efficiency, which likely hinders learning transfer. These results provide crucial insights into the mechanisms of specificity and transfer in perceptual learning from the perspective of brain network dynamics.

title: The Well-Tempered Color Wheel: Toward a Unified Pedagogical Model for Additive and Subtractive Color Systems
affiliations: 1. TOBB ETU (TR)
abstract: **The Well-Tempered Color Wheel: Toward a Unified Pedagogical Model for Additive and Subtractive Color Systems** Traditional color education relies heavily on historical color wheel models that inadequately reflect the perceptual and physical foundations of human color vision. In particular, the widely used twelve-hue red–yellow–blue color wheel conflates additive and subtractive color systems and misrepresents complementary color relationships. These inconsistencies contribute to persistent conceptual confusion, especially in contexts that require accurate reasoning across both digital and printed media. This study introduces the Well-Tempered Color Wheel, a perceptually coherent model that unifies additive and subtractive colors within a single diagrammatic framework. The proposed model defines complementary color relationships through numerical inversion in red–green–blue space and aligns these relations with subtractive color behavior. Inspired by musical temperament systems, slight perceptual adjustments are introduced to achieve global symmetry, consistent color opponency, and pedagogical clarity. Unlike traditional color wheels, this model explicitly incorporates achromatic reference points—including black, white, and gray—in order to stabilize luminance and contrast relationships. This structure enables intuitive visualization of both light-based and pigment-based color mixing while preserving the instructional advantages of a twelve-hue format. The Well-Tempered Color Wheel does not propose new perceptual mechanisms. Instead, it offers a representational correction that aligns commonly used educational and experimental color diagrams with established principles of color perception. By integrating additive and subtractive color logic within a unified perceptual framework, the model clarifies fundamental misconceptions regarding primaries, complements, and system boundaries. This approach has direct implications for visual perception research, experimental stimulus design, and interdisciplinary color education. The proposed model supports more accurate reasoning about color contrast, complementarity, and inversion across media, providing a robust perceptual reference tool for both scientific and educational applications.

title: Scotopic population receptive field properties throughout the visual hierarchy
affiliations:
1. Edmond and Lily Safra Center for Brain Sciences, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem (IL)
2. Department of Neurology, Hadassah Medical Organization and Faculty of Medicine, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem (IL)
abstract: Scotopic vision has several low-level limitations relative to photopic vision, including reduced acuity and a foveal scotoma. High-level visual abilities such as reading and face recognition are retained, although the cortical mechanisms supporting this remain incompletely characterized. Here, we used population receptive field (pRF) modeling to examine cortical representations of the visual field under scotopic conditions, focusing on pRF eccentricity and size across the visual hierarchy. Fourteen normally sighted subjects completed pRF mapping during fMRI scanning under photopic and scotopic conditions, using a stimulus that incorporated faces, houses, and letters to engage higher-level regions. A Gaussian model was fit to each voxel’s responses to estimate pRF size and position. Retinotopic areas (V1, V2d, V3d, V2v, V3v, hV4) were defined individually based on photopic pRF data, while category-selective regions (FFA, OFA, PPA, TOS, MT+) were defined using a photopic functional localizer. As expected, fewer voxels responded to the pRF stimulus under scotopic than photopic conditions, and responsive voxels exhibited higher mean eccentricity. However, when restricting analysis to voxels responsive in both conditions, there were only limited differences in mean eccentricity or in the overall distribution across eccentricity bins. Additionally, pRF sizes were smaller under scotopic conditions in most regions (V1, V2d, V3d, V3v, hV4, PPA, TOS) at 5-8-deg eccentricity. These findings indicate that pRF modeling with complex stimuli can effectively probe scotopic representations in high-level visual cortex. The shift towards peripheral processing under scotopic conditions appears to result at least partially from loss of the central visual field representation. Reduced pRF sizes under scotopic conditions may reflect either modeling artifacts or compensatory adaptations to low resolution in the rod system. Further work is needed to clarify these effects and extend them to additional visual regions.

title: The impact of simulated colour vision defects on game performance
affiliations: 1. The University of Manchester (UK)
abstract: Background: Congenital colour vision defect (CCVD) affects approximately 8% of males and 0.5% of females, with red-green defects being the most common type. Digital games are a common leisure activity that requires visual processing under different task demands. This study investigates whether simulated red-green CCVD affects game performance. Methods: Two games with different visual demands were used: Zuma’s Revenge (pattern-based matching task) and Star Wars Battlefront II (dynamic action shooting task). Participants who are experienced with game play and with normal colour vision completed six visual conditions: normal vision, simulated protan, simulated deutan, mild protan simulation, mild deutan simulation, and greyscale. Performance was measured using game scores. Short interviews were conducted after each condition to explore perceived difficulty. Results: Preliminary data from 10 participants showed a significant effect of visual condition on performance in Zuma’s Revenge, F(5,45) = 19.95, p < .001, partial η² = .689. Significantly lower performance in the greyscale condition compared to normal, protan, mild protan, and mild deutan conditions (all p ≤ .007). Significant differences were also observed between normal and deutan (p = .003). In contrast, no significant effect of condition was found for Star Wars Battlefront II, F(5,45) = 0.748, p = .592, partial η² = .077, with similar mean scores across conditions. Interview responses indicated that simulated colour vision defects were perceived as more challenging and less enjoyable, even though the performance was not significantly affected. Conclusion: The impact of simulated colour vision defects on game performance appears to depend on task demands. Pattern-based tasks showed greater performance differences, whereas dynamic environments may rely more on motion and other visual cues. These findings support the feasibility of using game-based tasks as an outcome measure in future research involving individuals with congenital colour vision defects.

title: Independent adjustment of luminosity, saturation and hue for probing the color appearance of simultaneous contrast
affiliations: 1. Univ. Grenoble Alpes, Univ. Savoie Mont Blanc, CNRS, LPNC (FR)
abstract: We present a method that allows the luminosity (k), saturation (s) and hue (ξ) of a stimulus pattern displayed on a computer screen to be varied independently. The display’s color space resides in a metric vector space where the angles between RGB vectors encode their spectral correlations. The parameters ksξ define a hyperboloid (k determines the surface level, s its eccentricity, and ξ the angular position on the hyperboloid) that is contained within a cone. In the first configuration the cone’s surface intersects the RGB vectors. In the second configuration the cone and hyperboloid are oriented so that their constant‑saturation planes are orthogonal to the vector representing the spectral luminous‑efficiency function V(λ). A subsequent hyperbolic rotation aligns the zero‑saturation condition (s = 0) with the gray axis. The apertures of both the cone and the hyperboloid were expanded to obtain independence between luminosity and saturation. We carried out a simultaneous‑contrast experiment in which participants adjusted the color of a circular stimulus on a neutral‑gray background to match the appearance of the same circle surrounded by a color‑inducing annulus. The test set consisted of three isoluminant desaturated colors—red, green and blue—while the inducing set comprised six isoluminant saturated color—red, yellow, green, cyan and magenta. Prior to the main task, a training session required participants to first match the color of a test pattern (chosen from the test set) to that of a different reference circular pattern, both presented on neutral gray. This second configuration produced more accurate adjustments, as indicated by a smaller distance between test and reference during training and a larger adjustment distance during the experimental phase. Analyses showed that adjustments were consistently opposite to the inducing annulus and that an interaction existed between the test and inducing patterns.

title: Quantifying the Munker–White effect using an interactive colour-matching application
affiliations:
1. Centro de Investigación en Tecnologías Gráficas, Universitat Politècnica de València (ES)
2. Universitat Politècnica de València (ES)
abstract: Colour perception is strongly shaped by visual context, as illustrated by Munker–White-type colour assimilation illusions: the same physical colour can appear different when viewed against backgrounds with non-uniform geometric and chromatic characteristics. Although the phenomenon is well known, there are few systematic quantitative data on the magnitude and direction of these perceptual deviations, which limits comparisons across studies and the development of predictive models. We present an interactive application developed in Python with the support of artificial intelligence tools, designed to quantify in a reproducible manner the chromatic variation induced by the Munker–White illusion using colour-matching tasks. In each trial, a fixed-colour target patch is shown with a superimposed pattern of coloured stripes (a Munker–White-type stimulus), alongside a physically identical comparison patch presented without stripes on a neutral background. Conditions are parameterised by three chromaticities: the stimulus colour, the background colour, and the colour of the superimposed stripes. Six base patterns are used and, for each, an inverted condition swaps the background and stripe colours while keeping the stimulus constant, yielding 12 adjustment conditions. Each observer adjusts the colour specifications of the sample patch using controls that manipulate CIE LCh values (lightness, chroma and hue) until an apparent match with the reference patch is achieved. The difference between the physical colour and the adjusted colour provides a direct measure of effect magnitude for each condition, expressible via ΔE metrics in CIELAB space. Preliminary results from one observer show robust perceptual shifts on the order of several tens of ΔE units, with sign reversals when the background–stripe relationship is inverted. This tool enables the generation of standardised quantitative data on the Munker–White effect and provides a foundation for future models capable of predicting colour appearance as a function of visual context.

title: Prototypical colour selections and their associations with emotion concepts across 35 countries
authors: International Colour Emotion Association Survey Group
affiliations:
1. Institute of Psychology, University of Lausanne (CH)
2. School of Social Work, University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Western Switzerland (CH)
3. Computer Vision Center / Computer Science Department, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (ES)
abstract: Colours and emotions are tightly linked, seemingly on a universal level. However, previous cross-cultural studies often relied on presenting colour terms rather than colour patches, limiting insights into how colour relates to emotions as a perceptual stimulus. Here, we investigated colour-emotion associations with a novel two-step approach examining i) what participants chose as prototypical colours for the 11 basic colour categories and turquoise, and ii) how these self-selected colour patches are associated with 20 emotion concepts.  We collected these data within the framework of the International Colour-Emotion Association Survey. At data extraction, we had data from 6995 participants across 35 countries and 38 languages. Participants were asked to first select the best example for each colour category (i.e., the prototypical colour) using a digital colour picker. Then, participants used the Geneva Emotion Wheel to associate each self-selected prototypical colour with one, several, or none of the 20 emotion concepts.  We examined the variability of the median colour choices per country in terms of hue, lightness, and chroma in the CIE LCh colour space. The highest agreement across countries was observed for white on lightness and chroma (SD = 0.00), and for red on hue (circular SD = 0.75). Conversely, the lowest agreement was observed for blue on lightness (SD = 7.03), turquoise on hue (circular SD = 15.9), and green on chroma (SD = 5.87). For colour-emotion associations, their overall patterns showed high similarity across countries, with an average pattern correlation of r = 0.92 (range = 0.73-0.96). Similarly, correspondence analysis indicated consistent spatial relationships between colour categories and emotion concepts structured primarily along the dimensions of valence-lightness (55.6% of explained variance) and arousal-warmth (21.7% of explained variance). These results support the universality and stability of colour-emotion associations across countries when working with both, colour terms and self-selected prototypical colours.

title: Language-specific structure of color space: Linking language and perception in Cantonese and Hakka
affiliations:
1. Guangzhou College of Business and Technology (CN)
2. Research Group EPAEG - Ergonomics, Psychological Aesthetics, Gestalt (DE)
3. University of Bamberg (DE)
abstract: Color naming varies across languages, yet little is known about how fine-grained differences between closely related languages structure color space and their relationship with perceptual factors like color categorization and appreciation. Cantonese and Hakka are two major Sinitic varieties spoken in southern China. They share a common writing system and cultural background, but differ substantially in phonology and vocabulary. This makes them particularly suitable for isolating linguistic effects from broader cultural differences. We recruited university students from Guangdong province (Hakka speakers: N = 27, mean age = 21 Cantonese speakers: N = 78, mean age = 22). All participants were fluent in Mandarin in addition to their respective languages. We first compiled non-basic color terms for each language (Hakka: 56 Cantonese: 68) based on interviews, dictionaries, and online sources. During the experiment, we presented participants with color terms from their respective languages and asked them to select the corresponding color appearances using a custom color-picker interface (sRGB), which we then transformed into CIELAB space. Cluster analyses revealed systematic differences between the two languages. Both groups exhibited eight cluster centers but with distinct category structures (Cantonese: red, yellow, green, teal, blue, purple, white, black Hakka: red, yellow, green, purple, brown, white, grey, black). Critically, in the blue–teal–green region, Cantonese partitioned the color space into three distinct clusters. In contrast, Hakka showed a single broader cluster spanning this region, with its centroid located between the Cantonese green and teal clusters, indicating a coarser categorical structure. These findings demonstrate that closely related languages can systematically differ in how they segment color space, even within a shared cultural and geographical context. Building on the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis, we will next examine whether these language-specific structures relate to differences in perceptual sensitivity, providing a controlled test of language-perception relationships.

title: Mapping a spatially varying metric in RGB color space using large-scale behavioral data
affiliations:
1. Giessen University (DE)
2. Danish Technical University (DK)
3. Utrecht University (NL)
4. KU Leuven (BE)
abstract: Current color difference metrics are based on sparse measurements of subsets of the three-dimensional color space. Recovering the full structure of perceptual sensitivity would require dense behavioral data across many color locations that until now seemed to be out of reach of experimental methods. We developed Colympics, a gamified psychophysical paradigm designed to obtain such data more efficiently. Observers view displays containing 50 colored items and select those that do not match the majority (reference) color under time pressure, receiving rewards for correct responses and penalties for errors. Target colors differ from the reference along multiple directions and amplitudes. Each unit of measurement therefore yields 50 binary decisions for a single reference color. A full dataset consists of 35 reference colors arranged on a body-centered cubic lattice in RGB space. Across 28 observers, this resulted in more than 100,000 decisions, with individual datasets ranging from approximately 1,600 to 21,000 decisions and stable performance between 67% and 77% correct. At each sampled location, perceptual distances were characterized by combining responses across directions in color space. This yields a local description in the form of a symmetric positive-definite tensor, corresponding to an ellipsoid of equal perceptual difference. These local estimates were aggregated across observers into a median metric field using the Frobenius norm, while preserving anisotropy and orientation. Comparison of individual ellipsoids with the median field shows substantial agreement in shape and orientation after removing overall size (median similarity 0.745 on a scale from 0 to 1). At the same time, observers differ systematically in sensitivity, reflected in approximately twofold variation in ellipsoid size. Agreement is stronger at the observer level than at the stimulus level. This approach provides a promising route toward a color space metric that can be adapted to stimulus conditions and that captures individual differences in perceptual sensitivity.

title: Peripheral limits of chromatic sensitivity in head-centered coordinates for ideal HMD design
affiliations:
1. Japan Broadcasting Corporation - NHK (JP)
2. NHK Foundation (JP)
abstract:
An ‘ideal’ head-mounted display (HMD) can be defined as one that provides a visual experience indistinguishable from that obtained with the naked eyes. To achieve this, display performance should match or exceed the capabilities of the human visual system, while avoiding unnecessary excess that would result in inefficient resource use. To determine ideal HMD specifications, it is therefore essential to characterize human visual performance with eye movements allowed and to describe visual sensitivities in head-centered coordinates.

The experimental apparatus comprised four curved displays (each with a radius of curvature of 1,000 mm and a visual angle of 69 degrees width) arranged on a virtual sphere centered at the observer’s right eye and placed radially in the upward, downward, nasal, and temporal directions. The visual stimuli were natural scenes and their pixelwise shuffled counterparts, which disrupted spatial structure while preserving pixel-level statistics. In each stimulus, peripheral regions were achromatized while maintaining the original luminance distribution. Observers viewed the stimuli monocularly with free eye movements, while their heads were stabilized using a chinrest.

A two-interval forced-choice task was employed, in which intact and partially achromatized stimuli were presented. Observers reported the interval containing an achromatic region. The eccentricity of the chromatic–achromatic boundary for each direction was adaptively estimated using the QUEST procedure.

Threshold eccentricities did not differ significantly between stimulus types, indicating that spatial structure had little influence on the extent of the color-sensitive region. The mean threshold eccentricities were approximately 55 (upper), 68 (lower), 64 (nasal), and 82 degrees (temporal), which closely matched the peripheral eccentricity limits for detecting spatial frequency components above 1 cpd, as reported in our previous study.

These results characterize the color-sensitive area in head-centered coordinates and offer practical guidelines for pixel arrangement and rendering precision in HMD systems aiming for ideal visual fidelity.

title: The effect of stimulus duration on various simultaneous contrast effects: an exploratory online study
affiliations:
1. Hokkaido University (JP)
2. Ritsumeikan University (JP)
abstract: Previous reports suggest that simultaneous contrast effects, such as lightness/brightness contrast (Kaneko & Gilchrist, 2020 Kaneko & Murakami, 2012), color contrast (Kaneko & Murakami, 2012), or the tilt illusion (Wenderoth & Johnstone, 1988), were stronger in shorter duration conditions. The simultaneous contrast effect is observed across many other visual features, but it is unclear whether this temporal dependency is generalized to other variations.  In this study, we explored the effect of duration on five varieties of simultaneous contrast effects: brightness, color, luminance contrast (Chubb illusion), spatial frequency, and tilt. The experiment was conducted online. The target stimulus was presented repeatedly on the left side of the display, and the adjustable probe stimulus (which remained visible throughout) was presented on the right. The participant’s task was to adjust the probe’s brightness/color/contrast/spatial frequency/tilt with a slider to match the appearance of the test. Each presentation of the test and its surround was for 1, 5, or 30 frames, but it was repeated multiple times with a 30-frame blank interval in between until the adjustment was complete. Each condition was repeated twice in a session. Data collected from participants who completed all the trials (N=82 after outlier removal) showed a weak to moderate within-condition reliability (Pearson’s r between .19 and .62). We replicated the stronger effects in the shorter-duration condition for brightness contrast and the tilt illusion, but not for color contrast. In addition, the results suggest the enhancement of the effect at shorter durations for spatial frequency and luminance contrast. Our preliminary data suggest that the stronger contrast effect in brief presentations may be common across various visual features. We discuss the pros and cons of an online study of visual psychophysics involving temporally sensitive stimuli.

title: Attention-Driven Excitatory Neurometabolic Dynamics in the Human Visual Cortex: Evidence from Task-Based fMRS
affiliations:
1. Institute of Neuroscience, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (TW)
2. Department of Education and Research, Taipei City Hospital (TW)
abstract: Sustained attention, encompassing the maintenance of both external and internal focus over time, is essential to effective perception and learning. Distributed brain networks supporting sustained attention have been extensively documented, including prefrontal, cingulate, thalamic, and visual cortices. Although recent studies have highlighted the visual cortex's involvement in early-stage attention modulation, its underlying neurochemical mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Our prior work has demonstrated that excitatory neurotransmitters, particularly glutamate (Glu) and the combined glutamate-glutamine signal (Glx), play a critical role in perceptual learning—a process that typically requires prolonged and focused attentional engagement. Here, we applied time-resolved functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS) at 3T to examine whether sustained attentional demands modulate Glx levels in the visual cortex. Five healthy adults completed three noontime sessions across consecutive days using a block design with alternating rest and visual stimulation periods. A vigilance task during central fixation ensured continuous attentional engagement. Each session comprised four spectra acquired via the PRESS sequence (TR = 2s, TE = 30 ms, 160 time points) yielding 40 time-resolved data points (temporal resolution = 32s). Spectra with CRLB >15% were excluded for quality control, and attentional performance was quantified by vigilance task response accuracy. Time-resolved analysis revealed significantly elevated Glx concentrations during stimulation relative to rest blocks (F(443)=24.01, p<0.001), with no significant change in GSH, NAA, or creatine. In contrast, time- averaged spectra (temporal resolution = 320s) failed to capture this effect, underscoring the necessity of fine temporal resolution. Furthermore, Glx concentrations exhibited a significant positive correlation with attentional performance (r = 0.59, p = 0.041). Together, these findings demonstrate that visual cortical Glx is dynamically modulated by visual stimulation, with modulation magnitude further shaped by attentional demands, suggesting a potential link between attention-driven Glx signatures and early sensory processing mechanisms, possibly contributing to perceptual learning.

title: Using Eye Tracking to Understand Imperfect Knowledge of both Object Identities and Object Locations in the Multiple Object Awareness Paradigm
affiliations: 1. University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: In everyday environments, people frequently need to maintain awareness of multiple moving objects simultaneously. Traditional Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) and Multiple Identity Tracking (MIT) paradigms typically assess performance using binary accuracy measures, which may underestimate the information observers retain about their environment. The Multiple Object Awareness (MOA) paradigm addresses this limitation by allowing multiple response attempts, enabling the measurement of graded awareness. Here we used the MOA paradigm in combination with eye tracking to examine whether observers retain partial information about both the locations and identities of moving objects. Across two experiments, participants were asked to track coloured squares moving within a display. After a period of time, all squares stopped moving and were replaced with grey disks. Participants were then asked to indicate the location of a target square. We analysed the number of clicks required to identify the target, spatial proximity of incorrect responses, colour similarity between selected items and the target, and eye movement behaviour during tracking. Our results indicated that incorrect selections were systematically closer to the target location and more similar in colour than expected by chance, indicating the presence of imprecise spatial and identity representations. Eye movement measures provided converging evidence linking this graded awareness to attentional and working memory allocation: greater fixation time on the target predicted fewer attempts required to locate it, whereas longer intervals since the last fixation were associated with reduced precision, particularly under higher tracking load. These findings provide converging evidence that visual awareness during multiple object tracking is graded rather than all-or-nothing.

title: A model for perceptual traveling waves grounded in Normalization
affiliations:
1. Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Integrative Neuroscience and Cognition Center (FR)
2. Department of Psychology, New York University (US)
3. Center for Neural Science, New York University (US)
4. Institut Universitaire de France (FR)
abstract: Attention rhythmically fluctuates at low frequencies (<20 Hz) creating cycles of increased and decreased perceptual performance, supported by brain oscillations at corresponding frequencies (VanRullen, 2016 Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2019 Kienitz, Schmid and Dugué, 2022). Recent work showed that these oscillations can propagate across the retinotopic visual cortex as Traveling Waves –smooth phase shifts propagating across cortical space (Dugué and Chavane, 2025). Critically, behavioral empirical evidence suggests that traveling waves can modulate perceptual cycles in space, i.e., perceptual cycles can travel across the retinotopic space (Fakche and Dugué, 2024). Here, we propose a biophysically-plausible computational model to explain traveling waves in the primary visual cortex (V1) and predict the consequences on perceptual cycles. We make use of the principles developed in an existing V1 model of perceptual traveling waves during binocular rivalry –a phenomenon where the dominance of a rival image progressively shifts to the suppressed image as an illusory perceptual wave (Cardoso, Li, Heeger and Dugué, 2025). The model posits that these perceptual waves are driven by attentional modulation and mutual inhibition to drive competition between the rival images, and rely on the phenomenological principle of normalization –a canonical computation explaining how attentional allocation modulates visual cortex responses (Carandini and Heeger, 2012). We first extended this model using the ORGaNICs framework, a class of biophysically-plausible recurrent neural circuits which have divisive normalization as an emergent property (Heeger and Mackey, 2019). Using this framework applied to the neurophysiological constraints of V1, we replicated the previous model of binocular rivalry with an emphasis on biophysical plausibility. We then assessed the generalizability of the model predictions to empirical data other than binocular rivalry and in which perceptual cycles propagate across the retinotopic space. Together, we characterized the circuit-level mechanisms of traveling waves and offer a model to guide future behavioral predictions.

title: Visual attention without multisensory support: single-channel perception constraints in military FPV drone operators
affiliations: 1. University of Latvia, Faculty of Education Sciences and Psychology (LV)
abstract: Military FPV (first-person view) drone operators work in a perceptual condition rarely studied in controlled settings: enclosed goggles deliver a single monocular video feed as the sole perceptual input, with no vestibular, proprioceptive, or aerodynamic feedback. Auditory input is further restricted by operational constraints. This configuration eliminates the multisensory redundancy that normally supports attentional reorienting. Models that predict graded, load-proportional exclusion of peripheral information would expect monitoring to resume as task demands decrease. The present data could suggest a different pattern. Nine semi-structured interviews with military drone operators (Latvian National Guard and Ukrainian combat FPV pilots), analysed through thematic coding, identified attentional phenomena specific to this single-channel condition. Three convergent findings emerged. First, operators report that flight parameters displayed within the visual feed become functionally inaccessible during target engagement, with several describing complete loss of awareness of peripheral display elements, including active blinking alarms. Second, trainee pilots who attempt to shift attention from the video stream to flight parameters lose aircraft control instantaneously, suggesting a discrete attentional toggle rather than graded reallocation. Third, the attentionally accessible region contracts spatially toward the display centre during engagement, with parameters at screen edges remaining functionally undetected leading operators to reconfigure indicator layouts accordingly. Together, these observations point to attentional exclusion that is discontinuous rather than graded, and spatially structured rather than uniform. Operators spontaneously compensate through a voice-linked co-pilot, the only available cross-modal channel. These convergent phenomena - arising under reduced sensorimotor embodiment and constrained multisensory integration - suggest that single-channel visual operation constitutes a distinct perceptual regime, with implications for understanding how bodily feedback contributes to attentional flexibility.

title: Similar Effects but Separate Mechanisms: Attention in Multistability and Visual Search
affiliations:
1. University of Bamberg (DE)
2. Research Group EPÆG - Ergonomics, Psychological Æsthetics, Gestalt (DE)
3. Bamberg Graduate School of Affective and Cognitive Sciences (BaGrACS) (DE)
4. University of Iceland (IS)
abstract: Visual attention enables selective prioritization of relevant information, shaping both what we perceive and how efficiently we act on it. Two well-documented phenomena that reflect this influence are volitional control in multistable perception and attentional priming in visual search. In multistable perception, attention allows observers to bias or modulate perceptual alternations between competing interpretations of an ambiguous stimulus. In visual search, repeated selection of a target feature facilitates faster detection, reflecting attentional priming. Despite their conceptual similarities, it remains unclear whether these effects rely on shared underlying mechanisms.  Here, we directly compared these phenomena within the same participants by using a shared stimulus feature, the direction of a sphere’s rotation. In the multistable perception task, participants viewed an ambiguous rotating sphere and attempted to modulate the rate of perceptual switches between alternative rotation directions. In the visual search task, participants identified a target defined by its rotation direction, allowing us to quantify attentional priming through repetition benefits. This within-subject design enabled us to assess whether individual differences in attentional control generalize across tasks. Participants showed robust effects in both paradigms: they successfully influenced perceptual dynamics in multistable displays and exhibited reliable attentional priming in visual search. However, individual performance did not correlate across tasks. This dissociation suggests that, although both phenomena are shaped by selective attention and share similar behavioral signatures, they rely on mechanisms that are at least partially distinct. These findings clarify how attention operates across different perceptual contexts and highlight the importance of distinguishing between superficially similar effects when developing models of visual attention and perceptual selection. All data and analysis code are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/HJWSU

title: Classifying Focused and Switched Attention Based on Eye Tracking Across Single and Dual Tasks
affiliations: 1. Somareality (AT)
abstract: Attention can be either allocated in a focused manner towards a single task or distributed across multiple tasks, requiring ongoing attentional switching. Distinguishing between these two attentional states is important in real world environments, such as driving, medical training, and aviation. The present study aimed to validate our Attention Type Classifier (ATC) that uses eye tracking data to differentiate between focused and switched attention. Participants wore mobile eye tracking glasses while completing two tasks intended to demonstrate two attentional states. In the single task, participants preformed a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) paradigm, where participants responded to infrequently shown numbers embedded within a stream of letters. This was expected to demonstrate focused attention due to the sustained attentional processing at a single task. In the dual task, participants performed the same RSVP at the centre, while simultaneously monitoring the four corners of the screen for a Gabor patch and reporting its orientation (e.g., tilted left or right). This required repeated shifts of attention between the central and peripheral tasks, therefore inducing attentional task switching. Results demonstrated that our ATC algorithm classified a significantly higher probability of switched attention during the dual task, compared to the single task. Behavioural data supported this, with reduced accuracy and slower reactions times observed under the dual task, indicating reduced attentional resources for the RSVP task. Accuracy did not differ between the central and peripheral tasks within the dual task, suggesting that attention was distributed in a similar manner across both single tasks rather than prioritising one task over the other. Overall, these findings demonstrate that eye movement patterns provide reliable markers of attentional states. The ability of our ATC algorithm to distinguish between focused and switched attention in controlled settings provides a foundation for extending this towards naturalistic environments.

title: Traveling Waves in Attentional Orienting and Reorienting
affiliations:
1. Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Integrative Neuroscience and Cognition Center (FR)
2. Sorbonne Université, Institut du Cerveau - Paris Brain Institute - ICM, Inserm, CNRS, AP-HP - Hôpital de la Pitié Salpêtrière - DMU Neurosciences - Neuro ICU (FR)
3. Institut Universitaire de France (FR)
abstract: Attention –the selection and facilitation of sensory information processing– is associated with low-frequency neural oscillations across distributed brain regions (Kienitz et al., 2022). Specifically, sustained attentional orienting is commonly associated with alpha-band oscillations (8-12Hz), whereas during attentional reorienting, theta-band oscillations (4-7Hz) dominate. Despite the inherently spatio-temporal nature of attention, most studies have examined it primarily in either the spatial or temporal domain alone, thereby limiting explanatory power. Recent work suggests that alpha oscillations propagate across the cortex as traveling waves during sustained orienting of spatial attention (Alamia et al., 2023 Fakche et al., 2024). Our latest work demonstrated that TMS-induced theta traveling waves causally contribute to visual search, highlighting their potential role in exploratory attention (Kong et al., 2026). Yet, the role of traveling waves across distinct attentional processes remains to be clarified. Here, we assessed the functional role of low-frequency traveling waves in attentional orienting and reorienting using simultaneous MEG-EEG recordings with psychophysics. Human participants (N=20) performed an orientation discrimination task where an auditory cue directed visual attention either toward the upcoming target location (valid –attention is sustained at that location) or the distractor location (invalid –attention reorients to the target location, i.e., exploration). We first confirmed successful attentional manipulation behaviorally (higher sensitivity in valid trials) and electrophysiologically (stronger alpha power in ipsilateral MEG-EEG sensors relative to the attended location in the cue-to-stimulus period). We then characterized single-trial traveling waves properties (i.e., direction, normalized velocity) and compared them across attentional conditions. Our results indicate that distinct patterns of low-frequency traveling waves differentiate sustained from exploratory attention. Moreover, combining MEG and EEG provides a complementary perspective on the spatio-temporal features of these traveling waves, shedding light on their potential anatomical pathways. Together, our findings support a functional role for low-frequency traveling waves in mediating sustained and exploratory attention.

title: Real-time tracking of pupil-phase fluctuations reveals state-dependent changes in temporal attentional capacity during the attentional blink
affiliations: 1. NTT Communication Science Laboratories (JP)
abstract: Pupil diameter is widely used as an index of arousal and neuromodulatory activity. For example, sustained changes in pupil diameter (i.e., baseline pupil size) have been linked to arousal levels and behavioral performance across a wide range of cognitive tasks. In addition to the sustained pupil responses, recent studies showed that pupil dynamics exhibit slow fluctuations (<0.2 Hz), which reflect ongoing brain-state transitions. Specifically, the slow pupil fluctuations correlate with large-scale neural dynamics, including sensory cortical activity and the default mode network. The finding suggests a possibility of using pupil-phase fluctuations to track cognitive performance, particularly in tasks that reflect temporal limits of cognitive capacity. Here we addressed this issue using an auditory attentional blink paradigm. Participants were required to detect two auditory targets (T1 and T2) embedded in rapid auditory streams. The effective attentional capacity was defined by the T2 detection rate given that T1 was detected correctly (T2|T1).
