In experiment 1, trial-by-trial analyses of the slow pupil fluctuations revealed a phase-dependent modulation. The probability of T2|T1 detection increased approximately 0–2 s following the onset of the pupil dilation phase. To test whether this phase-dependent modulation reflects a causal influence of ongoing brain-state, we implemented a closed-loop design in Experiment 2. Pupil diameter was monitored in real time, and target presentation was triggered during either the pupil dilation or constriction phases, respectively. Results showed that the target detection rate was better when the targets were presented during the pupil dilation phase than when they were presented during the pupil constriction phase, suggesting a potential influence of pupil phase on attentional capacity. Our results suggest that temporal attentional capacity is not fixed but fluctuates with ongoing brain-state dynamics, highlighting slow pupil fluctuation as a distinct physiological marker of cognitive state.

title: The effects of action preparation on attentional resource allocation: behavioral and pupillometric evidence
affiliations:
1. School of Psychological Sciences, University of Haifa (IL)
2. Institute of Information Processing and Decision Making, University of Haifa (IL)
3. Department of Cognitive and Psychological Sciences, Brown University (US)
abstract: Preparing a motor action has been previously shown to enhance perceptual discrimination, yet the mechanism underlying this enhancement remains unclear. One candidate account holds that action preparation results in allocating additional resources to task-relevant stimuli. The present study examined this hypothesis across two experiments using behavioral performance and the pupillary light response (PLR) as a measure of covert attentional resource allocation.  Given that the pupil responds rather slowly, Experiment 1 examined whether the action-preparation perceptual benefit extends to longer stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). Participants indicated whether two consecutive targets, separated by varying SOAs (300–1500ms), had the same orientation. In the ‘no-action’ condition participants only performed this discrimination task. In the ‘pointing’ condition they also directly acted on the 2nd target by pointing at it, thus, they were required to prepare the action during the SOA. Replicating prior findings, we observed a significant main effect of condition: perceptual sensitivity (d′) was higher in the pointing condition. Yet, there was no condition x SOA interaction, suggesting that action preparation enhanced perception robustly across a wide range of temporal intervals. Experiment 2 extended this paradigm by incorporating PLR measurements to directly probe attentional allocation. In this experiment, half of the screen was white and half black, and the targets appeared on either side, equally often. Given that covertly shifting attention into darker regions increases pupil size while covertly shifting attention to lighter regions decreases pupil size, the difference in pupil size between target-on-black and target-on-white trials serves as an index of attentional engagement. Results show larger pupil-size difference in the pointing condition than in the no-action condition, suggesting that action preparation actively recruits additional attentional resources. Together, these findings provide the first converging behavioral and physiological evidence that action-induced perceptual enhancement may be mediated by the allocation of attentional resources.

title: Polarization Perception and Neural Adaptation in Haidinger's Brush Psychophysics: From Normative Data to Albinism
affiliations: 1. University of Padova (IT)
abstract:
Haidinger's brushes (HB) are entoptic phenomena arising from dichroic absorption of polarized light by macular carotenoids aligned within Henle's fiber layer (HFL). Despite their potential as a non-invasive psychophysical index of macular integrity, key parameters governing their perception remain poorly characterized.

In a first study, we systematically investigated the role of neural adaptation in HB perception in 37 healthy individuals. Using a custom apparatus combining two blue LED sources (468 nm) with a rotating linear polarizer, we measured rotational speed thresholds (RST) across seven polarization levels. RST decreased linearly with the logarithm of polarization level, establishing a quantitative framework linking neural adaptation dynamics to macular pigment density. The estimated average polarization threshold was 9.7 ± 1.2%, lower than previously reported values, attributable to the broader range of rotational speeds explored. Critically, lower RST at maximum contrast predicted lower polarization thresholds, suggesting RST as a robust individual-level biomarker of macular function.

Building on this normative framework, we then applied the paradigm to three individuals with oculocutaneous albinism — a condition characterized by reduced macular pigment density and disrupted HFL architecture. Remarkably, all participants perceived polarization-dependent entoptic phenomena at 100% polarization, but reported qualitatively atypical patterns: asymmetric, peripherally localized, with aberrant motion descriptors. No false alarms occurred at 0% polarization. These deviations likely reflect HFL disorganization rather than pigment absence.

Together, these findings establish HB psychophysics as a sensitive, accessible tool for probing macular structural integrity across physiological and pathological conditions.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Measuring affective influences on sustained attention in ME/CFS, using a modified Gradual-Onset Continuous Performance Task
affiliations: 1. University of Leicester, Leicester (UK)
abstract: Cognitive difficulties in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) are often reported during sustained attention and executive control tasks. Neuroimaging studies suggest that these difficulties may reflect impaired recruitment and regulation of task-relevant networks, alongside difficulty in managing effort and internally driven signals, such as fatigue. The gradual-onset continuous performance task (gCPT) measures variability in reaction time (RT) as an index of attentional state. This study used a modified gCPT to examine whether affective stimuli influence attentional performance over time in young healthy adults (n = 23). Displays contained sequences of faces that morphed linearly from one face to the next and participants reported the gender of each face with a speeded button press. Blocks contained neutral-only or mixed neutral and emotional expressions. Trial-to-trial RT fluctuations indexed attentional instability, with extreme RT deviations classified as out-of-zone. Context sensitivity reflected differences between neutral-only and mixed-block trials, allowing examination of how emotional context influenced performance. Preliminary analyses indicated that attentional performance varied as a function of task context, with differences observed in RT, attentional stability, and behavioural response profiles. Extreme RT deviations were more frequent in neutral-only blocks than mixed blocks, and attentional stability changed over time. Behavioural profile analyses further suggested substantial individual differences in how participants responded to emotional context. These findings provide a behavioural baseline for testing whether attentional stability and sensitivity to emotional context are altered in ME/CFS.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Visual-Inertial Egocentric Metric Depth Estimation for Tabletop Activities of Daily Living
affiliations: 1. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract:
Neurodegenerative movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease or essential tremor impact the patient’s ability to independently perform the tabletop activities of daily living (ADLs) such as drinking and eating. While exoskeleton assistive devices offer a great opportunity to support these patients in tabletop ADLs by suppressing the pathological components of the intended movement, they require motion trajectory estimation, intention prediction, and scene understanding for effective assistance. 

Depth estimation is especially crucial for determining the relative position of the tabletop objects-of-interest to the patient. Current depth estimation approaches either leverage special hardware (e.g. stereo cameras), which is not available in our mobile sensor setup, or fine-tuning of deep monocular metric methods with a vigorously gathered dataset. Such a dataset would require tens of experimental setups with different tables and users in various environments with an egocentric depth camera.

We address this challenge by exploiting the biomechanical constraints of a person sitting at a table and utilizing inertial measurements in addition to monocular visual information from the Neon eye-tracking eyeglasses. Although the hardware setup of Neon is not sufficient for visual-inertial odometry, it is nonetheless useful for improvement over visual-only metric depth estimation.

The novelty of our method lies in the use of inertial measurements for table normal estimation, which allows us to reliably calculate metric depth of table plane pixels and, by using deep relative depth estimation and depth prior incorporation, of tabletop objects. After building a scene depth map during system initialization, we utilize visual feature tracking to estimate camera pose and scene depth after motion, maintaining a robust understanding of the scene in real-time. Our method achieves the mean distance estimation error of 2.5 cm with the runtime of 0.01 seconds per frame compared to 11 cm and 0.48 seconds of Depth Anything 3.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Objective quantification of panretinal visual function using flicker-ERG thresholds
affiliations: 1. University of Freiburg (DE)
abstract: Assessment of retinal function in advanced panretinal disease is challenging, as the measurement range of standard clinical measures like visual acuity or conventional electroretinography (ERG) is often exceeded. While the psychophysical ‘full-field stimulus threshold’ (FST) has gained importance in the context of gene therapy, its subjective nature introduces variability due to non-retinal factors such as cognitive processes and individual decision criteria. In a pilot study with healthy participants, we tested a method to objectify retinal function by determining photopic electroretinographic thresholds using weak full-field 30-Hz flicker stimuli superimposed on a luminance pedestal. We recorded responses at nine flash strengths around the perceptual threshold. In contrast to standard clinical flicker ERG recordings, to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio for near-threshold responses, twenty 3-second segments were averaged. Response amplitudes were quantified using Fourier analysis, and a retinal sensitivity score was determined by extrapolating statistically significant responses to zero amplitude. Initial results demonstrate that specifically tailored ERG protocols can reliably quantify retinal function near or even below the perceptual threshold. The ERG-based threshold provides a more direct, objective measure of retinal function than FST, independent of post-retinal processing. The approach piloted here can easily be extended to patients with advanced panretinal disease to monitor disease progression and evaluate efficacy in gene therapy trials.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Robust across trates and staits The stability of the attentional spotlight across autism spectrum disorder, aging, and task manipulations
affiliations: 1. Utrecht University, Helmholtz Institute (NL)
abstract: Visual attention helps us navigate our surroundings by continuously selecting relevant spatial information for more extensive processing. Here, spatial attentional selection is often conceptualized as an attentional spotlight. Previous data suggests there might be stable differences between individuals in the size of the spotlight directly related to trait differences such as a diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Here, we aimed to replicate and extent previous work on these trait differences by including individuals with- and without an official diagnosis of ASD and including a sample of older adults. Besides investigating trait differences in the spotlight size, we also addressed state differences by manipulating task characteristics, specifically cue size and target predictiveness. To this end, we conducted a series of experiments with an exogenous cueing paradigm in which we varied the distance from the cue to the target to map the attentional spotlight. \n\nResults showed no trait differences in the spatial characteristics of the attentional spotlight between individuals with a diagnosis of ASD and individuals without a diagnosis. Furthermore, while overall performance was lower for the older adults compared to younger adults, our results indicated that the size of the attentional spotlight remains similar between age groups. Regarding the state differences of the spotlight size, we found that the size of the cue does not influence performance and that target predictability only selectively benefits top-down expectations near the cued location, not farther locations. Together, our results indicated no group differences in the spatial characteristics of the attentional spotlight across heterogeneous samples. Furthermore, as measured by our paradigm, the size of the spotlight appears relative stable despite our modulations, suggesting the size of the spotlight is surprisingly stable.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Atypical responses to spatial frequency and contrast in the color and motion preferring columns of extrastriate cortex in individuals with amblyopia
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, University of York (UK)
2. Athinoula A Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging, Massachusetts General Hospital (US)
3. Department of Psychology, Northeastern University (US)
4. Department of Ophthalmology, University of California Irvine (US)
5. Department of Ophthalmology, Harvard Medical School (US)
6. Department of Ophthalmology, Boston's Children Hospital (US)
7. Picower Institute for Learning and Memory, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (US)
8. Department of Radiology, Harvard Medical School (US)
abstract: Amblyopia is a monocular visual deficit that persists after optical correction and is often a result of strabismus or anisometropia. The deficit is attributed to atypical visual processing in the brain. We examined how extrastriate visual cortex responded to different contrasts and spatial frequencies in a group of amblyopes (n=16) and controls (n=8). We used high-resolution fMRI to assess how motion- and color-selective columns in visual areas V2-V4 are tuned to spatial frequency and contrast and how this tuning is influenced by amblyopia. We measured responses in motion and color selective columns to five, log-spaced, spatial frequencies (0.1-5.8 c/deg) and five, log-spaced, contrasts (1.25-99%). We tested binocularly and each eye separately in different sessions. For both groups, and all eye conditions, the contrast sensitivity and spatial frequency preference showed differences between motion and color columns in cortical representations of 3-8° eccentricity, but not for 0-3°. The differences at 3-8° manifested in tuning to lower spatial frequencies in motion than color selective columns.  In the representation of 0-3°, color and motion columns were similarly tuned to high spatial frequencies.  Group differences were most pronounced in the representation of 0-3° for monocular conditions – particularly for the amblyopic eye - and were not limited to color selective columns.   However, the group differences interacted significantly with column, spatial frequency, contrast and, predictably, the eye stimulation condition. Atypical visual processing in amblyopia therefore manifests as different spatial frequency responses that depend on the eye of stimulation and the cortical column. The results indicate that amblyopia is not limited to atypical processing in color preferring columns, which depend on preferential inputs from parvocellular units. The magnocellular stream, which inputs preferentially to motion columns, is also affected.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Microstructural reorganization of cerebral white matter measured with 7T-MRI in adult amblyopia
affiliations:
1. University of Pisa (IT)
2. University of Florence (IT)
3. IRCCS Stella Maris (IT)
4. IMAGO7 Center (IT)
5. Institute of Neuroscience, National Research Council (IT)
6. Maastricht University (NL)
abstract: Amblyopia is a developmental disorder caused by abnormal visual input early in life, leading to persistent visual deficits and reorganization of the visual cortex and optic radiations. However, alterations extend beyond the visual areas and tracts previous studies reported changes of white matter integrity in non-visual areas, including increased fractional anisotropy (FA) in the bilateral uncinate tracts of adult amblyopes compared with controls (Tsai et al., 2019). Here we extended these results using 7T diffusion-weighted MRI and whole brain probabilistic tractography, which we complemented with the automated reconstruction (pyAFQ) of 30 white matter tracts. Fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) derived from the diffusion tensor were extracted from each tract to quantify microstructural properties we focused on associative tracts and studied 15 individuals with mild monocular anisometropic amblyopia (Snellen acuity in the worse eye between 0.5 and 6/10, between 16 and 49 years old) and 23 controls (no visual deficit between 22 and 40 years old). Repeated-measures ANOVAs including age as covariate revealed a significant tract-by-group interaction for both FA (F = 2.085, p = .022 after Greenhouse-Geisser correction) and MD (F = 2.090, p < .001). The group-difference was significant in three major tracts (all outside the occipital lobe): left posterior arcuate, right superior longitudinal, and left uncinate. This consisted of reduced MD together with increased FA in amblyopes.   Our findings indicate that amblyopia is associated with widespread microstructural reorganization extending beyond the visual cortex. For associative tracts, the changes are not necessarily disruptions, as we find enhanced organization indices in amblyopes compared with controls. This might reflect the relatively mild clinical profile of our sample, which selectively included non-strabismic individuals with relatively preserved visual acuity. This research was funded by the ERC-CoG grant PredActive.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Beyond low-level vision: magnocellular contribution to mirror image discrimination
affiliations:
1. Psychological Sciences Research Institute, Université catholique de Louvain (BE)
2. Institute of Neuroscience, Université catholique de Louvain, Belgium (BE)
abstract: The magnocellular and parvocellular pathways of the visual system are known to contribute different types of low-level information to visual perception. Here, we tested the hypothesis that the magnocellular pathway may also contribute to the ability to discriminate mirror images. This hypothesis was motivated by three lines of evidence. First, damage to the dorsal stream has been shown to affect patients’ ability to discriminate mirror images. Second, the occipito-parietal dorsal stream mostly receives magnocellular pathway inputs. Third, neuropsychological case studies reported patients whose difficulty to discriminate mirror images depended on the extent to which the stimuli engaged the magnocellular pathway. We will present the results of four complementary studies supporting this hypothesis. In study 1, magnocellular efficiency (indexed by flicker fusion threshold) correlated with the specific difficulty of children diagnosed with dyslexia in detecting mirror errors (relative to phonological errors) in a lexical decision task. In study 2, magnocellular efficiency correlated with the difficulty of adults diagnosed with dyslexia in discriminating mirrored geometrical shapes. In Study 3, we show that this relationship is specific to aspects of orientation processing assumed to depend on the dorsal stream. Finally, Study 4 showed that decreasing magnocellular efficiency by fast flicker adaptation disproportionately impairs the detection of mirror errors compared to phonological ones in a lexical decision task. Together, these findings provide evidence that the magnocellular stream contribution extends beyond low-level vision, playing a functional role in mirror image discrimination. It also offers new insights into possible origins of mirror errors in dyslexia.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: A subcortical-prefrontal pathway for unconscious visual categorization in humans
affiliations: 1. South China Normal University (CN)
abstract: While subcortical pathways are known to support residual vision in blindsight, their role in high-level perceptual processing in the healthy human brain remains poorly understood. We employed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and continuous flash suppression (CFS) to investigate the subcortical representation of ‘toolness’ (tools vs. non-tools) and shape (elongated vs. stubby) during unconscious processing. Both univariate and multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) revealed significant toolness representation in the ventral anterior (VA) nucleus of the left thalamus, and the left striatum (STR) of the basal ganglia. At the cortical level, this unconscious representation was restricted to Area 9a and anterior 10p within the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), bypassing primary visual areas. Background connectivity analysis showed that elongated tools selectively increased functional coupling between the bilateral VA and left Area 9a, and between the right VA and left STR. Furthermore, dynamic causal modeling (DCM) identified a functional thalamocortical pathway originating in the left VA and projecting to the left Area 9a that specifically contributed to toolness representation under CFS. These findings provide evidence for a dedicated subcortical-prefrontal shortcut in healthy humans that facilitates high-level visual categorization entirely outside of conscious awareness. This circuit likely reflects an evolutionary mechanism for the rapid, unconscious processing of ecologically relevant objects through their motor affordances.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: The Neural Correlates of Visual Discomfort and the Relationship with Autistic-Like Traits
affiliations: 1. University of Birmingham (UK)
abstract: Visual discomfort is common in the general population and heightened in clinical groups such as migraine and epilepsy. A prominent theory suggests that this discomfort arises from cortical hyperexcitability, supported by findings that certain visual features associated with discomfort (e.g., high contrast, striped patterns, mid-range spatial frequencies) also elicit increased neural responses. However, the neural mechanisms of visual discomfort are as of yet unclear. Moreover, autistic individuals who have also been observed to report frequent discomfort to these same parameters as well as show early evidence of atypical neural excitability remain under-researched in the discomfort literature. Therefore, this study aims to clarify which visual parameters are most uncomfortable, how these map onto neural markers of excitability, and how autistic-like traits may affect visual discomfort and the neural response. Adults from the general population (N = 31 so far) viewed contrast-reversing gratings presented at a temporal frequency of 7.2 Hz that varied in spatial frequency and either luminance contrast or chromatic separation and colour pairing. Participants then rated their visual discomfort for each on a visual analogue scale. EEG recorded steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP), and autistic-like traits were measured using the Autism Quotient. Preliminary findings suggest that autistic-like traits were unrelated to both discomfort and SSVEP amplitude. Additionally, although the stimuli rated as more uncomfortable (high contrast, large chromatic separation, red colour pairs) often produced the largest SSVEP amplitudes, there was an inconsistency for spatial frequency. While mid-frequency gratings (3cpd) elicited the largest SSVEP amplitude, both low (0.5cpd) and mid spatial frequencies were rated as more uncomfortable than high (9cpd). Our findings so far suggest that visual discomfort does not map directly onto cortical excitability for all visual parameters. The spatial frequency rated as most uncomfortable does not elicit the strongest neural response, challenging the hyperexcitability account of visual discomfort.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Aperiodic EEG Slopes Reveal Baseline and Load-Dependent Visual Exposure in Migraine
affiliations:
1. Department of Neuroscience, Aysel Sabuncu Brain Research Center, Bilkent University (TR)
2. Institute for Cognitive Neurology and Dementia Research, Medical Faculty, Otto-von-Guericke University Magdeburg (DE)
3. Neuroscience and Neurotechnology Center of Excellence (TR)
4. Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Middle East Technical University (TR)
5. Departments of Neurology and Algology, Faculty of Medicine, Gazi University (TR)
6. Neuropsychiatry Education Research and Application Center, Gazi University (TR)
7. Departments of Anatomy, Faculty of Medicine, Gazi University (TR)
abstract: Migraine has been associated with altered visual processing during the interictal period, including visual hypersensitivity and increased susceptibility to sensory exposure. One proposed mechanism is an altered excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance in the visual cortex, which impairs filtering and hence increases internal neural noise. In EEG, the aperiodic spectral exponent has been suggested to reflect internal noise at the population level and E/I balance in cortical activity, but its representation in migraine remains unclear. We used equivalent noise paradigms designed to challenge sensory processing. We measured the aperiodic spectral exponent (1/f slope) and individual alpha frequency (IAF) during eyes-open (EO) and eyes-closed (EC) resting states before and after demanding equivalent noise tasks in patients with episodic migraine without aura (n=13) interictally and healthy non-headache controls (n=12). We aimed to assess both trait-like group differences and state-dependent changes following visual exposure. Behaviorally, migraineurs showed impaired performance and diminished sensitivity relative to controls, reflected in elevated internal noise estimates, particularly during motion estimation. Migraineurs showed a reduced aperiodic exponent relative to healthy controls, together with a slower IAF across states, suggesting altered baseline cortical dynamics within an occipito-parietal ROI. Following the equivalent noise tasks, migraineurs exhibited a significantly flatter aperiodic exponent during EO recovery across a broad electrode cluster.  Within-group comparisons showed that migraineurs had steeper slopes during EC than EO in pre- and post-task, while controls showed this difference only in the pre-task period.  Migraineurs exhibit a distinct adaptation failure to visual stimulation, characterized by a sustained shift in aperiodic activity, indicating disrupted E/I balance and elevated internal noise. While eye closure partially reduces this neural noise, the recovery remains incomplete. Therefore, aperiodic EEG measures offer a physiological marker of sensory overload in migraine (Funding: The Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkiye, 225K067).
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Illusions that are not Illusions: Misleading cross-level comparisons
affiliations:
1. LMU (DE)
2. University Eye Hospital (DE)
abstract: Visual illusions – as Oliver Braddick has provocatively argued – are too broad a category to be characterized by simple criteria such as non-veridicality or perceptual error. In the present analysis, we want to elaborate, in the context of Dejan Todorovic’s augmented framework for illusions, on a class of classical visual illusions which we propose to call “misnamed illusions”. The common characteristic of these is that the percept is veridical even though it is based on differing physical attributes. Within Todorovic’s framework, the alleged perceptual error in many pictorial displays arises not within perceptual appearance but stems from a comparison between heterogeneous representational domains, like physical measurement and appearance. Examples include Adelson’s checkerboard and the Lotto-Purves Colour Cube. There, the alleged mismatch between luminance and brightness or brown and orange colour arises as a consequence of the perceptual mechanism of colour constancy. In a simplified framework for a general audience, we can thus distinguish between misnamed illusions, which arise from misleading cross-level comparisons, and genuine illusions, in which the discrepancy is intrinsic to perceptual appearance itself, i.e., relations that are directly available for comparison within the same perceptual field. As an example for a genuine colour illusion, we would put forward the “Lilac chaser”.

title: EEG correlates of perceptual (un)certainty are not due to variability in signal timing
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, Medical Center – University of Freiburg (DE)
2. Faculty of Medicine, University of Freiburg (DE)
3. Perception and Cognition Lab, Institute for Frontier Areas of Psychology and Mental Health (DE)
4. Faculty of Biology, University of Freiburg (DE)
5. Eye Center, Medical Center – University of Freiburg (DE)
abstract: Information available to our senses is inherently incomplete and varies in ambiguity and visibility. This results in variability of stability and certainty of perceptual interpretations. We compared the EEG evoked by ambiguous and low-visibility stimuli with that of disambiguated and high-visibility stimulus variants. The amplitudes of two Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) (P200 and P400) showed an inverse relationship with perceptual uncertainty (“ERP Uncertainty Effects”) across very different stimulus categories and complexity levels. The ERP analysis does not resolve whether amplitude effects reflect differences in strength or temporal variability of neural signals across stimulus repetitions. In this study, we investigated this question by analysing the EEG data in the frequency domain.  Using four stimulus types, we presented Necker lattices and smiley faces with either low or high perceptual certainty. Stimuli were presented discontinuously and participants (n=21) indicated their percept by key press. We analysed the EEG with a time-frequency analysis, comparing total power and phase variability (Intertrial Coherence, ITC) between low and high certainty stimulus variants in the 4-8 Hz frequencies (reflecting the P200 and P400 ERPs).  We replicated the ERP Uncertainty Effects, with high perceptual certainty having higher power compared to low perceptual certainty. For the Necker lattices, the ITC did not significantly differ between perceptual certainty levels. For the smiley faces, there was a significant difference between the ITC in the P400 time window with perceptual certainty having less temporal variability. However, this ITC difference could not explain the ERP Uncertainty Effects.  Our results indicate that the ERP Uncertainty Effects arise from differences in signal strength and not temporal variability. This suggests these effects result from the number and strength of underlying neural generators. The ITC difference for the smiley faces seem to be independent of the ERP Uncertainty Effects and might be due to the unique processing of faces.

title: Predictability of stimulus ambiguity but not of timing modulates perceptual (un)certainty estimation
affiliations:
1. Faculty of Biology, University of Freiburg (DE)
2. Perception and Cognition Lab, Institute for Frontier Areas of Psychology and Mental Health (DE)
3. Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, Medical Center, University of Freiburg (DE)
4. Faculty of Medicine, University of Freiburg (DE)
5. University College Freiburg (DE)
abstract: Sensory input though inherently noisy can be more or less reliable. Less reliable input, like the ambiguous Necker lattice, induces perceptual uncertainty, while reliable input, like disambiguated variants thereof, induces perceptual certainty. In EEG correlates, this is reflected in low (uncertainty) and high (certainty) ERP (event related potential) amplitudes. These “ERP (Un)Certainty Effects” are quite large (Cohen’s d of 0.6 - 1.2) and generalize over multiple stimulus categories and complexities. These findings, however, are based on experimental paradigms in which per condition only one stimulus variant was shown repeatedly with fixed blank screen ISI (interstimulus intervals). In these studies, predictability of successive stimuli was high and so far, it is unknown how this impacts the ERP Uncertainty Effect. Here, we tested the influence of predictability of stimulus ambiguity (i.e., induced perceptual certainty level) as well as predictability of timing on the ERP Uncertainty Effects. In Experiment 1 (n = 20), predictability of ambiguity in consecutive stimuli was removed by presenting both stimulus variants (ambiguous and disambiguated) in random order but with fixed ISI of 0.4 s. In Experiment 2 (preliminary, n = 15), predictability of timing was removed by showing stimuli with three mean ISI in jittered or non-jittered conditions (0.3 s – jitter: ± 0.01 s, 1 s – jitter: ± 0.1 s and 3 s – jitter: ± 0.2 s). Both stimulus variants were shown in separate conditions ensuring predictability of ambiguity. Randomized presentation of both ambiguous and disambiguated variants did not produce ERP Uncertainty Effects. In contrast, neither ISI length nor the presence or absence of a temporal jitter had an influence on the effects. It seems that predictability of stimulus ambiguity is essential for perceptual certainty estimation. When predictability of ambiguity is given, however, it is robust to modulations of ISI duration and predictability of timing.

title: Listening to negative music sharpens visual size perception
affiliations: 1. Liaoning Normal University (CN)
abstract: Emotions profoundly influence visual perception, yet it remains unclear whether negative emotions induced by music can cross-modally modulate visual size perception, and what causal role the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) plays in this process. Using a prime paradigm and the classic Ebbinghaus illusion as an index of visual size perception, the present study addressed these questions using high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) technique. Participants performed a size-matching task following prior exposure to music excerpts that induced positive, negative, or neutral emotional states. Experiments 1 and 2 consistently revealed that negative music significantly reduced the illusion magnitude compared to neutral or positive music. Experiment 3 applied tDCS over bilateral DLPFC (F3/F4) and found that active stimulation eliminated or even reversed the emotion-induced modulation of the illusion. Experiments 4 and 5 used HD-tDCS to independently manipulate excitability of the left or right DLPFC. Results consistently showed that under sham stimulation, negative music significantly reduced the illusion magnitude than positive music. However, enhancing (anodal) or suppressing (cathodal) excitability of either the left or right DLPFC eliminated this emotional modulation. These findings provide clear evidence that music-induced negative emotions cross-modally modulate visual size perception, and the DLPFC plays a critical causal role in this process. This study advances our understanding of cross-modal emotion-perception interactions and has implications for non-invasive neuromodulation interventions in affective disorders.

title: Alpha-band MEG reveals shared representations of perceived and imagined simple visual features
affiliations:
1. Macquarie University (AU)
2. The University of Sydney (AU)
3. UNSW (AU)
4. University of York (UK)
5. University of Geneva (CH)
abstract: Visual imagery is the ability to generate images in the mind’s eye without concurrent retinal input. While previous fMRI research has shown that low-level features such as orientation and colour can be decoded from imagery in visual regions, MEG and EEG decoding has primarily focused on complex categorical stimuli (e.g. houses and faces). Here, we targeted low-level visual features, specifically colour and shape, to investigate whether such information can be reliably decoded within category using MEG (e.g. red triangle vs red circle). Participants with moderate to strong imagery ability (verified via the binocular rivalry imagery paradigm) imagined simple coloured shapes for six seconds and rated their imagery vividness on a trial-by-trial basis while undergoing MEG. We applied time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis to examine when perceptual and imagery-related information was represented in MEG signals. Cross-decoding between perceptual and imagery conditions revealed shared representations selectively in the alpha band. During imagery, shape information (circle vs triangle) emerged earlier than shape–colour conjunctions (e.g. red circle vs red triangle). Colour alone could not be reliably decoded, potentially reflecting limitations in task design or weaker feature-specific representations. The emergence of shared representations primarily in the alpha band aligns with recent evidence suggesting that alpha oscillations support top-down reinstatement of sensory information during a range of cognitive tasks.

title: EEG correlates of the bias towards vertical motion perception during observation of the ambiguous motion quartet
affiliations:
1. Institute for Frontier Areas of Psychology and Mental Health (DE)
2. Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, Medical Center, University of Freiburg (DE)
3. Faculty of Medicine, University of Freiburg (DE)
4. Center for Behavioral Brain Sciences, Otto-von-Guericke University (DE)
5. Eye Center, Medical Center, University of Freiburg (DE)
abstract: The motion quartet consists of two dot pairs being alternatively present and absent at the diagonal corners of a centrally (visual field) located imaginary rectangle. Observers’ perception becomes ambiguous and alternates between two dots apparently moving either horizontally or vertically, with a bias towards vertical motion in the case of equal horizontal and vertical dot distances (aspect ratio =1). This vertical motion bias has been explained by less effortful intra-hemispheric processing in the case of vertical motion percepts, compared to more effortful inter-hemispheric processing of horizontal motion percepts. In the present study we tested this hemisphericity hypothesis.  Five motion quartet stimuli with different degrees of subjective ambiguity (varying point aspect ratios: 0.5, 0.7, 0.85, 1, 1.2) were presented discontinuously in separate experimental blocks and 13 participants indicated reversals in perceived motion direction by key press. We compared latency and amplitude of event-related potential (“ERP”, resulting from the EEG) correlates of horizontal and vertical motion percepts, expecting shorter latencies and smaller amplitudes of motion ERPs for vertical compared to horizontal motion percepts.  In an exploratory analysis, we identified two ERP components with larger amplitudes for vertical compared to horizontal motion percepts: One earlier ERP component at about 150 ms after stimulus onset with a posterior distribution, followed by a later component at about 280 ms and with both posterior and anterior activity clusters. We found no EEG evidence for timing differences in the processing of the two perceived motion directions.  Our results suggest a pattern of recurrent activity between posterior and anterior brain areas underlying the well-known vertical bias in perception of the ambiguous motion quartet. Whether, and if yes, how our EEG results are related to the hemisphericity hypothesis, needs to be shown in follow-up studies.

title: Repositioning Perceptual Illusions as a Medium for Active Learning in Higher Education
affiliations:
1. University of Aveiro (PT)
2. William James Center for Research (PT)
abstract: While perceptual illusions are widely used as illustrative tools in teaching Sensation and Perception courses, they are often reduced to passive, in-class demonstrations, limiting their potential to foster deep conceptual understanding. Given their intrinsically interactive nature, perceptual illusions instead lend themselves to active, student-centred learning approaches. The present work introduces and examines the pedagogical project Illusions Workshop, implemented in an undergraduate Psychology course on Perception and Attention, which seeks to reposition illusions as a central medium for active learning. Over the course of a semester, students worked in small groups to collaboratively design and construct interactive demonstrations of perceptual phenomena. This process was supported by access to a dedicated workshop space equipped with digital fabrication tools (e.g., 3D printers and laser engravers) and a range of construction materials (e.g., cardboard and foam board). In parallel, students conducted theoretically grounded analyses of the perceptual mechanisms underlying their chosen phenomena, drawing on the relevant scientific literature. The integration of conceptual and hands-on components was continuously supported through structured tutoring and formative feedback. The project culminated in a public dissemination event - “Illusions Day” - during which students presented their demonstrations to the academic community, combining scientific communication with experiential and inquiry-based learning. The pedagogical impact of the initiative was evaluated using a pre-post design, incorporating both multiple-choice items targeting core concepts in perception research and open-ended questions addressing understanding and engagement. The findings are discussed in terms of their implications for disciplinary learning in perception science, the development of transferable skills (including problem-solving, project planning, collaboration, and science communication), and student engagement within higher education contexts.

title: Does imagination really modulate pupil size?
affiliations: 1. The University of Queensland (AU)
abstract: The pupil constricts in response to light. Imagining a bright light has also been shown to subtly constrict the pupils. It has been suggested that pupil size modulation via the imagination relies on the same neural architecture as real sensory information processing. We have made several attempts to directly and conceptually replicate this effect of pupil size modulation via imagery, and have found mixed results. Interestingly, the strength of the effect seems to be contingent on the type of imagined content (e.g., realistic scenes seem to work better than basic shapes), and how the person is told about the to-be-imagined content (e.g., priming with examples vs. text-based descriptions). We relate these findings to several self-report measures of the imagination, and it remains to be seen if these modulations will prove to be a useful means of distinguishing people who report having weak or vivid imagined visual experiences.

title: Does the pen really levitate? Testing the possibility of demand characteristics in reports of the illusion of levitation
affiliations: 1. University of Bergen (NO)
abstract: Reports of the illusion of levitation suggest that objects can appear to float mid-air when their physical support is visually occluded. The present study examines whether such reports reflect a genuine perceptual experience or are potentially influenced by demand characteristics, i.e., participants’ interpretation of the experiment's purpose and subconscious change in behavior to fit the presumed goal of the study. In our 2 × 3 between-subjects design, participants are randomly assigned to one of the six experimental conditions. The first factor is stimulus visibility: in one condition, participants directly view a pen positioned in a way that may give the impression of levitation, whereas in another condition they are positioned so they cannot see the pen as levitating and are only asked to imagine it as such. The second factor is the type of occluder used to “hide” the support underneath the putatively levitating objects: a small occluder, a wide occluder or a transparent control occluder. By assessing spontaneous mentions of levitation in an open-ended report, followed by a rating of the extent to which the pen appears to be levitating on a 0–10 scale, we test whether participants in the non-visible condition are as likely to report levitation as those in the visible condition. Similar patterns of reporting across conditions might suggest that reports of levitation are not driven by visual perception alone, as would be inferred from the previous studies on the illusion of levitation. The results of our research are forthcoming and will be presented at the conference.

title: Visuospatial perspective-taking within different reference frames: The role of perspective change and mental rotation strategies
affiliations:
1. Bournemouth University (UK)
2. University of Trento (IT)
abstract: Mental representations of space can be generated and communicated within different reference frames and perspectives. Visuospatial perspective taking can also be affected by the degree of perspective change, which refers to the angular disparity between the physical and the target perspective. The present study investigated for the first time the effects of angular disparity and individual differences in mental rotation strategies on people’s ability to process spatial relations within different spatial reference frames (SRFs). Sixty-three healthy adults completed a task involving third-person-, object-, and environment-centered judgements of spatial relations between two objects under orthogonal and non-orthogonal degrees of perspective change while their use of self-based and object-based mental imagery strategies was also recorded. Results revealed significantly lower accuracy rates and higher response latencies in environment-centred spatial processing compared to third-person- and object-centred processing. Furthermore, performance was overall slower and less accurate under non-orthogonal angular disparity conditions compared to orthogonal perspective changes however, environment-centred accuracy was comparable across the two angular conditions. Finally, irrespective of the degree of perspective change involved, both self-based and object-based mental rotation strategies were used across all SRFs and associated with better performance. However, individuals favoured a self-based mental rotation strategy, particularly in the third-person- and object-centred frames. These findings confirm that at least partially distinct systems are involved in mentally representing space under different SRFs and that spatial perspective taking can be more challenging under non-orthogonal degrees of perspective change. The present findings also highlight the importance of mental visual imagery abilities in the form of self- and object-based mental rotation strategies in efficient spatial perspective taking.

title: Time-to-collision estimation within and beyond the Oppel-Kundt illusion
affiliations: 1. Johannes Gutenberg University (DE)
abstract: In the Oppel-Kundt illusion (OKI), a horizontal interval filled with vertical lines appears longer than an adjacent unfilled interval of the same physical length. In a previous study, we demonstrated that the OKI affects time-to-collision (TTC) estimation of an object moving through the space covered by the illusion. This temporal effect is comparable in magnitude to its spatial counterpart. In the present study, we investigated whether this effect extends into peri-illusional space. In 540 trials per participant (N = 30), a circular object moved from left to right at three speeds and was occluded at the end of the left interval. In a prediction-motion task, participants judged when the object would reach the end of the right interval. The left interval remained unfilled and constant, whereas the right interval varied independently in length and filling. We varied the relationship between the moving object and its background in three ways. First, we separated the object’s trajectory from the illusion by displacing it vertically below it. Second, the object remained below the illusion space, and we extended the three vertical lines defining the beginning and end of the intervals so that the lines reached into the space traversed by the object. Third, we reduced these lines to three dots such that the space below the object was equally segmented without intersecting its trajectory. Our results show that the effect of the OKI on TTC estimates extends into peri-illusional space. Surprisingly, extending the end lines of the intervals reduced this effect, whereas the illusion was almost fully restored when the interval boundaries were indicated by dots. Our findings suggest that the elongated end lines of the extrapolation interval define a new space that is not affected by the illusion, whereas isolated points do not.

title: Illusion of absence: Capturing the perception of occluded space using EEG
affiliations:
1. Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition, and Behaviour - Radboud University (NL)
2. University of Bergen (NO)
3. Lund University (SE)
abstract: The perception of occluded scene regions can involve the illusion of absence, wherein the region behind the occluder is perceived as empty. An object appearing out of a seemingly empty space should be surprising. In this EEG study, we measure the P3 component of event-related potentials to capture the neural correlates of surprise when objects are uncovered from behind an occluder. We expect an increased P3 in response to uncovering an object from behind a small occluded area compared to a large one. We will present preliminary data of this ongoing study. The findings of this study will help us better understand the neural mechanisms involved in perception of occluded space. Moreover, the ability to perceive what is completely hidden behind an occluder is crucial for road safety. For example, the supporting structures of a car on both sides of the windscreen can create the false perception that the occluded space behind them is empty, which can lead to an accident. This way, our study helps us understand the driver’s perspective on the road. This study was supported by the Research Council of Norway (Project No. 334817).

title: Top-down control of attention via search for targets and via inhibition of distractors are not two sides of the same coin
affiliations: 1. Department of Cognition, Emotion and Methods in Psychology, University of Vienna (AT)
abstract: Current theory discusses links between two types of top-down control of attention during visual search. On one hand, observers can configure (positive) top-down search templates in their memory that guide attention towards searched-for stimuli matching the template. On the other, observers can inhibit known distractors in a top-down way. However, it is debated how top-down inhibition of (attention capture by) distractors works. First, participants could use (negative) templates to proactively inhibit capture by template-matching distractors. Second, alternatively, top-down inhibition might work reactively, following attention capture by a distractor matching the negative template. Here, we investigated how efficiently observers used top-down templates for inhibition during negative search, and how the resulting performance effect corresponds to the individual observer’s top-down-dependent capture during positive search. During positive search, in an adapted Additional-Singleton-Protocol, observers searched for a color-defined target. Besides the singleton-target, displays contained several non-singleton distractors and one singleton-distractor in a non-target color or in a template-matching (target-similar) color. Here, distraction by target-similar distractors exceeded that by non-target color distractor, indicating individually varying degrees of top-down dependent attention capture. During negative search, observers searched for a singleton-target that was missing a predefined distractor color present either in a singleton-distractor, or in all (non-singleton) distractors. Behavioral and eye-tracking data suggested that an individual’s degree of top-down dependent capture during positive search was not related to the same individual’s degree of inhibition of the matching (singleton) distractors during negative search. In fact, during negative search, distractors matching the template for inhibition captured attention and reduced search efficiency, as predicted by reactive inhibition theory. These findings suggest that top-down templates for inhibition do not operate proactively, as positive search templates do, challenging the idea of a common origin of different types of top-down control of attention during visual search.

title: Dynamic visual search modelled with foveated observer
affiliations: 1. University of Helsinki (FI)
abstract: A natural part of vision is scanning the environment with eye movements, reflecting the foveated nature of the visual system. Our everyday environment is dynamic, often requiring rapid decisions based on shifting visual input. While a great deal is known about how we gather visual information in static settings, dynamic environments remain less studied and poorly understood. We studied how object movement and velocity affect visual search. We measured the eye movements and behavioural data of 16 participants in a visual search experiment with five different object velocities: 0, 3, 6, 8, and 11 deg/s (random-walk motion). The stimulus comprised 10 Gabor patches at different orientations (vertical target and distractors at ±25° or 50° from the target), against a background of dynamic Gaussian noise. Peripheral visibility was measured in a separate detection experiment. Increasing object velocity impaired search performance, with slower reaction times (β = 0.0249 s/velocity, p = .002) and reduced accuracy (β = −0.0048, p = .001). Critically, there was no speed–accuracy trade-off, and interactions in scanpath length (β = 22.12 deg, p < .001) and fixation dispersion (β = −3.13 deg²/velocity, p < .001) indicated that higher velocities primarily altered search behaviour in target-absent searches, leading to more constrained visual exploration. To account for human performance, we modelled dynamic visual search using a novel foveated evidence-accumulation Bayesian observer model. The model uses sensory noise and decision criterion as free parameters while being constrained by replayed human eye movements and sensitivity (visibility), allowing us to isolate perceptual limitations from oculomotor strategies. This straightforward foveated observer model with temporal accumulation explained the increase in reaction times and decrease in performance in dynamic search. Overall, the core difficulty of visual search in dynamic environments lies in perceptual constraints imposed by object velocity, rather than in altered search strategies.

title: Sharing Practices in Vision Research: Current Approaches and Future Directions
affiliations:
1. University of Southampton (UK)
2. New Mexico State University (US)
3. University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (US)
4. Harrisburg University (US)
abstract: Sharing data and other outputs from scientific research can be useful for several different purposes. These include: (1) analytic reproducibility, which involves re-running existing analyses reported in an associated paper (2) direct replication, which involves reusing the software/materials needed to run an experiment and (3) secondary data analyses, which involve analyzing shared datasets to ask new research questions. Here, we report on our recent projects examining sharing practices in vision research to provide an overview of our field’s current approaches, as well as highlighting ways that we can collectively improve our sharing practices. At present, the sharing of metadata is limited, which makes it difficult for others to reuse existing datasets. Without metadata, other researchers are often forced to make ‘educated guesses’ about shared files and their contents (e.g., identifying which files are raw data, and what variables are represented in each column of a dataset). Dataset producers diverge considerably regarding column naming conventions, representing a significant barrier to dataset reuse in the absence of accompanying metadata. Raw data is rarely shared, making it difficult for others to conduct secondary data analyses. Finally, shared outputs are generally difficult to find via internet searches, because research outputs shared online are often not linked clearly to associated publications (e.g., titles and abstracts are often not included alongside shared outputs). Despite these issues, there are several simple routes that we review in order to move forward and enhance sharing practices, ensuring that outputs are not only more easily found by others, but more easily reused by others as well. These focus on enhancing the metadata shared by researchers alongside their outputs, including the use of the ‘Find It – Access It – Reuse It’ scorecard that we have recently developed.

title: The Effect of Person Presence And Object Salience On Visual Search Time In Virtual Reality
affiliations:
1. University of Kent (UK)
2. University of York (UK)
abstract: Visual perception research often employs two distinct methodologies: highly controlled laboratory experiments and more-ecologically valid but less controlled real-world studies. Virtual reality (VR) offers a middle ground between these two methods, allowing for immersion within complex environments whilst retaining experimental control. Here, we demonstrate how such VR methods can be used to study visual search behaviour. We used high-fidelity avatars to explore the combined effect of person presence and stimulus salience on visual search time. Participants were asked to locate books in a virtual library. In half of the trials, the target objects presented had high or low salience. In addition, avatars were present in half of the trials and absent for the remaining trials. Our data shows that participants were faster to locate high compared to low salience objects. In addition, target objects were located faster when avatars were absent than present. However, the effect of avatar presence was only observed for low saliency targets, suggesting that person presence only distracted from the search when targets were harder to find. This experiment serves to validate these animated avatars as useful research tools to study visual perception in complex settings and solidifies VR as a method to understand social cognition in naturalistic contexts.

title: Reliable but Distinct: Visual Search Across Tasks
affiliations:
1. École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (CH)
2. Neuro-Cognitive Psychology & CITEC, Bielefeld University (DE)
abstract: Visual tests often show weak inter-correlations despite good test-retest reliability. These findings limit the applicability of these tests since test validity is low. Here, we tested to what extent visual search tasks correlate with each other. We used four conjunction tasks that varied in shape, colour, and orientation (n=32) and a letter search task (upright T among Ls). Each task was performed with three set sizes (2, 4, and 8 items). To evaluate test-retest reliability, each task was repeated four times.   Reliability was moderate to strong in nearly all conditions except one. Conjunction search tasks based on shape, color, and orientation were moderately to strongly correlated with each other. The letter search was only weakly correlated with these tasks. This dissociation may reflect reliance on different underlying mechanisms in feature-based and object-based search. This interpretation is further supported by factor analysis, which identified three factors. While the first four tasks loaded strongly onto the first two factors, the letter search task loaded primarily onto the third factor with minimal associations with the first two factors. Hence, these findings highlight how correlational analyses can provide insights into distinct underlying mechanisms in visual search.

title: Not All Searches Are Equal: Prevalence Effects Differ in Interactive Search Compared to Visual Search
affiliations: 1. University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: When carrying out a search for a target, manipulation with the environment and/or the individual objects within it may be required to successfully detect the target. These searches are known as interactive searches. Many real-life interactive searches involve searching for targets that are unlikely to be present or are said to have low target prevalence. Here, we conducted two experiments to examine the exhaustiveness of interactive search, focusing on whether searchers were less exhaustive when prevalence was low. For both experiments, we found a standard low prevalence effect for response accuracy, such that low prevalence targets were more likely to be missed than high prevalence targets. However, we found strong evidence against the influence of prevalence upon all measures of exhaustiveness during target-absent trials. In other words, contrary to traditional low prevalence visual search findings, changes in response accuracy were not a result of reductions in exhaustiveness. We conclude that, during interactive search, even when prevalence is low, searchers utilize a ‘no stone unturned’ strategy. When following this strategy, searchers become unwilling to provide an ‘absent’ response without checking most, if not all, possible places, regions or areas in a display that could contain a target.

title: Semantic scene structure guides visual search: Evidence from conceptual object clustering in real-world scenes
affiliations: 1. University of California, Davis (US)
abstract: Visual search in naturalistic scenes is remarkably efficient, yet the scene properties that drive this efficiency remain poorly understood. While visual clutter has been shown to be a real-world analogue of set size, less is known about whether the semantic organization of a scene, how meaningfully its objects cluster together in conceptual space, independently shapes search behavior. Here we operationalize object set size in both semantic and physical space using k-medoids clustering of object labels in ConceptNet Numberbatch semantic representational space, and object segmentations as proxies for spatial object clusters (Tachihara et al. 2025). Fifty participants searched for arbitrary target objects in 115 familiar real-world indoor scenes spanning six categories (kitchen, bathroom, office, bedroom, living room, dining room) while eye movements were recorded. Scene-level weighted correlations revealed that semantic clustering reliably predicted mean search reaction time (r = 0.343, p < .001). Scenes with more semantic clusters, reflecting greater conceptual fragmentation of the object inventory, were associated with slower search. While spatial clustering did not independently predict search behavior in our models, the semantic clustering effect was confirmed in generalized linear mixed effects models controlling for target eccentricity and target size. These results suggest that the conceptual organization of a scene's object inventory shapes attentional guidance during search, with implications for how semantic representations support visual cognition in naturalistic environments.

title: Catching insects: threatening images which do not capture attention
affiliations: 1. University of Vienna (AT)
abstract: In visual search tasks, threatening stimuli such as snakes or spiders capture attention more than neutral stimuli. This suggests a threat advantage in the capture of human visual attention. Our project focuses on such a potential threat advantage for insects. In altogether 6 experiments (N = 132), we asked observers to search for photographs and sketches of insects (of various species) among neutral images. So far, results suggest that a threat advantage does not apply to insects. Even though observers rate insect images consistently as more threatening than neutral images (e.g., plants, birds), insect images do not capture attention more than neutral images. Our results also question the established understanding of threat advantage, showing that manipulations such as priming can mimic threat advantages in visual search.

title: Modelling visual foraging: the role of errors and assumptions in theory building
affiliations: 1. University of Essex (UK)
abstract: Visual foraging is a continuous search behaviour in which a participant searches for multiple items. The cognitive factors that affect visual foraging behaviour have now been studied in a range of experimental paradigms: for instance, studies have shown that the perceived value of targets affects selection decisions, and that the difficulty of the foraging task affects how people make choices between sticking with the same target type or switching to another. We have built a theory of target-by-target visual foraging behaviour that uses parameters informed by these experimental results (implemented as a generative Bayesian model, FoMo). Here, we consider how studying the limitations of this model can help us to develop our psychological theories of foraging behaviour. Firstly, we consider an example where human behaviour diverges from FoMo model predictions, discussing what these model ‘errors’ can tell us, and how they led us to implementing methods for modelling ‘scanning’ strategies in FoMo. Secondly, building models involves making our assumptions explicit, which can help us identify aspects of behaviour we do not yet fully understand. We illustrate this with an example where we studied the effect of target scarcity on foraging behaviour. Finally, we consider how we can use baseline models to further explore areas for improving FoMo, using an example where we tested a new target selection decision rule for the model. To conclude, we discuss how these principles may be more broadly applicable to computational modelling work and theory building in vision science.

title: Modeling two distinct modes in visual search: Implications for V1 mechanisms in bottom-up attention
affiliations: 1. Sun Yat-sen University (CN)
abstract: We analyzed behavioral and gaze data from a visual search task designed to test the V1 Saliency Hypothesis (V1SH). Observers searched for a target ‘homo-pair’ of disks (both black or both white) embedded in a cluttered scene of uniformly oriented ‘hetero-pairs’ (one black and one white disk). The orientation of each pair was defined by the line connecting the disk centers. Target pairs were oriented either parallel or perpendicular to background distractors, randomly interleaved across 400 trials. A V1 neuron's on/off receptive subfield is more activated by the white/black disk in the stimulus. Because V1 neurons are suppressed by nearby neurons tuned to similar orientations, a target parallel—rather than perpendicular—to background hetero-pairs suffers less iso-orientation suppression. This triggers a higher V1 firing rate, making the parallel target more salient according to V1SH. Search behavior fell into two distinct modes: an exploratory mode, characterized by multiple saccades and a reaction time (RT) distribution with a high mean and heavy tail; and a rapid saliency-driven mode, where observers reported the target with zero to a few saccades, yielding an RT distribution with a short mean and light tail. To assess learning effects, we used Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods to fit RT data to a Hidden Markov Model, assuming the probability that a trial triggers the saliency-driven mode changes linearly with trial experience. Results show that parallel targets have a significantly higher probability of triggering the saliency-driven mode. Crucially, this ‘parallel advantage’ is robust in early trials and maintains its magnitude without growing as experience increases. These findings support V1SH, demonstrating that V1 is the neural mechanism underlying bottom-up attention—an inherent mechanism that does not require learning.

title: Prior Learning Influences Attentional Suppression after Target Relocation in Contextual Cueing
affiliations:
1. Department Psychologie, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (DE)
2. NICUM – Neuroimaging Core Unit Munich, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (DE)
3. Munich Center for Neurosciences – Brain & Mind, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (DE)
abstract: Visual search can be facilitated by repeated visuospatial contexts that guide attention towards likely target locations (contextual cueing). Prior work has employed different target-context mappings: target locations may be uniquely associated with specific repeated contexts (fixed mapping) or shared across repeated and nonrepeated displays (variable mapping). Although both regimes yield contextual cueing behaviorally, they differ in cue predictiveness and may therefore rely on distinct underlying representational formats. Variable mappings reduce cue predictiveness, favoring independent learning of the target location and the distractor context, whereas fixed mappings promote learning of specific target-distractor associations. Our study examined how these differences affect contextual adaptation after the relocation of the target in previously learned contexts, with the lateralized ERP component, distractor positivity (PD), as an indicator of distractor suppression. In Experiment 1 (N = 50), participants performed a visual search task involving repeated and nonrepeated contexts (variable mapping). Following an initial learning session, the target was relocated within an otherwise unchanged context in the relocation session. The results showed that behavioral contextual cueing was disrupted after relocation, and an early PD emerged at the new target location, indicating suppression of the relocated, but now task-relevant target position. Because the initial target location was not uniquely associated with a specific context during learning, it might not evoke strong misleading predictions and was therefore not actively suppressed. In Experiment 2 (N = 25), nonrepeated displays were removed and repetitions of the invariant contexts were doubled (fixed mapping). Following target relocation, an early PD was instead observed at the old target position, reflecting suppression of previously learned but now misleading context-target associations.  These findings suggest that attentional suppression is shaped by the structure of prior learning: variable mappings engage suppression of newly relevant target location, whereas fixed mappings recruit suppression of context-target bindings to overcome memory-driven biases.

title: First Things First: Selection Behavior in Real-World and Virtual Interactive Search.
affiliations: 1. University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: Interactive search, an extension of visual search, describes search tasks that require both visual inspection and physical manipulation of objects. In visual search, attentional selection is often guided by similarity to the target. However, in interactive search all relevant visual information is not always immediately available, requiring searchers to decide how to interact with their environment to uncover obscured visual information. Here, we investigated selection behavior in interactive search across two independent experiments. In both experiments, participants searched four cubes to locate a target “T” shape attached to one face of one of the cubes. In Experiment 1, participants physically interacted with tangible cubes, picking them up and rotating them whilst their interactions were recorded using optical motion-capture. In Experiment 2, participants performed an analogous task in a virtual environment, using a mouse to click and rotate cubes presented on a computer screen. In both experiments, two cubes contained a letter on each face (information-rich) whereas the remaining two contained a letter on only one face (information-poor). We predicted that participants would adopt an “easy-first” strategy, prioritizing the inspection of information-poor cubes before information-rich cubes. Our reasoning here was that whilst objects containing more shapes would provide a greater quantity of visual information to the searcher, examining these cubes would also come at a cost in terms of processing time and cognitive effort. Analyses revealed a divergence in selection behavior across environments. In real-world interactive search, participants preferentially inspected information-rich cubes with no change in this preference over trials, whereas in virtual interactive search, participants prioritized information-poor cubes, and this bias increased as trials progressed. These findings suggest that the weighting of time and effort costs relative to the likelihood of an object containing the target differs between otherwise equivalent real-world and virtual tasks.

title: Cross-channel Neural Adaptation Reveals Shared Emotion Representation of Biological Motion and Face in the Right Superior Temporal Sulcus.
affiliations:
1. Shanghai Normal University (CN)
2. Chinese Institute of Psychology (CN)
abstract: Emotional perception from biological motion (BM) and facial expressions is essential for social interaction, yet their shared neural processing mechanism remains unclear. The present study adopted a visual adaptation paradigm combined with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to explore the neural basis of BM emotion processing and its cross-category association with facial emotion perception. Behavioral results revealed robust emotion-specific adaptation aftereffects for BM: prolonged exposure to emotional BM biased subsequent ambiguous BM emotion perception toward the opposite valence, and this effect was independent of low-level retinotopic features and vanished under inverted BM presentation. A consistent inversion-dependent adaptation pattern was also observed for facial emotional stimuli. Critically, bidirectional cross-category emotion adaptation aftereffects were confirmed between facial expressions and BM, verifying the existence of common emotional neural representations across the two stimulus categories. Neuroimaging results further demonstrated that BM emotion processing elicited significant neural adaptation in the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), whose neural adaptation magnitude was tightly correlated with individual behavioral aftereffect strength. Moreover, facial emotion adaptation significantly modulated right pSTS neural responses to subsequent BM emotional stimuli. Collectively, these findings indicate that the right pSTS serves as a core neural module for BM emotion processing, and mediates domain-general shared representation of emotional information from both body motion and facial cues, revealing the key neural mechanism underlying cross-category emotional perception integration in social cognition.
