title: Reflexive attention to biological motion formed by arrows with opposing orientation: Impaired in individuals with high autistic traits
affiliations:
1. State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Science and Mental Health, Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CN)
2. Department of Psychology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CN)
abstract: Biological motion (BM) is a potent social signal capable of guiding human attention, a phenomenon termed social attention that underpins adaptive behavior and interpersonal interaction. Although extensively studied in laboratory settings, social attention is typically examined using simplified, isolated cues, leaving unresolved whether it possesses reflexive properties distinct from nonsocial attention. This study developed a dual-cue paradigm that embedded oppositely-oriented arrow cues within BM sequences, directly assessing reflexive nature of BM-induced attention using a conflict-resilience criterion. Results confirmed that BM cues, despite being reduced to kinematic information within incongruent directional signals, robustly directed attention. Furthermore, this potency persisted even for local BM signals lacking global configuration but disappeared upon removal of essential biological characteristics, highlighting the crucial role of local motion cues in guiding attention under perceptual conflict. Crucially, BM-driven reflexive attention was negatively correlated with autistic traits. Individuals with higher autistic traits failed to utilize BM cues to direct attention, yet showed intact arrow-driven attention, manifesting specific deficits in social rather than nonsocial attention. These findings uncover an intrinsic processing advantage for social signals in complex contexts that appears compromised with increasing autism-like characteristics, providing a novel paradigm with profound implications for early diagnosis and intervention in autism.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Motion Perception and Optical Flow

title: Perception of object velocity during visual simulation of ego movement
affiliations: 1. Univ Gustave Eiffel, COSYS, PICS-L (FR)
abstract: Moving observers need to be able to estimate the displacement of other objects in the scene in order to avoid collisions. Previous studies have reported that the visual system uses information in optic flow to subtract the retinal motion component due to self-movement to recover scene-relative object motion – a mechanism called flow parsing. This study investigates whether such mechanism plays a role in speed perception. Using a two-interval forced-choice procedure, participants were confronted in one of the two intervals to randomly moving dots (the reference condition) and in the other to a cloud of dots moving radially – either expanding or contracting. During each intervals participants were confronted to a probe moving horizontally toward the centre of the screen, and were asked to indicate which of the two was going faster. In the reference condition, the probe velocity was fixed at 3,6 deg.s-1. In radial conditions, it was adjusted using four interleaved staircases starting at 4,2 or 3,0 deg.s-1, in expanding or contracting flow. To prevent reliance on strategies unrelated to speed perception, both the initial position (i.e., eccentricity) and the duration of probe presentation were randomly varied. Our results show that radial motion plays a role in the perception of the probe’s speed in comparison to random motion. In accordance to flow parsing theory, participants judge the velocity of probe as slower in contracting optic flow and as faster in expanding optic flow. As a next step, we aim to extend this paradigm to biological motion. Because it provides structured, articulated kinematic cues that enhance motion perception, we hypothesize that this type of movement strengthens scene-relative object motion perception. In applied context of driving simulation this raises the question of how we perceive the movement of a pedestrian about to cross the road in front of us.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Motion Perception and Optical Flow

title: Why do changes in pupil diameter cause illusory visual motion?
affiliations:
1. University of Sussex (UK)
2. University of Lincoln (UK)
3. York University (CA)
4. Dartmouth College (US)
abstract: In the Rotating Snakes (aka Peripheral Drift) motion illusion a stationary pattern that contains repeated asymmetrical luminance gradients can appear to move episodically, triggered by saccadic eye movements, pattern onsets, and blinks. Last year we reported evidence from pupillometry that the illusory movement is caused by transitory changes in the retinal luminance of the pattern due to reflexive changes in pupil diameter following eye movements, pattern onsets and blinks. In this research we tested whether computational models of human cortical motion processing can account for apparent motion induced by luminance change.  The Adelson-Bergen motion energy sensor is widely used to model low-level motion detection, but our implementation of the standard model was unable to account for the illusion. We therefore tested a variant of the model in which the responses of direction-selective units were half-wave rectified prior to computing motion direction, creating separate ON and OFF sensors consistent with responses in cortical neurons. Both types of sensor were found to signal motion in asymmetrical illusion patterns, in the correct direction for OFF sensors and in the reverse direction for ON sensors.   OFF signals are already known to evoke stronger cortical responses that ON signals in humans, macaques and mice, and OFF stimuli are 25% more effective at driving motion perception than ON stimuli. If OFF responses in our model are weighted more strongly that ON responses in the direction computation, the ON/OFF model can predict the direction of the illusion. The weighted ON/OFF model can also explain the motion seen in a number of standard displays (as can the original Adelson-Bergen model). Variations in reported illusion strength in the population could be due to individual differences in ON/OFF weighting and in pupil motility. Supported by Leverhulme Trust Emeritus Fellowship EM-2023-043 (GM), and NSERC Discovery RGPIN-2019-03989 (PC).
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Motion Perception and Optical Flow

title: Interaction Rules as a Framework for Collective Motion Perception Beyond Templates
affiliations: 1. University of Münster (DE)
abstract: The visual system excels at segmenting objects from dynamic, non-rigid motion. While internal templates could facilitate the recognition of objects in biological motion (e.g. point-light walkers) or elastic deformations (e.g. point-light cloth), fluid systems such as bird swarms, smoke or water, lack a fixed geometry for a template. Instead, they underlie motion or interaction rules based on physical forces or intra-system dynamics. We hypothesize that the visual system extracts these rules as a functional substitute for templates. Using a novel 'Point-Light Swarm' (PLS) stimulus, we investigated whether 'alignment' as an interaction rule can be detected in collective 2D motion. Alignment was implemented based on Vicsek’s algorithm by which motion directions of all points within a defined spatial interaction-relation are replaced by the average direction (Vicsek, Phys. Rev. Lett., 1995). In two experiments, we varied the presentation duration (1500, 500, 100 ms) and the initial configuration (random or grid-based locations) of the PLS. In the first experiment, we used a distance-based interaction algorithm and varied interaction radii. To investigate the effect of the number of neighbours, we used a topological (neighbour-based) interaction framework in the second experiment. Participants had to detect the presence of alignment in a 2-AFC task. Results show that sensitivity (d') increases with the amount of interaction, either through larger radii or more neighbours, before reaching a plateau. Increase was stronger and plateau level was higher for 1500 ms and 500 ms stimulus-duration than for 100 ms. These findings show that alignment in PLS motion can be detected rapidly, even at duration of 100ms, but benefits from longer presentation duration. This implicates that the visual system either better integrates cues that are present at 100 ms over longer time or utilizes emergent cues that only develop after the initial 100 ms due to the interaction rules.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Motion Perception and Optical Flow

title: Conflicting motion cues in Gabor stimuli: evidence for separate position- and phase-based motion mechanisms
affiliations: 1. University of Oxford (UK)
abstract: Visual motion can be described by changes in the phase of Fourier components (phase cues), and changes in the position of salient features (position cues). Gabor stimuli can be constructed which place these cues in opposition, by displacing the gaussian window (position cue) in a different direction to the phase displacement of the sinusoid carrier (phase cue). We propose that these cues are processed by two independent motion systems with distinct spatiotemporal frequency sensitivities across the retina, with higher spatial frequency sensitivity for phase cues and a steeper eccentricity-dependent decline for position cues. We tested reported motion direction for two-frame apparent motion Gabor stimuli (n=7), rendered in 6 conditions: phase displacement only position displacement only or containing simultaneous phase and position displacements in conflicting motion directions of 45, 90, 135, and 180o. Stimuli were presented at 7 spatial frequencies at the fovea and 10 degrees eccentricity (fovea: 0.81 cpd to 16 cpd periphery: 0.3 cpd to 5.9 cpd), for 50 trials for each condition. Reported motion direction in the conflicting conditions at the fovea was biased towards the position cue, with a small but significant effect of the phase cue, particularly at higher spatial frequencies. In the periphery, the phase cue exerted a stronger effect on reported motion direction that could not be compensated for by simple scaling of spatial frequency between the fovea and periphery, supporting our proposal of two independent systems with changing spatiotemporal sensitivity across the retina. Furthermore, we demonstrated that participants’ own sensitivity to phase and position cues, measured in the isolated cue conditions, predicted the weighting of the phase cue in determining reported direction for the 4 conflicting cue conditions, at both fovea and periphery, across all spatial frequencies.

title: The role of visual contextual cues on motion extrapolation: A single horizon line biases the Representational Horizon
affiliations:
1. William James Center for Research, Department of Education and Psychology (PT)
2. Department of Education and Psychology, University of Aveiro (PT)
3. Institute of Electronics and Telematics Engineering, Department of Electronics, Telecommunications and Informatics (PT)
abstract: The perceived offset position of a moving target is systematically displaced forward, in the direction of motion (Representational Momentum RM), downward, in the direction of gravity (Representational Gravity RG), and along the horizon implied by the visual context (Representational Horizon RH). The latter has been shown to depend on visual context orientation, particularly in exterior settings where horizon cues are salient. Building on this evidence, the present study examined whether RH can be reliably biased by minimal visual cues that efficiently imply a horizon axis and investigated their differential impact on motion extrapolation phenomena. Participants observed moving targets following various trajectories, overlaid on a randomly chosen visual context depicting either a combined ground and sky gradients, an isolated ground or sky gradient, or a single horizon line context rotated -22.5º, 0º, or 22.5º relative to the true vertical. Upon the target's vanishing, participants indicated its last seen location with a trackball. Spatial localizations were subjected to a discrete Fourier decomposition procedure to obtain independent estimates of RM, RG, and RH. Outcomes showed that RH direction consistently followed the horizon implied by the visual context across all conditions. Furthermore, RM magnitude increased with the sky gradient and decreased with the ground gradient, indicating sensitivity to ecological features. These findings underscore the pivotal role of horizon information in visuospatial orientation and contribute to a better understanding of extrapolation phenomena.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Motion Perception and Optical Flow

title: The Role of Size and Texture in the Perceived Onset Position of a Moving Target
affiliations:
1. William James Center for Research, Department of Education and Psychology (PT)
2. Department of Education and Psychology, University of Aveiro (PT)
3. Institute of Electronics and Telematics Engineering, Department of Electronics,  Telecommunications and Informatics (PT)
abstract: When observers are asked to indicate the spatial location at which a moving target first appears, their judgements are systematically displaced backward along the direction of motion, a phenomenon coined as the Onset Repulsion Effect (ORE). Previous research has shown that this effect is particularly pronounced for ascending targets, revealing a vertical anisotropy in onset spatial localization. Furthermore, by manipulating perceived target mass through kinematic information or direct sensorimotor experience, prior studies have shown that the magnitude of the ORE increases for targets judged as heavier. These findings have led to the proposal that the ORE may reflect a cognitive tendency to attribute a ‘natural history’ to dynamic events, similar to the preparatory windup before throwing an object, resulting in a backward overcompensation of onset location. The present study investigated whether visual cues commonly used to infer object mass in everyday perception, namely size and texture, modulate onset spatial localization. Two experiments were conducted in which participants localized the onset position of moving targets that varied in size alone (Experiment 1) or in size combined with surface texture (Experiment 2). The results revealed that target size reliably modulates the magnitude of the ORE, with larger targets producing greater backward displacements, thus extending previous findings to visual size cues. In contrast, surface texture had no effect on onset localization, suggesting that the ORE is selectively sensitive to mass-related information and that its modulation depends on the representational level at which such information is inferred. The results are discussed in relation to stored representations of object dynamics and the role of embodied causal expectations in shaping spatial localization
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Motion Perception and Optical Flow

title: Mind the Affective Gap: Human vs. Machine Perception of Emotion in Biological Motion
affiliations: 1. Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan
abstract: We humans are superior in detecting important social signals such as gender and emotion from reduced visual stimuli such as biological motion, however, affective computing from whole-body movements is still at its infancy. Here we present a series of experiments in behavioral studies, neuroscience, and machine learning to showcase the challenges and opportunities to decode social communicative signals from body motion. These studies utilize DIEM-A, a multicultural diverse body movement database for emotions including over 10,000 short animations recorded from two Asian regions depicting 14 emotional categories. We discovered clear gaps between human participants and AI models in their responses in (1) cultural variation, (2) visual contexts, and (3) motion reasoning. First, human participants outperformed a deep learning model (Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network) at identifying hostile body movements, but equally well at identifying friendly signals. The cultural bias from human observations was absent in AI model, implying that they use different operation principles. Secondly, human participants can reliably extract embodied emotions from task-irrelevant information such as environmental background and the performers’ gender/size, but the performance from a visual language model (VLM, Gemini 2.5 flash) was heavily modulated by the richness of the visual background (avatar > point-light displays > video footage). Finally, to understand why the models diverge, we analyzed the natural language explanations generated by the VLM and compared them to human descriptions of the same videos. Humans prioritize kinematics cues (e.g., ‘step,’ ‘turn,’ ‘look up’), and VLMs prioritize abstract interpretations (e.g ‘suggests,’ ‘threat,’ ‘energy’) and bypass the raw physical observations.  Affective computing such as emotional intelligence has been identified as the next key milestone for tele-communication development. However, we are still far from understanding the nature of it. title: Tuning flow parsing effects with Gabor patch stimuli
affiliations:
1. University of Manchester (UK)
2. Andrew Mayes Centre for Cognitive Neuroscience (UK)
abstract: The flow parsing (FP) mechanism contributes to recovery of scene‑relative object movement during observer self‑movement and is thought to operate via global filtering (subtraction) of optic flow. FP‑consistent behaviour has been robustly demonstrated using optic‑flow fields composed of limited‑lifetime elements, but it remains unclear to what extent FP depends on low‑level stimulus attributes that are more precisely controlled in narrowband stimuli. Clarifying this dependency could provide insights for the neural implementation of FP.We measured FP effects using hemifields of mini‑Gabor patches, providing oriented narrowband local motion signals. In a preliminary experiment, patch attributes were manipulated to signal movement towards elements either at a single depth or at random depths within the scene. 50 Gabor patches were sampled uniformly in the scene and oriented, as a function of location, to signal global expansion or contraction. In Same‑Depth (S) conditions, Gabor spatial frequency, diameter and depth were 3 cpd, 2° and 1m respectively. In Random‑Depth (R) conditions, depths were sampled randomly between 0.5 and 1.5 m and Gabor parameters were scaled appropriately with depth. Across conditions, patch speeds were consistent with forward or backward observer motion at 0.75 m/s. Participants made 2AFC leftward/rightward movement judgements for a probe presented 5° from central fixation, in the hemifield opposite the flow. Probe velocity was controlled by interleaved Kesten staircases and psychometric functions were fitted to the resulting data. FP was characterised by the bias in the point of subjective stationarity.  FP‑consistent biases were observed in S and R conditions, but were larger for R, suggesting this stimulus provides more robust input to the FP mechanism. These results demonstrate that FP can be driven by local narrowband stimuli, offering a promising tool for probing low‑level computations and neural pathways underlying FP.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Motion Perception and Optical Flow

title: Response activation by complex animal silhouettes: Double dissociation between response priming and custom-made masking functions
affiliations: 1. University of Kaiserslautern-Landau (DE)
abstract: Previously, dissociations between the time-courses of response priming and visual awareness have only been reported for simple geometrical and color stimuli. Here we use the recent technique of “induced dissociations” to extend those findings to more complex stimuli. Participants are presented with animal silhouettes as primes and targets and are asked to respond either to the looking direction of the target animal or to identify the looking direction of the masked prime animal. Prime visibility is controlled by a metacontrast mask that consists of the superimposed silhouettes of both looking directions. Mask contrast is systematically coupled to prime-target SOA in two different ways to induce qualitatively different masking functions without affecting the time-course of priming. We show that response priming effects increase with SOA no matter whether prime discrimination performance increases or decreases. Our results indicate for the first time that double dissociations between response priming and visual awareness of the critical prime feature extend beyond simple stimuli and to visually complex, semantically relevant materials.

title: Active exploration reveals individual differences in material discrimination
affiliations:
1. Toyohashi University of Technology (JP)
2. University of Oxford (UK)
abstract: Understanding which visual cues support material discrimination is a central question in material perception. While this has traditionally been studied using passive viewing paradigms, recent works have adopted active exploration paradigms. This allow observers to move their viewpoint or manipulate objects, enabling the investigation of how diagnostic cues are actively acquired. However, it remains unclear how such cue-acquisition strategies vary across individuals. In the present study, we examined individual differences in cue-acquisition strategies during an active material discrimination task and whether these differences can be predicted by image- and video-computable features. Twenty participants explored virtual objects in a head-mounted display by moving their heads and manipulating the stimuli using handheld controllers judging whether each object appeared more metallic or glass-like. The stimuli varied continuously from glass to metal and included diverse shapes and illumination environments. Exploratory behavior was categorized into actions such as pulling the object, approaching it, and viewing it from above or below. Principal component analysis revealed two dominant dimensions: overall exploration duration and relative reliance on viewpoint changes versus object manipulation. Clustering identified two strategy groups: one relying primarily on viewpoint changes with shorter exploration durations and other relying more on object manipulation with longer durations. Despite these differences, both groups exhibited comparable increases in discrimination sensitivity across trials. Furthermore, simple models based on single image- and video-based features (e.g., temporal luminance changes and optic flow) were used to predict participants’ responses. Despite their simplicity, some models achieved high discriminability (d’ > 2) for certain participants, although predictive performance varied substantially across individuals. These findings suggest that although observers can adopt diverse strategies sufficient to support increases in discrimination sensitivity, different individuals likely rely on different visual cues during active material discrimination.

title: Active gaze sampling differentially shapes the use of motion and image cues in gloss perception
affiliations:
1. Toyohashi University of Technology (JP)
2. University of Oxford (UK)
abstract: Gloss perception is a fundamental visual function that involves estimating the physical properties of object surfaces, and specular flow is known to play a critical role in this process. However, how motion-based and image-based information is integrated during active viewing and whether gaze behavior directly contributes to the use of these cues in perceptual judgments remain unclear. Here, we investigated how physical stimulus properties and gaze behavior jointly contribute to gloss judgments. Participants viewed rotating objects in a virtual environment and judged whether they appeared glossy or not. In addition to a “shiny” condition, in which specular reflections moved across the surface, we employed a “sticky” condition in which reflections were attached to the surface and rotated with the object. Eye movements were recorded, and optical flow and static image features around fixation were analyzed alongside temporal changes in gaze. Perceived gloss was enhanced in the shiny condition but markedly reduced in the sticky condition. Compared with luminance-based features (five features 72.6%), random forest models predicting gloss judgments revealed that optic flow-based features (five features) achieved higher accuracy (76.7%). Crucially, when actual gaze trajectories were replaced with random trajectories, the performance of the luminance-based model significantly decreased, whereas the optic flow-based model maintained its performance. These findings indicate that motion-based information contributes more robustly to gloss perception than static image information does and suggest that gaze-dependent sampling primarily supports the acquisition of localized image cues, whereas motion-based cues are more globally available. These findings highlight the importance of active exploration in shaping the availability and utilization of visual information for material perception, suggesting that the contribution of visual cues may depend on whether they are acquired through self-generated or externally driven sampling.

title: Predicting gloss perception across asymmetric scene conditions
affiliations:
1. Justus-Liebig-Universtät (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior (DE)
abstract: Perceived gloss depends not only on the reflectance of a surface, but also on distal scene factors such as illumination, viewpoint, and object shape. As a result, the discriminability of two surfaces can vary substantially across scene conditions ranging from easily discriminable to perceptually equivalent. Here, we investigate whether perceived equivalence and discriminability of two surfaces across asymmetric scenes can be predicted using image-computable models. We rendered surfaces with five levels of surface roughness using combinations of ten illuminations, ten viewpoints, and ten shapes. We then calculated perceived visual differences between neighbouring roughness levels within each combination of scene factors using a visual difference predictor (VDP Mantiuk et al., 2023). Based on the average of the predicted perceptual differences within each scene, we selected three scenes with the highest differences (“high-VDP”) and three with lowest differences (“low-VDP”). If VDP predicts gloss perception across asymmetric scene conditions, sensitivity to gloss changes should differ the most between those scene sets. To test this, we fit psychometric functions for each scene based on observers’ gloss judgments in a 2AFC task comparing our chosen scenes to an asymmetric comparison with a near-median VDP value. We find that VDP predicts biases and sensitivity in gloss perception across different scenes, even though it is based on measuring visibility of differences within particular scenes. Specifically, in the “low-VDP” scenes, surfaces appeared rougher and sensitivity to gloss changes was reduced. These findings suggest that image metrics such as VDP can not only predict sensitivity to material changes within a scene, but can be a useful tool for predicting bias and sensitivity across asymmetric scene conditions.

title: Beyond Vision: How Sound Shapes Predictions of Material Dynamics
affiliations: 1. Middle East Technical University (TR)
abstract: Humans effortlessly infer the physical behavior of the things around them without formal knowledge of physics, a capacity described as “intuitive physics”. While this internal physical engine relies primarily on visual input, its multisensory foundations remain underexplored. Here, we examined how observers predict materials’ dynamic behaviors using audiovisuals of real-world materials, and whether material sounds modulate these judgments. In two experiments, participants predicted material behavior across five categories (fine granular, coarse granular, metals, hard metals, fluids). In Experiment 1, participants (n = 30) rated silent videos in 120 trials:  15 (materials) × 2 (exploratory behaviors: shaking, pouring) × 4 (dynamic behaviors: piling, splattering, spreading, and resting). Experiment 2 (n = 23) used the same design but included congruent and incongruent natural material sounds. Results revealed a systematic effect of material structure on participants’ predictions of material dynamics regardless of the sound condition. As the particle size of materials increased from fine to coarse granulars to metals and hard materials, piling up ratings consistently decreased, whereas splattering predictions increased. Fluids deviated from this trend, unsurprisingly receiving the highest ratings for splattering and the lowest for piling up. Fluids were also predicted to spread the most, followed by hard materials, granulars, and metals. Predictions for resting showed less consistent structure. Presenting the material sounds influenced judgments in a selective manner, affecting specific material dynamics (e.g., reliably increasing splattering ratings of fluids, piling up of hard materials and fine granulars, resting of metals and coarse granulars) rather than producing a general shift in ratings across conditions. Our findings support an overall visual reliance for predicting materials’ behavior, while suggesting that sounds can enhance material-specific inferences under certain conditions. Ongoing work isolating auditory signals will further clarify the independent and combined contributions of sensory modalities to material-related intuitive physics.

title: Seeing Materials from Sparse Motion: The Role of Configurational Information
affiliations: 1. JLU Giessen (DE)
abstract: Motion alone can evoke vivid impressions of materials, even in the absence of texture, color, or surface information. This is well demonstrated by dynamic dot materials (DDMs), displays that depict materials using only a few dots attached to or embedded within a moving object. However, it remains unclear which features of these displays our visual system extracts to infer material.  DDMs carry three potentially informative cues: global shape, conveyed by the overall configuration of moving dots, local motion, conveyed by the trajectories of individual dots, and relative motion, conveyed by the dynamic configurational relations among neighboring dots. We tested the contributions of global shape and local motion in a separate study. Here, we target relative motion by manipulating dot density and by scrambling the dot configuration within DDMs. Lowering dot density reduces the amount of available relative motion and weakens the shape information in the display. Scrambling dots completely disrupts this configurational information. We rendered DDMs at five density levels ranging from low to high, depicting materials from five different categories (smoke, liquid, jelly, rigid-breakable, and fabric). For each animation, we rendered an original and a scrambled version (representative stimuli: https://tinyurl.com/dynamic-dot-materials). 125 observers viewed these animations and classified them as depicting independent motion, structured motion, or recognizable material. Our results show that intact DDMs were frequently perceived as materials even at low to medium density, whereas scrambled DDMs were rarely perceived as materials, despite sharing identical motion statistics. Increasing the dot density in intact condition shifted the probability of responses from independent motion to material percept. This suggests that the visual system relies on configurational dynamics of moving dots to infer material from sparse motion. Increasing the dot density increases the reliability with which configurational relations and shape information can be recovered, thereby aiding the perception of material from motion.

title: Skin parameters predict individual differences in surface pleasantness
affiliations:
1. Center for Tactile Internet Human in the Loop, Dresden University of Technology (DE)
2. Chair of Psychology of Learning and Instruction, Dresden University of Technology (DE)
3. INM - Leibniz-Institute for New Materials (DE)
abstract: Perceptual judgements of physical objects and their properties, such as the smoothness of fuzzy skin of a peach, are typically highly consistent across individuals, whereas affective evaluations (e.g., pleasantness) tend to be more divisive. While previous work has linked such variability to prior experience and dispositional factors, the potential contribution of individual differences in skin properties remains largely underexplored. This is notable given the established role of skin parameters in shaping the perception of haptic features.  To fill this gap, we conducted a study in which 56 participants explored surfaces varying in physical roughness (18.3, 25.8, 46.2, 58.5, 125, 269, 425 µ) using their index finger and rated perceived roughness and pleasantness in counterbalanced sessions. Skin hydration and elasticity were measured prior to and after each session. Expectedly, participants were able to discern different roughness levels as indicated by the increase in perceived roughness with increasing physical roughness. Next, we modelled pleasantness ratings of participants as a function of physical roughness using linear and quadratic functions. In the quadratic group, pleasantness varied minimally across small differences in roughness but showed stronger changes across wider ranges of roughness. Interestingly, for some individuals, pleasantness was highest at the intermediate roughness levels.  Model comparison based on the Bayesian Information Criterion (ΔBIC > 2) was used to classify participants into two groups. This resulted in an even number of participants assigned to each response profile. Individuals exhibiting a quadratic relationship between roughness and pleasantness showed significantly higher skin hydration both before and after the pleasantness session. Similarly, these individuals showed a greater skin elasticity, although this difference was observed only prior to the pleasantness session. Together, these group differences suggest that people with more hydrated and elastic skin tend to have higher pleasantness thresholds when exploring rough surfaces.

title: Hearing Softness: Pitch and Temporal Qualities of Sounds Influence Material Perception
affiliations: 1. Middle East Technical University (TR)
abstract: Material perception emerges from the integration of multiple sensory modalities, and it is increasingly understood that sound-symbolic words can elicit particularly vivid material impressions, especially when they are presented spoken. At the same time, a growing body of work shows that prosodic variation in speech systematically shapes how people perceive and evaluate objects, actions, and affective states, yet its role in material perception remains largely unexplored. For instance, it is unclear whether prosodic variation alone can alter representations of material quality. To test this, we conducted three psychophysical experiments using a two-interval forced-choice paradigm to examine how pitch and temporal rate influence perceived material qualities. Participants selected which of the two sounds better matched material-related adjectives that capture core softness dimensions, such as wetness, roughness, granularity, surface softness, and compliance. In Experiment 1 (N=31), manipulations were applied to Turkish sound-symbolic words. Robust, dimension-specific effects emerged: pitch modulated judgments of heaviness, silkiness, and wetness, whereas temporal rate influenced judgments of heaviness and roughness, demonstrating systematic effects of prosody in perceived material qualities. In Experiment 2 (N=31), the same manipulations were applied to natural material sounds. Similar but weaker effects were observed, suggesting that prosody, in a broader sense, can influence material perception beyond language, though to a lesser extent. In Experiment 3 (N=24), pitch and temporal manipulations were applied to pure tones (beeps) as a non-verbal control. No consistent trends emerged, indicating that low-level acoustic variation alone is insufficient to elicit patterns of judgment in material perception. Together, these findings suggest that prosodic characteristics of verbal and non-verbal signals modulate perceived material properties through interactions with semantic and sensory context, and provide new evidence for the context-dependent nature of multisensory material representations.

title: Distinct ERP subtypes generalize across tasks and observers and are associated with endogenous EEG fluctuations, not stimulus encoding
affiliations:
1. Lausanne University Hospital (CH)
2. Lausanne University (CH)
3. The Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
abstract:
Human perception and behavior exhibit structured fluctuations over time, often interpreted
as reflecting latent internal states. Such states can be derived from both behavioral and neural
data, typically yielding a small number of recurring patterns, some of which generalize across
tasks. However, the relationship between behaviorally and neurally defined states remains
unclear, as neural states show inconsistent associations with behavior. Here, we addressed
three questions using a multitask EEG dataset (face and motion detection VEPCON) and a
trial-clustering approach applied to single-trial ERPs. We tested whether neural states (1)
recur across tasks, (2) reflect differences in stimulus processing, and (3) are associated with
prestimulus activity. Clustering revealed two states in each task. A state classifier trained in
one task generalized to the other, indicating that at least one state recurs across tasks with a
stable topography. Despite marked differences in ERP morphology, we found no evidence for
differences in stimulus processing: decoding, ERP components (e.g., N170), and mixed-model
analyses showed no consistent effects of state. In contrast, states were reliably associated with
differences in prestimulus EEG activity, particularly in the location and magnitude of alpha
bursts. Overall, these results suggest that neural states identified via trial clustering can
generalize across tasks but are primarily linked to endogenous prestimulus fluctuations rather
than differences in stimulus-related processing.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Evaluating Linear-Quadratic-Gaussian Models of Continuous Psychophysics Across Mouse- and Eye-Tracking Datasets
affiliations:
1. School of Psychology, University of Southampton (UK)
2. Laboratoire des Systèmes Perceptifs, CNRS, ENS, PSL University (FR)
3. Department of Psychology, New York University (US)
4. Institute of Psychology, Centre for Cognitive Science, Technical University of Darmstadt (DE)
5. Department of Engineering, Cambridge University (UK)
abstract: Continuous psychophysics is a successful paradigm  to estimate visual functions (Bonnen et al., 2015): using a target-tracking task, harder-to-see targets are tracked less faithfully. Tracking performance can be quantified from the peak, lag, and width of the cross-correlation between target and tracking velocities, but these measures are intercorrelated. Fitting a Kalman filter model to the tracking data yields a single observation-noise parameter, but, like cross-correlation parameters, it conflates perception with motor and cognitive factors. To address this issue, we fitted a Linear-Quadratic-Gaussian (LQG) model (Straub & Rothkopf, 2022) to estimate separate parameters for visual noise, motor noise, and cognitive costs. We analysed five datasets (Bonnen et al.’s original dataset plus four in-house datasets pooled N=27) spanning mouse- and eye-tracking, with manipulations of visual and motor noise. LQG parameter estimates differed in magnitude between mouse- and eye-tracking datasets. Across the mouse-tracking data, intercorrelations between cross-correlation parameters and the visual noise parameter from the LQG model suggested that the visual noise parameter provided a reliable summary index of cross-correlation metrics (peak–noise: r=−0.32 lag–noise: r=0.44 width–noise: r=0.31 all p<.001). Eye-tracking data largely replicated this pattern (peak–noise: r=−0.34 lag–noise: r=0.47 all p<.05), with one exception: the relationship between width and visual noise was reversed (r=−0.27, p<.05). Surprisingly, despite these intercorrelations, the visual noise, motor noise, and cognitive costs parameters extracted from the LQG model did not consistently track the experimental manipulations of visual and motor noise imposed in our in-house datasets. Overall, our findings indicate that the LQG framework is promising and can be applied to different types of tracking data and experimental manipulations. However, our results also motivate extending the framework to incorporate more sophisticated models of motor control and decision making, to better partition tracking performance into perceptual, motor, and cognitive components.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Temporal Dynamics of Structural and Semantic Information During Visual Neural Decoding
affiliations: 1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
abstract: According to visual hierarchy theory, when we perceive an image, we first detect its contours and edges before accessing the high-level semantic content of the image. While this processing hierarchy is well established in the literature, the precise EEG time points at which structural and semantic information become separately decodable remain unclear. To address this gap, we investigated the temporal dynamics of structural, object-level, and semantic visual information decoding from human EEG recordings. We used the THINGS-EEG2 dataset containing EEG recordings from 10 participants viewing 16,540 unique object images. For each image, we computed seven visual target representations spanning the processing hierarchy. Full-image and background-removed visual embeddings were obtained using CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training), a vision-language model that encodes images into a rich semantic embedding space. For structural representations, we first extracted edge maps using DexiNed, a deep edge detection network. Rather than encoding these edge maps with CLIP, which we found produces nearly identical embeddings for all edge maps regardless of content, we instead applied HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients), that captures local gradient orientations directly from pixel values, yielding highly discriminative structural embeddings.Semantic embeddings were generated from BLIP-2 captions at scene and object levels. Separate MLP decoders were trained across six non-overlapping windows (0–800ms) and evaluated using zero-shot retrieval. Preliminary results show that decoding accuracy peaks between 100 and 300ms after stimulus onset. Structural HOG features show a directional advantage in early windows (100–200ms) relative to semantic targets, providing initial support for a temporal hierarchy, though the separation remains modest. Background context contributes minimally to decoding, with isolated object and full image conditions tracking almost identically. By the time of the conference, we aim to refine our decoding pipeline to further isolate these temporal stages, providing stronger empirical support for a hierarchical account of visual processing.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Retinotopic specificity of the perceptual effects of focused transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the primary visual cortex
affiliations:
1. University of Plymouth (UK)
2. University of Iceland (UK)
abstract: Non-invasive magnetic and electrical stimulation have been extensively used to investigate the causal role of visual areas in perception, yet their focal resolution remains insufficient to effectively dissociate neighbouring but functionally distinct regions of the visual cortex. Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) presents a novel opportunity to modulate neural activity of sub-regions within the early visual cortex with millimetre precision. While the neuromodulatory effects of TUS have been demonstrated by sonicating broad regions of the primary visual cortex (V1), the perceptual effects and spatial specificity of TUS within V1 remain unexplored. Here, we investigate whether TUS targeting a retinotopically defined sub-region of V1 produces a change in perception at a predicted location in visual space. Using structural and functional MRI, we create individualised full-field retinotopic maps by fitting population receptive field models and combining them with a surface-based Bayesian prior. We then model the acoustic propagation of ultrasound into retinotopically labelled V1 and project these results into visual space, allowing us to identify an ‘active’ location predicted to receive the highest acoustic intensity, therefore the strongest perceptual effects, and a nearby ‘control’ location in V1 predicted to receive negligible acoustic energy. Participants then complete a two-alternative forced-choice orientation discrimination task during neuronavigated TUS to V1, with stimuli presented at either the ‘active’ or ‘control’ location on each trial. TUS trials are interleaved with sham trials, accounting for TUS auditory confounds, in a double-blind design. We hypothesise TUS will produce measurable changes in orientation discrimination performance restricted to the ‘active’ visual location predicted by our modelling. Pilot results are expected at the time of this poster presentation. In characterising the spatial specificity of TUS perceptual effects, this approach establishes a framework for future studies to dissociate the causal contributions of early visual areas to perception at an unprecedented scale for non-invasive neuromodulation.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Suggestions that there is no visual binding problem ignore evidence
affiliations: 1. The University of Queensland (AU)
abstract: The visual binding problem refers to an apparent need to integrate information concerning different types of visual feature from signals spread across functionally specialised regions of cortex. In a seminal ECVP keynote address, Peter Lennie argued that the visual binding problem does not exist, as visual neurons tend to encode for multiple visual features in tandem, so there is no need to recombine the products of specialised visual analyses. Subsequent review articles have reiterated these arguments, and have reasserted that there is no visual binding problem. But these arguments have ignored key evidence of situations where the perceptual binding of colours and of movements fails, and where the wrong combinations of colour and of movement can become bound in perception. In this presentation I will demonstrate two such situations, and another two situations where specialised components of the human visual system promote different experiences of a stimulus that do not cohere, but rather engage in a perceptual rivalry. I will also point out that arguments against the existence of a visual binding problem have mis-characterised evidence of links between selective visual deficits and focal brain damage. Lennie’s contribution to vision science was seminal. It led to evidence suggesting that the visual binding problem is not the same problem that was once envisaged. However, ignoring evidence that substantiates the existence of occasionally erroneous perceptual binding processes will not make the binding problem go away. It would just mean that models and theoretical accounts of human vision are only partially informed
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Shape-based Figure-Ground Organization in Vision Transformers
affiliations:
1. University of Toronto (CA)
2. Vector Institute (CA)
3. McGill University (CA)
4. UC Irvine (US)
abstract: Separating figure from ground is a fundamental aspect of perceptual organization. In the human visual system, figure-ground organization has been shown to rely on several shape-based cues such as surroundedness, convexity and symmetry. Early deep neural networks trained for object recognition, on the other hand, have been shown to strongly rely on texture information. Recent work suggests that this texture-bias might be overcome by Vision Transformers, and in particular, by large self-supervised models, in which object-centric perceptual organization  appears to emerge without the need for human labels. In this work, we systematically test a broad range of Vision Transformers for their ability to use shape-based cues for figure-ground organization. To this end, we fit linear probes to predict figure-ground assignment from intermediate representations, both for natural images, and for three sets of controlled stimuli where only surroundedness, convexity and symmetry are valid cues. Our results show that several Vision Transformers are able to use shape cues for figure-ground organization. Moreover, for some of these models, figure-ground probes trained on natural stimuli generalize to synthetic stimuli that isolate individual cues. In summary, our study demonstrates the ability of Vision Transformers to learn shape-based cues from the statistics of natural images. For some models, the link between figure-ground segregation and shape properties further reflects known biases of human visual perception. Understanding the internal processing of these models in greater detail is thus a promising future direction for studying the mechanisms of perceptual organization in human visual perception.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Why the information capacity of visual working memory cannot be measured in bits
affiliations:
1. University of Cambridge (UK)
2. University of Zagreb (HR)
abstract: The fidelity with which visual features can be recalled declines with the number of items represented in working memory, implying a limit on the brain's capacity for storing visual information. In the context of information theory, the process of storing and retrieving memories has been characterized as transmission of information through a noisy channel. If the channel capacity is fixed (e.g. to N bits) the ability to reconstruct a set of stored features will decrease in a predictable manner with set size. To assess this prediction, we developed a novel method based on the mutual information between stimuli and responses in cued recall tasks. In a crucial advance, this method accounts for the presence of “swap errors”, where one of the non-cued items is reported, which would otherwise distort information estimates. Applying our method to new and existing experimental data reveals a non-linear relationship between mutual information and share of capacity that is inconsistent with encoding in a fixed number of bits. We further show that the mutual information varies across feature dimensions, and with changes in stimulus range, in ways that are not predicted by a fixed capacity channel and cannot be accounted for by differences in perceptual acuity. While the information theoretic prediction assumes encoding can be flexibly reconfigured to make optimal use of a channel’s capacity, our observations instead match predictions of a relatively inflexible sample-based encoding mechanism, which we argue is consistent with the constraints imposed by the biology of the visual system. These findings are relevant to current debates about working memory recruitment of sensory cortex, and re-coding of visual information into more abstract mnemonic formats.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Biases in orientation perception reflec­t sparse predictive coding rather than Bayesian inference
affiliations: 1. Cardiff University (UK)
abstract: Early vision is frequently characterised as Bayesian inference. For instance, natural scenes are dominated by horizontal and vertical orientations (‘cardinals’). The visual system is hypothesised to incorporate this environmental regularity as a prior, potentially implemented via the preponderance of V1 neurons tuned to cardinals relative to oblique orientations. While this framework has successfully driven research, inconsistencies have emerged. Brain-decoding studies demonstrate that the neural representation of orientation is biased toward cardinals, which Bayesian models account for via the prior. Yet psychophysical studies report biases away from cardinals, which Bayesian models informed by efficient coding explain via likelihood asymmetry. No extant model, however, can account for attractive neural and repulsive behavioural biases concurrently. Here, we reconcile these inconsistencies. Using MEG-decoding in human observers, we manipulate stimulus precision via contrast, and find neural biases towards cardinals. Critically, bias is greater for high- than for low-precision stimuli. This pattern is incompatible with the effect of an orientation-prior, but can account for repulsive psychophysical biases. Unlike neural decoding, psychophysical measurements are necessarily relative, involving comparison of stimuli. The larger attractive bias we decode for high- compared to low-contrast stimuli should thus manifest behaviourally as a (seemingly) repulsive bias. Consistent with this notion, psychophysical testing in the same observers revealed biases away from cardinals when matching orientations of low- and high-contrast stimuli. We reproduce this pattern of neural and behavioural biases in-silico using a sparse predictive-coding network. Our network performs inference over image contents holistically, rather than over isolated features such as orientation. When trained on natural images, it spontaneously develops V1-like receptive fields with non-homogeneous orientation-tuning preferences. This non-homogenous tuning, together with sparsity-inducing lateral inhibition, is the key mechanism underpinning the bias pattern. Overall, our findings are inconsistent with Bayesian accounts of early vision, but provide novel mechanistic insight, reconciling psychophysical and neuroimaging results.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Bridging Computational Models, Brain Activity, and Behaviour: A Python Toolbox for Advanced RSA
affiliations:
1. University of Leeds (UK)
2. Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (IT)
3. University of Edinburgh (UK)
4. Columbia University (US)
5. Harvard University (US)
6. Mount Sinai (US)
7. Université de Montréal (CA)
8. Western University (CA)
abstract:
Understanding visual processing requires connecting complex computational models, such as deep neural networks, to large-scale neural and behavioral datasets. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) provides a central framework for this by allowing vision scientists to compare representational geometries across brains, computational models, and behavior. However, mapping high-dimensional vision models to noisy biological data presents distinct statistical challenges.

To address these challenges, we introduce rsatoolbox, an open-source Python library implementing recent methodological advances in RSA. The toolbox provides improved dissimilarity estimators, including cross-validated distances that eliminate the positive bias caused by measurement noise, alongside a novel Poisson symmetrized-KL divergence designed to specifically handle the variance of neural spiking data. Furthermore, it offers advanced comparators for Representational Dissimilarity Matrices (RDMs). These include whitened metrics to account for correlated errors in fMRI or M/EEG data, and a computationally efficient rank correlation coefficient (Kendall’s \\rho_a) for evaluating model architectures.

Crucially, rsatoolbox establishes a rigorous inferential framework for evaluating visual models. It implements a two-factor bootstrap procedure that enables inferences to confidently generalize across both independent subjects and distinct visual stimuli simultaneously. The package also features visualization tools, such as multidimensional ‘model maps’, to clearly communicate complex pairwise comparisons between candidate vision models and neural data. By integrating with the broader Python neuroscience ecosystem, rsatoolbox equips vision scientists with a standardized, robust platform to explore neural geometries across fMRI, M/EEG, spiking, and behavioral data, supporting the discovery of the computational mechanisms underlying visual perception.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: When (timing) is determining visual system organization
affiliations:
1. Bar-Ilan University (IL)
2. UCL (UK)
abstract: The dominant role of any sensory system is to allow the organism to sense its environment (“NOW”), plan its potential (re)action according to its goals given the current surroundings and events (“SOON”), and learn (acquire knowledge) from current experiences for the future (“LATER”). While these are critical for survival (whether the organism is standstill, moving slowly or extremely fast through its environment), the prevailing model of human visual system organization mainly concerns and is mainly based on data from organisms that are located in one place in their environment. Thus, the temporal relevance of visual information for the behaving organism has been critically overlooked. In fact, the speed at which we move through the environment probably dictates and qualitatively changes “the what” and “the where” our visual system is tuned to (e.g. when running or driving but not when seated - information very far from us becomes highly relevant to our survival as our body may approach it very soon). I assume timing is the key factor determining what and where the visual system would be most sensitive to. Therefore, I propose a novel overarching comprehensive visual system organization framework that addresses the prevailing model’s limitations. The novel framework suggests the visual system is composed of 3 main visual pathways, each revolving around a pivotal egocentric time range: the “now” pathway (processing all the visual changes happening now across the visual field, mostly visual motion), the “soon” pathway (processing all visual information that may likely be relevant in the next 3s, today’s dorsal/”where”/”how” pathway), and the “later” pathway (processing information that may be relevant later on, today’s ventral/”what” pathway). I will follow this with multiplicity of predictions stemming from this model and highlight outstanding questions for new directions of research.
session_title: Poster Session 2 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Gallery of Fakes: An Eye-tracking Investigation of How Perceived Inauthenticity Impacts the Aesthetic Appreciation of Faces vs. Artworks
affiliations: 1. University of Toronto (CA)
abstract: Is an object any less beautiful just because it is a fake? Authenticity status can have a rather complex and multifaceted effect on the aesthetic perception of various stimulus categories. Previous work has shown that copies and forgeries of paintings tend to receive lower monetary and aesthetic evaluations compared to the original artwork (Locher et al., 2015 Rabb et al., 2018), whereas faces with makeup or plastic surgery tend to elicit lower social/moral judgments, but are not penalized in aesthetic ratings compared to natural faces (Liang et al., 2023). These findings highlight a point of potential nuance in the aesthetic appreciation of inauthentic stimuli, modulated by the stimulus type. However, there has yet to be any work directly comparing the costs of “fake beauty” in artworks versus faces, despite the substantial parallels in their social implications (e.g., greater monetary profits through the misrepresentation of identity). As such, we implemented an eye-tracking paradigm to characterize the aesthetic and oculomotor signatures of perceived authenticity status. Participants were first primed with a label corresponding to a high (faces = natural, paintings = original), medium (faces = makeup, paintings = copy), or low authenticity status (faces = plastic surgery, paintings = forgery), and were then shown an image of a human face or still-life painting. Their free-viewing eye movements were recorded during the stimulus presentation period, and they were subsequently asked to rate the image on their familiarity, liking, impressiveness, and desire to engage with it. The results of this experiment will contribute novel insights into the cognitive impact of perceived authenticity on the aesthetic appreciation of faces versus artworks, providing a holistic view into the psychophysiological effects of “fake beauty” and revealing possible consequences associated with modern image manipulation in contexts such as advertising, news, social media, and entertainment.

title: Designing resilient cities: Greenery, rectilinearity, and sociality as key factors in aesthetic preferences
affiliations:
1. Univ. Grenoble Alpes, Univ. Savoie Mont Blanc, CNRS, LPNC (FR)
2. Campbell Family Mental Health Research Institute, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CA)
3. Université Clermont Auvergne, CNRS, LAPSCO, CHU Clermont-Ferrand (FR)
abstract: Urban nature-based solutions are increasingly recognized for their role in climate change adaptation however, their success also depends on their visual appeal, which can influence public acceptance and engagement. This study investigates how visual features—specifically building shape, presence of greenery, and cues of sociality—affect aesthetic evaluations of architecture, drawing on principles from neuroaesthetics and visual perception research. Forty-three participants (41 females, Mage =20.93, SDage =4.34, ages 18–44) were divided into three experimental groups (positive or negative semantic information, and control) and asked to rate the aesthetics of buildings varying in perceived shape, greenery, and sociality using a visual analogue scale. Results showed a preference for rectilinear forms, the inclusion of greenery, and higher sociability cues, with a notable interaction between building shape and greenery. Semantic information did not significantly influence aesthetic ratings. These findings underscore the role of visual cues and their interactions in shaping environmental aesthetic preferences, offering insights for both architectural design and future research on visual perception in urban environments.

title: Aesthetically Reframing the Unwanted: Perceptual Modulation of Evaluative Judgments for Negatively Connoted Medical Stimuli
affiliations: 1. University of Bamberg (DE)
abstract: Medical assistive devices are strongly associated with negative affective priors, providing a useful test case for examining how perceptual and multisensory factors modulate evaluative judgments under biased conditions. We investigated whether systematic variation in visual presentation, spatial context, and haptic access alters the perceptual representation of ostomy products along dimensions of aesthetics, ergonomics, and activity-related affordances. Across two experiments, we combined continuous spatial arrangement paradigms with forced-choice psychophysics and eye tracking. In Experiment 1, participants arranged physical products along adjective-defined continua (e.g., beautiful–ugly, dynamic–static, user-friendly–complicated) under visual-only versus visuo-haptic conditions, enabling the extraction of perceptual scaling functions and cross-dimensional structure. In Experiment 2, participants performed paired-comparison judgments on images of products presented on the body (frontal vs. lateral viewpoints), while gaze behavior was recorded to assess attentional allocation and feature weighting. Results show that evaluative judgments are systematically modulated by low- and mid-level perceptual cues, despite strong negative priors. Contextualized body presentations shift judgments toward increased perceived normality and activity compatibility, particularly for lateral views that reduce canonical object salience. Products exhibiting features consistent with everyday object categories (e.g., textile-like appearance) are mapped closer to positive regions in perceptual space, suggesting category-based predictive influences. Visuo-haptic integration selectively enhances judgments along ergonomics-related dimensions, indicating modality-specific weighting in multidimensional evaluation. Eye-tracking data reveal that attentional selection is biased toward features diagnostic for category reclassification, supporting a predictive processing account in which perceptual inference minimizes conflict between sensory input and prior expectations. These findings demonstrate that evaluative representations of negatively connoted objects are plastic and context-dependent, and can be systematically shifted through controlled manipulation of perceptual variables. The study provides a framework to reframe an entire product sector such a medical assistive devices.

title: Quantifying Beauty – Comparing the results of ratings and pairwise comparisons
affiliations: 1. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: In most empirical aesthetic research, data on the aesthetic appeal of stimuli is obtained by asking participants to rate them on a Likert scale, requiring them to indicate, for example, their perceived beauty on a scale from 1 (not at all beautiful) to 7 (very beautiful). This rating method has many advantages, as it is easy to implement and allows multiple dimensions of an aesthetic impression to be evaluated simultaneously. Pairwise comparison on the other hand can be useful when small effect sizes are at play or individual differences are of interest. In two studies, we compared the two methods and investigated (a) whether measuring aesthetic judgments using both methods yields comparable results and (b) how stable the individual aesthetic judgments are over time for the two methods. In the first study, we compared judgments of the beauty of chair images repeating each judgment ten times. The beauty assessments obtained using the two methods were very similar. Furthermore, regardless of method, repeated measurements within participants were strongly correlated, suggesting that their perception of beauty is consistent and does not change substantially over time. In contrast to this, taste typicality, the correlation between one participant and the leave-one-out average of all other participants, was only moderately positive on average, indicating a wide range of opinions. In the second study, we tested whether these results would generalize to other stimuli by using abstract artworks. Similar results were obtained, except for even lower values of taste typicality in ratings between participants. In summary, this systematic comparison of the two evaluation methods provides insight into their respective advantages and disadvantages, which will be discussed in the poster.

title: What can visual perceptual sensitivity tell us about individual differences in appreciation?
affiliations: 1. KU Leuven (BE)
abstract: To what extent can differences in how we visually perceive images and patterns explain differences in how we appreciate them? In this study, we assessed individuals’ pairwise preferences for image pairs within five different sets (images of paintings, abstract patterns, natural scenes, photographs of neatly organized compositions, and natural textures) at two timepoints (two months apart). For 253 participants, we also measured threshold-level sensitivity for differences in lightness, chroma, hue, shape, orientation, and size using interleaved staircases, for two reference values per feature dimension. Moreover, participants completed several questionnaires to characterize their perceptual and aesthetic processing abilities and experience (incl. VAIAK, VAST-R). Preliminary analyses indicate that individual differences in perceptual sensitivity were positively correlated across features (r = .01–.44), and that perceptual sensitivity was positively correlated with aesthetic sensitivity as measured with the VAST-R (r = .17–.30). Furthermore, especially orientation and shape sensitivity correlated positively with preferences for order (except for paintings r = .04–.34) and with preferences for complexity in natural scenes (r = .19–.30). Further analyses will dive deeper into modeling the perceptual sensitivity data and explore how different person characteristics, like individual differences in perceptual sensitivity, personality, and art expertise, interconnect in predicting individual differences in aesthetic appreciation across different stimulus sets.

title: Art wins: Higher Valuation Responses to Op Art Compared to Matched Optical Illusions
affiliations:
1. Seoul National University (KR)
2. Korea University (KR)
3. University of Bamberg (DE)
abstract: The question of how we approach visual art differently from non-art has long been of interest in perceptual science and empirical aesthetics. Here, we used two visually similar yet conceptually distinct categories of images to probe this question: Op Art and optical illusions. The former takes inspiration from the latter, but is approached as an object of aesthetic appreciation, whereas the latter is used primarily as a study object in perceptual science. We asked 47 Op Art-naïve participants to review 48 randomized stimuli in a 2×2 design with factors Type (Op Art vs optical illusions) and Color (achromatic vs chromatic). Optical illusions were selected to resemble the Op Art works as closely as possible. Participants reported how much they would be willing to pay for each image. Total viewing time and normalized valuation were analyzed as dependent variables.  A repeated-measures ANOVAs revealed a significant Type × Color interaction for valuation (F(1,45)=6.70, p=.013). The main effect showed that Op Art was valued more highly overall than illusions, but the effect of color reversed across stimulus type: chromatic illusions were valued more highly than achromatic ones, whereas achromatic Op Art was valued more highly than chromatic Op Art. A comparable interaction pattern was also observed for viewing time (F(1,46)=10.39, p=.0023), with correlations between viewing time and valuation positive and similarly strong in all four categories (r >.431). Overall, our results show that Op Art was valued more than illusion stimuli, despite the broad visual similarity between the two categories. At the same time, the robust positive correlations indicate that valuation and viewing engagement are closely linked across stimulus categories. Our findings constitute a first step into exploring the features of Op Art in perceptual science with future work diving into comparison of computational descriptors.

title: Eyes-CREAM: From Eyes to Compositional Relations—An Esthetic Annotation Model
affiliations: 1. KU Leuven (BE)
abstract: Artistic composition plays a vital role in aesthetic appreciation. Even when individual elements are visually appealing, a poor spatial organization can diminish the overall aesthetic quality of an artwork. While effective composition can enhance aesthetic appeal, the concept of composition remains abstract and difficult to quantify. To bridge the gap between objective metrics and subjective appreciation, we hypothesize that humans process composition by spontaneously establishing the spatial relations between different image regions. This internal structure can be extracted in the form of contours by analyzing their gaze patterns. Moving beyond basic photographic rules (such as the rule of thirds, central emphasis, or the presence of leading lines), this project introduces a model to automatically extract “compositional annotation” contours from viewer gaze patterns. These annotation contours capture both the relationships among visual elements and the higher-level geometric structure emerging from them. We used an eye tracking dataset comprising 40 photographs and 40 paintings with strong composition, viewed by 43 participants. The eye-movement data are first processed using an edge bundling algorithm. Then, each visual stimulus is divided into small grids to extract localized directional flow vectors. Using Gestalt principles of proximity and good continuation, prominent flow vectors are interpolated to generate the final annotation contours. Initial results indicate that the model successfully generates meaningful compositional contours from eye movement data. Future work will validate the annotated composition contours against expert annotations. By transforming the abstract artistic concept of composition into concrete mathematical contours, this work bridges human perception and computational aesthetics as a step towards human-like machine evaluation and perhaps even generation of visual aesthetics.

title: Physical Plausibility, Animacy, and Pleasantness in Bouncing Motion
affiliations:
1. Department of General Psychology, Univeristy of Padova (IT)
2. Department of Social, Political and Cognitive Sciences, University of Siena (IT)
abstract: Bouncing is a perceptually rich event in which an object falls under gravitational acceleration and collides with a rigid surface. Across four experiments, we examined how the physical parameters of a bouncing event influence judgments of physical plausibility, perceived animacy, and motion pleasantness. Experiments 1 and 2 showed that bounces with a physically plausible coefficient of restitution (C ≤ 1) were judged as more physically plausible and less animate than bounces violating energy conservation (C > 1). Moreover, motions consistent with gravitational acceleration (i.e., uniformly accelerated or decelerated) were perceived as more physically plausible than motions with constant velocity. Physically implausible bounces were not only judged as more animate, but also as more pleasant, indicating a positive association between animacy and pleasantness. However, pleasantness was strongly modulated by kinematic structure: bounces with uniform acceleration or deceleration were rated as more pleasant than constant-velocity bounces, despite this factor having little impact on perceived animacy. Experiment 3 showed that this effect cannot be reduced to familiarity, as it persisted when the motion was rotated by 180 degrees. Finally, Experiment 4, using eye-tracking, suggests that this effect may be driven by perceptual fluency: uniformly accelerated or decelerated motions are more predictable and easier to track. Overall, the findings highlight the interplay between physical plausibility, perceived animacy, and motion pleasantness in the perception of dynamic events.

title: Perceptual and Aesthetic Sensitivity to Systematically Manipulated Image Composition
affiliations: 1. KU Leuven (BE)
abstract:
Image Composition is said to influence human preference, yet it has rarely been
operationalized and tested empirically in rich images. In this study, we focus on three art-
theoretical principles often mentioned to underlie composition: Balance, Emphasis, and
Repetition. In three online experiments, we directly manipulated and validated them
separately, and tested their effects on aesthetic preference.
Using a mix of generative AI and manual editing, we generated 180 images consisting of 60
motifs (realism and fantasy), with three intensity levels of each Composition principle (less,
base, more). In addition to participants' rankings, we recorded demographic backgrounds, art
interest and knowledge, and the qualitative reasoning behind their choices.
To verify our stimuli, our first Experiment (N=37) had participants rank image triplets from ‘least’ to ‘most’ for each compositional principle. Results from Plackett–Luce (PL) models showed that the manipulations performed as expected in nearly every instance, with only three exceptions. In Experiment 2 (N=152) we asked participants to rank image triplets with the same motif by their compositional quality or personal preference. While both criteria followed the expected patterns of ‘more’ being ranked above the baseline condition and ‘less’ being ranked below it (all PL), composition rankings showed a significantly stronger effect than preference rankings in the ‘more’ condition (Z = 2.05, p = 0.041, Wald-type -test). To further test these effects, Experiment 3 (N=348) utilized a 2AFC design where participants chose between image pairs (across motifs) based on composition or preference. Analysis of item-level worth estimates (PL) indicated that, on average, the experimental manipulation successfully shifted rankings of composition, yet failed to produce a consistent effect on participant preference. Across three experiments, our manipulations consistently influenced participants' rankings and choices regarding image composition but had a much weaker or negligible impact on participants' personal preferences.

title: Does a stabilized image-like visual stimulus disappear?　—Phenomenological investigation of the percept of visual images driven by miniature eye movements—
affiliations:
1. Institute of Arts, School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Shinshu University (JP)
2. Department of Medical Sciences, Faculty of Health and Medical Sciences, Aichi Shukutoku University (JP)
3. Department of Orthoptics, Faculty of Health Sciences, Fukuoka International University of Health and Welfare (JP)
4. Institute of Textile Science and Technology, School of Science and Technology, Shinshu University (JP)
abstract: This study developed a device to present visual stimuli synchronized and coupled with miniature eye movements of flick (microsaccade), drift, and tremor. Using this custom-made device, we presented a stabilized retinal image-like stimulus to investigate changes in the percept of visual images. Eye movements were sampled at 500 Hz, output as analogue data, and input into the device. The attenuation and gain variable frequency filters installed in the presentation device were adjusted according to the characteristics of the three types of miniature eye movements. By activating and/or deactivating these filters individually, the data were transmitted to a presentation screen equipped with 1,024 (32×32) red LEDs (subtended 0.81º×0.81º ), each with a diameter of 2 mm (subtended 1.53’), to generate a stabilized retinal image-like stimulus. When a Necker cube, the letter “HB”, and other figures (e.g., face) were individually presented on a 0.81º×0.81º screen for one minute of observation, the following introspections were reported by nine participants: a) All participants reported that the image generally “became blurred” and disappeared partially b) some perpendicular lines of the Necker cube disappeared and reappeared intermittently c) when luminance of the stimulus was decreased (19.85 to 3.11 cd/m2), the characters “HB” disappeared almost completely and later reappeared d) individual attenuation of flick or drift did not markedly change the percept of the stabilized image e) when tremor was attenuated alone, the percept changed relatively to that of the stabilized image, suggesting that percept of the stabilized image may rely mainly on tremor movement.
