These findings suggest that among the three types of eye movements, tremor may have a greater influence on the percept of the stabilized image, while flick and drift may interact in a supportive manner. Additional studies are required to elucidate the detailed properties and functions of miniature eye movements.

title: Intermittent Utilization of Sensory Input in Human Visuomotor Tracking
affiliations:
1. East China Normal University (CN)
2. Shanghai Jiao Tong University (CN)
abstract: Whether visuomotor control continuously incorporates sensory input or relies on intermittent updates remains debated. While most prior studies naturally assume continuous moment-to-moment integration of incoming information, alternative accounts propose that visuomotor control is primarily driven by intermittent internal predictions, with only occasional input-driven corrections. Here, we analyzed human tracking performances with continuously moving targets using a mixture modeling approach. At each time point, responses were assumed to arise either from a Kalman filter–based tracking process (“update”), in which sensory inputs are incorporated, or from an input-independent state (“no-update”), in which responses are decoupled from current sensory information. A global parameter, termed update sparsity, quantified the proportion of time during which responses were not driven by incoming input. Across four experiments manipulating target color channels and trajectory structure, update sparsity was found to be consistently high (85%–95%) and systematically increase with regularity of the target moving trajectory. This pattern indicates that participants incorporated visual information into motor control only intermittently, relying less on online sensory input when target motion was more predictable. These findings suggest that the contribution of sensory input is dynamically modulated rather than continuously enforced. Together, the results challenge the assumption of continuous sensory integration in visuomotor control and instead support a framework in which control is dominated by internal prediction, with sensory information incorporated in a temporally sparse, intermittent manner. This model also provides a quantitative account of how visuomotor control balances prediction and online sensory input under varying environmental structure.

title: Tool Perception as a Temporally Dynamic Evaluative Process: Evidence From an Eye-Tracking Study
affiliations:
1. University of Trieste (IT)
2. Suor Orsola Benincasa University (IT)
abstract: Recent accounts of tool perception have moved beyond manipulation-based views, proposing that tool processing reflects a dynamic process recently conceptualized as action reappraisal, integrating semantic, mechanical, and sensorimotor information. However, how tools are processed in isolation versus context, how attention is allocated to both tools and objects, and how these processes unfold over time remain unclear. In an eye-tracking study, participants (N = 30) freely observed isolated tools, thematically consistent tool-object pairs, and inconsistent pairs over a 2800 ms time window. Growth Curve Analysis was used to examine (1) the proportion of looking toward functional versus manipulation areas of the tool across all conditions, and (2) the proportion of looking toward the tool versus the object in paired conditions. Visual attention toward tool areas differed across conditions over time. Early attention was mainly focused on functional areas across all conditions. In the isolated condition, however, attention toward the manipulation area already increased within the first 500 ms. Over time, attention shifted toward manipulation areas and stabilized in the consistent and isolated conditions during the late stage. In contrast, the inconsistent condition showed a less linear trajectory, with a late re-engagement of functional areas. Analysis of tool–object dynamics showed that visual exploration systematically started from the object and then shifted toward the tool in both paired conditions. Crucially, attention to the object remained higher in the inconsistent condition across most of the time window. These findings suggest that tool perception unfolds as a temporally dynamic evaluative process. The object appears to define the action problem, whereas the tool constrains how the action can be implemented. When this mapping is unclear, attention to the object remains higher and tool processing returns to earlier evaluative stages. Overall, the results provide support for reasoning-based accounts of tool perception.

title: Mapping a perceptual feature space for transsaccadic object correspondence
affiliations:
1. Sensorimotor learning unit, Department of Psychology, University of Marburg (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior, Universities of Marburg, Giessen, and Darmstadt (DE)
3. Experimental Psychology, Department of Psychology, Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
4. Theoretical Cognitive Science, Department of Psychology, University of Marburg (DE)
abstract:
Peripheral vision is primarily used to select potential targets for further inspection in foveal vision. Across saccades, presaccadic peripheral information must be combined with the matching postsaccadic foveal input. This transsaccadic object correspondence (TOC) is established by using specific features, such as shape, texture, displacement, size, and contrast. While previous studies demonstrated the relevance of individual features, it remains unclear how multiple features are weighted and how they interact in TOC.

To explore TOC in a multidimensional stimulus space, we created a photorealistic ‘fruit morph’ stimulus set. This involved independently morphing an eggplant and an orange along the feature dimensions of texture/color and shape. With 100 steps for each feature, this resulted in a continuous space of 10,000 images. We conducted a postsaccadic target selection task where observers made a horizontal saccade towards a peripheral stimulus object. Perisaccadically, this object was replaced by two vertically displaced candidates, and observers executed a corrective saccade to the candidate perceived as the closest match.

This configuration required at least three stimuli differing in shape/texture coordinates. To determine discriminability thresholds and estimate feature weights for specific correspondence probabilities, we applied an information-theoretic approach for multidimensional adaptive sampling. We maximized the mutual information between model parameters and the expected response in every trial, using a gradient-based optimizer.

We demonstrate that a multidimensional perceptual stimulus space can be mapped based on binary response data from corrective saccades. Even though the stimulus space is continuous, we find that features are not equally weighted in TOC. Instead, texture is twice as important as shape in establishing transsaccadic object correspondence in our stimulus set. This illustrates how multiple object features are integrated and traded off when establishing correspondence across eye movements.

title: From saliency to semantics: a large-scale lifespan study on gaze and scene understanding
affiliations:
1. Experimental Psychology, Justus Liebig University (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior (DE)
abstract: Moment-to-moment gaze shifts are fundamental to exploring complex visual environments in high detail. But what governs the decision of where to look next? While early models emphasized low-level visual saliency, recent evidence suggests that high-level semantic relevance, specifically global scene understanding (SU), is a superior predictor of spatial gaze distribution. To quantify an object’s relevance for SU, we utilized a computational approach recently validated by Murlidaran and colleagues: we automatically generated multiple AI-provided descriptions of a scene, visually blocking every object in turn. For each blocked object we computed the resulting semantic dissimilarity to the description of the original scene using Sentence-BERT embeddings. By mapping these difference scores back onto their corresponding object pixel masks, we generated a map of object weights for global scene understanding. We then compared the gaze patterns from 6,720 participants (ages 5–72) across 40 naturalistic scenes with visual objects including people. By correlating object dwell time distributions with SU maps, automatically generated local meaning maps (DeepMeaning, Hayes and Henderson), and low-level-saliency, we observed two key findings: First, we replicated that SU-relevance is the strongest predictor of gaze behavior, a result that holds across all age groups. Second, while the predictive power of low-level saliency declines during the first two decades of life, the influence of SU-relevance and local meaning maps significantly increases. These results reveal a clear developmental transition from stimulus-driven saliency toward meaning-driven exploration, with global scene understanding emerging as the primary driver of gaze decisions as the visual system matures.

title: Looking back: Individual regression rates during reading covary with returns during scene viewing
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
2. Department of Neuroscience and Behavior, Barnard College (US)
abstract: Eye movements offer a unique window into visual perception and cognitive processes. Research on reading has shown that regressive saccades – eye movements that revisit previously fixated words – are associated with comprehension and reading difficulties such as dyslexia. Nevertheless, regressions can also occur when fluent readers are confronted with simple texts. Our aim was to investigate whether regressions are driven by reading-specific processes or reflect general mechanisms of visual sampling.  Using an individual differences approach, we conducted an eyetracking study with 128 German university students. Participants first read lines from a German encyclopedia for children and completed a multiple-choice comprehension test, confirming that all participants read and understood the lines without problems. Participants then completed a free-viewing task of 200 naturalistic scenes. This allowed us to quantify individual regression rates during reading, as well as return rates – the tendency to move the eyes back to previously fixated objects or regions during scene viewing. The results revealed robust individual differences with high internal consistency for both, the frequency of regressive saccades during reading and return saccades during scene viewing (r = 0.944 for reading and r = 0.930 for scene viewing). Notably, these measures were significantly correlated across participants (r = 0.24, p < .01), suggesting they share overlapping mechanisms. We aim to further explore these mechanisms in ongoing work. Specifically, we hypothesize that both individual regression and return rates are related to poorer executive control of saccades. We therefore predict that participants with higher rates of return and regressive saccades also show a weaker performance in antisaccade tasks. Ultimately, this research could reveal which general mechanisms of visual sampling shape reading and – perhaps – reading-related difficulties.

title: When Minds Wander and Blank: Oculomotor Signatures of Endogenous Distraction
affiliations: 1. University of Verona (IT)
abstract: To an external observer, we may appear fully engaged with the external environment, while our conscious experience is frequently hijacked by self-generated content or by states of mental absence, systematically distracting us from the task at hand. States of Mind Wandering (MW) and Mind Blanking (MB) occur throughout daily experience, with individuals spending 30-50% of waking hours in task-unrelated thoughts. Despite growing recognition, these phenomena are inconsistently conceptualized as endogenous forms of distraction competing with external attentional demands. To address these limitations, we developed a novel paradigm investigating how internally oriented states function as distractors and interact with salient external distractors. We implemented a modified version of Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) with Go/No-Go responses, featuring a saccadic response for all trials and manual response for GO trials. To modulate the emergence of MW and MB, we also included a reverse SART task, in which the ratio between Go and No-Go trials is inverted. Mental states were assessed with the Experience-Sampling method, while eye tracking recorded gaze parameters, allowing us to extract oculomotor measures including saccadic reaction times, spatial accuracy and rate of saccadic omission. While the reverse SART was not effective in modulating the emergence of off-task mental states, we found that both behavioral and oculomotor performance was significantly lower during MW and even more so during MB. In addition, we also discovered an interaction between mental states and the presence of visual distractors, which was significant during MW but not during MB, showing a distinct impact of the distractor during MW. The results of this study contribute to the characterization of frequent off-task mental states by providing objective markers with eye-tracking measures, to better understand how they impact daily functioning.

title: Pre-saccadic attention enhances peripheral object perception regardless of scene-based spatial expectations
affiliations: 1. Univ. Grenoble Alpes, Univ. Savoie Mont Blanc, CNRS, LPNC (FR)
abstract: During visual scene perception, visual acuity is maximal at fixation and decreases with eccentricity. Although pre-saccadic attention has been shown to enhance perception of simple stimuli at eccentric locations, it remains unclear whether this benefit extends to object perception in the context of complex scenes processing and whether it interacts with perceptual effects of context-based predictions. The present study addressed these questions using two gaze-contingent display experiments. Experiment 1 examined whether saccade preparation toward an object improves its perception compared to a saccade toward another location or no saccade. Participants maintained central fixation while covertly attending to scene images. A spatial cue indicated a parafoveal location and specified whether participants should saccade toward it or maintain fixation. The cue could indicate either a target object’s location or another location in the scene. The target object disappeared either when participants initiated a saccade or after a brief delay if they maintained fixation. Participants were then presented with an object, either the target or a distractor absent from the scene, and indicated whether they had previously seen it. Results revealed higher accuracy in trials with a saccade toward the target object than another location or without a saccade. Experiment 2 tested whether this benefit interacts with spatial expectations in the scene context. The cue always pointed to the target object’s location, and the spatial congruence of the object within the scene was manipulated (expected or unexpected location). Participants either performed a saccade toward the cued location or maintained fixation. We again observed higher accuracy when a saccade was made to the target object than when no saccade was initiated. However, this effect was not modulated by the object’s spatial congruence within the scene. Overall, the results demonstrate a robust benefit of pre-saccadic attention for peripheral object perception independently of context-based spatial expectations.

title: Eye tracking metrics for evaluating the cognitive impact of spectacle lens design
affiliations:
1. Carl Zeiss Vision International GmbH (DE)
2. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: With increasing age, our eyes lose the capability to focus on close objects. A common solution for this condition, called presbyopia, are Progressive Addition Lenses (PALs), spectacle lenses with different areas for far and near vision. The gradual change of correction power between these areas unavoidably leads to optical aberrations, causing peripheral blur that can impact performance and cognitive demand in everyday tasks. Changes in pupil size and blink rate have been linked to cognitive load in controlled laboratory tasks, but their validity in more naturalistic settings with gaze and vergence changes remains unclear. Here, we test whether these eye tracking metrics can evaluate the cognitive impact of different PAL designs. Thirty-two experienced PAL wearers performed a pegboard task, a visuomotor near task requiring fine hand-eye coordination. Each participant performed the 3-minute test three times with each of two PAL designs: an optimized PAL, which uses wearer-specific parameters to reduce peripheral blur, and a standard PAL. Both lens pairs were worn in a mobile eye tracker frame. In this within-participant design, we evaluated task performance, subjective cognitive load (NASA-TLX questionnaire) and eye tracking metrics as objective markers for cognitive demand, including mean pupil diameter, pupil size variability, and blink rate. The optimized PAL design significantly improved task performance and reduced subjective cognitive load. While the pupil measures showed no significant differences, blink rate is significantly higher with the improved PAL, indicating reduced cognitive demand. We conclude that pupillometry-based cognitive load markers might be less sensitive in naturalistic tasks with frequent gaze changes. However, blink rate can support the evaluation of the cognitive impact of lens blur. The results underscore the benefit of optimized lens design and suggest blink rate as an objective metric for vision correction solutions.

title: Primed for Action: How Humans Decode Actions from Almost Nothing
affiliations:
1. Newcastle University (UK)
2. University of Surrey (UK)
abstract: Why do humans find actions easy to recognise compared to state-of-the-art machines? While machines struggle with naturalistic egocentric action videos, people can recognise them from minimal spatiotemporal features. We previously identified Minimal Recognisable Configurations (MIRCs) in Epic-Kitchens-100 videos which were correctly (Easy) or incorrectly (Hard) categorised by our computer-vision network. High-level (e.g., active object, active hand) and mid-level (e.g., orientation, motion) critical features for action recognition were determined from these MIRCs. Here we used eye-tracking to converge on critical features and establish whether people’s eye-movements can explain why machines found some actions hard. We further tested whether contextual top-down information can affect people’s performance and eye movements, as machines predominantly use bottom-up information. Participants (N=36) were briefly presented with a static prime image (400ms), then viewed the original or MIRC video and identified the action while eye movements were recorded. Primes were the middle frame of the original video. Objects were removed or the frame was phase-scrambled to progressively reduce contextual information. Normalised Scanpath Saliency (NSS) was used to compare which features predicted where participants looked. Active objects (NSS=1.60) and orientation (NSS=1.16) were the best predictors, outperforming active hands (NSS=0.75). The predictive ability was higher for features in Hard (NSS=0.69) than Easy (NSS=0.51) videos. For priming, unedited primes produced higher accuracy and shorter first fixation durations (78%, 299ms) than phase-scrambled primes when viewing MIRCs (57%, 330ms). Our results suggest that egocentric action recognition is dominated by the active object and edge orientation features. Furthermore, contextual priming facilitates recognition and initial gist extraction, but not further search for visual features. Overall, participants were more likely to fixate critical features for Hard videos and could recognise Easy videos by fixating regions with lower feature activation. Incorporating human strategies such as increased attention to critical features can improve action recognition by machines.

title: Divisive-normalisation improves CNN training efficiency and generalisation
affiliations: 1. University of Luxembourg (LU)
abstract: Deep neural networks exhibit robustness and generalisation issues not seen in humans. They are also less data-efficient learners than humans, requiring considerably more training samples to accurately identify novel exemplars of known categories. Building-in mechanisms to improve generalisation could mitigate both issues by reducing reliance on learning appearance variations from data. We show that a biologically-inspired divisive-normalisation mechanism can improve the generalisation and data-efficiency of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) when trained on ImageNet1k. We implement a novel activation function, HAND (Homeostasis, Accelerating Nonlinearity, Divisive-nomalisation), where the homeostasis is implemented with batch normalisation to keep neurons active, the accelerating nonlinearity is a squaring operation, and divisive-normalisation closely matches the standard formulations and is applied across all channels in each feature map. A ConvNeXt using HAND as the activation function requires 25 training epochs to reach the same accuracy on the test-data as the unmodified model achieves after 200 epochs. Furthermore, when using an equal number of training epochs, HAND produces higher accuracy on the test-set and similar or improved generalisation performance on the common corruptions data, across different CNN architectures trained using a variety of data augmentation techniques. When the volume of training data is reduced and unevenly distributed between classes (Long-tailed ImageNet) the improvements in performance are even larger. Using the ModelvsHuman benchmark to assess generalisation, both in terms of accuracy and consistency with human categorisation decisions, shows HAND is beneficial when the number of parameter updates, or the number of training samples, is limited. These improvements do not come at the cost of a reduced ability to reject samples from unknown classes. On the contrary, out-of-distribution detection is generally improved. HAND can, therefore, reduce the required training time and/or the required volume and variety of training data, helping to reduce the divergence between CNNs and human image classification.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Evaluating Bayesian Representational Similarity Measures between Neural Networks
affiliations: 1. University of Luxembourg (LU)
abstract: Deep learning models are successful models of visual perception, motivating efforts to better understand their internal processing. Although various methods have been proposed to compare representations, it remains unclear which methods one should use. Here, we expand and extensively test BayesCompare, a Bayesian approach based on linear readouts to measure the similarity of network representations. In BayesCompare, the dissimilarity between two representations is computed using a divergence, Bhattacharyya or Kullback-Leibler (KL), or a distance, Jensen-Shannon (JSD), Total Variation, 2-Wasserstein, or Hellinger, between prior predictive distributions. We evaluate BayesCompare in comparison to representational similarity analysis (RSA), GULP, distance correlation, Jaccard similarity and centered kernel alignment using 5 instances each of six ImageNet-trained neural network architectures trained with slightly different recipes. First, we quantify each method's ability to retrieve the corresponding layer from instances of the same architecture with the silhouette score. All tested metrics can discriminate corresponding layers from other layers decently (all silhouette scores ≥ 0.75). However, our KL divergence, Bhattacharyya, and JSD measures yield particularly high scores, showing that BayesCompare can improve layer retrieval over existing methods. Second, because layers transform features incrementally, representational similarity should decrease the more processing steps occur between layers. We quantify how well metrics fulfill this expectation using Kendall's Tau. All divergences within BayesCompare yield very similar results, matching existing methods as well, which sometimes score slightly higher and sometimes slightly lower. Third, we measure the metrics' consistency under different random image sets and set sizes with the intraclass correlation coefficient. All BayesCompare metrics yield highly reliable results even with a set size of 50, while RSA shows the lowest consistency. These results establish BayesCompare as an effective way of measuring representational similarity while being easy and fast to compute and give strong guidance on which variants one should use.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: EZ-SDM: Closed-form estimation of spherical evidence accumulation for three-dimensional perceptual reports
affiliations: 1. Choice Modelling Centre, University of Leeds, Leeds, UK
abstract: Many visual decisions require a continuous directional report in three-dimensional space, including judgements of motion direction and heading. Hyperspherical diffusion models provide a process account of such responses by representing evidence as a multivariate diffusion process that terminates at a spherical boundary. The response is the boundary-hitting direction, while the first-passage time determines decision time. Despite this natural geometry, these models remain difficult to use because parameter estimation usually depends on computationally intensive numerical likelihood methods. We introduce EZ-SDM, a closed-form, moment-based estimator for the three-dimensional spherical diffusion model with a fixed boundary, centrally initiated accumulation, and diffusion scale fixed for identification. The estimator exploits a structural property of the model. Decision time and response direction are independent, response directions follow a von Mises-Fisher distribution on the unit sphere, and the directional distribution and dimensionless timing moments are linked through the same concentration parameter. The mean response vector identifies drift direction and directional concentration. Combining its resultant length with the mean and variance of response time then yields explicit estimates of drift magnitude, boundary radius, and nondecision time. Simulations across a broad parameter range show accurate recovery of the generating parameters and close prediction of the joint response-time and directional distributions. Estimation requires only sample moments and is therefore orders of magnitude faster than numerical likelihood evaluation. Recovery deteriorates mainly when directional concentration is very weak or the number of observations is small, making the estimator's limits transparent. EZ-SDM provides a practical measurement model for continuous three-dimensional perceptual reports. It supports rapid model checking, parameter screening, and initialization of more elaborate hierarchical models, while preserving the spherical geometry of the underlying decision process.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Scaling the Map: Task-Adaptive Assembly Supports Flexible Hierarchical Navigation
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, Sun Yat-sen University (CN)
2. School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences, Peking University (CN)
abstract: While humans navigate hierarchical structures by composing modular sub-maps, the neural architecture supporting this flexibility remains unclear. A resource-rational system faces a fundamental trade-off: integrating all scales into a unified map would impose high metabolic costs and risk interference between global and local coordinates. Alternatively, the brain might maintain representations in a disaggregated format, binding them selectively as task demands dictate. Leveraging a novel hierarchical navigation paradigm, we tested whether the brain implements a dynamic binding mechanism. Using fMRI and representational similarity analysis, we found that the medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) consistently maintained a scale-invariant global scaffold. Critically, the hippocampus (HPC) selectively encoded fine-grained local details only when required, with the strength of this representation predicting individual behavioral accuracy. Rather than being directly integrated into the mOFC scaffold, these modular hippocampal representations were bridged by the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) to enable functional assembly. These findings reveal that compositional cognitive maps are maintained as discrete, modular units, assembled into a functional whole via mPFC-mediated binding—a mechanism that balances representational efficiency with behavioral flexibility.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Bayesian linear encoding to evaluate models on neuroimaging data
affiliations: 1. University of Luxembourg (LU)
abstract: Introduction. Evaluating the similarity of deep neural networks to human brain data is a crucial method to test mechanistic models of cognition. Several methods to perform these evaluations exist, and although each method approaches the problem from a different angle, recent research suggests that available metrics may not be optimal: very different networks achieve similar performance in large scale benchmarks and fitting seems to push network representations to be too similar to discriminate them from each other.  Methods. We evaluate a Bayesian linear encoding model that allows for the computation of brain similarity without explicitly fitting the feature weights by operating on the kernel matrix. To assess the reliability of our method, we calculate the correlation of model rankings between subjects, for our method and other state of the art methods. We use two DNNs in our initial evaluation: ResNet50 and ViT/B-16. Results. Preliminary results show a slightly higher correlation across subjects for our method (mean τ=0.91), than for a frequentist encoding model (mean τ=0.88).  Conclusion. Our proposed method constitutes an interesting addition to existing tools for brain similarity, achieving slightly better results while being much faster to compute and avoiding common steps such as dimensionality reduction and hyper-parameter setting through cross-validation by operating on the model‘s kernel matrix.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Content-specific and raw occipital alpha oscillations serve distinct functional role in predictive visual perception
affiliations: 1. Department of Imaging Neuroscience,  University College London (UK)
abstract: Predictions about future events significantly influence how we process sensory signals. In previous work, we demonstrated that predicted shape representations exhibit oscillatory activity in the alpha band (10–11 Hz) during pre-stimulus intervals. Here, we extended these findings by having participants perform a shape identification task that directly relied on the shape predictions, allowing us to link the neural correlates of prediction to subjective perception. We used magnetoencephalography (MEG) combined with multivariate decoding to examine the content and frequency characteristics of perceptual predictions and relate them to behaviour. The shape identification task involved auditory cues predicting which shape was likely to appear. To make the identification of the shapes challenging, they were embedded in white noise. First, we found that valid prediction cues improved both identification accuracy and reaction times. Signal detection theory analyses revealed that participants were significantly biased toward reporting the predicted shape (i.e., reduced criterion), without a change in sensitivity (i.e., similar d-prime). We replicated our previous finding that predicted shape representations fluctuate in the alpha band (10–11 Hz). Logistic regression analyses further revealed that this content-specific alpha power predicted perceptual biases induced by the predictions. That is, when content-specific alpha power was high, participants were more likely to perceive the predicted shape. In contrast, higher raw sensor-level occipital alpha power was associated with a greater likelihood of reporting the unpredicted shape. These results suggest that content-specific alpha fluctuations and general occipital alpha power serve distinct functions in visual perception. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that sensory predictions are represented in pre-stimulus alpha oscillations and that these oscillatory signals shape how we perceive the world.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Learning-Based Neurodynamical Model of Perception-Action Coupling
affiliations: 1. Hertie Institute, University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: Visual perception and action execution influence each other reciprocally. These bidirectional interactions recruit a wide network of cortical areas. It remains poorly understood how such coupled dynamic neural representations of action perception and control are established by learning. METHODS: We propose a neural model that is based on neural fields that represent visual and motor dynamics. The vision field receives external inputs derived from real image sequences of hand movements, where observed poses are extracted using a deep neural network model. The motor field encodes actions in terms of self-sustained propagating activity and generates the output that drives a hand avatar, thereby enabling closed-loop visuomotor feedback. Connectivity in the neural field model is established through Hebbian learning from sequential and correlated sensorimotor activity. Model behavior is evaluated under conditions matching behavioral experiments in which the congruence between executed and observed actions is systematically varied. RESULTS: After learning, each neural field supports sequential selectivity. The coupling between the visual and the motor field supports synchronous localized activity patterns in both fields. The trained model reproduces several psychophysical results on perception-action interaction within a unified framework. Specifically, the model captures the modulation of visual performance during concurrent motor execution, and higher visual-motor relative-phase variability in the anti-phase than in the in-phase condition. CONCLUSIONS: Our model provides a theoretical account of how coupled dynamic representations for action perception and control can be established by Hebbian learning. It offers predictions about how learning shapes the strength and structure of the coupling between these representations.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Oscillatory and aperiodic neural dynamics jointly organize visual perception over time
affiliations: 1. New York University Abu Dhabi (AE)
abstract: Temporal integration is a fundamental operation in vision, allowing the nervous system to accumulate sensory evidence over brief intervals and maintain stable perception despite internal noise and external uncertainty. A prominent proposal is that rhythmic neural activity in the alpha band (~8–13 Hz) provides a temporal scaffold for perception, with its frequency defining the temporal resolution of perceptual processing. However, empirical evidence remains inconsistent, with debates over mechanisms linking alpha oscillations to perception, potential confounds between detection and integration, and growing recognition that both oscillatory and aperiodic neural dynamics may jointly shape visual temporal processing. To address this challenge, we developed a novel sustained visual integration paradigm designed to minimize detection confounds and account for perceptual bias, combined with resting-state EEG to probe interactions between aperiodic and oscillatory neural dynamics in visual temporal integration. Participants (n = 83) viewed sustained alternating gratings varying in alternation speed, inducing the perception of either two interchanging gratings (segregation) or a fused plaid (integration). Faster individual alpha rhythms predicted higher temporal resolution (i.e., increased segregation), while a steeper aperiodic spectrum (i.e., lower neural noise) predicted a steeper psychometric slope, indicating greater perceptual precision. Individuals with slower alpha frequencies and flatter spectra (i.e., higher neural noise) showed stronger serial dependence on prior judgments, indicating reduced sensory precision and increased weighting of prior experience. Subjective confidence increased with faster alpha rhythms, reflecting the clarity of sensory evidence and its consistency with previous responses. Together, these findings suggest that perceptual interpretation, confidence, and history effects in temporal integration reflect the joint influence of alpha rhythms and aperiodic neural activity. Mechanistically, faster alpha rhythms and lower neural noise may enhance perceptual resolution by generating more precise sampling frames per time unit, leading to finer temporal perception, reduced reliance on prior experience, and greater subjective confidence.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Baseline Visual Capacity Gates the Efficacy of High-Frequency tRNS on Spatial Resolution
affiliations:
1. National Magnetic Resonance Research Center (UMRAM), Bilkent University (TR)
2. Department of Neuroscience, Aysel Sabuncu Brain Research Center, Bilkent University (TR)
3. Neuroscience and Neurotechnology Center of Excellence (NOROM), Department of Anatomy, Faculty of Medicine, Gazi University (TR)
abstract: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) is a promising neuromodulatory approach for altering visual cortical processing, yet findings remain inconsistent regarding how different stimulation frequencies modulate neural mechanisms. These inconsistencies may partly reflect high inter-individual variability, potentially driven by state-dependency and task demands. To address this, we investigated how baseline visual capacity predicts the responsiveness to frequency-specific tRNS. Healthy adults completed demanding orientation discrimination tasks under high-frequency (101-640 Hz), low-frequency (0.1-100 Hz), and sham stimulation over the visual cortex. To capture individual differences in baseline visual state, visual capacity was assessed using a separate contrast detection task. Moving beyond single-point accuracy, visual performances were psychophysically modeled using the complete contrast sensitivity function (CSF), allowing the extraction of specific structural limits, including the spatial frequency at peak sensitivity, the high-frequency cutoff, and integrated-area parameters. Results confirm that tRNS effects were fundamentally state-dependent rather than uniformly facilitatory. Specifically, hf-tRNS improved visual resolution and overall visibility primarily in individuals whose baseline visual states allowed them to benefit from the stimulation, whereas these effects were absent under lf-tRNS. Our findings reveal a distinct mechanistic divergence between frequency ranges, suggesting that hf-tRNS, but not lf-tRNS, selectively interacts with the existing contrast sensitivity profile to refine spatial resolution. We suggest that this frequency-specific engagement potentially reflects the recruitment of fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons, which may lead to enhanced lateral inhibition and improved discrimination. Furthermore, by demonstrating that these effects are gated by baseline visual capacity, we provide a framework to account for the inter-individual variability and conflicting results prevalent in neuromodulation research. Therefore, we highlight that incorporating individual baseline states into stimulation protocols is essential for achieving consistent and predictable neuromodulatory outcomes. (Supported by TUBITAK 424K278, BIDEB 2211 BAGEP Award of the Science Academy-Turkiye).
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: A multivariate approach linking alpha activity and aperiodic EEG features to perception and cognition
affiliations:
1. Psychophysics and Neural Dynamics Lab, Department of Radiology, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Vaudois and University of Lausanne (CH)
2. The Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
3. Research Institute of Cognitive Neurosciences, Free University of Tbilisi (GE)
4. Laboratory of Psychophysics, Brain Mind Institute, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (CH)
abstract: Perceptual science is often driven by the aim of linking behavioral phenomena to neural activity, such as relating the EEG alpha rhythm (8–12 Hz) to perception and cognition. Almost all studies in the field correlate the outcome of one single perceptual or cognitive task with the individual alpha frequency or power. Here, we adopted a multivariate approach, using a protocol that combines resting-state and task-based EEG recordings (N = 22) with a battery of eight canonical tasks, including orientation discrimination, temporal integration, bistable perception, the Stroop task, spatial attention, visual search, and working memory. We assessed associations between behavioral measures (accuracy and reaction times) and EEG features, including alpha peak frequency and amplitude, as well as aperiodic slope and offset. We found only weak and sparse correlations among behavioral measures, with stronger consistency mainly for reaction times across tasks, but not for accuracy. EEG features show moderate test–retest reliability but no clear or consistent relationship with behavior. Overall, these results indicate that the relationship between EEG alpha features and perceptual and cognitive performance is far from a simple one-to-one mapping and instead exhibits substantial heterogeneity.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Computational Modelling and Neural Mechanisms

title: Unsupervised Discovery of Oculomotor Deficits in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy via Deep Temporal Clustering of Saccade Velocity Profiles
affiliations:
1. Marburg University (DE)
2. Queen's University (CA)
3. University Hospital UKGM (DE)
4. Monash University (AU)
abstract: Background/Objective: Traditional saccade analysis in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) relies heavily on established discrete metrics (e.g., peak velocity, amplitude). While these metrics hold clinical value, they discard the continuous temporal dynamics of the eye movement. In this study, we propose a novel, featureless computational approach using deep sequence modeling to uncover disease-specific oculomotor phenotypes (OculoMotifs). Methods: High-resolution continuous gaze data from PSP patients and healthy controls (CTRL) were segmented into individual saccades. Instead of extracting summary statistics, the unextracted, variable-length velocity sequences were fed directly into a bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network. After training the model to classify subjects using a multiple-instance learning framework with attention, we sought to interpret the learned physiological representations. We extracted the high-dimensional hidden states from the trained GRU encoder for each individual saccade. To mitigate the curse of dimensionality, we applied Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to compress the feature space, followed by unsupervised K-Means clustering to map the saccades into distinct behavioral subtypes based purely on their temporal dynamics. Results: This data-driven clustering revealed profound structural differences in the oculomotor repertoires of the two groups. The network autonomously isolated specific saccadic phenotypes (OculoMotifs), such as distinct downward/oblique trajectories with robust velocity profiles, that were abundant in healthy controls but entirely absent in the PSP cohort. Other saccade subtypes were significantly rarer in the patient group, directly reflecting the oculomotor limitations caused by the disease. Conclusion: In conclusion, using AI to analyze continuous eye movements is not just highly accurate for diagnosis it also helps to discover new, interpretable signs of the disease. By examining how the model groups these movements, we can understand and explain which eye functions are impaired due to neurodegeneration. title: VisionBridge: A Knowledge Graph-Augmented Multimodal Framework for Cross-modal Image Understanding in Individuals with Visual Impairments and Blindness
affiliations:
1. Program of Digital Humanities and Creative Industries
2. Department of Computer Science and Engineer, National Chung Hsing University
abstract: Human perception is inherently multisensory. While sighted individuals primarily rely on visual information to understand their surroundings, individuals with visual impairments and blindness construct perceptual representations by integrating tactile exploration, auditory information, semantic memory, spatial cognition, and prior experience. However, recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain largely vision-centred, generating image descriptions that emphasize visual appearance rather than perceptually meaningful information. These systems frequently depend on visual vocabulary such as colour, shape, and appearance, provide limited support for non-visual cognitive representation, and may generate inaccurate or hallucinated content. As a result, current AI-based image description systems remain insufficient for supporting independent image understanding and meaningful cross-modal perception among individuals with visual impairments and blindness. To address this challenge, this study proposes VisionBridge, a knowledge graph-augmented multimodal framework that reconceptualizes image understanding as a process of cross-modal perceptual representation rather than conventional image captioning. The framework integrates multimodal large language models with a structured semantic knowledge graph to organize visual objects, spatial relationships, tactile characteristics, auditory information, functional attributes, and cultural context into an interconnected perceptual network. Instead of providing a single static description, VisionBridge supports multilingual speech interaction, enabling users to actively explore image content through natural dialogue according to their own perceptual needs and cognitive strategies. By grounding multimodal reasoning within structured semantic knowledge, VisionBridge is expected to improve semantic consistency, reduce hallucination, and generate image descriptions that more closely correspond to non-visual mental representations. Beyond improving accessible audio description, the proposed framework provides a computational model for investigating how visual information can be transformed into multisensory knowledge that supports cross-modal perception. This work contributes to research on perceptual artificial intelligence, multisensory cognition, and accessible human–computer interaction, offering a novel approach toward inclusive AI systems for individuals with visual impairments and blindness.

title: Individual differences in children’s decision making in visual motion and orientation tasks: understanding the sources of variability
affiliations: 1. University of Birmingham (UK)
abstract: Previous studies have shown that children’s visual perception becomes faster and more accurate with age. These studies have focused predominantly on mean differences across age groups, but a key unresolved issue is the large amount of variability across children. In this pre-registered study, an unselected sample of 200 children aged 7 to 10 years participate in visual motion and orientation tasks, at two time points in order to address this issue. By assessing test-retest reliability of children’s performance, we aim to show whether there are meaningful differences between children, or alternatively whether measurement noise alone is the source of variability in previous research. Assuming that there is meaningful variation, we aim to see whether characteristics related to neurodiversity predict performance on motion and orientation tasks. Children are asked to respond according to the overall direction of moving dots and the orientation of gratings in visual motion and orientation tasks respectively. Children are tested at two time points (7-18 days apart), and the order of the two tasks is counterbalanced across participants. Based on a preliminary analysis of 53 participants, we see moderate test-retest reliability on motion (ICC=0.50) and orientation (ICC=0.64) tasks. We also find that higher autistic quotient scores are associated with increased accuracy in the orientation task. This supports the idea that autistic traits may be related to prioritising accuracy when making decisions. No other relationships between the developmental characteristics (reading ability, intolerance of uncertainty, or ADHD strengths and weaknesses) and performance are shown to be significant. In the full dataset, these relationships will be explored further and supplemented with diffusion model analysis to decompose performance into distinct processing stages.

title: Pointing performance of low vision individuals when selecting a target among flankers in virtual reality : effect of pointing techniques and pointing visual feedback
affiliations:
1. Aix Marseille Univ, CNRS, CRPN (FR)
2. Aix Marseille Univ, CNRS, LPL (FR)
3. 2Clubdes3 (FR)
4. Centre Monticelli Paradis d’Ophtalmologie (FR)
5. Université Côte d’Azur, Inria (FR)
abstract: Individuals with Central visual Field Loss (CFL) have difficulty to perform visually-guided pointing tasks in Virtual Reality (VR). To improve the accessibility of VR pointing tools, we investigated the ability of these individuals to point at a target among flankers that induced different levels of crowding. A psychophysical approach in a controlled VR environment was used with different pointing conditions.  Experiments were implemented with the open-source PTVR toolbox (https://ptvr.inria.fr/) in a VR headset (Vive Pro). Patients with CFL (N = 60) had to select a 2° diameter target dot by pointing at it under monocular viewing. Pointing was achieved with a hand-contingent pointer seen as a « laser beam » or with a head-contingent pointer seen as a 6° diameter reticle (crossed design). The target was displayed alone or inbetween two vertically-aligned identical flanker dots. Target/flankers distance (Δ) varied from 7.4° to 2.6°. In two independent groups, the target started to flicker as soon as it was pointed at (feedback condition) or not (no-feedback condition). Selection was validated by pressing the hand controller’s trigger. Pointing performance was assessed by measuring selection accuracy and selection times.  Main results show that average accuracy for head- and hand-pointing are about 0.96 and 0.89 respectively. For both techniques, accuracy decreases when Δ decreases. The rate of this decrease is higher with hand-pointing than with head-pointing, and is similar for both feedback conditions. On average, head-pointing induces lower selection times than hand-pointing.  This study describes conditions where CFL persons are able to efficiently use hand- and head-pointing techniques with similar accuracy. This should allow patients having neck, or hand, weaknesses to choose hand-, or head-pointing respectively. Our work also provides quantitative recommandations to improve pointing for low vision individuals when interfaces contain packed items inducing crowding.
