title: Visual discomfort to flicker and dynamic bandpass noise in autistic and non-autistic children
affiliations: 1. University of Birmingham (UK)
abstract: Autistic children often experience differences in sensory processing including heightened reactivity to visual information (e.g., flickering light or motion) which can cause discomfort. However, little is known about the exact visual parameters that cause discomfort in autistic children, and whether this differs from non-autistic children. In this pre-registered study, autistic and non-autistic, cognitively able children aged 6 to 14 years rated their visual discomfort for uniform flicker and dynamic bandpass noise stimuli using a visual analogue scale.  Uniform flicker stimuli flickered sinusoidally between two grey levels (0.8 Michelson contrast) at temporal frequencies of 1.875, 3.75 or 15Hz. Dynamic bandpass noise stimuli were presented at varied central spatial frequencies and spatial frequency bandwidths, with 1 octave filtered central temporal frequencies of 1 or 16Hz, unfiltered temporal frequencies, or translational drift at 1 or 16Hz.   Preliminary analyses of 17 autistic and 27 non-autistic children reveal increased visual discomfort for higher temporal frequencies (15-16Hz) for uniform flicker and dynamic bandpass noise in both autistic and non-autistic children. Dynamic bandpass noise was rated higher for visual discomfort than static bandpass noise. Autistic children showed a larger increase in visual discomfort from 1Hz to 16Hz compared to non-autistic children for dynamic bandpass noise. Surprisingly, autistic children showed reduced visual discomfort ratings overall compared to non-autistic children, although this may be due to a higher proportion of girls in the non-autistic sample to date.   These preliminary data suggest visual discomfort is greater for temporal frequencies at which the early visual system has peak sensitivity, supporting the notion there are universal principles leading to visual discomfort of temporal visual information. They also suggest, while autistic and non-autistic children may differ in how they rate visual discomfort relative to their own baseline, autistic children may be more greatly affected by increases in temporal frequency compared to non-autistic children.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Allocentric visuospatial working memory is selectively preserved against age-related cognitive decline
affiliations: 1. University of Cambridge (UK)
abstract: In visuospatial working memory (VSWM), both egocentric information relative to the observer and allocentric information about the spatial relationships between objects can contribute to recall. Previous work (Aagten-Murphy & Bays, 2019) found that resources for storing information from these two sources are limited, but independent. In adults, VSWM declines with age, but whether the two memory systems deteriorate equally is not known.  To disentangle the contributions of ego- and allocentric processing to age-related VSWM decline, we conducted two online experiments with a total of 160 young (18–30 years) and older (60–70 years) neurotypical healthy adults. In Experiment 1, participants viewed an array of colored disks and, after a brief delay, reported the remembered location of the disk matching a color cue. A larger gray disk was either present throughout the entire trial (LM-PRESENT), supporting its use as a spatial landmark, or only during stimulus presentation (LM-ENCODING). In Experiment 2, the single landmark disk was replaced by a cluster of smaller disks we manipulated the reliability of allocentric information by varying the width of their distribution. During the delay, a new cluster was drawn from the same distribution (LM-PRESENT) or the cluster disappeared (LM-ENCODING).  We fit the data with a model optimally combining egocentric location information with allocentric information about location relative to the landmark when it is visible at recall (LM-PRESENT only). Allocentric precision is assumed to peak at the location of the landmark and decline exponentially with distance from it. While egocentric memory fidelity was lower in older than in younger adults, as expected (BF10 = 78), we found evidence against age-related differences in peak allocentric precision (BF10 = 0.359) and its decline with distance (BF10 = 0.522). This dissociation indicates selective preservation of allocentric working memory during healthy aging and establishes a baseline for investigating neurodegenerative disorders.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: The Effect of Executive Dysfunction on Visuospatial Skills in Mild Cognitive Impairment
affiliations:
1. MSc. Program, Graduate School of Health Sciences, Istanbul Medipol University, Istanbul, Türkiye
2. Department of Neurology, İstanbul Medipol Mega University Hospital, Istanbul, Türkiye
3. Neuroscience Research Center (SABITA), Istanbul Medipol University, Istanbul, Türkiye
4. Ergotherapy Department of Ergotherapy, Faculty of Health Sciences, Istanbul Medipol University, Istanbul, Türkiye
abstract: Aim: Understanding the relationship between executive functions and visuospatial skills in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is important for identifying early indicators of cognitive decline. The present study aimed to investigate the relationship between executive function problems and visuospatial functions in Mild Cognitive Impairment.      Method: A total of 104 patients diagnosed with MCI were included in this retrospective study. Global cognitive function was assessed using the Standardized Mini-Mental State Examination. Executive functions were evaluated with a battery including the Clock Drawing Test, verbal fluency tests (K-A-S, animal naming, and fruit naming), Trail Making Test time difference (TMT-TD), and Stroop Test time difference. Visuospatial abilities were assessed using the Benton Judgment of Line Orientation (BJLO) and Benton Facial Recognition Test (BFRT), while attention was evaluated using Digit Span Tests. Participants were divided into two groups based on executive functioning: impaired executive functioning (IEF) (n = 59) and preserved executive functioning (PEF) (n = 45), and analyzed accordingly. Results: The IEF group showed statistically significantly lower performance in line orientation among visual-spatial skills (p<0.05), while face recognition performance did not show a significant difference between the groups (p>0.05). Detailed analyses revealed that individuals with impaired TMT had statistically significantly lower BJLO test scores compared to those with TMT test scores within the norm (p<0.05), but Stroop test performance did not change according to visual perceptual skills (p>0.05).  Conclusion: This study highlights the interaction between executive skills, particularly cognitive flexibility and decision-making, and spatial skills in MCI.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Visual discomfort to spatial frequency statistics of natural images in autistic and non-autistic adults
affiliations: 1. University of Birmingham (UK)
abstract: Visual discomfort has been linked to deviations from the spatial frequency statistics observed in natural scenes, which generally follow a 1/f distribution. Atypical sensory processing is widely reported in autism, and some evidence suggests sensory sensitivity may vary by gender. However, it remains unclear whether deviations from natural image statistics differentially influence visual discomfort in autistic and non-autistic individuals, and whether such effects vary by gender.   The present study investigated whether autistic individuals report greater visual discomfort than non-autistic individuals when viewing natural images that vary in their deviation from the 1/f spatial frequency distribution, and whether these effects differ by gender.   170 participants (78 autistic, 92 non-autistic) completed an online image-rating task in which they viewed one of five 200-image subsets from the McGill Calibrated Colour Image Database and rated each image as “comfortable” or “uncomfortable.” Participants’ screens were calibrated during the study, so each image was displayed at approximately 10° visual angle. The spatial frequency structure of each image was extracted, and images were categorised into low, medium, and high deviation from 1/f. The proportion of images rated as uncomfortable within each category was analysed using a 2×2×3 mixed-design ANOVA.  Results revealed a significant main effect of group, with autistic participants reporting a higher proportion of images as uncomfortable than non-autistic participants. A significant main effect of spatial frequency deviation was also observed, however pairwise comparisons were not significant. No effects of gender or interactions were found.   These findings indicate that autistic individuals report greater visual discomfort, while the influence of spatial frequency deviations appears modest for natural images. This is inconsistent with the suggestion that visual discomfort is related to deviation from natural image statistics. The results highlight group differences and provide a basis for future research under more controlled conditions to identify contributing factors.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: The effects of extended virtual reality (VR) use on visual and sensorimotor functioning and visually-induced motion sickness (VIMS)
affiliations:
1. Toronto Metropolitan University (CA)
2. KITE Research Institute -  University Health Network (CA)
abstract: Our perception of the surrounding environment depends on the successful integration of sensory inputs, including information from the visual and proprioceptive systems. This is especially necessary when interacting with simulated environments, such as virtual reality (VR). Over the past 30 years, VR technology has gained rapid popularity in domains such as military training, education, and healthcare, with an estimated 171 million users worldwide. Yet, some studies indicate that up to 80% of individuals may experience visually-induced motion sickness (VIMS) while using VR, exhibiting symptoms such as eyestrain, blurred vision, and dizziness. Our understanding of side effects lasting beyond VR usage is also inconclusive for example, reduced sensorimotor performance has been observed up to 6 hours after VR exposure, and more severe aftereffects have been reported following prolonged use. These symptoms may be attributed to the accommodation-vergence conflict that arises in VR: whereas accommodation and vergence are normally coupled to maintain clear vision in the real world, these mechanisms are decoupled in VR as the visual scene is presented at a fixed distance  The proposed study will therefore examine the effects of extended VR exposure on VIMS, visual functioning, and sensorimotor performance. Participants will engage in a VR exercise game for 40 minutes, with subjective reports of VIMS and performance on sensorimotor (eye-hand coordination) and visual functioning (depth, acuity, motion perception, near-point accommodation and convergence, and binocular accommodation and vergence) tasks assessed before and after game exposure. Preliminary results reporting VIMS severity, visual functioning, and sensorimotor coordination variation before and after VR exposure will be presented. An increase in subjective VIMS scores and a reduction of sensorimotor and visual functioning performance is anticipated. Such findings may contribute to the continued development and improvement of virtual technologies for a wide range of users.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Counterintuitively Enhanced Masking Performance in Adults Born Preterm
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, Bilkent University (TR)
2. Department of Neuroscience, Aysel Sabuncu Brain Research Center, Bilkent University (TR)
abstract: Preterm birth can lead to a range of motor, cognitive, and perceptual complications, including poorer performance across various visual tasks in both children and adults. Despite differences in visual perception, the neural mechanisms remain largely unknown. One potential mechanism affected by preterm birth is cortical reentrant processing, which characterizes the bidirectional flow of information within the visual system and constitutes a core component of visual perception. Developmental evidence suggests that feedback processing is not yet fully mature in early infancy and that this mechanism may be particularly vulnerable to the effects of preterm birth. Visual masking paradigms provide a useful tool for investigating these bidirectional processing dynamics. Within this framework, preterm birth may disrupt the balance between feedforward and feedback processes, thereby altering the dynamics of visual information processing. In the present study, we tested this possibility by comparing masking performance between adults born preterm and those born at term. The experiment employed an object substitution masking (OSM) paradigm with five trailing mask durations (0, 50, 100, 150, and 300 ms). Data were collected from adults born at term (N = 23) and preterm (N = 19). Accuracy was measured using a four-alternative forced-choice task. The results revealed no significant interaction between mask duration and group, but significant main effects of mask duration (p < 0.001) and group (p < 0.001). Overall, individuals born preterm showed higher accuracy (72%) than those born at term (60%). This pattern was observed when both the target and the mask were black, but not when both were white  (preterm vs. term accuracy: 70% vs. 67%). These findings demonstrate a counterintuitively better performance in adults born preterm in a masking paradigm, likely reflecting atypical development of reentrant mechanisms, more specifically, those related to feedback processing, involved in visual perception following preterm birth.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Does Executive Function Resolve Spatial Interference, and Does Navigation Strategy Influence this Interaction?
affiliations:
1. Bournemouth University (UK)
2. University of Plymouth (UK)
abstract: Spatial navigation in dynamic environments requires not only the formation of spatial representations but also the ability to resolve interference between competing representations of overlapping routes. While the role of the hippocampus in spatial memory is well established, less is known about how executive control processes support navigation under conditions of interference. To address this gap, the present study carried out two experiments.\n The first experiment (N = 40) aimed to examine whether core components of executive function, working memory updating, mental set shifting, and inhibitory control predict susceptibility to proactive and retroactive interference during spatial navigation. Participants completed a virtual navigation task comprising three routes designed to induce interference through overlapping landmarks. Executive function was assessed using the Digit Span task, Stop-Signal Task, Trail Making Test, and Wisconsin Card Sorting Test.  Preliminary findings showed that accuracy was numerically lower at interference intersections compared to unique intersections in both proactive (Route 2) and retroactive (Route 3) conditions however, these differences did not reach statistical significance. No significant associations were observed between executive function measures and interference performance. However, updating ability was significantly associated with more efficient initial route learning, suggesting that executive control contributes to route encoding and acquisition under standard task condition.  Building on this rationale, the second experiment (N = 77) introduced an instructional manipulation to systematically guide encoding strategy, contrasting landmark-based associative encoding with sequence-of-turns encoding. By constraining how participants encode spatial information, this experiment examined how encoding strategy affects interference-related demands. Data collection for this experiment has been completed, and analysis is ongoing. Findings from Experiment 2 will be presented at the conference.
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Pseudoneglect Does Not Decrease with Reduced Arousal Following Sleep Deprivation – A Study Using Both Free Visual Exploration and Behavioral Measures
affiliations: 1. Institute of Psychology, Jagiellonian University (PL)
abstract: Phenomenon of pseudoneglect manifests as a subtle attentional bias toward left hemisphace that occurs frequently in a healthy population. Although being easily replicable and sharing some of the attributes with the unilateral neglect syndrome, its’ mechanisms remain unclear. Several studies pointed to arousal as a key factor modifying its’ magnitude, or even presence. Our aim was to replicate those findings, while also disentangling the effects of two main drivers of low arousal: sleep deprivation and circadian rhythms.  In order to investigate whether reductions in arousal influence pseudoneglect, an experiment with 44 right-handed participants (29 women, 0 non-binary) between 18 and 30 years old was conducted. First, during a baseline phase, subjects had to maintain a healthy sleep schedule, which was monitored by actigraphy. It was followed by an experimental night with a full sleep deprivation, during which they performed the free-viewing task, greyscale task and the landmark task under three conditions: normal arousal in the evening (8 p.m.), reduced arousal at the circadian trough (5 a.m.), and following all-night sleep deprivation (9 a.m.). Arousal and vigilance were carefully monitored using behavioral measures.  As expected, arousal levels were lowest at 5 a.m. and 9 a.m., without differences between them. However, visual exploration patterns as measured with the three tasks did not differ across conditions, with all sessions showing a robust and comparable leftward bias.   These findings suggest that transient reductions in arousal, whether induced by circadian phase or sleep deprivation, do not diminish  pseudoneglect. Our results contribute to the ongoing debate on the mechanisms underlying  spatial attentional biases  and  indicate  that factors other than global arousal may play a more critical role.   Financial support: the study was supported by a grant awarded to Aleksandra Smus by the Rada Kół Naukowych Uniwersytetu Jagiellońskiego (RKN/2025/2A/020)
session_title: Poster Session 3 · Clinical, Developmental, and Applied

title: Vanishing balls: Representational momentum in real, accelerating motion
affiliations: 1. University of Aberdeen (UK)
abstract: Observers typically tend to perceive the final position of an occluded moving object as displaced forward along its trajectory, an effect known as Representational Momentum (RM). Most evidence for RM effects comes from screen-based studies using implied motion or constant velocity. Here, we examined RM in a more ecologically valid setting using real, accelerating motion. Participants viewed balls (cricket vs. tennis) rolling down a 3m long inclined track while wearing noise-cancelling headphones. Occlusion was triggered at three randomly selected positions (102, 146 and 192 cm) using embedded markers and shutter glasses. In Experiment 1 (N=20), participants sat mid-track and followed the ball with head and eye movements, reporting its last seen position prior to occlusion. In a second condition, they estimated the moment the ball reached the end of the track after occlusion using button presses. In Experiment 2 (N=20), participants viewed the ball rolling towards them from the end of the track (i.e., without head movements, reduced sensorimotor engagement), again reporting its last seen position. Without head movements, robust forward displacement was observed across all occlusion points. With head movements, RM was present only for the early occlusion but not for later ones. This challenges the notion that forward displacement arises directly from oculomotor processes. Two accounts may explain this pattern. First, head movements may enhance continuous sensory updating, reducing reliance on prediction. Alternatively, tracking may rely mainly on velocity signals and only partly incorporate acceleration, which could contribute to changes in perceived position as motion unfolds. In the timing task, endpoint estimates were more accurate for later occlusions, with early occlusions showing an overestimation of time-to-end, consistent with limited use of acceleration information. Together, the results show that RM for real, accelerating motion depends on viewing conditions, highlighting an interaction between predictive processes and online sensorimotor information.

title: A Repulsive Bias Away from the Straight-Ahead in Perceived Heading as Determined by Continuous Psychophysics
affiliations: 1. York University (CA)
abstract: Earlier work has shown that perceived heading can be either biased towards the straight-ahead or away from the straight-ahead. An egocentric-allocentric distinction has been suggested as a potentially unifying solution, where egocentric responses lead to attraction towards the straight-ahead while allocentric responses are connected to repulsion from it. We investigated the egocentric prediction of this hypothesis using a novel, egocentric heading perception task based on continuous psychophysics. We immersed participants in a virtual environment where they experienced optic flow consistent with self-motion that changed every 200 ms based on a random walk, i.e., the direction for the next interval was determined by adding a value sampled from a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 10° to the current direction. Participants continuously aligned a joystick with their perceived heading. Each heading (0-360° in the x-z plane) was equally likely to occur. Participants performed this task with either SLOW or FAST simulated self-motion and in a CONTROL condition in which they had to align the joystick with an arrow that was continuously changing its direction rather than with their perceived heading. We found repulsive biases away from the straight-ahead for all three conditions, with the CONTROL condition displaying the weakest bias and the SLOW condition showing the strongest bias. Finding such repulsive biases in our egocentric task goes against the egocentric versus allocentric explanation for biases during heading estimations. However, our results are consistent with another account of biases in heading perception (Sun et al., 2025 PLOS Computational Biology) that posits that smaller response ranges lead to attraction while wider response ranges (such as our 360°) lead to repulsion.

title: Eye-head coordination in twisting movements with different amounts of rotation
affiliations: 1. Nihon University (JP)
abstract: Gymnasts use visual information to achieve spatial orientation and to control their bodies while airborne. Previous research has reported that during turning movements involving 180° and 360° rotations about the longitudinal axis, gymnasts exhibit gaze patterns characterized by gaze stabilization at takeoff and before and after landing, as well as patterns showing brief gaze stabilization during the turn. However, it remains unclear whether similar gaze strategies are used in movements involving a greater amount of rotation. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to clarify the coordination of eye and head movements during a straight jump with one-and-a-half turns and to examine how this coordination differs from that observed in twisting movements involving up to 360° of rotation. Participants were male collegiate gymnasts. The experimental task was a straight jump with one-and-a-half turns, involving a 540° rotation about the longitudinal axis. Eye movements were measured using electrooculography (EOG). Simultaneously, head movements were recorded using two digital high-speed cameras. Head rotation angles were calculated from the video recordings, and their relationship to eye movements was analyzed. The results showed that while the head rotated continuously in one direction, the eyes repeatedly moved in the opposite direction. In other words, in a 540° twisting movement, the strategy observed in jumps with a half or full turn, namely a large predictive gaze shift toward the forward-facing direction at landing, may be less likely to occur. These results suggest that gymnasts may use different gaze strategies for spatial orientation depending on whether the twisting movement involves up to 360° or 540° of rotation.

title: The contribution of proprioception to size constancy in perception and action: an fMRI study
affiliations:
1. University of Trento (IT)
2. Karolinska Institutet (SE)
3. La Trobe University (AU)
abstract: Size constancy allows the visual system to maintain stable representations of object size despite changes in viewing distance, supporting accurate perception and action. Although extensively studied, the mechanisms underlying size constancy remain only partially understood, particularly regarding the contribution of non-visual signals such as proprioception. Here, we investigate how proprioceptive depth cues are integrated with retinal information to support size constancy in both perception and action. We conducted an fMRI experiment using glow-in-the-dark spheres presented at two viewing distances (near vs. far) and two physical sizes (2.5 cm vs. 5 cm). The experiment was performed under restricted viewing conditions (darkness monocular viewing through a 1-mm pinhole) to remove all depth cues. Participants were asked to either grasp or manually estimate its diameter with their right hand, while their left hand held the pedestal on which the sphere was placed, providing a measure of distance. Regions of interest were independently defined using an object localizer to identify ventral and dorsal stream regions, including the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and intraparietal sulcus (IPS), and a retinotopic localizer to map early visual cortex (V1). In addition, a region of interest in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) was defined based on coordinates derived from the literature. To further characterize the directionality of information flow within this network, we performed Dynamic Causal Modeling (DCM), allowing us to test how proprioceptive and visual signals interact at the level of effective connectivity. Our findings reveal a functional dissociation between visual pathways: ventral stream regions within LOC are primarily sensitive to task demands and object size, whereas dorsal stream regions within IPS are preferentially modulated by viewing distance. These findings suggest that size constancy emerges from complementary contributions of ventral and dorsal pathways, integrating retinal and proprioceptive information to support stable perception and action across changes in distance.

title: Material properties are accounted for during motor-imagery
affiliations:
1. Experimental Psychology, Justus Liebig University (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior, Universities of Marburg, Giessen, and Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: To successfully grasp objects, we have to take their physical properties—such as compliance, surface friction, orientation and weight—into account. These different properties are often estimated visually. However, there are cases when such properties cannot be seen directly (e.g., the weight of an opaque milk carton depends on how full it is, but this cannot be seen directly). Here we sought to test whether the imagined or expected properties of objects impact both real and imagined actions. Thirty participants carried out two counterbalanced tasks. In one task, participants were to reach, grasp and transport a cylinder made of brass or styrofoam to a target location. The material was either visible or wrapped in thin paper and placed in front of the participants at four different orientations (0°, 60°, 90°, 120°). Participants were informed of the material hidden beneath the paper. Movements were tracked with a Qualisys infrared motion tracking system and timings for each phase were calculated by identifying key frames of hand and object movements. The second task consisted of motor-imagery, where participants had to imagine carrying out the movements. Participants rested their dominant hand at the resting position while pressing a button with their non-dominant hand to collect timings of their imagined movements. After each trial, participants provided a rating on a 4-point scale of imagery vividness and difficulty. For analysis, trials with reaction times 3 standard deviations outside of the participant means were excluded as outliers before performing a repeated measures ANOVA. Material knowledge affected reaching and transport phases for both imagined and performed movements with and without visual material cues, indicating that mere knowledge of an object’s constituting material alone carries information of properties useful for action-planning and execution.

title: Testing models of the cognitive structure of perceivable human actions
affiliations: 1. University of York (UK)
abstract: Several models have been proposed to explain the cognitive structure underpinning our perception of human actions. These studies have conceptualized this structure as a domain specific ‘action space’ defined by a limited number of important dimensions that describe the meaningful information on which we evaluate actions. However, these different models have disagreed on both the number of dimensions, and what action qualities each dimension represents. To help resolve these differences we retested Vinton et al.’s (2023) 4-D action space model whilst considering additional qualities identified by other models. We combined Vinton’s original dataset where participants rated 240 different controlled actions against 23 action characteristics, with ratings of the same actions against 8 new characteristics derived from all the other action space model dimensions. We used an EFA-to-CFA approach to determine the optimal model of action space and assess which action qualities define that space. Action space was best modelled by 5-factors. Two substantial dimensions originally identified by Vinton (Friendliness, Formidableness) each explained 18-19% of the variance. Whilst 3 smaller dimensions each explained 10-8% of the variance these included Abduction (as per Vinton) and additionally Locomotion and Environmental Interaction. We interpret this representation of action space as having 2+3 dimensions. We confirm previous research showing friendliness and formidableness are the two most important action qualities and likely represent action specific signals of the social cognition dimensions of warmth and competence respectively. Differences between earlier studies of action space can be attributed to non-representative samples of actions or the use of static images of actions.

title: Shared and idiosyncratic components of spontaneous blink timing profiles during sports driving
affiliations:
1. NTT Communication Science Laboratories (JP)
2. Institute of Science Tokyo (JP)
abstract: Natural behaviour requires continuous regulation of vision, attention, and action. However, underlying shared cognitive-state dynamics are difficult to recover in extended visuomotor tasks because overt performance and physiology vary substantially across individuals. We examined whether spontaneous eye blink behaviour, an underused behavioral marker linked to visual-cognitive state and broader task-related processes, reveals common structure during simulated sports driving. Eleven non-expert drivers completed repeated laps in a high-fidelity formula-car simulator on a race track while wearing a head-mounted eye tracker. Sessions manipulated temporal demand using fast and slow pace instructions. Blink events were aligned to position along the track and summarized as spatial blink-intensity profiles, allowing comparison across laps, drivers, and pacing conditions. Despite apparent between-driver differences in overall blink rate and profile shape, blink timing showed reliable within-driver locking to course position across laps. We then fit a parsimonious latent-template model that decomposed each individual profile into a shared course-locked component, an individual sensitivity to that component, and an individual intercept. This shared structure was similar across fast and slow sessions, whereas faster driving was associated with a lower overall blink level. Blinking was reduced during dynamically demanding parts of driving, especially under braking and higher lateral acceleration, indicating a close relationship between blink timing and the control state of the vehicle. At the same time, the full spatial organization of blinking was not accounted for by these kinematic factors alone, suggesting contributions from other course-linked factors. These findings show that spontaneous blinking during naturalistic driving is not merely noisy physiology, but contains reproducible structure linked to the temporal and spatial organization of behaviour. More broadly, the results position blink timing as an accessible behavioural marker for studying active vision and internal-state dynamics in ecologically rich tasks.

title: Visual aftereffects emerge from non-visual reaching adaptation
affiliations: 1. School of Psychology,  South China Normal University (CN)
abstract: Although it is well established that motor behaviors modulate early sensory processing, the nature and functional role of these top‑down signals remain unclear. Here, to address this question, we tested whether repeated execution of reaching movements in a single direction (denoted as reaching adaptation) could selectively modulate visual orientation tuning and induce a visual orientation aftereffect. This reaching-adaptation paradigm was inspired by the classic visual-adaptation paradigm, which is widely used to test for feature-specific neural populations versus shared representations across features or even modalities. If reaching adaptation induces aftereffects similar to visual adaptation, it would suggest that feedback signals during reaching selectively modulate visual orientation tuning. We found that reaching without visual feedback led to the following presented visual bar being perceived towards the direction of the reach, i.e., an attractive aftereffect. This finding was consistently observed for both leftward and rightward adaptation and for both left and right hands. Hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling (HDDM) further showed that this effect was primarily mediated by changes in sensory evidence accumulation, rather than being solely attributable to decision-level processes. The existence of cross-modal adaptation indicates a shared representation between feedback of reaching direction and visual orientation. Consistent with a shared representation, we also found that the vertical reaching direction on the next trial was attracted toward the orientation of a visual bar presented on the previous trial. Together, these findings demonstrate that even without visual feedback, the top-down feedback signals from motor to sensory cortex do not merely modulate global states such as arousal or attention instead, they carry feature‑selective information that bidirectionally interacts with visual features to enhance each other’s response gain.

title: Seeing others act: the dissociation between sensory processing and top-down cognitive control during joint agency
affiliations: 1. School of Psychology, South China Normal University (CN)
abstract: Humans perceive self-generated and other-generated sensory information differently. While joint action toward a common goal is thought to allow the brain to ‘adopt’ a partner's actions into its own predictive framework, direct neural evidence for this sensorimotor internalization remains elusive. We investigated this by training pairs of participants to perform simultaneous keypresses. Before and after training, EEG was recorded while participants listened to auditory stimuli generated by themselves, their partner, or a computer. Behaviorally, training significantly reduced keypress asynchrony and increased subjective Sense of Agency (SoA) ratings for the partner. Neurally, we observed classic sensory attenuation (reduced N1 and P2 amplitudes at fronto-central sites) for self-generated compared to computer-generated sounds. Critically, no such attenuation occurred for partner-generated sounds even after training. Furthermore, while the temporal Tb component showed attenuation for the self, it exhibited sensory enhancement for the partner. Beyond primary sensory processing, we examined top-down modulatory mechanisms using the theta-band weighted phase lag index (wPLI) between fronto-central and temporal regions. Theta wPLI was significantly lower for self-generated than computer-generated sounds. Notably, the wPLI for partner-generated sounds decreased after training, and this reduction correlated with the subjective increase in SoA. These results suggest a functional dissociation in joint agency: while primary sensory levels maintain a clear distinction between self and other, top-down cognitive control mechanisms are adapted to treat a partner's actions similarly to one's own. These findings challenge the notion of a complete sensorimotor ‘merging’ in joint action, pointing instead to a high-level integrative framework.

title: Attunement to Object Size Affects Locomotor Strategies During Fly Ball Interception
affiliations:
1. Universitat de Barcelona (ES)
2. Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (US)
abstract: Prominent heuristics for fly ball interception, such as LOT and GOAC models, rely on optical angles and their higher order derivatives but have largely ignored the possible role of the object's physical size. However, attunement to object size could play a role in the control of locomotor interception by allowing fielders to scale optical variables. This study tested the hypothesis that when intercepting moving objects on foot, fielders' movements are influenced by an adaptation or attunement to the objects’ physical size. Participants intercepted fly balls in a virtual reality environment via a head-mounted display. Balls were projected to eight possible landing locations surrounding the subject's initial position. To test the attunement hypothesis, the experiment manipulated ball size across blocks. In Block 2, the ball size (diameter) was 0.15 m on 90% of trials, but increased to 0.18 m on 10% ‘catch trials’. In Block 4, the ball was 0.18 m on 90% of trials, but decreased to 0.15 m on 10% catch trials. This design allowed for the comparison of fielders' trajectories for physically identical stimuli where the only difference was the size to which the fielder was attuned. As predicted, baseline trajectories were similar on matched normal trials. However, trajectories diverged significantly on catch trials, suggesting that subjects’ movements were affected when they were not properly attuned to the ball’s physical size.  Crucially, individual subjects exhibited two diametrically opposed behavioural patterns on catch trials. When presented with an unexpectedly small ball, one group of participants retreated backward, consistent with misinterpreting the slower optical expansion as a distant, high-altitude ball. Conversely, another, larger group moved forward, consistent with misinterpreting the exact same information as a slow-moving ball dropping short. These findings demonstrate that fielders become robustly attuned to physical size, employing idiosyncratic control strategies to resolve optical ambiguities during interception.

title: Estimating the difficulty of segmentation tasks using ideal observers and neural networks
affiliations:
1. Technical University of Darmstadt (DE)
2. Centre for Mind, Brain and Behaviour (CMBB) (DE)
abstract: Visual segmentation is still an open problem in both biological and machine vision. Understanding how segmentation can be performed optimally requires a setting where the generative process of an image is fully known. Dead leaves images provide exactly this. They are synthetic images generated by layering randomly shaped, colored, and textured objects. Importantly, they capture many statistical regularities of natural images while the generative process is known. This allows the derivation of the Bayes-optimal ideal observer for segmentation. However, exact inference for this ideal observer is computationally tractable only for small patches of up to 3×3 pixels, and the number of possible segmentations grows super-exponentially with patch size, making the ideal observer infeasible for larger patches. Neural networks offer a potential solution: as general function approximators, they have been shown to approximate the decisions of ideal observers and solve segmentation problems, though whether this extends to approximating an ideal observer for segmentation remains to be investigated. First, we evaluate the ideal observer for dead leaves segmentation. We show that it is well calibrated and identify image features that make segmentation easier or harder. We then train fully convolutional neural networks on dead leaves segmentation using ground-truth segmentations and compare their predictions to those of the ideal observer on 3×3 patches. The network not only achieves comparable performance but also produces similar predictions, indicating that both models make similar errors. This holds not only in-distribution but also across many out-of-distribution conditions, though predictions diverge further from the training distribution. Finally, we evaluate network generalization to larger 7×7 patches, where the ideal observer is intractable, and find that the network achieves reasonable segmentation performance. These results suggest that neural networks trained on ground truth segmentation can be used to approximate ideal observer segmentation and help in estimate task difficulty.

title: How stable is preference for visual curvature across stimuli and over time?
affiliations: 1. Human Evolution and Cognition group, Department of Psychology, University of the Balearic Islands (ES)
abstract: Visual contour is relevant to object perception and affective evaluation. Substantial evidence supports a reliable hedonic preference for curvilinear contours over angular ones. However, recent studies indicate that this preference is modulated by contextual and individual factors. A possible source of heterogeneity is individual differences in hedonic sensitivity to curvilinear and angular stimuli. The objective of this study is to investigate the intra-individual and temporal consistency of hedonic sensitivity to curvature across four types of stimuli: meaningless shapes, indeterminate paintings, drawings of everyday objects, and interior spaces. One hundred participants rated their liking of the stimuli three times over a two-week period in a test-retest task. Ninety-two participants completed the third session, in which they also rated the perceived curvilinearity of the stimuli. The results show that, in all three sessions, participants did not show a significant preference for curvature in interior spaces or objects, although a slight tendency towards it was observed. In the other two stimulus types, curvature preference was clearly significant across sessions. Hedonic sensitivity to curvature for each participant and stimulus type was calculated as the difference between the estimated individual slopes for angular and curved stimuli. The correlations among stimulus types within each session were moderate to high, and gradually increased from the first to the third session. The correlations between sessions were high for meaningless shapes, and moderate to high for paintings and objects. However, test-retest reliability results showed that temporal consistency varied depending on the stimulus type, highlighting intra-individual variability. This research contributes to our understanding of hedonic sensitivity to curvature by offering insights into its dynamics across stimuli and time points. We propose that consistency may serve as a criterion supporting the existence of a given hedonic preference.

title: Low confidence for perceptual completion of partially occluded objects
affiliations:
1. General and Biological Psychology, Department of Psychology Philipps University of Marburg (DE)
2. Laboratoire des Systèmes Perceptifs, Département d’études cognitives, École Normale Supérieure, PSL University, CNRS (FR)
abstract: The visual system is very good at completing the missing information in proximal gaps that are caused by anatomical constraints (e.g. scotomas) and in distal gaps that are caused by partial occlusion from other objects or by self-occlusion. Previous studies have shown that perceptual completion of proximal gaps occurs outside of our awareness and that observers report high confidence for the inferred information in those gaps. Here, we investigated whether similar metacognitive biases would emerge for perceptual completion of distal gaps when some stimulus parts are physically absent. We ran three experiments using stimuli that were either intact (full stimulus), partially cutout (stimulus with gap), partially occluded (amodal completion) or induced (modal completion). In Experiment 1, participants performed an orientation discrimination task and a confidence rating for their perceptual decision. In Experiment 2, participants performed a Vernier acuity task and a confidence rating for their perceptual decision. In Experiment 3, participants performed a continuity-discontinuity decision task for two consecutive stimuli and made a forced-choice confidence judgment selecting the decision they felt more confident about. We examined whether participants report high confidence for amodal and modal completion in comparison to a full stimulus or a stimulus with gap. Across three experiments with different tasks, we found that participants had the highest confidence for full (non-occluded) stimuli, whereas amodal and modal completion led to comparable confidence as stimuli with gap. These findings show that there is low confidence for perceptual completion of distal gaps. Moreover, seeing a physical gap or an occlusion had similar effects on confidence judgments. In combination with previous research, our results suggest that the visibility of gaps in sensory information and occlusion critically influence metacognitive confidence.

title: Is visual memory platonic? Image memorability transfers to scene descriptions
affiliations: 1. Justus-Liebig University (DE)
abstract: Some images are consistently remembered better than others (Isola et al., 2011). This inherent image memorability can be predicted surprisingly well by a residual neural network which is sensitive to semantic image features (ResMem Needell & Bainbridge, 2022). Large-scale human data also suggests that memorability is mostly driven by semantic features (Kramer et al., 2023). This raises the question whether image memorability depends on visual features or at least in part is independent of modality. Here, we tested whether the memorability of scene images transfers to short textual descriptions of those scenes. Across multiple surprise memory experiments we confirm that this is the case, regardless of whether scene descriptions were generated by humans or multimodal large language models. Furthermore, new images produced with generative AI from descriptions alone reproduce the memorability of original images. Together, these findings provide strong evidence that the memorability of scene images does not hinge on visual features on display, and that language serves as an efficient and faithful compression of memory-relevant visual content. They are consistent with the notion of converging representations across vision and language modalities, in line with recent proposals in the context of AI (Huh et al., 2024) and reminiscent of Plato’s concept of an ideal reality. We plan to test whether this alignment between visual and semantic memory is specific to surprise memory of scenes or generalises to other types of images and tasks.

title: What Does 'Curvy' Mean to You?: Distinct Patterns in the Perceptual Space of Curvature
affiliations: 1. University of Toronto (CA)
abstract: Curvature is widely treated as a fundamental dimension of visual shape perception, yet its perceptual structure and defining features remain underspecified. We asked how curvature-related shape variation is organized in perceptual space and which geometric features observers use when judging similarity. In Experiment 1, we constructed a controlled space of 1D line-contour stimuli that parametrically varied smoothness, number of vertices, and turning angle, and participants performed a triplet odd-one-out task under either general or curvature-focused instructions. In Experiment 2, we extended this approach to 2D abstract shapes that independently varied smoothness, number of vertices, and range of vertices, again collecting odd-one-out similarity judgments. From these relational judgments, we derived pairwise similarity estimates and used representational similarity analysis with multidimensional scaling to reconstruct the implied perceptual spaces. Across both instruction conditions and both stimulus sets, curvature-related similarity could not be reduced to a single axis: accurate reconstructions required multiple dimensions, some of which were selectively associated with particular physical features while others reflected joint contributions from several features. Clustering of participant-level feature weights revealed stable subgroups that, for 1D contours, relied primarily on either smoothness or number of vertices, and for 2D shapes, on either smoothness or a joint weighting of vertex number and range. These findings indicate that curvature is a multidimensional perceptual construct emerging from the integration of several geometric cues, and that perceived “curvature” depends on how observers differentially weight these cues when organizing shape similarity.

title: From image statistics to perception: Dead Leaves as controlled naturalistic stimuli
affiliations:
1. Technical University of Darmstadt (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior (DE)
abstract: A central goal of vision science is to understand how the visual system processes natural inputs. Across many tasks, including rapid scene categorization, perceptual grouping, and visual search, performance depends strongly on low-level image statistics. In natural scenes, however, these statistics are tightly entangled with semantic content. This makes it difficult to isolate their respective contributions to perception. Dead leaves images provide a controlled intermediate stimulus between simple laboratory patterns and fully natural images. They are generated by sequentially layering simple shapes, or leaves, sampled from parameterized distributions. The resulting images are cluttered and capture key statistical regularities of natural scenes, including power spectra, contrast distributions, and occlusion structure. At the same time, they contain minimal semantic content. This makes them well suited for studying how statistical regularities affect visual inference. Here, we introduce deadleaves, an open source Python package for generating standardized yet highly customizable dead leaves stimuli. The package enables researchers to dissociate image statistics from semantics, construct controlled stimulus sets matched to natural image statistics, and probe their role across perceptual tasks in humans and computational models. It supports precise manipulation of object geometry, and appearance, and provides exact ground truth segmentation with full generative control. We present the core features of deadleaves and demonstrate its use in applications to natural image statistics, perceptual organization, image segmentation, and aesthetics. Together, this framework provides a flexible testbed for studying the role of low level image statistics across a wide range of visual behaviors.

title: Perceived Meaning of Scene Patches: Effects of Eccentricity and Surrounding Context
affiliations: 1. Kiel University (DE)
abstract: In order to select scene regions for foveal inspection, the visual system must estimate the meaning of potential fixation targets. In naturalistic scenes, targets are typically processed with the limited spatial resolution of the visual periphery. However, existing semantic models of fixation prediction do not account for differences between central and peripheral vision. In order to test the hypothesis that such differences also influence perceived meaning, we extended the Meaning Map approach (Henderson & Hayes, 2017), which aggregates ratings of isolated scene patches into spatial distributions of meaning. We examined how these ratings change when patches are viewed in parafoveal and peripheral vision. Using a gaze-contingent paradigm, circular patches (2.25° diameter) were maintained at fixed eccentricities (up to 12° visual angle) to prevent direct foveation. Participants rated how meaningful (i.e., informative or recognizable) the patches were. We hypothesized that meaning recognition would decrease with increasing eccentricity. This pattern was supported overall however, in a substantial subset of cases, meaning ratings were higher in the periphery, driven by both stimulus properties and participant strategies. These findings suggest that the standard instruction we used may not generalize to extrafoveal vision. In an ongoing follow-up experiment, we therefore altered the instructions by asking participants to rate the usefulness of patches for an unspecified follow-up task. Unlike the previous experiment, the patches were not only presented in isolation, but also surrounded by meaningless textures or blurred scene content. We expect that meaning perception is facilitated by truthful scene context and complicated by uninformative textures. Collectively, the present data suggest that semantic models of attention and fixation should consider that eccentricity and context shape meaning perception outside foveal vision.

title: Boats in the sky and dolphins in the grass: Neural markers of object-background semantic consistency in adults and young infants
affiliations:
1. The MARCS Institute for Brain, Behaviour & Development, Western Sydney University (AU)
2. School of Psychology, Western Sydney University (AU)
3. School of Computer, Data and Mathematical Sciences,  Western Sydney University (AU)
abstract: Humans are highly attuned to the statistical regularities of our visual environment, including the surrounding context in which we tend to encounter specific objects. Existing work shows that we recognise and remember objects in semantically-consistent scenes better than those in inconsistent ones, and that the former evoke stronger neural representations in the brain. Behavioural and eye-tracking evidence indicates that sensitivity to object-scene relations emerges within the first year of life however, the neural mechanisms supporting semantic consistency effects in infancy have yet to be established. Here we addressed this by recording scalp EEG from a large infant sample aged 2-12 months (n = 61) and adult observers (n = 22) as they viewed upright and inverted objects superimposed on semantically consistent or inconsistent backgrounds (e.g., dolphin-water vs. dolphin-grass). Decoding analyses of adult data revealed robust representations of both object and background categories which were strengthened by consistent object-background relations between 200-300ms. Both decoding types were also modulated by object orientation, but over a briefer and earlier time window. For infants, decodable object representations (e.g., dolphin vs. tractor vs. airplane …) were only evident for upright object presentations, and strongest when those upright objects appeared on semantically consistent backgrounds. In the infant sample, decoding of the background scene itself (e.g., grass vs. water vs. sky) was comparatively stronger, emerging regardless of the superimposed object’s orientation or semantic consistency. These results contribute to the emerging field of infant neural decoding and provide new insight into how knowledge of object–scene relationships develop over the first year of life.

title: Near-optimal feature combination for superordinate classification of unencountered objects
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior (DE)
abstract: Visually classifying objects into superordinate classes like “animal” or “plant” is challenging because radically different items (e.g., “peacock”, “shark”) must be grouped together. This becomes even harder when facing entirely novel objects that have never been encountered before. We sought to uncover the visual features and computations underlying superordinate classification for such novel objects. We probed participants’ visual feature spaces by having them generate sixteen unfamiliar (i.e., made up) and eight familiar (i.e., real) exemplars for 10 superordinate classes (animal, building, clothing, furniture, appliance, instrument, plant, tool, vehicle, and a general “object” class). Thirty-two other observers then classified and rated typicality for these drawings. Their responses were correlated strongly with the classes that prompted the drawings, and typicality ratings were consistently much lower for unfamiliar than for familiar drawings. This confirmed that observers can generate genuinely novel yet easily classifiable drawings. We then asked 180 further participants to mark and label the drawings’ defining “parts” (e.g., “head”, “window”, “handle”). There was high distinctiveness in features between classes, which presumably aids superordinate classification. However, we also observed sparse, highly variable features within classes, substantiating the computational challenge of superordinate classification. Importantly, we found that classification of unfamiliar object drawings was extremely well predicted by an optimal Bayesian classifier that derives its classification from feature likelihoods and priors yielded from familiar objects (r = 0.9). Therefore, superordinate classification appears to combine semantic-level features approximately optimally to generalise to novel exemplars. We suggest that we use such compositional feature representation both for classifying objects together despite substantial differences in visual appearance, and to imagine—and draw—new things.

title: Keeping track of object files for identical objects
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (DE)
2. Berlin School of Mind and Brain, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (DE)
3. Department of Psychology, Technische Universität Chemnitz (DE)
abstract: Object files are temporary representations that store and update object-specific information across spatial and temporal gaps (Kahneman et al., 1992). They can be measured as object-specific preview benefits (OSPB): following a preview of digits displayed within separate and visually distinct objects, reaction times are faster to a target digit that reappears in the same object, compared to it reappearing in a different object. We examined whether OSPBs can be established using visually identical objects rather than geometrically distinct shapes. Trials started with a preview display showing single digits within two Gabor patches. The digits then disappeared for 300 ms, during which patches either blinked briefly (static condition), moved continuously, or suddenly jumped to a new location. Finally, a target digit appeared in one of the two Gabors, which participants were asked to rapidly identify via button press. The target could be one of the previewed digits appearing in the same or a different object, or a new digit altogether. Catch trials, in which the preview paired a digit with a letter, were interleaved throughout, ensuring attention to the preview display (Sasi et al., 2023). Three groups of participants (Exp 1: n=21 Exp 2: n=20 Exp 3: n=19) completed this task, which differed across experiments in the number of possible target digits, retinal eccentricity, or surface features of objects. In Experiment 1 (four possible digits, 6.36 dva eccentricity), we found a significant OSPB only in the static condition. Experiment 2 (three possible digits, 4.24 dva eccentricity) showed an OSPB in the static and continuous condition. In Experiment 3, we added surface features to the Gabors to enhance object distinctiveness. With this variant, we found an OSPB in the continuous condition only. In addition to these differences, our findings demonstrate that distinct temporary object representations can be established between highly similar objects.

title: The unseen face in the crowd: Ensemble perception incorporates invisible face
affiliations:
1. Tohoku University (JP)
2. National Taiwan University (TW)
abstract: Our visual system rapidly extracts ensemble statistics from multiple visual stimuli. However, it remains elusive whether awareness of individual items is necessary for ensemble perception. Here, we tested whether ensemble statistics incorporates unseen stimuli. In each trial, participants judged the mean emotion intensity of three faces, with an additional concurrently presented and interocularly suppressed face. We found that the average emotion rating of the three faces was biased toward the emotion intensity of the unconscious face, suggesting that the ensemble perception incorporates the invisible stimulus. In subsequent experiments, we first ruled out the possibility that the effect was driven by response bias. Furthermore, by including either suppressed emotional or neutral faces, we found that the ensemble emotion judgment could be biased in either direction. This effect persisted even when different emotions were randomly intermixed within the same block, suggesting that the effect was not driven by demand characteristics following a break in suppression. Together, our results show that ensemble perception integrates both conscious and unconscious faces, broadening its known limits.

title: Quantity over quality? The impact of the number of faces to learn and of their appearance on the robustness of facial representations
affiliations: 1. Psychology and Neuroscience of Cognition, University of Liège (BE)
abstract: For decades, researchers have sought to identify the factors that support robust face learning. Prior work has shown that exposure to varied images improves later recognition. Because image variation can include changes in viewing conditions, pose, expression, or appearance, our research has focused specifically on the role of facial appearance—kept stable or made variable through changes such as hairstyle, hair colour, or makeup. This focus was rooted in the idea that an efficient face‑learning system should refine memory representations only when necessary, after exposure to changes in appearance. Some of our earlier studies showed that memory representations were more robust when participants learned four faces with variable appearances compared to four faces with stable appearances. However, other studies found either no difference between the two conditions or better performance for stable faces when only two faces were learned per condition. To clarify these discrepancies, we conducted a preregistered study manipulating both the number of faces to learn (four, eight between‑subjects) and appearance (stable, variable within‑subjects). 236 participants learned faces from the same set of static images. As predicted, recognition performance was higher in the four‑face condition than in the eight‑face condition, indicating a cost of increased learning load. We also found a main effect of appearance, but no significant interaction between appearance and number of faces. Nonetheless, paired comparisons revealed higher recognition performance for variable faces in the eight‑face condition, whereas no difference between appearance conditions was observed when only four faces were learned. These findings suggest that learning load strongly influences recognition performance, and that the effect of appearance may depend on the allocation of limited memory resources in a given learning context. Learning load may therefore help explain inconsistencies in the face‑learning literature and should be considered in future research.

title: Decoding Neural Responses to Real and Synthetic Faces: Evidence from EEG
affiliations:
1. MARCS Institute for Brain, Behaviour and Development, Western Sydney University (AU)
2. School of Psychology, Western Sydney University (AU)
3. School of Computer, Data, and Mathematical sciences, Western Sydney University (AU)
abstract: The increasing realism of synthetic AI-generated faces presents challenges for human visual perception and judgement. Although behavioural studies suggest that observers cannot reliably distinguish real from synthetic faces unless under certain conditions, recent work suggests that they evoke differentiable neural processes. The present study investigated what drives the neural decoding of real from synthetic faces. Electroencephalography (EEG) signals were recorded while participants viewed 900 real and synthetic faces varying in realism (realistic vs. unrealistic), availability of information (external vs. internal features), face regions (whole vs. segmented face) and orientation (upright vs. inverted). Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis was used to decode stimulus category (real vs. synthetic) from neural activity, separately for each manipulation (e.g., whole vs. segmented). Results indicated that neural responses to real and synthetic faces were reliably separable over brief time windows, and that neural discriminability between real and synthetic faces may be modulated by the realism of the stimuli, the availability of information and the facial region (eyes, mouth). These findings provide further evidence that EEG-based decoding may capture early neural sensitivity to differences between real and synthetic faces, even when behavioural performance do not reliably separate these categories. This suggests that the visual system may encode subtle differences between real and synthetic faces at early stages of processing. More broadly, this work contributes to understanding how the human visual system adapts to increasingly realistic synthetic stimuli, with implications for models of face perception and the detection of AI-generated content.

title: Behind the Mask: A New Viewpoint on Face Identity Recognition at First Glance.
affiliations:
1. Université de Lorraine, INTERPSY (FR)
2. Université de Lorraine, CNRS, IMOPA (FR)
abstract: The human visual system demonstrates remarkable efficiency in rapidly and accurately recognizing individual faces. However, this ability can be compromised by variations in viewing conditions, such as changes in viewpoint, or by the occlusion of critical facial features, for instance by face masks. Moreover, although numerous studies have shown that face masks substantially impair facial identity recognition, most have relied on the use of facial stimuli presented in a frontal view, over extended durations, as well as on explicit behavioral tasks. Here, we aimed to explore the impact of viewpoint and mask-wearing on the implicit recognition of facial identity at first glance. To this end, electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings were conducted on 25 participants during the presentation of the same (unfamiliar) face identity at a frequency of 6 Hz, with the insertion every fifth image of different face identities, leading to a face identity recognition (FIR) response at 1.2 Hz (6 Hz/5) and its harmonics (2.4 Hz, etc.) directly observable in the frequency spectrum. Different 60-s stimulation sequences were presented with unmasked and masked faces and from different viewpoints (frontal, ¾ right and ¾ left), while participants performed a bar color change detection task. The neural FIR response recorded over the bilateral occipito-temporal cortex was markedly reduced by mask-wearing. Furthermore, while no effect of viewpoint was found for masked faces, the FIR response was significantly reduced for three-quarter views compared to frontal views for unmasked faces. Overall, our findings highlight a frontal-view advantage for first-glance face recognition, facilitating the extraction of facial features and promoting holistic face processing. They also underscore a substantial impact of mask-wearing on face recognition, with no viewpoint-related optimization, resulting from the occlusion of lower-face features and the disruption of holistic face perception.

title: Seeing Faces: Exploring Perceptual Disorders in Glaucoma Patients Through Event-Related Potentials
affiliations:
1. Université de Lorraine, INTERPSY (FR)
2. Lille university hospital (FR)
3. Université de Lille, CNRS, Lille Neurosciences & Cognition (FR)
abstract: Glaucoma is an age-related ocular pathology characterized by a progressive degeneration of the optic nerve and retinal ganglion cells. Without medication, it leads to a visual field defect, starting in the periphery and progressing towards the center. Behavioral studies have reported face recognition deficits in patients with glaucoma. However, the origin and nature of this impairment remained unclear. The present study aimed to explore the neural correlates underlying face perception deficits in this pathology using event-related potentials (ERPs), with a particular focus on the N170 occipito-temporal component, a well-established electrophysiological marker of face structural encoding and holistic face processing. During ERPs recording, 17 patients with open-angle glaucoma and 17 age-matched control participants performed an orientation decision task involving two categories of stimuli (faces and cars), presented in both upright and inverted orientations. In both groups of participants, the accuracy rate on the behavioral task was high (approximately 97%). Contrary to the P1 component, the N170 exhibited a significantly delayed latency and lower amplitude in patients. Additionally, although the N170 amplitude was larger for faces than for cars in both patients and controls, the two groups differed primarily in their response to faces, suggesting a specific impairment in the structural encoding of faces in glaucoma patients, leading to the extraction of an inadequate facial representation. Finally, when the two groups were combined, a weak face inversion effect was observed on the N170 amplitude, indicating impaired holistic face processing however, this effect may reflect an overall effect of aging. In conclusion, this study confirmed abnormalities in face perception in patients with glaucoma and extended previous behavioral findings by highlighting that these alterations would arise at early perceptual stages of face processing, as indicated by the modulations of the N170 component.

title: Developmental changes in Mooney face perception from early childhood to adulthood
affiliations:
1. Niigata University (JP)
2. Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JP)
3. Rikkyo University (JP)
abstract: Humans can robustly perceive faces from limited information. A well-known example is the perception of Mooney faces— two-tone black-and-white face images with degraded individual features (e.g., eyes and mouth) (Mooney, 1957). The detection of Mooney face is observed even in infants (Doi et al., 2009 Otsuka et al., 2012 Yamanaka et al., 2025). However, little is known about how this ability develops beyond infancy. To fill this gap, we examined this ability from early childhood to adulthood.  Participants were divided into three age groups: fourteen 4–10 years, twelve 15–18 years, and eight adults. Upright face preference (Chien, 2011) was measured using Mooney faces with four levels of degradation (Levels 1–4). Level 1 stimuli were comparable in visibility to those previously shown to be detectable by infants (Yamanaka et al., 2025). The experiment consisted of two blocks. In the first block, upright and inverted Mooney faces with the same degradation level were presented side-by-side across 32 trials. The second block presented upright and inverted photographic faces across 8 trials. Each trial lasted 10 seconds, and participants’ gaze was recorded using an eye tracker. Because a two-way mixed-design ANOVA revealed no significant main effect of age group and relevant interaction, data were pooled across age groups for further analysis. Two-tailed one-sample t-tests against chance level (0.5) showed significant upright face preference for Level 1 (t(33) = 3.17, p = .003, d = 0.54), Level 2 (t(33) = 3.41, p = .002, d = 0.80), Level 3 (t(33) = 4.19, p < .001, d = 0.74), and photographic faces (t(33) = 3.52, p = .001, d = 0.38). These findings suggest that participants aged 4 years through adulthood can reliably detect Mooney faces up to Level 3.

title: Face and Scene Learning: A Trade-Off in the Context of Appearance Variability
affiliations: 1. University of Liège (BE)
abstract: In daily life, we meet individuals in varying contexts, and their appearance may change to varying degrees between encounters. Although variability in appearance may initially make face learning more challenging, prior research has demonstrated that it ultimately enhances recognition accuracy (Devue & de Sena, 2023, Cognition). Here, we investigated whether memory advantages from exposure to variable appearances come at the cost of memory for contextual information and for face-scene associations. We hypothesised that inner features of faces that were learned with variable appearances would be memorised in a robust but decontextualized manner, leading to improved recognition performance for faces but not for scenes or face-scene associations. In contrast, we expected that faces with a stable appearance and the surrounding scenes should be memorised in a global manner, yielding relatively poorer face recognition with better scene recognition and stronger face-scene associations. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a pre-registered study (N = 64) examining how variability in appearance (stable vs. variable hair colour and style) influences face and scene learning. Participants learned six images of eight new faces, each embedded in two distinct scenes. After a 5-min delay, face recognition was tested using pictures displaying only inner facial features. Scene recognition and memory for face-scene associations were also tested to investigate memory for the extrinsic context and decontextualisation, respectively. Eye-tracking data were collected throughout the entire experiment to determine the spatial distribution of visual attention. Results show better overall recognition for scenes associated with stable faces and for their association. A trend also suggests that exposure to variability may improve inner-feature recognition, even though these features were fixated less in that condition. Taken together, these findings suggest that variability in facial appearance favours the encoding of inner facial features at the expense of contextual information.

title: Robust face identity codes in the Super-Recogniser brain
affiliations:
1. The MARCS Institute for Brain, Behaviour and Development, 
Western Sydney University (AU)
2. School of Computer, Data and Mathematical Sciences, 
Western Sydney University (AU)
3. School of Psychology, The University of New South Wales (AU)
4. School of Psychology, Western Sydney University (AU)
abstract: Super-Recognisers are individuals with an exceptional ability to remember and individuate human faces. Processing differences between super-recognisers and typical viewers are typically inferred from behavioural tasks that explicitly ask participants to attend to face identity, but the neural mechanisms underpinning these differences are not understood. Building on recent work showing differences in brain activity between super-recognisers and typical viewers (e.g., Faghel-Soubeyrand et al., 2024 Nador et al., 2025), we asked whether super-recognisers superior abilities are founded on differences in the dimensional structure of neural face identity coding. We recorded 64-channel electroencephalography as 23 Super-Recognisers and 21 typical controls viewed rapid sequences of faces representing 40 different identities (10 different images of each person). For each participant, we used time-resolved Representational Similarity Analysis to derive pairwise dissimilarities for the 40 identities, then examined how consistent this representational geometry was between each pair of observers using correlation. Our results showed that compared to controls, Super-Recognisers exhibited heightened consistency with each other during a mid-latency interval (300-500ms). Moreover, while identity information was reliably decodable in both groups, individual identities were more separable for Super-Recognisers during this same time window. These results suggest that Super-Recognisers have more differentiated neural representations of face identity than typical viewers do, and that dimensional structure of face identity codes is meaningfully related to superior performance on overt face recognition/matching tasks.
