title: A Reexamination of Infants’ Discrimination of Mooney Faces
affiliations:
1. Rikkyo University (JP)
2. Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JP)
3. Nigata University (JP)
abstract: Some previous studies suggest that infants use various strategies to discriminate between faces  and that face discrimination is highly robust to information degradation (e.g., masks, caricatures). We previously investigated the ability of 6–18-month-old infants to discriminate between faces in the Mooney face condition (faces degraded into two-toned black-and-white images) (Takashima et al., 2025), employing the visual paired comparison task (e.g., DeBolt & Oakes, 2023), a simplified version of the habituation method. We found no evidence that infants could discriminate individuals from Mooney faces. However, it is possible that a more sensitive experimental method with longer habituation trials may reveal evidence of Mooney face discrimination in infancy. In the present study, we conducted an experiment using a familiarity/novelty preference procedure with 6–18-month-old infants (final sample: N = 24). The experiment began with six familiarization trials (15 seconds × 6 trials). In each familiarization trial, a pair of Mooney faces depicting the same individual was presented side by side. After the six familiarization trials, two test trials (10 seconds × 2 trials) followed. In each test trial, two Mooney faces were presented side by side: one depicting the same individual as in the familiarization stimuli and the other depicting a novel individual. Infants’ gaze behavior toward the visual stimuli was recorded using an eye tracker.  We expected that if the infants could discriminate between individuals from Mooney faces, they would show significant visual preferences for the novel face in the test trials. However, no significant novelty preference was observed (two-tailed one-sample t-test: t (23) = 1.70, p = .102[NS1] , d = 0.35). Given that the much more sensitive method adopted in the present study failed to find evidence of face discrimination, infants in this age range may be unable to discriminate individuals from Mooney faces.

title: Visual Preferences for Familiar Faces in Chimpanzees: Effects of Social Separation and Long-term Memory.
affiliations:
1. Japan Women's University (JP)
2. Institute for the Evolutionary Origins of Human Behavior, Kyoto University (JP)
abstract:
Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) are highly social primates that, like humans, generally exhibit visual preferences for the faces of conspecifics and kin. However, previous findings on visual preferences for familiar individuals have been inconsistent: some studies report preferences for former groupmates, whereas others find no such bias for current groupmates. To determine whether these preferences reflect simple familiarity or long-term memory associated with social separation, we examined the effect of cohabitation recency on visual attention in this species.

In Experiment 1, using eye tracking, we presented pairs of images consisting of either a ‘past groupmate’ or a ‘current groupmate’ alongside a ‘novel individual.’ We measured total looking time and first-look latency (the time required to first orient to each stimulus). The results clearly revealed a significant preference for familiar individuals—indicated by longer looking times—only when images of past groupmates were presented. No significant differences were found in first-look latencies, suggesting that familiarity did not modulate initial reflexive orienting.

In Experiment 2, we examined whether this preference was driven by the ‘recency of the photograph’ or by ‘social separation.’ We paired novel faces with images of current groupmates taken either in the ‘past’ (approximately 20 years ago) or ‘recently’ (within 1 year). No significant familiar-face preferences or latency differences were observed in either condition. This indicates that the visual novelty of older photographs alone does not elicit a preference.

These findings suggest that visual preferences for faces in chimpanzees are not induced by simple familiarity or by the visual novelty of older photographs, but rather by the social context of long-term separation. This study demonstrates that chimpanzees maintain robust long-term representations of former social partners even after decades of separation. Furthermore, these results suggest that such social memories are reflected in sustained looking behavior rather than in initial visual orienting.

title: Near-vision scene categorization across eccentricities using a Humphrey-inspired spatial framework
affiliations:
1. LPNC (FR)
2. GIPSA-LAB (FR)
abstract: Ageing is associated with progressive visual changes, including reduced access to fine details, particularly in near vision due to declining accommodative capacity. Despite their ecological relevance, near-vision constraints are rarely considered in studies investigating visual processing across the visual field. The present study introduces a novel scene categorization paradigm that organizes the scene display to align with the Humphrey 30-2 visual field test, a standardized clinical test used to evaluate visual field sensitivity across eccentricities. This organization enables sampling of categorization performance across eccentricities in near vision. This work constitutes a feasibility study conducted in young adults with normal vision to validate the methodological implementation of this approach before its application to ageing populations. Grayscale photographs of indoor and outdoor scenes were presented binocularly at a viewing distance of 30 cm within concentric annular regions spanning 0° to 30° of visual angle. Stimuli were designed using a partition of the visual field into five cortically equivalent annular regions based on a cortical magnification function, ensuring that each region corresponded to an equivalent surface of primary visual cortex. The eccentricity boundaries were 0-2.8°, 2.8-7.1°, 7.1-12.7°, 12.7-20.1°, and 20.1-30.0°. Participants performed a categorization task (indoor vs. outdoor) while maintaining central fixation. On each trial, a stimulus corresponding to one of the five eccentricity regions was presented. Stimuli were displayed for 200 ms in Experiment 1, based on Humphrey perimetry duration, and for 100 ms in Experiment 2, based on rapid scene categorization tasks. Performance varied across eccentricities in a non-monotonic manner, with higher error rates at central locations and better performance at near-peripheral positions, indicating that scene categorization in near vision does not rely solely on central vision, consistent with previous findings. These findings demonstrate that the proposed paradigm provides a reliable framework for assessing visual performance across eccentricities in near vision.

title: Age-related changes in visual field asymmetries
affiliations:
1. Institute of Psychology, Jagiellonian University (PL)
2. Centre for Brain Research, Jagiellonian University (PL)
3. Doctoral School in the Social Sciences, Jagiellonian University
4. Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science, New York University (US)
abstract: Visual perception is not uniform across the visual field. Extensive research indicates that performance in a wide range of visual tasks is typically superior along the horizontal relative to the vertical meridian (horizontal–vertical anisotropy, HVA) and enhanced along the lower compared to the upper vertical meridian (vertical meridian asymmetry, VMA). While the HVA becomes more pronounced through adolescence and the VMA emerges during adolescence (Carrasco et al., 2025), it remains unclear whether and how they evolve across the adult lifespan. Neuroimaging evidence links individual differences in the VMA in a visual working memory task to microstructural properties of the early visual cortex that vary with age (Papiernik-Kłodzińska et al., 2026). This raises the possibility that aging alters the spatial organization of visual performance. To test this, we compare young (18–30 years) and older (60–80 years) adults in an orientation discrimination task. Gabor patches are presented at four cardinal locations (upper, lower, left, and right) at 6° eccentricity, with contrast individually thresholded to achieve ~80% accuracy across the locations prior to the main task.  During the task, participants indicate whether the target stimulus is tilted clockwise or counterclockwise from the vertical. Fixation is monitored using eye-tracking, and trials with fixation breaks are repeated at the end of each block. Older adults are screened using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) to ensure a cognitively healthy sample. We will report HVA and VMA indices derived from discriminability (d′) differences across locations and assess age-related differences in their magnitude. We hypothesize that aging reshapes polar angle asymmetries in visual performance, potentially reflecting underlying neuroarchitectural changes in the aging visual system.

title: Illusory uniformity of connectedness and peripheral numerosity perception
affiliations:
1. University of Bologna, Department of Psychology (IT)
2. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Previous research has shown that exposure to textures with center-periphery discontinuities can, under some conditions, lead to the illusory impression of a uniform texture, in which the quality of the central stimulus extends to the periphery (e.g., Otten et al., 2017). Furthermore, it has been shown that for the texture composed by dots and lines, if the lines connect the dots, the apparent numerosity of the dots is reduced (e.g. Franconeri et al., 2009 He et al., 2009). In our first experiment, we verified that the illusion of uniformity also applies to the connectedness of dots. We had observers judge whether the dots in the peripheral region of a texture were connected, while orthogonally manipulating the connectedness of the central region. The results confirmed that, despite not being informative, the central portion of the texture produced a congruent bias on peripheral perception: dots in the periphery appeared more connected when the central portion was connected, and vice versa.   In our second experiment, we investigated whether the illusory connectedness induced by the central stimulus also biases the perceived numerosity of the peripheral stimulus. To this end, observers compared the number of dots in a peripheral sector of the texture with that in a subsequent central probe. The physical density of dots in the peripheral sector varied between trials, and the presence of connected or unconnected dots in the center varied orthogonally. The PSE tracked peripheral numerosity, confirming that observers attended to the peripheral stimulus however, there was no significant effect of the connectedness of the central stimulus, failing to provide evidence for an effect of illusory connectedness.  We speculate that other perceptual biases, such as the general reduction in perceived peripheral numerosity or other biases related to stimulus regularity, might have dominated the observers’ judgements, overshadowing the effect of connectedness.

title: Examining spatial and temporal processing of low spatial frequency sine and square gratings
affiliations: 1. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: Early vision models aim to explain how visual information is encoded in the first stages of the visual system. Interest in such models has grown in recent years, as they improve human–machine alignment when used as pre-processors for deep neural networks (DNN) (Dapello et al., 2020). Progress, however, partly depends on high-quality data to constrain the parameters of nonlinear models (Wichmann, 1999). One influential study in the field of spatial vision is Campbell and Robson (1968). In it, they propose that the initial encoding of visual information is in independent, narrowly tuned spatial-frequency channels. Despite its influence, the study relied on only two observers and the method of adjustment, making the data less than ideal for constraining the parameters of early vision models. An often overlooked finding is the elevated square-over-sine sensitivity ratio at low spatial frequencies, exceeding the predicted value of 4/π. This has been attributed to harmonics of low-frequency stimuli falling into more sensitive mid-frequency channels. This hypothesis can be tested by reducing harmonic contributions. Short presentation durations or high temporal frequencies shift the contrast sensitivity function (CSF) from bandpass to lowpass (Kelly, 1979), which should lower the square-over-sine ratio toward 4/π . Green, Corwin, and Schor (1981) confirmed this using 25ms presentations, though again with limited participants and the method of adjustment. Here, we replicate and extend these classic findings using a two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) design with sufficient participants and trials to ensure statistical power. We test spatial frequencies of 0.25, 0.5, 1, and 2 cpd across presentation durations of 33, 333, and 1067 ms, along with a 15Hz flicker condition. This design allows us to probe both spatial and temporal summation. Together, our experiments provide a much extended replication of a seminal spatial vision study, making the results suitable for constraining parameters of early vision models.

title: Improving a fast and modular image-computable psychophysical spatial vision model
affiliations:
1. University of Tübingen (DE)
2. CS@Max Planck (DE)
abstract: To explain the initial encoding of pattern information in the human visual system, the standard psychophysical spatial vision model is based on channels specific to spatial frequency and orientation with the human contrast sensitivity function (CSF) as the envelope of the sensitivities of the individual channels, followed by divisive normalization (contrast gain-control). Schütt and Wichmann (2017, Journal of Vision) developed an image-computable implementation of the standard model and showed it to be able to explain data for contrast detection, contrast discrimination and oblique masking and to some extent natural-image masking. Furthermore, the model induces a sparse encoding of luminance information. Reichert and Wichmann (2024, VSS) provided a modern, efficient, automatically differentiable implementation of this model in the deep-learning framework PyTorch enabling easy and fast training of model parameters on image data. We extend Reichert and Wichmann's implementation by allowing learning of the lapse rate as a hyper-parameter. This can drastically improve its deviance (up to 100 %) on the same contrast-discrimination data as Schütt and Wichmann. We capture the dependence of the fitted parameters on presentation duration. Moreover, we discuss individual differences in the fitted parameters and how these differences might in addition be captured. An advantage of our model is its modularity and automatic differentiation because this facilitates rapid implementation, addition, and testing of new components of the standard spatial vision model. We use the model’s fast inference, specifically, to estimate confidence intervals for and the loss landscapes between model parameters. Furthermore, our extensible framework allows the integration of this psychophysically validated model into larger image-processing pipelines with elements such as retINRF (Velasco-Salido et al., 2026, ECCV) to account for retinal processing or downstream convolutional neural networks (CNNs) such as VOneNet (Dapello et al., 2020, NeurIPS), where it may increase performance or energy efficiency due to its relative simplicity.

title: Enhancing the Sensitivity of the Redundant Target Paradigm
affiliations: 1. Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (DE)
abstract: The redundant target effect refers to the well-established principle that responses are faster to two simultaneous targets than to one. Beyond its theoretical interest, the phenomenon has attracted attention as a tool to probe residual visual capacities (controversially termed “blindsight”) within the blind field of patients suffering from homonymous hemianopia. Residual visual capacities are inferred when the redundant target significantly accelerates responses, even when it is presented in the blind field. Yet, a recent review showed that classic versions of the redundant target paradigm (RTP) have limited sensitivity, with almost half of patients failing to show the effect for one versus two targets presented in their sighted hemifield, meaning the RTP frequently misses even undisputed visual capacities. This study aimed to enhance the sensitivity of the RTP through optimizing the experimental design in healthy participants. In Experiments 1 and 2, target saliency (1: numerosity, 2: size), asymmetric configurations, and bimanual versus unimanual responses were investigated: the largest redundancy gains occurred for bimanual responses and asymmetric configurations, specifically a low-saliency target in the single condition and an additional high-saliency target in the redundant condition. As manipulating size yielded a slight advantage, this approach was adopted in Experiment 3.  In Experiment 3, the presumed blind-field (large) target was further advantaged by presenting it slightly before the small target. Healthy participants were asked to respond only to the small target, while the large target preceded it by variable stimulus-onset asynchronies (SOAs). Reaction time benefits increased with SOAs. At the single-case level, 85% of participants showed a significant effect at the longest SOA, rising to 96% when trials across SOAs were combined, underscoring the importance of increasing the number of trials. This optimized RTP could thus provide a highly sensitive test of blindsight.

title: Scene visibility is shaped by interactions between central and peripheral visual field information
affiliations:
1. LPNC, University Grenoble Alpes (FR)
2. Laboratoire de Psychologie Sociale et Cognitive, University Clermont Auvergne (FR)
abstract: Past studies have shown mutual interactions between information extracted in central and parafoveal or peripheral vision in the context of scene categorization, where information from one visual field influences categorization in the other one. The present study examined whether such interactions also influence scene visibility across the visual field. Experiment 1 (n = 32) addressed the influence of peripheral information on scene visibility in central vision while Experiment 2 (n = 29) addressed the opposite. In both experiments, scene information in the target visual field (a central disk in Experiment 1 or a peripheral ring in Experiment 2) was embedded in noise and participants performed a scene-in-noise and a noise-in-scene detection task. providing complementary measures of scene visibility. We manipulated information available in the non-target visual field which was either congruent, incongruent or meaningless relative to the target visual field. Detection thresholds were estimated using adaptive 1up-1down staircases, to obtain Scene-in-Noise and Noise-in-Scene detection thresholds for each condition of visual information in the non-target visual field. Results showed that in both experiments meaningful and structured information in the non-target visual field (congruent or incongruent) improved scene perception in the target visual field compared to meaningless information. Experiment 2 indicated that peripheral scene visibility is further improved by the presence of congruent central information. These findings are interpreted in the context of the predictive processing framework, suggesting that high-level information extracted in one visual field can be used to generate predictions that improve perception of degraded information in the remaining visual field.

title: The ERP Neural Response to Symmetry is Dependent upon Temporal Order
affiliations: 1. University of Stirling (UK)
abstract: The difference in the Event Related Potential (ERP) response to symmetry and noise, termed the Sustained Posterior Negativity (SPN) is believed to be a task-invariant biomarker of automatic symmetry perception. Most ERP studies of symmetry have used single-interval forced-choice (1IFC) designs, disregarding the temporal order of events and their continuity/predictability over time. Here, we use a 2IFC design in two separate experiments (symmetry vs. colour detection), combined with machine learning models, to examine how temporal order and task affect ERP responses to symmetry. Critically, if the SPN response is automatically generated by the presence of symmetry, no temporal-order effects or task differences would be present. We used three conditions: two fixed-order where the stimuli in each trial were the same, i.e., symmetry before noise (SN) or vice-versa (NS), and a random condition where each trial could be either SN or NS. We found that (a) for fixed SN trials the classic SPN effect was observed (symmetry lower than noise 250-600 ms after stimulus onset) while for fixed NS trials this effect reversed for the symmetry detection task, and was absent in the colour detection task (b) N1 component was found to encode stimulus position, with larger amplitude for first stimulus (c) P1 component showed sensitivity to symmetry with amplitude being larger for symmetry compared to noise (d) classification of single trial EEG epochs using EEGNeX and EEGConformer achieved highest accuracy for fixed-order conditions (~72%/~64%), but performance dropped to chance (~49%/~52%) when models trained on one fixed-order condition (SN) were tested on the other (NS). These findings suggest that decoding relied on condition-specific temporal structure rather than a general symmetry response, contradicting the notion that the SPN reflects a task-invariant automatic process, and highlighting the role of stimulus predictability and presentation order in shaping ERP-based to symmetry perception.

title: Cardiac cycle and visual performance: beyond a categorical phase effect
affiliations: 1. The University of Tokyo (JP)
abstract: Visual perception is not isolated from the bodily rhythm. A growing literature suggests that the phase of the cardiac cycle, namely cardiac systole and diastole, modulates visual perception. However, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here, we asked whether a simple 2IFC contrast discrimination task is modulated by the cardiac phase at which stimuli are presented.  In our pilot study, ten participants judged which of two sequentially presented Gabor patches had higher contrast. Using online physiological signal processing, one stimulus was timed to a systolic anchor (250 ms after the preceding ECG R-peak) and the other to a diastolic anchor (75% of the current R–R interval). The contrast difference between the two Gabors was parametrically varied, and external visual noise (Low/High) was added to manipulate visual sensitivity independently. R-peaks were re-detected offline from raw ECG only trials in which the two stimuli fell in opposite cardiac phases were retained for analysis, yielding around 739 trials per participant.  Psychometric fitting confirmed that external noise elevated the JND (Low = 0.061, High = 0.079). However, the previously reported cardiac phase effect, defined as the mean accuracy difference between systole-target and diastole-target trials, was not significant in either noise condition. In an exploratory analysis, we asked whether trial-by-trial variability in cardiac timing, rather than categorical phase, could explain performance. For each trial, we computed the mismatch between the predicted and actual timing of the next heartbeat, estimated from preceding R–R intervals. The directional mismatch related to accuracy: trials on which the next heartbeat arrived later than predicted were associated with better discrimination. These findings suggest that visual contrast discrimination is sensitive not to a fixed systole–diastole dichotomy but to beat-to-beat deviations in cardiac timing, pointing to a dynamic rather than categorical link between cardiac signals and vision.

title: Good times for vision science: reading the time from an analogue clock as a visual task
affiliations:
1. Centre for Brain Research, Jagiellonian University (PL)
2. Neurocognitive and Experimental Psychology Lab, Free University of Berlin (DE)
abstract: Reading the time from an analogue clock is a visual task with three advantages that rarely coincide: it is naturalistic, can be easily studied under experimental control, and requires specific skills. Yet, unlike other such tasks (e.g. reading text), it has received little attention in the scientific literature. Here, we aim to fill this gap and establish ‘clock reading’ as an experimental task for vision science. To break this new ground, we conducted two crowd-sourced online experiments (total N = 866). The first experiment assessed the difficulty of reading 144 different times (from midnight to noon) separated by five-minute intervals. On each trial, participants saw a numeral-free clock face for two seconds and typed the time they read afterwards. To minimize within-experiment learning, we divided the sample into twelve groups, and each group saw only 13 unique times (including a training trial). The average accuracy of responses per participant was 0.7. Intriguingly, it was markedly lower for times with the minute hand located on the left side of the dial. The second experiment had an identical trial structure, but it used a 24-element subset of the 144 times that, based on the first experiment, covered the range of times spanning from the easiest to read to the most difficult ones. It tested whether the presence of numerals and longer presentation duration affect clock reading accuracy. We found that the former factor had a stronger facilitatory effect than the latter. Overall, our results show that the procedure from the second experiment provides a good measure of an individual’s ability to read the time from an analogue clock. Therefore, it can be used in future research on still unexplored perceptual and cognitive aspects of clock reading. Funding: National Science Centre, Poland (2024/55/D/HS6/02157) and Polish National Agency for Academic Exchange NAWA (Ulam Programme).

title: Distinguishing objective and subjective prediction error in the human brain
affiliations:
1. University College London (UK)
2. University of Amsterdam (UK)
3. Birkbeck University of London (UK)
abstract: Under predictive coding accounts of perception, the brain continuously generates predictions about incoming sensory input, with mismatches between predictions and actual input generating prediction error signals that drive learning and perceptual updating. Prediction error signals have been shown to evoke amplified neural responses in sensory, striatal, and brainstem regions. In prior work, these prediction error signals have typically been characterised using the objective statistics of the environment - for example, by contrasting high- versus low-probability events, or by modelling trial-by-trial prediction error magnitudes using normative learning models. However, while it seems that predictions errors may be processed implicitly, some error signals are accompanied by conscious experience – for example, a subjective experience that an event was unexpected. Due to the focus on objective statistics, little is known about the mechanisms by which subjective experience of structure drives perception and learning. Intriguingly, recent behavioural work from our lab (Clarke et al, 2026) has shown that reported expectations and surprise explained more unique variance in perceptual decision speed and accuracy than that captured by objective stimulus statistics and model-derived prediction errors. To investigate the neural mechanisms supporting the representation of subjective relative to objective probabilistic structure, we recorded fMRI in 30 participants performing an auditory-visual associative learning task, in which visual Gabor orientations were predicted by preceding auditory tones with 75% or 25% probability. Participants rated the expectedness of each outcome on every trial, allowing us to compare subjective prediction error magnitude against objective prediction errors derived from different computational learning models. We show how brainstem, sensory and frontal structures differentially encode probabilistic structure and our subjective experience of it. Specifically, we consider how subjective experience of expectation and expectation violation may shape the neural encoding of prediction errors in ways that have been overlooked with previous focus on pure objective structure.

title: Colours of Consciousness: Testing Predictive Mechanisms of Subjective Experience through Synesthetic Training
affiliations:
1. Donders Centre for Cognition (NL)
2. Radboud University (NL)
3. Tilburg University (NL)
abstract: Understanding how the brain generates subjective experience remains a fundamental challenge. The Predictive Processing Framework (PPF) proposes a bold answer: conscious perception reflects the brain’s predictions rather than incoming sensory input directly. If true, systematically altering predictions should directly alter what we experience this claim has rarely been tested empirically. We address this question using grapheme–colour synesthesia (GCS) as a model of prediction-driven perception. In GCS, achromatic letters reliably evoke colour experiences, illustrating how internal models shape perceptual content. We manipulate prediction strength in non-synesthetes (N = 24) using a longitudinal “reading-in-colour” paradigm, in which participants are trained on systematically coloured texts with parametrically varied letter–colour probabilities and letter frequencies. Their performance is compared to that of developmental synesthetes (N = 24). Participants complete behavioural and pupillometry sessions before and after training. Subjective colour experience is assessed using detailed questionnaires, while pupil dilation indexes prediction error and information gain. Using information-theoretic measures, we test whether physiological responses scale with model-derived estimates of information gain, and whether the intensity of reported colour experience scales with the strength of learned predictions, indexed by pupil dynamics. This approach enables a direct, quantitative link between computational theory, physiological signals, and phenomenology. By showing that experimentally induced predictions shape both physiology and conscious experience, this work provides a stringent test of the PPF’s central claim. More broadly, this work contributes to the development of pupil dynamics as a tractable, non-invasive marker of subjective experience and offers a framework for studying how the brain constructs perceptual reality.

title: Paradoxical influences of prediction are resolved across time
affiliations:
1. University College London (UK)
2. Birkbeck, University of London (UK)
abstract: It is widely thought that the brain uses expectations to optimise perception, yet theoretical accounts disagree about the form of this optimisation. Bayesian accounts propose that perception is biased towards expected events, rapidly generating more veridical experiences, whereas cancellation accounts argue that unexpected inputs are perceptually prioritised as they are more informative. A recent opposing process theory reconciles these views by proposing a temporal reversal in prioritisation: perceptual processing is pre-emptively biased towards what is expected, followed by later enhancement of only particularly surprising inputs that are informative for learning and model updating.  We tested this account across two EEG studies using time-resolved decoding. In Study 1, we leveraged expectations acquired over a lifetime of experience concerning action outcomes. Participants observed avatar action outcomes that were either expected or unexpected given their own movements. Decoding revealed a temporal reversal: representations of task-relevant expected outcomes were enhanced from before stimulus onset, followed by a later post-stimulus advantage for unexpected outcomes. Study 2 examined whether this later advantage for unexpected events depends on the degree of surprise. Participants learned cue-outcome relationships that were subsequently violated during the EEG session, allowing outcome probability to be parametrically manipulated. Behavioural performance tracked trial-wise surprisal, indicating sensitivity to graded outcome probabilities. Preliminary decoding results suggest that later enhancement occurs selectively for highly surprising outcomes. Together, these results support the opposing process theory. By exerting distinct influences across time, expectations can render perception more veridical, while still allowing for the accurate perception of particularly surprising events that are important for updating our beliefs or ongoing courses of action.

title: Distinct Representations of Probabilistic Context in Perception and Eye Movements
affiliations:
1. Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone, Aix-Marseille University (FR)
2. Central European University, Center for Cognitive Computation (AT)
abstract: Perceptual decisions and eye movements are shaped by sensory information and expectations about the environment, reflecting experience-dependent internal models. Yet, they do not always adapt to context in the same way, suggesting they may rely on partly different internal representations.  In direction-biased motion tasks, anticipatory eye movements track the most frequent direction while perceptual discrimination is sometimes biased toward the least frequent one. Less is known about visually-guided eye movements. Here we ask whether perception and eye movements rely on a shared representation of context in a direction-biased random dot kinematogram (RDK) task, or distinct computational strategies. Thirteen observers (N = 13) performed a direction discrimination task in two conditions, reporting leftward or rightward motion in an RDK in a 2-AFC decision-making paradigm, while eye movements were recorded. The experiment comprised two phases: an adaptive staircase to estimate RDK direction discrimination thresholds, followed by a main task in which motion coherence varied randomly across trials. Crucially, motion direction probabilities shifted from unbiased (50/50) to biased (80/20), either abruptly (JUMP) or gradually (RAMP). In the JUMP condition, perceptual decisions were robustly biased toward the less frequent direction, a counterintuitive effect that persisted across trials and replicated prior findings, including an independent online experiment (N = 24). This deviates from normative predictions that favor the more frequent direction. Anticipatory eye movements were instead biased toward the more frequent direction, as was early visually guided smooth pursuit, though the latter appeared primarily driven by recent trial history with no clear influence of global probability. In the RAMP condition, the same pattern of oculomotor adaptation was observed, whereas the perceptual bias toward the less frequent direction was reduced, though it remained present. Together, these preliminary findings suggest a partial dissociation between perceptual and oculomotor processes, potentially governed by distinct internal representations of probabilistic context.
session_title: Poster Session 4 · Cognition, Decision Making, and Confidence

title: The effect of word meaningfulness on recognition performance during brief presentation
affiliations: 1. Institute of Psychology, Vilnius University (LT)
abstract: We investigated whether memory has a greater capacity for meaningful words compared to random letter strings in brief presentations. The study consisted of two experiments. Both experiments involved presenting a 3 x 4 letter array for a duration of 50 ms. The first experiment was performed without masking, while in the second experiment, masking was presented immediately after the stimulus presentation. The array consisted either of random letters or meaningful four-letter words. Each session included 100 trials with a random presentation of either letters or words. After each presentation, subjects reported what they had seen by filling an empty array with all remembered letters in their correct spatial positions.  We found that the number of correctly identified letters increased when the letters formed meaningful words. This effect was observed in both masking and non-masking conditions. In the random letter condition, subjects recalled between 2 to 5 letters without a mask and 1 to 3 letters with a mask. In the meaningful word condition, subjects recalled 1 to 3 words (4 to 12 letters) without a mask and 1 word (4 letters) with a mask. These findings suggest that information is not stored in memory as visual information and later accessed letter by letter by attention rather, it is passed to the semantic center for analysis immediately after the stimulus display. Additionally, we noted substantial individual variability in recalling meaningful words from brief presentations.

title: Does the visual adaptation of causality spread across objects?
affiliations:
1. Institut für Psychologie, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (DE)
2. Angewandte Humanwissenschaften, Hochschule Magdeburg-Stendal (DE)
abstract: Humans report a vivid impression of launching when one object approaches another object, which moves in the same direction upon touching. This perception of causality can be altered by visual adaptation: after prolonged exposure to launch events, observers are less likely to report perceiving a launch in subsequent ambiguous test events, ranging from launching to passing events by manipulating the disc overlap of these two objects. In Experiment 1 (n=12), we tested whether adaptation to causality spreads to different parts of an object even if those parts did not have direct contact with the other object involved in the launching event. The adaptor stimulus consisted of a single disc colliding with a vertical stack of five discs (each 1.5 dva in diameter), of which the point of collision was always at the bottom of the stack. Test events were presented at one of three vertical locations relative to the larger object: center, top, and bottom. We found adaptation effects only for test events that were presented at the bottom, indicating strong spatial specificity with no evidence for a spread of causality. In Experiment 2 (n=12), we examined whether a larger moving object colliding with a single disc would elicit the same spatial specificity. This time, the adaptor stimulus consisted of a vertical rectangle colliding with a single disc. Here, we observed evidence for a spread of adaptation in the launching object. Adaptation effects emerged at the center and top locations, but not at the bottom. Crucially, an additional adaptor stimulus designed to control for motion offset did not produce adaptation effects. Together, these findings suggest that perceived causality relies on spatially precise mechanisms tied to the point of contact however, adaptation can also spread to parts of an object that had no direct contact with the launched object.

title: Selective responses to ordered sequences of letters and numbers with EEG frequency tagging
affiliations:
1. University of Lorraine (FR)
2. KU Leuven (BE)
3. University of Luxembourg (LU)
abstract: Memory for sequences of items is an important aspect of human cognition, but its representation is debated. Sequential memory may be represented more through relative item order, or more through collective chunks of items. One challenge is that variable explicit ordering or memory tasks are used in experimental research. We introduce a relevant task-free approach to record sequence-specific responses with EEG frequency tagging. Participants, uniformed about item sequences, were simply instructed to detect fixation-cross shape changes. Participants were shown rapid sequences of seven repeating items (letters, numbers, or colors) at a rate of 0.15 s per item, i.e., 6.7 Hz. If these sequences of items are automatically chunked, we expected to observe sequence-specific responses at 0.95 Hz (i.e., 6.7 Hz/7) and its harmonics. Selective sequence-specific responses were recorded to familiar, ordered letter sequences (ABCDEFG), suggesting that this letter string may be represented as an integral chunk. In contrast, we did not observe selective sequence responses to familiar, ordered sequences of an incomplete chunk of numbers (1234567). However, when this sequence was reshaped into a continuous fluid pattern (123456765432), a selective sequence response did occur. Overall, EEG frequency tagging of sequences appears to be a promising approach to investigate representations of sequences in memory. The present results suggest that the presentation of ordered sequences without an order-related task does not automatically elicit an order-recognition brain response. Instead, the results are in line with associative models with holistic chunking for sequential memory.

title: Too Much of the Same Thing: Overweighting Correlated Visual Evidence
affiliations:
1. University of Bergen (NO)
2. University of California, Berkeley (US)
abstract: In socioeconomic decisions, people routinely treat correlated evidence as independent, overestimating its value. For example, a news story retold by several tabloids might be perceived as more truthful than when reported by a single outlet, despite originating from a single source. This phenomenon coined 'correlation neglect' is widely studied, yet its mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that this inability to account for correlations is not limited to socioeconomic decision-making but is also present in low-level perceptual decisions. Observers averaged color or orientation stimuli that were drawn randomly on each trial from a multivariate normal distribution. The distribution's covariance matrix was set in such a way that the features for half of the matrix were correlated, while in a control condition, no correlation was present. An ideal observer, aware of this task structure, would downweight correlated information. In contrast, the real observers consistently overweight correlated information across color and orientation experiments, indicating that they are not just neglecting the correlations, but treat correlated stimuli as more informative. We discuss mechanisms underlying this bias to visual correlations, which offer potential insights into the underlying cause of correlation neglect in socioeconomic decision-making.
session_title: Poster Session 4 · Cognition, Decision Making, and Confidence

title: Interactions between the brainstem and visual cortex in processing surprise.
affiliations:
1. University College London (UK)
2. Maastricht University (NL)
3. University of Amsterdam (NL)
abstract: To navigate the world as efficiently as we do, our perceptual systems integrate prior knowledge with sensory signals. According to predictive processing accounts, laminar organisation in the cortex supports this integration: top-down predictions about sensations activate deep layers of sensory cortex, input synapses onto middle layers, and the prediction error is computed in superficial layers. Furthermore, it has been proposed that, after large prediction error signals in the cortex, subsequent catecholamine release supported by brainstem structures might reactively amplify unexpected sensory representations. By capturing visual cortex and brainstem activity simultaneously with 7T fMRI, we investigated how these processes interact to determine what we perceive. During pre-scanning training, participants learned to associate auditory tones (high or low) with an on-screen Gabor patch (CW or CCW), where p(CW|low) = p(CCW|high) = 1. During scanning, participants were still exposed to expected tone-Gabor pairings on 75% of trials (p(CW|low) = p(CCW|high) = 0.75) but these were accompanied by unexpected pairings on the other 25%. Behaviourally there was evidence that participants learnt in the anticipated fashion - reaction times were faster for expected than unexpected trials in early scanning blocks and the effect declined across time. We test the idea that the laminar profile of visual cortex exhibits preferences according to purported predomination of unit types, with the expected represented with higher fidelity than the unexpected in deep layers and the converse preference in superficial layers. We also ask whether brainstem structures – specifically the Locus Coeruleus, the Raphe Nucleus, and the Ventral Tegmental Area – are more responsive to the unexpected, as well as how the brainstem and visual cortical effects interact. We discuss the implications of this novel 7T fMRI examination of brainstem-laminar sensory interactions for our understanding of perceptual processing and learning.
session_title: Poster Session 4 · Cognition, Decision Making, and Confidence

title: Tracking Word Order in Reading: Evidence from Eye Movements and Fixation-Related Potentials
affiliations:
1. Bournemouth University (UK)
2. Northumbria University (UK)
3. University of Lancashire (UK)
abstract: In a recent eye tracking study, Atanasov et al. (2025) reported limited evidence for early parallel lexical processing during reading. The present study extends this work by manipulating the word order of a target word pair (transposed vs. non-transposed) and sentence final word grammaticality (grammatical vs. ungrammatical), while introducing a balanced grammaticality judgment task (50% “yes”, 50% “no” answers) and co-registering participants’ eye movements and EEG. This design enables a direct test of claims that word transposition effects may arise earlier than is detectable in eye movement data and are more sensitively indexed by neural measures. Preliminary eye movement results replicate the original Atanasov et al.’s findings. No parafoveal effects of word transposition are observed in the Pre-Target region. Disruption caused by word transposition is first detected at Target Word 1, and to a reduced extent at Target Word 2, with transpositions eliciting longer reading times. In the Post-Target region, reading times are longest when participants encountered an ungrammatical sentence final word for the first time. Overall, these findings support a view that processing is incremental and cue driven, with disruption being localised to the point of fixation of the ungrammaticality. Ongoing fixation-related potential analyses will determine whether earlier neural effects are detectable, providing a stronger test of parallel processing accounts.

title: How do humans see horse faces?
affiliations:
1. Bournemouth University (UK)
2. Equine.Training (UK)
3. Writtle School of Agriculture, Anglia Ruskin University (UK)
4. University of São Paulo (BR)
abstract: There is increasing interest in the scientific literature regarding which facial cues reliably indicate pain and affect in horses, with an aim to improve their welfare. Although pain and discomfort ethograms have been published, little is known about the human ability to spontaneously perceive pain and affect from the faces of horses without such guides. Our previous research (Gregory et al., 2025) was the first to show how some psychological traits (social anxiety) but not others (empathy) predict perception of pain in horse faces, and that equine care-giving experience predicts accuracy of pain ratings. However, no research has assessed which features are attended to when humans assess horse faces for pain. As such, we examined participants’ eye movements whilst they viewed thirty images of horse faces,  displaying a range of expressions, for five seconds each, and then rated levels of perceived pain, arousal and valence. Participants also completed online questionnaires assessing a range of psychological traits and their horse care-giving experience. Subsequently, interest areas were assigned to each face according to key regions associated with pain and affect cues, and dwell time % to each was calculated.  Overall, we found that participants with horse-care experience looked mostly at the eyes (33%), followed by the upper-face, then the nose/muzzle, then ears, and finally the mid-face (4%). There was a medium positive correlation between years of horse-care experience and gaze to the eyes, and a medium negative correlation between gaze to the ears and years of horse experience. Relationships between psychological traits, pain ratings and dwell time to the AOIs will also be presented. Current findings indicate that horse experience, which we previously showed predicted pain rating accuracy, is associated with increased gaze to the eyes, suggesting the eyes are a critical feature for determining pain and affect in horse faces.

title: Eye-movement manifestations of differential safety-behaviour strategies in social anxiety
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Social-cognitive theories (e.g. Clark & Wells, 1995) suggest individuals with social anxiety (SA) employ both avoidance and impression management safety-behaviours to reduce anxiety. The avoidance sub-type manifests primarily as eye-contact avoidance. Cognitive behavioural therapies aim to reduce eye-contact avoidance in SA in favour of increased engagement with positive social cues (e.g. Yoshinaga et al., 2024).  However, both safety-behaviour types are thought to increase feelings of self-focussed attention, increasing anxiety. Despite the theory, the relationship between SA, feelings of self-focus and objective attention measured by eye-tracking, have not been examined during a live social interaction.  Therefore, we recorded eye-movements of non-clinical participants with high (HSA  N= 34), moderate (MSA N = 34), and low (LSA N = 18) SA during a live video call where a confederate interviewer displayed different  emotional expressions (positive, neutral, negative) and where participants’ self-camera was either visible or not (directly manipulating self-focus, as in Vriends et al., 2017). State anxiety, state social anxiety, and feelings of self-focus were also measured.  HSA participants reported greater self-focus, and higher state SA, which was unaffected by self-camera visibility. HSA made fewest fixations to the interviewer’s eyes/face, particularly when the confederate had a neutral/negative expression. The MSA group made more fixations to the interviewer’s eyes than the HSA group, despite reporting equivalent state anxiety.  All participants increased interviewer-directed gaze during a positive expression whilst reducing interviewer-directed gaze when the self-camera was visible.  This study provides the first evidence for differential safety-behaviour strategies according to SA level: HSA showed avoidance, whereas MSA showed behaviour consistent with impression management: making more eye contact, a socially desirable behaviour. Self-focus was highest in HSA individuals, suggesting avoidance may be associated with higher self-focus than impression management, but turning the self-camera on/off did not impact feelings of self-focus.
session_title: Poster Session 4 · Social Perception and Emotion

title: Efficiency of Gaze and Covert Attention Allocation to Gesture-Like Peripheral Cues
affiliations: 1. KU Leuven (BE)
abstract: Gaze and gestures are central components of social interaction, but little is known about how visual attention is allocated to gestures in dynamic conversational contexts. In natural conversations, observers typically fixate faces while gestures occur in peripheral regions, suggesting that gesture perception may rely strongly on covert attention. We developed a novel experimental paradigm designed to approximate conversational turn-taking under controlled conditions. Participants stood in front of a large presentation screen displaying two stick figures positioned at conversational distance and size, forming a naturalistic three-person situation. Digits were presented in rapid succession in parallel at both “face” locations. Sometimes digits were replaced by target stimuli. The side on which the targets appeared switched from time to time. Participants were instructed to detect these targets and responded via button press. Information about the upcoming target side – analogous to a change of speaker – was conveyed by peripheral cues presented below the face locations, within the gesture space. Crucially, efficient task performance required maintaining fixation on the relevant face location while extracting cue information mainly from the periphery. A control group performed the identical task, but stimuli were embedded in visually matched, non-social configurations instead of stick figures. Eye movements were recorded using head-mounted eye tracking. Eye-movement data showed that gaze remained predominantly directed at the target stream regions, with only limited overt shifts toward the cue locations. Nevertheless, behavioral results (hit rates) revealed reliable cueing benefits, indicating that participants effectively used peripheral information to anticipate the target locations. This work demonstrates that conversational gaze behavior can be approximated experimentally and suggests that maintaining fixation on the face region, while processing gestures peripherally, may serve as an efficient and functionally advantageous strategy in conversations. These results further highlight the critical role of covert attention in processing communicative gestures during dynamic social interactions.

title: Decoding Bodily Emotion Dimensions: Interdependence Between Valence, Arousal, and Sociality
affiliations:
1. The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (HK)
2. Research Institute of Electrical Communication, Tohoku University (JP)
3. National Chung Cheng University (TW)
4. Research Institute of Electrical Communication, Tohoku University (JP)
abstract: Dimensional theories map affective states across different dimensions, such as arousal (strength or intensity), valence (degree of pleasantness or unpleasantness), and dominance (the degree of control an individual perceives). While facial, semantic, and vocal stimuli have demonstrated supporting evidence for the interdependence of emotional dimensions underlying general core affect, it remains unknown whether the bodily emotional expressions share the same dimensional construct across different emotion categories. We address this gap by asking 134 participants (62 Taiwanese and 72 Japanese) to rate their perceived arousal (0 = low, 10 = high), valence (-5 = negative, 5 = positive), and sociality (0 = towards self, 10 = towards others) on 486 point-light displays of 6 professional performers from a multi-cultural bodily emotion database, DIEM-A. The stimuli include four basic emotions (anger, fear, joy, and sadness) and five social emotions (gratitude, guilt, jealousy, pride, and shame) at three intensity levels (high, medium, and low). We discovered significant interrelations among the three dimensions. Regarding the valence-arousal relationship, a quadratic model outperformed linear fitting, revealing the lowest arousal ratings for neutral stimuli and gradually increasing arousal ratings as perceived valence increased toward both positive and negative sides for all emotions. Additionally, the valence-sociality relationship differed by emotion category: valence was positively associated with sociality for social emotions but showed no significant correlation for basic emotions. These findings provide empirical evidence that bodily emotion perception shares a similar valence-arousal structure with established models of affect and uniquely introduce sociality as a critical third dimension for differentiating social from basic emotions in bodily actions. This study advances a more holistic dimensional model of bodily emotion, suggesting that the visual perception of biological motion inherently encodes social intent alongside core affect.
session_title: Poster Session 4 · Social Perception and Emotion

title: Temporal dynamics of neural representations of social and object relations
affiliations:
1. Neural Computation Group, Justus Liebig University Gießen (DE)
2. Institut des Sciences Cognitives Marc Jeannerod, Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique & Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1 (FR)
3. Center for Applied Computer Science and Data Science, Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
4. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior, Philipps University Marburg, Justus Liebig University Giessen, and Technical University Darmstadt (DE)
5. Cluster of Excellence “The Adaptive Mind”, Justus Liebig University Giessen, Philipps University Marburg, and Technical University Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: Understanding the physical world requires understanding how things are related to each other in visual scenes. The temporal dynamics of relational representations remain largely unexplored. In this study we used electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate the time course of relational representations in minimalistic social and non-social visual scenes. Participants viewed pairs of humans (e.g. two humans shaking hands) or objects (e.g. an egg and an egg cup) (200 ms). Each pair was shown in a typical configuration for interacting (‘typical’ pairs), and an atypical configuration (‘atypical’ pairs) in which the items’ positions were swapped. In addition, pairs varied along different dimensions: Human pairs differed for type of interaction (communicative or physical) and interaction structure (reciprocal or transitive) whereas object pairs differed for functional structure (functionally constrained or interacting objects). EEG signals were analyzed using time-resolved representational similarity analysis (RSA). Results showed an early dissociation between social and non-social scenes beginning around 50 ms after stimulus onset. We also observed a typicality effect for human pairs where typical and atypical configurations produced distinct neural representations from ~90 ms. Typicality effects were much less pronounced for object pairs. Additional analyses revealed distinct neural representations for reciprocal versus transitive human pairs (from ~200 ms), and functionally constrained versus interactive object pairs (from ~160 ms). Together these findings demonstrate that relational information is rapidly encoded during visual perception, and suggest that social interactions evoke particularly strong and early relational representations in the visual system.
