title: The effect of dementia on art over a lifespan: do portraits tell a more personal story of cognitive decline?
affiliations:
1. Heriot-Watt University (AE)
2. Loughborough University (UK)
abstract: For an individual to create art a range of perceptual and cognitive functions are required. Our previous research has demonstrated that perceptual and cognitive systems are impaired as a result of developing dementias (e.g. Wilcockson, et al., 2019). Recently, our research indicated that linguistic analysis could be utilised to identify within an author’s writing career their use of language was affected by dementia (Pattison, Begde, & Wilcockson, 2026). This was found to be ten years prior to a dementia diagnosis, indicating a long preclinical period for dementias. Therefore, these results indicate that it is possible to retroactively analyse the work of artists who ultimately receive a dementia diagnosis to identify when in their career their perceptual and cognitive systems are impaired as a result of their developing dementia. In order to explore this hypothesis in the visual arts, six artists were identified three artists who created art who ultimately received a dementia diagnosis and three artists who created art into their old age but did not experience dementia. For each artist, a subset of paintings was collected, with each painting created at a different period across the artist’s lifespan. Image statistics were then calculated for each of the pieces of art, so that we could analyse within-subject changes in art style, but also between-subject differences between dementia and normal ageing artists. Overall, the results would indicate whether the early stages of cognitive decline affect the creation of art, potentially ten years earlier than clinical diagnosis. If this is the case, then it may ultimately be possible to consider using art as a diagnostic marker for cognitive decline.

title: Colour, Balance, Dynamics, and Liking in Self‑Arranged Suprematist Compositions: An Interactive Art Study
affiliations: 1. Giessen University (DE)
abstract: What makes a composition engaging? Drawing on the formal vocabulary of Suprematist art, this study explored how colour, compositional instruction, and personal preference influence the creation and aesthetic evaluation of self‑arranged works. Ten Suprematist art works were rendered as paper cut‑outs in two conditions: an original chromatic palette and a monochromatic variant featuring black shapes on a white background. Each of twenty art naïve participants produced three distinct compositions (“stable,” “dynamic,” and “interesting”) by arranging the cut‑outs before transcribing them digitally. Participants then rated their own works and the originals on perceived balance, stability, dynamism, liking, and interest. They started with the black shapes, two weeks later they repeated the process with the chromatic ones.  Compositionallayouts were quantified with measures of symmetry, mass distribution, spatialdispersion, and angular deviation from cardinal axes. Findings indicated that in stablecompositions shapes were vertically stacked near the lower pictorial field, whereas in dynamic compositions shapes displayed larger angular deviations and a more dispersed spatialspread. Interesting compositions were characterized by greater variation inorientation and positioning the chromatic set produced slightly largerdeviations. Inthe rating data, colour heightened the sense of balance in stable arrangements,amplified the impression of dynamism in both the original and self‑createddynamic works, but had no significant effect on perceived stability.Compositions labeled “interesting” received the highest liking and balancescores, colour further boosted both liking and perceived interest. Our results suggest that perceived attractiveness and aestheticpreference are contingent on the task directive, the number of shapes used,structural variety in orientation and placement, and that shape colourprimarily serves as an affective amplifier for dynamism, balance, and liking.This study demonstrates the value of participatory construction paradigmspaired with individualized preference ratings for probing the perceptualorganization principles that govern artwork interpretation.

title: Towards tRanslational Inclusive Art & Design, Co-designed by Science, designers and the General Public, Used by Designers: lessons from real-world data collection
affiliations:
1. University of Bristol, Bristol Business School (UK)
2. University of Bristol, Bristol Veterinary School (UK)
3. University of Bristol, School of Psychological Sciences (UK)
abstract: Current approaches to evaluating public art often rely on metrics such as community engagement, aesthetic value, and economic impact, but do not consider alignment with cognitive and perceptual capacities and diverse cultural and socio-economic backgrounds, as these factors can make environments feel either welcoming and engaging or, conversely, overwhelming and alienating. In this project, we introduce a co-design approach that simulates and tests different artwork designs within their intended environments in a virtual test space, while quantifying experience through physiological markers of engagement. We report on a case study in Higher Education in which we co-developed, in collaboration with professionals, and test-trialled a prototype contextualised design tool using VR technology. Participants were fitted with an Oculus Quest 1 headset and were able to freely explore the space by walking before sitting on one of the physical seats provided. Once seated, grey moveable floor-to-ceiling panels appeared to enclose the seating area. The panels changed designs between stress-inducing, high-contrast repetitive patterns, nature images, and abstract counterparts generated from the same images using neural style transfer techniques, allowing control over semantic content while varying abstraction. Participants’ experiences were captured through audio recordings and physiological measures (E4 wristband: BVP, HR, EDA, skin temperature, accelerometer), time-locked to panel transitions. Time-series transformer networks applied to BVP and EDA data achieved high classification accuracy when training and validation sets were drawn from the same participant pool. However, accuracy dropped substantially when validation involved entirely unseen participants. The reasons for this reduced generalisability are discussed. Findings also highlighted that nature images in a built space intended for conversation felt out of context and distracting. This illustrates the need for the development of contextualised tools to define and measure sensory stressors of environments in relation to their intended purpose.

title: Influence of Olfactory Stimuli on Aesthetic Evaluation and Impression of Paintings
affiliations:
1. Doshisha Women's College of Liberal Arts (JP)
2. Kansai University (JP)
3. Yokohama National University (JP)
abstract:
Recent museum exhibitions increasingly incorporate multisensory experiences however, empirical research comparing viewers' impressions with and without ambient scents remains limited, as most existing literature focuses on case studies within specific gallery environments. This study investigated how olfactory stimuli influence the subjective impression of paintings, the perceived time of day and season, through a controlled psychophysical experiment.

Four distinct paintings served as visual stimuli: ‘Terraces in Cagnes,’ ‘L'Estaque,’ ‘Peonies, Lilas and Tulips’ (Renoir), and ‘Le Moulin Rouge’ (Lautrec). Four aroma oils, ylang-ylang, cardamom, Japanese cypress, and geranium, were selected as olfactory stimuli. Twenty female participants first evaluated the paintings alone, then evaluated 16 unique painting–scent combinations using the Semantic Differential method with 15 adjective pairs and categorical scales for the perceived time of day (six categories) and season (four categories).

The results showed that olfactory information significantly influenced visual evaluations. Geranium increased ‘bright’ ratings, especially for ‘Peonies, Lilas and Tulips’. Notably, for this still-life, which was frequently categorized as ‘nighttime’ in the visual-only condition, the addition of scents significantly decreased ‘night’ ratings. While the low-luminosity background in this painting may serve as a visual cue for nighttime, the results suggest that olfactory stimuli re-directed the viewers' attention toward the vivid floral subjects. This shift in attentional focus potentially modulated the perceived time of day by overriding ambient visual features. Factor analysis further revealed that the addition of cardamom and geranium resulted in higher overall ratings for ‘pleasant’ and ‘clear,’ whereas ylang-ylang led to lower ‘pleasant’ ratings.

Findings suggest that scents do not merely provide background atmosphere but actively modulate cross-modal perception, affecting both sensory attributes and temporal interpretations. This research highlights the potential of integrated olfactory–visual design in enhancing the aesthetic experience in gallery environments.

*This study was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP23KK0185.

title: The Perception of Biolocomotion: Revisiting Michotte’s ‘Caterpillar Effect’
affiliations:
1. University of Siena (IT)
2. University of Padova (IT)
abstract: Beyond his seminal and widely recognized work on perceptual causality, Michotte also explored the phenomenon of biolocomotion, demonstrating how single moving shapes can evoke the impression of a living being. Specifically, he described an autonomous movement generated by a rectangle alternating the motion of its ‘head’ and ‘tail’ sections. This creates the phenomenal impression of a ‘self-advancing caterpillar’ through phenomenally elastic and organic cycles of expansion and contraction. In this study we investigated the optimal conditions for the perceived naturalness and pleasantness of this effect. Thirty-two participants viewed 18 animations of a black rectangle (initial length: 2.5 cm) moving in caterpillar mode. We manipulated three variables: expansion length (0.5L, L, 2L), speed (2.47, 4.94, 9.88 cm/s), and direction. Participants rated naturalness and pleasantness on a 0-1 scale and provided qualitative descriptions of any perceived animal resemblance. Results show a significant interaction between length and speed: short motions were perceived as more natural at slow-to-medium speeds, while fast speeds were preferred for long motions. Overall, naturalness follows an inverted U-shaped function of the log-ratio between length and speed. While pleasantness followed similar patterns, speed exerted a stronger independent effect, with higher speeds generally rated more positively. Qualitative analysis revealed that ‘caterpillar’ descriptions strongly correlated with both naturalness and pleasantness. However, the two constructs do not completely overlap, as not all ‘caterpillar’ stimuli were judged equally pleasant. Notably, associations with other crawling animals (e.g., snakes, worms, or snails) correlated negatively with both ratings. This suggests that naturalness and pleasantness do not merely reflect any association with a living creature, but rather how the motion of a living being appears prototypical.

title: Boundary Extension in Renaissance frescos
affiliations: 1. University of Padova (IT)
abstract: Boundary Extension (BE Intraub et al., 1992) refers to a systematic bias individuals tend to remember having seen a wider portion of a scene than was presented. We tested whether the same effect is found for scenes in Renaissance frescoes, given the use of linear perspective to create a sense of space. We conducted four online experiments. Participants were presented with pairs of images and judged differences in viewing distance, from −2 (“much closer”) to +2 (“much farther”). In the first experiment, BE was replicated using 40 photographs of outdoor scenes taken with a 35 mm lens. In the second experiment, the same design was applied to 40 images from Renaissance frescoes, which were matched in size to the photographs. In this case, BE was not observed. The third experiment included 30 photographs and 30 frescoes from the previous experiments, with the two types interleaved, and confirmed BE only for photographic stimuli. This discrepancy could be due to the absence of depth-of-field (DoF) in frescoes. A fourth experiment was conducted where frescoes were digitally manipulated. Blur was applied to peripheral regions through a custom MATLAB script designed to approximate naturalistic DoF, with a progressive blur corresponding to a simulated aperture of f/4. Blur was only present in the baseline image (the intermediate view). Although previous studies have found evidence of BE with artificially induced DoF (Hafri et al., 2022), our results did not show evidence of BE in frescoes. This may be due to the nature of the images, which may not depict sufficiently open or panoramic scenes, or to limitations in the realism of the simulated DoF or of the frescoes compared to photographs. It can also be important that observers are aware that they are looking at frescos, which by definition are flat images on walls.

title: Symmetry, Curvature, and Boundary Complexity in Haptic and Visual Aesthetic Appreciation
affiliations: 1. Justus Liebig University (DE)
abstract: Aesthetic judgments play a fundamental role in everyday experiences of objects,  environments, and in the appreciation of art - for example, when admiring a smartphone for its sleek design or when enjoying the dynamics in a line drawing. While most research on aesthetic judgments has focused on visual objects, recent work indicates that touch elicits aesthetic experiences (e.g., Carbon & Jakesch, 2012). Yet, a direct comparison of aesthetic judgments in vision and touch is still scarce. Here, we systematically examined how symmetry, global curvature, and boundary complexity of 2D raised black shapes on white square backgrounds influence aesthetic judgments across the two modalities. Employing a within-participant design, 12 participants either explored (blindfolded) a given shape with their dominant index finger for 15 seconds or visually inspected it for the same amount of time. Following each exploration, the stimulus was rated on a 100-point scale on aesthetic appeal, and in two separate blocks, also judged on perceived symmetry and complexity, respectively. The order of blocks was the same across participants. An LMM analysis with the fixed factors modality, symmetry, global curvature, and boundary complexity revealed that overall, aesthetic appeal differed in visual and haptic modalities. In terms of stimulus features, the results show that only symmetry determined appeal, with symmetric shapes being rated as more appealing, in both modalities. We also find a strongly significant two-way interaction between global curvature and modality: while pointy shapes were judged more appealing visually, curvy shapes were preferred haptically. Taken together, these results suggest that, while visual and haptic aesthetic judgments may be governed by some common principles, each modality may also be sensitive to different factors, such as global shape curvature. These modality-specific idiosyncrasies might arise from the distinct ways eyes and hands explore the environment to meet different affective and functional needs.

title: The Effects of Contrast Modulations on Aesthetic Appreciation and Eye Movements in Monet’s Paintings
affiliations:
1. Bogazici University (TR)
2. Bilkent University (TR)
3. Freie Universität (DE)
abstract: Aesthetic appreciation is shaped by the way the visual system processes information through two primary pathways: The dorsal-stream, which is primarily involved in spatial processing, motion, and visually guided action and is often linked to the processing of luminance-defined information, and the ventral-stream, which is more strongly associated with object recognition and hue-contrast processing. Although most experimental aesthetics research focused on semantic ambiguity, the present study examines lower-level perceptual ambiguity, which arises from the selective reduction of specific contrast type. Impressionist painters such as Claude Monet appear to have exploited this phenomenon through equiluminance, producing shimmering and spatially unstable visual impressions as in “Impression, Sunrise”. Sixty-six Boğaziçi University students viewed five original Monet paintings and digitally manipulated versions of selected regions of interest (ROIs) presented in three conditions: luminance-contrast-only, hue-contrast-only, and mixed-contrast. Eye movements were recorded and aesthetic appreciation was assessed with the AEQ and ARS scales. We hypothesised that the hue-contrast-only and luminance-contrast-only conditions would elicit fewer but longer fixations, along with higher aesthetic ratings, reflecting increased cognitive effort to resolve perceptual ambiguity. Results, on the other hand, showed that aesthetical preference scale scores and total fixation counts remained stable across conditions, suggesting that Monet's compositional structure is sufficiently robust to preserve its integrity despite ROI-based contrast manipulations. However, ROI fixation duration percentages were found to be higher in the hue-contrast-only condition, indicating that the allocation of visual attention across focal regions may be directly shaped by contrast condition. Significant effects of presentation was also observed, with ROI fixation duration percentages decreasing following repeated exposure. Moreover, interactions between contrast condition and painting suggested that the impact of contrast is modulated by the unique layout of each artwork. Overall, the results suggest that Monet’s compositional structure constrains gaze robustly, while local attentional allocation remains sensitive to ROI-based contrast manipulations.

title: Audiovisual emotional congruency modulates gaze dispersion and aesthetic evaluation of paintings
affiliations:
1. Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University (NL)
2. Department of Communication and Cognition, Tilburg School of Humanities and Digital   Sciences, Tilburg University (NL)
abstract: Audiovisual congruency shapes aesthetic experience, yet the role of visual exploration in this process remains poorly understood. Building on prior fMRI work demonstrating increased cortical activation under audiovisual emotion incongruency (Yilmaz et al., 2025), we investigated how pairing paintings with emotionally congruent or incongruent music affects gaze behavior and beauty ratings. Sixty-one participants viewed happy or sad paintings accompanied by music that was either emotionally matched (e.g., sad painting, sad music) or mismatched (e.g., happy painting, sad music). Eye movements were recorded, and gaze dispersion, which is defined as the spatial variance of fixation patterns, was used to quantify exploratory viewing. Aesthetic evaluation was assessed via beauty ratings after each trial. First, the results of a generalized linear mixed-effects model showed that incongruent music-painting combinations significantly increased gaze dispersion, indicating broader, less focused visual exploration under emotional incongruency. A second generalized linear mixed effects model then examined whether gaze dispersion predicted beauty ratings. Although the spatial distribution of fixations was largely stable across conditions, individual differences in dispersion reliably predicted aesthetic experience: people with more dispersed gaze reported lower beauty ratings. Importantly, audiovisual congruency moderated this relationship, revealing a robust negative effect of gaze dispersion on beauty that was significantly enhanced under incongruent conditions. These findings can suggest that aesthetic experience is not determined solely by stimulus properties but depends on how people visually engage with the paintings. Future analyses will examine the influence of individual differences on gaze behavior, including arts and music experience, cognitive flexibility, personality traits, and emotional state, to reveal how distinct participant clusters differ in their exploratory behavior. Furthermore, we will investigate the degree to which gaze patterns remain consistent within individuals.

title: Empathy in artworks: Combining evidence from pupillometry, facial EMG and self-reports
affiliations:
1. University of Limassol (CY)
2. Cyprus University of Technology (CY)
abstract: Empathic responses to visual art have been shown to engage multiple pathways with psychophysiological evidence generally stronger for figurative than non-figurative content (Gerger, Pelowski, & Leder, 2017). In non-figurative artworks, patterns and forms engage empathic processes differently, potentially reflecting a greater reliance on top-down cognitive interpretation given their lack of animate content (Melcher & Bacci, 2013). Yet objective evidence which does not rely on self-reports studies single aspects of empathy. Grounded in the distinction between cognitive, affective, and motor empathy, the focus of this multi-modal psychophysiological study is to investigate whether empathic responses towards non-figurative art (abstract artworks and landscapes that retain natural scenes without human figures) can be measured objectively and be compared to figurative artworks. Participants (N=27, m=12/f=15 Mean age=33.50, SD=5.90) viewed abstract, landscape, and figurative artworks across three condition blocks: cognitive empathy (valence identification), affective empathy (intensity of felt emotion), and passive viewing. Responses were assessed using self-reports, pupillometry, and facial EMG on a baseline-corrected and valence-specific basis. Participants showed accurate cognitive-based empathic responses in all three artwork types (figure, landscape, abstract) while affective-based empathic responses were more intense for figurative and landscape art, but also evident for abstract art. Motor empathic responses were detected for all artwork types, as evidenced by significant facial muscle activation above baseline. Results suggest that prevailing theories of aesthetic empathy are differentially operative across the three empathic pathways. Motor empathic responses across all artwork types support embodied simulation as a content-independent mechanism (Freedberg & Gallese, 2007), while the content-independence in valence identification suggests a top-down interpretive engagement during cognitive empathy. Sharing emotion even with abstract art—though with reduced intensity, suggests that affective empathy may depend on the availability of a hypothetical persona (Levinson, 1996), an experiential referent possibly more readily evoked by depictions of natural scenes.

title: Categorical storage of de-prioritized visual working memory content
affiliations: 1. Utrecht University, Helmholtz Institute (NL)
abstract: Multiple items can be maintained in visual working memory (VWM) with different levels of priority (e.g., relevant now versus later). An emerging view, largely based on neuroimaging work, is that VWM content is stored in early visual cortex only when fine-grained detail is required. This occurs when items are prioritized, for instance to support precise recall or perceptual comparison. Instead, when VWM content is deprioritized, storage relies more on downstream regions, including parietal cortex where representations were shown to be more categorical. This framework leads to a clear prediction. If deprioritized items are stored in regions that do not support fine detail, then retrieving them into a prioritized state should reveal a loss of precision. Critically, such representations should also become more categorical. We tested this prediction using an existing dataset of three experiments (Wang et al., 2025). Participants memorized two colors for two consecutive delayed reproduction tasks using a continuous color wheel. One item was prioritized (cued for imminent report), whereas the other was temporarily deprioritized (relevant for later report). To quantify categorical structure, we conducted separate behavioral experiments (using the same experimental setup as Wang et al.) to identify color categories and map their prototypes and boundaries. Results showed that recall precision was lower for previously deprioritized items, indicating information loss. Also, color reports were generally biased toward (rather than away from) category prototypes, demonstrating influences of category membership on recall. Crucially, this bias was strongest for previously deprioritized items. These findings show that deprioritized VWM contents are stored in a more categorical format, consistent with a transfer from early visual cortex to higher-level regions. Although this flexibility supports efficient resource allocation, it comes at a cost: transfers are not lossless and systematically transform memory content. Categorical coding may support robust behavior in natural contexts, despite reduced precision.

title: Emotional valence does not automatically shift spatial attention: evidence from the conceptual cueing effect
affiliations: 1. University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: Embodied cognition theories share the idea that mental concepts are represented through combinations of sensorimotor features, yet how these features are selected and organised into concepts is debated. In the conceptual cueing effect, abstract words direct spatial attention to locations congruent with their valence (e.g. ‘HAPPY’ orients upwards Meier & Robinson, 2004). Existing theories disagree on how this link between word semantics and spatial directions is established. Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) explains that activating abstract concepts automatically shifts spatial attention towards semantically congruent locations because concepts are inadvertently re-expressed in terms of sensorimotor relations. Theory of Event Coding (TEC) instead holds that the influence of abstract concepts on spatial attention is modulated by the task relevance of their associated spatial features. Clarifying which theory best explains the association between spatial directions and abstract concepts is key to understanding how concepts are represented in an embodied manner.   In two experiments, we examined conditions necessary for observing the conceptual cueing effect, thereby testing the explanations offered by the CMT and TEC. We adopted a previous study’s paradigm wherein participants viewed a centred cue word and discriminated the shape of a subsequent target appearing above or below the fixation point (Gozli et al., 2013). Participants responded to emotional (e.g. ‘JOY’ or ‘SAD’) or directional (e.g. ‘ABOVE’ or ‘BELOW’) cue words, while varying the task relevance of cue valence across two conditions. We compared participants’ reaction time, hit rate, eye movements, and pupillometric responses. Although our setup elicited strong spatial cueing effects using explicit directional cues in all conditions, we did not obtain a clear cue-target congruence effect with emotional cues as described in the original study. These results challenge the Conceptual Metaphor Theory, as they indicate that at least for emotional words, spatial attention is not automatically directed to the valence-congruent spatial locations.

title: Attention Modulates Duration Perception for Accelerating but Not Uniform Motion
affiliations: 1. University of West London (UK)
abstract: In a prior study, we showed that both visual gravity and uniform motion (operationally defined as linear acceleration and non-accelerating radially expanding optic flow, respectively) produced systematic distortions in duration reproduction. Specifically, reproductions increased with magnitude (e.g., stronger acceleration or faster speed), showing overestimation at 500 ms, a motion-type-dependent indifference point at 1000 ms, and underestimation at 2000-3000 ms, with uniform motion reproduced longer than gravitational motion. Because temporal distortions are often linked to attentional processes, we tested whether attention modulates the effects of magnitude (H1) and motion type (H2). Building on our previous study, thirty-two adults (M age = 28.7) performed a dual task: they viewed the same gravitating (1g, 2g, 3g) or uniformly moving (9.8, 19.6, 29.4 m/s) radial optic flow for 500, 1000, 2000, or 3000 ms with a word or nonword presented during the animation, followed by a duration reproduction and a lexical decision response. Attentional load was manipulated via lexical frequency (lower frequency English words = high load higher frequency = low load). Attentional load significantly reduced lexical sensitivity (d' = 2.39 vs. 1.64 for low and high load, respectively z = 14.44, p < .001) and shifted criterion from neutral to conservative (c = 0.04 vs. 0.47 for low and high load, respectively z = 16.60, p < .001). Critically, attentional load affected temporal reproduction,  with gravitating motion producing longer reproduction in high load (p < .05, partial η² = .15 Δ = 18.47 ms), supporting H2 but not H1, since the magnitude function did not interact with attentional load. The results showed that attention does not uniformly account for temporal distortions instead, its influence depends on motion type, with accelerating motion (but not uniform motion) relying on attentional resources during temporal encoding.

title: Test-retest reliability of split-field pupillometry in the assessment of pseudoneglect
affiliations: 1. Jagiellonian University (PL)
abstract: Measuring spatial biases in the orienting of covert attention is inherently challenging. Traditionally, research on pseudoneglect and hemispatial neglect has relied on tasks requiring overt behavioral responses, which substantially constrain the scope of investigation. Recently, however, split-field pupillometry (also known as the split-screen task) has been proposed as an alternative approach. When the screen is split vertically into two halves with opposite luminance (white-left/dark-right vs. dark-left/white-right), spatial biases can be inferred by comparing PLR amplitudes across conditions. For example, a stronger response to the left hemifield is typically interpreted as evidence of pseudoneglect, as reported at the group level in prior studies. Conversely, patients with hemispatial neglect tend to exhibit stronger PLR responses to the right hemifield. To evaluate the suitability of split-field pupillometry for studying individual differences and repeated-measures designs, its test–retest reliability must first be established. In the present study, 30 neurologically healthy participants completed a split-field pupillometry task across three separate sessions, each spaced at least 24 hours apart. Measurement consistency was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficients derived from Bayesian hierarchical models. In this sample, the reliability of the spatial pupil bias index (defined as the difference in PLR amplitude between left- and right-sided stimulation) ranged from poor to moderate, indicating substantial within-subject variability across sessions. Although a larger sample size might improve the precision of these estimates, the current findings suggest that split-field pupillometry may have limited utility for certain experimental designs requiring stable individual-level measures. Reliability may, however, be higher in clinical populations, such as patients with hemispatial neglect.

title: Many experimental studies of visual attention are massively underpowered
affiliations:
1. University of Southern Denmark (DK)
2. Karolinska Institutet (SE)
abstract: Rosenholtz (2024) argued that visual attention required a Khunian paradigm shift to address unexplained anomalies in studies of visual attention. While we agree that experimental studies produce conflicting results, we show that such conflicts are to be expected, given the quality of many experimental studies. In particular, many studies use sample sizes that have a low probability of showing statistical significance for the effects of interest.  For example, based on data from around 75,000 participants, the classic Posner spatial cuing task shows a difference of response times for valid and invalid cues of around 39 milliseconds, with a standard deviation for the difference of 107 milliseconds. Calculations show that to have 80% power to demonstrate a basic cuing effect requires a sample of N=62, but a meta-analysis of spatial cuing studies indicates that experimental studies typically use N=18, which corresponds to power of 36%. Worse still, many modern studies investigate deviations in the basic effect. A study looking for a difference between the cuing effect for a control group and an experimental group that produces half the cuing effect requires samples of N1=N2=480 to produce power of 80%. Studies with the typical sample size have power of only 8%, so they should produce anomalies but these anomalies do not need to be explained because they largely represent noise. Many other paradigms for visual attention have similar characteristics. The problem is easily addressed by including power analyses as a standard part of experimental design.

title: Roles of Early Visual Cortex in Global Interaction Between Attention and Visual Consciousness: Evidence from TMS
affiliations: 1. Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CN)
abstract: Clarifying the interactive process between attention and consciousness is a key issue. We previously developed a novel paradigm that dissociates top-down and bottom-up attention while simultaneously probing visual awareness. By combining stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) data, we found that top-down attention does not directly promote conscious experience, but rather facilitates it by inducing a global attentional capture process marked by global coupling between the frontal brain and the posterior brain. Under this globally coupling state, how the activity of the early visual cortex affects the global attentional capture process and conscious experience, as well as which aspects of conscious experience are influenced, are the questions further addressed in this study. Combining this paradigm with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the early visual cortex in the unilateral hemisphere, we performed interventions at three time points (0 ms/100 ms/200 ms relative to image onset) and asked participants to verbally report the visibility level and specific content of the images. The phosphenes induced by TMS were contralateral to the visual field, indicating that TMS successfully altered the local visual activity. However, the attentional capture effect was not modulated by TMS stimulation, and this effect was symmetric between the two stimulation hemispheres, suggesting that attentional capture is indeed a global effect. In terms of conscious experience, TMS improved both visibility rating and content coding of consciousness. Importantly, the intervention effect on the visibility rating was hemispherically symmetric, while the effect on consciousness content was significantly different between the two hemispheres. These results indicate that the early visual cortex is involved in both the global mechanism that determines the visibility level of conscious experience and the local mechanism that determines the content of conscious experience. The above findings provide new insights into the role of the early visual cortex in the interaction between attention and visual consciousness.

title: Does attention to different body parts cause differences in body size adaptation?
affiliations: 1. Nottingham Trent University (UK)
abstract: The misperceptions of one’s body shape and size are a growing health concern. Perceiving oneself to be larger or smaller than one really is (body size and shape misperception) can contribute to health concerns such as eating disordered behaviours, high body dissatisfaction, and poor mental health. Visual adaptation has been identified as a mechanism that may explain these misperceptions. Visual adaptation is the phenomenon whereby exposure to a certain body type (e.g., very thin bodies) causes an aftereffect whereby subsequently viewed bodies appear distorted in the opposite direction (heavier than they really are). Attention has been shown to modulate the direction and magnitude of this effect. For example, individuals with higher levels of body dissatisfaction pay more attention to thin ‘idealised’ bodies and consequently experience more pronounced aftereffects of body size overestimation (Stephen et al., International Journal of Eating Disorders, 52(1), 79-87).  Here we looked at whether attention to specific areas of the body drive this adaptation effect – an aspect that has not previously been investigated. The experiment employed a modified Posner cueing task to manipulate participants visual attention to specific body areas. In a three by two between-subjects design, participants were directed to either the shoulders, stomach, or lower legs on either a narrow or a wide body using an arrow cue. Adaptation was measured by comparing their body size perception before and after the Posner adaptation task. Body size perception scores were assessed using the method of adjustment producing points of subjective normality. The results showed that the Posner design was successful at inducing aftereffects in the opposite direction to the size of the adaptation body. We observed no difference between directing attention towards different body areas possibly suggesting that body size adaptation is not dependent on which areas of the body are attended.

title: Preparatory global feature-selective attention to colour
affiliations:
1. University of Southern Denmark (DK)
2. University of Aberdeen (UK)
3. Michigan State University (US)
abstract: Many experiments in humans and animals have observed a “global” facilitation of attended features across the entire visual field, even when spatial attention is focused on a single location. Such global selection of attended features is assumed to enable guided visual search. However, global facilitation of features has only been observed while attention is actively focused on a relevant stimulus. This differs from the situation in visual search, where the target location is not yet known during the search. Here, we investigated whether the global spread occurs during preparatory attention, before the presentation of the attended physical stimulus, which would provide empirical support for its role in guiding visual search. Participants attended to superimposed fields of either orange or blue randomly moving dots on either the left or right side of fixation with the task of detecting brief coherent motion targets. Recordings of steady-state visual evoked potentials elicited by the flickering stimuli allowed concurrent measurement of the time course of feature-selective attention in visual cortex on both the attended and the unattended sides. When the onset of dots on the attended side was delayed relative to the unattended side, we observed a global feature-selective enhancement prior to the onset of the attended side dots. We propose that this spread of preparatory attention to relevant features is crucial for guided visual search.

title: Gradual Change Blindness to Blur: Implications for Video Coding
affiliations:
1. Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NO)
2. University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (US)
abstract: Large changes can go unnoticed if they coincide with a visual disruption. Even changes occurring right in front of us can go undetected when they occur slowly and continuously. This change blindness presents a compelling opportunity for perception-driven video coding: gradually increasing compression ratio (and thus reducing video quality) may go unperceived under certain conditions. We carried out a preliminary proof-of-concept study in which we studied the effect of change blindness on gradually increasing blur. We systematically varied display duration and blur level in phase-scrambled images. We first established a baseline threshold. The observed detection thresholds were similar to predictions from the ViCE blur discrimination model, validating that model for scene images. We then measured detection when blur was introduced gradually. Thresholds were significantly higher, both when participants knew where the change would occur (location cued) and when they had to search for it (location uncued). In the absence of a cue, we were able to substantially blur the entire image before the change was detectable, suggesting non-trivial perceptual headroom that compression pipelines could potentially exploit. With both cued and uncued gradual changes, detection occurred earlier with longer stable display times between increments. This gradual change blindness could be exploited for compression algorithms via gradual blur as pre-processing.

title: Limits of Cross-Task Generalisation of Category-Selective Neural Codes
affiliations: 1. University of Nottingham (UK)
abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that tasks with shared underlying structure can share neural task representations, even if the tasks operate over distinct stimuli, leading to the proposal that many tasks are solved using reusable amodal neural representations. For example, prefrontal populations that are category-selective in one task (e.g., distinguishing cats from dogs) are also selective in another task (e.g., distinguishing sports cars from sedans). Such generalisation can accelerate learning and better use limited neural resources. However, when stimuli can be encountered in multiple tasks and therefore require different task-specific stimulus-response mappings, neural cross-task generalisation can lead to interference, making generalised representations inefficient. Tasks with low cross-task interference may thus favour generalisation, while tasks with high potential interference may favour independent, task-specialised representations. Here we examined how neural task representations adapt when they suddenly transition from a low- to a high-interference regime. 32 human participants completed a new visual category learning paradigm as we measured task-specific category-selective neural patterns using electroencephalography. Participants learned to categorise simple visual shapes in two separate categorisation tasks consisting of distinct stimulus sets and distinct category boundaries. In the low-interference session (day 1), category-selective neural patterns generalised between tasks, indicating the use of a shared, task-independent categorisation code. In the next session (day 2) we created interference by introducing new stimuli which were shared across both tasks but needed to be categorised differently in them. While we could still decode categories in both tasks, these codes no longer generalised between tasks, indicating that interference led to task-specific neural representations. Curiously, the previously learned stimuli continued to be represented in a task-generalised code. Taken together, our results show that efficient, generalisable neural task codes adapt flexibly to resolve interference by warping neural category representations to maintain generalisation where possible while orthogonalising stimulus representations with potential interference.

title: Causality perception under visual uncertainty
affiliations:
1. Technical University of Darmstadt (DE)
2. University College London (UK)
3. Philipps-Universität Marburg (DE)
abstract: Causality perception occurs in simplified 2D animations of two-object collisions, where a launcher approaches a stationary target that moves upon contact (“launching displays”). Observers viewing centre-to-centre collisions usually report perceiving more causality, the more launcher and target moving direction are aligned. In this work, we extend a previous account that views causality perception as a mismatch between an observer’s real-time observation of the target moving angle and their initial prediction of the target moving angle. Here, we investigated whether observers’ perception of the launcher moving angle is retrospectively influenced by a later observation of the target moving angle. We expected that participants assess the compatibility between predictions and observations to evaluate causality, but also reconcile violations of predictions by retrospectively adjusting their observation of the pre-collision state (postdiction). 32 participants performed three randomly-interleaved tasks on consecutive trials: 1. viewing a launching display until the collision and indicating the predicted target trajectory 2. viewing a full launching display (pre- and post-collision) and rating the causality of the collision on a slider scale and 3. viewing a full launching display (as in 2) and then indicating the launcher’s starting point. Both predictions of target trajectory and postdictions of launcher starting point showed a repulsion away from cardinal directions. Observers’ postdictions seemed to show a weak, but systematic dependence on target moving angle, supporting the idea of a retrospective reconciliation of mismatching sensory evidence in launching displays. A probabilistic model implementing a predictive mechanism of causality perception produced causality judgments that aligned well with our behavioural data. This model shows that prediction, postdiction and causality judgments exhibit a direction-dependence. In our current account, we cannot discriminate between predictive and retrospective components of causality judgments, which remains an objective for future research.

title: The effect of self-generated action on visual perception: testing magnocellular and parvocellular contributions
affiliations:
1. Center for Psychiatry, Justus Liebig University (DE)
2. School of Psychological Sciences and Sagol School of Neuroscience, Tel-Aviv University (IL)
abstract: Voluntary actions are thought to modulate sensory processing through predictive mechanisms such as efference copies. While attenuation of self-generated stimuli is well established in tactile and auditory domains, evidence in vision remains inconsistent, with studies reporting attenuation, enhancement, or no effect. One possible source of this variability is the involvement of different visual pathways. In eye-movement paradigms using simple grating stimuli, low- and high-spatial-frequency information has been shown to be differentially affected by action, suggesting pathway-specific modulation. However, it remains unclear whether similar effects generalize to voluntary button presses and more complex naturalistic stimuli.  Present behavioral study investigated whether action-related modulation depends on spatial frequency, thereby biasing magnocellular (low spatial frequency LSF) and parvocellular (high spatial frequency HSF) processing. Participants (N = 34) categorized briefly presented naturalistic images (cats, birds, cars, airplanes) as animate or inanimate under active (self-triggered) and passive (externally triggered) conditions. Stimuli were filtered to isolate LSF and HSF information.  Accuracy was significantly higher for LSF than HSF stimuli, indicating robust effects of spatial frequency. However, no significant differences were observed between active and passive conditions, and no interaction between action and spatial frequency emerged. Reaction times showed a similar pattern. Finally, exploratory analyses of run effects and individual differences indicated learning-related improvements across runs, but provided no additional evidence for reliable action-related effects. These findings suggest that, within this paradigm, self-generated actions do not reliably modulate visual perception, even when low- and high-spatial-frequency processing is selectively engaged. More broadly, they indicate that action-related effects in vision may depend on stimulus characteristics, task design, or the type of action used to generate sensory consequences, and may therefore be more subtle or context-dependent than in other sensory modalities.

title: Distort Enough and It Lives: Dynamic Local Shape Deformations Drive Animacy Perception
affiliations:
1. Middle East Technical University (TR)
2. Social Sciences University of Ankara (TR)
3. École Normale Supérieure - PSL (FR)
4. Justus-Liebig University (DE)
abstract: Prior work showed that local shape distortions can parametrize rigid and non-rigid transparent layers. Here, we investigated the role of non-rigid motion in animacy perception through local shape distortions. Two psychophysical experiments were conducted using the Eidolon Factory, a toolbox that enables parametric distortion of images along two independently controlled dimensions: intensity (reach) and locality (grain). In the first experiment, we examined whether dynamic local shape distortions and movement direction were sufficient to elicit animacy attribution. We used a 2 (movement type: animate vs. inanimate) x 2 (motion direction: upward vs. downward) x 4 (shape type: ellipse to rounded rectangle) within-subjects design (N = 16). Participants adjusted distortion parameters such that each stimulus either appeared to them being self-propelled (animate) or being dragged (inanimate). Results revealed that reach values of the observer settings were significantly higher in the self-propelled condition than in the dragged condition, while grain values did not differ systematically. Reach values for upward motion were also significantly higher than those for downward motion, whereas no significant difference was observed in grain values. Shape type did not elicit any effects on either reach or grain values. Based on these results, we conducted a forced choice experiment, using a 2 (movement type: self-propelled vs. dragged) x 2 (movement direction: upward vs. downward) within-subjects design (N = 28). Here, participants viewed nine pairs of clips consisting of stimuli at three reach levels and three grain levels with either upward or downward motion and selected the stimulus they perceived as animate. Findings confirmed that reach values are the primary cue driving animacy judgments, and that participants reliably distinguished animate from inanimate stimuli despite substantial inter-individual variability. Together, these results suggest that low-level local shape distortions constitute a viable and parametrically controllable cue for perceived animacy.

title: Task Relevance in Response Priming with Occlusions: A Feature Flip-flop Across Occluders Thickness
affiliations: 1. RPTU University of Kaiserslautern-Landau (DE)
abstract: This study investigates how stimulus visibility modulates response priming across two visual dimensions, colour and shape. Participants performed a priming task with coloured shapes (red/blue circles/squares) presented at fixation, responding to a subsequent target based on either its colour or shape. Prime visibility was manipulated using a pair of grey occluders positioned either horizontally or vertically, with occluder thickness varied in width to reduce the visibility of the prime. Robust priming effects were observed in both tasks. We found that priming was task-dependent: only the colour of the prime influenced responses in the colour task, whereas only the shape of the prime influenced responses in the shape task. The respective task-irrelevant features did not display measurable priming effects, consistent with a dimension-specific gating mechanism. We refer to this pattern as a “feature flip-flop,” whereby only task-relevant features are permitted to activate the motor response. In addition, priming magnitude decreased with increasing occluder thickness, indicating that reduced prime visibility weakens response activation. Importantly, the feature flip-flop pattern persisted across visibility levels. These findings suggest that response priming is jointly constrained by stimulus visibility and task-dependent conditions, highlighting the role of action-trigger conditions in controlling feature-to-response activation.

title: Latent states in continuous perception revealed by a hierarchical Bayesian HMM
affiliations:
1. University of Mannheim (DE)
2. Koç University (TR)
3. Lausanne University Hospital and University of Lausanne (CH)
4. Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (CH)
5. he Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
abstract: Human performance in perceptual, mnemonic, and cognitive tasks naturally fluctuates. Recent research using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) applied to forced-choice tasks has linked these fluctuations to transitions between different modes of processing: an external mode, in which perception more faithfully reflects the sensory input, and an internal mode, in which perceptual decisions are biased by prior experience. Here, we extend this framework to continuous report tasks, an increasingly common paradigm, using a hierarchical Bayesian HMM. The proposed model classifies trial-by-trial perceptual decisions as arising from an internal mode (modeled as attractive serial dependence), an external mode, or an uncertain mode in which observers guessed. We applied this model to a publicly available dataset of motion direction reproduction. We found that the proposed approach successfully identified latent states and their transition dynamics across most observers in the current dataset. In particular, it distinguished states characterized by strong serial dependence from more unbiased responses and further captured variations in response precision across states. In ongoing work, we aim to benchmark model performance and optimize parameters across a large collection of datasets. This approach has the potential to provide a general tool for characterizing internal state dynamics in perceptual performance using continuous report measures.

title: Symbiotic Brain-Machine Drawing via Visual Brain-Computer Interfaces
affiliations: 1. University of Glasgow (UK)
abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are evolving from research prototypes into clinical, assistive, and performance enhancement technologies. Despite the rapid rise and promise of implantable technologies, there is a need for better and more capable wearable and non-invasive approaches whilst also minimising hardware requirements.  We present a non-invasive BCI for iterative selection-based mind-drawing that infers a subject's internal visual intent through iterative selection of adaptive visual probes presented on a screen encoded at different flicker-frequencies and analyses the steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs). Gabor-inspired or machine-learned policies dynamically update the spatial placement of the visual probes on the screen to explore the image space and reconstruct simple imagined shapes within approximately two minutes or less using just single-channel EEG data. Additionally, by leveraging stable diffusion models, reconstructed mental images can be transformed into realistic and detailed visual representations. Whilst we expect that similar results might be achievable with e.g. eye-tracking techniques, our work shows that symbiotic human-AI interaction can  increase BCI bit-rates by more than a factor 5x, providing a platform for future development of AI-augmented BCI.

title: Progressive Reconfiguration of Perceptual Decision-Making by Learned Expectations
affiliations:
1. The University of Osaka (JP)
2. Kansai University (JP)
abstract: Decisions in uncertain environments rely on the accumulation of sensory evidence, guided by prior expectations. Predictive coding theories propose that expectations modulate the precision with which evidence is weighted in drift-diffusion models (DDMs), this precision corresponds to the slope of drift rate, mirroring the perceptual gain in predictive coding. Yet, how learned expectations dynamically reconfigure evidence accumulation over time remains poorly understood. Here, we extend DDMs with three components for expectation-driven modulation: starting-point bias (motor-preparation bias), drift intercept (directional bias), and drift slope (perceptual gain). To test this model, we collected behavioral data in a two-stage cued proportion judgment task, where participants judged whether black or white dots were more numerous after a cue. Twenty participants first completed a learning stage (100 trials) to learn cue-stimulus associations. During this stage, color cues (red/white) were statistically linked to the dominant color of the dot stimulus (e.g., red cues predicted white-dominant displays). In the test stage (300 trials), cues retained no predictive validity (coherence: 0.35--0.65). To track how expectation-driven effects evolve over time, we partitioned the test stage into three phases (100 trials each) and fitted eight competing DDMs---each compnent independently cue-dependent or shared---in a hierarchical Bayesian framework. Models were compared using trial-level leave-one-out cross-validation based on the expected log pointwise predictive density (ELPD). Crucially, the best model shifted across phases. The first phase favored the motor-preparation-bias-only model, yet the null model remained competitive (ΔELPD = 0.94). The second phase favored the null model. In the third phase, however, the model with both motor-preparation bias and perceptual gain performed best. By dissociating perceptual gain from motor-preparation bias, we demonstrate that learned expectations recruit perceptual gain as an additional component. This contribution emerged later yet persisted alongside the motor-preparation bias, which suggests that expectation-driven perceptual modulation is sustained rather than transient.

title: No evidence for choice-induced modulation of temporal binding in a replication of Barlas & Obhi (2013)
affiliations: 1. Heinrich Heine University (DE)
abstract: When we generate a sensation, for instance by pressing a button to produce a tone, the time between action and ensuing sensation appears compressed. The phenomenon termed temporal binding is commonly studied using visual timing paradigms such as the Libet clock and has traditionally been interpreted as an implicit marker of the sense of agency, i.e., the feeling of having produced the action. According to this account, intervals between action and sensation are perceived as shorter when sensations are interpreted as consequence of one`s own actions. In contrast, recent findings challenge this idea and suggest that temporal binding arises from attention- and expectancy-based processes, rather than from a subjective sense of agency. \nIn the light of these developments, we have conducted a conceptual replication of Barlas & Obhi (2013), a study that presented evidence supporting an agency-based account. In their paradigm, they used three conditions in which participants could choose between either one, three or seven buttons to trigger a tone. Stronger temporal binding was found when participants had more choice options. The authors interpreted the increase in temporal binding to reflect enhanced agency under greater choice. In our conceptual replication of this study, however, we found no significant differences in binding strength between one, three or seven choice options. This failure to replicate the original effect calls into question the role of choice-induced agency for temporal binding and suggests that the effect may be better explained by more general cognitive processes.

title: Ticket to Change: Dynamic Descriptive Social Norms as a Route to Sustainable Travel Behavior
affiliations: 1. ZHAW (CH)
abstract: Climate change mitigation requires interventions to promote more sustainable travel behavior, and digital booking platforms may provide a promising way to do so. The present study tested whether dynamically implemented descriptive norms on these booking platforms can increase the probability of switching from plane to train. To test this assumption, observers (N = 517) were presented with a scenario of a mandatory school trip from Zurich to Vienna. Thereby participants were randomly assigned either to the control condition or to one of the two descriptive norm conditions (weak vs. strong). In the weak norm condition, the ticker, which displayed the number of peers who had already switched to train, slowly counted up from a low number (“16”), in the strong norm condition it counted up from a higher number (“162”). Contrary to our assumptions, the weak norm was more effective in promoting switching to train than the strong norm, relative to the control condition. One possible explanation is that the weak norm matched the size of a relevant peer group more, thereby increasing perceived social relevance. Furthermore, reaction time (RT) analysis revealed that in the control condition, but not in the descriptive norms conditions (weak, strong), participants showing longer RTs switched significantly less to the train–possibly due to the absence of a normative cue, longer RTs or deliberation facilitates the generation and weighting of counterarguments against the sustainable option. Alternatively, longer RTs may reflect increased decision conflict toward the default option (the plane) in the absence of a normative cue. Additionally, prior behavior–assessed as self-reported travel-related CO2 emissions–influenced switching to train: participants with stated lower previous CO2 emissions showed higher switching rates, particularly in the descriptive norm conditions (weak, strong). Overall, descriptive norms appear to influence judgement by perceived group relevance, deliberation processes, and prior behavior.

title: The Role of Food Product-Related Humor in Instagram Feeds
affiliations: 1. ZHAW (CH)
abstract: Globally, obesity is on the rise. Furthermore, food products advertised on social media are mostly unhealthy. But how can healthier food products be promoted? Maybe trough productrelated humor? To test this, 631 observers were presented with an artificial social media feed that included a target post about chickpea pasta as a healthy food product. Thereby observers were randomly assigned to one of the following target post conditions: A control condition without humor was compared with two humorous conditions (product-unrelated vs. productrelated). While the product-unrelated condition had no relation between humor and product features (e.g., fiber content), there was one in the product-related condition. To assess the effects of these conditions in promoting healthy food products, we measured observers’ purchase intention for the chickpea pasta. The results, however showed no differences between the conditions. But could humor also have an indirect effect, via mediator variables (e.g., perceived humor, post attitude, product attitude)? The subsequently calculated path model indeed, revealed two significant indirect effects. The use of product-unrelated humor (vs. control condition) had a negative indirect effect on purchase intention. Specifically, product-unrelated humor decreased product attitude, which in turn translated into a lower purchase intention. On the other hand, the use of product-related humor (vs. productunrelated) had a positive indirect effect on purchase intention via perceived humor, post attitude and product attitude. Hence, humor only unfolds its persuasive potential when it is related to the product. To conclude, product-related humor might be able to promote healthier products on social media.

title: Perceptual Learning of Visual Crowding and Location-Specific Transfer in Patients with Central Vision Loss and Normally Sighted Controls
affiliations:
1. University of Regensburg (DE)
2. University Hospital Regensburg (DE)
abstract: Individuals with central vision loss (CVL) frequently develop a preferred retinal locus (PRL) on the intact peripheral retina, adopting eccentric fixation as a compensatory strategy. Visual crowding impairs the recognition of peripherally presented targets when flanked by distractors and is considered a main obstacle to everyday visual functioning in CVL, affecting tasks such as word recognition and reading. Visual crowding has been shown to be reduced through perceptual learning. Thirteen patients with CVL and 13 age-matched normally sighted controls completed an 8-day training protocol on a Landolt C gap detection crowding task with radially and tangentially arranged same-sized circle flankers. Learning success was operationalized as a reduction in critical target-to-flanker distance. Training was conducted at the PRL and an equally eccentric but unutilized control retinal location (CRL). Patients fixated at their PRL, while each matched control trained at the corresponding locations under central fixation. Pre- and post-training, all participants were assessed in letter visual acuity, Vernier hyperacuity, contrast sensitivity, a lexical decision task, and a reading test. All measures except reading were performed at both PRL and CRL. Both groups showed significant learning across locations. Radial-tangential anisotropy was detected only in controls at both locations. Patients demonstrated better crowding performance at the PRL than the CRL, whereas controls showed no location-dependent difference. Transfer to word recognition and visual acuity was significant exclusively at patients' PRL, while controls improved comparably at both PRL and CRL. Reading speed improved in patients but not in controls. No changes in Vernier hyperacuity or contrast sensitivity were observed in either group. These findings indicate location-specific transfer to other visual tasks in CVL patients after crowding training, reflecting preferential resource allocation to the PRL, and support perceptual learning as a rehabilitation approach for central vision loss.

title: Transient downregulation of excitatory activity facilitates skill learning in older adults
affiliations: 1. University of Regensburg (DE)
abstract: Previous studies have shown that the ability to acquire new skills is preserved into older age, suggesting that Hebbian-like synaptic plasticity in sensory-motor areas remains intact. At the same time, there are intrinsic biological changes in the aging brain, including an increase in neural activity, which constrain transient glutamatergic signaling required to induce synaptic plasticity. Here, we investigated whether older adults engage neuronal mechanisms that transiently regulate levels of excitatory activity in early sensory areas, thereby enabling the induction of synaptic plasticity. Participants (60 – 79 years old, n = 20) trained on a visual orientation detection task leading to visual perceptual learning (VPL), a type of visual skill learning. The concentration of glutamate, a major excitatory neurotransmitter, was measured in a volume-of-interest in the occipital lobes (primarily consisting of early visual areas V1 and V2) with functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS) before, during and after training. The results showed that training enhanced detection performance for the trained orientation, consistent with VPL, whereas no improvement was observed for an untrained control orientation. Glutamate concentration decreased within an interval of twenty minutes after the end of training relative to the pretraining concentration. A mediation analysis showed that this reduction of glutamate mediated the impact of pretraining glutamate levels on the formation of VPL. In contrast, a control group of young adults (18 – 30 years old, n = 20) increased glutamate concentration associated with VPL over the same posttraining interval. These results suggest that transient downregulation of excitatory activity in early sensory areas facilitates the induction of synaptic plasticity and supports skill learning in older adults.

title: Extending RL–WM Dynamics Beyond Discrete Choice: Evidence from a Continuous RLWM Paradigm
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology, University of Cambridge (UK)
2. University of California, Berkeley (USA)
3. University of Cambridge (UK)
4. University of Leeds, Leeds (UK)
abstract: Understanding human learning requires disentangling the contributions of multiple interacting cognitive systems. Rather than arising from a single mechanism, the learning process reflects the joint operation of working memory (WM) and reinforcement learning (RL), which support rapid, updating, and gradual value-based learning, respectively. Previous investigations of this interaction have largely relied on discrete alternative-choice paradigms, where response spaces are inherently categorical. While these designs have yielded important insights, they constrain decision-making to predefined options and may obscure how WM and RL operate in more naturalistic, continuous environments. In the present study, we examine WM–RL dynamics using a continuous version of the RLWM task, eliminating discrete response targets and allowing actions to vary along an unconstrained dimension. Behavioral data were collected from 85 participants, followed by a surprise test phase. Consistent with prior findings, results indicate that under high WM load, RL plays a greater role in shaping learning by gradually strengthening stimulus–response associations that are later recalled more reliably. Although WM facilitates rapid early learning, these quickly acquired associations are more susceptible to forgetting, whereas associations learned more gradually under greater reliance on RL show enhanced retention. Importantly, because continuous responses provide richer information than traditional accuracy-based measures, we fitted a three-component mixture model to decompose response variability. While mixture models have primarily been used to characterize memory performance in recall-based paradigms, this study extends their application to continuous RLWM data. The model-based analyses converged with behavioral findings and further revealed how working-memory load modulates the contribution of different learning processes. These findings demonstrate that the canonical interaction between WM and RL generalizes beyond discrete choice paradigms to continuous response spaces, underscoring the robustness of this dual-system account of learning. Future work should explore how reward value further influences learning asymmetries in continuous domains.

title: Retrocueing benefits in visual working memory are disrupted by distraction but not by the need to maintain unprioritised memory contents
affiliations: 1. University of Nottingham (UK)
abstract: Visual working memory (WM) declines with ageing. Predictive cues, directing attentional prioritisation of memory contents reliably improve accuracy and reduce reactions times in younger adults, but there is conflicting evidence regarding whether this ability declines or is maintained in older adults. While some work suggests preserved internal attention, it may 1) become more vulnerable to distraction by an intervening, attention-demanding task, or 2) rely on the ability to drop unprioritised contents to free up resources. Here we developed a visual WM retrocueing task to test these two possibilities. Younger (18-35) and older (60+) adults recalled two items per trial, allowing us to test a) cueing benefits when the cued item was tested first, b) when it was tested second after recalling an uncued item acting as a distractor, and c) any reduction in recall accuracy of uncued items compared to no-cue trials, suggesting that participants had dropped items to free resources for the cued item. Both younger and older adults benefitted when the cued item was recalled first, with the size of the benefit comparable between groups. This benefit came at no apparent cost to subsequent recall of an uncued item in either group, suggesting that cueing benefits do not require dropping other contents. However, when the cued item was recalled second, only the younger group showed a cue benefit. Therefore, preserved internal attention in ageing appears to be impaired by distraction but not by the need to maintain unprioritised contents. Eye-tracking and EEG data have also been recorded. Lateralised posterior alpha rhythms and microsaccades have been used as markers of internal attention in younger adults and we predict ageing effects which reflect those in behaviour. These neural and behavioural markers will give further insight into how these processes change as we age and how we might preserve WM ability.

title: Seeing an Event Isn’t Enough: Phenomenal Causality Modulates Attentional Capture But Not Automatically
affiliations: 1. Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences, Zhejiang University (CN)
abstract: Phenomenal causality is perceived solely from physical cues, reflecting the perceived necessity between two motions. It is perceived automatically and independently of higher-level reasoning. Some researchers suggest that phenomenal causality may function like a Gestalt cue, integrating two motions into a unified whole in a nature way, but this hypothesis has not been empirically tested. Prior work showing that Gestalt-based perceptual integration carries over into visual working memory (VWM) representation provides a basis for examining whether phenomenal causality yields a similar integrative effect. Across three experiments, we investigated whether phenomenal causality shapes how VWM interacts with attention. Experiment 1 used a classical VWM-guided attention paradigm and manipulated causality through time interval. Participants memorized two disc colors and their causal relation before completing a visual search and a memory tasks. VWM-guided attention emerged only in the causality condition. Experiment 2 replicated this results by manipulating motion-path, again demonstrating that causally linked motions were represented as a single event in VWM that guided attention, whereas non-causal motions were not. Experiment 3 tested whether such integration occurs automatically. Participants memorized only one disc's color (i.e. target color) and completed a search task without intentionally encoding the discs' relation. If integration were automatic, both colors would be encoded and guide attention in the causality condition. However, results revealed only the target color guided attention, indicating that VWM does not automatically encode the non-target color even when it is perceptually organized by causality. Together, it shows that phenomenal causality can restructure how multiple motions are represented and used to guide attention, but only when explicitly encoded. This work highlight event structure as a critical determinant of how VWM shapes attentional selection offering new insight into how dynamic event structure shapes cognition.

title: Beyond Intrinsic Priority: How Contextual Distinctiveness Modulates Social Information Selection
affiliations:
1. Zhejiang University (CN)
2. South China Normal University (CN)
abstract: The human visual system often prioritizes self-relevant stimuli, such as one's own name, a phenomenon termed the self-processing advantage (SPA). However, it remains a matter of debate whether this priority stems from a fixed, intrinsic quality of self-representation or a flexible process governed by contextual factors. In this study, we employed a modified attribute amnesia paradigm to investigate how the social composition of a visual display modulates the automatic encoding of person names into working memory. Across a series of experiments, we manipulated contextual distinctiveness by varying the categorical composition of the potential name set, while holding task structure constant. Our results show that the SPA is highly sensitive to relative contextual distinctiveness. When the self-name serves as a unique social category, it reliably captures cognitive priority. Notably, this benefit extends to other familiar identities under high-distinctiveness conditions, indicating that uniqueness is a primary driver of automatic visual encoding. Conversely, when the self's distinctiveness is diluted within a diverse social context, the SPA is eliminated. Crucially, under matched competitive constraints where the self and another highly familiar identity share distinctiveness, self-relevance acts as a tie-breaker to reclaim processing priority.  These findings demonstrate that the self-processing advantage is not an inevitable intrinsic privilege but is flexibly shaped by relative contextual distinctiveness. This study highlights the dynamic nature of how the visual system prioritizes socially relevant information based on the informational structure of the immediate context.

title: A Unifying Framework of Competing History Biases and Memory Failures in Visual Working Memory Representations
affiliations: 1. Koç University (TR)
abstract: We present an analytical framework to account for history biases in visual working memory (VWM) representations. A variety of history biases shape target representations, ranging from stable categorical attractors (intercardinal orientations, canonical colors) to transient session-level summaries (central tendency of the stimulus distribution) and trial-by-trial serial dependencies. These sources of bias have typically been treated independently, or those deemed irrelevant removed via residualization, post-hoc. The proposed framework offers a unified perspective that can comprehensively account for all these history biases in VWM representations. Specifically, we applied a stochastic model to an in-house rapid serial visual presentation attentional blink data where participants had to encode and reproduce two sequential targets’ orientations (T1 and T2).  The model assumes that VWM representations are continuous traces that drift and diffuse over delay, while simultaneously accounting for memory failures. T2 responses were best captured by a full model dependent on the memory state. Specifically, when T2 (subsequent target) is “remembered”, its representation drifts towards the stable categorical attractors (e.g., intercardinal orientations) and the global mean of the T2 orientation distribution while drifting away from the preceding target in the same trial (T1). When the T2 is “forgotten”, the model probabilistically assigns the response to one of three memory failure substates: a swap error (reporting T1 for T2), a categorical guess (e.g., an intercardinal orientation), or a random guess (a uniform response). To further validate this analytical framework’s generalizability, we applied reduced variants of the model to serial dependence datasets, demonstrating how these overlapping biases dynamically influence VWM representations. The model is currently under further development. This framework unifies several lines of research and offers better understanding of human VWM without applying post-hoc statistical corrections to the data.
