title: Preserved covert attention but altered oculomotor dynamics in myopia
affiliations:
1. University of Lausanne (CH)
2. Lausanne University Hospital (CH)
3. New York University (US)
abstract: GOAL: Covert attention enhances visual perception across the visual field, often with pronounced effects in the periphery, where sensory uncertainty is highest. Individuals with myopia, even when corrected, exhibit reduced acuity and contrast sensitivity in the peripheral visual field compared to emmetropes. Here, we investigated whether  the extent of covert attention effects and their corresponding oculomotor responses vary as a function of myopia. METHODS: Participants, all with corrected-to-normal vision, performed two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) tasks to discriminate the orientation of tilted Gabor patches. Stimuli were presented at 6° eccentricity on the horizontal meridian while participants maintained central fixation. Endogenous (voluntary) and exogenous (involuntary) attention were manipulated using informative central and uninformative peripheral cues, respectively,  shortly before the stimuli appeared. Cues were valid, invalid, or neutral, and presented randomly. Tilt thresholds for each participant were determined using a Weibull staircase (80% accuracy). Microsaccades were recorded throughout the trial. RESULTS: Both groups exhibited robust endogenous and exogenous attentional effects: valid cues increased performance (d’), while invalid cues decreased performance, compared to neutral cues. The magnitude of these attentional benefits and costs were comparable between myopes and emmetropes. In both experiments, participants exhibited a microsaccade bias toward the target during the response preparation period, however, this bias was significantly reduced in the myopic group.  CONCLUSION: Myopia, a condition associated with axial eye elongation and typically developing in late childhood, leads to peripheral visual deficits. Our findings indicate that covert attention remains functional in myopia and may partially compensate for these sensory deficits in corrected-to-normal adults. However, the attenuated microssaccades dynamics suggest that, while attentional benefits are preserved, downstream processes–potentially related to decision stages–may be altered in myopia.

title: Sustained and selective attention in multiple object tracking
affiliations:
1. Research Centre for Brain and Behaviour, Liverpool John Moores University (UK)
2. University of Southern Denmark (DK)
3. University of Aberdeen (UK)
abstract: Selective attention supports many aspects of perception and goal-directed behaviour, yet its relationship to everyday attentional experience remains poorly understood — laboratory studies typically examine attention over timescales of only a few seconds, while measures of real-world attention rely predominantly on vigilance-based tasks. To address this, we examined selective attention during multiple object tracking in two experiments, both using frequency-tagging and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) to index prioritisation of targets over distractors.  Experiment 1 focused on individual differences, asking whether trait distractibility reflects the strength of selective attention or the ability to sustain it. Forty-eight participants completed a multiple object tracking task and a validated inattention questionnaire. Unexpectedly, participants with higher distractibility scores showed steeper improvements in tracking accuracy across the session, outperforming less distractible individuals by the end. At the neural level, ASRS scores were positively correlated with overall SSVEP amplitudes, yet the strength of attentional selection -- the difference in SSVEPs elicited by targets and distractors -- did not vary with self-reported distractibility, suggesting that this trait is associated with stronger sensory responses rather than impaired selective attention. Experiment 2 employed a continuous tracking paradigm, removing inter-trial breaks to quantify time-on-task effects. Participants completed a continuous 20-minute tracking task where SSVEPs indexed selection within each 60-second interval. Attention modulation indices (AMIs) weakened progressively within each trial, yet the average trial AMI strengthened across the session, suggesting that attention is not just sustained but dynamically updated throughout the experimental task. Selection was also reduced immediately preceding tracking errors, confirming that lapses in sustained attention predict tracking failures.  Together, these findings show that selective attention during multiple object tracking reflects both trait-like individual differences and time-varying dynamics that can help characterise attention in everyday life.

title: Behavioral and Neural Correlates of Selective Attention in Adults Born Preterm
affiliations:
1. Department of Neuroscience, Bilkent University (TR)
2. Department of Psychology, Bilkent University (TR)
abstract: Preterm birth has been linked to long-term visual–perceptual difficulties, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. These difficulties are most commonly attributed to dorsal stream dysfunction, although evidence remains inconsistent. An alternative account proposes a more global impairment in visual processing. To test this, we combined psychophysics and fMRI to examine selective attention in adults born preterm and term-born controls. Participants performed letter (8 control, 9 preterm) and motion tasks (6 control, 6 preterm) under attended and unattended conditions, with peripheral distractors presented either simultaneously or sequentially. In the attended condition, they detected luminance decreases in the peripheral distractor in the unattended condition, they identified a central letter or motion while ignoring peripheral distractors. Perceptual grouping was manipulated to dissociate top-down and bottom-up attentional influences. Psychophysical results showed that motion thresholds were significantly affected by perceptual grouping (p = 0.002) and distractor presentation (p = 0.008), with higher thresholds in no-grouping and sequential conditions. There was a strong main effect of attention in letter tasks (p < 0.001), along with interactions between attention and distractor presentation (p = 0.004) and among attention, grouping, and birth status (p = 0.01). Notably, the preterm group showed a smaller increase in thresholds between attended and unattended conditions in the no-grouping condition. fMRI analyses (7 control, 7 preterm) that focused on V1, V4, and hMT+ regions, revealed a significant interaction between attention and birth status in V4 (p = 0.01), displaying that the control group but not the preterm group showed higher BOLD signals in attended conditions. A similar pattern was numerically observed in hMT+. Additionally, sequential distractor presentation elicited higher BOLD responses across groups (p = 0.02), supporting biased competition. The results indicate a partially differentiated pattern of selective attention between preterm- and term-born adults.

title: Evaluating Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) in a dry EEG system using a gamified Posner task
affiliations:
1. VPixx Technologies (CA)
2. Université du Québec en Outaouais (CA)
3. Wearable Sensing (US)
abstract:
Rapid invisible frequency tagging (RIFT) is a promising method for noninvasively monitoring spatial attention. In the RIFT paradigm, luminance modulations at >50 Hz are used to embed invisible flicker in a high-speed display. A growing body of literature shows that this flicker produces robust steady-state evoked responses in the visual cortex and beyond. The relative amplitude and coherence of the response serve as clear metrics of dynamic spatial attention, distinct from overt gaze behaviour. Thus, RIFT offers a unique window into attention while remaining completely undetectable to the participant.

No study to date has examined RIFT in dry-electrode EEG. Given the comfort and accessibility of dry electrode headsets, establishing a proof of concept for RIFT in dry EEG is a critical step toward real-world BCI and performance-monitoring applications where wet EEG and MEG are impractical. In addition, characterizing the impact of mental load and attentional resource allocation on the RIFT response is essential for developing a comprehensive RIFT analysis pipeline for online operator performance monitoring.

In this work, we present SpaceRIFT, a gamified Posner cueing paradigm. Participants maintain central fixation while four peripheral display regions are tagged at distinct frequencies (Experiment 1) and phases (Experiment 2). A valid-cue phase establishes baseline attentional modulation, followed by a ‘damaged computer’ phase in which cue reliability is degraded. Neural responses are recorded using either dry-electrode EEG (Wearable Sensing) or wet-electrode EEG (Brain Vision).

Analyses will characterize the functional frequency range and phase resolution supported by dry-electrode EEG, establishing the operational RIFT window available in an accessible, deployable system, and relate behavioural indices of mental load and cue reliability to trial-wise neural responses. We expect that dry electrode EEG will support a well-defined operational RIFT window, with converging behavioural–coherence relationships aligned with wet EEG benchmarks.

title: Top-down temporal attention influences visual perception through frequency-distinct modulations
affiliations:
1. Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics (DE)
2. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: Just as attention gates our conscious perception in space, the brain proactively prioritizes moments in time based on temporal regularities and allocates resources accordingly, resulting in performance benefits at attended moments. However, the neural mechanisms underlying temporal attention are not yet fully understood. One intriguing possibility relies on the now established link between fluctuations in visual perception and the neural state at the moment of stimulus presentation, such as the momentary phase of endogenous oscillations. Through this, temporal attention might affect visual perception if knowing the timing of an upcoming stimulus could be used to proactively align the optimal oscillatory phase to the moment of the predicted target onset. While this has been shown for periodic streams and attributed to oscillatory entrainment, it is unclear whether such mechanism is also involved in aperiodic, memory-based attention. In a series of experiments, we investigated whether temporal attention as guided through memorized time intervals operates through phase alignment in the occipital cortex. Participants conducted challenging visual discrimination tasks under delayed response protocols, to minimize involvement of anticipatory motor activity. Temporal predictions were provided through periodic streams or cue-interval memorized associations, and participants provided both objective discrimination performance and subjective perception. We found that memory-based temporal cueing increased phase alignment in the delta band (0.5-3 Hz) to an equal degree as rhythmic entrainment. However, alpha band (8-12 Hz), where the temporal window of optimal perception is much narrower, did not show clear phase modulation. Additionally, temporally guided anticipatory suppression of alpha-band amplitude was decoupled from the observed perceptual benefits of both subjective and objective perception. Taken together, these results show that low-frequency phase alignment can occur in the absence of oscillatory entrainment, and reveal that temporal attention changes interactions between alpha activity and behaviour compared to spontaneous fluctuations.

title: Are attentional state fluctuations impervious to task load?
affiliations: 1. University of Leicester (UK)
abstract: Our ability to focus visual attentional resources fluctuates on a moment-to-moment basis, producing periods of stable and unstable performance (Esterman et al., 2013 Rosenberg., 2026). While increasing task load typically impairs performance, it remains unclear whether impairments arise from modulating fluctuations between underlying optimal and suboptimal attentional states. Here, we used reaction time variability and pupillometry to index fluctuations in attentional state in a novel orientation discrimination task. Task difficulty was manipulated block-wise by the presence or absence of task irrelevant colour variation in displays. We expected fluctuations in performance to depend on task difficulty, such that increased load would alter the temporal structure of attentional state fluctuations. While the presence of colour distractors reduced accuracy significantly, this did not affect reaction time variability. Independently of colour distractors, lower accuracy was observed during periods of high reaction time variability, while pupil size was associated with reaction time variability but not performance directly. We found no reliable evidence that colour distractors modulated reaction time variability or pupillometric markers of attentional fluctuation. Instead, the observed relationship between pupil size and reaction time variability suggests these fluctuations were largely independent of our load manipulation and may reflect intrinsic factors.

title: The effects of attention and causal structure on the neural representation of naturalistic movies
affiliations:
1. CIMeC, University of Trento (IT)
2. Donders Institute, Radboud University (NL)
abstract: Events are often linked by cause-and-effect relationships that our brain uses to anticipate future perceptual inputs, such as dark clouds preceding a rainstorm. Here, we investigated how disrupting these causal relationships influences neural representations of perceptual features. Specifically, we tested whether the brain updates its internal models automatically after a prediction is violated or requires top-down attention.  In a MEG experiment, 54 participants watched 8-minute-long movies while either attending to the movies or performing a distraction task. In the attended condition, catch trials required participants to judge whether the movie continued in an expected manner, whereas in the distraction condition they judged whether briefly appearing shapes were the same or different. This design allowed us to assess whether predictions were formed automatically or required top-down attention. Crucially, the movies were also played either forward or backward. Because natural events unfold in a fixed causal order, reversing the movies produces clear violations of the underlying causal structure without altering the frame-by-frame visual input.  We used dynamic RSA, a novel extension of representational similarity analysis, in which temporally variable models of stimulus features are compared to neural data. This allows us to test directly when and to what extent these features are represented in the brain.   Preliminary analyses showed that low-level visual features including luminance and optical flow were represented in a lagged manner (360-560 ms and 100-120 ms, respectively) in early visual regions (V1, V2, and V3/V4). Attention enhanced these representations, whereas reversing the causal structure produced no consistent effect on representational dynamics. Body posture was represented in LOTC at 300-500 ms, with neither attention nor movie direction modulating this representation.  These preliminary findings suggest that while attention shapes early sensory processing, neural representations of both low-level and higher-level visual features may be robust to violations of causal event structure.

title: Attentional deployment in the visual field includes both task- and observer-specific components
affiliations: 1. Aalborg University (DK)
abstract: Visual attention studies often distribute stimuli on an imaginary circle to minimise foveal and low-level confounds (e.g., Sørensen, Vangkilde, & Bundesen, 2015). While the Theory of Visual Attention (TVA Bundesen, 1990) formally allows spatial variation, it is frequently applied in ways that assume homogeneity across the visual field and is seldom examined directly (with rare exceptions, e.g., hemifield lateralisation Habekost & Rostrup, 2006). Here, we challenge this assumption by demonstrating systematic and stable spatial structure in attentional deployment. Revisiting data from Sørensen, Vangkilde, and Bundesen (2015), we estimate attentional weights (w) across six equidistant spatial positions over repeated sessions and task contexts. Replicating previous reports of inter-individual spatial biases (Nordfang, Staugaard, & Bundesen, 2018), we observe pronounced and idiosyncratic deviations from spatial uniformity. Critically, these spatial profiles exhibit substantial within-subject stability across sessions, forming an attentional “fingerprint” of the observer. Importantly, previous work has demonstrated that attentional measures can be highly sensitive to methodological factors, including eye movements and practice effects (Petersen & Kyllingsbæk, 2013). In contrast, the spatial weighting profiles observed here remain robust across sessions, indicating that they capture stable aspects of attentional deployment rather than transient task artefacts. However, these fingerprints are not fixed. Partial-report paradigms systematically reshape spatial weighting profiles across sessions, whereas whole-report paradigms yield comparatively stable configurations. This dissociation suggests that partial report engages adaptive or strategic control processes that dynamically modulate spatial selection. Together, these findings indicate that attentional weights reflect both stable individual structure and task-dependent dynamics. More broadly, they challenge the comparability of TVA-derived parameters across paradigms and highlight the need to account for individual spatial profiles when interpreting measures of visual attention.

title: The brain inhibits salient, but not non-salient, distractors in the control of eye-tracking.
affiliations: 1. Lancaster University (UK)
abstract: Numerous studies have examined factors that influence whether attention is captured by distractors, often focusing on the roles of bottom-up factors like target salience and top-down control. While these studies tend to emphasize the capture of attention, in everyday situations, we are typically adept at suppressing visual distractions to focus on the object of interest. This raises key questions: How is suppression of distractors achieved? Is attention solely drawn to the most salient object, or does processing at the distractor's location play a role? How long does this inhibition last, and is it based on the distractor’s identity or location? Can this inhibition handle multiple distractors, and how important is distractor saliency? To address these questions, the Inhibition of Recent Distractor (IRD) Task, introduced by Crawford et al. (2005), (Smith & Crawford 2024) was used. In this task, a peripheral target is presented along with a distractor, followed by a new target appearing either at the previous target’s location (T-T), a new location (T-N), or the previous distractor’s location (T-D). Initial findings showed active inhibition of the distractor’s location for up to 5 seconds, which is location-based. Recent studies confirmed the IRD effect and highlighted the importance of distractor saliency in suppressing multiple distractors. References: Crawford, T. J., Higham, S., & Hill, S. (2005). The Inhibitory Effect of Recent Distracter. Vision Research, 45(27), 3365-3378. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2005.07.024 Smith, E., & Crawford, T. (2024). The inhibitory effect of a recent distractor: Singleton vs multiple distractors. Experimental Brain Research, 242(7), 1745-1759. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00221-024-06846-3

title: Pre-saccadic modulation of vergence response
affiliations:
1. Philipps-Universität Marburg (DE)
2. Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior (DE)
3. Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone, CNRS, Aix-Marseille Université (FR)
4. Philipps-Universität Marburg (DE)
abstract: We use a combination of saccades and vergence to redirect our gaze across direction and depth in three-dimensional space. Vergence eye-movements typically precede saccadic eye-movements, demonstrating that the visual system is able to dynamically extract disparities not at the fovea to drive vergence. Here, we investigated the vergence responses induced by brief pre-saccadic disparity steps. The stimulus consisted of three random-dot stereograms (RDSs), each 7° in diameter, presented at fixation, 8° above fixation, and 8° below fixation. Each trial started with a randomized interval of central fixation. Then, a cue instructed the participants either to make a saccade to one of the peripheral RDSs or to continue fixating at the center. Following a random delay after cue onset (150 - 350 ms), a disparity step (target) of -1.5°, -0.75°, 0°, 0.75°, or 1.5° was introduced either at the center or at the peripheral RDSs resulting in four conditions: i. central cue and central target ii. central cue and peripheral target iii. peripheral cue and central target and iv. peripheral cue and peripheral target. The target was presented for 100 ms before the screen turned blank. Participants responded to disparity steps in all conditions, but the strength of this vergence response was modulated by the saccadic plan. In the fixation conditions, vergence responses were stronger for disparity steps at the fovea (i) than in periphery (ii) as expected. Remarkably, in the saccadic condition, responses were stronger for peripheral target (iv) than for central target (iii). Moreover, vergence responses at the fovea when the participants made a saccade to periphery (iii) were weaker than when they maintained central fixation (i), suggesting some disengagement of attention from the pre-saccadic location. Together, our results demonstrate that vergence responses are modulated by saccadic planning. Supported by German Research Foundation (Project numbers: 524696675 EXC-3066 TAM)

title: Testing models of sensory cue integration with physiological measurements
affiliations: 1. University of Reading (UK)
abstract: Contemporary models of sensory cue integration propose that by combining sensory cues we gain a more precise sensory estimate compared to that available from the cues in isolation. This is achieved by weighting cues in proportion to their relative reliability, and their reliability relative to a priori information about the perceptual property being estimated. Cue weighting is typically measured behaviourally, e.g. via a two alternative forced choice experiment. However, theoretically, one could determine cue weighting using data from any level of the perceptual hierarchy, e.g. from physiological response through to perceptual decision. Here, we derive equations allowing one to test cue integration using cue weights inferred from the gain function relating physiological responses to a varying driving stimulus. We apply this model to an extensive preexisting data set of vergence and accommodative responses (measured with a Remote Haploscopic Photorefractor) to distance targets (0.5, 1, 2 and 3 dioptres) varied to isolate individual cues of disparity, blur and angular subtense (Horwood and Riddell, 2008). We find that combined cues physiological gain functions can be predicted by that of individual cues. This being clearer for vergence compared to accommodative responses. Our results offer a novel way in which to test models of sensory cue integration, which complements current behavioural methods. We highlight the assumptions and limitations of this approach, as well as its ability to disambiguate between competing models of cue integration.

title: Bridging the Latency Gap: A Neurocomputational Model of Predictive Remapping
affiliations: 1. University of Technology Chemnitz (DE)
abstract: Visual perception remains remarkably stable across saccadic eye movements despite rapid and large displacements of the retinal image. This stability is thought to rely, in part, on predictive remapping processes that update spatial representations in anticipation of eye movements. However, the functional role and temporal characteristics of these mechanisms remain debated. In this study, we investigate neural dynamics in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) of monkeys performing a spatial foraging task, which investigates spatial updating during visual search, described by Mirpour & Bisley (2016). The data revolves around neural activity profiles in present and future receptive fields across saccades under different stimulation conditions (target, distractor, empty). We use a neurocomputational model of spatial perception based on gain fields, integrating retinal input with corollary discharge (CD) and proprioceptive eye-position (PC) signals to generate distributed spatial representations.\nBy systematically manipulating model components, we isolate the contributions of individual signals to the observed dynamics. Our results show that predictive remapping, arising from the interaction of corollary discharge, proprioceptive eye-position, and presaccadic visual signals, is sufficient to account for the rapid emergence of postsaccadic representations in LIP. While the required phasic CD signal peaks around saccade onset, the PC signal update has to be late after saccade.

title: Skilled badminton players maintain gaze on the opponent’s upper body in a live return task
affiliations:
1. NTT Communication Science Laboratories (JP)
2. The University of Tokyo (JP)
abstract: Anticipating an opponent’s action is critical in badminton return, yet little is known about how gaze behavior is temporally organized around shuttle impact. This study examined the temporal structure of gaze behavior in a live badminton return task, comparing skilled and less-skilled players under ecologically valid conditions. Eighteen male university badminton players (10 skilled, 8 less-skilled response-time analysis: n = 17) returned 40 randomized shots (smash, cut, drop, clear) while wearing a mobile eye tracker. Gaze was analyzed relative to shuttle impact, focusing on fixation onset and duration within three areas of interest: the opponent’s upper body, lower body, and the racket–shuttle contact point. Performance was assessed using return errors and response time derived from waist-mounted acceleration.  Skilled players made fewer return errors than less-skilled players (1.9 vs. 9.3) and responded faster (147 vs. 204 ms). Their typical gaze pattern was “shuttle → upper body → contact point” (9/10), whereas many less-skilled players mainly shifted gaze directly from the shuttle to the contact point (6/8). Skilled players fixated the opponent’s upper body for longer (383 vs. 79 ms) and the contact point for a shorter duration (227 vs. 426 ms). They also shifted gaze to the contact point later than less-skilled players (172 vs. 350 ms before impact), indicating that they maintained gaze on the opponent’s upper body until closer to shuttle impact. In contrast, the onset of the first upper-body fixation did not differ between groups. Upper-body fixation duration was negatively correlated with response time. These findings suggest that rather than simply looking at different locations, skilled players differ in how they time the shift of gaze from predictive body cues to impact-related information. This timing-dependent visual strategy may be important in badminton and may also reflect a more general principle of anticipation in fast interceptive actions.

title: Sensory, motor and cardiac coupling during visual foraging
affiliations:
1. University College London (UK)
2. Hebrew University of Jerusalem (IL)
abstract: Natural vision involves active exploration of the environment, with observers choosing when and where to sample information. Observers must therefore navigate the inherent trade-off between exploiting high quality information during visual fixations and exploring for information in different locations by making a saccade. Previous work demonstrates that perceptual sensitivity and the probability of making saccades fluctuate at 4 to 8 Hz. This suggests a temporal segregation of exploration and exploitation in natural vision, reflected in the rhythmic alternation between fixations and saccades. Furthermore, these rhythms might be modulated by other endogenous biological fluctuations, like the cardiac cycle, which induces variation in perceptual and saccadic processes. To investigate how these rhythmic processes are nested across timescales, we have designed a novel visual foraging task that allows measurement of perceptual and saccadic rhythms during continuous, naturalistic behaviour. Participants make freely initiated saccades between multiple gratings, and respond to brief low-contrast targets that are displayed on top of the currently fixated grating. The probability of a target appearing depletes as a function of time fixating that grating, encouraging visual exploration of the display. We can therefore investigate detection performance in conjunction with the timing of freely-initiated saccades and microsaccades. Preliminary analyses of pilot data (n=5) suggest the presence of fast (~8Hz) oscillations in detection rates following saccade landing on a new grating. Future analyses on a full dataset of 40 participants will investigate how (micro)saccadic rhythms are coupled to perceptual rhythms and the slower cardiac cycle. Overall, we aim to show the interplay of biological rhythms that underlie natural vision and provide a mechanistic account of the temporal coordination of exploratory visual behaviour.

title: VoroGaze AOI: A User-Friendly Voronoi-Based Shiny App for Fixation Analyses
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Choosing areas of interest (AOIs) in eye-tracking research is often a subjective process that not only raises questions about the reliability and validity of the results, but also makes comparisons across studies difficult. The Voronoi tessellation method divides an image into regions around predefined landmarks such that each location is assigned to its nearest landmark. This method has been proposed as a more objective solution that is robust to noise, particularly for faces and other stimuli with clearly defined features. However, commercial software has not implemented Voronoi-based AOI analysis, meaning that applying this method often requires complex custom coding. To address this issue, we present VoroGaze AOI, a user-friendly Shiny app for AOI creation and fixation analysis, which runs in a standard web browser. Users simply upload a fixation report and the relevant stimuli, and place landmarks on each stimulus. The app then computes AOIs based on these landmarks and generates fixation summaries. VoroGaze AOI will be made freely available to all interested researchers.

title: The Cardinal Bias: Intrinsic Structure of Visual Exploration Revealed by Eye Movements
affiliations:
1. State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Science and Mental Health, Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CN)
2. Department of Psychology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CN)
abstract: The human visual system optimizes its behavior when exploring the environment, allocating eye gaze based on stimulus salience, task goals, and statistical probabilities. However, it remains largely unknown where gaze naturally falls when these guiding factors are absent, neutralized, or isotropic. Here, we report a robust “Cardinal Bias” in eye-movement patterns during visual search. When searching for a weak target embedded in 1/f noise within a circular display, participants directed more fixations toward the four cardinal directions (up, down, left, right) than toward the four oblique ones, despite equal target probabilities on these axes and randomized background textures. Remarkably, this cardinal preference persisted even when targets never appeared along the cardinal and oblique axes, or when they followed a uniform distribution within the search display, albeit target probabilities reshaped the distribution of fixations. In addition, participants were unaware of this cardinal bias, and naive online participants could not predict it, suggesting that visual exploration follows a hidden structure without explicit efforts. Eye movements have long been considered guided by a priority map that integrates various attentional factors. Our findings provide novel evidence that this priority map possesses an intrinsic mode independent of obvious guiding factors, implying a spatial reference frame aligned with Earth’s gravity for visual exploration.

title: Transsaccadic integration of facial information
affiliations: 1. Technische Universität Chemnitz (DE)
abstract: If an object of interest appears in the periphery, an observer typically makes a saccade to place it in their fovea. The visual system can be highly efficient in this scenario by using both separated target inputs - peripheral and foveal information - optimally for perception. This process is called optimal transsaccadic integration and has been shown for low- to mid-level visual features. It is unknown whether this efficacy holds for more complex perceptual judgements and higher-level visual features. Here, we addressed this open question and tested optimal transsaccadic integration of facial information. Sixteen participants judged the sex of faces (female or male) they saw either only presaccadically in the periphery, only postsaccadically in the fovea, or across saccades at both retinal locations. If participants integrate optimally, perception across saccades should be more precise than perception of only one of the inputs alone and match predicted precision by maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE). We measured perceptual precision by fitting psychometric functions per condition and participant and deriving the just-noticeable difference (JND). We also derived the points of subjective equality (PSE) to investigate perceptual bias. We found JNDs to be significantly lower (i.e. higher precision) in the transsaccadic condition compared to the best JNDs from the single-input conditions. In addition, transsaccadic JNDs matched JNDs predicted by maximum-likelihood estimation. These results suggest optimal transsaccadic integration of facial information. PSEs revealed a robust male bias in the periphery and no bias in the fovea and across saccades. Further comparison to MLE predictions revealed that peripheral and foveal biases were weighted optimally by their reliabilities across saccades. Our results demonstrate that optimal integration can extend to complex perceptual judgements, such as the sex of faces. This suggests that transsaccadic integration is not limited to low- or mid-level features but may also operate on more abstract representations.

title: Age effects on value-based gaze allocation in natural images
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University (DE)
2. 2Chemnitz University of Technology (DE)
abstract: Our environment provides a plethora of visual information that requires efficient attentional selection, typically associated with gaze shifts. Whereas basic oculomotor parameters are remarkably robust during aging, there is evidence for substantial age effects when naturalistic stimuli are explored. In particular, there seems to be a bias towards appetitive stimuli. At the same time, object-level visual salience might become more relevant in the face of declining sensory capacities. We investigated age effects on gaze behavior and how those are shaped by valence and visual salience. A total of 32 older adults (60-80 years) and 31 younger adults (20-36 years) participated in our study and their gaze behavior was recorded during free viewing of natural scenes in which object valence and salience were varied systematically. We found that salience drives gaze guidance similarly in both older and younger adults. In contrast, we found a more pronounced modulation of gaze parameters by valence in older adults than in younger adults. In particular, appetitive valence reduced time to first fixation and increased dwell time. The variability of gaze control was not linked to individual differences in executive functions, indicating separate underlying mechanisms. Our findings corroborate that gaze guidance in natural images is subject to age effects and suggest a dominant role of top-down processes.

title: Manual response planning as a cue elicits weak contextual saccadic adaptation
affiliations:
1. Lille University (FR)
2. CNRS (FR)
abstract: Contextual saccadic adaptation refers to the oculomotor system’s ability to maintain distinct adaptive states depending on context. Previous work, including ours, has established that this process is highly selective. Specifically, motor-related cues directly affecting the saccade drive contextual adaptation, whereas purely perceptual cues are largely ineffective. This is consistent with the idea that contextual adaptation depends on how strongly a cue engages motor processes relevant to the saccadic system. Here, we asked whether manual response preparation can act as a contextual cue for saccadic adaptation, as in saccadic motor planning. Participants performed a double-step adaptation task in which two opposite intra-saccadic step (ISS) directions were paired with two contexts. During fixation, a symbolic arrow indicated which hand (left or right) to use. Participants prepared the response before the saccade and executed the button press within 300 ms after saccade onset. The mapping between response hand and ISS direction was counterbalanced across participants. We reasoned that if motor preparation alone is sufficient, manual response preparation should allow contextual saccadic adaptation, whereas if contextual learning is specific to oculomotor planning, no effect should be observed. We observed an intermediate pattern: four out of nine participants showed significant contextual adaptation, but the effect remained weaker than with strongly motor-related cues such as saccade sequences.  These findings may reflect a gradient of motor relevance. Manual response preparation can partially structure adaptation, possibly through eye–hand coordination, but remains insufficient to serve as a robust contextual cue for separate adaptive states. In contrast, cues directly shaping the saccadic motor plan are the most effective, suggesting that contextual learning primarily depends on effector-specific motor planning.

title: Pre-microsaccade enhancement of the current and future stimulus locations in foveal V1
affiliations: 1. Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan (ISR)
abstract: Microsaccades are miniature saccades performed during visual fixation that were shown to play a pivotal role in active sensing. Recent studies suggested that pre-microsaccade attention may underlie the enhanced visual processing at the stimulus site. However, the neuronal mechanism underlying this phenomenon at the foveal scale remains unknown. Using voltage-sensitive dye imaging, we investigated the neural responses to uninstructed, spontaneous microsaccades in the fovea of the primary visual cortex (V1) in monkeys. We found that before a microsaccade onset toward a stimulus, the neuronal activity at the current and future landing stimulus sites was enhanced. This enhancement was spatially confined to the current and future landing stimulus sites, which appeared to merge along the microsaccade trajectory in V1. Finally, we found that a pre-microsaccade increased synchronization at the current stimulus site. Our findings shed new light on the neural modulations preceding microsaccades and suggest a link to neural signatures of attention.

title: Revolutions Around a Hue Circle: Individual Differences in Steady-State Visual Evoked Potentials May Reveal Six Lobes and Complex Cardinal Opponency in Cortical Chromatic Coding
affiliations: 1. Fielding Graduate University (US)
abstract: Kaneko et al. (2025) analyzed individual differences in steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) recorded occipitally in response to a flickering checkerboard swept around a cone-contrast hue circle. By examining inter-individual correlational patterns and applying nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS), they identified lobes at six primary and four secondary hue positions, as well as four dimensional components. Building on that work, I argue here that five aspects of those results challenge simple opponent-process explanations and motivate new models of cortical color coding. 1.  No simple opponency. Neither the correlational nor the NMDS components showed sidelobes appearing 180° opposite the test stimulus, and no dimension aligned cleanly with either cardinal axis. 2.  Six primary lobes, separated by ~60°, were evident in the correlational patterns and first two NMDS dimensions, consistent with prior electrophysiological and psychophysical literature. 3.  Four additional lobes emerged in the third and fourth NMDS dimensions. The 10 lobe positions coincide with the psychophysical hue-scaling components from Emery et al. (2023), with lobes spaced approximately every 30° in the full four-dimensional solution. 4.  Complex opponency. All four dimensions show multi-lobe opponent structure with poles at non-complementary, non-cardinal hue angles. 5.  Complex cardinal opponency. Three dimensions show a dominant peak at a cardinal hue direction, opposed by multiple non-complementary lobes. These patterns raise fundamental questions: do the patterns observed in group data reflect genuine neural mechanisms within individual observers? Do these candidate neural codes influence color perception? I hypothesize that the answer is yes in both cases. Future work using masking paradigms can directly address the first the second remains an open target for perceptual studies.

title: Estimating L:M cone ratio with an objective SSVEP based version of the OSCAR test.
affiliations:
1. The Sussex Colour Group, School of Psychology, University of Sussex (UK)
2. Department of Psychology, University of Cambridge (UK)
3. Experimental Psychology, University College London (UK)
4. Institute of Ophthalmology, University College London (UK)
abstract: Previous research has established that the ratio of long- to medium wavelength-sensitive cones in the human retina (L:M cone ratio) varies substantially between individuals. It is unclear how the retinal cone mosaic develops in early life and what environmental factors may contribute to variation in L:M cone ratio. Existing research has been limited to adults as methods typically involve heterochromatic flicker photometry (HFP), where the observer adjusts the relative intensities of two alternating lights until minimal flicker is perceived. One such test is the Objective Screening of Colour Anomalies and Reductions (OSCAR) test (Jordan & Mollon, 1997, Colour Vision Deficiencies XIII, Kluwer) which uses a unique waveform where red and green LEDs modulate their amplitudes in counterphase around a constant mean. This has the advantage that the stimulus appears a stable yellow throughout the range of counterphase modulation depths. However, the OSCAR test and other existing tests cannot be used with infants as infants are unable to make adjustments or report what they perceive. We propose a novel method of measuring perceived flicker without a requirement for participant responses, using steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs) measured with electroencephalography (EEG). We measured SSVEPs from the occipital lobe in adult participants in response to a CRT-based version of the OSCAR test. Our CRT-based OSCAR test cycled through a range of possible depths of 26.67 Hz counterphase modulation of the red and green primaries. We derived L:M cone ratio estimates as the minima of SSVEP responses as a function of counterphase modulation depth. We discuss our preliminary findings and ways to maximise the efficiency of the method.  One future application of the method will be to use it to estimate L:M cone ratio in infants longitudinally to characterise cone ratio development.

title: Food-selectivity and colour tuning curves in the ventral visual pathway
affiliations: 1. University of Sussex (UK)
abstract: Trichromatic vision is crucial for evaluating food objects. This seems to be reflected in the newly-discovered ventral food streams – these regions of the ventral visual pathway are both food-selective and colour-biased. However, it is not currently known how the neural representations of food and colour are connected in these regions. Are there colour tuning curves in the ventral food streams for canonically coloured objects (e.g., when an image of a banana is presented on a display do the ventral food streams show activation patterns shaped as a tuning curve centred around yellow)? We set up a 3T fMRI study to investigate whether there are food-specific colour tuning functions in the ventral food streams. Four participants took part in four 1h scan sessions. We identified food-selective regions by using a functional localiser: we showed participants images of food, faces, places and objects in grayscale and colour on a colour calibrated display. To measure putative colour tuning functions, each participant saw 2 food objects rendered in greyscale and in 5 different hues (original hue, and hue-rotated: -90°, -37°, 37° and 90°), where saturation and luminance were controlled. Food-colour stimuli were presented peripherally for 2s while participants performed a central 2N-back task. After the scan sessions, participants took part in two behavioural tasks to select typical food colours and rate the naturalness of the food objects. We found food-selective ROIs in the ventral visual pathway that also respond to colour (vs grayscale non-food objects). Our preliminary analysis of stimulus responses in the food-selective ROIs did not reveal consistent colour tuning curves. We speculate that the 2N-back task may have been too cognitively demanding to activate the neural representations of the food colours, especially when the food objects were presented in the periphery.

title: Disadvantage of active visual search for a coloured target in immersive virtual environments
affiliations:
1. Department of Electrical & Electronic Engineering, University of Manchester (UK)
2. Leeds Institute of Textiles and Colour, University of Leeds (UK)
3. Virtual Reality Research (VR2) Facility, Division of Psychology, Communication & Human Neuroscience, University of Manchester (UK)
abstract: Everyday human vision typically involves active exploration of three-dimensional environments, with freedom to move and change viewpoint. Yet many perceptual judgments are still studied using simplified stimuli on computer displays in passive viewing conditions, with unclear implications for real-world performance in outdoor three-dimensional scenes. One way to investigate how viewing mode affects visual perception is through surface-colour judgments during target search in immersive virtual reality scenes. Twenty-two complex virtual reality scenes modelled on outdoor hyperspectral images were used to compare surface-colour matching under active and passive observation. On each trial, a swatch was presented whose colour was sampled from the selectable scene area, and participants attempted to find the surface from which it came. In the active condition, they stood in 3D scenes and could move their head and body to explore beyond the initial viewpoint of each scene, although both targets and selectable surfaces were restricted to the regions initially visible from that viewpoint. In the passive condition, participants were seated and viewed a virtual monitor displaying 2D screenshots of the regions, taken from the initial viewpoint of the corresponding active scenes. Twenty participants completed both viewing conditions, wearing a head-mounted display in each condition. A preliminary analysis showed that passive visual search was more accurate and somewhat faster than active visual search. These findings suggest that making viewing more realistic in immersive environments does not necessarily improve visual judgments. One possible explanation is that active viewing in those environments increases attentional demands, despite providing a more natural mode of observation.

title: A systematic characterisation of steady-state visually evoked potentials as a function of contrast, spatial and temporal frequency and colour
affiliations:
1. School of Psyhology, University of Sussex (UK)
2. Experimental Psychology, University College London (UK)
3. Institute of Ophthalmology, University College London, (UK)
4. School of Philosophy, Psychology and Language Sciences, University of Edinburgh (UK)
abstract: The human visual system transforms light into perceptual experiences of colour through a series of retinal and cortical processes. While early stages of colour information processing by the visual system are well characterised, cortical colour mechanisms remain less understood. Contrast sensitivity functions (CSFs), typically measured with behavioural psychophysics, have been widely used to describe how sensitivity to achromatic and chromatic contrast varies as a function of spatial and temporal stimulus properties. Steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs) can be measured as electroencephalography (EEG) signals at the temporal frequency of a modulating stimulus. Whilst SSVEPs are commonly used to address a range of questions about perception, attention and cognition more generally, our understanding of how low-level stimulus properties impact SSVEP amplitudes remains limited. This in turn limits the interpretability of results derived from SSVEPs. Specifically, SSVEP contrast response functions (CRFs) remain to be characterized in detail over a range of spatial and temporal frequencies and colour axes. We measured SSVEP-based CRFs for gratings varying systematically across colour axes (cardinal and intermediate cone-opponent axes and luminance), temporal frequencies (1.5–40 Hz), and spatial frequencies (0.15–7.5 cycles per degree). We present results from three participants and describe our process of optimising the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in our analysis pipeline. Our work provides a base for linking psychophysical CSFs with EEG-derived CRFs captured using SSVEPs. Systematic EEG-derived CRFs can be used to improve the design and interpretation of studies using SSVEPs to investigate visual perception.

title: Effects of coloured lighting on perceived atmosphere
affiliations: 1. University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: Architects, artists, and designers have long used coloured lighting to shape the atmosphere of scenes and artworks. The complex sensory, cognitive, and emotional nature of perceived atmosphere has been challenging to its scientific investigation. Nevertheless, we have previously shown in a series of online studies that associations between lighting colours and atmosphere in pictures are systematic, robust, and largely independent of depicted scene content. The results also suggested that colour–atmosphere relationships are categorical rather than based on gradual colour similarity. We thus investigated how different atmospheres are distributed across continuous colour space in a controlled laboratory experiment. Participants adjusted the chromaticity of lighting rendered in CIELAB to maximise atmospheres in pictures. This was done for 15 atmosphere descriptors across five AI-generated scenes designed to reflect different lighting applications. Results showed that participants associated atmosphere descriptors with similar colours as in the online studies. Consistent with the online studies, ‘tense’ atmospheres (i.e., ‘scary’, ‘hostile’, and ‘threatening’) produced associations with both red and green across observers. In this case, the average adjustment is not representative, as it corresponds to a colour between red and green that participants almost never adjusted for tense atmospheres. Therefore, we binned colour matches across participants to dissociate atmosphere similarity from colour similarity. Using principal component analysis, we mapped the atmosphere descriptors into a three-dimensional space defined by their colour associations. In this space, cognate atmosphere descriptors (e.g., cosy, calm, and relaxed) clustered, showing that colour-based similarities reflect relationships between atmospheres. Colour-based similarities between pairs of atmosphere descriptors were positively correlated between laboratory and online studies despite their methodological differences. Together, these findings show that coloured lighting systematically affects perceived atmosphere, and that these effects generalise across fundamentally different scenes. The resulting colour-based atmosphere space can guide manipulations of perceived atmosphere through coloured lighting in professional practice.

title: Impact of Change in ipRGC Stimulation Levels on Process of Adaptation and Time Required
affiliations:
1. Nara Women's University (JP)
2. Doshisha Women's College (JP)
3. Yokohama National University (JP)
abstract: Recent reports have indicated that intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) affect color perception as well as brightness, suggesting that they may influence the chromatic adaptation process.  To identify the trends in the temporal changes in chromatic response under lighting conditions with varying levels of ipRGC stimulation, we prepared five lighting conditions only the level of ipRGCs stimulation varied while the luminance and chromaticity of the front wall were held constant. The experiment was conducted in the white-surfaced space equipped with two color-changing (RGB) luminaires and two tunable white LED luminaires. The luminance of the front wall was 105 cd/m2 and the xy-chromaticity values were (0.333, 0.333). A total of 20 different lighting scenarios were established by combining these five lighting conditions. After an initial 6-miniutes adaptation period under the first lighting condition, the lighting was switched to the test condition. Participants evaluated color appearance of the front of the wall under the test lighting conditions at intervals of 0, 10, 20, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240 seconds using the elemental color scaling method. The participants were three females in their twenties. It was shown that the saturation of the lighting decreased as a function of adaptation duration, but ipRGCs stimulation intensity was switched from low to high, the color appearance was greenish, conversely, when it was switched from high to low, the color appearance was reddish. It was also shown that except for one participant, the chromatic response returned to zero within 240 seconds under all lighting conditions. These results indicate that not only cones but also ipRGCs contribute to color perception and color adaptation.

title: Can Colour Signal Urban Economic Status? The Role of Chromatic Information in Perceiving Urban Inequality and Wealth
affiliations: 1. School of Psychology, University of Sussex (UK)
abstract: Economic inequality can harm social cohesion and interpersonal connectedness (Gobel & Carvacho, 2024). Inequality may be salient at different levels of urban geography and different levels of cognition.  In an earlier investigation, we examined whether low-level visual statistics of urban environments can signal economic conditions. We obtained a dataset of over 3,000 colour-calibrated GoPro images from London, and paired the locations with local economic data. We found that chromatic statistics including hue and brightness distributions, average chromaticity difference (Penacchio et al., 2023), and pixel-level greenness were strong predictors of Gini coefficient – an objective measure of economic inequality calculated at the neighbourhood level (Suss, 2023) - and median house price (Nabil et al., ECVP 2025). In the present experiment, we asked whether viewers can successfully predict economic conditions from images, and how colour affected this judgment. Participants (N = 80) viewed our GoPro images presented as virtual tours of London streets. Following the prior evidence that colour could signal objective inequality, we presented both colour and greyscale versions of the same streets as a between-participant condition. We found that participants' perception of income inequality and overall wealth of neighbourhoods was unaffected by the removal of colour. Moreover, participants successfully predicted the relative wealth of the streets in both conditions, though their estimate of income inequality within a neighbourhood was inaccurate. Their responses on affective states, social engagement, ethnic diversity and perceived greenness provided further insights into how people perceive urban areas with varying economic conditions and varying visual statistics. The combined results show that, although the economic conditions of modern urban environments may be predicted from their chromatic visual statistics, people are not tuned into this signal when they make socio-economic judgments based on street appearance alone. These results have implications for our understanding of how sensory information influences socio-economic judgments.

title: Colour Effects on Facial Anger Perception: a Personalised Colour Paradigm with Neurodivergent and Neurotypical Participants
affiliations: 1. Univeristy College London, Institute of Environmental Design and Engineering (UK)
abstract: Colour is a well-established modulator of emotion perception, with the red-anger link being the most consistently reported association. However, its mechanism remains debated, spanning physiological cues, semantic priming, and culturally learned associations. A further complication is that colour preference is highly individual, so paradigms using uniformly applied group-level colours (e.g., a fixed red) may lack explanatory power, particularly for neurodivergent (ND) individuals who differ in both facial emotion decoding and sensory processing. This paradigm disentangles perceptual and individual-level factors in colour-driven emotion perception. Participants completed continuous trait measures (Autism Spectrum Quotient, Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised, Empathy Quotient) and a Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue test. Each participant then selected personal comfort and clarity colours by adjusting hue, chroma, and lightness. Four colour conditions were generated per participant: comfort, clear, opposite of comfort, and an achromatic (lightness-only) baseline. Face stimuli (FACES database) were preprocessed to retain only lightness information (L* channel), and each participant's selected a*b* values were applied to produce personalized L*a*b* stimuli. On each trial, two colour-conditioned versions of different faces were presented sequentially for 2 s each, followed by a forced-choice judgment of which appeared angrier. Each participant completed 72 trials, with face-colour pairings fully counterbalanced so that every face appeared in every colour condition. This design isolates colour effects from luminance confounds, dissociates contributions of hue, chroma, and lightness, and counterbalances group-level colour-emotion associations across participants. Eight participants (4 ND, 4 NT) completed a pilot of this paradigm. Preliminary results suggest that faces shown in each participant's comfort colour were selected as angrier significantly less often than in other conditions, across both ND and NT participants. Exploratory patterns across ND trait scores and colour sensitivity suggest that variability in colour-driven emotion effects may track continuous individual traits rather than a categorical ND/NT distinction.

title: Bright Is White: The Role of the Brightest Area Cue in Virtual Reality
affiliations: 1. Justus Liebig University (DE)
abstract: The brightest region in a scene is a well-known cue for human colour constancy and is widely exploited in camera white-balancing algorithms under varying illumination. This principle is often referred to as the “bright is white” assumption, namely that the visual system treats the brightest relevant surface in a scene as a proxy for the illuminant. However, its relative contribution remains debated, in particular in complex and naturalistic environments. This study investigates the role of the brightest area cue in colour constancy experiments, with a focus on how experimental design and scene complexity influence its effectiveness. A controlled 3D virtual environment was created using Unreal Engine and presented via a Varjo Aero headset. Building on prior findings, we hypothesised that the impact of silencing the brightest area cue depends on the availability of other cues. We designed a new scene containing multiple objects that convey the brightest area information, all consistently positioned within the participants’ field of view. Two conditions were tested: (1) a Baseline condition with all cues available, and (2) a Maximum Flux condition in which the brightest area cue was silenced. Illumination conditions included neutral, yellow, and blue lighting. We observed a significant decrease in colour constancy performance in the Maximum Flux condition compared to the Baseline. This contrasts with prior work using more complex scenes where performance remained stable despite cue removal, but aligns with earlier studies employing simplified environments. These results support the hypothesis that the contribution of the brightest area cue is strongly modulated by scene design and cue availability. When the white objects are large and relevant, silencing the cue reduces performance. This highlights the importance of experimental context in studying perceptual mechanisms and suggests that colour constancy relies on a flexible integration of multiple cues rather than a single dominant factor.

title: A common framework for comparing brightness and contrast under spatial context
affiliations: 1. Technische Universität Berlin (DE)
abstract: A surrounding region modulates both brightness and contrast perception, and gain control models have been proposed for both—suggesting a common underlying mechanism. Yet the two domains are rarely studied with the same methods and stimuli, making cross-domain comparison difficult. Perceptual scaling provides a common framework to address this. Perceived brightness and contrast can each be expressed as perceptual scales: functions of stimulus properties and contextual factors such as surround contrast or orientation. Maximum Likelihood Conjoint Measurement (MLCM) estimates such scales from pairwise comparisons, agnostic to stimulus domain—quantifying how each stimulus factor contributes to perception. Previously, we (Vincent, Aguilar, Maertens ECVP 2024) established this using MLCM to measure brightness induction effects, showing it captures induction across a broad luminance range.\nHere, I extend perceptual scaling to contrast perception and its context effects. A high-contrast surround reduces perceived contrast—an effect known as surround suppression—and does so in an orientation-selective manner: parallel surrounds suppress more strongly than orthogonal ones. For achromatic gratings, perceptual scales show stronger suppression for parallel than orthogonal surrounds. For chromatic (red-green) gratings, I find the same pattern, but with an additional selectivity: color. A red-green surround suppresses a red-green center a blue-yellow surround does not—regardless of orientation. Suppression thus requires the surround to match the center in both color and orientation simultaneously.\nCross-domain comparison also requires comparable stimuli. Surround suppression is classically measured with bipolar gratings brightness induction with uniform fields. Intermediate stimuli—unipolar gratings and oriented noise textures—share the spatial structure of gratings but retain center-surround luminance differences, bridging the two domains. With shared methods and comparable stimuli, gain control model predictions become directly testable, opening the possibility of a single model class that predicts how context affects both perceived brightness and contrast.

title: iTrak: Using A Novel Approach To Show That Preferred Fixation Location Remains Stable In Adults
affiliations:
1. Dartmouth College (US)
2. University of California, Santa Barbara (US)
abstract: Individuals show consistent preferences for the position at which they first fixate on a face, known as their preferred fixation location (PFL). While stable within individuals, the vertical position of this PFL varies widely across observers. Each observer also has an optimal fixation location (OFL), where recognition performance is highest. Typically, PFLs and OFLs are closely aligned, and performance declines rapidly as fixation moves away from this point (retinotopic tuning). Stability in these positions over time seems advantageous to ensure observers reliably fixate their OFL. However, preliminary evidence of higher PFLs in younger adults than older adults (Peterson et al., 2019) and decline in discrimination for eyes but not mouths as adults age (Fry et al. 2023) indicate that one’s PFL position may drift down the face with age. We investigate the age-related shift in PFLs and the link between PFL and retinotopic tuning using iTrak, a novel approach to ascertaining first fixation locations remotely. iTrak presents a target face followed by a grid of character bigrams each for 200ms, and the participant's report of which character bigram they saw indicates their first fixation position. In this study, participants completed a sex discrimination task in a free-fixation paradigm to generate their PFLs and a forced-fixation paradigm to estimate retinotopic tuning curves. The free-fixation task (N=43, age range=18-64) showed no correlation between age and vertical PFL (r=-.05, p=.73). The forced-fixation task (N=19) showed a negative correlation between distance from PFL and sex discrimination performance (r=-.52, p=.02). These findings indicate that PFLs remain stable with age, while the match between PFLs and OFLs demonstrates that iTrak effectively determines eye position. Our future research will aim to validate the iTrak method further by comparing the eye position data it generates to that collected with laboratory-based eye-tracking.

title: Ambient and focal dichotomy in face perception
affiliations:
1. Vision Action Cognition - Université Paris Cité (FR)
2. Integrative Neuroscience and Cognition Center - Université Paris Cité (FR)
abstract: Eye movements reflect exploration strategies that correspond to two processing modes: an ambient mode at the beginning of exploration (short fixations – large saccades), associated with rapid and global information extraction, followed by a focal mode (long fixations – small saccades), linked to finer and more selective sampling. The aim of the current study is to establish a functional link between these modes, their perceptual consequences, and their neural signatures.  In an eye-tracking experiment, a set of faces was presented to 22 participants who performed two forced-choice tasks presented in separate counterbalanced blocks: (1) Ensemble: estimate the average emotion of the faces (2) Identity: identify one of the faces among those presented. The set size (4, 8, 12 faces) and presentation duration (500, 1500, 3500 ms) were randomly selected for each trial.  The results replicate the oculomotor signatures of the two modes, with an increase in fixation duration during exploration, and reveal a dissociation: for the ensemble task, performance was better for short durations but was not modulated by face number, reflecting early and rapid processing. Conversely, the identity task showed an effect of face number and presentation duration, with better performance for smaller sets and longer presentations. This is consistent with an initial ambient mode supporting rapid extraction of global information, followed by a more detailed analysis during the focal mode. A second study using EEG will test whether ambient and focal modes are also characterized by distinct neural patterns, thereby linking oculomotor behavior, neural representations and information processing modes.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: Spatially Structured Emotional Regularity Enhances Working Memory for Faces
affiliations: 1. Department of Psychology and Center for Brain and Cognitive Sciences, School of Education, Guangzhou University (CN)
abstract: Structured regularities across multiple items can support visual processing. However, whether such regularities in emotional faces can be extracted to facilitate working memory, and whether this facilitation is modulated by emotional valence, remains unclear. To address these questions, we conducted two behavioral experiments using working memory tasks. Participants were required to memorize multiple faces with varying emotional intensities and, after a delay, adjusted a test face to match the intensity of the cued face. In Experiment 1, four faces were arranged horizontally. In the structured condition, emotional intensity increased linearly from left to right. In Experiment 2, faces were arranged in a 2 × 2 grid. In the structured condition, emotional intensities increased clockwise from a starting position, with four possible starting positions creating four regularity patterns. In both experiments, the unstructured condition involved random assignment of the four intensities to positions. The results showed that in Experiment 1, memory precision was higher in structured than in unstructured conditions. In Experiment 2, this facilitation effect was consistently observed across all regularity types, indicating that the benefit generalized across spatial configurations rather than being specific to a particular one. In addition, across both experiments, memory precision was higher for negative than for positive emotions. Taken together, these findings suggest that spatially structured regularities in emotional faces can be extracted to facilitate working memory performance. Moreover, this facilitation is robust across spatial configurations and is modulated by emotional valence, with a bias toward negative emotions.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: How do People Use Social Information From Avatars in a Virtual Reality Search Task?
affiliations:
1. University of Kent (UK)
2. University of York (UK)
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is a useful tool for behavioural research due to its ability to immerse users within naturalistic environments whilst retaining control over experimental variables. Thus, VR can help bridge the gap between two distinct methodologies: highly controlled laboratory studies in sterile settings, and more ecologically valid but noisier real-world research. Here, we show how VR can be used to explore how people utilise cues given by avatars in a visual search task. In this experiment, we placed participants in an immersive beach environment populated by several high-fidelity avatars. The task was to find a target shell close to each avatar, with the avatars either giving helpful or unhelpful cues to the location of the target. We informed half of the participants that an avatar that gave a happy facial expression when approached would provide helpful information, while an avatar that gave a disgusted expression would provide unhelpful information. The other half of participants were not informed of this contingency. We measured how long it took participants to find the target shell, focusing on the effects of instruction given and the helpfulness of the avatars. We found that the helpfulness of the avatar impacted search times, but only when participants were given explicit instruction to attend to the social cues of the avatar. This demonstrates that people are capable of using social information given by avatars to aid them in visual search, but may not do so intuitively. The findings of this study show how VR can be used to explore social cognition in more naturalistic contexts.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: Magnetoencephalography reveals the neural time course of illusory face perception in vertically symmetrical random noise images
affiliations: 1. University of New South Wales (AU)
abstract: The perception of illusory face-like form in random patterns or objects, referred to as face pareidolia, is thought to reflect a coarse internal template used by the visual system to detect biological faces early on in the visual processing hierarchy. The visual features of real-world face pareidolia exemplars can vary widely (e.g., illusory faces seen in clouds versus power sockets), which makes it difficult to control for variation in low- to mid-level image features across stimuli. Here, we measured the neural activity associated with illusory face perception in randomly generated fractal noise patterns, matched exactly in symmetry and image statistics, using magnetoencephalography (MEG). We then applied multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to investigate the time course of the neural representations of fractal noise stimuli reported by observers as containing versus not containing illusory faces. We further compared these data with the time course of neural responses to images of biological human faces and regular (not face-like) objects. For classifying the presence versus absence of pareidolic faces in the fractal noise stimuli, the classifier exhibited above chance decoding accuracy from soon after stimulus onset, reaching a peak accuracy of over 65% at around 500ms, just after stimulus offset. Furthermore, cross decoding analyses, whereby the classifier was trained on brain activity in response to biological faces and random non-face objects and tested on fractal patterns that did and did not evoke pareidolia, similarly showed above chance accuracy from early after stimulus onset. Such cross decoding indicates that the neural representations of real face images and pareidolia-inducing noise patterns contain shared information regarding the presence of face-like structure in a stimulus.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: Attentional biases in engagement with and disengagement from ambiguous facial expressions
affiliations: 1. Chuo University (JP)
abstract: Ambiguous facial expressions have frequently been shown to bias emotion recognition depending on individual traits and contextual information (e.g., Richards et al., 2002). Furthermore, facial ambiguity can influence social impressions (Kaminska et al., 2020). These findings suggest that ambiguous facial expressions are socially important stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether such expressions capture attention. The present study investigated attentional engagement and disengagement biases toward ambiguous facial expressions using a modified dot-probe task (Rudaizky et al., 2014). We predicted the attentional biases upon engagement with and/or disengagement from ambiguous facial expressions due to their social significance. In Experiment 1, the results did not provide significant evidence for attentional engagement or disengagement biases toward ambiguous facial expressions. However, against the prediction, we observed a trend suggesting that attention was more easily disengaged from ambiguous expressions than from neutral expressions, though it was not significant. This earlier disengagement may indicate that ambiguous facial expressions are quickly interpreted based on the current social context or the viewer’s traits or state. In Experiment 2, we tested this hypothesis in a preregistered study by refining the method used in Experiment 1. We directed participants’ attention to facial expressions by including catch trials and then obtained similar results to those in Experiment 1. These findings suggest that ambiguous facial expressions do not necessarily capture attention, but instead may facilitate interpretation during the registration, allowing viewers to efficiently make appropriate behavioral responses in social situations.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: Effects of Face Masks on Trustworthiness Judgments and Person Identification
affiliations: 1. Jissen Women's University (JP)
abstract: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, mask wearing has become widespread, increasing the frequency with which people encounter masked faces in daily life. However, masks occlude the lower half of the face, potentially impairing person identification and facial expression recognition. As emotional cues become less visible, impressions of trustworthiness may also be affected. The present study examined the effects of mask wearing on impression formation and person identification. If masks hinder facial recognition and thereby influence impression formation, individuals who experience greater difficulty identifying a person across masked and unmasked conditions should judge masked faces as less trustworthy (Hypothesis 1). In addition, participants may form weaker representations of age groups encountered less frequently in daily life, making them harder to identify than more familiar groups (Hypothesis 2). Fifty-one university students participated. In Task 1, participants viewed paired images of the same person with and without a mask and indicated which face appeared more trustworthy. In Task 2, they judged whether pairs of masked and unmasked faces depicted the same individual. For female faces, participants who more frequently judged the two images as depicting the same person tended to rate unmasked faces as more trustworthy, whereas those who made fewer such judgments tended to rate masked faces as more trustworthy. For male faces, unmasked faces were generally rated as more trustworthy. Stimulus-level analyses indicated that “different person” judgments increased particularly for women in their 20s and men in their 60s. Overall, Hypothesis 1 was not supported, whereas Hypothesis 2 received partial support. Because most participants were male, recognition accuracy for opposite-sex faces may have been lower. Future research should further examine the relationship between person identification and impression formation to clarify underlying mechanisms in face perception.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: Optimizing transcranial electrical stimulation for enhancing face identification
affiliations:
1. Bournemouth University (UK)
2. Fulbright University Vietnam (VN)
abstract: Face identification is an essential skill used in everyday social interactions, contributing to one’s social and personal life. It is also important in forensic scenarios that rely on identification of others, such as eyewitness identification and identity checkpoints. Brain damage or abnormal development can lead to impairments in face identification, which in turn can have negative consequences for both mental health and national security. Thus, finding methods to improve face identification is crucial. Transcranial electrical stimulation (TES) is an emerging method for enhancing face identification however, research pertaining to its efficacy has been inconsistent (Willis et al., 2019). This is likely due to the different tasks and stimulation parameters employed across studies.
