This study aims to determine the optimal stimulation parameters (transcranial direct current vs. random noise stimulation) for improving face identification. Initial findings (N = 34) from a repeated measures ANOVA showed no significant effects of stimulation type on face identification. These results, while unexpected, are consistent with some literature reporting inconsistent effects of TES, likely due to individual differences (Kho et al., 2023). However, a larger sample may yield different results. Nonetheless, findings from this research will allow significant advancements in neuroscience and practical interventions in visual cognition. References Kho, S. K., Keeble, D., Wong, H. K., & Estudillo, A. J. (2023). Null effect of anodal and cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on own-and other-race face recognition. Social Neuroscience, 18(6), 393-406. Willis, M. L., Costantino, A. I., Nitsche, M. A., Palermo, R., & Rivolta, D. (2019). Anodal tDCS and high-frequency tRNS targeting the occipitotemporal cortex do not always enhance face perception. Frontiers in neuroscience, 13, 78.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: ´Who’s left out? A systematic analysis of exclusion criteria in developmental prosopagnosia research
affiliations: 1. Department of Psychology, University of Copenhagen (DK)
abstract: Developmental prosopagnosia (DP) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by severely impaired face recognition. Over the last ~20 years, research on DP has increased substantially, but many core questions remain unresolved. By systematically analyzing the exclusion criteria applied in studies of DP, we aim to characterize the participants included in this research, and in particular those who are not.  266 unique studies of DP were published from 1991 to 2025, and 186 of these describe exclusion criteria. A total of 300 specific criteria were used in different combinations across studies (mean = 3,9 criteria), with the most common (’Abnormal vision’) used in 54 papers. Following an iterative categorization process, we identified 11 overall categories of exclusion criteria. The most frequent were: Neurological (128 papers) Visual (112) Other developmental (86) and Psychiatric (78).  By mapping out the specific criteria and overall categories, we show that the exclusion of participants in studies of DP has at the same time been A) strict (many exclusion criteria applied) and B) unsystematic (the same criteria not applied across studies). A) raises the concern that the population of DPs studied to date may in essence be ’super prosopagnosic,’ i.e., representing particularly pure and dramatic cases with few comorbidities or associated deficits. This has been important for establishing DP as an entity independent from e.g., autism, but it makes it difficult to establish how DP may relate to other neurodevelopmental or psychiatric conditions. B) indicates that the same type of cases may not be included across studies. This may have contributed to the perceived heterogeneity of DP but leaves it unknown if the syndrome itself is heterogeneous, or whether this reflects selection bias. Importantly, as consensus criteria for who are included and excluded from the DP group are not established, estimating the prevalence of DP remains impossible.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: Idiosyncratic visual sampling reflects functional differences in facial information use
affiliations: 1. University of Fribourg (CH)
abstract: Over the past decade, individual differences in visual sampling strategies during facial identity processing have attracted growing interest. These differences are stable over time, generalize to real-world scenarios, and relate to neural responses. However, the core functional role of these interindividual differences remains unclear. Specifically, it is still unresolved whether they reflect simple preferences in where observers fixate to extract facial information, or meaningful differences in the visual information used to recognize identity. To address this question, we tested a large sample of young healthy adult Western observers in a face identification task. Observers first performed the task under free-viewing conditions while their eye movements were recorded, allowing us to characterize their sampling strategy. Based on these data, we identified groups of observers with similar fixation patterns (e.g., preferential fixation of the eyes or the mouth). In a complementary task, participants completed the same recognition paradigm using a Bubbles reverse-correlation technique, enabling us to identify the diagnostic facial information each observer used for successful identification. The resulting single-subject classification images were then aggregated according to the observer groups derived from the eye-movement data. Our results reveal systematic differences across groups, indicating that observers who sample faces differently rely on distinct subsets of facial information to perform the task. Specifically, observers who preferentially fixated the eyes relied more on information from this region, whereas those who sampled the mouth relied more on information from lower facial regions. Importantly, differences in sampling strategies and information use were not predictive of overall recognition accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that idiosyncratic sampling strategies reflect a genuine functional difference in information use. Together, they provide the first direct mechanistic explanation of idiosyncratic gaze behavior during face identification, suggesting that observers do not rely on the same facial information and further questioning the universality of these strategies.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Face Perception and Recognition

title: Modulatory Role of Fronto-Parietal Beta-Band tACS in Stream-bounce Illusion
affiliations:
1. Department of Neuroscience, Aysel Sabuncu Brain Research Center,  Bilkent University (TR)
2. Department of Biomedical Engineering, Ankara Medipol University (TR)
3. Department of Psychology, TED University (TR)
4. Institute of Cognitive Neurology and Dementia Research, Otto-von-Guericke University Magdeburg (DE)
5. Neuroscience and Neurotechnology Center of Excellence (NÖROM), Department of Anatomy, Faculty of Medicine, Gazi University (TR)
abstract: The stream-bounce illusion is an established paradigm for investigating the dynamics of audiovisual processing, in which temporally proximate sound significantly increases the likelihood that two moving objects are perceived as bouncing rather than streaming. Previous findings indicate that beta-band oscillatory synchronization (~20 Hz) within a fronto-parieto-occipital network is associated with this illusion. However, it remains unclear whether frequency-specific modulation of this activity can causally influence perceptual outcomes. To address this, we applied frequency-specific transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) over the fronto-parietal network while participants performed a classical stream-bounce task. Participants were randomly assigned to two frequency control groups (n = 13 per group), both receiving 19 Hz beta, sham, and a group-specific control stimulation in the theta and gamma bands (5 Hz and 41 Hz, respectively). The behavioral results showed a significant main effect of SOA, with bounce perception decreasing monotonically as the temporal gap between visual and auditory events increased, in line with stream-bounce literature. Relative to sham, theta stimulation was associated with significantly reduced bounce perception, whereas gamma and beta stimulation showed no significant difference. A significant interaction between SOA and beta stimulation was observed, suggesting beta stimulation weakened the suppressive effect of SOA on bounce perception, potentially reflecting a widening of the temporal binding window. An additional analysis comparing sham performance across the two control groups revealed no significant difference, confirming baseline equivalence. These findings provide causal evidence that beta-band oscillatory activity modulates the temporal window of audiovisual processing, extending correlational findings and highlighting the frequency-specific nature of oscillatory contributions to multisensory perception, with broader implications for understanding atypical multisensory processing in clinical populations. Funding. The Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (BIDEB 2211-A).
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Can a vestibular training reduce dizziness and motion sickness?
affiliations: 1. Johannes Gutenberg-Universität (DE)
abstract: Motion sickness comes in many forms, car sickness, air sickness, or cybersickness. As the vestibular system is involved in all of these cases, dizziness or disorientation, nausea, and eye-strain are often named as the major symptoms. We investigated whether a vestibular training can reduce these symptoms. The training consisted of a short (8 min) exercise routine. Volunteers performed the training over the course of two weeks. We measured subjective and objective symptoms after exposure to a nauseating virtual bicycle ride before and after the training period. In addition to dizziness and motion sickness ratings, we assessed postural reactions to a rotating and pitching visual environment while standing upright, as well as post-rotatory motion sensations. The results show that two weeks of training significantly reduced dizziness, whereas the improvement of nausea was surprisingly small. We discuss the potential of the training to serve as a resilience training against different forms of motion sickness.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Movement Reduces Tactile Intensity While Prediction Preserves Precision
affiliations: 1. Heinrich Heine University (DE)
abstract: Somatosensory gating is often described as reduced tactile intensity during movement, yet it remains unclear whether this bias reflects motor preparation or requires a movement episode. We investigated tactile gating by dissociating perceptual bias from discrimination precision in vibrotactile intensity judgments across two experiments. In Experiment 1, a Go/NoGo cue determined whether participants executed or withheld a movement, and the tactile probe was delivered after the cue when participants knew whether movement would occur. Perceived intensity showed a clear execution dependency: bias shifts were present on Go trials but absent on NoGo trials, in both active and passive movement contexts. In contrast, discrimination precision showed additional sensitivity to control state, with selective modulation when an action was prepared and then cancelled (Active NoGo). In Experiment 2, we tested whether bias can emerge before movement onset by presenting tactile probes in a pre-movement interval versus during movement execution. Perceived intensity was already reduced in the pre-movement period relative to a stationary baseline, whereas discrimination precision remained stable under predictable kinematics. Together, these findings indicate that typical intensity- bias gating tracks movement occurrence (and is not explained by foreknowledge alone), while pre-movement contexts can already bias intensity judgments without degrading discrimination. More broadly, somatosensory gating comprises dissociable components: an execution-linked bias in perceived intensity and a precision component that is sensitive to predictive/control demands.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Similarities Between Multisensory Integration of PPPD Patients and Controls
affiliations:
1. University of Manchester (UK)
2. Andrew Mayes Centre for Cognitive Neuroscience (UK)
3. Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust (UK)
4. Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust (UK)
5. Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust (UK)
6. NHS Lothian (UK)
abstract: Persistent Postural Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD) is a functional neurological disorder characterised by chronic dizziness and balance impairment. One theory suggests symptoms arise from inappropriate multisensory integration, with atypical overweighting of visual relative to vestibular information. We are currently investigating multisensory integration of PPPD patients and age and IQ matched control participants in two tasks: i) heading recovery and ii) Scene-Relative Object Movement (SROM) discrimination. In this interim analysis we present data on a subset of our larger study (30 patients and 25 control participants). Participants were presented with self-movement information and judged (2AFC) either the direction of self-movement (Left/Right) relative to straight ahead (heading task) or SROM (Up/Down) of another object in the scene (SROM task). Self-movement information was provided physically via a 6 degrees-of-freedom motion platform, visually via optic flow presented in a head-mounted display, or using both modalities. The motion of the self or the object was controlled by interleaved Kesten staircases, which enabled us to obtain psychometric parameters for the perceptual bias and precision. At the group level, there are clear signs of integration in the heading task, but less evidence for integration in the SROM task. Critically, there is little evidence for differences in integration between patient and control groups in either task. In particular, we find no evidence for overweighting of visual relative to vestibular information about self-movement in PPPD. Furthermore, while individual differences in integration are present, this is true for both groups. Although our data collection is ongoing, these preliminary findings present a challenge to the integration hypothesis of PPPD, since we find no overweighting of visual information for patients, and similar integration for patients and controls across both tasks.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: The effect of recent perceptual history on the stream/bounce effect
affiliations: 1. The University of Queensland (AU)
abstract: The stream/bounce illusion arises when two identical targets approach from opposite sides of a display, coincide at the point of coincidence (POC), and continue to the opposite sides. Observers typically perceive the motion as “streaming”, in which the targets pass through each other with their motion unchanged, or as “bouncing”, in which the targets reverse direction at the POC. When a brief transient at the POC is presented, responses are biased toward bouncing. In transient free trials, responses are biased toward streaming when these trials are intermixed in a block. Previously, Grove et al. (2016) reported support for the cognitive inference account of this illusion by rendering the motion trajectories unambiguous with vertical offsets of the targets. Target histories were manipulated by targets shifting their trajectories up to four times before the POC. Bounce responses increased with the number of trajectory switches. Here we expand on this approach by making the targets visually distinct, employing random dot patches that differed in dot density by 0, 10, 20, 30, or 40%. Target histories were manipulated by swapping the targets’ identities 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4 times before the POC. The magnitude of the stream bounce effect - the difference in the percentage of reported bounces between sound and no sound trials - increased with the number of identity swaps. Interestingly, this effect was largest for targets whose identity differed most, contrary to the effect of vertical trajectory shift. These results add to existing support for the cognitive inference account of the illusion and show different outcomes for identity-based manipulations and spatial manipulations of the stream/bounce display.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: How action consequences induce regression to the mean
affiliations: 1. Heinrich Heine University (DE)
abstract: We have shown previously that the perceived intensity of self-produced stimuli regresses toward the mean. Classic accounts of sensory attenuation research rely on movement and movement plans. However, this approach is confounded by co-occurring sensations like visual and tactile feedback when e.g. moving your arm towards a key to press it, which might distract attention from the produced stimulus. Here, we disentangle these components by isolating the factors of movement, prediction, and tactile feedback in order to differentiate between prediction and distraction by self-generation. Participants were asked to judge the loudness of two consecutive tones after either performing a movement to trigger the first tone, receiving a tactile stimulus during the presentation of the first tone, or experiencing both together. The results showed that predictability did not influence auditory regression the effect was present regardless of whether the tone was predictable or not. The involvement of an additional action or stimulus was sufficient to produce the regression compared to a neutral baseline. In a second experiment, participants performed a similar task but received different levels of vibrotactile distraction while listening to the first tone. The results showed that the level of vibrotactile distraction influenced the regression: the stronger the distraction, the steeper the regression. We conclude that regression to the mean, expressed as sensory attenuation and enhancement, is driven by distraction and independent from movement planning. As a result of distraction, listeners become less precise and rely more strongly on their mean hearing level, which the regression indicates to be around 60 decibel.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: When self-generated touch is not just attenuated: Magnitude estimation reveals changes in perceptual sensitivity
affiliations: 1. Heinrich Heine University (DE)
abstract: Classical accounts for sensory perception propose that self-generated stimuli are perceived as weaker because of predictive forward models, whereas movement-related tactile gating leads to a general reduction in perceived intensity. However, most evidence is based on tasks where two stimuli are directly compared and do not address how perception changes across a broader range of intensities. Here, we used magnitude estimation to examine how self-generated and movement-related vibrotactile stimuli are perceived across multiple intensities. Participants performed goal-directed finger movements on a keyboard while receiving vibrotactile stimulation either during movement, at keypress on the active finger, or at keypress on the passive finger, alongside a no-movement baseline. The relationship between physical and perceived intensity was modelled using Stevens’ power law, allowing to dissociate changes in overall response level and sensitivity for intensity differences. Results reveal clear differences between conditions. Compared to the baseline condition, stimulation during movement resulted in reduced perceptual sensitivity. In contrast, both self-generated conditions showed increased sensitivity, with participants distinguishing more strongly between different intensities. Notably, this effect was most pronounced when stimulation occurred on the active finger. While stimulation during movement leads to a general reduction in perceived intensity, consistent with tactile gating, self-generated stimulation shows a different pattern. This challenges the idea that action-related perception is primarily characterized by attenuation. Instead, it suggests that the brain flexibly adjusts perceptual sensitivity depending on context. Rather than uniformly reducing self-generated input, the sensory system enhances differences when signals are behaviorally relevant and suppresses them when they are not. Our results point to a dynamic reweighting of sensory information, rather than a simple reduction of predicted input. The underlaying mechanism may support more precise sensorimotor behavior by enhancing the distinction between weaker and stronger sensory signals, therefore allowing for finer control and adjustments.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Designing an SSEP-compatible redundant signals paradigm: Tag–target interactions shape multisensory effects
affiliations: 1. University of St Andrews (UK)
abstract: Multisensory integration enhances perception and behaviour, often leading to shorter reaction times when multiple signals are presented simultaneously, a phenomenon known as the redundant signals effect (RSE). In many cases, multisensory speed-ups exceed predictions from statistical facilitation and violate so-called Miller’s bound, suggesting genuine cross-modal interactions. To enable future investigation of the neural mechanisms underlying this effect, we developed a novel RSE paradigm compatible with steady-state evoked potentials (SSEP). Auditory (noise sounds) and visual (Gabor patches) stimuli were frequency-tagged using amplitude modulation (sound) and phase modulation (vision), with tag frequencies counterbalanced (2.5 vs. 3.75 Hz). Behavioural targets were changes in carrier frequency and Gabor orientation. In a 2×2 design (n=19), targets were presented either synchronous or asynchronous with modality-specific frequency tags. Visual, but not auditory, responses were slower when targets were synchronous with their corresponding frequency tag. Critically, in multisensory conditions, this slowing increased the RSE and produced larger violations of Miller’s bound. To further probe this synchrony effect, a second experiment (n=20) manipulated visual tagging and target features. When phase modulation defined the behavioural target, unisensory response times were unaffected, and neither RSE nor violations of Miller’s bound were modulated. In contrast, when orientation changes served as targets alongside phase tagging, visual responses were selectively slowed, consistent with a masking-like interaction. These findings demonstrate that interactions between frequency tagging and target features can systematically bias behavioural measures of multisensory integration.  This highlights the importance of stimulus design in SSEP-compatible paradigms and identifies frequency tag–target combinations as a critical factor in studying the neural basis of multisensory processing.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Processing of spatial and pitch auditory deviants in visually impaired children
affiliations:
1. Unit for Visually Impaired People, Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia (IT)
2. DIBRIS, University of Genova (IT)
3. Institution for Human & Machine Cognition (US)
abstract: Human auditory system is highly sensitive to changes in the sound environment, enabling rapid detection of salient events through automatic and controlled attention. However, it remains unclear how early sensory experience, particularly reduced visual experience, influences the salience of auditory changes, especially for spatial localization. Individuals with visual impairment (VI) may exhibit enhanced auditory abilities due to cross-modal plasticity, raising the question of whether and how pitch and spatial features interacts. We tested 22 children (13 sighted, mean age = 10.2 years 9 VI, mean age = 9.52 years) using an active auditory oddball task with three deviant conditions: spatial, pitch, and combined (pitch+space). Behavioral performance was assessed using Signal Detection Theory measures (d′, criterion) and reaction times (RT) analyzed with generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs). Neural activity was recorded with a 64-channel EEG system to examine event-related potentials (ERPs). A significant group x condition interaction for d′ (p = 0.005) showed that sighted children maintained comparable sensitivity across conditions, whereas VI children exhibited higher sensitivity in the combined condition compared to spatial condition (p = 0.003). RT analyses revealed a significant group x condition interaction (p = 0.007), driven by VI children responding faster in the combined condition compared to pitch condition (p = 0.002), while no significant differences were observed in sighted group.  Exploratory ERP analyses suggest possible group differences in early auditory components (P2a, P2b), whereas later components (P300) appear broadly comparable across groups. No overall auditory advantages emerged for either group. However, these findings suggest that reduced visual experience may shape how auditory features contribute to perceptual salience and attentional guidance, particularly under conditions requiring multi-feature integration.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: The Dynamic Weight Illusion—A novel illusion revealed in immersive mixed reality
affiliations:
1. University of Southampton (UK)
2. University of Wisconsin-Madison (US)
abstract: Humans can easily infer an object’s weight from both its appearance and its physical interactions with the environment. Alongside static cues such as size and material, dynamic cues (e.g. motion and deformation) provide informative evidence about mass, yet they are difficult to isolate and manipulate in real-world experiments. Here, we used immersive mixed-reality (MR) to examine whether visual deformation cues affect perceived heaviness under visuo-haptic conflict, and whether such effects resemble classic size- and material-weight illusions, where “lighter-looking” objects are perceived as heavier than identically weighted “heavier-looking” objects. In a preliminary Virtual Reality study, participants (N=22) provided vision-only weight ratings for virtual objects varying in size, material appearance, or dynamic interaction–depicted by animations of objects impacting and deforming a cloth surface to varying degrees. These ratings confirmed the expected ordering of heaviness judgments based on visual information and allowed us to select stimulus pairs that elicited comparable vision-only weight expectations in each condition. We used these selected pairs in a subsequent MR experiment where participants (N=21) lifted identical physical cubes via handles while viewing co-registered virtual counterparts. High-precision motion capture ensured accurate alignment between the physical objects and their virtual renditions during lifting, allowing manipulation of visual cues while physical mass was held constant. Smaller-looking objects were judged as heavier despite identical mass (p<.001), replicating the size-weight illusion. In contrast, material appearance did not produce a material-weight illusion (p=.718). Strikingly, dynamic cues produced an illusion in the opposite direction: objects that produced a larger cloth deformation were judged as heavier (p<.001). Our findings suggest that representations of object weight are qualitatively different when inferred from observed dynamics rather than size and material, leading to weight illusions in opposite directions.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: Interaction of Location and Frequency in Tactile Action Priming
affiliations: 1. Justus Liebig University (DE)
abstract: Touch research has typically treated mechanoreceptive channels as independent sensory filters (Bolanowski et al., 1988) and action control as operating on abstract spatial codes (Gallace & Spence, 2008). Here, we tested whether vibration frequency is integrated with location during tactile priming. Building on four-channel models that distinguish RA I and Pacinian pathways (Bolanowski et al., 1988), we presented suprathreshold vibrotactile primes (~0.2 RMS, 120ms) and targets (1.0 RMS, 120ms) at 40Hz and 240Hz. Prime and target were separated by a 250 ms interval, allowing them to be perceived as distinct events (Kuroki & Nishida, 2024). Participants performed a 2AFC localization task. Stimuli were delivered to ring and index fingers of the right hand, which defined the left and right target locations, respectively, and participants reported target location with spatially corresponding left/right keypresses using their left hand. Prime-target pairs were arranged in a 2×2 design crossing Location Congruency and Frequency Congruency. Reaction times were analysed with linear mixed-effects models and accuracy with generalized linear mixed-effects models. The critical effect was a robust Location Congruency × Frequency Congruency interaction, significant in both reaction time and accuracy, p<0.001, indicating violation of simple additivity between spatial frequency factors. Crucially, on same-location trials, prime and target frequency still interacted strongly in both reaction time and accuracy, p<0.001, demonstrating a within-channel advantage over cross-channel pairings within-channel pairings were 30.8ms faster at 40Hz and 26.4ms faster at 240Hz. The reaction-time model further revealed a three-way interaction with target frequency, p=0.001, showing that tactile spatial priming is not channel-neutral, the binding effect differed across 40 and 240Hz targets: the efficiency of the spatial decision depends on the frequency relationship between prime and target. These findings suggest that a vibrotactile prime carries forward an integrated location and frequency trace, revealing that spatial and channel information are rapidly combined in touch.
session_title: Poster Session 6 · Multisensory and Other Senses

title: The role of volitional control in distinguishing mental imagery from perception
affiliations: 1. Department of Imaging Neuroscience, University College London (UK)
abstract: Perceptual reality monitoring (PRM), the ability to distinguish mental images from external perception, is known to be affected by imagery vividness. However, vividness is unlikely to be the only factor at play: hyperphantasics, who experience exceptionally vivid imagery, do not typically hallucinate. Here, we investigated whether volitional control is an additional determining factor of PRM by testing whether involuntary imagery is more likely to be mistaken for perception than voluntary imagery. We developed a novel method to induce involuntary imagery in a controlled way. N=139 participants underwent a training session where sounds were repeatedly paired with specific images, leading to involuntarily experiencing these images when sounds alone were played. Participants then performed a task where sounds triggered associated images during concurrent presentation of congruent or incongruent visual stimuli, and indicated whether a stimulus was present (detection) and its identity (discrimination). A separate sample (N=64) performed the same task but voluntarily generated the images indicated by the sounds.  The paradigm successfully elicited involuntary conscious imagery in 83% of participants (as indicated by self-reports). Both imagery types led to more presence responses for congruent than incongruent trials, but crucially, this congruency effect was larger for involuntary imagery. Furthermore, this extended to discrimination responses, suggesting involuntary imagery more strongly affected not only whether but also what participants perceived. These findings suggest that volitional control, alongside vividness, is a key determinant of PRM, which has important implications for understanding conditions characterized by involuntary imagery, such as PTSD and psychosis.

title: Generative adversarial learning explains why imagination feels less real as we grow up
affiliations:
1. Department of Imaging Neuroscience, University College London (UK)
2. Prolific (UK)
3. Experimental Psychology, Division of Psychology and Language Sciences, University College London (UK)
4. Institute of Ophthalmology, University College London (UK)
abstract: Because sensory input is often incomplete and ambiguous, the brain uses prior experience to make educated guesses about what it is seeing. To do so, it develops internal models generating predictions about incoming sensory signals.  These same models can also generate sensory signals in the absence of input, through imagination. However, as generative models develop with age, it seems that our ability to generate vivid imaginations decreases rather than increases. In this work, inspired by a machine learning framework called Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), we test the hypothesis that this paradox could arise from an interaction between the generative model and a separate reality monitor. GANs learn a generative model via an adversarial feedback loop with a discriminator. The discriminator learns to distinguish real images from generated images, while the generator learns to generate images that are realistic enough to fool the discriminator. We trained GANs on two different image sets and tracked the adversarial dynamics throughout training. Results show that in both datasets, early in training, low-quality generated images were more often misclassified as real compared to later stages, despite later images being more realistic. Our results suggest that, in early development, poor imagination may be more easily mistaken for reality because the reality monitoring system is underdeveloped. In later stages of development, although world models remain relatively stable, the reality monitoring system continues to improve, making imagery feel less real. Follow-up analyses provided concrete hypotheses about the development of world models and reality monitoring. In both datasets, the development of high-level visual features scaffolded the generation of low-level features in generated images. Additionally, the discriminator relied on representations distinct from those used in object classification for reality inferences. Overall, this framework explains key developmental phenomena and makes testable predictions about the development of imagination and reality monitoring.

title: The Influence of Scene Context on Imagery-Perception Confusions
affiliations:
1. University College London (UK)
2. Radboud University (NL)
abstract: The scene context shapes how we perceive objects within it. When objects are ambiguous, we rely on scene information to identify them. Contextual expectations arise from our inner models of the world, enabling efficient action in our surroundings. However, contextual influences may extend beyond object identification. Our brain constantly updates predictions to make sense of the world, and these predictions may also shape what we judge as real versus imagined. Previous behavioral studies show that simultaneous imagery increases perceptual detection responses, suggesting imagery is sometimes confused for perception. Here, we asked whether scene context enhances this confusion. In two online experiments (N₁=98 N₂=73), participants detected objects that gradually appeared within congruent or incongruent scenes. In half of the blocks, participants simultaneously imagined the stimulus while detecting it and in the other half they only detected the stimulus. On every trial, participants gave a detection response and an imagery vividness rating. Both experiments showed a main effect of imagery, as well as an interaction between imagery and scene congruency on detection responses, suggesting participants were more likely to confuse imagery for perception when it was congruent with the scene. Computational modeling suggests that scene context increases the sensory strength of imagery, thereby increasing the likelihood it crosses a ‘reality threshold’. These results extend laboratory findings to ecologically valid settings and reveal that contextual expectations shape not only what we perceive, but also whether we judge it as real. This deepens our understanding of how the brain navigates the boundary between perception and imagination.

title: Environmental and Neural Correlates of Geometrical Illusion Susceptibility
affiliations:
1. Center for Environmental Neuroscience at Max Planck Institute for Human Development
2. Center of Neurodevelopmental Disorders at Karolinska Institutet
3. Department of Comparative Cultural Psychology at Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology
abstract: Despite decades of research, the mechanisms underlying susceptibility to geometric illusions remain poorly understood. Many classic illusions rely on depth cues and perspective assumptions to infer three-dimensional structure from two-dimensional retinal input, implicating visuospatial integration and scene conceptualization. Empirical research suggested that individuals living in 'carpentered' environments, characterized by straight lines, right angles, and rectangular structures, may be more susceptible to certain geometric illusions, yet the robustness and underlying mechanisms of this association remain unclear (Gregory, 1985). The hippocampus may be relevant here, as it has been linked both to visuospatial integration and scene conceptualization, and to the integration of memory and past experience with incoming sensory input (Kok & Turk-Browne, 2018). Building on Axelrod and colleagues (2017), who identified the parahippocampal cortex as a correlate of Ebbinghaus and Müller-Lyer illusion susceptibility, we hypothesized that gray matter volume (GMV) in the hippocampus and parahippocampus, as well as daily urban exposure, would be associated with higher illusion susceptibility. 105 participants completed eight geometric illusions (Müller-Lyer, Ebbinghaus, T, Horizontal-Vertical, Ponzo, Delboeuf, Poggendorff, Zöllner) online. Structural T1 MRI data were analyzed using voxel-based morphometry. In an additional twin sample, we examined urban exposure, quantified via Geoinformation System data, and illusion susceptibility, controlling for genetic and shared-environment confounds. Inter-illusion correlations were generally low. Significant positive associations emerged between Müller-Lyer susceptibility and hippocampal GMV, and between T illusion susceptibility and parahippocampal GMV. Urban fabric was likewise positively associated with T illusion susceptibility. These findings suggest that hippocampal and parahippocampal structures support scene-based spatial inference in illusion perception, drawing on the hippocampus's broader role in scene construction and integrating sensory input with prior knowledge. The association between urban fabric and T illusion susceptibility further suggests that internalized assumptions about depth and perspective may be calibrated by the geometry of one's environment.

title: Drawings of visual hallucinations vary systematically as a function of the parameters of hallucination-induction stimuli
affiliations:
1. University of Sussex (UK)
2. The Hochschule Bielefeld – University of Applied Sciences and Arts (DE)
3. Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CA)
abstract: Visual hallucinations occur across contexts ranging from psychedelic experiences to neurological disorders, yet their phenomenological structure remains difficult to characterize. Stroboscopic light stimulation provides a controlled means to rapidly induce vivid visual hallucinations under laboratory conditions. These hallucinations reliably include geometric forms theorised to reflect low-level visual processing in a manner similar to other low-level hallucinations. While this phenomenon serves as an experimental model of hallucinations that originate from lower-order brain regions, research has traditionally relied on verbal reports or rating scales that fail to capture their geometric complexity. To address this, we developed and validated novel image-recreation methods in which participants use an interface to produce images of their visual hallucinations. Across three experiments with over 200 participants, we show that quantitatively measured low-level image features are reliably recoverable at the population level using these methods. We applied this paradigm to establish a quantitative mapping between stroboscopic parameters and hallucinatory phenomenology across stimulation frequencies ranging from 2.5 to 80 Hz. Increasing frequency was associated with higher perceived brightness and reduced contrast, despite constant overall light luminance. We found that beta band stimulation (15 Hz) produced hallucinations which were higher in detail and complexity than other frequencies, challenging the long-standing notion that alpha-band stimulation maximises hallucination intensity. Further, we observed a broader repertoire of geometric forms than typically described in existing observations and computational models. An improved characterization of the contents of visual hallucinations across contexts can provide new empirical constraints on how the functional architecture of the cortices constructs visual experiences in normal and altered states.

title: Decoding imagination: Reading the mind’s eye
affiliations:
1. University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland, HES-SO Valais-Wallis (CH)
2. Center for Integrative and Complementary Medicine, Division of Anesthesiology, Lausanne University Hospital & University of Lausanne (CH)
3. The Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
4. Computational Neuroscience Labs, ATR (JP)
abstract: Mental imagery, i.e., a sensory experience occurring without external stimulation, has been shown to contribute to disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder but also chronic pain and anxiety. It is a promising therapeutic target. While the neural mechanisms of mental imagery largely overlap with those of perception, the temporal dynamics of when and how a mental image might be elicited or changed remain underexplored.  This project aims to track complex mental imagery in healthy individuals using high-density electroencephalography (EEG) and multivariate pattern analysis. Currently, we seek to decode neural representations of imagined complex scenes under two conditions: structured imagery, prompted by a strict visual stimulus (Experiment 1), and less restricted imagery, prompted by a brief description (Experiment 2).  So far, five healthy adults (mean age ± SD: 27±2.5 4 men), out of a planned sample of seventy, have completed both experiments. Each experiment consisted in 120-150 trials per scene category (family, nature, pipe), with a 3-sec prompt, a 3-sec imagery period and a 1000-1200ms inter-stimulus interval.  Preliminary decoding results from data collected up to early August 2026 will be presented, including: (1) cross-validated decoding of visual stimulus data from Experiment 1 (e.g., decoding accuracy, confusion and temporal generalization matrices), and (2) decoding of mental imagery under varying degrees of restriction (Experiments 1 and 2) using classifiers trained on visual data from Experiment 1. Based on prior evidence of strong overlap between perception and imagery, we expect significant decoding of complex imagined scenes with these classifiers.  These results may indicate how information about complex scenes can be decoded from brain activity under varying degrees of control, and whether temporal EEG dynamics differ between perception- and imagery-based neural patterns. This approach will then be applied to a third experiment examining freely occurring imagery (i.e., people’s “happy place”) elicited by an auditory cue.

title: Testing interference between visual imagery and perception in visual cortex
affiliations: 1. Donders Institute, Radboud University (NL)
abstract: Visual imagery relies on top-down activation of visual cortex representations that are also activated when perceiving these objects. However, most evidence for this comes from studies without any concurrent visual input, while such top-down signals would typically have to co-exist with simultaneous bottom-up input in daily life. Given their neural overlap, we hypothesized that concurrent imagery and perception can result in mutual interference, especially if the representations of imagined and perceived content are similar. To investigate competitive interactions within visual cortex, we asked participants to imagine or perceive objects from three real-world object categories (fruits, tools, crockery) on their own, or while other objects from one of these categories were simultaneously presented in the periphery. Using fMRI, we measured multivariate voxel activity patterns evoked by (1) imagery of a single object, (2) perception of a single object, (3) concurrent imagery and perception, and (4) perception of multiple objects. Our design allows us to investigate and quantify imagery-perception interaction across the visual hierarchy, and compare it to competition between multiple perceived objects. Preliminary analyses show that imagery in isolation evokes reliable neural activity resembling perception in early visual cortex. This imagery signal is, however, strongly reduced by concurrent visual input, even though the visually-presented objects were presented at a different retinotopic location than the imagined object. Further analyses will focus on comparing the effect of distracting visual input between early and higher-level visual regions and the effect of category-matching vs. mismatching visual input, shedding light on the interactions between bottom-up input and top-down signals in visual cortex.

title: State-Dependent Neural Architecture of Mental Imagery: Insights from Hypnosis and NREM Parasomnias
affiliations:
1. Center for Integrative and Complementary Medicine, Division of Anesthesiology, Lausanne University Hospital & University of Lausanne (CH)
2. The Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
3. University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland, HES-SO Valais-Wallis (CH)
4. Centre of Sleep Research and Investigation, Lausanne University Hospital & University of Lausanne (CH)
abstract: Mental imagery (MI) is central to everyday human experience, and is progressively understood as part of the pathophysiology of different illnesses, including some sleep disorders such as non-rapid eye movement (NREM) parasomnias. Nevertheless, there are open questions about the neural underpinnings of naturally occurring MI processes, how these can be modulated (e.g. by hypnosis), and how these are affected by neuropsychological disorders. We hypothesized that the neural mechanisms of MI should change following a hypnotic induction, and should differ between healthy participants and patients with NREM parasomnias. We measured electroencephalography (EEG) while people were engaged in a MI task (i.e. “happy place” MI), that we administered following or not a hypnotic induction to healthy participants and patients with NREM parasomnias. Patients completed the same task again after following a treatment using either hypnosis or standard of care (i.e. psychoeducation).  Assuming that the brain can be considered a complex system, we applied measures of neural information content to quantify changes in hypnotic and non-hypnotic MI, as these measures have been previously shown to successfully describe human awareness and consciousness levels. In addition, microstate characteristics have also been found to vary with similar tasks (i.e. meditation, mind wandering) and neuropsychological disorders. We thus investigated whether measures of signal complexity, and microstate characteristics and their dynamics, change with hypnosis.  In healthy participants (N= 41), we found that brain complexity during MI changes with a hypnotic induction, but only for participants with medium susceptibility. Hypnosis modulates both state characteristics and dynamics of microstates, but susceptibility does not. Patients (N = 41) show drastically reduced complexity during MI when compared to controls, unaffected by suggestibility. Analyses are ongoing. These preliminary results show that a hypnotic induction changes essential characteristics of brain processes involved in MI, and that these processes are impacted by disease.

title: Feeling of Presence Is Associated with Interoceptive Accuracy and Multisensory Experiences under Sensory Deprivation
affiliations: 1. NTT Communication Science Laboratories (JP)
abstract: Feeling of Presence (FoP) refers to the feeling that another intentional agent is present nearby when, in fact, there is no one else (Nenadalová & Řezníček, 2025). To better understand the factors associated with FoP, we examined how internal bodily information (interoception) and subjective sensory experiences are related to FoP. Participants performed a change-report task under sensory deprivation conditions, reporting perceived changes in the room using a lever to indicate the perceived intensity of environmental changes. The degree of lever tilt was used as an operational measure of FoP intensity, with greater tilt reflecting a stronger FoP. Despite no actual changes, participants reported perceived changes, and FoP intensity correlated with interoceptive accuracy (p < .05). After the task, participants completed a questionnaire in which they indicated the sensory modalities associated with their experience of FoP. Participants reported the perceived change through multiple sensory modalities: visual (20.8%), auditory (54.2%), skin sensations (50.0%), a general feeling (e.g., “it just felt that way” 64.6%), and other modalities (6.3%). Participants also rated the intensity of perceived changes for each modality (1–100 scale). FoP intensity correlated with visual sensations (p < .001), skin sensations (p < .001), general feeling (p < .05), and overall perceived changes (p < .05). Additionally, interoceptive accuracy correlated with skin sensations (p < .05) and perceived changes (p < .05). A linear model revealed significant effects of skin sensations (p < .001), other modalities (p < .05), overall perceived changes (p < .005), and unusual experiences (p < .05) to FoP intensity. These findings suggest that FoP is associated with individual differences in interoceptive sensitivity and subjective sensory experiences, including hallucinatory-like perceptions. The observed correlations indicate that both internal bodily information and reported perceptual changes are systematically related to FoP under sensory deprivation.

title: A visually anchored scale for visual imagery reveals dissociable perceptual dimensions and category-specific structure
affiliations:
1. University of Iceland (IS)
2. University of Akureyri (IS)
abstract: Visual imagery varies widely across individuals, from aphantasia (no imagery) to hyperphantasia (highly vivid imagery), yet most measurement tools rely on verbal self-report with limited external anchoring. We introduce the Visual Imagery Visually Anchored Scale (VIVAS), which asks participants to reconstruct mental images of objects from six categories (animals, buildings, faces, food, manmade objects, and novel objects) along three perceptual dimensions (opacity, sharpness, and color saturation) using visually presented anchors. VIVAS was administered to a probability-based panel randomly selected from the National Registry of Iceland 205 participants were included. VIVAS dimensions were highly related but not interchangeable: individual differences in color imagery reliably dissociated from those of opacity and sharpness visual imagery may therefore partly separate into structural clarity and chromaticity. Imagery also differed systematically across categories. Novel objects elicited the weakest imagery, highlighting a central role for familiarity in shaping imagery strength. Food items showed selectively enhanced color imagery, consistent with the functional importance of color for evaluating edibility and with the overlap between food- and color-selective regions in visual cortex. Structural clarity showed minimal category specificity beyond familiarity effects. VIVAS total scores did not differ by gender, age, education, or device type, supporting robustness for online administration. VIVAS correlated moderately with the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ), well below the ceiling set by each instrument's reliability, and individual-level dissociations were striking: some participants scoring in the bottom 10% on one measure fell in the top quartile on the other. Verbal and visually anchored measures therefore capture complementary, and sometimes divergent, facets of imagery with implications for how aphantasia and hyperphantasia are defined and identified. These findings position VIVAS as a reliable, visually grounded complement to existing verbal questionnaires it captures both overall imagery strength and meaningful dimension- and category-specific structure that standard self-report tools cannot easily assess.

title: Brain Responses to Visual Symmetry in Early Infancy
affiliations: 1. York University (CA)
abstract: Visual symmetry is abundant in natural and man-made environments and plays an important role in object recognition and perceptual organization. Brain imaging studies have demonstrated robust responses to reflection symmetry in several regions of visual cortex, often using dot patterns with one or more axes of reflection. Another approach has used the wallpaper groups, 17 regular textures that comprise the complete set of possible symmetries in the 2D plane. Each wallpaper group contains a unique combination of fundamental symmetries, including reflection and rotation. While reflection typically produces the strongest brain responses, adult visual cortex also responds robustly to the other symmetry types present in the wallpaper groups, including rotation. Here we extended this work to infants, recording brain responses to reflection (group PMM) and rotation (group P4) from 18 participants aged 2-8 months using high-density electroencephalography (EEG). Infants viewed full-field (24º visual angle) wallpaper textures in a Steady-State Visual Evoked Potentials paradigm in which PMM and P4 textures alternated with matched phase-scrambled control images that preserved low-level visual properties while removing global structure. This paradigm allows separate measurement of symmetry-specific responses and low-level image update responses driven by contrast changes at each image transition. Image update responses were robust for both PMM and P4, indicating that our infant participants were equally willing to look at the stimuli in both conditions. We also found adult-like responses to reflection symmetry in infants, but rotation symmetry produced responses that were much less adult-like, and perhaps not measurable at all. To our knowledge, these are the first measurements of brain responses to symmetry in early infancy. Our results suggest a learned component of symmetry processing and raise the possibility that infants may learn to perceive reflection earlier than rotation, possibly due to differential exposure during the initial months of life.

title: Temporal dynamics of acuity and contrast sensitivity with uncrowded and crowded stimuli in healthy and amblyopic observers
affiliations:
1. University of Freiburg (DE)
2. Berlin University of Applied Sciences and Technology (DE)
abstract: Visual acuity (VA) in healthy observers depends on stimulus presentation duration, reflecting multiple temporal mechanisms across different time scales. Amblyopia has been associated not only with crowding but also with altered temporal processing. However, evidence remains inconclusive. Contrast sensitivity (CS) has been proposed as a clinically relevant, although frequently ignored, measure of visual performance. We investigated how stimulus duration affects VA and CS in healthy and amblyopic observers under conditions of crowding. By comparing optotype and grating stimuli, we aimed to differentiate between shape recognition and resolution acuity, and to investigate their differential temporal dynamics, particularly in amblyopia. The Freiburg Visual Acuity and Contrast Test (FrACT) was used with crowded and uncrowded Landolt Cs as well as sinusoidal gratings. VA and CS were assessed at presentation durations of 0.1 s, 1.0 s, and 10 s in healthy participants and compared to amblyopic observers. In healthy participants, uncrowded VA was significantly better at 1.0 s compared to 0.1 s for all stimuli, with a further small but significant improvement at 10 s. Compared to uncrowded VA, crowded VA was identical at 0.1 s but worse at 1.0 s and 10 s. CS increased significantly with duration for crowded and uncrowded optotypes as well as for gratings, but was not affected by crowding. Preliminary amblyopic data suggest, as expected, increased crowding effects of presentation duration are qualitatively similar but appear less pronounced. This study extends previous findings on duration effects to crowded optotypes and to CS in healthy observers and provides an initial account of duration effects in amblyopic vision. The differential effects of crowding on VA versus CS may be related to the involvement of partly different neuronal substrates. In amblyopia, the present pilot data are consistent with the assumption of altered temporal aspects of processing.

title: Do Visual Field Asymmetries Affect Ensemble Perception?
affiliations: 1. University of Iceland (IS)
abstract: Peripheral vision is characterized by lower spatial resolution, larger receptive fields and systematic crowding that reduces access to individuated elements. Additionally, visual field asymmetries have been reported in the literature with weaker crowding, higher spatial frequency and contrast sensitivity in the lower visual field compared to the upper visual field. There has also been an advantage reported along the horizontal meridian that the performance is weaker along the vertical meridian. Constraints such as crowding are explained by compulsory pooling or integration of information across space, in which the visual system may rely on summary representations rather than detailed encoding of individual items. Ensemble perception has been suggested as a mechanism that allows observers to obtain summary statistics from groups of objects. However, it remains unclear whether these summary representations are computed uniformly across the visual field or whether they are constrained by visual field asymmetries. We investigated whether accuracy (deviation from the ensemble mean) and variability (the circular standard deviation of orientation judgments across trials) vary across visual field locations or remain location independent. Participants were presented with a fixation cross and 9 white lines for 150 ms. Afterwards, participants were presented with a single white line in the center and were asked to adjust the line so that it matched the average orientation of the lines from the previous display. Our results showed that the accuracy and variability of the adjustment responses revealed no clear asymmetries across the visual field. Although peripheral vision is not uniform for individuated object perception (as evidenced by crowding), pooling across multiple items in an ensemble task may reduce the impact of these asymmetries. In individuation tasks such as crowding, pooling affects access to individual elements and enhances these asymmetries.

title: Illusory Motion Parallax in Virtual Reality: The Role of Scene Context and Viewing Geometry
affiliations: 1. Centre for Vision Research, York University (CA)
abstract: Under natural viewing conditions, binocular disparity and motion parallax are ordinarily coupled cues to three-dimensional structure. In stereoscopic virtual reality, however, binocular disparity can be presented without the head-contingent viewpoint updates that define motion parallax, creating conditions in which a physically static scene appears to move with the observer. The present study investigates this illusory motion parallax and evaluates the hypothesis that it arises from predictive processing: disparity-defined depth generates an expectation of motion parallax, and when that expected signal is absent, the resulting mismatch is experienced as reversed parallax.  Across five experiments in head-mounted virtual reality, we examine the perceptual conditions under which this illusion emerges and how its strength is modulated. Experiment 1 demonstrates that the effect depends on binocular disparity and disappears under monocular viewing. Experiment 2 shows that the perceived motion follows the direction predicted by reversed parallax. The central contribution of the study concerns the role of scene context and viewing geometry. Experiment 3 demonstrates that the illusion is strongly shaped by surrounding scene structure, with the largest effects in minimal scenes and weaker effects in more structured environments. Experiment 4 reveals that the illusion increases with steeper viewing angles. Experiment 5 shows that the illusion weakens as observer distance from the display increases. Taken together, these findings indicate that illusory motion parallax is not a fixed consequence of cue conflict, but a context-sensitive percept shaped by both environmental structure and the observer’s spatial relation to the display.  These results support a forward-model account in which stereoscopic depth generates predictions of head-coupled parallax, and the absence of the expected signal is experienced as motion. More broadly, they show that depth-cue integration in immersive displays depends jointly on predictive mechanisms, scene context, and viewing geometry.

title: Transcranial alternating current stimulation affects visual crowding and redundancy masking differently: A resting-state EEG study
affiliations:
1. Sabancı University (TR)
2. École Normale Supérieure, PSL University (FR)
3. İstanbul Medipol University (TR)
abstract: The ability to recognize objects in peripheral vision is fundamentally limited by surrounding objects. This phenomenon, visual crowding (VC), has been causally linked to beta oscillations (15-25 Hz) in the right parietal cortex: higher parietal beta power predicts improved crowding performance, and online 18-Hz tACS over P4 selectively boosted beta power and reduced crowding. A related but distinct phenomenon, redundancy masking (RM), is the systematic underreporting of identical items. While RM and VC share characteristics, such as their dependence on eccentricity and inter-item spacing, several key differences suggest that their underlying neural mechanisms are different. We applied online 18 Hz tACS over P4 to compare the effects of parietal beta stimulation on VC and RM, testing whether they rely on shared or dissociable oscillatory dynamics.   In a within-subject design, participants (N=8) completed two sessions, one active tACS and one sham, separated by one week to prevent carryover effects. In each session, 5-min eyes-closed resting-state EEG was recorded before and after stimulation to assess tACS-induced changes. Both tasks were performed under online 18-Hz tACS over P4. VC stimuli were verniers flanked by lines RM stimuli were arrays of lines (set sizes: 3-5). Participants reported the offset direction in the Vernier task, and the perceived number of lines in the RM task. Active tACS produced higher VC accuracy compared to sham, replicating the finding that beta-tACS reduces crowding. Conversely, active tACS increased RM compared to sham. While post-stimulation EEG power changes were not significant, the direction of beta change (+0.21 dB) followed a trend consistent with previously reported beta upregulation associated with reduced crowding. These findings suggest a dissociation between neural mechanisms of VC and RM. Parietal beta oscillations may play opposing functional roles depending on tasks and stimuli, facilitating discrimination of crowded targets and deteriorating detection of items in repeating patterns.

title: The role of spontaneous fluctuations in attention in perceptual filling-in
affiliations: 1. Maastricht University (NL)
abstract: Filling-in occurs during the perceptual disappearance of a blank figure presented on a textured background.Current models propose a two-stage process: the figure’s boundary representation weakens through adaptation, allowing the background texture to spread into the figure’s region via long-range horizontal connections in early visual cortex. Here we tested whether attention, which modulates lateral connectivity in early visual cortex, also influences filling-in. First, we found that filling-in was preceded by a reduced pupil size, which is related to general arousal and selective attention. To differentiate between a reduction in general arousal and selective attention leading to filling-in, we used electroencephalography to track alpha oscillations as a neural correlate for attention. Furthermore, we modelled a typical alpha power lateralized distribution from recordings during a standard lateralized attention paradigm and assessed the correlation of the alpha power distribution preceding filling-in onset with this model. We found a high lateralization of alpha power and a high correlation with the lateralization task a few seconds preceding filling-in onset, suggesting that attention is directed towards the figure before filling-in. In addition to the electroencephalography measurements, we ran a parallel psychophysics study with a novel gradual continuous performance task (gradCPT) to track attentional states in a dual-task paradigm preceding filling-in. The results from this task suggested that that filling-in episodes were preceded by distributed low attention across the visual field before filling-in. The results target together suggest that low attentional states predict perceptual filling-in. Low attentional states may reduce figure-ground segregation and thereby may facilitate the spreading of background-related activity from the background into the cortical region occupied by the figure – resulting in perceptual filling-in.

title: Beyond visual resolution: Redundancy masking as a limiting factor of foveal vision
affiliations:
1. École Normale Supérieure, PSL University, CNRS (FR)
2. University Eye Hospital, University of Bonn (DE)
abstract: Visual resolution—the ability to resolve fine spatial detail—is highest at the fovea. Hence, individual elements are most accurately discriminated within foveal vision. However, individuation of multiple items is not determined by resolution alone. In redundancy masking, a compression of information by the visual system, items in peripheral vision that can be resolved are not perceived. Whether redundancy masking occurs in the fovea is unclear. Here, we investigated this question.  Participants were presented with arrays of three to five lines for 83.3 ms. We varied eccentricity (0.5° and 1° inter-line spacing: 0.03°), directions from fixation (left, right, up, and down), and line width (0.03°, 0.04°, and 0.05° length = 0.4°). Eye tracking ensured that stimuli were presented only after participants maintained fixation for one second. In the main experiment, participants reported how many lines they perceived (enumeration task). After the main experiment, a two-line resolution task was used to measure resolution. Observers often reported fewer items than were presented, across both eccentricities and in all directions. The magnitude of underreporting increased as line width decreased and the number of lines increased.  The results showed that participants with higher accuracy in the resolution task had less underreporting in the enumeration task. Importantly, underreporting despite sufficient visual resolution points to a limitation independent of resolution. Based on a pre-specified criterion (>90% in the resolution task), we excluded participants with lower accuracy. Underreporting remained substantial, and the correlation was no longer observed.  These results show that redundancy masking also occurs in the fovea, despite its peak visual resolution. Strong underreporting persisted when visual resolution was clearly sufficient, indicating that resolution cannot account for the effect. Taken together, these findings suggest that redundancy masking is another limitation in foveal vision, resulting in systematic underreporting of items.

title: How the brain unifies a divided visual field: neural dynamics of foveal-peripheral interaction during the uniformity illusion using RIFT
affiliations: 1. Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University, Nijmegen (NL)
abstract:
Human vision relies on two complementary streams: foveal vision provides high acuity within a narrow field, while peripheral vision covers a wide field at lower resolution. Despite these striking differences, we experience a unified visual world. How the brain constructs this unified percept from two fundamentally different streams — and whether it does so by replacing one with the other or by actively integrating both — remains unresolved.
We address this question using the uniformity illusion, in which sustained fixation on a stimulus that differs in orientation between (para)foveal and peripheral regions causes the whole pattern to appear uniform, typically governed by the foveal feature. This illusion offers a unique window into foveal-peripheral interaction: it isolates the moment at which the brain imposes a unified representation on conflicting inputs, and allows us to ask whether peripheral signals are suppressed and replaced, or whether both streams remain active and are weighted according to their reliability.
We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) while participants viewed orientation-defined textures in a factorial design crossing orientation difference magnitude with physical stimulus change. Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) was applied separately to foveal and peripheral regions at distinct frequencies, providing continuous, independent measures of neural excitability in each stream. Critically, nonlinear interactions between the two tagged streams generate intermodulation components — a direct index of foveal-peripheral signal integration that cannot arise from parallel processing alone.
By contrasting illusory uniformity with veridical uniformity and with prediction-confirming stimulus changes, we can dissociate the neural signatures of perceptual state, signal weighting, and active integration. Together, these measures address whether the unified visual percept reflects active filling-in or Bayesian integration of conflicting foveal and peripheral signals.

title: Behavioural Training Fails to Reduce Plant Awareness Disparity in Numerosity Perception
affiliations: 1. University of Padua (IT)
abstract: Despite plants accounting for most of Earth’s biomass, humans systematically neglect them and underappreciate their ecological relevance. This phenomenon, termed Plant Awareness Disparity (PAD), extends beyond explicit attitudes or knowledge deficits to influence basic perceptual and cognitive functions, including numerosity estimation. Previous research shows that the number of plant stimuli is consistently underestimated compared to animals and inanimate objects. Whether this bias can be reduced through repeated task practice, however, remains an open question. In the current work, a total of 54 participants took part in five repeated testing sessions requiring rapid numerosity judgments of briefly presented arrays containing animal, mineral, or plant images. We examined category-specific changes in performance across sessions using mixed-effects modelling of estimation errors. Our results revealed a robust practice effect between the first and second sessions, indicating improved overall performance with repeated exposure to the task. Importantly, this improvement was not accompanied by any reduction in the plant-specific bias. Throughout all sessions, plant numerosities remained systematically underestimated compared with both animal and object stimuli. Taken together, our findings support the view that PAD reflects a more persistent feature likely rooted in semantic processing rather than in low-level perceptual constraints. Thus, interventions aimed at reducing PAD may be more effective if they focus on conceptual representations and understanding of the role of plants in the environment, rather than relying solely on repeated exposure or simple task practice.

title: Visual serial dependence in joint action contexts
affiliations:
1. Lausanne University Hospital (CH)
2. University of Lausanne (CH)
3. The Sense Innovation and Research Center (CH)
4. University of Modena and Reggio Emilia (IT)
5. Goethe University Frankfurt (DE)
abstract: Serial dependence in perceptual decision-making has typically been studied in individual tasks, where observers are biased by the history of stimuli and responses they experience alone. Here, we investigated the role of social interaction by embedding an orientation reproduction task in a joint context. Pairs of participants viewed the same oriented stimulus, while the task to report the orientation was randomly assigned to one of them on each trial. We measured serial dependence bias and response precision as a function of whether the preceding trial was performed by the same observer, a human co-actor, or a computer. In a first experiment, we found dissociable effects of the joint context on bias and precision: while an attractive bias toward previous orientations was observed across all conditions, response precision increased when participants performed the task with a human co-actor compared to a computer. In a second experiment, we assigned different response tools to the observer and the co-actor to control for response-related effects. We replicated the increase in precision in the joint condition. Additionally, we found modulations of the bias due to the type of response tool only when the same observer acted on consecutive trials. These findings suggest that social interaction with a human co-actor leads to increased precision in stimulus encoding, while serial dependence operates across agents. In addition, a component of serial dependence linked to stimulus–response mapping appears to remain specific to the individual.

title: Beyond Simple Accumulation: Selective Integration of Visual Features Over Time
affiliations: 1. EPFL - Swiss Federal Technology Institute of Lausanne
abstract: Feature integration is essential for perception. Whereas in cross-modal perception, reliability-weighted cue integration models dominate, integration in vision is usually explained by simple feature summation, visual persistence, or temporal filtering. Here, we tested vernier offset integration in the Sequential Metacontrast Paradigm (SQM), in which two streams of diverging lines are perceived as expanding from the center to the periphery. When one line contains a vernier, observers perceive this offset on all other lines - even though these lines are physically straight. When two offsets are presented in the same direction, observers perceive a larger combined offset. By contrast, recent findings showed that when the two offsets are presented in opposite directions, observers do not perceive an averaged or canceled offset, but instead report one offset or the other, revealing feature competition rather than simple accumulation. Obviously, temporal summation cannot account for these results. Allowing straight and offset features to differ in reliability improved the fit of the simple summation model. However, the best account was obtained by combining this model with a selective integration rule that Gaussianly down-weighted discrepant signals, similar to outlier rejection. Hence, feature integration in SQM follows selective integration rules resembling those known from cue integration in cross-modal perception, suggesting that sophisticated integration principles may operate even for low-level visual features.

title: The Role of Feature Covariation in Serial Dependence
affiliations: 1. University of Iceland (IS)
abstract: Information from the past can bias our interpretation of the present. A commonly observed example of this is serial dependence, where current stimulus reports seem to incorporate features of prior stimuli. This effect has been observed across multiple stimulus dimensions, including orientation, facial identity, duration, and numerosity. Serial dependence might be so widespread because stimuli often do not change much over time, meaning that recent stimuli generally remain informative when interpreting ambiguous current stimuli. Similarity of task-irrelevant stimulus features has been found to enhance serial dependence. For example, moving stimuli which are the same colour produce stronger serial dependence in motion direction judgements. Possibly because this similarity creates the impression of stimuli as persistent objects. However, real-world objects often exhibit more complex feature relationships, where multiple attributes covary. For example, an object’s apparent shape and colour may change together as a function of lighting or viewpoint. In such cases, covariation between features could signal meaningful change rather than stability. Thus, secondary features may not only promote perceptual continuity but also provide cues indicating changes in primary features. In the present study we aimed to test the effect of secondary feature covariation on serial dependence. Participants completed an orientation reproduction task using Gabor stimuli whose colour either covaried systematically with orientation or varied randomly. We hypothesized that covarying secondary features might reduce serial dependence by acting as task-relevant cues which reduce stimulus uncertainty. Preliminary results indicate that feature co-variation reduces serial dependence compared to stimuli with uncoupled features. These results refine our understanding of the conditions under which serial dependence arises and highlight how feature relationships can modulate perceptual stability.
