title: Perception of total length, mean size and numerosity of line segments
affiliations:
1. Université Rennes 2 (FR)
2. University of Aberdeen (UK)
abstract: The visual system efficiently extracts summary statistics from sets of objects, including mean size and numerosity. However, preliminary findings indicated that the total perceived length of sets of line segments is systematically underestimated, suggesting that cumulative magnitude is not directly perceived. Here, we tested whether the perceived total length (T) can be approximated by the product of perceived mean size (M) and perceived numerosity (N) for sets of n line segments. In a within-subject design, 16 participants completed three blocked conditions where psychometric functions were obtained for the mean length (M), total length (T), and numerosity (N) of the test set containing 4, 8 or 12 (n) line segments. Data were analysed using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs). In the total length condition, points of subjective equality (PSEs) revealed a strong underestimation relative to the reference, increasing monotonically with n whilst precision (inverse of the just-noticeable difference, JND) degraded in parallel. In the mean length condition, PSEs indicated a moderate overestimation, with bias varying across values of n. However, precision remained stable, consistent with an efficient averaging mechanism. In the numerosity condition, PSEs showed underestimation at the smallest n, reduced and similar at larger values, with precision unaffected.\nThus, only total length showed a deterioration of both accuracy and precision with increasing n. The multiplicative model failed to predict the observed biases in the total length condition, with the discrepancy growing with n, and tended to underestimate the observed JNDs.\nExtending previous studies on area perception to line segments, our results support a reliance on indirect, noisy computation rather than direct extraction of cumulative length.

title: Recent history attracts and repels perceptual decisions depending on surprise
affiliations: 1. University College London (UK)
abstract: Past sensory experience shapes our perceptual decision-making in the now. Popular models frame these effects as either attracted towards or repelled away from recent percepts. For example, after previously seeing a vertically-oriented edge, an attraction involves reporting off-vertical edges as more vertical and repulsion means seeing them as more horizontal. The last decade has seen different explanations for such intriguing dependencies, with some accounts highlighting a possible role for predictive processes – under the assumption that we predict the world should remain stable. However, present accounts are unable to explain what determines whether predictive influences are attractive or repulsive. We therefore turn to a new model that explains paradoxical serial dependence influences in terms of prediction. This ‘opposing processes’ model proposes that effects might turn from attractive to repulsive depending on the level of surprise elicited by the mismatch between predictions – in this case past events – and sensory evidence. We test this model on a large amount of recently-collated trial-by-trial data from 22 different orientation and motion direction continuous reproduction studies. Across the entire dataset, we show that our model outperforms previously-proposed alternatives. Specifically, our model uniquely accounts for the flip from attraction to repulsion according to the level of deviation between current and past events – attraction with small deviations and repulsion with larger discrepancies. We additionally show that this flip occurs with smaller deviations when there is higher perceptual precision, in line with a mechanism of strong counter-factual evidence leading to surprise-mediated repulsion. A final analysis predicts the amplitude and direction of trial-by-trial predictive biases on perceptual decision-making using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. These findings thus account for apparently contradictory findings of serial dependence, including null results, and show how these contradictions may relate mechanistically to those found in the predictive processing literature.

title: Serial dependence across the visual field: perceptual stability without polar angle asymmetries
affiliations: 1. Háskóli Íslands (IS)
abstract: The visual system integrates current inputs with past information to reduce noise and stabilize perception over time, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Such integration often results in an attractive biases toward previously seen inputs, particularly under uncertain conditions. Uncertainty in visual perception is especially pronounced in peripheral vision due to retinal and cortical constraints. Consistent with this, prior work has demonstrated stronger serial dependence in the periphery compared to central vision. In addition, perceptual performance varies across the visual field, with known polar angle asymmetries favoring the horizontal over the vertical meridian and the lower over the upper visual field. However, the influence of these asymmetries on serial dependence remains largely unexplored. The present study aimed to address this by examining whether the polar angle asymmetries modulate the strength of serial dependence. Twenty participants performed an orientation adjustment task with stimuli presented above, below, left, or right of fixation at 9 degrees in the visual periphery. In addition, data from a separate study examining visual field asymmetries in an orientation averaging task were reanalyzed to extend these findings to serial dependence when summary statistics are extracted. Serial dependence was observed across all locations, but neither its magnitude nor response precision differed as a function of polar angle. In contrast, serial dependence was significantly stronger when consecutive stimuli appeared at the same spatial location, in line with previous findings of retinotopic specificity. At the same time, its persistence across locations suggests contributions beyond strictly retinotopic mechanisms. Together, these findings indicate that while serial dependence is not strictly location-specific, it is modulated by the location coherence between current and previous visual inputs.

title: Category-specificity in stimulus-history effects
affiliations:
1. University of Florence (IT)
2. CNR Institute of Neuroscience (IT)
abstract: A coherent perceptual experience requires distinguishing, over time, information belonging to the same object from information signaling a new one. This balance between continuity and sensitivity to change relies on stimulus-history effects: perception can be attracted to prior input (serial dependence), promoting continuity, or repelled from it (adaptation), facilitating the detection of novel objects. If these mechanisms support segmentation, they should be tuned to features defining object identity. Color is a highly salient feature that segments the visual scene into meaningful categories. Within this structured environment, perceiving numerosity separately for each group provides information about resources and threats, guiding ecologically relevant behaviors. Accordingly, prior categorical context may modulate the strength and direction of stimulus-history effects in numerosity perception. Previous work showed that adaptation to high numerosities produces stronger underestimation when the subsequent stimulus shares the same color than when colors are incongruent. Here, we asked whether the same holds for other history effects. Twenty-two adults performed a numerosity estimation task. In two sessions, low and high numerosity ranges were associated with different colors (blue and green), followed by a third interleaved session preserving the numerosity–color mapping. In single-range sessions, responses expanded to cover the full response range. In the interleaved session, responses instead converged toward the global mean of the two numerosity ranges. Crucially, random interleaving created both category repetition and alternation streaks, enabling a direct test of how local categorical statistics shape stimulus-history effects. We observed attractive serial dependence at the 1-back lag, convergence toward neutrality at the 2-back lag, and a repulsive, adaptation-like effect at longer lags. Critically, short-lag attraction was category-independent, whereas long-lag repulsion emerged only under category repetition. These findings suggest that stimulus-history effects operate dynamically depending on temporal and categorical structure of the environment, with category-general attraction promoting continuity and feature-specific repulsion supporting differentiation.

title: Interaction between Metacognitive Factors & Biases In Visual Perception
affiliations:
1. University of Warwick (UK)
2. Koç University (TR)
abstract: Serial Dependence (SD) is a sequential perceptual bias and captures influences of recent history on current visual percepts. While the low-level perceptual origins of SD are well investigated, its modulation by high-level metacognitive factors, e.g., confidence, is not as clear. In the current study, we investigated how local and global confidence judgments influence the magnitude of SD in a delayed orientation estimation task. We also examined whether the relationship between local and global confidence judgments is modulated by SD effects. Participants reproduced orientations of Gabor patches and rated both trial-based (local) and block-level (global) confidence across blocks varying in set size (3, 6, or 9). This design also allowed us to test whether global confidence estimates were directly impacted by local confidence and block set size. Contrary to existing evidence, we observed a serial dependence effect that was not modulated by local confidence judgments, both for the previous and the current target responses. In addition, global confidence showed no signs of a reliable SD effect. However, a serial effect was observed for metacognitive estimates themselves. Linear mixed-effects models showed that both previous confidence and current error independently predicted local confidence. Global confidence was influenced by prior global confidence estimates and block-wise error, but not set size. Taken together, these findings show the dynamic nature of metacognitive computation in relation to recent perceptual history. One's confidence can be predicted from one's own past at different levels, yet the evidence on how much this alters perceptual biases, as SD, is limited.

title: Serial dependence in ensembles depends on representation coherence
affiliations: 1. University of Iceland (IS)
abstract: Serial dependence describes the attractive bias of current perceptual reports toward recently observed stimuli and is often interpreted as an adaptive mechanism that stabilizes perception over time. Previous work has shown that serial dependence increases under conditions of uncertainty, suggesting that observers rely more strongly on prior information when current sensory input is unreliable. However, most studies have examined single-item stimuli, leaving open how these principles generalize to ensemble perception, where observers extract summary statistics from multiple elements. While recent work has demonstrated serial dependence in ensemble representations, it remains unclear whether variability within ensembles modulates the strength of this effect. Here, we investigated serial dependence in an orientation averaging task. On each trial, participants viewed nine oriented Gabors and subsequently reported the mean orientation. Ensemble variability was manipulated by varying the spread of orientations within each display. Contrary to predictions based on uncertainty alone, we found that serial dependence was stronger for low-variability ensembles and reduced for high-variability ensembles. This effect cannot be attributed to stimulus similarity, as ensemble means were randomly sampled and did not differ systematically across variability conditions. Accordingly, average orientation differences between consecutive trials were similar for low- and high-variability ensembles. Instead, our findings show that variability modulates serial dependence in a manner that contrasts with previous accounts based on uncertainty. This suggests that temporal integration depends not only on uncertainty, but also on the coherence of the current ensemble representation. Low-variability ensembles may provide a more stable summary signal, allowing stronger influence from previous stimuli, whereas high-variability ensembles may yield less coherent representations, weakening temporal integration despite increased uncertainty.  In addition, our findings raise the possibility that, although uncertainty in single-object paradigms is known to modulate serial dependence, variability within ensemble representations may not be used to guide temporal integration in the same way.

title: Using RIFT to assess the effects of prediction and surprise on visual processing
affiliations:
1. Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (DE)
2. Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University, Nijmegen (NL)
abstract: Predictions are widely argued to modulate visual processing, both in terms of expectation suppression/surprise enhancement effects during stimulus processing, and in terms of pre-activated sensory templates prior to stimulus onset. However, the precise neural mechanisms, temporal dynamics, and feature-specificity of these effects have remained unclear, in part due to challenges in assessing them in humans in a temporally-resolved and feature-specific manner. Here, to address these challenges, we study the effects of predictability on bottom-up visual processing using magnetoencephalography (MEG) and Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) —  an emerging method to track top-down modulation of early visual cortical activity. Participants view a continuous stream of snowflake-shaped stimuli composed of two overlapping symbols, a “+” and an “x”. Each trial consists of a pre-stimulus period in which the snowflake template is shown, followed by a stimulus period in which one symbol is highlighted relative to the other. Stimuli are presented in either a repeating rhythm (xx++) or an alternating rhythm (x+x+), with occasional violations creating expected and surprising events. The different rhythms allow us to control for the number of stimulus repetitions, disentangling surprise from low-level adaptation effects. The two symbols are invisibly frequency-tagged at different frequencies, enabling continuous, stimulus-specific tracking of cortical responses both during the pre-stimulus template period and during stimulus processing. With this approach, we can reveal precisely which feature information is modulated in early visual cortex by predictability and surprise, along with the temporal dynamics of those modulations. Together, these findings will clarify the neural mechanisms of visual expectation effects and demonstrate that RIFT can track feature-specific cortical modulations beyond covert spatial attention — opening the door to a much broader range of cognitive and perceptual phenomena.
session_title: Poster Session 7 · Ensemble, Numerosity, Texture, and Serial Processing

title: The impact of action semantics on visual expectancy learning
affiliations: 1. University of Lille (FR)
abstract: Expectancy learning, the ability to anticipate future events on the basis of environmental cues, is a key component of adaptive behavior. It has been extensively studied through Pavlovian conditioning (pairing of a neutral stimulus with a biologically important event) in animals and contingency assessment task (after being exposed to a stimulus flow, the participants have to indicate whether a specific stimulus can be predicted on the basis of another) in humans. Because of its roots in the animal learning tradition, this kind of research have rarely looked at the impact of variables reflecting higher-order semantic relations between stimuli.  The present study assessed whether action semantics could impact expectancy learning in a visual contingency assessment task. Participants were exposed to rapid stimulus streams. Each stimulus represented an object and was presented for 300 ms. A stream involved two kinds of stimuli: cues and outcomes. At the end of a stream, participants performed predictive judgments about whether a specific outcome could be predicted from a specific outcome. Beside the objective predictive relation between the cues and outcomes, we manipulated the semantic relation between the target cues and outcomes which could either be related through an action semantics or semantically unrelated.  We found that irrespective of the objective predictive relations between the stimuli, action semantics were making participants more likely to judge there was a predictive relation between them. This suggests that higher-order semantic relations between stimuli might bias the detection of predictive relations between stimuli, independently of the objective statistical structure of the environment.

title: Sensitivity in Scene Typicality Judgments: Linking Pairwise Choice and Rating Scales
affiliations:
1. Institute of Psychology, Czech Academy of Sciences (CZ)
2. University of Muenster (DE)
abstract: People do not treat categories as uniform sets instead, they perceive some exemplars as more typical than others. These differences can reflect the internal structure of a category (e.g., variation among dog breeds) or more subtle feature cues (e.g., how typical a particular kitchen appears). In a previous study, participants rated the typicality of 1,500 images of kitchens, bedrooms, and living rooms on a 0–100 scale, with each image evaluated by 25–50 raters. We computed the mean typicality score for each image, but it remains unclear how sensitive participants are to variations on this scale and how those numeric differences translate into judgmental preferences. To address this question, we selected 24 images from each category, sampling three images from each of eight typicality quantiles. Three new participant groups (N = 101 for kitchens, N = 114 for bedrooms, and N = 96 for living rooms) completed 276 binary-choice trials, selecting the more typical exemplar in each pair. Responses were modeled using a Bradley–Terry framework, and the resulting preference coefficients were compared with the previously obtained mean typicality ratings. The two measures showed strong correspondence (r = .826 for kitchens, r = .869 for bedrooms, r = .924 for living rooms), allowing us to align the scales. The analysis indicated that a difference of approximately 10 points (9.3–11.6) on the 0–100 scale doubled the odds that participants selected the higher-rated exemplar in pairwise comparisons. Expressed differently, rescaling the original ratings to a 7-point Likert scale suggests that a 1-point difference between two images corresponds to a 73–78% probability of selecting the more typical exemplar (odds = 2.71–3.45). Our experiments show that the average typicality ratings are highly predictive of actual human choice behavior.
session_title: Poster Session 7 · Scene and Object Perception and Recognition

title: Blended scenes deviate in typicality but preserve perceptual similarity
affiliations:
1. Institute of Psychology, Czech Academy of Sciences (CZ)
2. University of Muenster (DE)
abstract: When studying scene perception, an important factor is scene similarity. Recent advances in generative models allow us to create artificial scenes that are composites of several images, and these blends remain highly meaningful with respect to scene structure. In this study, we explored three questions: (1) How closely do blended scenes resemble their source images? (2) Can behavioral similarity judgments be predicted using deep feature representations? (3) How do blends differ from source images in perceived typicality?  We selected 115 images from four scene categories (two indoor, two outdoor). Using OpenAI's GPT-Image 1.5 model, we generated blends in three conditions: within the same category, between different categories within the same domain (indoor or outdoor), and across domains (combining indoor and outdoor scenes). These blends were evaluated in an online study (Prolific, N = 80) using a rating task in which participants viewed a blend alongside its two source scenes and adjusted a slider to indicate which source the blend more closely resembled. For each image, we extracted deep features from multiple layers of AlexNet (conv3, conv5, fc6, and fc7) pretrained on the Places365 database. We also estimated image typicality using the ChatGPT-4 model, leveraging our recent evidence that LLM-based typicality scores serve as a reliable proxy for human norms in scene categorization. Results showed strong agreement between behavioral similarity and deep-feature similarity (r > .70 across all tested convolutional and fully connected layers). Blended scenes were rated as markedly less typical than their source images, with typicality reduced by approximately 20-30% relative to the original value or the scale range. This decrease was observed not only for cross-category blends but also for within-category blends. These findings indicate that while deep features capture perceptual similarity well, the blends are perceived as atypical rather than as simple averages of their components.

title: Dissociating contribution of convexity and perceived distance in allocation of attention to 2D stimuli
affiliations:
1. University of Padua (IT)
2. University of Southern Denmark (DK)
abstract: Some studies suggest preferential allocation of visual attention to objects perceived as near rather than far in 2D and 3D representations. However, when stimuli are depicted using 3D cues such as shading, they can modulate perceived depth but may fail to disambiguate important shape properties such as convexity, which can be influenced by shading-based cues (e.g., light-from-above). We investigated whether perceived distance and convexity can be dissociated by replicating the paradigm of West et al. (2013) and adapting it to 2D stimuli. In their study, convex/near and concave/far spheres were presented in a temporal order judgment task using different stimulus onset asynchronies (24, 48, 60, 120 ms) to test prior-entry effect (i.e., the tendency for attended stimuli to be perceived earlier in time). We conducted an exact replication, then isolated perceived distance with linear-perspective stimuli and convexity using 2D-closed-contours with a sinusoidal-boundary on one side. We hypothesised that convexity would produce a stronger prior-entry effect than concavity and that this effect would exceed that driven by perceived distance when both cues were present. When only distance cues were available, we expected a bias toward the near stimulus. We estimated the Point of Subjective Simultaneity (PSS) and compared reaction times (RT) between stimuli in each experiment. Replication showed a positive PSS and faster responses for near/convex stimuli. With 2D-distance alone, we found no reliable differences between stimuli. In contrast, with closed-contour, prior-entry favoured concave over convex parts. Although the hypotheses were partially supported, these results suggest that convexity and perceived distance rely on distinct mechanisms of attentional allocation in 2D vs. 3D stimuli. This divergence may be interpreted within a probabilistic framework of 2D contour processing, whereby inward (convex) curvature is more expected in closed shapes, whereas outward (concave) curvature is statistically less frequent and therefore more informative.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Object Size Adaptation
affiliations: 1. Department of Neurosciences, Psychology, Drug Research and Child Health (NEUROFARBA), University of Florence (IT)
abstract: Perceptual experience is continuously shaped by recent sensory history through adaptive mechanisms that recalibrate neural representations. Previous work has shown that size adaptation alters perceived object size and is associated with activity in early visual cortex, yet its temporal dynamics remain unresolved. Moreover, recent evidence from numerosity adaptation indicates that the similarity between adaptor and test stimuli in their low-level features determines the strength of adaptation effects, suggesting that some adaptation phenomena may involve post-categorical processes. Here, we combined psychophysics and EEG to determine when size adaptation effects arise along the visual hierarchy and whether such recalibration is influenced by stimulus similarity.  Participants performed a 2AFC size discrimination task between two circular stimuli presented on either side of a central fixation point (baseline condition), with one stimulus fixed at 5° diameter and the other varying around this value. The same task was then performed following exposure to a large adapting circular stimulus for 4 seconds, with the color of the adaptor and test stimuli either matching (congruent condition) or differing (incongruent condition) across blocks. Behaviorally, adaptation to large stimuli induced a compression of perceived size, consistent with previous findings. Importantly, the magnitude of adaptation was modulated by feature congruency, with stronger effects observed in color-congruent compared to incongruent conditions. At the neural level, an early response around ~100 ms was the first component modulated by adaptation, although this modulation was not sensitive to color congruency. In contrast, congruency-dependent modulation emerged at a later stage, around ~200-300 ms and beyond, with enhanced responses for congruent relative to incongruent conditions. These findings indicate a temporal dissociation between early adaptation effects and later modulation by feature congruency, suggesting that perceptual recalibration may not be limited to low-level sensory mechanisms but may depend on interactions across feature dimensions, consistent with object-based categorization processes.

title: Response in the frequency-contrast plane: reproduction of modern psychophysics with image quality models.
affiliations: 1. Universitat de València (ES)
abstract: Models for image quality assessment are traditionally based on vision science and, more recently, on machine learning. Years ago, reproducing the classical human response to frequency-contrast patterns was enough to get good quality metrics (Daly, 1990 Teo and Heeger, 1994). For this reason, it is important to check the behaviour of current metrics with basic stimuli in this plane. In this work, we use new data gathered using modern psychophysics in the frequency-contrast plane to evaluate image quality models. In this evaluation, models face the same task as humans in Maximum Likelihood Difference Scaling and Ordinal Embedding experiments. In particular, we compare 5 state-of-the-art models. We also evaluate the Mean Squared Error for convenient reference.  In this type of experiments, two stimuli and a reference stimulus are presented, then, the observer decides which is more similar to the reference. For models, we simulate the experiment by taking the distance computed by each metric between the reference and the two stimuli. In particular, the stimuli are Gabor patches or narrow band noise of certain frequency, orientation and RMSE contrast. These stimuli can come with a background with controlled frequency and orientation. In this setting, one can keep the frequency the same and change only the contrast (unidimensional case), or mix both variables (multidimensional case).  In our results, all models have a response that increases with contrast. Obviously, RMSE has a linear response, while some models certainly have a saturating response. Models have a limited frequency bandwidth, but not exactly like humans. Likewise, no model properly reproduces masking effects. In conclusion, no model faithfully reproduces human behaviour in the frequency-contrast plane. This finding is consistent with studies that suggest that a better performance in image quality does not imply models that reproduce low-level vision facts.

title: Differentiating image-based strategies for viewpoint discrimination.
affiliations:
1. Queen Mary University of London (UK)
2. Bristol University (UK)
abstract: When we compare objects seen from different viewpoints, what information are we using? In classic studies of mental rotation, the linear relationship between response time and angular disparity between two viewpoints was taken as evidence that observers mentally rotate a structural, 3D representation of the object. However, angular disparity will often be correlated with the degree of change in the 2D image. Therefore, viewpoint comparison may reflect sensitivity to image-level cues rather than, or alongside, classic linear rotation. In this study, we dissociate four candidate cues in a triadic viewpoint discrimination task: angular disparity, cumulative image displacement (CID), direct image displacement (DID), and static image similarity. Participants viewed a reference image alongside two comparisons and chose which was closer in viewpoint to the reference. We created a novel stimulus set with unfamiliar abstract 3D objects and geometrically regular objects to vary whether observers could infer the 3D structure of the objects. We included conflict trials in which different cues made divergent predictions. Using mixed-effects logistic regression, we find that all four candidate cues significantly predicted choices, with image-based cues - particularly image similarity and DID - emerging as stronger predictors than CID and angular disparity, in terms of effect size. In conflict trials, choices were most strongly driven by image similarity, with accuracy falling substantially when only displacement-based cues supported the correct response. Participants also differed substantially in which cues they relied on, while most tracked image similarity, a minority relied more heavily on displacement-based cues and showed lower overall accuracy. These findings suggest that viewpoint comparison is not a unitary process - observers may not rely solely on mental rotation of a 3D structural representation, but instead favour 2D image-based heuristics, with meaningful individual variation in how different sources of visual information are weighted.

title: Object-Scene congruency and visual similarity interact to support scene memory
affiliations: 1. University of Warwick (UK)
abstract: We can remember a plethora of different scenes, but effective retrieval of scene information is selective and dependent on many factors. Prior research suggests that the memorability of an image is not only influenced by how visually similar it is to others, but also how congruent it is to the surrounding scene context (Pandya et al., 2024 Rémy et al., 2013). However, there is a dearth of literature investigating whether the visual similarities between different scenes, and object-scene congruency interact to predict scene memory. In this study, participants rated the congruency of different object-scene pairs, followed by a surprise 3-alternate forced choice (3-AFC) memory task for scene images. Each trial consisted of a set of three images of same scene category. To test whether visual similarity has an influence on scene memory, and whether low or high-level visual features are relevant, we extracted feature representations through AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model. Feature values were extracted at each layer and averaged across the set to generate trial-level measures of visual similarity spanning from low-level visual features (brightness, contrast) to high-level constructs (eye, wheel etc.). Generalised linear mixed effects models were first fitted to test whether feature-specific similarities and object-scene congruency interact to jointly predict scene memory. The results indicate that higher-level feature layers were found to negatively predict scene memory accuracy, such that greater visual similarity between images was linked to poorer performance. This effect was moderated by object–scene congruency As congruency increased, the negative influence of similarity on recognition accuracy weakened. The findings suggest that schema-based knowledge about the world aids memory, such that object-scene congruency acts as a compensatory mechanism modulating the cognitive need to use more higher-level perceptual features to support scene memory.

title: Object typicality in indoor scenes: Does the choice of response method matter?
affiliations:
1. Institute of Psychology, Czech Academy of Sciences (CZ)
2. Department of Psychology, Faculty of Arts, Charles University (CZ)
abstract: Typicality ratings can be used to characterise objects in scenes, with recent work showing that object frequency and specificity are useful for scene categorisation (Wiesmann & Võ, 2023). In this study, we investigated whether the choice of response method affects typicality estimates for objects drawn from three indoor room categories.  During a pilot experiment using preliminary subset of 35 stimuli, 45 Czech-speaking participants (37 women, 8 men M(age) = 24.5, SD = 8.0) rated typicality for objects from indoor scene photographs (kitchen, bedroom, living room) using three methods: rank ordering (participants ordered list of objects from most to least typical for a given room), an object-anchored Likert scale (participants saw two images of the same object from different angles and rated how commonly it appears in each of three rooms), and a room-anchored Likert scale (participants were given room context and rated a list of objects for that room). All measures showed high inter-rater agreement (ICC(2,k) > .97 Kendall's W = .80 for kitchen and bedroom, .70 for living room) and strong cross-method convergence across all pairwise comparisons (Spearman ρ = .76 – .98). Despite this convergence, the response method affected absolute ratings: object-anchored task produced higher typicality estimates than room-anchored task across all rooms. This difference varied across room categories, being largest for the living room and smallest for the kitchen, potentially reflecting how strongly each room is associated with a fixed set of objects. An expanded experiment, using a human-annotated object set derived from 1,500 indoor scene photographs, is currently underway and will allow these patterns to be examined with greater precision. Complete typicality ratings and their cross-method comparison will be presented at the conference.

title: Dissociable effects of object relatedness and scene congruency on visual recognition
affiliations:
1. Sichuan Normal University (CN)
2. Yunnan University (CN)
3. University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: Visual object recognition is shaped by both global scene context and local relations between co-occurring objects, yet their relative contributions and temporal dynamics remain unclear. We examined how scene congruency and object relatedness jointly influence recognition in two experiments. In Experiment 1, participants categorized target objects embedded in semantically congruent or incongruent scenes. Reaction times revealed a reliable scene-congruency benefit, with faster recognition for targets appearing in congruent backgrounds. In Experiment 2, we added a second contextual object that was either related or unrelated to the target, together with a no-background baseline, while recording EEG. Behaviorally, object relatedness strongly modulated performance: targets were recognized more slowly and less accurately when paired with a related contextual object than with an unrelated one. Moreover, relatedness interacted with scene congruency: when the contextual object was related, congruent scenes facilitated recognition, whereas when it was unrelated, incongruent scenes produced faster responses.  ERP analyses revealed dissociable processing stages. In the no-background condition, relatedness modulated the N170, suggesting an early influence of foreground structure. Across conditions, unrelated pairs elicited larger P2 amplitudes, consistent with more efficient attentional selection. The N3 was sensitive to both scene congruency and object relatedness when a background was present, indicating later contextual integration, while the N4 was primarily affected by relatedness. Time-resolved MVPA further showed that object relatedness was decodable earlier and more robustly than scene congruency.  Together, these findings suggest that in multi-object scenes, local object-object structure can exert a stronger and more sustained influence on recognition than global scene gist.

title: The role of behavioural goals in shaping representations in the ventral visual pathway
affiliations: 1. CIMeC, Trento University (IT)
abstract: How does the brain represent the visual environment? Classic theories of object vision focus on object recognition however, human object vision is far from being solved, and accumulating evidence points to the complexity of the multidimensional representational space that underlies visual representations. In a series of neuroimaging studies, we investigate the role of action-related dimensions in shaping the organisation of visual cortex representations. In the first study, we examined responses to images of body parts and objects with different degrees of action-related properties. In the left lateral occipitotemporal cortex, we identified a topographically organised action gradient, with overlapping activations for bodies, hands, tools, and manipulable objects along a dorsal–posterior to ventral–anterior axis, culminating at the intersection of body parts and objects exhibiting higher action-related properties. In the second study, we confirm and extend these results by showing that manipulable food, which conveys grasping affordances, maps onto the same action gradient in the lateral occipitotemporal cortex by overlapping with other manipulable and action-effector objects such as tools. Importantly, topographic deep neural networks trained on object recognition were unable to capture the same spatial organisation observed in the lateral occipitotemporal cortex. Together, these results suggest that, to understand object vision, we need to move beyond object recognition, often considered the final goal of visual perception, and take into account the role of behavioral goals, such as object interaction, in shaping the organisation of object space in the visual cortex. Understanding the core mechanisms underlying this object space could inform the development of computational models that perceive and represent the world in a human-like manner.
