title: Visual Awareness and Action: Testing Dual-Task Immunity in Online Motor Corrections to Unperceived Changes
affiliations: 1. Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (DE)
abstract: Humans often act in dynamically changing environments that require rapid motor adjustments, and the motor system is capable of modifying ongoing actions in response to unperceived changes. Goodale et al. (1986) demonstrated that participants could adjust their pointing movements to compensate for targets that were displaced during saccadic eye movements, even though they were unaware of the displacement. The current study examines whether such adjustments remain robust under cognitive load and systematically tests whether target shifts truly go undetected. Participants perform pointing tasks with gaze-contingent target shifts, under single- and dual-task conditions. In this paradigm, the target is displaced during a saccade and due to visual sensitivity being highly reduced during saccades (known as saccadic blindness), these displacements typically go unnoticed. To test whether the motor system is immune to the dual-task interference, eye and hand movement parameters were compared between single- and dual-task conditions. Results showed clear dual-task interference in primary saccades, which were slower (as measured by reaction time and peak velocity) and less accurate in the dual-task condition. This reduction in performance was subsequently compensated by larger and more frequent secondary saccades. Additionally, the increase in pointing errors as a function of target displacement amplitude was steeper in the dual-task condition. Finally, a separate two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task which measured perceptual awareness to target displacements, revealed chance-level performance across most displacement magnitudes, with above-chance performance only for the largest displacement in the direction of the saccade. Overall, the findings suggest that increased cognitive load disrupts online motor corrections to environmental changes, even when perceptual awareness of those changes is limited. Goodale, M. A., Pelisson, D., & Prablanc, C. (1986). Large adjustments in visually guided reaching do not depend on vision of the hand or perception of target displacement. Nature, 320(6064), 748-750.

title: The role of vision in the size-weight illusion
affiliations: 1. Ludwigs-Maximilians-Universität München (DE)
abstract: The size-weight illusion (SWI) – smaller objects are perceived as heavier than larger objects of equal mass – remains incompletely understood despite over a century of research (Nicolas et al., 2012). Building on Buckingham and Goodale (2010), the present study examined the contribution of online visual feedback to sensorimotor and perceptual manifestations of the SWI. Participants lifted three cubes of different size but identical mass, while grip and load forces were continuously recorded via a force transducer. A between-subject design was employed across three vision conditions, differing in the degree of visual information available during lifting: full vision (unobstructed view of both object and sensor), only early vision (neither object nor sensor visible during lifting), and sensor only vision (sensor visible object occluded). Visual access was manipulated using LCD-goggles and a physical occlusion cover. Force analysis revealed comparable grip and load force profiles under full-vision and sensor only vision conditions. In contrast, complete visual occlusion during lifting resulted in globally elevated grip and load forces, indicating a greater reliance on conservative force estimates in the absence of any visual feedback. Critically, these findings demonstrate that appropriate anticipatory force calibration can be achieved without direct visual access to the object during lifting. With respect to perceptual outcomes, both the occluded and limited-vision conditions were associated with an attenuation of the perceptual SWI relative to full vision, implicating visual feedback as a modulatory factor in the conscious experience of the illusion. Buckingham, G., & Goodale, M. A. (2010). Lifting without seeing: The role of vision in perceiving and acting upon the size weight Illusion. PLoS ONE, 5(3), 3–6. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0009709 Nicolas, S., Ross, H. E., & Murray, D. J. (2012). Charpentier’s papers of 1886 and 1891 on weight perception and the size-weight illusion. Perceptual and Motor Skills, 115(1), 120–141. https://doi.org/10.2466/24.22.27.PMS.115.4.120-141

title: Quantifying the impact of monocular visual blur on control of upper-limb movements in virtual reality
affiliations:
1. University of Leeds (UK)
2. Independent Researcher (UK)
abstract: Accurate reach-to-grasp movements are necessary for everyday tasks and rely on binocular visual information to support visuomotor planning and online control. Previous research in real-world environments have demonstrated that monocular visual blur alters reach-to-grasp kinematics, evidenced by reduced movement speed and impaired grasp accuracy. However, research identifying thresholds at which this occurs, as well as the extent of individual differences in visuomotor function, remain limited.   We sought to identify the threshold at which monocular visual impairment begins to impact the planning and execution of prehension. We conducted experiments in virtual reality (VR), which offers a platform for the precise manipulation of visual input, including the ability to tailor visual blur to each individual or experimental condition, and allows for the efficient switching between conditions. We investigated the threshold of motor impairment by degrading vision monocularly at 5 levels of increasing blur. Participants were required to reach, grasp, and lift a virtual object, which was calibrated with a real-world object to ensure accurate haptic feedback while grasping. Upper-limb kinematics were quantified using motion capture to assess markers of movement planning and execution, such as reach velocity, grip aperture and deceleration time. We hypothesised that movement kinematics will be increasingly impacted with greater severity of monocular visual blur. We predicted slower movement velocities and altered grip aperture scaling, reflecting changes in visuomotor planning and control. Preliminary results showed increased movement time, lower peak velocities and altered grip aperture scaling under stronger blur.   This study improves our understanding of the visual threshold at which monocular visual impairments impact motor planning and control and may inform clinical thresholds for intervention for individuals with monocular visual impairments. Future research may provide insight into how VR may be utilised in the development of cost-effective and accessible at-home visual interventions and further non-clinical research on visually-guided action.

title: Shape-related biases in volume and weight perception
affiliations: 1. University of Southampton (UK)
abstract: In the shape-weight illusion, objects are perceived as lighter or heavier depending on their shape. For example, spheres are perceived as heavier than tetrahedrons of matched weight and volume. Opposite biases occur in size perception: spheres appear smaller than volume‑matched tetrahedrons. If perceptually smaller objects are perceived as heavier, this pattern would be consistent with the size-weight illusion, whereby the smaller of two weight‑matched objects feels heavier. However, perceived size alone does not account for the shape-weight illusion across all shapes, and surface area has been proposed as an alternative predictor of perceived weight. Alternatively, a 'sensorimotor mismatch' could contribute to the illusion, whereby forces misapplied based on perceived size may influence perceived weight. For example, objects that appear larger may be grasped with excessive force and consequently be perceived as lighter. We measured the shape-weight illusion using four shapes (sphere, tetrahedron, cuboid, and H‑shape presented in three sizes), chosen to decorrelate perceived volume and surface area. Thirty participants provided magnitude estimates of object volume in a visual task and of object weight in a visuo‑haptic lifting task. Objects were lifted via a handle equipped with force-torque transducers to record grasping forces and torques. We observed clear shape‑related biases: cuboids and spheres were perceived as the largest and smallest shapes, respectively spheres and tetrahedrons were perceived as the heaviest and lightest. Thus, there were discrepancies between size and weight biases, but these were not explained by surface area. Additionally, we observed systematic differences in grip force and torque, but found no evidence for a sensorimotor mismatch. Instead, force patterns were aligned with shape‑dependent stabilisation requirements during lifting. We propose that sensorimotor factors related to grasp stability – such as grip force and torque during lifting – may contribute to the shape-weight illusion alongside perceived volume.

title: Visually-guided human grasping behaviour with fully articulated hands
affiliations:
1. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
2. University of Southampton (UK)
3. Technical University of Darmstadt (DE)
abstract: Humans possess a remarkable capacity to grasp and handle objects. To achieve this seemingly effortless task, we need to visually select appropriate contact regions on the surface of the object and shape the multiple joints of our hand accordingly to reach a stable grasp. Despite the wide range of possible grasps in everyday behaviour, most research has been conducted under highly constrained conditions, often emphasizing precision grip grasps and reducing hand-object contact to mere points rather than extensive regions. Here, we aimed at characterizing human grasps under more natural conditions by removing these constraints and allowing for full articulation of the hand. Our contribution is two-fold: First, we developed a method to measure contact regions on hands and objects by combining components from deep learning, motion tracking and computer graphics to reconstruct a full 3D mesh of the hand and object from video data, which allowed analyses of both hand poses and hand-object contact. Then, we collected a comprehensive dataset (N=40) of human grasping behaviour featuring a wide variety of objects and tasks across multiple sessions. First, participants pantomimed grasps from a standard taxonomy of 33 grasp types. Second, participants each grasped 14 (out of total of 28) objects with (1) precision grip (2) multi-digit and (3) unconstrained conditions. Third, we examined the influence of the task which participants performed with the object (use hand over turn horizontally turn vertically heft). Our results showed that participants rarely used precision grip, yet they were highly consistent in their grasping strategies, which manifested in consistent contact regions and highly stereotyped hand poses across repetitions and participants. Our findings both demonstrate a novel way to measure hand-object contact during grasping and extend our insights into grasping behaviour to more naturalistic scenarios.

title: How visual and auditory cues affect preferred distances in human-drone interaction
affiliations: 1. Experimental Psychology, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (DE)
abstract: Drones are becoming increasingly common in everyday environments, which raises the question if and how they impinge on one’s personal space when interacting with a drone. Personal space requirements serve protective and regulatory functions, and a variety of cues influence when we start to feel intrusion into our personal space. In this study, we investigated how the visual size and the acoustic properties of a delivery drone affect the closest comfortable approach distance. In a virtual reality setting, participants completed a stop-distance task in which a drone approached them and they had to make it stop at the closest comfortable distance. We manipulated three factors: the drone’s physical size (small, medium, or large) the pitch of its motor sound (-40%, -20%, original sound, +20%, or +40% matched for subjective loudness) and its overall volume (two levels). All three factors significantly affected the preferred distance to the drone: participants allowed smaller drones to approach more closely than larger ones. Louder noise increased the space requirement, and lower-pitched noise afforded closer proximity as compared to high-pitched noise. These findings have direct implications for the design of the drone itself as well as for the design and evaluation of the personal space requirements in human-drone interaction.

title: Immersive environments influence egocentric target representation
affiliations:
1. York University (CA)
2. Justus Liebig University Giessen (DE)
abstract: When using virtual reality, people sometimes walk into objects or walls even when in a familiar real world environment. We have shown that while immersed in virtual reality and pointing to previously seen objects in the real world, pointing endpoints are based primarily on the locations of objects in the current virtual environment. On each trial participants performed a simple walking task in virtual reality and then pointed to the remembered location of the real-world door. The virtual environment could be aligned or misaligned to the real world. We found that participants were either just pointing at what they could see or that the egocentric representation of the unseen environment was overwritten by the currently seen environment. This indicates that egocentric target representations are weakened when performing tasks in virtual environments. To further test this, 20 participants performed a similar walking task and had to point to the location of the door in the real world while they saw either a virtual replica of the real world room or just a black environment. In a preliminary analysis we found that after walking, pointing was not affected by the visual input. This suggests that the egocentric target representation was overwritten. However, if participants had been stationary, they pointed closer to the virtual (instead of the real world) door when pointing with vision compared to when being in the dark environment. This suggests that participants were primarily pointing based on what they saw, i.e. they relied more strongly on environmental (allocentric) than egocentric cues however, they might still have access to the egocentric target representation.

title: Color, Geometry and Gender: Spatial Navigation Strategies in Non-Euclidean Virtual Reality
affiliations:
1. Department of Basic Psychology, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid (ES)
2. Department of Information Systems, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (ES)
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) enables environments that violate Euclidean geometry for example, corridors can overlap in physical space while appearing entirely distinct to the user. Such partially non-Euclidean spaces offer a practical strategy for expanding virtual worlds within constrained physical areas, yet their effects on spatial cognition remain poorly understood. We investigated how partial non-Euclidean geometry affects path integration and homing performance. Thirty-six participants (23 men, 13 women ages 18-56) navigated four VR labyrinths using an Oculus Quest 2: two Euclidean and two partially non-Euclidean, each with or without colored wall cues. Mazes were matched for goal distance (~16 m) and the number of bifurcations (7). Movement data were recorded and processed to extract trajectories, distance, time, and errors. There was no significant increase in navigational errors in non-Euclidean mazes (p = .59), despite traveling substantially greater distances (60.75 m vs. 30.50 m, p < .001, r = .34). These findings align more closely with cognitive graph theory (localized, path-based spatial representations) than with the global metric maps predicted by cognitive map theory. Colored walls significantly reduced wrong turns on the outward journey (p = .05, r = .13), serving as navigational cues. However, color had no significant effect on return navigation, suggesting that landmark benefits do not persist through the homing phase. No statistically significant gender differences were found. These results show that partially non-Euclidean VR spaces are navigable without increased error, supporting their use in immersive applications.

title: Global and Local Environmental Statistics Jointly Shape Visually Guided Motor Planning
affiliations: 1. UC Berkeley (US)
abstract: Visually guided action depends on balancing speed and accuracy. This speed–accuracy tradeoff (SAT) is usually treated as a fundamental constraint, often framed as a single optimization between time and error. Yet the brain also uses prior information and environmental statistics to improve performance, and the computations that enable this remain unclear. Standard models of visuomotor control emphasize Bayesian inference, in which prior information is combined with sensory input to estimate the current state. Here, we show instead that adaptive motor planning relies on two complementary computations that exploit different statistical structures in the environment. One process uses global summary statistics to speed planning for frequently encountered targets, consistent with use-dependent learning. By shifting decision boundaries, it accelerates action selection and reduces planning variability, but also introduces an attractive bias toward the mean trajectory. A second process tracks local, trial-by-trial statistics and generates a repulsive sequential bias tuned to environmental autocorrelation, counteracting this error. In visually guided reaching movements, these sequential effects matched efficient coding predictions and conflicted with Bayesian accounts: current movements were biased away from previous movements, variability decreased when successive reaches were similar, and the repulsive bias increased with intrinsic motor variability. Together, these findings support a factorized control architecture in which global statistics speed action selection while local statistics preserve accuracy, showing how visually guided movements can become both faster and more accurate without simply relaxing the SAT.

title: Impact of novel action semantics on the early visual processing of objects
affiliations: 1. Univ. Lille, CNRS, SCALab – Sciences Cognitives et Sciences Affectives (FR)
abstract: Action semantics refer to multimodal representations encompassing manipulation knowledge (e.g., object grasp and use), functional knowledge (e.g., tool function), and sensory consequences related to object use. In support of embodied cognition approaches, action semantics was found to enhance object processing in various identification tasks. The present research aims to investigate whether novel action semantics can also enhance early stages of visual processing. To that aim, we are running an ongoing experiment (n=8/66) to test the effect of novel action semantics on object detection. Healthy young adults (age=23±1.6, 6 women) were exposed to novel 3D objects in virtual reality and had to learn their name and function in one of two training conditions (n=4 by group) varying in manipulation experience (functional use vs. perceptual judgments). We used breaking Continuous Flash Suppression (bCFS), and its variant, reverse-bCFS, to study access to and disappearance from consciousness, respectively. We also used an exogenous version of the Posner-cueing task to investigate attentional capture of learned objects (presented as cue). Facilitation or inhibition effects were calculated as RT[valid object cue – invalid object cue]. Preliminary bCFS results indicate that object detection was faster in the functional use group than in the perception group (median RTs: 4.5±2.9 vs. 6.5±1.8 s, d=0.82). Congruently, reverse-bCFS data suggest that object disappearance from consciousness was slower in the functional use group than in the perception group (median RTs: 5.2±2.7 vs. 3.6±2.9 s, d=0.58). In the Posner-cueing task, inhibition magnitude was similar between the functional use and perception groups (mean RTs: -19.8±8.3 vs. -18.7±12.1 ms, d=-0.10). These preliminary results suggest that high-level object features related to action semantics can elicit faster access to consciousness. Forthcoming data will further help to determine to what extent action semantics may have a top-down facilitatory effects on object detection.

title: Does distractor homogeneity have the same effects on visual search and visual foraging?
affiliations:
1. Philipps-University Marburg (DE)
2. Brigham and Women's Hospital (US)
3. Harvard Medical School (US)
abstract: In visual search, greater distractor-distractor similarity makes search easier while greater target-distractor similarity makes search harder (Duncan & Humphreys, 1989). While this principle is widely supported in single-target visual search paradigms, it’s unclear whether distractor homogeneity has a similar impact on multiple-target visual foraging tasks. In our foraging tasks, observers repeatedly search for multiple targets within “patches” under time constraints and are allowed to decide when to move to a new patch. From an optimal foraging perspective, the Marginal Value Theorem (MVT) (Charnov, 1976) predicts that the current patch should be left once the instantaneous rate of target collection drops below the overall rate in the environment. This paradigm therefore enables simultaneous investigation of foraging efficiency and patch-leaving behavior. The present study tested how distractor homogeneity affects visual foraging behavior in perceptual (color) and categorical (letter) foraging tasks. Distractor homogeneity was manipulated within subjects. Results showed a dissociation across the tasks. In the categorical letter foraging task, higher distractor homogeneity was associated with improved foraging performance, reflected as higher target collection rates and fewer uncollected targets across different levels of distractor homogeneity. Patch-leaving behavior remained also consistent with MVT, showing that observers adjusted their leaving decisions based on their overall collection rate. However, the homogeneity conditions did not produce expected differences in foraging performance during perceptual color foraging. These findings indicate that distractor homogeneity affects visual foraging behavior differently across domains and highlight the need for further investigation into the underlying perceptual mechanisms of foraging in dynamic visual environments.

title: Neural representations of relational-based attentional template in frontoparietal network
affiliations:
1. Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences, Zhejiang University (CN)
2. Liangzhu Laboratory, State Key Laboratory of Brain-machine Intelligence, Zhejiang University (CN)
3. Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Neurocognitive Development and Mental Health, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China (CN)
abstract: Goal-directed attention relies on attentional templates – internal representations of target stimuli. While traditional views hold that templates represent exact feature values (e.g., specific color or orientation), recent theories propose a functional distinction between a relational “guiding template” (e.g., 'redder') and a veridical “target template” (e.g., red). To isolate the guiding template and its neural substrates, we conducted a behavioral (Experiment 1, N = 20) and an fMRI (Experiment 2, N = 20) experiment using a cued visual search task. In both experiments, participants reported the orientation of a target bar located inside a circle matching the cued color. Behavioral results from Experiment 1 showed that distractors matching the relational property of the cue (e.g., “redder” than the uncued color) captured significantly more attention than distractors that were equidistant in color space but mismatched the relational property (e.g., “yellower”). In Experiment 2 (fMRI, N = 20), multivoxel pattern analysis revealed that the frontoparietal network, specifically the inferior frontal junction (IFJ) and intraparietal sulcus (IPS), represented the relational information during preparatory attention. Crucially, the cross-decoding of neural activity patterns in these regions, performed across distinct color pairs sharing the same feature relationship, was reliably above chance level. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) further corroborated that these templates were structured by relational rather than feature proximity. Together, our findings identify the critical brain regions underlying the relational format of target template during attentional guidance.

title: Salient intra-object features dominate the contents of the visual search template: Electrophysiological evidence
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: When searching for an object, we must mentally represent its features as a ‘search template’ (aka attentional set). Although evidence suggests we can search for multiple features simultaneously, it remains unclear whether we do so when searching for a multi-feature target. Based on the hypothesis that individuals use the most efficient 'good enough' template, we predicted that participants would prioritise only the most salient target feature. Participants (N = 18) searched a 4-item array for a ring-shaped target defined by two colours: a salient primary colour (80% proportion of the ring) and a secondary colour (20% proportion). They judged target presence/absence and identified an embedded line orientation on target-present trials (44% of trials). To assess which specific features were prioritised, target-absent trials contained a probe colour on one non-target ring, matching either the primary feature, secondary feature, or a task-irrelevant feature. Probes were either large (80% proportion of ring) or small (20%), allowing assessment of bottom-up salience as well. Behaviourally, the primary colour produced notably greater interference, particularly as a large probe. ERP results revealed that both primary and secondary colour (but not irrelevant) probes elicited an N2pc, reflecting attentional selection however, the large primary feature probe elicited a substantially larger N2pc than all other probes, and was closest in magnitude to the target N2pc. Notably, despite only eliciting a moderate N2pc, the small primary colour probe was the only probe to elicit an N1pc, consistent with early attentional orienting. Together, these findings suggest that individuals prioritise the most salient target feature during visual search, and rapidly engage, then discount, items sharing this feature that are implausible targets. The current results are therefore consistent individuals utilising a 'good enough' template strategy by prioritising intra-object salient features, despite multiple features being task-relevant and required to identify the target.

title: Investigating the learning of statistical regularities during visual foraging.
affiliations:
1. Univ. Bordeaux, LabPsy (FR)
2. Univ. Lille, CNRS, SCALab (FR)
3. Univ. Iceland, Icelandic Vision Lab (IS)
abstract: In contrast to traditional visual search paradigms that focus on detecting a single target, visual foraging tasks require identifying multiple targets among distractors within a single display. This makes them particularly useful for examining how attention is allocated over time. Building on previous findings from single-target visual search studies, we explored whether sensitivity to statistical regularities can guide target selection during visual foraging. To address this question, we used an exhaustive conjunction foraging task in which both targets and distractors varied along two features: shape and color. Two types of statistical regularities were compared, namely frequency and conditional probability. Participants had to search for and select (with the computer mouse) all the targets that appeared randomly within two of the sixteen possible screen quadrants. In the Probability condition, targets always co-occurred across a specific pair of quadrants (conditional probability = 1), meaning that when targets were present in one quadrant, they were also present in its paired location, although such events were relatively infrequent overall. In the Frequency condition, targets appeared more often overall, but their co-occurrence across paired quadrants was less consistent (conditional probability = 0.5). Participants completed 200-trial learning phase, followed by a 20-trial switch phase in which targets appeared in novel quadrant pairings. Reaction times were analyzed separately for initial selections and interquadrant transitions. In addition, mouse trajectories were examined as an index of spatial exploration. It was hypothesized that both reaction times and trajectory length would progressively decrease over the course of the learning phase, reflecting acquisition of spatial regularities, and subsequently increase during the switch phase following disruption of these regularities. At the time of submission, we have conducted two experiments with 40 and 16 participants, respectively. Preliminary findings show learning effects, as indicated by reductions in both reaction times and trajectory-length measures over time.

title: Low salience intra-object features are neglected from the visual search template: Evidence from Inattentional blindness
affiliations: 1. Bournemouth University (UK)
abstract: Everyday visual tasks, such as locating a friend in a crowd, require complex visual search. Unweighted scanning is inefficient, meaning we are thought to rely on top-down attentional templates of a target object’s features. However, little is known about how multiple features within a single object affect visual search. Does it involve analysis of all relevant features?, or do we use a ‘good enough’ template which selectively focuses on the most salient features? We explored this using an inattentional blindness paradigm across two pre-registered experiments. Participants searched a photo-realistic crowd scene for a person wearing clothing made up of two colours: a large-proportion salient primary colour (e.g., green) and a smaller secondary colour (e.g., purple counterbalanced), and identified the person's gender. Midway through the task, an unexpected star-shaped stimulus appeared in the periphery. This critical stimulus was varied across groups, and was either the primary colour, secondary colour, or a task-irrelevant (e.g., orange) colour (counterbalanced). Immediately after, participants were probed on their awareness of its location and shape. After refining awareness criteria in Experiment 1 (N = 236 group sizes = 75-84 https://osf.io/vg4cy), participants were most likely to notice the critical stimulus when it matched the primary colour. Notably, the secondary colour was no more likely to be detected than the irrelevant colour. This pattern was replicated in a larger pre-registered sample in Experiment 2 (N = 360 120 per group https://osf.io/3psyd), with primary colour detected most frequently, and secondary colour detection no different than the irrelevant colour. These findings demonstrate that intra-object feature salience shapes the contents of top-down attentional templates. Low-salience features appear to be excluded from the template, leading to increased inattentional blindness. This suggests that visual search is not a comprehensive analysis of all target features, but is instead driven by the most perceptually dominant ones.

title: Cross-modal foraging for human action
affiliations:
1. University of Iceland (IS)
2. University of Malta (MT)
abstract: Human foraging tasks are used to study how attention operates when multiple targets must be selected over time. Previous work has shown that visual synchrony can improve foraging performance consistent with accounts based on local grouping of targets (Makarov et al., 2024, 2025). However, cross-modal cues were only effective in these studies when participants explicitly searched for visual targets defined in terms of a specific temporal rate, a rate also shared by the sound or haptics cues. Here, we begin to explore whether these patterns also apply to a dynamic action-based task using point-light figures. Participants completed a time-limited task in which one of four actions (chopping, mowing, pumping or sweeping) was specified as the target action at the start of each trial. Actions were taken from the Vanrie & Verfaillie (2004) motion capture database. Participants selected as many targets as possible within 60 seconds. At any moment, 40 figures were visible in a 10 × 6 grid, including 10 targets and 30 distractors. The point-light figures were rotated randomly in depth and had limited lifetime, fading in and out and reappearing at new locations, creating a continuously changing display that reduced grid-based search strategies while maintaining a constant target/distractor ratio. Target actions were presented under three conditions: asynchronous (action-phase randomized for each target), visually synchronized, and visually synchronized with sound (e.g., a chopping sound for chopping). Distractor figures were sampled randomly from 16 additional actions and had no synchronization with respect to phase. Preliminary results replicate our previous findings with non-biological stimuli: There was a clear advantage for visual synchronization, but no additional benefit for adding a congruent sound.

title: The Efficiency of Multiple Distractor Inhibition During Visual Search
affiliations:
1. University of Bristol (UK)
2. Birkbeck, University of London (UK)
abstract: In daily life, we encounter visually salient distractions that must be managed to successfully navigate our environment. Research has demonstrated that attentional capture by highly salient stimuli can be avoided under certain circumstances. Most studies, however, focus on the inhibition of a single salient distractor, and less is known about whether multiple salient distractions presented simultaneously influence one another during inhibition. Across four experiments, using behavioural and ERP measures, we examined how spatial proximity and feature similarity between two salient distractors influence their inhibition during visual search. Observers searched for a shape-defined target among target-coloured (non-salient) distractors and one or two salient nontarget-colour distractors, which could have the same or two different colours. Behavioural measures revealed efficient suppression of both one and two salient distractors, indexed by faster response times when a salient distractor was present (Experiment 1) and reduced probe report accuracy at salient versus non-salient distractor locations (Experiment 2). Crucially, when there were two distractors, the magnitude of suppression was not influenced by their spatial layout (adjacent vs separated) or colour (same vs different), indicating that these factors do not affect suppression efficiency. In the ERP experiments, the lateralised Pd component was used to track inhibition of individual salient distractors, by placing one distractor laterally and the other on the midline. Pd was smaller for adjacent compared with separated distractors, while distractor features (same versus different colour) had no effect (Experiment 3). This Pd reduction did not reflect reduced suppression but instead perceptual grouping of adjacent lateral and midline distractors, reducing overall Pd amplitude relative to displays with two lateral salient distractors (Experiment 4). Overall, results indicate that the suppression of two salient distractors and single-item suppression are similarly efficient, and that multiple-item suppression is not sensitive to the spatial layout or colour of distractors.

title: Generative models can explain (or at least help us understand) individual differences in cognition
affiliations:
1. University of Essex (UK)
2. University of Aberdeen (UK)
abstract: Nearly all experiments in cognition and visual perception involve taking multiple measurements from each participant. This includes taking multiple recordings of the same concept (e.g., recording response time on a number of trials), and taking multiple measurements per trial (e.g., response time and accuracy). The number of measurements expands as we add in eye-tracking metrics, EEG statistics, and so on. Researchers interested in individual differences typically assume that these measurements are i) mutually independent and ii) free from confounds, before taking simple summary statistics and then applying correlation procedures. A general theme of research on individual differences in our field has been a lack of correlations. I argue that, on reflection, this shouldn’t be surprising, as the measurements we put into our correlations are imprecise composites of multiple causal factors. For example, it is well established that reaction times are influenced by learning and inter-trial serial dependencies. This means that participants in a hypothetical visual search experiment may all have identical “skill” in search, but could exhibit wildly different RTs due to differences in learning rates and serial dependency effects. I present simulated data to demonstrate how such processes can both mask correlations and produce spurious correlations. A potential solution to my hypothetical problem is the use of generative models with latent parameters. I provide an example in the form of FoMo, which decomposes performance in visual foraging into a small number of per-participant parameters.

title: N2pc as attention selection marker: insensitive to distributional distractor probabilities.
affiliations: 1. University of Iceland (IS)
abstract: Previous research on Feature Distribution Learning (FDL) has shown that observers implicitly encode the probability distributions of distractor features in visual search displays. These representations are remarkably rich, extending well beyond simple summary statistics such as the mean. However, the neural mechanisms supporting the encoding and use of such feature probabilities remain poorly understood. In the present study, we examined whether learned distractor probabilities modulate the N2pc - a well-established electrophysiological marker of attentional selection. Twenty-four participants performed a modified FDL visual search task in which they searched for an oddly colored target among 36 colored diamonds and reported its location in the upper or lower half of the display. During an initial learning phase, the color distribution of distractors remained constant across trials to facilitate implicit statistical learning. In subsequent test trials, role reversals were introduced so that a former distractor color became the target, with its prior probability (as a distractor) systematically varied. Behavioral results confirmed successful implicit learning of distractor distributions: search times were significantly slower for targets whose colors were close to the mean of the previously learned distractor distribution compared to targets farther from it. In contrast, analysis of the N2pc component (measured as contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference wave amplitude in the 200–300 ms post-stimulus window) revealed no modulation by distractor probability. These findings indicate that while observers form detailed probabilistic representations of distractor features that influence search efficiency, such learning does not directly scale the amplitude of early attentional selection as indexed by the N2pc. This dissociation suggests that statistical regularities in the environment may primarily affect later stages of processing or operate through more subtle temporal dynamics rather than the overall strength of attentional deployment. This work was supported by the Icelandic Centre for Research (Rannís grant 239774-052) awarded to S.H.R.

title: Looking-without-seeing in visual search occurs for salient but not non-salient targets
affiliations:
1. Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics (DE)
2. University of Tübingen (DE)
abstract: Attention in visual search is often controlled by both bottom-up saliency and top-down priority. According to the V1 Saliency Hypothesis and the Central-peripheral Dichotomy theory, gaze during search is guided exogenously by saliency signals generated in primary visual cortex (V1), particularly in the peripheral visual field, and by goal-directed target recognition, particularly in the central visual field. Liang et al. (2023) provided evidence in a search task for a homo-pair of dots (both white or both black) as a search target among uniformly oriented hetero-pairs of dots as non-targets. They observed a parallel advantage — the target was easier to find when it was parallel rather than perpendicular to the non-targets. This advantage is a signature of V1 saliency mechanisms (by properties of V1 responses to these dot-pairs). It indicated that the target was more salient than the non-targets to enable looking-without-seeing: the target captured gaze even when it was too peripheral to be recognizable in crowded non-targets, purely by its bottom-up saliency (Liang and Zhaoping, 2025). Since hetero-pairs evoke substantially weaker V1 responses than homo-pairs in isolation (Smith et al., 2002), a hetero-pair target among uniformly oriented homo-pairs should be non-salient and should not evoke looking-without-seeing. The current study tested this prediction. As predicted, the hetero-pair target required a longer search time and exhibited instead a perpendicular advantage, signifying that it was indeed less salient than the non-targets. Furthermore, looking-without-seeing was absent, such that gaze during search relied exclusively on top-down looking-by-seeing. Specifically, the probability of a saccade reaching the target exceeded chance level only when the target’s eccentricity was sufficiently small to allow at least a partial recognition of the target before the saccadic onset. These results, compared against our replication of Liang et al. (2023), demonstrate that bottom-up V1 saliency is necessary for peripheral gaze capture without recognition.

title: Graded Colour Salience in Pre-attentive Visual Search: Evidence from Set-Size Independent Detection
affiliations:
1. Yamagata University (JP)
2. Mapleline co. Ltd (JP)
abstract: It is widely recognised that certain colours attract attention rapidly, although their precise identity cannot be determined prior to perceptual processing. This observation implies the operation of pre-attentive mechanisms in visual attention. According to Feature Integration Theory, basic visual features such as colour are processed in parallel at a pre-attentive stage, producing feature-based pop-out that is independent of set size. However, subsequent developments, notably the Guided Search model, propose that parallel feature activation feeds into a priority map that guides focal attention. Within this framework, even in pop-out conditions, differences in feature salience may yield graded differences in detection latency. The present study examined colour salience using a visual search paradigm with 27 participants (aged 19–45 years) with normal trichromatic colour vision. Observers searched for a pre-specified target colour among multiple distractors and responded via key press. Red, green, and blue stimuli were positioned equidistant from the achromatic point in CIE 1976 L*a*b* colour space, and set size was varied across three levels. Reaction times were unaffected by set size, indicating efficient search consistent with feature-based pop-out as predicted by Feature Integration Theory. However, detection latency differed significantly across colours, with red detected more rapidly than green or blue. From the perspective of Guided Search, this pattern suggests that although colour-defined targets are processed in parallel, their relative salience differentially weights activation within the priority map. Importantly, colour salience is context-dependent, influenced by luminance, adaptation, task demands, and background contrast. The findings therefore do not imply intrinsic superiority of red, but rather demonstrate that, under pop-out conditions, chromatic signals can guide attention with graded efficiency.

title: Seeing the Bias: Hemifield‑Dependent Remapping of Sensory, Sighting, and Acuity Eye Dominance
affiliations: 1. University of Hong Kong (HK)
abstract: Eye dominance may refer to sensory, sighting, and acuity dominance, yet their correspondence across the visual field is unclear. Here, we indexed these three dominance metrics across 17 visual field locations: the fovea and 16 locations at 3° and 6° eccentricities along 8 polar angles. Sensory dominance was indexed with a dichoptic motion coherence threshold task, sighting dominance with a pointing alignment task, and acuity dominance with a grating acuity task. Results revealed that along the horizontal and oblique meridians, both sensory and sighting dominance shifted from foveal dominance toward the left eye in the left hemifield and toward the right eye in the right hemifield. There were no shifts in sensory or sighting dominance along the vertical meridian. In contrast, acuity dominance exhibited weak overall magnitude and lacked systematic field-variations. Consistent with their spatial similarities, sensory dominance significantly predicted sighting dominance across the visual field, and this within-subject correlation was selective to the meridians exhibiting hemifield asymmetries. Acuity dominance showed negligible correlations with the other two metrics. We speculate that both sensory and sighting eye dominance tap into binocular combination processes at the primary visual cortex (V1), where the contralateral eye is weighted more strongly due to structural asymmetries across the visual pathway. In contrast, acuity dominance likely reflects monocular optical and retinal factors independent of binocular interactions, explaining its spatial invariance and weak correlations with other dominance metrics.

title: Neural Signatures of Eye Dominance
affiliations: 1. The University of Hong Kong (HK)
abstract: Eye dominance is a multifaceted phenomenon, yet it is often studied as a unitary construct. Using 3T fMRI, we examined whether the neural mechanisms underlying acuity (resolution), sighting (spatial/motor), and sensory (suppressive) dominance reflect shared or divergent processes. To isolate these mechanisms while controlling for visual input, we used identical orthogonal sinusoidal gratings (45/135 deg) across all experimental conditions. Sensory eye dominance was assessed under an event-related design, by presenting orthogonal gratings dichoptically to induce rivalry.  This allowed for the mapping of alternations between ‘dominant’ and ‘non-dominant’ eye percepts.  Acuity and sighting dominance were evaluated using a block design where gratings were presented monocularly to either the dominant or non-dominant eye.  Finally, observers were tested under binocular presentation wherein identical gratings were presented to both eyes.  In all conditions, participants were asked to indicate whether the perceived grating was tilted clockwise or counterclockwise.  By maintaining constant visual input and task demands across conditions, we dissociate the neural correlates of 'eyedness' based on functional demand. In line with behavioural data from our laboratory, we find that eye dominance is not a unitary property of the visual system, but rather a dynamic, task-dependent allocation of neural resources across both early circuits (V1) – presumably reflecting interocular suppression – and across the dorsal and ventral streams.

title: Examining the Role of Sensory Eye Dominance on Perceptual Memory
affiliations: 1. The University of Hong Kong (HK)
abstract: Sensory eye dominance (SED) refers to preferential weighting of one eye’s information over the other. Here, we examined whether perceptual memory could be a functional advantage of SED. To index SED, we used two types of tasks: a rivalrous task that presented letters of opposite contrasts to each eye and an integrative task that involved the dichoptic presentation of coherent and randomly moving dots to the two eyes. To test perceptual memory, we presented two sine-wave gratings of random orientations sequentially and asked observers to remember the target (first) grating’s orientation while ignoring the second, distractor grating. Observers adjusted a white line to match their memory of the target grating’s orientation. Perceptual memory accuracy was quantified as an orientation error, calculated as the response angle minus the target‘s angle. We manipulated the distractor grating’s orientation, which could be different from that of the target grating in either the clockwise or the counterclockwise directions. We also manipulated which eye the target and the distractor gratings were presented to: they could be presented to both eyes, both to the dominant eye only, both to the non-dominant eye only, or one to each eye. We found that memory errors were biased by both the distractor’s orientation (e.g., clockwise distractors led to clockwise memory errors, and vice versa) and the eye to which the target and the distractor were presented to. Memory errors were smaller when the target and the distractor were presented to different eyes than when they were presented to the same eye, and this advantage was only found when the target was presented to the dominant eye. That is, the dominant eye exhibited reduced memory interference by a perceptually similar distractor.  The data suggest that SED affects the strength of encoding of information in perceptual memory.

title: Effects of Focal Distance Mismatch in Binocular Displays on Visual Performance
affiliations: 1. Meta Reality Labs (US)
abstract: Purpose: This study explores the impact of display focal distance (DFD) mismatch, defined as the difference in focal distances presented to each eye by a stereoscopic display, on visual performance. Understanding how DFD mismatch affects visual performance is critical for optimizing augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) systems, where mismatches in focal distance can disrupt depth perception and visual comfort. Methods: Thirty-nine participants with normal vision (monocular acuity >20/25, stereopsis <70 arcmin) performed a visual discrimination task using four Landolt Cs. The experiment systematically varied DFD mismatch between 0.0D and 2.0D, simulating different focal distances for each eye. The nominal (mean) DFD was kept at 1.0D. Our task relied on binocular fusion and focus latency, a metric sensitive to both binocular fusion and focus, measured via AEPsych adaptive sampling. The latency values were normalized to baseline (0.0D DFD mismatch). Both AR and VR conditions were tested, with DFD mismatch applied only to the stimulus (AR) or both stimulus and background (VR). Results: Increasing DFD mismatch resulted in significant declines in visual performance, with the latency increasing by ~200ms (~35–40%) at 2.0D mismatch. Cumulative distribution analysis showed that a DFD mismatch of 0.25D or less caused minimal performance impact (<10% in <5% of participants), consistent with clinical guidelines. The effect was similar across AR and VR conditions. These findings can inform product design: maintaining DFD mismatch ≤0.25D in AR/VR devices minimizes perceptual risk and supports optimal user experience.

title: Concurrent Use of Visual Information from Different Horizontal Directions with Independently Controlled Binocular Viewing
affiliations:
1. National Institute of Technology, Numazu College (JP)
2. Nagaoka University of Technology (JP)
3. Toyama Prefectural University (JP)
4. Nagoya Institute of Technology (JP)
5. Toyohashi University of Technology (JP)
abstract: Human observers normally rely on coordinated eye and head movements to obtain visual information outside the current field of view. If the horizontal viewing directions of the two eyes are controlled independently like as chameleon, visual inputs from different directions can be made available at the same time. However, when different scene information is presented to the two eyes, interocular conflict may induce binocular rivalry or suppression, limiting the effective use of information from both views. It therefore remains unclear whether spatially separated visual information can be used concurrently under independently controlled binocular viewing. We examined this question in a virtual reality experiment with 24 participants. The experiment used a 2 x 2 within-subjects design. Viewing control was either head-only viewing or head movement combined with independent control of the two eyes using an analogue stick. Task condition was either a single visual search task or a dual task combining the same search task with an additional frontal reaction task. In the search task, participants searched for targets appearing around the observer and reported the number displayed on the target surface. In the reaction task, they responded to a color change in a frontally presented object. Reaction times in the frontal reaction task were significantly shorter with independent binocular control than with head-only viewing. This reduction was not accompanied by an overall increase in search time. Search time also showed no main effect of task, indicating that adding the frontal reaction task did not produce a significant overall cost in search performance. These results do not demonstrate fully parallel processing of information from different directions. They suggest, however, that independently controlled binocular viewing can allow observers to use spatially separated visual information concurrently in a way that improves frontal reaction performance without an overall decrement in visual search.

title: Contributions of internal noise and efficiency to the stereoscopic anisotropy
affiliations: 1. Department of Experimental Psychology, Faculty of Psychology, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Campus de Somosaguas (ES)
abstract: A well-known anisotropy exists in human stereopsis: the visual system exhibits higher sensitivity to horizontal sinusoidal disparity corrugations at low spatial frequencies than to vertical corrugations. The underlying mechanism, cortical locus or functional role of this effect remains unclear. Various theories have attempted to explain it through the size of summation fields or the number of available channels, but none provides a clear explanation. In this study, we used a noise masking paradigm to isolate and quantify the roles of internal noise and processing efficiency in the anisotropy. We measured disparity thresholds at four spatial frequencies (0.1, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8 cpd) masked by white noise of different power densities using a Bayesian staircase procedure. As predicted, detection thresholds increased as a function of noise power. Fitting an equivalent noise model to the threshold data revealed that the horizontal mechanism's performance advantage is driven by both a reduction in internal noise and a higher efficiency relative to the vertical mechanism. Interestingly, while efficiency reached its maximum at 0.2 cpd for both orientations, the horizontal mechanism maintained higher efficiency across all spatial frequencies tested. Our data provide strong evidence for orientation-specific mechanisms in disparity computation, demonstrating that internal noise is a key contributor to the observed stereoscopic anisotropy.

title: SimpleStereo: Keeping Stereo Vision in Retinal (vs World) Coordinates + QualiaNet: An Experience-Before-Inference Network
affiliations: 1. Columbia University (US)
abstract: We present two computational models – SimpleStereo and QualiaNet – which reflect the two stages – Experience and Inference – of visual processing on our account. 1. EXPERIENCE: SimpleStereo models our visual experience of stereo vision as a retinal disparity map relative to fixation. This keeps stereo vision in retinal (rather than world) coordinates, and rejects the idea that stereo vision is attempting to reconstruct 3D geometry. SimpleStereo departs from traditional models of stereo vision in three fundamental ways: First, it keeps stereo vision in absolute (vs relative Parker, 2007) disparity, since depth being nearer vs. further than fixation is a fundamentally different visual experience. Second, it rejects thinking of stereo matching in terms of a geometric “correspondence problem” (Marr & Poggio, 1979). Instead, stereo vision fuses whatever is on the two foveae, and then depth from disparity radiates outwards from that initial retinal anchor. Third, it rejects depth from disparity as geometric reconstruction. Instead, the Linton Stereo Illusion demonstrates that depth from disparity is simply a linear function of retinal disparity. Pilot data suggests z = 5.4x, where x is disparity, and z is the x-axis angular size match (in degrees) of the perceived z-axis depth. The resulting model of stereo vision transforms our understanding of visual space from a fully articulated 3D space, to fixation plus nearer/further than fixation. 2. INFERENCE: QualiaNet seeks to infer the 3D world based on this impoverished model of visual space. On our account, stereo vision does not provide us with absolute distance. Instead, we infer absolute distance based on “a cognitive association between (a) vivid stereo depth and (b) closer distances (reflecting our experience of an environment where disparity falls-off with distance2)” (Linton, 2018). We demonstrate that a CNN (QualiaNet) can learn to accurately estimate absolute distance based simply on a disparity map relative to fixation.

title: Investigating the detection and discrimination of perceived depth from disparity with stimuli that target either local or global stereopsis
affiliations: 1. McGill University (CA)
abstract: Some individuals with otherwise normal vision have been found to exhibit deficits in stereopsis. The reported prevalence of this “stereo-anomaly” varies from 2% to 30% and seems to depend on the stimulus and task design. Recent work (Baldwin et al. 2024, iScience 27:109879) found 17% of individuals who could detect a disparity-defined target in a spatially bandpass random dot stereogram (RDS) could not discriminate the direction of disparity (with a further 14% simply having more difficulty with the discrimination task). In this study, we set out to determine whether the deficit identified in global stereopsis (with bandpass RDS stimuli) would transfer to the case where targets are shown in local stereopsis (bandpass circles). We recruited 25 adults with normal vision and measured stereoacuity thresholds across four tasks: local detection, local discrimination, global detection, and global discrimination. In each of our tasks, disparity was controlled by a pair of interleaved staircases. Stereoacuity thresholds were obtained by fitting a psychometric function. Comparing the two stimulus types (local and global) and tasks (detection and discrimination) using a linear mixed-effects model, we found thresholds were significantly higher (≈2×) for local stereopsis compared to global stereopsis. There was no significant effect of task. In contrast with Baldwin et al (2024), we did not find any participants were unable to perform the global discrimination task, though the distribution of the discrimination/detection threshold ratios was bimodal. Three individuals had specific difficulty with the local discrimination task, to the extent that thresholds could not be estimated from their data. The stereo-anomaly evident in our data is milder than that reported in previous studies. We consider this may be due to subtle differences in stimulus and task design, and in the method used to present dichoptic stimuli (polarisation here, compared to anaglyph in some previous work).

title: Linear perspective with and without foreshortening
affiliations:
1. McGill University, Montreal (CA)
2. Keio University (JP)
abstract: Linear Perspective is the depth cue formed by parallel lines that lie along the line of sight that in the retinal image converge towards a vanishing point. There are however two distinct potential cues to depth in linear perspective: the orientation variation orthogonal to the line of sight and the diminishing separation between the lines as they converge, i.e. foreshortening.  To determine which cue is the most salient for depth perception we used Gabor micropatterns to decouple the two cues, with the variations in micropattern orientation defining the orientation cue and variations in spatial frequency and density defining the foreshortening cue. We simulated an inclined textured ground plane that either varied solely in the orientation cue or with both orientation and foreshortening cues.    Subjects either adjusted the aspect ratio of an ellipse until it appeared to lie flat on the plane or adjusted the relative size of two discs positioned at the beginning and end of the plane in order to test for the well-known Ponzo illusion.   The ellipse measurements showed no consistent evidence for the role of the orientation cue either on its own or when added to the foreshortening cue.  On the other hand the Ponzo task showed a small illusion of around 4% for the orientation cue alone.  In the combined cue condition the orientation cue added about 5% to the total size of the Pono illusion, but this translated to a proportional increase of 90%.  Our results suggest that with micropattern-based displays perceived inclination varies considerably with the measurement method and that the benefit of the orientation cue is best manifest when combined with the foreshortening cue.
